{"request_id":"8fd783ca8d2e1a97fdee68fa","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is remarkable! I must meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from the bench and paced the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is only a source of inspiration for me. You might find nothing special in him. I find everything in him. He is most present in my work when no image of him appears. He is, as I said, a hint of a fresh style. I see him in the sweep of certain lines, in the beauty and fine shades of certain colours. That is all.”

“Then why won’t you show his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I put into it an expression of this strange artistic devotion. I never cared to speak of it to him. He knows nothing about it, and never shall. But the world might suspect it, and I will not expose my soul to their shallow, prying eyes. They will not put my heart under their microscope. There is too much of me in that piece, Harry—far too much!”

“Poets are not as careful as you. They know passion sells. Today a broken heart brings many editions.”

“I despise them for it,” Hallward cried. “An artist should create beautiful things but put nothing of his own life into them. We live in an age when men treat art as if it were a diary. We have lost the sense of beauty in itself. One day I will show the world what it means; and for that reason the world will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you are wrong, Basil, but I won’t argue. Only the intellectually lost argue. Tell me, is Dorian Gray very fond of you?”

The painter pondered a moment. “He likes me,” he said at last. “I know he likes me. Of course, I flatter him terribly. I take a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I will regret. Usually he is delightful to me, and we sit in the studio and talk about a thousand topics. Now and then, though, he is terribly careless and seems to enjoy hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I have given my whole soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his buttonhole, a bit of decoration to gratify his vanity, an ornament for a summer day.”"}

{"request_id":"b49fd4eb0990da5d672e014a","rewritten_text":"Mrs. Clay’s feelings had overruled her ambition, and she gave up the chance to keep scheming for Sir Walter for the young man’s sake. Yet she has brains as well as emotions; and now it is uncertain whether his shrewdness or hers will win in the end—whether, after stopping her from becoming Lady Elliott, he might not end up coaxed and charmed into making her Lady William instead.

There is no doubt Sir Walter and Elizabeth were appalled and humiliated by losing their companion and discovering her deceit. True, they could turn to their grand cousins for solace, but they would long feel the sting of flattering and fawning on others without being flattered and followed in return—only half a pleasure.

Anne, satisfied early on that Lady Russell meant to love Captain Wentworth as she ought, had no real shadow on her happiness except the knowledge that she had no relatives to offer him whom any sensible man could appreciate. It was there she felt her own inferiority most. The difference in their fortunes meant nothing; it never troubled her for a moment. But to have no family ready to welcome and value him, nothing respectable, harmonious, or affectionate to offer in return for all the merit and warm reception she found in his brothers and sisters, caused as sharp a pain as her mind could feel amid otherwise strong happiness. She had only two friends to add to his circle, Lady Russell and Mrs. Smith. He was, however, very ready to attach himself to both. Lady Russell, despite her past faults, he now admired wholeheartedly. Though he did not have to say he thought she was right to separate them originally, he could say nearly everything else in her favor. As for Mrs. Smith, she had many claims that quickly and firmly recommended her.

Her recent kindness to Anne was reason enough, and their marriage, instead of costing her a friend, gave her two. She was their first visitor once they were settled, and Captain Wentworth, by helping her recover her husband’s West Indian property—writing letters for her, handling business, and carrying her through every small difficulty with the energy of a brave man and devoted friend—fully repaid every service she had given, or ever intended to give, his wife."}

{"request_id":"e892bc5bda66a86c9e974826","rewritten_text":"I rushed over and scooped her into my arms, covering her with kisses while I begged, “Talk to me, darling, please! What’s wrong?”

Her head sagged against my chest, and she whispered, barely audible, “Hello, Central.”

“Quick!” I shouted to Clarence. “Call the king’s homeopath, now!”

Two minutes later I was kneeling beside the child’s crib, and Sandy was sending servants racing in every direction throughout the palace. I saw the situation almost instantly—membranous croup. I bent close and murmured, “Wake up, sweetheart! Hello, Central.”

She opened those soft eyes, slow and cloudy, and managed to say, “Papa.” That was a relief—she still had fight left in her. I sent someone for sulphur, and I grabbed the croup kettle myself; I don’t sit around waiting for doctors when Sandy or the child is sick. I knew how to care for both of them, and I’d done it before. This little one had spent half its short life in my arms, and many times I could hush its troubles and coax a laugh through those tear-sprinkled lashes when even its mother couldn’t.

Sir Launcelot, decked out in his finest armor, came striding down the great hall on his way to the stock exchange; he served as president, holding the Siege Perilous, which he’d bought off Sir Galahad, since the Round Table now doubled as their trading floor. Seats at it cost so much you wouldn’t believe me if I told you. Sir Launcelot was playing the bear and had cornered one of the new ventures, about to squeeze the shorts that day—but so what? He remained the same Launcelot, and the moment he glanced in while passing the door and realized his favorite was ill, that settled it. Bulls and bears could claw each other all they wanted; he’d come right in and stand guard over little Hello-Central with everything he had. And that’s exactly what he did. He pitched his helmet into a corner, and within thirty seconds he’d fitted a fresh wick into the alcohol lamp and had the croup kettle heating. By then Sandy had draped a blanket canopy over the crib, and we were set.

Sir Launcelot stoked the heat, and together we loaded the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a dash of lactic acid, then topped it off with water and fed the steam pipe under the canopy. Everything was squared away, and we settled down on either side of the crib to stand our watch."}

{"request_id":"734bbf7198dd8da6c8cba65b","rewritten_text":"“Take heed to what I say; I have mastered the dialect of despair: it is engraven in me, for I am Despair itself, a being at once exultant and melancholy. Yet those words deceive, for though the wave runs dark it is not bitter. We sink down, whisper a kindly good night with closed lids, and when we rouse again, we are liberated. Come, tarry no further, thou loitering one! See the gracious draught! Behold, it is a spirit of kindness, not a mortal maiden, who calls thee, and with beseeching tones (would they might draw thee!) entreats, Come and drink.”

As I spoke I fastened my gaze upon his face, and his surpassing loveliness, the celestial pity shining in his eyes, the gentle yet earnest protest and amazement that sat on him even before he uttered a word, altered the tension of my mood, stripping me of desolate defiance and leaving only the tenderest sorrow. I noted his eyes moist as well while he gathered both my hands into his; and seating himself beside me, he spoke:

“This is a mournful act to which you would guide me, beloved friend, and your misery must be profound indeed to instill such gloomy purposes. You yearn for death, yet tremble before it, and wish me to share the passage. But I possess less daring than you, and even at your side I shrink from dying. Hear me, and then decide whether you ought to enlist me in your scheme, even if with that overwhelming rhetoric of despair you could render grim death so alluring that fair heaven would seem obscured. Listen, I beseech you, to one who has himself fostered desperate designs, and burned with restless longing for the grave, yet at last has trodden the phantom beneath his feet and dulled its sting. Come, since you have personated Despair to me, I will now become Una to you and draw you safely from his murky cave. Hear me, and be softened by words from which all selfish fire has fled.

“We comprehend not the meaning of this vast world; its baffling intermingling of good with ill. Nonetheless we are set here and commanded to live and to hope. What it is we should hope for I know not; but some good lies before us which we must pursue; that is the charge laid upon us in this life. Should misfortune assail, we must struggle with her; we must thrust her aside and still advance to seek that which our very nature craves. Whether this hope of future good is but a schooling for another life I cannot tell; or whether it is only that we, as laborers in God’s vineyard, must lend our efforts to level the road for those who follow.”"}

{"request_id":"6b142d4e3d515bde38d389cb","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No response.

“TOM!”

Silence.

“What’s come over that boy, I’d like to know? You, TOM!”

Still no reply.

The old lady slid her spectacles down and peered over them around the room; then pushed them back and glanced beneath them. She hardly ever looked straight through them for anything as trifling as a boy; they were her ceremonial pair, the pride of her heart, meant for “style” rather than duty—she could have seen through a couple of stove lids just as clearly. She paused, perplexed, then said, not in a harsh tone but loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I swear, if I get hold of you I’ll—”

She did not finish, for she was already stooping and poking beneath the bed with the broom, needing all her breath to punctuate each jab. She dragged out nothing but the cat.

“I never saw the like of that boy!”

She moved to the doorway, stood there, and gazed out at the tomato vines and “jimpson” weeds that passed for a garden. No Tom. So she raised her voice at a slant meant to carry and called:

“Y-o-u-u TOM!”

A faint sound came from behind, and she turned just in time to grab a small boy by the slack of his roundabout and halt his dash.

“There now! I might have guessed that closet. What have you been doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what. Forty times I’ve told you if you didn’t leave that jam be I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch wavered in the air—the danger was dire—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady spun around, snatching her skirts to safety. The boy bolted instantly, scrambled up the tall board fence, and vanished over it.

His Aunt Polly stood astonished a moment, then let out a gentle laugh.

“Bother the boy, can’t I ever learn anything? Hasn’t he tricked me often enough that I’d be on guard by now? But old fools are the biggest fools there are. Can’t teach an old dog new tricks, so they say. Yet my stars, he never plays them the same way two days running, and how’s a body to guess what’s next? He seems to know just how long he can tease me before I blow my stack, and he knows if he can stall me a minute or make me laugh, everything’s lost again and I can’t give him a lick.”"}

{"request_id":"0b6d7cf6b1b5d07275723219","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost finished their cycle. It was now late May; the woods wore their freshest green, and the sweet scent of newly cut grass filled the fields. I hoped that the gentle air and the lovely face of nature might help me inspire him with calm feelings, and stir in him a sense of peace and love to prepare him for the trust I was determined to win from him.

I therefore chose one of those evenings for my attempt. I asked him to walk with me and led him to a nearby beech wood whose light shade shielded us from the slanting, dazzling rays of the setting sun. After walking in silence for some time, I sat down with him on a mossy mound. It is strange, but even now I can see the place: the slender, smooth trunks were wrapped in ivy, whose glossy dark-green leaves contrasted with the white bark and the pale leaves of the young beech shoots growing from their parent trunks. The short grass was mixed with moss and partly covered by the dead leaves of the previous autumn that the wind had gathered into little heaps here and there. A few moss-covered stumps were scattered about. The leaves were gently stirred by the breeze, and through their green canopy you could glimpse the bright blue sky. As evening advanced, the distant trunks were reddened by the sun, the wind fell completely still, and a few birds flew past us to their evening rest.

So there we sat, and when you hear all that happened—all that tore our souls even in this peaceful place, which, without those strange passions, might have been a paradise for us—you will not wonder that I remember it as I looked upon it then, hoping its calm might give me calm and inspire me not only with courage but with persuasive words. I noticed all these details almost absent-mindedly while I tried to arrange my thoughts for what I meant to do. My heart pounded as I worked myself up to speak to him, for I was resolved not to be turned away, yet I trembled to imagine how my words might affect him. At last, with much hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the excessive affection—you showed me when you first returned, I hope, will excuse me in your eyes for daring to speak to you, though with the tender love of a daughter, yet also with the freedom of a friend and equal.”"}

{"request_id":"b8d9b5481dcde0111074242f","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Master Will—really I am,” the servant answered quickly. “Almost to the end now.”

“Out to the end!” Legrand almost screamed. “You’re saying you’re at the end of that branch?”

“Soon be at de end, massa—o-o-o-oh! Lord have mercy! What’s this on the tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, delighted. “What is it?”

“It’s nothing but a skull. Somebody left his head up here, and the crows ate every bit of the meat.”

“A skull, you say! Fine. How is it fastened to the branch? What holds it there?”

“Sure enough, massa; let me look. Why, this is a curious thing, I swear—there’s a big nail in the skull that fastens it to the tree.”

“Good. Now, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you—understand?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Pay attention, then. Find the left eye of the skull.”

“Hum! hoo! that’s funny! There isn’t any eye left at all.”

“Damn your stupidity! Do you know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that—know all about it. I chop wood with my left hand.”

“Of course! You’re left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now I suppose you can find the left eye of the skull, or where it used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long silence. Finally the servant asked, “Is the left eye of the skull on the same side as the skull’s left hand too? Because the skull doesn’t have any hands. Never mind! I’ve got the left eye now—here it is! What should I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it, as far as the string will reach—but be careful not to let go of the string.”

“All done, Master Will; easy to put the bug through the hole. Look out down below!”

During this talk none of Jupiter’s body could be seen, but the beetle he had lowered now hung at the end of the string and shone like a globe of polished gold in the last rays of sunset, a few of which still lit the hill where we stood. The scarab hung clear of every branch, and if dropped would have fallen at our feet. Legrand at once grabbed the scythe and cleared a circular space, three or four yards wide, just beneath the insect. When he finished, he told Jupiter to let go the string and come down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"dbec9775e59f115fece0a346","rewritten_text":"If you refuse and prefer to rely on my patience and the mercy of those you have wronged, sit in that chair without a word. It has been waiting for you for two whole days.”

Monks muttered something unintelligible but still wavered.

“You will act quickly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and your other choice is gone forever.”

Still the man hesitated.

“I have no desire to bargain,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and because I defend the dearest interests of others, I have no right to.”

“Is there—” asked Monks, his tongue faltering, “is there no middle course?”

“None.”

Monks looked anxiously at the old gentleman, but read only severity and resolve in his face, so he walked into the room and, shrugging his shoulders, sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and return when I ring.”

The men obeyed, leaving the two alone.

“This is fine treatment, sir,” said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “It is because the hopes and wishes of our youth were bound up with him and that fair girl of his blood and kin who rejoined her God while still young, leaving me solitary and lonely. It is because he knelt with me beside his only sister’s deathbed when he was still a boy, on the morning that—though Heaven decided otherwise—would have made her my young wife. It is because my scarred heart clung to him from then on, through all his trials and faults, until he died. It is because old memories fill my heart, and even the sight of you brings back thoughts of him. It is because of all this that I am moved to treat you gently even now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and blush for your unworthiness to bear the name.”

“What has the name to do with it?” the other asked after studying his agitated companion in sullen wonder. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow, “nothing to you. But it was hers, and even after all these years it still brings back to me, an old man, the glow and thrill I once felt when I heard it from a stranger. I am very glad you changed it—very, very.”

“This is all very grand,” said Monks (to keep his assumed name) after a long silence, during which he jerked himself to and fro in stubborn defiance while Mr. Brownlow sat shading his face with his hand."}

{"request_id":"5efe560aa0b3a6c0a0f23334","rewritten_text":"“Are you speaking of—Mr. Knightley?”

“Why, of course I am. I could never have imagined any one else—and I thought you understood that. When we discussed him, it seemed the plainest thing in the world.”

“Not quite,” Emma replied with constrained composure, “for everything you said then appeared to concern another person. I might almost declare that you actually mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill. I am certain you spoke of the favor Mr. Frank Churchill conferred on you in defending you from the gipsies.”

“Oh! Miss Woodhouse, how could you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember perfectly what I said at the time. I told you I could not wonder at your affection; that, considering the assistance he provided, it was entirely natural—and you agreed, expressing yourself fervently about how deeply you felt that obligation, even detailing your sensations as you saw him step forward to your aid. The impression remains vivid.”

“Oh dear,” cried Harriet, “now I recall what you mean, but I was thinking of something quite different then. It was not the gipsies—it was not Mr. Frank Churchill I intended. No!” (with a touch of pride) “I was thinking of a far dearer moment—of Mr. Knightley’s approaching me to dance when Mr. Elton refused to stand up with me, and when there was not another partner available. That was kindness itself; that was true compassion and generosity; that was the service that first made me feel how far he surpasses every other creature on earth.”

“Good heavens!” exclaimed Emma. “This has been a most unhappy—most lamentable error!—What can be done?”

“You would not have supported me, then, had you understood me? At least, I cannot be worse off now than I should have been if the other had been the person; and now—it _is_ possible—”

She paused for a few seconds. Emma remained silent.

“I cannot wonder, Miss Woodhouse,” she continued, “that you perceive a vast difference between the two, in relation to me or to anybody. You must esteem one five hundred million times higher than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—that if—strange as it may sound—yet they were your own words, that _more_ astonishing things have occurred, that matches of _greater_ inequality have been made than between Mr. Frank Churchill and me; and so it seems as if even such a thing as this may have taken place before—and if I should be so unspeakably fortunate as to—if Mr. Knightley should actually—if _he_ ignores the disparity, I trust, dear Miss Woodhouse, you will not oppose it or try to create obstacles.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b1cb6ef31abce314fb5ac3d5","rewritten_text":"The storm howled all night, but nothing noteworthy happened. The next morning, when they came down to breakfast, the dreadful bloodstain was back on the floor. “I don’t think it’s the Paragon Detergent’s fault,” said Washington. “I’ve tried everything. It must be the ghost.” He scrubbed the stain away again, but the following morning it returned. On the third morning it was there too, even though Mr. Otis had locked the library himself and taken the key upstairs. Now the whole family was intrigued. Mr. Otis began to think he had been too firm in denying ghosts existed, Mrs. Otis announced she wanted to join the Psychical Society, and Washington started drafting a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the Persistence of Bloodstains Connected with Crime. That night, any remaining doubts about the reality of apparitions vanished forever.\n\nThe day had been warm and sunny, and in the cool evening the family went out for a drive. They did not return until nine o’clock, when they had a light supper. Their conversation never touched on ghosts, so there were none of those basic conditions of expectant belief that often come before sightings of supernatural events. The topics they discussed, as I later learned from Mr. Otis, were just the usual subjects for cultured Americans of the better sort: the great advantage of Miss Fanny Davenport over Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of getting green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the best English homes; Boston’s importance in developing the world-soul; the convenience of the baggage-check system on trains; and the pleasant sound of the New York accent compared with the London drawl. They never mentioned anything supernatural, nor did Sir Simon de Canterville come up. At eleven o’clock the family went to bed, and by half past eleven all the lights were out. Some time later, Mr. Otis woke up because he heard a strange noise in the hallway outside his room. It sounded like clanking metal that drew closer every moment. He got up at once, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He stayed perfectly calm and felt his pulse; it was steady. The odd noise continued, and he clearly heard footsteps with it. He put on his slippers, took a small oblong bottle from his dressing case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"722ff6ab3967f9012b88a853","rewritten_text":"I told myself I didn’t want to get mixed up in that kind of business.

When I came downstairs in the morning the parlor was closed, the watchers were gone, and only the household, widow Bartley, and our group were around. I studied their faces to see if anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell.

Around midday the undertaker arrived with his helper. They set the coffin in the middle of the room on two chairs, lined up our chairs in rows, and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were full. I saw the coffin lid looked the same as before, but I didn’t dare peek under it with people nearby.

Then folks started flocking in, and the cousins and the girls took the front row at the head of the coffin. For half an hour the visitors filed past slowly in single file, looked at the dead man’s face for a moment, and some shed a tear. Everything stayed quiet and solemn, except for the girls and cousins holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, heads bowed, sobbing a little. The only other sounds were shoes scraping the floor and noses being blown—because people always blow their noses more at funerals, unless it’s church.

When the place was packed, the undertaker glided around in his black gloves and soothing ways, adding the last touches, settling people and things, making no more sound than a cat. He never spoke. He moved folks, squeezed in latecomers, opened a path, and did it all with nods and hand signs. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the softest, smoothest, stealthiest man I ever saw, and he didn’t have any more smile to him than a ham.

They had borrowed a melodeon—a weak one—and when all was ready a young woman sat down to play it. It was pretty squeaky and colicky, and everyone joined in singing, and Peter was the only one who had anything good out of it, if you asked me. Then Reverend Hobson began slow and solemn, and started to speak, when the wildest uproar broke out in the cellar that anyone ever heard; it was just one dog, but he made a fierce racket and kept it up without stopping. The parson had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"b4a823a1f9822dec7e0d87bf","rewritten_text":"Her situation was truly one of uncommon trial and perplexity. Though she felt the keenest longing to unravel the mystery that hid Oliver’s past, she could not betray the trust that the wretched woman she had just spoken with had placed in her, as a young, innocent girl. The stranger’s words and demeanour had struck Rose Maylie deeply; mingled with her affection for Oliver, and nearly equal in strength and warmth, was her earnest wish to lead the forsaken creature back to repentance and hope.

They intended to remain in London only three days before setting off for several weeks to a distant part of the coast. It was already midnight of the first day. What could she plan that might be carried out within eight-and-forty hours? And how might she delay the trip without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them, and would stay for the next two days; yet Rose knew too well the excellent gentleman’s impetuous temper, and could foresee the anger with which, in the first burst of his indignation, he would regard the agent of Oliver’s capture. She could not trust him with the secret, when no experienced person could back up her plea for the girl. These were ample grounds for the utmost caution and discretion when telling Mrs. Maylie; the lady’s first impulse would surely be to consult the worthy doctor in the matter. Seeking any legal adviser, even had she known how, was hardly to be considered for the same reason. She did, for a moment, think of turning to Harry; but this brought back the memory of their last parting, and it seemed an unworthy thing to summon him home when—tears sprang to her eyes as she followed this line of thought—he might already have learned to forget her, and to be happier apart.

Tossed by these conflicting thoughts; leaning now toward one plan, then another, and again recoiling from all as each new argument rose before her; Rose spent a wakeful, troubled night. After more self-communing the following day, she reached the desperate resolve to seek Harry’s counsel.

“If it grieves him,” she pondered, “to return here, how grievous must it be for me! Yet perhaps he will not come; he may send a letter, or he may come in person and carefully avoid seeing me—he did when he left. I hardly expected it, yet it was better for us both.” With that, Rose set down the pen and turned aside, as if even the paper that was to bear her message should not witness her tears."}

{"request_id":"bd4214c7f8af77a4d2033e7a","rewritten_text":"This marriage is entirely right. I didn’t think so at first, but I admit it now. The gods created Sibyl Vane for you. Without her you would have been unfinished.”

“Thanks, Basil,” replied Dorian Gray, squeezing his hand. “I knew you’d understand me. Harry is so cynical he frightens me. But here comes the orchestra. It’s dreadful, but it lasts only five minutes. Then the curtain goes up, and you’ll see the girl to whom I’m going to devote my whole life, the one to whom I’ve already given everything good in me.”

Fifteen minutes later, amid a wild storm of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onto the stage. Yes, she was undeniably beautiful—one of the loveliest creatures Lord Henry thought he had ever seen. There was something fawn-like in her shy grace and startled eyes. A faint blush, like the reflection of a rose in a silver mirror, touched her cheeks as she glanced at the packed, enthusiastic house. She retreated a few steps, and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward sprang to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat motionless, as if in a dream, staring at her. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, murmuring, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of Capulet’s house, and Romeo in his pilgrim costume had entered with Mercutio and the others. The orchestra, such as it was, struck up a few bars, and the dance began. Through the crowd of awkward, shabby actors, Sibyl Vane moved like a being from a more refined world. Her body swayed as she danced, like a plant drifting in water. The curves of her neck were like those of a white lily. Her hands seemed carved from cool ivory.

Yet she was strangely lifeless. No joy appeared when her eyes met Romeo’s. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,
and palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

with the brief exchange that followed, were delivered in a completely artificial way. Her voice was lovely, but the tone was entirely wrong. It was off in color. It drained all vitality from the verse. It made the passion seem unreal.

Dorian Gray turned pale as he watched her. He felt confused and worried. Neither of his friends dared say anything to him. To them she now seemed utterly incapable."}

{"request_id":"5456ee5b7f1cc5cb0b360208","rewritten_text":"“You’ve reared an artificial soul and spirit in him, ma’am, utterly unfitting for someone of his station: as the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, who are practical philosophers, would tell you. What have paupers to do with soul or spirit? It’s ample that we let ’em keep living bodies. Had you kept the boy on gruel, ma’am, none of this would have occurred.”

“Dear, dear!” exclaimed Mrs. Sowerberry, lifting her eyes devoutly toward the kitchen ceiling. “This is what comes of being generous!”

Mrs. Sowerberry’s generosity to Oliver had consisted of a lavish measure of all the grimy scraps nobody else would eat; so there was much meekness and self-sacrifice in her standing, of her own free will, beneath Mr. Bumble’s heavy charge, though, to be fair, she was entirely guiltless in thought, word, or deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, when the lady’s eyes dropped back to earth, “the only plan now, that I know of, is to leave him in the cellar a day or two, until he’s a bit starved down; then take him out and keep him on gruel through his apprenticeship. He comes of bad stock. Excitable temperaments, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both nurse and doctor said that mother of his forced her way here through difficulties and agony that would have killed any well-disposed woman, weeks beforehand.”

At this point in Mr. Bumble’s speech, Oliver, hearing merely enough to realize some mention was being made of his mother, began kicking again with such fury that every other sound was drowned. Sowerberry reappeared just then. Oliver’s offence, with those exaggerations the ladies felt best calculated to inflame his wrath, was explained, whereupon he unlocked the cellar door in a flash and hauled his mutinous apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver’s clothes were ripped from the beating he’d taken; his face mottled with bruises and scratches; his hair hanging over his brow. The hot flush had not faded, however; and as he was hauled from his confinement, he glowered courageously at Noah and looked entirely undaunted.

“Now, you’re a fine young fellow, aren’t you?” said Sowerberry, giving Oliver a shake and a cuff on the ear.

“He insulted my mother,” Oliver answered.

“Well, suppose he did, you ungrateful little wretch?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She earned what he said, and more.”

“She didn’t,” said Oliver.

“She did,” said Mrs. Sowerberry.

“It’s a lie!” said Oliver.

Mrs. Sowerberry broke into a torrent of tears.

This deluge of weeping left Mr. Sowerberry no real choice. Had he hesitated for a single instant to punish Oliver severely, it must be plain to every knowledgeable reader that he would have been, by all precedents in marital quarrels, a brute, an unnatural husband, an insulting creature, a base imitation of a man, and various other delightful characters too numerous to list within the confines of this chapter."}

{"request_id":"6d04f630d7de095160a6f00b","rewritten_text":"Shall I be carried to the skies on soft, flowery beds of ease while others fight to win the prize and sail through bloody seas?

People thought he was a marvelous reader. At church sociables he was always asked to read poetry; when he finished, the ladies would raise their hands, let them fall into their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads as if to say, “Words fail us; it is too beautiful, far too beautiful for this earthly world.”

After the hymn, the Reverend Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin board and read notices of meetings, societies, and other matters until it seemed the list would run on to the crack of doom—a strange custom still kept up in America, even in cities, in this era of plenty of newspapers. Often, the less reason there is to keep a tradition, the harder it is to discard it.

Then the minister prayed. It was a generous, detailed prayer: it pleaded for the church and its little children; for the other churches in the village; for the village itself; for the county; for the State; for the State officers; for the United States; for the churches of the United States; for Congress; for the President; for the officers of the Government; for poor sailors tossed by storms; for the oppressed millions under European monarchies and Eastern despotisms; for those who have the light and good news yet lack eyes to see or ears to hear; for the heathen on faraway islands; and it ended by asking that the words he was about to speak find grace and favor, like seed planted in fertile soil, yielding a thankful harvest of good. Amen.

Dresses rustled, and the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it—if he even managed that. He was restless throughout. His mind kept count of every element of the prayer without meaning to—he was not listening, but he knew the territory well and the minister’s usual route through it. Whenever a bit of new material was added, his ear caught it and his whole being objected; he thought additions were unfair and underhanded. In the middle of the prayer a fly settled on the back of the pew before him and tormented his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands, wrapping its arms around its head and polishing it so vigorously it seemed almost to come off, exposing the thin thread of its neck; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them down as if they were coat-tails; going through its whole toilette with perfect calm, as though it knew it was completely safe."}

{"request_id":"169ae8e566d3ea200272ed70","rewritten_text":"But there was no cheer in the little town that same calm Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s family were putting on mourning clothes, full of grief and tears. An unusual stillness held the village, though it was usually quiet enough. The townspeople went about their business absent-mindedly and spoke little, though they often sighed. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children; their games held no joy, and they gave them up one by one.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself drifting around the empty schoolyard, feeling very low. Nothing there soothed her. She murmured to herself:

“Oh, if I only had a brass andiron knob again! But I haven’t got anything now to remember him by.” She swallowed a sob.

After a moment she muttered:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that—not for the whole world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

The thought broke her, and she wandered off with tears running down her cheeks. Soon a bunch of Tom’s and Joe’s friends came by, stood looking over the picket fence, and spoke softly about how Tom did this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe said something that—now that they thought about it—seemed like a sign of doom. Each one pointed out the exact spot where the boys had stood, then added something like, “and I was standing just here—just like I am now, suppose you were him—I was this close—and he smiled just like this—and then something ran all over me, you know—awful—and I never thought what it meant, but now I can see!”

They argued over who saw the dead boys last, each claiming that gloomy honor and supplying proof, though the stories were bent a bit. When they finally agreed who actually saw the boys last and spoke the final words, those lucky ones adopted a kind of sacred importance, and the others gaped and envied them. One poor fellow, who had nothing else to brag about, said with obvious pride:

“Well, Tom Sawyer he thrashed me once.”

But that bid for glory fell flat. Almost all the boys could say the same, which ruined the distinction. The group wandered off, still sharing memories of the lost heroes in hushed voices."}

{"request_id":"f2efffcfa33d2d5454552797","rewritten_text":"This was invitation enough.

“Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been taken by a young man of large fortune from the north of England. He came down on Monday in a chaise-and-four to see the place, liked it so much that he made an agreement with Mr. Morris at once, plans to move in before Michaelmas, and some of his servants will be in the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, of course! A single man with four or five thousand a year. What a wonderful opportunity for our girls!”

“How so? How can it matter to them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife answered, “how can you be so aggravating? You must know I expect him to marry one of them.”

“Is that his purpose in settling here?”

“Purpose? Nonsense, how can you say that! But it is very likely that he may fall in love with one of them, so you must visit him as soon as he arrives.”

“I see no need for that. You and the girls may go—or you may send them alone, which might be better; since you are as handsome as any of them, Mr. Bingley might like you best of all.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I certainly had my share of beauty, but I do not claim anything extraordinary now. When a woman has five grown daughters, she should stop thinking about her own beauty.”

“In those cases, a woman usually has little beauty left to think about.”

“But, my dear, you must go to see Mr. Bingley when he comes to the neighborhood.”

“That is more than I promise, I assure you.”

“But think of your daughters. Imagine what a good match it would be for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go for that reason alone; normally, you know, they never visit new arrivals. Indeed, you must go, for it will be impossible for us to call on him if you do not.”

“You are overly particular, surely. I dare say Mr. Bingley will be happy to see you; and I will send a few lines with you to assure him of my full consent to his marrying whichever of the girls he prefers—though I must give a special recommendation for my little Lizzy.”

“I insist you do no such thing. Lizzy is no better than the others; I am sure she is not half as pretty as Jane, nor half as good-humored as Lydia.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"4454fe307dd23fb9fdef6b0f","rewritten_text":"He had never suspected his own influence. He followed her into the shrubbery without any plan of testing it. He came only from the anxiety to see how she was taking Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish aim, only the wish, if she gave him the chance, to comfort or advise her. Everything else sprang from the moment, from what he heard and how it moved him. Hearing that she cared nothing for Frank Churchill—that her heart was free—sparked the hope that, eventually, he might win her love; but it was never a hope for the present. In a brief surge of eagerness over judgment, he had only dared to ask that she would not forbid him to try. The greater hopes that soon unfolded were all the more enchanting. The love he had hoped to earn, if possible, was already his. In half an hour he had gone from deep distress to a happiness so complete it could go by no other name.\n\nHer change matched his. This single half hour had given both of them the same treasured certainty of being loved, and had cleared away ignorance, jealousy, and distrust on both sides. He had long felt jealousy, dating back to the arrival, or even the expectation, of Frank Churchill. He had been in love with Emma and jealous of Frank Churchill from almost the same moment; one feeling had probably opened his eyes to the other. That jealousy drove him from the country. The Box Hill outing pushed him to leave; he meant to spare himself the sight of such permitted, even encouraged, attentions again. He left to learn to be indifferent, but he chose the wrong place. His brother’s house held too much domestic happiness; woman there appeared in too amiable a light; Isabella was too much like Emma—differing only in the few, obvious inferiorities that made Emma shine brighter—for him to accomplish much, even if he had stayed longer. Yet he persisted, day after day, until this very morning’s mail brought the news about Jane Fairfax. Then, with the gladness he could not help feeling, since he had never thought Frank Churchill worthy of Emma, and with so much tender concern and anxious care for her, he could stay away no longer. He rode home through the rain and walked over right after dinner to see how this sweetest and best of creatures, flawless in spite of all her faults, bore the discovery."}

{"request_id":"19be3eb8fd214f9b4ab741ae","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a very distinguished-looking old gentleman, and another younger one who had his right arm in a sling. And, my goodness, how the crowd yelled and laughed, keeping it up nonstop. But I didn’t see anything funny about it, and I figured it would take some effort for the duke and the king to find it funny, either. I expected they’d go pale. But no, neither of them turned a shade. The duke never even hinted he suspected what was going on, just strolled around cooing, pleased and contented, like a jug gently glugging out buttermilk; and the king gazed down so sorrowfully on the newcomers it looked like it hurt his heart to imagine there could be such crooks and scoundrels in the world. Oh, he did it beautifully. Lots of the leading townspeople crowded around the king to show they were on his side. The old gentleman who’d just arrived looked utterly confused. Before long he started to speak, and I could tell right away he sounded like an Englishman—not exactly like the king, though the king’s version was a pretty fair imitation. I can’t repeat the old gentleman’s exact words, or copy his voice, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise I never expected, and I’ll admit straight out I’m not in the best position to respond to it; because my brother and I have been unlucky—he’s broken his arm, and our luggage got set off at a town upriver last night by mistake. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can neither hear nor speak—and right now can’t even make decent signs, seeing as he has only one hand to do it with. We are who we say we are, and in a day or two, when my luggage catches up, I can prove it. But until then I’ll say nothing more, and go over to the hotel and wait.”

So he and the new mute started off; and the king laughed and blustered:

“Broke his arm—very likely, isn’t it?—and mighty convenient, too, for a fraud who has to use signs and hasn’t learned how. Lost their luggage! That’s rich!—and mighty clever—under the circumstances!”

He laughed again, and so did everyone else, except three or four, or maybe half a dozen. One of them was that doctor; another was a sharp-faced fellow carrying an old-fashioned carpetbag made of real carpet material, who had just come off the steamboat and was speaking to the doctor in a low voice, glancing toward the king once in a while and nodding—they were Levi Bell, the lawyer who’d gone up to Louisville; and another was a big rough fellow who came over and listened to everything the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

{"request_id":"4ba44cea7ad9745719d8fd0e","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, lightly resting his hand on the Doctor’s arm again after a short silence, “how would you explain this attack?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette replied, “there was a powerful and sudden revival of the thoughts and memories that first caused his illness. Some intense, painful associations came back vividly, I think. He likely feared for a long time that those memories would return—perhaps under certain conditions, perhaps on a particular occasion. He tried to prepare himself in vain; maybe the effort to prepare only made him less able to endure it.”

“Would he remember what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, hesitant.

The Doctor looked around the room in distress, shook his head, and answered quietly, “Not at all.”

“Now, about the future,” hinted Mr. Lorry.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining strength, “I have great hope. Since Heaven was merciful enough to restore him so quickly, I should have great hope. He gave way under the pressure of a complicated something, long feared and vaguely expected and resisted, and after the storm broke and passed, I hope the worst is behind him.”

“Well, well! That’s reassuring. I’m grateful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am grateful,” the Doctor echoed, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other points,” said Mr. Lorry, “on which I need guidance. May I continue?”

“You could do your friend no better service.” The Doctor offered his hand.

“To the first point, then. He is scholarly and unusually driven; he throws himself passionately into gaining professional knowledge, running experiments, many pursuits. Does he do too much?”

“I think not. His mind may simply need constant occupation. That might be partly his nature, partly the result of suffering. The less it is engaged with healthy work, the more it risks turning toward unhealthy thoughts. He may have noticed this in himself and acted on it.”

“You are sure he isn’t under too much strain?”

“I think I’m quite sure.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that would happen easily. There’s been heavy pressure in one direction, and it needs a counterbalance.”

“Excuse me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose for a moment he were overworked; would it show up as a return of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"d5ce154808d4fe0e2e19e93e","rewritten_text":"“I have to go, unsure of what awaits me; but I will come back here, or trail your group, as soon as I can. A single word, a single look, will decide whether I enter your father’s house tonight or never again.”

A letter like that could not easily be shaken off. Half an hour alone to think might have calmed her; but the ten minutes she had before being interrupted, burdened by her present constraints, did nothing for her composure. Each moment only stirred her more. It was happiness so intense it overwhelmed her. Before she even got through the first wave of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all walked in.

The urgent need to appear like herself sparked an immediate battle, but after a short while she couldn’t keep it up. She stopped understanding a word they were saying and had to plead illness as an excuse. They could see she looked very unwell, were alarmed and sympathetic, and insisted they would not leave her for anything. It was awful. If only they would go away and leave her to the quiet of that room, it would have been her cure; but to have them standing or hovering around her drove her to desperation, and she declared she would go home.

“Certainly, my dear,” cried Mrs. Musgrove, “go home this instant and take care of yourself so you’ll be ready for tonight. I wish Sarah were here to tend to you, but I’m no doctor. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

But a chair was out of the question. Worse than anything! To give up the chance of even a brief word with Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk up the town (and she was almost sure she would meet him) was unbearable. She objected strongly to the chair, and Mrs. Musgrove, whose mind ran only to one kind of illness, after confirming with some worry that there had been no fall, that Anne had not recently slipped and struck her head, that she was absolutely certain she had not fallen, could cheerfully let her go and count on finding her better that night.

Determined to leave no possible precaution undone, Anne forced herself and said—

“I fear, ma’am, it hasn’t been made completely clear. Please be kind enough to tell the other gentlemen that we hope to see your entire party this evening. {"request_id":"0b9a0699d00176c1d4c5e730","rewritten_text":"Mr Elliot looked up with such marked respect.”

“Quite delightful!” cried Mrs Clay, though she dared not glance at Anne. “Exactly like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I not call them father and son?”

“Oh! I place no restriction on anyone’s words. If you choose to have such ideas! But honestly, I hardly notice his attentions as anything beyond what other men show.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs Clay, raising her hands and eyes, and letting the rest of her surprise sink into a convenient silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you need not be so anxious about him. Remember, I invited him. I sent him away smiling. When I learned he truly meant to spend all of tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired the skill of her friend, who could show such pleasure in anticipating and greeting the very person whose presence must interfere with her main aim. Mrs Clay must inevitably hate the sight of Mr Elliot; yet she could wear the most obliging, calm expression, and seem perfectly content with the shortened chance of devoting only half as much time to Sir Walter as she would have otherwise.

To Anne, it was extremely distressing to see Mr Elliot enter the room, and quite painful to have him approach and speak. She had already suspected he could not always be sincere, but now she saw deceit in everything. His respectful attention to her father, compared with his earlier comments, was disgusting; and when she remembered his cruel conduct towards Mrs Smith, she could barely endure his present smiles, gentleness, and polished sentiments.

She was determined to avoid any change in behavior that might provoke a protest from him. She was keen to escape any questioning or attention. Still, she meant to be as decidedly cool to him as their relationship allowed, and to quietly step back from the needless intimacy she had been led into. So she was more cautious and more distant than the night before.

He tried to stir her curiosity again about where and how he might have once heard her praised; he very much wished to be encouraged by more questioning. But the magic was gone. He realized that the bustle and excitement of a public room were needed to ignite his modest cousin’s vanity; he discovered, at least, that it could not be managed now, amid the competing claims of everyone else."}

{"request_id":"902db7cc906171c4e9cdfae9","rewritten_text":"“Please think, ma’am,” said Oliver, tears forcing their way despite his efforts to hold them back. “Oh, remember how young and good she is, and how much comfort she brings everyone. I am sure—certain—quite certain—that, for your sake, because you are so good; for her own sake; and for the sake of all she makes happy, she will not die. Heaven will never let her die so young.”

“Hush!” said Mrs. Maylie, resting her hand on Oliver’s head. “You think like a child, poor boy. Still, you remind me of my duty. I forgot it for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old and have seen enough of illness and death to know the pain of parting from those we love. I have seen enough to know it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them. Yet this should comfort us even in sorrow, for Heaven is just, and such things teach us clearly that there is a brighter world than this, and the passage to it is quick. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how dearly!”

Oliver was amazed to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke, she checked her tears by one effort; straightening her posture and becoming calm and steady. He was even more surprised that this steadiness lasted, and that during all the care and watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie stayed ready and composed, carrying out all her duties with steadiness and, outwardly, even cheerfulness. But he was young, and did not yet know what strong minds can do in such trials. How could he, when even their owners seldom see their own strength?

A tense night followed. Morning brought the fulfillment of Mrs. Maylie’s fears. Rose had entered the first stage of a high and dangerous fever.

“We must be active, Oliver, and not give in to useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, pressing her finger to her lips as she looked into his face. “This letter must reach Mr. Losberne with all speed. It has to go to the market town, no more than four miles away by the footpath across the field, and from there be sent by express on horseback straight to Chertsey. The innkeepers will see to it, and I trust you to make sure it is done.”

Oliver could not speak; his face showed nothing but the urgent wish to start at once."}

content.text: {"request_id":"18dd7548260209c7fc5018b2","rewritten_text":"The following day the specter felt faint and spent. The dreadful suspense of the past four weeks had begun to tell on him. His nerves were utterly wrecked, and he flinched at the lightest rustle. For five days he stayed shut in his chamber, and finally resolved to abandon the issue of the blood-stain on the library floor. If the Otises did not care for it, plainly they did not merit it. They were clearly persons of a coarse, material nature, quite unable to grasp the emblematic value of sense-bound manifestations. The subject of spectral appearances, and the evolution of astral forms, was naturally a separate affair, beyond his power to regulate. It remained his solemn duty to show himself in the corridor every week, and to gibber from the broad oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of each month, and he could not perceive any honourable means of shirking his obligations. That his life had been exceedingly wicked was beyond dispute, yet he was scrupulous in every matter touching the supernatural. Thus, for the ensuing three Saturdays he paced the corridor between midnight and three o’clock, taking every conceivable step to avoid detection. He took off his boots, moved as softly as possible over the worm-eaten boards, donned a sweeping black velvet cloak, and carefully used the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit he found it extremely hard to bring himself to employ this last precaution. Nevertheless, one evening while the household were at dinner, he stole into Mr. Otis’s room and purloined the bottle. At first he felt somewhat abased, but later was sensible enough to acknowledge that the contrivance had many advantages and, to some extent, served his ends. Still, despite all his efforts, they would not let him alone. Strings were repeatedly stretched across the corridor, and he stumbled over them in the darkness, and once, when dressed as “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he received a nasty fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had constructed from the doorway of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult so infuriated him that he decided to make one last attempt to uphold his dignity and station, resolving to confront the insolent young Etonians the following night in his famed guise of “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”\n\nHe had not assumed that disguise for over seventy years; indeed, not since he had so terrified pretty Lady Barbara Modish with it that she abruptly ended her betrothal to the reigning Lord Canterville’s grandfather and fled to Gretna Green with dashing Jack Castleton, vowing that nothing on earth would persuade her to wed into a house that allowed such a hideous specter to pace the terrace at dusk."}

{"request_id":"4f511519d71ae99ebcce4ffd","rewritten_text":"It was within Warwick Castle that I met the curious stranger I am about to describe. Three traits drew me to him: his frank simplicity, his astonishing mastery of ancient armor, and the restful ease of his company—inasmuch as he supplied all the conversation. As modest folk tend to do, we drifted together at the rear of the group being guided through the halls, and he immediately began voicing observations that caught my interest. Speaking in a soft, pleasant, unhurried fashion, he seemed by degrees to slip out of this age and world into some distant era and forgotten realm; sooner or later he bound me in such a spell that I thought myself moving through the ghosts, shadows, dust, and decay of a hoary antiquity, conversing with one of its relics. Precisely as I might mention my closest associates or bitterest foes, or the neighbors most familiar to me, he spoke of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and every other illustrious name of the Round Table—and how incredibly old, indescribably old and faded and withered and ancient he appeared as he proceeded! Presently he turned and addressed me, as casually as another might refer to the weather or some routine concern—

“You know of transmigration of souls; are you acquainted with transposition of epochs—and of bodies?”

I replied that I had never heard of such a thing. He cared so little—equally as when one talks of the weather—that he did not even observe whether I answered or not. A brief pause followed, instantly cut off by the monotonous drone of the paid guide:

“Ancient hauberk, dating from the sixth century, era of King Arthur and the Round Table; reputed to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; observe the circular opening in the chain-mail over the left breast; no explanation; thought to have been made by a bullet after firearms were invented—possibly by Cromwell’s soldiers from spite.”

My companion smiled—not a modern expression, but one that surely vanished from general use ages upon ages ago—and murmured, apparently to himself:

“Wit ye well, I saw it done.” Then, after a short pause, he added: “I did it myself.”

Before I had recovered from the electric shock of that assertion, he had disappeared.

The whole evening I sat by the fire at the Warwick Arms, steeped in visions of bygone days, while the rain rattled against the panes and the wind howled round the eaves and corners. At intervals I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s bewitching volume, feasting on its rich wonders and exploits, inhaling the perfume of its archaic names, and dreaming anew."}

{"request_id":"65a9b94168524ea84ab96bda","rewritten_text":"“She and the children might do perfectly well here.”

“Ah, Papa—that’s something you’ve never managed yet, and I doubt you ever will. Isabella cannot stand staying behind when her husband goes.”

Sadly, this was too true to argue. Unwelcome as it was, Mr. Woodhouse could only give a resigned sigh; and since Emma saw how the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband dampened his spirits, she immediately steered the conversation to something that would lift them.

“Harriet must spend as much time with us as she can while my brother and sister are here. I’m sure she’ll enjoy the children. We are very proud of them, aren’t we, Papa? I wonder which one she’ll think is the handsomest, Henry or John?”

“Yes, I wonder which she’ll choose. Poor little darlings, they’ll be so happy to come. They love being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they do, sir. I’m sure I can’t think of anyone who doesn’t.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John is very like his mother. Henry is the eldest; he was named after me, not his father. John, the second, is named for his father. Some people are surprised, I believe, that the eldest wasn’t named after his father, but Isabella insisted on Henry, which I thought very sweet of her. And he’s a remarkably clever boy. They’re all remarkably clever, and they have so many charming little ways. They’ll come stand by my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, could you give me a piece of string?’ And once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives are only made for grandpapas. I think their father is far too rough with them.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you’re so very gentle yourself; but if you could compare him to other fathers, you wouldn’t find him rough. He wants his boys to be active and sturdy; and if they misbehave, he’ll give them a sharp word now and then; but he’s an affectionate father—certainly Mr. John Knightley is affectionate. The children are all devoted to him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and tosses them up to the ceiling in such a terrifying way!”

“But they love it, Papa; there is nothing they enjoy more. It’s such fun for them that if their uncle didn’t make them take turns, whichever one started would never let the other have a chance.”

“Well, I can’t understand it.”

“That’s true of all of us, Papa. Half the world can’t fathom what delights the other half.”"}

{"request_id":"0046eb013d965a7379a3251f","rewritten_text":"They know what a clever boy he is; they’ll give the Artful nothing less than life.”

“What do you mean by lagging and a lifer?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What’s the use of talking like that to me? Why don’t you speak so I can understand?”

Fagin was about to translate these mysterious expressions into plain speech—and, interpreted, Mr. Bolter would have been told they meant “transportation for life”—when the dialogue was cut short by the entrance of Master Bates, hands shoved in his pockets, face twisted into a semi-comical look of distress.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” said Charley, once he and his new companion were introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to identify him; and the Artful’s booked for a passage abroad,” replied Master Bates. “I’ll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband to visit him in before he sets out. To think of Jack Dawkins—flash Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—being sent overseas for a common two-penny-halfpenny snuffbox! I never thought he’d do it for less than a gold watch, chain, and seals at the very least. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables and go out like a gentleman, not like a common thief, without any honor or glory!”

With this outpouring for his unlucky friend, Master Bates dropped into the nearest chair, looking thoroughly dejected.

“What do you mean by saying he has neither honor nor glory!” cried Fagin, shooting an angry glance at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best among you? Could any of you touch him or even come near his scent? Eh?”

“Not one,” answered Master Bates, his voice thick with regret. “Not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” snapped Fagin. “What are you blubbering for?”

“Because it isn’t on the record, is it?” said Charley, driven to outright defiance of his venerable mentor by the pull of his sorrow. “Because it won’t show up in the indictment; because nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he stand in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe he won’t be there at all. Oh, my eyes, what a blow this is!”

“Ha! ha!” laughed Fagin, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter in a fit of chuckling that shook him as if he had the palsy. “Look how proud they are of their trade, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"07f6763a55eefd528302c191","rewritten_text":"His mind and temperament, while different from hers, would have fulfilled all her hopes. It would have been a union that benefited both: her ease and high spirits could have softened his nature and polished his manners, and his judgment, experience, and worldly knowledge would have offered her advantages of far greater value.

But no such fortunate marriage could now show the admiring public what true conjugal bliss looked like. A very different union, one that made the other impossible, was about to be formed within their family.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would be supported with any degree of independence. But she could easily guess how little lasting happiness awaited a couple brought together only because their impulses overpowered their principles.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. He briefly answered Mr. Bennet’s thanks with assurances of his willingness to do whatever he could for any member of the family, and ended with a plea that the topic never be raised to him again. The main purpose of his letter was to report that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

“It was very much my wish that he do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree that leaving that corps is highly advisable for his sake and my niece’s. Mr. Wickham intends to join the Regulars; among his former acquaintances he still has some who can and will assist him in the army. He has been promised an ensign’s commission in General ----’s regiment, currently stationed in the north. It is beneficial to have it so far from this part of the country. He makes respectable promises, and I hope that among different society, where both must protect their reputations, they will behave more sensibly. I have written to Colonel Forster to explain our current arrangements and to ask him to reassure Mr. Wickham’s creditors in and around Brighton that they will be paid soon, for which I have given my word. Could you take the trouble to deliver similar assurances to his creditors in Meryton? I will enclose a list, as he provided it. He has submitted all his debts; I hope at least he has not misled us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything should be settled within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and Mrs. Gardiner tells me that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south.”"}

{"request_id":"26c38d783267e1131706e4a0","rewritten_text":"He shivered and went back, closing the window behind him.

When he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it. He did not even look at the murdered man. He knew the only way to survive was to refuse to face what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait causing all his misery was gone from his life now. That was enough.

Then he remembered the lamp. It was an unusual Moorish piece, made of dull silver with steel arabesques and set with rough turquoises. His servant might notice it missing and start asking questions. After a brief hesitation, he went back and took it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the corpse. How still it was! How terribly white the long hands seemed! It looked like a hideous wax figure.

With the door locked behind him, he crept quietly downstairs. The wood creaked and sounded as if it were crying out in pain. He stopped several times and listened. No, everything was silent. It was only the echo of his own steps.

When he reached the library, he spotted the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden. He unlocked a secret cupboard in the wainscoting, the one where he kept his disguises, and put the items inside. He could burn them later. He checked his watch. It was twenty minutes to two.

He sat down to think. Every year—nearly every month—men were hanged in England for what he had done. There had been a madness for murder everywhere. Some red star must have come too close to Earth. And yet, what evidence pointed to him? Basil Hallward had left at eleven. No one had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet was asleep. Paris! Yes, Basil had left for Paris on the midnight train, just as planned. With his strange, private habits, it would be months before anyone was suspicious. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before then.

Suddenly an idea struck him. He put on his fur coat and hat and went out into the hall. He stopped, listening to the slow heavy steps of the policeman on the pavement outside and seeing the flash of the lantern in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

After a few moments, he lifted the latch and slipped out, closing the door gently behind him. Then he began to ring the bell."}

content.text: {"request_id":"e1644e11489bf6f2eedeb8db","rewritten_text":"Colonel Grangerford was a gentleman, plain and simple. He was a gentleman through and through, and so was his family. He was well born, as people say, and the Widow Douglas always claimed a man’s breeding counted as much as a horse’s; no one argued with her, because she was top aristocracy in our town. Pap repeated it too, though he was no more high-class than a mudcat. Colonel Grangerford stood tall and thin, with a dark, pale complexion and not a touch of red anywhere. He shaved his narrow face clean every morning, had the thinnest lips and nostrils, a sharp nose, heavy eyebrows, and eyes so black and deep-set they looked like they stared out from caves. His forehead was high, his hair black and straight and hanging to his shoulders. His hands were long and slim. Every day he put on a clean shirt and a full linen suit so white it almost hurt to look at. On Sundays he added a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane topped with silver. There was never any foolishness around him, not a bit, and he was never loud. He was as kind as any man could be—you could feel it, and that gave you confidence. Now and then he smiled, and it was a fine sight; but if he drew himself up like a liberty pole and lightning started flashing under his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree and only later find out what was wrong. He never had to tell anyone to mind their manners—everyone behaved when he was around. Folks loved his company too; he was like sunshine most of the time—he made everything seem like fair weather. And if he turned into a storm cloud, it was dark for only half a minute, and that was enough; nothing else would go wrong for a week afterward.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came downstairs in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs, greeted them, and wouldn’t sit again until they did. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter stood, mixed him a glass of bitters, and handed it over. He held it while Tom and Bob mixed their own, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” The colonel and his wife bowed just a touch and said thank you, and all three drank. After that, Bob and Tom dripped a spoon of water over the sugar and the bit of whiskey or apple brandy left in their tumblers, passed them to me and Buck, and we drank to the old folks too."}

{"request_id":"673dc63be6ab70956fcb9c0f","rewritten_text":"In my early years discontent never entered my thoughts, and whenever ennui threatened, the sight of nature’s beauties or the study of humanity’s excellent and sublime works could always engage my heart and restore buoyancy to my spirits. Now I am a blasted tree, lightning seared into my soul; I felt then that I would live on merely to display what I would soon cease to be—a wretched wreck of humanity, pitied by others and insufferable to myself.

We lingered at Oxford for some time, wandering through its surroundings and striving to recognize every spot linked with the most stirring period of English history. Our small exploratory excursions were frequently extended by the succession of objects that appeared. We went to the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and to the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my soul rose above its degrading, miserable terrors to reflect on the divine ideals of liberty and self-sacrifice of which these sights were monuments and reminders. For an instant I dared shake off my chains and gaze about me with a liberated and exalted spirit, but the iron had already bitten into my flesh, and I relapsed, trembling and despairing, into my wretched self.

With reluctance we left Oxford and traveled to Matlock, our next resting place. The countryside near this village recalled far more vividly the scenery of Switzerland; yet every feature was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the coronet of distant snowy Alps that constantly accompany the pine-clad mountains of my homeland. We toured the marvelous cavern and the small natural history cabinets, where curiosities are arranged just as in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. Henry’s utterance of the latter name made me tremble, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which was now linked with that dreadful scene.

Continuing north from Derby, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself back among the Swiss mountains. The patches of snow still lingering on the northern slopes, the lakes, and the rushing rocky streams were all beloved, familiar sights. We also formed some acquaintances who nearly managed to trick me into feeling happiness. Clerval’s joy was proportionately greater than mine; his mind unfolded amid men of talent, and he discovered within himself greater faculties and resources than he had ever thought possible while keeping the company of his inferiors."}

Telephone the king’s homeopath to come!” Within two minutes I was kneeling by the child’s crib, and Sandy was sending servants racing through every corridor of the palace. I understood at once—membranous croup. I bent close and whispered, “Wake up, sweetheart! This little one had spent much of her short life in my arms, and often I could chase away her troubles and coax a laugh through wet eyelashes when even her mother couldn’t. Sir Launcelot, in full armor, came striding down the great hall, heading to the stock-board. He presided there and sat in the Siege Perilous, which he had bought from Sir Galahad; the stock-board was now made up of the Knights of the Round Table, and they used the Round Table for business. Seats went for—well, you wouldn’t believe the price, so why mention it. Sir Launcelot was bearish and had cornered one of the new issues, ready to squeeze the shorts today; but as always he was true Launcelot, and when he looked in while passing the door and learned his favorite was sick, nothing else mattered. Bulls and bears could battle on their own; he would stay with little Hello-Central. And that’s what he did. He tossed his helmet into the corner, swapped in a fresh wick for the alcohol lamp in half a minute, and started heating the croup kettle. By then Sandy had draped a blanket canopy over the crib, and everything was set. Sir Launcelot stoked the heat, he and I packed the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid plus a dash of lactic acid, then filled it with water and slipped the steam spout under the canopy. With everything in order, we took our seats on either side of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"52d3a24c08b01c0e3e8305d0","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to calm you quite a bit. But what ran through your mind? What did you think we’d found?”

Huck was cornered—the man’s searching gaze was on him—he’d have given anything for a believable answer—nothing came—those eyes were drilling deeper and deeper—one foolish reply popped up—no time to judge it, so he went with it. Weakly he said, “Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Huck was too miserable to smile, but the old man laughed loud and delightedly, shaking his whole frame from head to toe, and said that a laugh like that was money in a man’s pocket because it slashed the doctor’s bill like nothing else. Then he added, “You poor kid, you’re pale and worn out—you’re not well at all—no wonder you’re a little flighty and off balance. But you’ll be fine. Rest and sleep will pull you through, I hope.”

Huck was annoyed with himself for being such a fool and showing so much suspicious excitement, since he had abandoned the idea that the bundle from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard the talk at the widow’s stile. He had only thought it probably wasn’t the treasure—he hadn’t known for sure—and so the hint of a captured bundle rattled him beyond control. Still, he was glad the little scene had occurred, because now he knew without question that that package wasn’t the package, and his mind was at ease and very comfortable. Everything seemed to be falling into place now; the treasure had to still be in No. 2, the men would be caught and jailed that day, and he and Tom could grab the gold that night without trouble or fear of interruption.

Right as breakfast ended there was a knock at the door. Huck leaped for a hiding place—he had no desire to be linked even remotely to the previous night. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including Widow Douglas, and noticed groups of townspeople climbing the hill to stare at the stile. Word had spread. The Welshman had to tell the night’s story to the guests. The widow expressed her gratitude loudly for being saved.

“Don’t mention it, ma’am. There’s someone you owe more to than me and my boys, maybe, but he won’t let me tell his name. We wouldn’t have been there without him.”"}
