{"request_id":"76f849fb5e4b4b43f5c49821","rewritten_text":"“I hope I will soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” said Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, eager to take this as a special compliment, smiled very graciously.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I assume,” he went on, “and know that he is my son, though he does not share my name.”

“Oh yes, and I shall be very happy to meet him. I am sure Mr. Elton will call on him right away, and we will both be delighted to have him at the Vicarage.”

“You are very kind. Frank will be extremely pleased, I’m certain. He is to be in town next week, if not sooner. We had notice of it in a letter today. I met the mail as I was out this morning, and seeing my son’s handwriting, I took the liberty of opening it, though it was not addressed to me—it was to Mrs. Weston. She is the one he writes to most; I hardly ever get a letter.”

“And you actually opened what was meant for her! Oh, Mr. Weston,” said Mrs. Elton, giving an affected laugh, “I must protest. That sets a very dangerous example! Please do not let your neighbors follow it. Upon my word, if this is what we are to expect, we married women must fight back! Oh, Mr. Weston, I never would have believed it of you!”

“Yes, we men are sad creatures. You must guard yourself, Mrs. Elton. This letter tells us—it is a short letter, written in haste just to alert us—that they are all coming up to town at once, because of Mrs. Churchill. She has been ill all winter and thinks Enscombe is too cold, so they are all moving south immediately.”

“Indeed—from Yorkshire, I believe. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, about a hundred and ninety miles from London, a long journey.”

“Indeed, very long. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance to people with great fortunes, Mr. Weston? You would be amazed at how my brother, Mr. Suckling, travels. You will hardly believe it, but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back again with four horses.”

“The trouble with the distance from Enscombe,” said Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand, has not been able to leave the sofa for a full week at a time. In Frank’s last letter, he said she complained of being too weak to enter her conservatory unless she had both his arm and his uncle’s.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"061bbb035c2643b8cf367c05","rewritten_text":"“I’m agreed. It’s the best idea. Just hold hands and swear we—” “Oh no, that won’t work for this. That’s fine for little trifling things—especially with girls, because they’ll go back on you and blab if they get mad—but there ought to be writing for something big like this. And blood.” Tom loved the idea. It felt deep, dark, and terrible; the time, the situation, and the surroundings matched it perfectly. He picked up a clean pine shingle in the moonlight, pulled a bit of red keel from his pocket, tilted it toward the moon, and slowly scratched out these lines, biting his tongue on each downstroke and easing up on the upstrokes. “Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about This and they hope they drop dead on the spot if they ever tell and rot.” Huckleberry admired Tom’s ease with writing and the grandeur of his words. He immediately pulled a pin from his lapel to prick his skin, but Tom stopped him. “Hold on! Don’t do that. A pin’s brass. It might have verdigris on it.” “What’s verdigris?” “It’s poison, that’s what. Just swallow some once—you’ll find out.” So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy pricked his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom managed to sign his initials, using the ball of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was done. They buried the shingle close to the wall with gloomy rituals and muttered spells, and the chains on their tongues were considered locked with the key thrown away. A figure crept quietly through a gap at the other end of the ruined building just then, but they didn’t see it. “Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this keep us from ever telling—always?” “Of course it does. No matter what happens, we have to stay quiet. We’d drop dead—you know that.” “Yes, I reckon so.” They kept whispering a while. Suddenly a dog let out a long, mournful howl just outside, barely ten feet away. The boys grabbed each other, shaking with fear. “Which of us is he after?” gasped Huckleberry. “I don’t know—look through the crack. Quick!” “No, you, Tom!” “I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"d922afe8acff1fdc7febc998","rewritten_text":"WHEN the wedding day arrived, about three weeks later, St. Peter’s filled to overflowing with a throng of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester read the service with great solemnity, and everyone declared they had never seen a more striking pair than bride and groom. Yet they were more than simply striking—they were content. Not once did Lord Arthur rue the trials he had endured for Sybil, while she, for her part, offered him the finest gifts a woman can bestow—adoration, gentleness, and affection. Reality had not shredded their romance. They always felt youthful.

Some years later, after two beautiful children were born to them, Lady Windermere came down to visit Alton Priory, that charming old estate the Duke had given his son as a wedding present; and one afternoon, as she sat beneath a lime-tree in the garden with Lady Arthur, watching the young boy and girl dart up and down the rose walk like flickering sunbeams, she suddenly clasped her hostess’s hand and asked, ‘Are you happy, Sybil?’

‘Dear Lady Windermere, naturally I am happy. Aren’t you?’

‘I have no time for happiness, Sybil. I invariably like the last person introduced to me; but generally, once I get to know people, they bore me.’

‘Don’t your lions amuse you, Lady Windermere?’

‘Oh heavens, no! lions are only entertaining for a single season. Once their manes are trimmed, they are the dullest creatures imaginable. Besides, they misbehave terribly if you treat them really well. Remember that dreadful Mr. Podgers? He turned out a complete fraud. Of course I didn’t mind that in the least, and even when he asked to borrow money I forgave him, but I could not tolerate his making love to me. He has quite soured me on cheiromancy. I am into telepathy now. Far more diverting.’

‘You mustn’t say a word against cheiromancy here, Lady Windermere; it is the only topic Arthur cannot abide being teased about. I assure you he takes it quite seriously.’

‘Surely he doesn’t actually believe in it, Sybil?’

‘Ask him yourself, Lady Windermere—here he comes,’ and Lord Arthur strolled up the garden carrying a huge bunch of yellow roses, the two children dancing about him.

‘Lord Arthur?’

‘Yes, Lady Windermere.’

‘You can’t truly believe in cheiromancy?’

‘Of course I do,’ replied the young man with a smile.

‘But why?’

‘Because I owe to it all the joy of my life,’ he murmured, dropping into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"917165bfdf4b132e28cc8917","rewritten_text":"“So now I’m the owner of a herd of knights,” said I as we rode away. “Who would have imagined I’d ever be listing assets of that variety? I won’t know what to do with them unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, an it please you, sir, and their squires.”

“A fine catch. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I understood thee not. That will I quickly tell.” Then she mused softly, tasting the words like they were sweetmeats: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; ay, even so; where do they hang out. Truly the phrase hath a fair and winsome savor, and is prettily turned. I will repeat it anon and anon in mine idlesse, so that of perchance I may learn it. Where do they hang out. Indeed! already it trippeth from my tongue, and because—”

“Don’t lose track of the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes; the knights, you remember. You were going to tell me about them. A bit ago, remember? Figuratively, the game’s started.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Step up to the plate. Meaning, set to your statistics and stop using up tinder before the blaze. Give me the lowdown on the knights.”

“I will, and gladly will begin. So they two departed and rode into a mighty forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

I knew I’d blundered the instant she began. I’d set her machinery running; that was on me. She’d be thirty days reaching the salient points. She generally launched without preface and ended without arriving anywhere. If you broke in she either ignored you and kept on, or mumbled a couple of words, then backed up and re-delivered the sentence. Interruptions only made matters worse; yet I had to interrupt—and often—to remain alive; a body would perish if he let her monotony drip over him all day long.

“Great Scott!” I groaned. She merely went back and started anew:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came unto an abbey of monks, and were well lodged. Then on the morn they heard their masses in the abbey, and so they rode forth till they entered a great forest; then Sir Gawaine espied in a valley by a turret twelve fair damsels, and two knights armed upon mighty steeds, and the maidens paced to and fro by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"abd280e1f1352dce788f83d3","rewritten_text":"“But,” I said, handing the slip back to him, “I’m still completely in the dark. Even if all the riches of Golconda were waiting for me as a reward, I’m certain I couldn’t earn them by solving this puzzle.”

“Yet,” said Legrand, “the solution isn’t nearly as difficult as you might think from first glancing at the symbols. These characters, as anyone could easily guess, form a cipher—that is, they carry a meaning. But from what we know of Kidd, I couldn’t imagine him capable of constructing one of the more complex cryptographs. I decided at once that this was a simple kind—one that would seem, to a sailor’s crude mind, utterly impossible without the key.”

“And you actually solved it?”

“Easily; I’ve solved others that were ten thousand times more complex. Circumstances, and a certain inclination of mind, have led me to take an interest in such riddles, and it’s questionable whether human ingenuity can devise a cipher that human ingenuity cannot, with proper effort, unravel. Once I had established connected, legible characters, I scarcely spared a thought for the difficulty of discovering their meaning.

“In this case—as in every case of secret writing—the first question concerns the language of the cipher, because the methods of solution, especially for the simpler types, depend on and vary with the nature of the language. Generally, there’s no option but to test (guided by probabilities) every language known to the solver until the right one appears. But with this cipher, the signature made everything easy. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ works in no language but English. If not for that clue, I would have begun with Spanish and French, as the languages most likely for a pirate of the Spanish Main to use for such a secret. As it was, I assumed the cipher was English.

“You’ll notice there are no spaces between the words. If there had been, the task would have been relatively easy. I would have started by comparing and analyzing the shorter words, and if a single-letter word had appeared, as would be likely (a or I, for example), I would have considered the solution certain. But with no separations, my first step was to identify the most common letters and the rarest ones.”"}

{"request_id":"5db4a4396cc3ac80173de858","rewritten_text":"Those dignified and frail old men were always seen bowing, and people believed that after bowing one customer out, they kept bowing in the empty office until they bowed another customer in.

The barrister shrewdly guessed that the banker would not speak so strongly without being morally certain. Though unprepared for the bitter truth he had to swallow, he managed it. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, wagging his courtroom forefinger at the Temple once he had done so, “my way out of this is to make all of you the ones in the wrong.”

It was a trick from an Old Bailey strategist, and it gave him great comfort. “You will not make me the one in the wrong, young lady,” said Mr. Stryver; “I’ll do that for you.”

So when Mr. Lorry visited that night as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, surrounded by books and papers deliberately scattered around him, seemed to have nothing on his mind less than the morning’s subject. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry and appeared absent and distracted.

“Well!” said the kindly envoy, after half an hour of useless attempts to bring him to the matter. “I have been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” repeated Mr. Stryver, coolly. “Oh, of course! What was I thinking of?”

“And I am sure,” said Mr. Lorry, “that our talk was correct. My opinion is confirmed, and I repeat my advice.”

“I assure you,” replied Mr. Stryver, very amiably, “that I’m sorry for it for your sake, and sorry for it for the poor father’s sake. I know it must always be painful for the family; let’s drop it.”

“I don’t follow you,” said Mr. Lorry.

“I expect not,” Stryver answered, nodding in a soothing and final way; “no matter, no matter.”

“But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted.

“No it doesn’t; I assure you it doesn’t. I assumed there was sense where there isn’t, and worthy ambition where there isn’t, and I’m relieved of my mistake, with no harm done. Young women have made similar foolish choices often before, and often paid for them in poverty and obscurity. From an unselfish view, I’m sorry it ended, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms; from a selfish view, I’m glad it ended, because it would have been bad for me in worldly terms—it hardly needs saying I could have gained nothing from it.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"42ce7ef7dd8d4c2da23c3873","rewritten_text":"Mrs. Otis, who, I should add, is no insignificant authority on Art—having enjoyed the privilege of several Boston winters during her girlhood—assures me these jewels have considerable monetary value and would command a high price if brought to market. Given that, Lord Canterville, I am certain you will understand how utterly impossible it would be for me to permit them to remain in any member of my household’s possession; in fact, such frivolous baubles, however fitting or even essential they may be for the dignity of the British nobility, would be utterly incongruous among those raised on the austere, and I believe enduring, doctrines of republican plainness. I ought perhaps to mention that Virginia is very keen you should allow her to keep the box as a keepsake of your unfortunate yet misdirected forebear. As it is exceedingly old and consequently somewhat shabby, you may feel inclined to grant her request. For my own part, I must admit it surprises me to find one of my children displaying any sympathy for medievalism in any shape, and I can only explain it by remembering that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a journey to Athens.\n\nLord Canterville listened very seriously to the worthy Minister’s discourse, occasionally tugging at his grey moustache to conceal an unbidden smile, and when Mr. Otis concluded, he grasped his hand warmly and said, “My dear sir, your delightful little daughter rendered my unfortunate ancestor, Sir Simon, an immense service, and my family and I owe her a great debt for her extraordinary courage and spirit. The jewels are plainly hers, and, by Jove, I dare say that if I were cruel enough to take them, the mischievous old knight would be up from his grave in a fortnight, giving me the very deuce of a time. As for calling them heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless the fact is recorded in a will or legal document, and these jewels’ existence has been entirely unknown. I assure you I have no greater claim to them than your butler, and when Miss Virginia matures I daresay she will enjoy having pretty adornments. Besides, you overlook, Mr. Otis, that you acquired the furniture and the ghost at a valuation, and anything belonging to the ghost passed immediately into your ownership, since, however lively Sir Simon may have been in the corridor at night, legally he was quite dead, and you bought his property outright.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"6de2b089740811ad5bbbeb73","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?” Oliver asked. “Hush!” the Dodger whispered. “Do you see that old fellow at the bookstall?” “The gentleman across the way?” Oliver answered. “I do.” “He’ll answer,” the Dodger said. “A first-rate plant,” added Master Charley Bates. Oliver glanced between them in sheer astonishment; but questions were out of the question, for the two boys slipped quietly across the street and crept up behind the old gentleman to whom they had pointed him. Oliver followed a few steps, unable to decide whether to go forward or back, and watched in silent wonder. The old gentleman looked thoroughly respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a velvet collar, white trousers, and tucked a neat bamboo cane beneath his arm. He had picked up a book at the stall and stood there reading with as much intentness as if seated in his own study armchair. Very likely he fancied himself so, for it was quite clear from his absorption that he noticed neither stall, street, boys, nor anything but the volume before him. He read straight on, turning a page when he reached the bottom, starting again at the top line, and proceeding with the utmost eagerness. Imagine Oliver’s horror as he lingered a few steps away, eyes stretched as wide as they could open, to see the Dodger slip a hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! To see him pass it to Charley Bates, and then watch both boys dart around the corner at full speed! In a flash, the entire mystery of the handkerchiefs, watches, jewels, and the Jew burst upon the boy’s mind. For a moment he stood, terror making his blood tingle as if he burned; then, dazed and frightened, he ran, scarcely aware of what he was doing, flying as fast as his legs would carry him. All this happened within a minute. The very instant Oliver started, the old gentleman felt for his pocket, missed his handkerchief, and spun around. Catching sight of the boy tearing away, he naturally assumed he was the thief; shouting “Stop thief!” with all his strength, he set off after him, book in hand."}

content.text: {"request_id":"03c373a0effa762e7308878e","rewritten_text":"He had not in the least suspected the sway he possessed. He followed her into the shrubbery without any intention of exerting it. His only object, in his worried desire to observe how she met Frank Churchill’s engagement, was to be at hand, should she permit, to comfort or advise her. All that followed sprang from the instant, the direct response of his feelings to what he heard. The exquisite assurance that she was wholly indifferent to Frank Churchill, that her heart lay entirely free of him, had birthed a hope that, eventually, he might win her own affection; but it was no immediate hope—only a momentary yielding of eagerness over prudence, craving merely to be told she did not forbid his efforts to gain her. The loftier hopes so gradually revealed were all the more entrancing. The love he had wished to be allowed to create, if he were able, was already his! In the course of half an hour, he had moved from utter distress to something so near perfect felicity that no other term would fit.\n\nHer transformation matched his. This same half-hour had given each the priceless certainty of being cherished, stripping away, for both, the same measure of ignorance, jealousy, or mistrust. On his side, jealousy had long been present, dating back to the arrival—or even the anticipated arrival—of Frank Churchill. He had loved Emma and envied Frank Churchill from nearly the same moment, one feeling perhaps revealing the other. Jealousy of Frank Churchill had drawn him from the neighbourhood. The Box Hill expedition had fixed his resolve to depart. He would spare himself the sight of such authorized, encouraged attentions again. He had gone to learn indifference. Yet he chose badly. His brother’s home contained too much domestic bliss; woman there showed too attractive a form; Isabella resembled Emma too strongly—differing only by those marked inferiorities that continually set Emma’s brilliance before him—for much progress to be possible, even had he stayed longer. Nevertheless, he remained resolutely, day after day, until this very morning’s post brought Jane Fairfax’s story. Then, filled with the gladness he could not help feeling—never having thought Frank Churchill worthy of Emma—there arose so much tender concern, so much urgent anxiety for her, that he could stay away no more. He rode home through the rain, and walked up immediately after dinner to learn how this dearest and best of all beings, perfect despite all her imperfections, sustained the revelation."}

{"request_id":"5590c20000adcd5f5158c366","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how mysterious they were! The soul had its own animal nature, and the body sometimes felt spiritual. The senses could become refined, and the intellect could sink low. Who could say where bodily impulse ended or the mental began? The neat definitions from ordinary psychologists felt shallow. Yet how hard it was to choose between the different schools of thought! Was the soul a shadow sitting inside the house of sin? Or was the body contained within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Separating spirit from matter was a mystery, and so was their union.

He wondered if psychology could ever become a precise enough science to reveal each small spring of life. As things stood, we always misunderstood ourselves and rarely understood others. Experience had no moral value. It was merely the name men gave to their mistakes. Moralists usually treated experience as a warning, claimed it had ethical power in shaping character, and praised it for teaching us what to follow and what to avoid. But experience held no motivating force. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly showed was that our future would mirror our past, and that the sin we once committed with disgust we would commit many times with delight.

To him, the experimental method was clearly the only way to reach any scientific understanding of the passions. Dorian Gray was a subject ready to hand and seemed likely to yield rich and fruitful results. His sudden, wild love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon worth studying. Curiosity surely played a large role in it, along with the desire for new experiences, yet it was not simple but a complex passion. Whatever boys’ crude sense-desire lay in it had been transformed by the imagination into something that seemed to the young man far removed from the senses, and for that very reason it became more dangerous. It was always the passions whose origins we lied about that ruled us most. Our weakest motives were the ones we knew and admitted to ourselves. Often when we thought we were experimenting on others, we were really experimenting on ourselves.

While Lord Henry sat lost in these thoughts, a knock sounded at the door, and his valet came in to remind him it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"f8c491b5132d4cbd9df7e91d","rewritten_text":"At noon on Saturday I strolled to the well and watched for a bit. Merlin was still burning smoke powders, flailing the air, and mumbling nonsense as fiercely as ever, though he seemed rather crestfallen, for he hadn’t coaxed a single bead of sweat from that well yet. At last I asked, “How does it look now, partner?”

“Behold, I am even now engaged upon the mightiest enchantment known to the princes of the occult arts in the Eastern lands; if this fail me, nothing can serve. Hold thy peace until I am done.”

This time he raised a smoke that blacked out the entire landscape, surely making life miserable for the hermits, for the wind was blowing their way and rolling over their dens in a thick, heaving fog. He poured forth torrents of speech to match, contorted himself, and slashed the air with his hands in astounding fashion. After twenty minutes he sank down panting, about spent. Then came the abbot with several hundred monks and nuns, and behind them a throng of pilgrims and a couple of acres of foundlings, all drawn by the immense smoke and all wildly excited. The abbot anxiously asked for the results. Merlin replied:

“If any labor of mortal strength could break the spell upon these waters, this last assay had wrought it. It has failed; from which I do now know that what I feared is truth established; the proof of this failure is that the most potent spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name none may utter and live, has cast his charm upon this well. No mortal breathes, nor ever shall, who can pierce the secret of that spell, and without that secret none may shatter it. The water will never flow again, good Father. I have done what man might. Let me depart.”

Naturally this threw the abbot into no small dismay. He turned to me with alarm written on his face and said, “Ye have heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all, then—pray, not all! Which part holds?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has laid a spell on the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we are undone!”

“Possibly.”

“But not surely? Ye mean, not surely?”

“That’s it.”

“Wherefore ye would say that when he declares none can break the spell—”

“Yes, when he says that, he says what is not necessarily so. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might stand some chance—some small, some trifling chance—of success.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"4ade73d1b542203283d6609c","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?” Oliver asked. “Quiet!” whispered the Dodger. “See that old fellow at the bookstall?” “The gentleman across the way?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.” “He’ll do,” the Dodger said. “A perfect setup,” added Master Charley Bates. Oliver stared at them in shock, but he had no chance to ask questions. The two boys slipped across the street, creeping close behind the old gentleman who had caught their attention. Oliver followed a few steps, unsure whether to approach or retreat, and gazed on in silent wonder. The old gentleman looked very respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, white trousers, and carried a neat bamboo cane under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood there reading as earnestly as if he were in his own study. He might well have imagined himself at home, for his focus was such that he noticed neither the stall, the street, nor the boys. He read straight through, turning a page when he finished a line and starting the next, absorbed with lively interest. Oliver watched from a few steps away, horror widening his eyes, as the Dodger slipped a hand into the gentleman’s pocket and pulled out a handkerchief. He saw him hand it to Charley Bates, and then both boys bolted around the corner at full speed. In a flash, the whole mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew came to the boy’s mind. He stood there for a heartbeat, his blood burning through his veins with terror, then, confused and scared, he ran as fast as his legs could carry him. All this happened in a minute. As soon as Oliver began to run, the old gentleman felt in his pocket, missed his handkerchief, and spun around. Seeing Oliver speeding off, he naturally assumed the boy was the thief, and, shouting “Stop thief!” with all his strength, chased after him, book still in hand."}

{"request_id":"603322dccb3c71c33db78848","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

Still no answer.

“What’s happened to that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!”

Silence.

The old lady pulled her spectacles down to look over them around the room. Then she pushed them back up and peered under them. She almost never looked through them for small things like the boy; they were her fancy pair, the pride of her heart, meant for show, not practical use—she could see just as well through a pair of stove lids. She looked puzzled for a moment and then said, not exactly furious, but loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well, I swear, if I catch you I’ll—”

She did not finish, because she was already bending down and poking under the bed with the broom, and she needed her breath for that. She dragged out nothing but the cat.

“I never did see the beat of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood there, and looked out at the tomato vines and jimpson weeds that made up the garden. No Tom. So she lifted her voice at an angle made for distance and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u, TOM!”

A slight noise sounded behind her and she turned just in time to grab a small boy by the back of his jacket and stop his escape.

“There! I might have thought of that closet. What were you doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that stuff?”

“I don’t know, aunt.”

“Well, I know. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve said if you didn’t leave that jam alone I’d skin you. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hovered in the air—the danger was serious—

“My! Look behind you, aunt!”

The old lady spun around and snatched her skirts out of harm’s way. The boy took off instantly, scrambled up the high board fence, and disappeared over it.

His aunt Polly stood surprised for a moment, then broke into a gentle laugh.

“Hang the boy, can’t I ever learn anything? Hasn’t he played enough tricks on me for me to be watching for them by now? But old fools are the biggest fools. Can’t teach an old dog new tricks, so they say. But goodness me, he never plays the same trick two days in a row, so how’s anyone supposed to know what’s coming? He seems to know just how long he can tease me before I lose my temper, and he knows if he can stall me for a minute or make me laugh, it’s all over and I can’t hit him a lick.”"}

{"request_id":"d4f19b5aa7f7f246cd2f39a0","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know me unless you read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. Mr. Mark Twain made that book, and he mostly told the truth. Sometimes he stretched things, but mostly it was true. That’s nothing. I never saw anyone who didn’t lie now and then, except maybe Aunt Polly, the widow, or Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly—Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all in that book, which is mostly true, with some stretches, like I said.

Here’s how that book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers hid in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars each—all gold. It was a heap of money when it was piled up. Judge Thatcher took it and put it out at interest, and it brought us a dollar a day each all year long—more than anyone could figure what to do with. Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me; but it was hard living in her house, with how steady and proper she was in everything. When I couldn’t take it anymore, I ran off. I got back into my old rags and my sugar-hogshead and felt free and happy. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was starting a band of robbers, and I could join if I would go back to the widow and be respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, along with a bunch of other names, though she didn’t mean any harm. She put me in those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and feel squeezed in. Then the old routine started up again. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to show up on time. At the table you couldn’t start eating right away; you had to wait for the widow to bow her head and mutter over the food, even though nothing was wrong with it—except that everything was cooked separate. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different; things mix up, share their juices, and taste better.

After supper she brought out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was eager to know all about him; but after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead a long time. Then I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t pay attention to dead folks."}

{"request_id":"cf6a0220523289f0d67a39b7","rewritten_text":"Indeed, he had arrayed himself as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” one of his most notable portrayals, and one the Cantervilles remembered only too well, for it truly sparked their feud with their neighbour, Lord Rufford. It was about quarter past two in the morning, and, so far as he could tell, the household slumbered. Yet as he sauntered toward the library to examine whether any vestige of the bloodstain remained, two figures suddenly sprang from a shadowy nook, flung their arms frantically above their heads, and screeched “BOO!” right in his ear.

Gripped by a panic quite excusable under such conditions, he bolted for the staircase, only to find Washington Otis stationed there with the large garden syringe; thus trapped by foes on every side and nearly brought to bay, he fled into the vast iron stove, which, luckily for him, lay unlit, and had to crawl home through flues and chimneys, reaching his own room in a dreadful state of grime, disorder, and despair.

After that night he ventured on no further nocturnal raids. The twins lay in ambush for him more than once and scattered the corridors with nutshells nightly, much to the irritation of their parents and the servants, but their efforts proved futile. Plainly his feelings were so hurt he refused to show himself. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his great treatise on the history of the Democratic Party, which had occupied him for years; Mrs. Otis arranged a splendid clam-bake that astonished the entire county; the boys devoted themselves to lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other national American pastimes; while Virginia rode the lanes on her pony, with the young Duke of Cheshire—who was spending the last week of his holidays at Canterville Chase—at her side. People generally concluded the ghost had departed, and Mr. Otis even wrote as much to Lord Canterville, who replied with delight at the tidings and sent his warmest compliments to the Minister’s estimable wife.

The Otis family, however, was mistaken, for the ghost still haunted the place and, though now nearly an invalid, had no intention of letting things end there, especially after learning that the young Duke of Cheshire was among the guests. The Duke’s great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost, and was discovered next morning sprawled on the card-room floor in such a powerless paralytic condition that, though he lived to advanced years, he could utter nothing ever again but “Double Sixes.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1fe7c34d60c2455cd4bd0b02","rewritten_text":"Soon his voice floated down in a kind of halloo.  “How much farther do I need to go?”  “How high are you?” asked Legrand.  “Ever so far,” the Black man replied. “I can see the sky through the top of the tree.”  “Forget the sky. Listen to me. Look down the trunk and count the branches below you on this side. How many have you passed?”  “One, two, three, four, five—I just passed five big branches on this side, sir.”  “Then climb one branch higher.”  A few minutes later the voice called out again, saying he had reached the seventh branch.  “Now, Jup,” Legrand shouted, clearly agitated, “work your way along that branch as far as you can. If you notice anything unusual, tell me.” At that point any lingering doubt I had about my poor friend’s sanity vanished. I had no choice but to conclude he had lost his mind, and I grew seriously concerned about getting him home. While I was debating what to do, Jupiter’s voice rang out again.  “Almost afraid to go much farther on this branch—it’s dead almost all the way.”  “Did you say it was a dead branch, Jupiter?” cried Legrand, his voice shaking.  “Yes, sir, dead as a doornail—done for sure—gone from this world.”  “What on earth am I to do?” asked Legrand, sounding utterly distraught.  “Do?” I said, glad for a chance to cut in. “Why, come home and go to bed. Come now! Be sensible. It’s getting late, and remember your promise.”  “Jupiter,” he shouted, ignoring me entirely, “do you hear me?”  “Yes, Master Will, hear you perfectly well.”  “Test the wood with your knife and see if it’s very rotten.”  “It’s rotten, sir, sure enough,” the man replied after a moment, “but not as rotten as it could be. I could risk going a little farther on the branch by myself, that’s true.”  “By yourself! What do you mean?”  “I mean the bug. It’s really heavy. Suppose I drop it first, then the branch won’t break with just the weight of one Black man.”  “You infernal scoundrel!” Legrand shouted, visibly relieved. “What do you mean by saying such nonsense? If you drop that beetle, I’ll wring your neck. Now listen, Jupiter—do you hear me?”  “Yes, sir, no need to shout at a poor Black man like that.”  “Good. Now pay attention. If you crawl out on that branch as far as you think is safe and don’t let go of the beetle, I’ll give you a silver dollar the moment you get down.”"}

{"request_id":"f95acf3e3cf52246fae8ad02","rewritten_text":"“I must leave, ignorant of what awaits me; yet I shall either return here or catch up with your party the instant I am able. A single word or glance will suffice to settle whether I enter your father’s house tonight or never again.”

It was not the sort of letter to recover from quickly. Half an hour alone to think might have calmed her, but the mere ten minutes that elapsed before she was disturbed, coupled with all the constraints of her circumstances, did nothing for her composure. Each moment seemed only to heighten the tumult. It was joy too intense to bear. And while she was still in the first rush of feeling, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta entered together.

The sheer obligation to appear her usual self prompted an immediate effort, yet after a time she could manage no more. The conversation passed her by completely; she could not follow a word and was forced to plead illness and withdraw. They immediately noticed how unwell she looked, were appalled and full of concern, and insisted they would not budge without her for anything. This was dreadful. If only they had departed and left her to the quiet of that room, it would have soothed her; but to have them all clustered around her in anxious attendance was maddening, and in desperation she declared she would return home.

“By all means, my dear,” exclaimed Mrs. Musgrove, “go straight home and take care, so you may be ready for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to tend you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

Yet the chair was out of the question. Worse than anything! To sacrifice the least chance of exchanging two words with Captain Wentworth during her quiet, solitary walk through town (and she felt almost sure she would meet him) was impossible. She vehemently opposed the chair, and Mrs. Musgrove, who considered only a single type of ailment, having anxiously assured herself there had been no fall involved; that Anne had not recently slipped and struck her head; that she was thoroughly certain no fall had occurred; could then let her go with a relieved heart, relying on finding her improved by evening.

Resolute not to overlook any precaution, Anne exerted herself and said—

“I fear, ma’am, that everything is not entirely settled. Please be so kind as to inform the other gentlemen that we expect your whole party tonight. I am afraid there may have been some misapprehension; and I especially wish you to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh! my dear, it is perfectly clear, I give you my word.”"}

{"request_id":"3d5929a02098d8574e7bbce1","rewritten_text":"“This marriage is exactly as it ought to be. I did not believe it in the beginning, yet now I concede it. For you the gods fashioned Sibyl Vane. Without her you would have been unfinished.”

“Thank you, Basil,” Dorian Gray replied, clasping his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical; he frightens me. But here comes the orchestra. It is dreadful, though it goes on only five minutes. Once the curtain goes up, you will behold the girl to whom I mean to give my entire life, to whom I have already surrendered whatever good is within me.”

Fifteen minutes later, amid a storm of applause, Sibyl Vane came onto the stage. She was indeed beautiful to behold—one of the most exquisite beings Lord Henry thought he had ever encountered. Something of a fawn lingered in her timid grace and startled gaze. A delicate flush, like the reflection of a rose in silver, touched her cheeks as she looked at the packed, eager audience. She retreated a step or two; her lips seemed to quiver. Basil Hallward sprang up and began clapping. Dorian Gray sat motionless, as if dreaming, fixed upon her. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, whispering, “Charming! charming!”

The setting was the hall of Capulet’s home; Romeo, in his pilgrim’s attire, had arrived with Mercutio and the rest. The orchestra, scant as it was, played a few bars, and the dance commenced. Amid a throng of awkward, poorly attired performers, Sibyl Vane moved like a being from some finer realm. As she danced, her body swayed like a water plant. The curves of her throat were those of a white lily. Her hands appeared wrought of cool ivory.

Still, she was strangely apathetic. No happiness appeared when her eyes fell upon Romeo. The few lines allotted to her—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

with the short exchange that followed, she delivered in a wholly artificial style. The voice remained exquisite, yet its tone rang entirely false. The colouring was wrong. It drained the verse of vitality. It rendered the passion unreal.

Dorian Gray turned pale as he followed her. He was both bewildered and uneasy. Neither friend dared speak to him. To them she appeared completely inept."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a0cac1f9cbca198122cb4663","rewritten_text":"April 7th. I rose early and, to my great joy, finally saw what could only be the northern Pole itself. There was no doubt about it. It lay directly below me; yet I had climbed so high that nothing could be seen clearly. From the progress recorded in my altitude numbers between six in the morning on April second and twenty minutes to nine that same day (when the barometer fell), it could be reasonably inferred that, at four in the morning of April seventh, the balloon had reached a height of no less than 7,254 miles above the sea. This elevation may seem immense, but the calculations I used probably produced a figure far below the truth. In any case I unquestionably saw the earth’s whole major diameter; the entire northern hemisphere spread beneath me like a flat map, and the equator formed the horizon around me. Your Excellencies may readily imagine that the narrow tracts within the Arctic circle, though directly beneath me and therefore not foreshortened, were still too small and too distant from my viewpoint to allow very precise study. Still, what I could make out was striking and unusual. Northward from that vast rim already mentioned—the practical limit of human discovery in these regions—stretched an unbroken, or nearly unbroken, sheet of ice. In the first few degrees of its extent the surface was fairly flat, farther on it settled into a plane, and finally, becoming noticeably concave, it ended at the Pole in a circular center, sharply defined, whose apparent diameter subtended an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its dusky color, shifting in intensity, was always darker than any other spot on the visible hemisphere, at times deepening into the blackest and most impenetrable shade. Beyond this little could be learned. By noon the circular center had shrunk considerably, and by seven in the evening I lost sight of it entirely, the balloon crossing the western edge of the ice and racing off toward the equator.\n\nApril 8th. I noticed a clear decrease in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a marked change in its general color and appearance."}

{"request_id":"c0b591b4fe79f7abdd19c3ee","rewritten_text":"I call on you, spirits of the dead, and you wandering agents of vengeance, to help and guide me in what I must do. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink deep of agony; let him feel the despair that torments me now. 

I began my invocation with such solemnity and awe that I almost believed the shades of my murdered friends heard me and approved my devotion, but fury seized me by the end, and rage choked my voice. 

Through the stillness of night, a loud and demonic laugh answered me. It rang in my ears long and heavy; the mountains echoed it, and I felt as if all of hell surrounded me with mockery and laughter. Surely in that moment I would have gone mad and ended my miserable life, except that my vow had been heard and I was meant for vengeance. The laughter died away, and then a familiar, hateful voice, seemingly right at my ear, whispered audibly, “I’m satisfied, miserable wretch! You’ve chosen to live, and I’m satisfied.” 

I lunged toward the spot where the sound came from, but the fiend escaped my grasp. Suddenly the broad disk of the moon rose and lit up his ghastly, twisted figure as he fled with more-than-human speed. 

I chased him, and for many months this has been my sole task. Guided by a faint clue, I followed the twists of the Rhône in vain. The blue Mediterranean appeared, and by strange chance I saw the fiend slip aboard a vessel bound for the Black Sea under cover of night. I booked a berth on the same ship, but he slipped away—I still have no idea how. 

Through the wilds of Tartary and Russia, even though he always slipped away, I never stopped tracking him. Sometimes peasants, terrified by this horrific apparition, showed me the direction he took; sometimes he himself, afraid that if I lost his trail I would give up and die, left signs to guide me. Snow fell on my head, and I saw the imprint of his huge footsteps in the white plain. You who are just starting life, to whom care is new and agony unknown, how could you understand what I have felt and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my torments; some devil’s curse clung to me, and I carried my own eternal hell. Yet a benevolent spirit still followed me, guiding my steps, and when I complained the most it suddenly pulled me out of obstacles that seemed impossible. Sometimes, when nature, overwhelmed by hunger, nearly collapsed, a meal appeared for me in the wilderness that restored my strength and courage."}

{"request_id":"a90a73ed6ef272fcbf74475c","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to ease your mind a good deal. But what gave you that shock? What were you expecting we’d turned up?”

Huck was in a tight corner—the questioning eye fixed on him—he would have bartered anything for a believable answer—nothing came—those probing eyes drove deeper and deeper—a foolish reply presented itself—there was no time to weigh it, so he tried it—weakly:

“Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Poor Huck was too miserable to grin, while the old man roared with delight, shaking every joint in his frame, and concluded by remarking that a laugh like that was cash in a man’s pocket since it cut a doctor’s bill down like everything. Then he went on:

“Poor old fellow, you’re pale and overdone—you’re not well at all—no wonder you’re a bit light-headed and off balance. But you’ll pull through. Rest and sleep will bring you round all right, I’m hoping.”

Huck smarted to think he had been such a fool and shown such a suspicious excitement, for he had abandoned the notion that the bundle from the tavern contained the treasure as soon as he’d overheard the talk at the widow’s stile. He had only supposed it wasn’t the treasure—he hadn’t known—and so the revelation of a captured parcel upset his self-control. Still, he was glad the fuss had taken place, since now he knew beyond doubt that this bundle wasn’t the bundle, and his mind was at ease and remarkably comfortable. In truth, everything seemed to be moving exactly as they wanted now; the treasure had to be still in No. 2, the men would be seized and locked up that day, and he and Tom could secure the gold that night without effort or any fear of interference.

They had barely finished breakfast when there was a knock at the door. Huck darted for a hiding spot, unwilling to be tied even in rumor to the previous night’s affair. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, the Widow Douglas among them, and noticed clusters of townsfolk climbing the hill to stare at the stile. So the story had got around. The Welshman had to recount the night’s events to the visitors. The widow voiced her gratitude for being saved.

“Don’t mention it, madam. There’s someone you owe more to than to me and my lads, likely, but he won’t let me speak his name. We’d never have been there except for him.”"}

{"request_id":"b2bb3719045233fb15e52d0b","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams to fade like this? Our name had been written “a little lower than the angels,” yet we proved no better than mayflies. We had called ourselves the “paragon of animals,” and lo, we were a “quintessence of dust.” We complained that the pyramids still stood while the embalmed body of their builder decayed. Alas, even the shepherd’s straw hut we passed on the road held more promise of longevity than the whole human race. How could we reconcile this dismal change with our past hopes and apparent powers?

Suddenly an inner voice, clear and articulate, seemed to say: Thus from eternity it was decreed; the steeds that carry Time forward had this hour and this end chained to them from the moment the void produced its burden. Would you try to read backwards the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Servant of the Omnipotent! eternal, changeless Necessity! You sit with tireless fingers weaving the indissoluble chain of events—I will not complain of your acts. If my human mind cannot accept that all that exists is right, still, since what is must be, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly we were not born to enjoy, but to submit and to hope.

Will the reader grow tired if I describe in detail our long journey from Paris to Geneva? If, day by day, I were to record in journal form the pressing miseries of our lot, could my hand write, or language provide words, equal to the variety of our woe, the crowding of one lamentable event upon another? Have patience, reader! Whoever you are, wherever you live, whether of a spiritual race or descended from some surviving pair, your nature will be human, your home the earth; here you will read of the acts of the extinct race and ask in wonder if those who suffered what you find recorded were made of frail flesh and soft bodies like yourself. Indeed they were—weep, then; for surely, solitary being, you will be tender-hearted. Shed compassionate tears; yet listen carefully to the tale, and learn the deeds and sufferings of your predecessors.

Still, the last events that marked our progress through France were so full of strange horror and heavy misery that I dare not linger over them. If I dissected each incident, every moment would contain a harrowing tale whose smallest detail would chill your young blood. It is right that I raise, for your instruction, this memorial to the lost race; but not that I drag you through the wards of a hospital, nor the hidden chambers of the charnel house."}

{"request_id":"3b24cb3281e04bceb0fe87c3","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret lowering herself to visit the Coles. The trip gave her plenty of pleasant thoughts the next day, and whatever she might have sacrificed in dignified solitude was more than compensated by the glow of popularity. She must have delighted the Coles—good people who deserved to be made happy—and left a reputation that would linger for a long time.

Perfect happiness, even in memory, is rare, and there were two points that still bothered her. She wondered whether she had betrayed one woman’s duty to another by sharing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings with Frank Churchill. It had hardly been right, but the idea had taken hold of her so strongly that it slipped out, and his readiness to accept everything she told him felt like a compliment to her insight—one that made it hard to be sure she should have kept quiet.

Her other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and in that she had no doubts. She sincerely and unquestionably lamented that her own playing and singing were inferior. She deeply regretted the idle hours of her childhood—and sat down to practice with determination for an hour and a half.

She was interrupted when Harriet arrived; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, she might have been comforted quickly.

“Oh! If only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t lump us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than a lamp is like sunlight.”

“Oh dear—I think you play better than she does. I’m sure I prefer hearing you. Everyone last night said how beautifully you played.”

“Anyone who knew anything about it must have felt the difference. The truth is, Harriet, my playing is just good enough to earn praise, but Jane Fairfax’s is far beyond it.”

“Well, I will always think you play just as well as she does, or that if there is any difference, nobody would notice it. Mr. Cole said you had excellent taste, and Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about your taste, saying he valued taste more than technique.”

“Ah! But Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw she had technique, but I didn’t know she had any taste. Nobody mentioned it. And I hate Italian singing—there’s no understanding a word. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know it’s only what she’s obliged to do, since she’ll have to teach.”"}

{"request_id":"11638e07d61441cb89ba3320","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke warmly of his sister’s skill.

“I am delighted to hear such a favourable report of her,” said Lady Catherine. “Pray tell her from me that she must not expect to excel unless she practises continually.”

“I assure you, madam,” he answered, “that she does not require that counsel. She practises habitually.”

“So much the better. One cannot practise too much; and when I next write to her, I shall insist upon her never neglecting it. I often remind young ladies that no proficiency in music can be acquired without steady diligence. I have repeatedly told Miss Bennet she will never play truly well unless she exercises more; and though Mrs. Collins has no instrument of her own, she is perfectly welcome—as I have frequently assured her—to come daily to Rosings and play the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She would inconvenience no one in that quarter of the house.”

Mr. Darcy looked slightly mortified by his aunt’s want of manners, and held his peace.

When the coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam recalled Elizabeth’s promise to play for him, and she immediately took her seat at the instrument. He drew a chair close beside her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then resumed talking to her other nephew, until he walked away and, moving with his customary deliberateness toward the pianoforte, placed himself where he could fully observe the lovely performer’s face. Elizabeth noticed his design, and at the first convenient pause turned toward him with a mischievous smile, saying—

“You intend to awe me, Mr. Darcy, by approaching with such solemnity to hear me. But I shall not be intimidated, even though your sister plays so admirably. There is a stubborn spirit in me that cannot endure being frightened at another’s pleasure. My courage always mounts with every attempt to cow me.”

“I shall not tell you that you err,” he replied, “for you cannot seriously suppose I have any wish to alarm you; and I have known you long enough to understand that you take great delight in sometimes professing sentiments that are not, in truth, your own.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this sketch of herself, and turned to Colonel Fitzwilliam: “Your cousin is giving you a very pretty illustration of me, and teaching you never to believe a word I utter. I am particularly unfortunate in meeting someone so well qualified to expose my true character, in a neighbourhood where I hoped to pass with some slight degree of credit.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b74cbab85a0a850f549949a0","rewritten_text":"Back in my day, in my own country, this money came from tariffs, and the citizen liked to imagine the foreign importer paid it. That belief comforted him, though in truth the American people paid it, and the cost was so evenly spread that the yearly charge to a man worth a hundred million dollars and to a day laborer’s nursing infant was exactly the same—each paid six dollars. Nothing could be fairer than that, I guess. Now, Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, and all the British Islands together held fewer than a million people. A mechanic’s average wage was three cents a day when he supported himself. By that measure the national government’s expenses were ninety thousand dollars a year, or about two hundred fifty a day. So, by using nickels instead of gold on a king’s-evil day, I hurt no one, displeased no one, made everyone happy, and saved four-fifths of that day’s national expense besides—a saving equal to eight hundred thousand dollars in my America. When I made the change, I drew on wisdom from a very distant source—the wisdom of my boyhood—for a truly wise statesman never scorns any wisdom, no matter how humble its origin. In my boyhood I always saved my pennies and donated buttons to the foreign missionary cause. The buttons satisfied the ignorant native as well as the coin, the coin served me better than the buttons; everyone was pleased and nobody harmed.\n\nMarinel took the patients in order. He examined each applicant; if the person failed, he was turned away; if he passed, he went on to the king. A priest spoke the words, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king stroked the ulcers as the reading went on; at last the patient graduated, received his nickel—the king hung it around his neck himself—and was dismissed. Would you expect that to heal? It certainly did. Any ritual will heal if the patient’s faith in it is strong. Near Astolat there stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared, so a girl who herded geese there said, and they built the chapel on that spot and hung inside a picture showing the event—a picture you would think dangerous for a sick person to see. Yet thousands of the lame and sick came there, prayed before it every year, and left healthy and whole; even the well could gaze on it and live."}

There Mr. Otis asked the station-master if anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but he could learn nothing. The station-master sent messages up and down the line and promised to keep a close watch for her, and after Mr. Otis bought a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper closing his shop, he rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away that was said to be a regular haunt of the gypsies because of a large common nearby. They woke the village policeman but got no news from him, and after riding all over the common, they turned back home and reached the Chase around eleven o’clock, exhausted and almost heartbroken. They found Washington and the twins waiting for them at the gate-house with lanterns, as the avenue was very dark. Not a trace of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley Meadows, but she was not with them, and they explained their sudden departure by saying they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and had left in a rush so they wouldn’t be late. They were even distressed to hear of Virginia’s disappearance, as they were grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of them had stayed behind to help search. The carp pond had been dragged, and the entire Chase had been carefully checked, but nothing was discovered. It was clear that, for that night at least, Virginia was lost to them, and Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house in deep despair, the groom following with the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a cluster of frightened servants, and in the library poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa, almost maddened by fear and anxiety while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a sad meal, as hardly anyone spoke, and even the twins were awed and quiet, being devoted to their sister. When they were done, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleas, sent them all to bed, saying nothing more could be done that night and that he would telegraph Scotland Yard in the morning to send detectives at once."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d8214cdca750f6e9ad86d68d","rewritten_text":"He rose and left the room with my nurse, and in another moment my father stepped inside. Nothing could have pleased me more just then than his arrival. I reached out to him and cried, “Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?” My father soothed me with assurances of their safety and tried, by lingering on these subjects so dear to me, to lift my spirits. Yet he soon realized that a prison is no place for cheerfulness. “What sort of place is this where you’re living, my son?” he said, looking mournfully at the barred windows and the squalid room. “You set out to find happiness, but misfortune keeps hounding you. And poor Clerval—” The name of my unlucky, murdered friend was more than I could bear in my weakened state; I burst into tears. “Yes, Father,” I answered, “some terrible fate hangs over me, and I must live to see it through, or I would have died on Henry’s coffin.” We weren’t allowed to speak for long, since my fragile health meant every precaution was needed to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin came in and insisted that my strength mustn’t be drained by too much emotion. Yet my father’s presence was like that of a guardian angel, and gradually my health returned. As my illness faded, I was consumed by a bleak, suffocating melancholy that nothing could disperse. Clerval’s image hovered before me, pale and murdered. More than once the turmoil these thoughts stirred made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Why, in heaven’s name, did they keep such a wretched, hated life alive? Surely it was so I could fulfill my fate, which now seemed near its end. Soon, very soon, death would still these throbbings and free me from the crushing weight of suffering that drove me into the dust; and while carrying out justice’s sentence, I too would find rest. Then death still seemed distant, though I longed for it constantly, and I often sat motionless and speechless for hours, wishing for some great upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins. The assize season was approaching. I had already spent three months in prison, and though still weak and in constant danger of relapsing, I was forced to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court convened. Mr. Kirwin took it upon himself to gather witnesses and organize my defense."}

{"request_id":"9df9b85add5fa7ac6a249ca8","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse—handsome, clever, and rich, with a comfortable home and cheerful nature—seemed to possess some of life’s best gifts, and had spent nearly twenty-one years with very little to trouble or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a loving, indulgent father, and because her sister married early, Emma had been mistress of the house from a young age. Her mother had died so long ago that Emma could only faintly remember her affection; in her place stood an excellent governess who had given her nearly a mother’s devotion.

Miss Taylor had lived with Mr. Woodhouse’s family for sixteen years, serving more as a friend than a governess. She loved both daughters, though she had a special fondness for Emma. Between them, the bond was more like that of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor stopped holding the title of governess, her gentle nature had kept her from imposing any restraint; and now that any hint of authority was long gone, they lived together as dear friends, mutually attached, with Emma doing just what she pleased. She respected Miss Taylor’s judgment, yet still followed her own will.

The real drawbacks of Emma’s situation were the ability to have rather too much her own way and a tendency to think too highly of herself. These were the only flaws threatening to tarnish her many pleasures. The danger went so unnoticed that she never counted them as misfortunes.

Sorrow did come—gentle sorrow—but not through any unpleasant realization. Miss Taylor married. That loss brought Emma her first real grief. On the day of her beloved friend’s wedding, Emma sat longer than ever before in somber thought. Once the ceremony ended and the newlyweds departed, her father and she were left to dine alone, with no third friend to brighten the long evening. After dinner, her father settled into his usual nap, and Emma had only her thoughts and the sense of what she had lost.

Everything about the event promised happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of impeccable character, comfortable fortune, suitable age, and agreeable manners. Emma found some comfort in recalling how selflessly and generously she had encouraged the match. Still, it felt like a dark day for her. She knew she would feel Miss Taylor’s absence every hour of every day. She remembered the kindness of sixteen years—the lessons and games since Emma was five, the unflagging dedication to keeping her attached and entertained when well, and the tender care through every childhood illness."}

{"request_id":"d58056f15867ef016cc18c5b","rewritten_text":"“On that point, then, I will remain entirely silent; and you may be sure that once we are married, I will never utter an ungenerous reproach.”

She had to interrupt him immediately.

“You are too quick, sir,” she exclaimed. “You forget that I have not answered. Let me do so without further delay. Thank you for the compliment you pay me. I understand the honor of your proposal, but I cannot do anything except decline it.”

“I am already aware,” Mr. Collins replied with a formal wave of his hand, “that it is customary for young women to reject the offers of the man they secretly mean to accept when he first asks for their favor, and that sometimes they refuse a second or even a third time. Therefore, I am not at all discouraged by what you have just said, and I hope to lead you to the altar before long.”

“Honestly, sir,” Elizabeth cried, “your hope is extraordinary after what I have stated. I assure you I am not one of those young women—if such women really exist—who are bold enough to gamble their happiness on being asked again. I am completely serious in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am sure I am the last woman in the world who could make you so. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am convinced she would find me entirely unfit for the role.”

“If it were certain Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins very gravely, “but I cannot imagine her Ladyship would disapprove of you. You may be certain that when I have the honor of seeing her again, I will speak most highly of your modesty, thrift, and other admirable qualities.”

“Really, Mr. Collins, any praise of me will be unnecessary. Allow me to judge for myself, and pay me the compliment of believing what I say. I wish you very much happiness and prosperity, and by refusing your hand, I do everything I can to keep you from being otherwise. In making the offer, you have satisfied your conscience regarding my family, and may take possession of the Longbourn estate when it passes to you without any self-reproach. Therefore, this matter may be considered completely settled.” Rising as she spoke, she would have left the room if Mr. Collins had not addressed her again—

“When I have the honor of speaking to you next on the subject, I shall hope for a more favorable reply than the one you have just given me; though I am far from accusing you of cruelty, because I know it is the established custom among women to turn down a man at his first application, and perhaps you have already said as much to encourage my suit as would be consistent with the true delicacy of your sex.”"}

{"request_id":"986a0fc165f0482f8a8dbc56","rewritten_text":"Country folk, butchers, drovers, hawkers, urchins, thieves, loungers, and vagabonds of every shabby order were jumbled in one heap; the drovers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and flung about, sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squealed, hawkers cried their wares, and shouts, oaths, and squabbles rose on every side; bells clanged and voices roared from every public-house; the jostling, shoving, driving, beating, whooping, and yelling; the hideous, jarring din reverberating from every corner of the market; and the grimy, unshaven, ragged wretches constantly running here and there, bursting in and out of the press, made it a deafening, bewildering scene that utterly confounded the senses.

Mr. Sikes, towing Oliver after him, forced a passage through the densest portion of the crowd and paid scant heed to the endless sights and sounds that so amazed the child. He nodded once or twice to a passing acquaintance, and, fending off as many invitations for a morning dram, pushed straight onward until they escaped the tumult, and, threading Hosier Lane, came out into Holborn.

“Now, young ’un!” cried Sikes, glancing up at St. Andrew’s clock, “close upon seven! step lively. Come, don’t be lagging already, Lazy-legs!”

With these words he gave his small companion’s wrist a jerk; Oliver, breaking into a half-run somewhere between a brisk walk and a trot, contrived to keep pace with the burglar’s rapid stride as best he might.

They kept on at this gait until Hyde Park Corner lay behind them and they were bound for Kensington; then Sikes slackened until an empty cart, some way in the rear, drew level. Spying “Hounslow” painted upon it, he asked the driver, with such politeness as he could muster, to carry them as far as Isleworth.

“Climb up,” said the fellow. “That your lad?”

“Ay; he’s mine,” answered Sikes, fixing Oliver with a hard stare and slipping his hand, as if unconsciously, into the pocket where the pistol lay.

“Your father steps rather smartly for you, eh, youngster?” the driver remarked, noting Oliver’s breathless state.

“Not a whit,” said Sikes, cutting in. “He’s used to it. Here, grip my hand, Ned. Up you go!”

So saying, he boosted Oliver into the cart; and the driver, pointing to a pile of sacks, bade him lie there and rest himself.

As milestone after milestone slid by, Oliver’s wonder grew at the destination his companion had in mind. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, Brentford were all left behind; yet they rolled on as steadily as though the journey had barely begun."}

{"request_id":"92dbe83d0752048131f9f912","rewritten_text":"“But,” I said as I handed the slip back to him, “I am just as confused as before. Even if the jewels of Golconda waited for me as a reward, I’m sure I couldn’t earn them by solving this riddle.”

“And yet,” Legrand replied, “the answer isn’t nearly as hard as a quick look at the characters might make you think. These characters, as anyone could guess, form a cipher—that is, they carry a meaning. But from what we know of Kidd, I couldn’t imagine him capable of creating any advanced cryptographs. I decided at once that this was a simple type—one that, to the rough mind of a sailor, would seem impossible without the key.”

“And you really solved it?”

“Easily. I’ve solved others ten thousand times more complex. Circumstances and a certain turn of mind have made me interested in such puzzles, and one may well doubt whether human ingenuity can make a cipher that human ingenuity, properly applied, can’t solve. Once I had connected, readable characters, I hardly gave a thought to the difficulty of finding their meaning.

“In this case—indeed, in every case of secret writing—the first question concerns the language of the cipher, because the method of solving it, especially when dealing with simple ciphers, depends on and shifts according to the nature of the language. Usually, there is no choice but to experiment, guided by probabilities, with every language known to the solver until the right one is found. But with the cipher before us, the signature removed all difficulty. The pun on the word ‘Kidd’ only works in English. Without that clue I would have begun with Spanish and French, the languages in which a pirate of the Spanish Main would most likely write a secret. As it was, I assumed the cryptograph was in English.

“You notice there are no spaces between words. If there had been, the task would have been much easier. In that case, I would have started by comparing and analyzing the short words, and if a single-letter word had appeared, as would be most likely—‘a’ or ‘I,’ for example—I would have considered the solution all but certain. But, since there were no spaces, my first step was to determine which letters appeared most often and which appeared least.”"}

{"request_id":"d3b98d6b3e84d33144ffa6d6","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from these dear friends—a secret he had nurtured since childhood, and although he cherished his fellow students, he would not entrust it to the delicacy or sympathy of any of them. He was in love. He feared the intensity of his longing might become their amusement; he could not endure having them profane it by treating as trivial and fleeting what he felt to be the core of his life.

Near his family estate lived a gentleman of modest means with three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, but her beauty merely crowned her other virtues—her mind was clear and strong, her nature angelically gentle. She and my father had been playmates from infancy: Diana, even as a child, had been a favorite with his mother. That partiality deepened as the bright, lively girl grew, and during his school and college holidays they were inseparable. Novels and all the devices by which civilized youth learn of passions before they truly feel them had left a deep impression on him, who was so unusually sensitive to every emotion. At eleven, Diana was his favorite playmate, but he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older, her sheltered upbringing left her more childish, at least in matters of feeling; she accepted his ardent declarations with innocence and returned them without understanding what they meant. She had read no novels and spent her time only with her younger sisters—how could she know the difference between love and friendship? When the unfolding of her understanding finally revealed the real nature of their bond, her heart was already pledged to her friend, and her only fear was that other attractions and fickleness might make him break his childhood vows.

But each day their feelings grew more intense and tender. This passion had grown as he grew; it had woven itself into every power and every sentiment and could only perish with his life. No one knew of their love but themselves; yet even though he dreaded, in everything else and even in this, the judgment of his companions for so truly loving one poorer than himself, nothing could shake his resolve to unite himself to her as soon as he could gather the courage to face the obstacles he was determined to overcome.

Diana was entirely worthy of his deepest devotion."}

{"request_id":"05b6428d988f32c833031def","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” the old lady exclaimed as he walked in. “Why haven’t you come to see me all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I never get a moment to myself,” Lord Arthur said with a smile.

“I suppose you mean you spend every day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense? I cannot understand why people make such a fuss about getting married. In my day we never dreamed of cooing in public, or in private either.”

“I promise you I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.”

“Of course; that’s the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. You men should take heed. On a fait des folies pour moi, and now I’m just a poor rheumatic creature, with a false front and a bad temper. If not for dear Lady Jansen sending me all the worst French novels she can find, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are useless except for taking fees. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur seriously. “It’s a marvelous thing invented by an American.”

“I don’t think I like American inventions, Arthur. I’m certain I don’t. I read some American novels lately, and they were pure nonsense.”

“Oh, but there’s no nonsense here, Lady Clem! I promise it’s a perfect cure. You must agree to try it.” Lord Arthur took a small box from his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is delightful, Arthur. Is it really a gift? That’s very sweet of you. And this is the wonderful medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I’ll take it at once.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem,” cried Lord Arthur, grabbing her hand, “you mustn’t do that. It’s a homeopathic medicine. If you take it without having heartburn, it might do you great harm. Wait until you have an attack and take it then. You’ll be amazed at the effect.”

“I’d like to take it now,” said Lady Clementina, holding the little transparent capsule up to the light, the tiny bubble of liquid aconitine floating inside. “I’m sure it’s delicious. The truth is, although I hate doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I’ll keep it for my next attack.”

“And when will that be?” Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}
