{"request_id":"c1a015599c272753243584bc","rewritten_text":"The next day was set for an explanation, so our honour would not suffer from delay. Drummle showed up with a polite note in Estella’s hand saying she had had the honour of dancing with him several times. That left me no choice but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and to refuse, as untenable, any idea that I could be found anywhere. Drummle and I then sat snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove contradicted everyone indiscriminately, and finally it was declared that good feeling had advanced at a remarkable pace.

I tell it lightly, but it was not light to me. I cannot convey how much it hurt to think that Estella would show any favour to a contemptible, clumsy, sulky boor so far below the usual standard. To this day I believe it sprang from the pure generosity and selflessness of my love for her that I could not bear the thought of her stooping to that hound. I would have been miserable no matter whom she favoured, but a worthier recipient would have caused me a different kind and degree of pain.

It was easy to learn, and I soon did learn, that Drummle had begun to trail her, and that she let him. Before long he was always chasing after her, and he and I crossed paths every day. He held on in a dull, stubborn way, and Estella held him on—now encouraging him, now discouraging him, now almost flattering him, now openly despising him, now knowing him well, now barely remembering who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers called him, was used to lying in wait and had his tribe’s patience. He also had a blockheaded confidence in his money and family importance, which sometimes served him well, almost acting like focus and determination. So the Spider, dogging Estella, outwatched many brighter insects, and would often uncoil and drop at just the right moment.

At a certain Assembly Ball at Richmond—there used to be Assembly Balls almost everywhere then—Estella outshone every other beauty. This blundering Drummle hung about her with so much tolerance from her that I resolved to speak to her about him. I took the next opportunity, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home and was sitting apart among some flowers, ready to go."}

{"request_id":"35be4bf3a52c1309f5b2bd59","rewritten_text":"The encircling oaks were the dwelling of a clan of nightingales—there you find me now; Idris, in the sweet bloom of youth, stands beside me—remember, I count but twenty-two years, and scarce seventeen summers have washed over the darling of my soul. The river, swelled by autumn rains, flooded the meadows, and Adrian, in his cherished skiff, occupied himself with the perilous amusement of tearing the highest branch from a drowned oak. Oh Adrian, art thou so weary of existence that thou flirtest thus with peril?—

He gained his prize and steered his boat through the torrent; we watched him anxiously, yet the current drew him away from us; he was compelled to land far below and take a wide circuit before he could reach us. “He is safe!” cried Idris, when he sprang ashore and waved the branch aloft as a sign of triumph; “we will await him here.”

We found ourselves alone; the sun had set; the nightingales began their melody; the evening star gleamed clear amid the yet unwaning light in the west. The azure eyes of my heavenly girl rested on that dear emblem of herself: “How the light quivers,” she murmured, “which is the star’s very life. Its flickering brilliance seems to confess that its condition, even like our own on earth, is shifting and unsteady; it fears, meseems, and it loves.”

“Look not on the star, beloved and generous friend,” I exclaimed, “seek not love in _its_ trembling beams; gaze not on far worlds; speak not of the mere fancy of emotion. Long have I held my peace; long to sickness have I yearned to speak, to offer to you my soul, my life, my whole being. Look not on the star, dear love—or do, and let that immortal spark plead for me; let it be witness and advocate, silent as it glows—love is to me as light to the star; while it remains uneclipsed by nothingness, so shall I adore you.”

Never to the world’s hardened eye can the ecstasy of that instant be disclosed. Still I feel her graceful figure resting against my surcharged heart—still do sight, pulse, and breath falter at the recollection of that first kiss. Slowly and wordlessly we went to meet Adrian, whose steps we heard drawing near.

I begged Adrian to come back after he had escorted his sister home. That same night, pacing the moonlit woodland paths, I poured my entire heart, its rapture and its promise, into my friend’s keeping. For a moment he seemed troubled—“I might have foreseen this,” he said; “what contention must follow now!”"}

{"request_id":"9c91066c84d1e840067c880b","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery horse, the same one that had carried him to victory in Greece; he exhausted himself with relentless exercise, drowning the torment of his troubled mind in physical strain.

He gradually came to his senses; at last, as if recovering from poison, he lifted his head above the fog of fever and passion into the clear air of calm reflection. He considered what ought to be done. He was struck by the amount of time that had slipped by while madness, rather than reason, guided his actions. A month had passed, and during that time he had not seen Evadne. Her influence, which had little connection with the lasting emotions of his heart, had greatly faded. He was no longer her slave—no longer her lover: he would never see her again, and by fully returning to himself, he would earn Perdita’s trust.

Yet, even as he resolved this, his imagination summoned the wretched home of the Greek girl, which she had refused to trade, out of principle, for a more luxurious one. He remembered her brilliance when he first met her; he remembered her life in Constantinople, surrounded by every mark of eastern magnificence; he thought of her current poverty, her daily toil, her lonely state, her cheek wasted by hunger. Compassion filled his chest; he would see her once more; he would devise a plan to restore her to society and the privileges of her rank; then their separation would naturally follow.

Again he reflected on how, throughout this month, he had avoided Perdita, fleeing from her as he fled from his own conscience. But now he was awake; all this would be set right, and future devotion would erase the memory of this sole stain on the serenity of their life. He grew cheerful as he thought of this and firmly mapped out the course he would follow. He remembered that he had promised Perdita to attend that very evening (the nineteenth of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector) a festival held in his honor. Let this festival be a good omen of happiness in the coming years. First, he would visit Evadne—not linger, but he owed her some explanation, some compensation for his long, unexplained absence—and then he would return to Perdita, to the neglected world, to duty, social splendor, and the enjoyment of power.

After the scene described earlier, Perdita had anticipated a complete change in Raymond’s behavior and habits. She expected open communication and a return to the affectionate routines that had been the joy of her life."}

{"request_id":"c8971537a8b93aff023df88d","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent to Adrian, chosen as arbiter. They had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and ravaged countryside, feeding their mutual hatred, and now they argued their causes with undimmed party spirit.

By questioning the deputies separately and after much inquiry, we learned the real situation in Paris. Since parliament appointed him Ryland’s deputy, all surviving English people had submitted to Adrian. He was our leader to guide us from home to unknown lands, our lawgiver, our guardian. When we first arranged our emigration plan, we never expected to stay apart, and command of the entire group, rising by degrees, ended with the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen events altered our plans and kept most of us separated from the supreme leader for nearly two months. They had crossed in two distinct groups, and once in Paris quarrels sprang up between them.

They had found Paris a desert. At first, when the plague appeared, returning travellers, merchants, and letters kept us informed of the disease’s progress on the continent. As deaths increased, this contact dwindled and stopped. Even in England, communication from one part of the island to another became slow and rare. No ship crossed the channel between Calais and Dover; or if a sorrowful voyager left the French shore to learn the fate of his family among us, often the greedy sea swallowed his little boat, or after a day or two he caught the plague and died before he could tell the tale of France’s desolation. We therefore remained largely ignorant of conditions on the continent and still clung to a faint hope of finding many companions in its wide stretch. But the same causes that devastated England had worked even more widely in the sister land. France was empty; along the long road from Calais to Paris not a single human being appeared. In Paris there were a few, perhaps a hundred, resigned to their fate, wandering the streets and gathering to talk of former days, still showing that brightness and even cheerfulness that seldom deserts people of that nation.

The English took Paris without resistance. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures lingered at the usual meeting-place in the Tuileries; they wondered why the islanders approached their doomed city—for in extreme misery people always imagine their own share of suffering is the worst, just as in intense pain we would trade the torment we endure for any other that might strike another part of the body."}

{"request_id":"4225379af32359bf70b51162","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, aghast at Sikes’s deed, fell into a chain of thoughts as to whether an upright life were not, after all, the wiser course. Convinced at length that it surely was, he turned away from the former scenes, bent on reforming himself in some fresh field of endeavour. He toiled severely and endured no small misery for a season; yet, being blessed with a contented temper and steadfast aim, he prospered at last; and, from a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he is now the blithest young grazier in Northamptonshire.

And now the hand that writes these lines trembles as it draws near the end of its labour, and would gladly spin out, for yet a brief while, the story of these adventures.

I could wish to tarry still with a few of those among whom I have so long dwelt, and partake of their happiness by trying to portray it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of early maidenhood, casting on her sheltered path a soft and gentle radiance that lighted every companion beside her and warmed their hearts. I would paint her the spirit and joy of the fireside ring and the merry summer party; I would follow her through the hot fields at noon, and listen to the low music of her sweet voice in the moonlit stroll; I would watch her abroad in all her goodness and charity, and at home in the smiling, tireless performance of household offices; I would portray her and her departed sister’s child rejoicing in their mutual love, spending long hours together conjuring images of the friends they had so sadly lost; I would call again before me those joyous little faces that gathered around her knee and drink in their lively chatter; I would remember the clear peal of laughter, and summon the sympathetic tear that glimmered in the gentle blue eye. These, and a thousand expressions, smiles, and inflections of thought and tongue—I would willingly summon them all again.

How Mr. Brownlow proceeded, day by day, to enrich the mind of his adopted boy with stores of learning, and how he became more devoted to him as the lad’s nature unfolded, revealing the thriving germs of all he hoped to see—how he traced in him fresh traits of his early friend, awakening in his own heart old recollections, mournful yet sweet and comforting—how the two orphans, schooled by hardship, remembered its lessons in pity for others, in mutual affection, and in fervent gratitude to Him who had shielded and sustained them—these are matters that need no rehearsal."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b43e25ad8f2178c044ebffba","rewritten_text":"Weeks slipped by, and my absorption in you only deepened. Then something new arose. I had already portrayed you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis in huntsman’s cloak with a gleaming boar-spear. Wreathed with heavy lotus blossoms you had sat at the prow of Adrian’s barge, staring across the murky green Nile. You had bent over a still pool in some Greek grove and beheld in the water’s quiet silver the wonder of your own reflection. All of it had been what art ought to be—uninvolved, ideal, distant. One day—sometimes I call it fatal—I resolved to paint an extraordinary portrait of you as you truly are, not dressed in bygone finery, but in your own clothes and era. Whether it was the realistic approach, or simply the marvel of your own nature presented to me with no mist or veil, I cannot say. Yet as I worked, each speck and veil of colour seemed to betray my secret. I feared others would discover my worship. I felt, Dorian, that I had confessed too much, that I had poured too much of myself into it. So I resolved the picture must never be exhibited. You were slightly irritated, but you had no idea what it meant for me. Harry, when I told him, laughed. I did not care. When the portrait was done and I sat alone before it, I knew I was justified…. After a few days it left my studio, and once free of the oppressive fascination of its presence, it struck me that I had been foolish to think I saw anything in it beyond your extraordinary beauty and my own skill. Even now I cannot shake the sense that believing the passion felt in creation truly appears in the work is a mistake. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and colour speak only of form and colour—that is the sum. I often think art hides the artist far more than it reveals him. So when I received that offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the centrepiece of my exhibition. It never occurred to me you would refuse. I understand now that you were right. The picture must remain unseen. Do not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have confessed."}

{"request_id":"208ed0946cc39f17f2cb8676","rewritten_text":"Knights and their armored mounts never moved at any great clip. Once they pushed as best they could, with the ground firm now and free of snow or mire, they might manage a seven-mile pace. They’d need to swap horses twice and would likely get in around six, a little after perhaps, but still with daylight enough to spot the white cloth I meant to tie around my right arm, the signal for me to take command. We’d surround the prison and whisk the king out at once. It would look grand and dramatic enough, though I would have chosen noon for the extra theatrical effect.

Next, to add more strings to my bow, I decided to hunt up some of the folk I had earlier recognized and reveal myself to them. That might get us out of this mess without needing the knights. Yet I had to be careful—risky business. I had to appear splendidly dressed, and one can’t just leap into finery. I’d have to advance gradually, buying outfit after outfit from shops spaced apart, each one a bit finer than the last, until I reached silk and velvet and was ready. So I set out.

But the plan collapsed in a flash. At the first corner I ran smack into one of our slaves skulking with a watchman. I coughed just then, and he shot me a look that pierced to the bone; I’m sure he thought he recognized the cough. I ducked into a shop at once, moved down the counter asking prices, and kept an eye sideways. The pair had stopped to talk, peering through the doorway. I resolved to slip out the back if there was one and told the shopwoman I needed to step out there to search for an escaped slave said to be hiding somewhere behind, explaining I was an officer in disguise, with my partner at the door holding one of the murderers. Would she kindly tell him not to wait, but to hurry to the far end of the back alley to catch the fellow when I flushed him out?

Fired with excitement at the chance to glimpse one of those already famous murderers, she rushed off straightaway."}

{"request_id":"3d9d60b5fc89934edb6e14b3","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was even more crowded than usual. Six Cabinet Ministers had come straight from the Speaker’s Levée with their stars and ribbons, every pretty woman wore her smartest gown, and at the end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsruhe, a heavy Tartar-looking woman with tiny black eyes and dazzling emeralds, speaking bad French at the top of her voice and laughing wildly at everything anyone said. It was truly a mixed crowd. Splendid peeresses chatted pleasantly with fierce Radicals, fashionable preachers rubbed shoulders with famous skeptics, a whole flock of bishops kept following a stout prima donna from room to room, several Royal Academicians stood on the staircase pretending to be ordinary artists, and they said the supper room was at one point packed with geniuses. It was one of Lady Windermere’s finest evenings, and the Princess stayed until almost half-past eleven.

As soon as the Princess left, Lady Windermere returned to the picture gallery, where a famous political economist was solemnly lecturing an indignant Hungarian virtuoso on the scientific theory of music. She began talking to the Duchess of Paisley. Lady Windermere looked astonishingly beautiful, with her proud ivory neck, big blue forget-me-not eyes, and heavy coils of golden hair. They were truly golden—not the pale straw color that now claims the name, but the gold woven into sunbeams or hidden in mysterious amber. They framed her face like a saint’s halo, though with a good measure of a sinner’s charm. She was a fascinating study of character. Early on she had learned the crucial fact that nothing resembles innocence as much as indiscretion, and through a string of reckless escapades, half of them quite harmless, she had earned all the privileges of a celebrity. She had changed husbands more than once—Debrett credits her with three marriages—but since she had never changed her lover, society had long ago stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, childless, and possessed of that excessive love of pleasure that keeps one young.

Suddenly she looked eagerly around the room and said, in her clear contralto voice, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” exclaimed the Duchess, giving a sudden little jump.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess; I can’t live without him at the moment.”

“Dear Gladys! you are always so original,” murmured the Duchess, trying to remember what a cheiromantist actually was and hoping it was not the same as a chiropodist.

“He comes to look at my hand twice a week, every week,” continued Lady Windermere, “and he says the most interesting things about it.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"f4f60678a4316d17fc9c73d8","rewritten_text":"At least he believed so. Yet who could be sure? … No. Nothing further had happened. Out of vanity he had spared her. Out of hypocrisy he had worn the guise of virtue. From mere curiosity he had experimented with self-denial. He saw that now. But this murder—was it destined to haunt him forever? Would his past forever weigh upon him? Was he truly going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence still stood against him: the portrait itself. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it so long? Once, seeing it change and wither had delighted him. Lately, no such delight remained. It had robbed him of sleep. Whenever he was away, dread seized him lest other eyes should behold it. It had cast sadness over his pleasures. Even its recollection had spoiled many a joyful hour. It had been like a conscience. Yes, it had been conscience. He would destroy it. He looked around and spotted the knife that had killed Basil Hallward. He had polished it many times until no stain remained. It shone, gleaming. As it had slain the painter, so it would slay the painter’s creation and all it symbolized. It would kill the past, freeing him once it was dead. It would end this monstrous existence of the soul, and without its ghastly rebukes, he would know peace. He grasped the knife and plunged it into the painting. A scream rang out, followed by a crash. The scream was so hideous in its anguish that the terrified servants awoke and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen crossing the square below halted and gazed up at the grand house. They continued until they encountered a policeman and led him back. He rang repeatedly, but no one answered. Apart from a light in one of the upper windows, the house lay in darkness. After a while, he withdrew to a nearby portico and kept watch. “Whose house is that, Constable?” the elder gentleman inquired. “Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” replied the policeman. They exchanged glances, sneering as they walked off. One was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle. Meanwhile, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed domestics whispered among themselves. Old Mrs. Leaf wept and wrung her hands. Francis was white as death. After about fifteen minutes, he roused the coachman and one of the footmen, and together they crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"1af7ef482edca599622f635b","rewritten_text":"Shall I call for them? Or for Miss Bates? She is closer still—and I cannot be sure Miss Bates would not read the others’ feelings as well as anyone. I think we do require a larger council. Suppose I go and ask Miss Bates to come?”

“Well—if you like,” replied Mrs. Weston with some hesitation, “if you believe she can be of any service.”

“You will glean nothing worth having from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and gratitude, but she will give you no information. She will scarcely attend to your questions. I do not see any benefit in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so entertaining, so very entertaining! I am extremely fond of listening to Miss Bates. And I need not bring the entire family, you know.”

Mr. Weston now joined them, and, when he heard what was intended, he sanctioned it decidedly.

“Ay, do, Frank.—Go fetch Miss Bates, and let us settle everything immediately. She will relish the plan, I am sure; and I know no fitter person to teach us how to clear away obstacles. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming rather too fastidious. She is a perpetual lesson in being cheerful. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! The old lady?”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great simpleton, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I did not instantly remember. Certainly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And off he ran.

Long before he returned, escorting the short, neat, quick-stepping aunt and her graceful niece, Mrs. Weston, like a good-tempered woman and a devoted wife, had re-examined the passage, and discovered the inconveniences much less formidable than she had imagined—indeed barely worth mentioning; and so the difficulty of deciding ended. Everything else, at least in theory, was entirely smooth. The minor arrangements of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper, arranged themselves; or were left as mere trifles to be settled whenever Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes chose.—Every invited person was certainly to come; Frank had already written to Enscombe to request remaining a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be denied. And it was to be a delightful ball.

Most heartily, when Miss Bates arrived, did she agree that it must be so. As an adviser she was unnecessary; but as one who approved (a much safer role) she was thoroughly welcome. Her praise, at once broad and detailed, eager and unceasing, could not fail to gratify; and for another half-hour they all paced back and forth between the various rooms, some proposing, some attending, and all rejoicing in the anticipation of what was to come."}

{"request_id":"f1986dc10a7b17672441ce10","rewritten_text":"If you want one for home use, I can give you an excellent piece, and I promise you will be pleased with it. May I ask who it is for? If it is for the police, or anyone connected to Scotland Yard, I am sorry but I cannot help you. The English detectives are really our best allies, and by counting on their stupidity, we are free to do whatever we wish. I would not part with one of them.

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “it has nothing to do with the police. The clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Dear me! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do nowadays.”

“I’m afraid you give me too much credit, Herr Winckelkopf,” said Lord Arthur, blushing. “In truth, I know nothing about theology.”

“So it is a completely private affair?”

“Entirely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room, returning in a few minutes with a round piece of dynamite about the size of a penny, and a charming little French clock, topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face lit up at the sight. “That is exactly what I want,” he exclaimed. “Now tell me how it goes off.”

“Ah! That is my secret,” replied Herr Winckelkopf, studying his creation with justified pride. “Let me know when you want it to explode, and I will set it to that exact moment.”

“Today is Tuesday, and if you could send it off right away—”

“That cannot be done; I have important projects to finish for friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might send it tomorrow.”

“Oh, that will be quite good!” said Lord Arthur politely. “If it is delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning, it will do. For the explosion, let it be Friday at noon exactly. The Dean is always at home then.”

“Friday at noon,” repeated Herr Winckelkopf, and he wrote it down in a large ledger on the bureau near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising, “please let me know how much I owe you.”

“It is such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I do not care to make a charge. The dynamite costs seven and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and the delivery about five shillings. I am only too happy to serve any friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"7124f9a79577be5ec7d46489","rewritten_text":"Without giving herself a moment to think, and hardly aware of her own feelings, Elizabeth finished that letter, grabbed the other, and opened it with intense impatience. It had been written a day after the first one ended.  “By now, my dearest sister, you must have my hurried letter; I hope this one will make more sense, but even though I’m not rushed, my head is so confused I can’t promise to be coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to say, but I have bad news that can’t wait. As foolish as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate to be certain it has already happened, because there’s far too much reason to fear they never went to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday; he left Brighton the day before, just hours after the express. Even though Lydia’s brief note to Mrs. F. claimed they were headed to Gretna Green, Denny mentioned he believed W. never meant to go there or to marry Lydia at all; that was repeated to Colonel F., who immediately panicked, left B., and went after them. He traced them easily to Clapham but no farther, because when they reached that place, they switched to a hackney coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All anyone knows after that is they were seen continuing on the London road. I don’t know what to think. After exhausting every inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. came into Hertfordshire, asking anxiously at every tollgate, and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but with no success—no such couple had been seen. With the kindest concern he came to Longbourn and shared his fears in a manner that did credit to his character. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F.; but no one can blame them. Our distress, my dear Lizzy, is terrible. My father and mother assume the worst, but I cannot think so ill of him. Many circumstances might make it more sensible for them to marry privately in town rather than follow their original plan; and even if he could devise such a scheme against a young woman of Lydia’s connections, which seems unlikely, could I believe she would be so devoid of sense? Impossible! Yet I am upset to find that Colonel F. is not confident they will marry: he shook his head when I voiced my hopes and said he feared W. was not a man to be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"048baa14b1df15107ab9faef","rewritten_text":"“Is that the sum of it? That is no great matter! Many fall under the Republic’s displeasure and must look out through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which is he?”

“I am. Inevitably, since I am the last.”

Jarvis Lorry has answered every preceding inquiry. He is the one who has stepped down and stands with his hand on the coach door, replying to a knot of officials. They stroll around the carriage and slowly climb onto the box to inspect the scant luggage on the roof; country-folk loiter about, crowd nearer the doors, and stare greedily inside; a small child, held by its mother, stretches out its tiny arm to touch the wife of an aristocrat sent to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.”

“We may depart, citizen?”

“You may depart. Forward, my postilions! A prosperous journey!”

“I salute you, citizens.—And so the first peril is over!”

Jarvis Lorry speaks again as he clasps his hands and lifts his eyes. Terror fills the coach, weeping breaks out, and the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveler is heard.

“Are we not travelling too slowly? Can they not be urged to greater speed?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would appear like flight, my darling. I must not press them too far; it would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see if we are followed!”

“The road lies clear, my dearest. Thus far, no one pursues us.”

Pairs and trios of houses slip past, lone farms, decaying structures, dye-works, tanneries, and such, stretches of open country, rows of leafless trees. The hard, uneven paving stones lie under us, deep soft mud to either side. At times we edge into the bordering mire to escape the clattering stones that shake us; at times we bog down in the ruts and sloughs there. Our impatient torment grows so intense that, in our frantic fear and haste, we feel for springing out and running—hiding—doing anything but halting.

Out from the open country and once more among crumbling buildings, isolated farms, dye-works, tanneries, and the like, cottages in pairs and threes, avenues of leafless trees. Have they tricked us, carrying us back by another route? Is not this the same place twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look behind, look behind, and see if we are chased! Silence! the posting-house.

Leisurely our four horses are unhitched; leisurely the coach rests in the little street, stripped of its team, showing no likelihood of moving again; leisurely the fresh horses come into sight, one after another; leisurely the new postilions appear, sucking and braiding the lashes of their whips; leisurely the old postilions count their coins, make false totals, and end in discontent."}

{"request_id":"5e1ad2fe81fd06b85fe45c5e","rewritten_text":"“Then listen! You!” Monks shot back. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother—whom he’d been separated from for ages, left Paris and brought me along. Maybe she wanted to guard his fortune; she certainly didn’t love him, and he didn’t love her. He never knew we were there, because his senses were gone, and he kept drifting in and out until he died the next day. In his desk we found two papers written the night he first became sick. Both were addressed to you,” he said to Mr. Brownlow, “and wrapped in a short note warning that nothing should be delivered until after his death. One was a letter to Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What about the letter?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter? A sheet covered back and forth with a confession full of remorse, begging God for mercy. He had duped the girl with some secret tale—promising he’d explain someday why he couldn’t marry her just yet—and she kept believing him until she trusted him too much and lost what could never be restored. She was only a few months from giving birth. He told her what he had planned to do to hide her disgrace, if he had lived, and begged her, if he died, not to curse his memory or blame herself or their young child for their sin, because all the guilt was his. He reminded her of the day he gave her the locket and ring that had her first name engraved on it, with space left for the name he hoped to add when he could finally marry her. He begged her to keep wearing it close to her heart, as she always had—and then he raved, repeating the same words wildly, like a man losing his mind. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, while Oliver’s tears fell in streams.

Monks said nothing.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “matched the letter. He wrote of the misery his wife had caused him; of your defiance, vice, malice, and corrupt passions, you his only son, raised to despise him; and he left you and your mother each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. The rest of his estate he split into two equal parts—one for Agnes Fleming, the other for their child, if the child were born alive and reached adulthood.”"}

{"request_id":"52471d2897ede361f64d98bf","rewritten_text":"From the steps where we had once embarked him, and ever afterward, I was on guard for any hint that we were suspected. I found none. We certainly had not been, and at that moment were not, watched or trailed by any boat. Had any craft hovered near us, I should have run for the shore, forcing her either to pass on or reveal her purpose. Yet we proceeded without the least sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and seemed, as I’ve remarked, naturally blended with the scene. It was striking (though the miserable life he had led might explain it) that he was the calmest of us all. He was no dullard, for he told me he wished to live to see his benefactor become one of the noblest gentlemen abroad; neither was he inclined to passivity or surrender, as I read him; but he had no intention of anticipating peril. When it arrived, he faced it, but it must arrive before he gave it thought.

“If you knowed, dear boy,” he said, “what it is to sit alongside my dear boy with my pipe, after being day by day between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the pleasure of liberty,” I replied.

“Ah,” said he, shaking his head soberly. “But you don’t know it the same as me. You’d have to be under lock and key, dear boy, to know it the same as me,—but I ain’t a-going to be low.”

It struck me as inconsistent that, driven by some dominant idea, he had risked his freedom and even his life. Yet I considered that perhaps freedom devoid of hazard stood too far from the habits of his existence to mean to him what it would to another man. I was near the truth, for after a short pause in his smoking he said:—

“You see, dear boy, when I was yonder, on t’other side of the world, I kept always looking this way; and it grew dull to be there, though I was growing rich. Everybody knowed Magwitch, and Magwitch could come or go, and nobody’s mind was put out about him. They aren’t so easy concerning me here, dear boy,—wouldn’t be, at least, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you will be entirely free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he answered, letting out a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And think so?”"}

{"request_id":"5257a5df4758be482ad487d9","rewritten_text":"When the wedding took place about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a whole crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester read the service with great solemnity, and everyone agreed they had never seen a handsomer couple than the bride and groom. Yet they were more than handsome—they were happy. Not once did Lord Arthur regret everything he had endured for Sybil, while she, in turn, gave him the greatest gifts a woman can offer a man: devotion, tenderness, and love. Reality never crushed their romance. They always felt young.

Some years later, after they had two beautiful children, Lady Windermere came to visit Alton Priory, the lovely old estate the Duke had given his son as a wedding present. One afternoon, while she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl race up and down the rose walk like flickering sunbeams, she suddenly took her hostess’s hand and asked, “Are you happy, Sybil?”

“Dear Lady Windermere, of course I’m happy. Aren’t you?”

“I never have time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last new person I’m introduced to, but generally, as soon as I get to know people, I grow tired of them.”

“Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?”

“Good heavens, no! Lions are only fun for one season. Once their manes are trimmed, they’re the dullest creatures alive. Besides, they behave terribly if you’re genuinely kind to them. Do you remember that awful Mr. Podgers? He was a complete fraud. Of course I didn’t mind that, and even when he tried to borrow money I forgave him, but I couldn’t stand his flirting with me. He made me absolutely loathe palmistry. I’m into telepathy now. It’s far more entertaining.”

“You mustn’t speak against palmistry here, Lady Windermere; it’s the one subject Arthur doesn’t like people teasing about. I assure you he takes it very seriously.”

“You can’t mean he believes in it, Sybil?”

“Ask him yourself, Lady Windermere—here he comes,” said Sybil, as Lord Arthur strolled up the garden with a large bunch of yellow roses in his hand, his two children dancing around him.

“Lord Arthur?”

“Yes, Lady Windermere?”

“You’re not telling me you believe in palmistry?”

“Of course I do,” the young man said with a smile.

“But why?”

“Because I owe all the happiness of my life to it,” he murmured, dropping into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"1207c74e8d84bed555108a3f","rewritten_text":"Her situation was a severe and unusual trial. She longed to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s past, yet she felt bound to respect the trust the miserable woman had placed in her, as an innocent young girl. The woman’s words and manner had moved Rose Maylie deeply; alongside her love for her young charge burned an equally strong desire to lead the outcast back toward repentance and hope.

They intended to stay in London only three days before traveling to a distant coastal town for several weeks. It was already midnight on the first of those days. What could she do within the remaining forty-eight hours? How could she delay the journey without arousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them and would remain so for two more days, but Rose knew the good doctor’s impulsive nature too well. She could foresee the fury with which he would, in his first burst of anger, treat the person responsible for Oliver’s capture. She dared not tell him the secret when no experienced advocate could support her plea for the girl. All these were reasons to act with great caution before confiding in Mrs. Maylie, whose first instinct would surely be to consult the doctor. Going to a lawyer, even if she knew how, was equally impossible for the same reason. She briefly thought of appealing to Harry, but that reminded her of their last parting; it felt unworthy to call him back when—tears filled her eyes at the thought—he might already have learned to forget her and might be happier away.

Tormented by these conflicting thoughts, pulled toward one plan and then another and rejecting each as it arose, Rose spent a sleepless, anxious night. After further reflection the next day, she made the desperate decision to consult Harry.

“If it pains him to return here,” she thought, “it will pain me just as much. Perhaps he will refuse; perhaps he will write, or he might come in person but carefully avoid me—he did that when he left. I hardly expected it, yet it was better for us both.” Rose then laid down the pen and turned away, as though even the paper meant to carry her message should not see her tears."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3609ab544f1e48ccb7b3ad8a","rewritten_text":"Raymond exulted in the keen sensations that attended the return of health; he felt that commanding the Athenians set him in a position fit for his aspirations, and in dreaming of taking Constantinople he anticipated an event that would stand like a beacon through the desolate ages, an achievement unmatched in human chronicles; when that city, rich in historical associations, whose wondrous site astonished the world, and which for centuries had remained the stronghold of the Moslems, should be redeemed from bondage and savagery and handed back to a race illustrious for intellect, refinement, and love of liberty. Perdita reposed on his regained companionship, his affection, his ambition and renown, as a Sybarite might sink into a sumptuous couch; every thought was rapture, each feeling seemed immersed in a soothing, congenial atmosphere.\n\nWe reached Kishan on the seventh of July. The weather throughout our pilgrimage had been tranquil. Daily, before dawn glimmered, we deserted the night’s lodge and watched the shade flee from hill and vale, while the sun’s golden pageantry drew nigh. The soldiers who accompanied us caught, with their native vivacity, an ardent delight from beautiful scenery. The uprising sun was celebrated with triumphant music, and between the strains the birds, heard in fragments, supplied the pauses. At noon we raised our tents in some shaded glen or leafy woodland among the mountains, while a rivulet babbling over pebbles invited grateful slumber. Our march at evening, more composed, yet surpassed the morning’s eager excitement. If the musicians played, without design they selected melodies of restrained feeling; a parting of lovers or a plaint for absence would be followed and concluded by a solemn hymn, which accorded with evening’s placid loveliness and lifted the spirit to lofty, devout meditation. Often every sound was hushed so that we might listen to the nightingale, the fire-flies fluttering in luminous rhythm, while the gentle coo of the aziolo promised fair skies to the wayfarers. Should we thread a valley? Soft shadows enclosed us, and crags wore lovely tints. Should we cross a mountain, Greece spread beneath us like a living map, her famed heights cleaving the clear air, her rivers running in silver lines through fertile fields. Hardly daring to breathe, we English travellers gazed with ecstasy on that magnificent landscape, so unlike the grave tones and pensive charms of our native scenes. Beyond Macedonia, the fruitful yet flat plains of Thrace offered fewer charms, but the road still held our interest. A vanguard announced our coming, and the villagers were soon astir to render homage to Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"bf7ad3594963eabc45e97478","rewritten_text":"No reference escaped his lips until their visitor wished them good night; but the moment he was gone, he turned to his daughter and remarked—

“Jane, I heartily congratulate you. You are going to be a most contented woman.”

Jane at once approached him, kissed his cheek, and thanked him for his kindness.

“You are an excellent girl,” he resumed, “and I take great satisfaction in believing you will be so well established. I have not the least doubt that you two will do admirably together. Your tempers are wonderfully alike. Each of you is so accommodating that no decision will ever be reached; so easygoing that every servant will impose upon you; and so liberal that you will be forever exceeding your income.”

“I hope not. Imprudence or heedlessness regarding money would be inexcusable in me.”

“Exceed their income! My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife exclaimed, “what nonsense is that? Why, he has four or five thousand a year, perhaps more.” Then to her daughter she cried, “Oh, my dearest Jane, I am beside myself with joy! I am sure I shall not close my eyes all night. I knew it would happen. I always said it must, in the end. I was convinced you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the instant I saw him when he first arrived in Hertfordshire last year, I thought how probable it was that you should be united. Oh, he is the most handsome young man that ever existed!”

Wickham and Lydia vanished from her thoughts. Jane stood far above every other child in her affection. At that moment she had regard for no one else. Her younger sisters promptly began to cultivate her favour for future pleasures she might be able to grant.

Mary requested access to the Netherfield library; Kitty pleaded vehemently for several balls there every winter.

From then on, Bingley was naturally a daily visitor at Longbourn; often arriving before breakfast and never leaving till after supper; except when some barbarous neighbor, not to be sufficiently detested, had invited him to dinner, and he felt duty-bound to accept.

Elizabeth now found very little opportunity for discourse with her sister; for while he stayed, Jane could spare attention for no one else. Yet Elizabeth considered herself of considerable use to both, during those intervals of separation that occasionally took place. When Jane was absent, he invariably attached himself to Elizabeth for the gratification of talking about her; and when Bingley was gone, Jane always pursued the same relief.

“He has made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by assuring me he had not the slightest idea of my being in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"971ede5c88fb2cb37bd3ae55","rewritten_text":"“On that point I shall remain entirely silent, and you may be sure that once we are married, I will never utter an unkind reproach.”

This had to be stopped immediately. “You are too quick, sir,” she said. “You forget that I have not answered. Allow me to do so without delay. Thank you for the compliment you pay me. I truly appreciate the honour of your proposal, but I must decline it.”

“I know well,” Mr. Collins replied with a solemn wave of his hand, “that young ladies usually refuse the man they secretly mean to accept the first time he applies, and sometimes even the second or third time. So I am not at all discouraged by your words, and I hope to lead you to the altar soon.”

“Honestly, sir,” Elizabeth exclaimed, “your hope is rather strange after my declaration. I am not one of those young women—if such exist—who dare to risk their happiness on the chance of being asked again. I am entirely serious in my refusal. You could not make me happy, and I am sure I would be the last woman to make you happy. Indeed, if your friend Lady Catherine knew me, I am convinced she would find me unfit in every way for the role.”

“If it were certain that Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins gravely, “but I cannot believe her Ladyship would disapprove of you. You may be sure that when I next have the honour of seeing her, I shall praise your modesty, thrift, and other delightful qualities.”

“Really, Mr. Collins, there is no need to praise me. Allow me to decide for myself and do me the honour of believing what I say. I wish you all happiness and wealth, and by refusing your offer, I am doing all I can to ensure you have both. By proposing, you have satisfied your feelings about my family, and you may take possession of Longbourn whenever it comes to you without any guilt. This business is therefore settled.” As she spoke, she rose and would have left the room, had Mr. Collins not stopped her.

“When I next have the honour of speaking to you on this subject, I hope for a more favourable answer than the one you have given now. Yet I do not accuse you of cruelty, for I know it is customary for your sex to reject a man on his first proposal, and perhaps you have already said as much to encourage my suit as is proper for a woman of true delicacy.”"}

{"request_id":"fe44cddffecb09ed3e9a97d0","rewritten_text":"Yet there was one secret he guarded even from these beloved companions; one he had cherished since his earliest days, and though he cherished his fellow collegiates, he would not expose it to their fineness of feeling or sympathy. He was in love. He feared the vehemence of his passion would become their jest, and he could not endure that they profane it by deeming that trivial and fleeting which he knew to be the very essence of his life.

A gentleman of modest means resided near his family estate, with three charming daughters. The eldest surpassed the rest in beauty, yet her loveliness merely accompanied other qualities—her mind was lucid, her character angelically gentle. She and my father had been companions since infancy: Diana, even as a child, enjoyed the favour of his mother; that partiality grew with the years of this graceful, vivacious girl, so that during his school and college holidays they were constantly together. Novels and the various means by which youth in civilized society learn of passions before truly feeling them, had exerted great influence over one so susceptible to every impression. At eleven, Diana was his preferred playmate, but he already spoke the language of love. Though she was nearly two years older, her schooling left her more childlike, at least regarding the understanding and expression of emotion; she accepted his fervent vows innocently and responded without comprehending their meaning. She had read no novels and was confined to the company of her younger sisters—how could she discern the distinction between love and friendship? And when her maturing mind revealed the true nature of their dealings, her heart was already pledged to her friend, and her only dread was that other allurements or inconstancy might prompt him to break those infant pledges.

Yet each day their attachment grew more fervent and tender. It was a passion maturing with his own growth; woven through every faculty and sentiment, to be lost only with life itself. None but their two hearts knew of this affection; and though in all else, and even here, he feared the criticism of his companions for loving one beneath him in fortune, nothing could for an instant shake his resolve to unite himself to her as soon as he could summon the courage to confront the obstacles he was fixed upon overcoming.

Diana was in every way worthy of his deepest devotion."}

{"request_id":"a7859c515f2d8ef7757f4e81","rewritten_text":"Now that no task occupied him, he crossed the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of the left, then reversed them, then swept a hand along his bearded chin, repeating the motions in steady alternation without pause. Rousing him from the vagabond reverie into which he always drifted after speaking was like hauling some feeble creature back from a faint, or trying, in hope of a revelation, to detain the spirit of a man at the point of death.

“Did you ask my name?”

“Indeed I did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that everything?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was neither sigh nor groan, he bent over the work again until the quiet was once more broken.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” Mr. Lorry inquired, his gaze steady upon him.

His gaunt eyes turned toward Defarge, as if to hand the question over; but no support coming from that side, they sank to the floor before returning to the man addressing him.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He slipped away again, for whole minutes, always repeating those rhythmic movements with his hands. At last his eyes crept back to the face they had abandoned; when they fastened on it, he started, resuming like a dreamer abruptly wakened and reverting to a subject from the night before.

“I asked leave to teach myself, and after a long time I obtained it with great difficulty, and I have made shoes ever since.”

As he reached for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry, still fixing his face, asked:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the floor, and he stared steadily at the interrogator.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry set his hand on Defarge’s arm—“do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Does no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time arise in your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

While the long-imprisoned man stared fixedly, in turn, at Mr. Lorry and at Defarge, faint traces of an intensely active intelligence in the middle of his brow struggled through the black haze that enveloped him. They clouded over again, weakened, and vanished; yet they had been visible."}

{"request_id":"4e95b1fbbe4fd419008bf990","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff replied.

“And just so the ladies are clear on the word ‘yokel,’ I take it you mean the culprit isn’t a countryman?” Mr. Losberne said with a smile.

“Exactly, sir,” Blathers replied. “So, this is about the robbery, then?”

“All of it,” said the doctor.

“Now, what’s this about the boy the servants keep talking about?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing at all,” replied the doctor. “One panicked servant convinced himself the boy had something to do with the break-in, but it’s nonsense—pure absurdity.”

“Easily dismissed, if that’s the case,” Duff remarked.

“He’s right,” Blathers said, nodding and idly twirling the handcuffs as if they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What’s his story? Where did he come from? He didn’t fall from the clouds, did he, sir?”

“Of course not,” said the doctor, shooting a nervous glance at the two ladies. “I know his whole history, but we can discuss that later. You’d prefer to see where the thieves tried to get in first, I assume?”

“Certainly,” said Mr. Blathers. “We should examine the scene first and question the servants afterward. That’s the standard procedure.”

They brought in lights, and Blathers and Duff, followed by the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and practically everyone else, went into the little room at the end of the hall and looked out the window. Then they went around across the lawn and looked in through the window. After that, someone handed them a candle to check the shutter, then a lantern to trace the footprints, and finally a pitchfork to prod the bushes. After all this, with everyone watching in breathless suspense, they returned inside, and Mr. Giles and Brittles reenacted their parts in the previous night’s adventure with melodramatic flair—some six times over—contradicting each other in only one important detail at first, and in no more than a dozen by the final performance. Once that was done, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a lengthy conference that, for secrecy and solemnity, made the most intricate medical consultation look like child’s play.

Meanwhile, the doctor paced restlessly in the next room, and Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with anxious faces.

“Honestly,” he said, stopping after a series of brisk turns, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

Though he’s innocent of the murder, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate about answering the advertisement—about claiming the orangutan. Even if they track the creature, they can’t prove I knew about the murder, or implicate me just because I knew something. Above all, I’m identified. The advertiser names me as the owner of the animal. I can’t know how much he really knows. If I fail to claim property so valuable, which people know is mine, I’ll at least make the animal itself seem suspicious. It’s not in my interest to draw attention to myself or the creature. I’ll answer the advertisement, reclaim the orangutan, and keep it hidden until this blows over.’” At that moment we heard footsteps on the stairs. “Be ready,” Dupin said, “with your pistols, but don’t show them or use them until I give the signal.” We had left the front door open, and the visitor entered without ringing, coming several steps up the staircase. Now, though, he seemed to hesitate. We soon heard him going down again. Dupin moved quickly to the door just as we heard him returning. He didn’t retreat a second time; instead he came up confidently and knocked on our door. “Come in,” Dupin said in a cheerful, hearty voice. A man entered. {"request_id":"87070ce4e241029968678e76","rewritten_text":"After joining in the general lamentations over the terrible consequences of this event—which Elizabeth saw as all but certain, and Miss Bennet could not say was entirely impossible—Elizabeth continued, “But tell me everything about it that I haven’t already heard. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they any idea before the elopement happened? They must have seen them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted he had often suspected a fondness, especially on Lydia’s part, but nothing that alarmed him. I feel so sorry for him. He behaved with the greatest care and kindness. He was actually on his way to us to assure us of his concern before he had any notion they had not gone to Scotland; once that fear spread, it hurried his journey.”

“And was Denny certain that Wickham would not marry? Did he know they planned to run off? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Colonel Forster questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan, and refused to give his real opinion. He no longer insisted they would not marry, and from that I hope he may have been misunderstood before.”

“And until Colonel Forster came himself, none of you, I suppose, doubted they were actually married?”

“How could such an idea even cross our minds? I felt a little uneasy—a bit fearful for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his behavior had not always been entirely proper. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only sensed how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then admitted, with very natural pride at knowing more than the rest of us, that in Lydia’s last letter she had been prepared for such a step. She had known, it seems, that they’d been in love for many weeks.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I don’t believe so.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit he did not speak as well of Wickham as he once did. He thought him reckless and extravagant, and since this dreadful business occurred, it’s said he left Meryton deeply in debt; but I hope that isn’t true.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secret, if we had revealed what we knew about him, this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But exposing someone’s past faults without knowing how they feel now seemed unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"9df865f99cd263e979ffb4a3","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was quite upset by the second postponement of the wedding, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her gown, did everything she could to persuade Sybil to end the engagement. Yet, devoted as Sybil was to her mother, she had given her entire life to Lord Arthur, and nothing Lady Julia said could shake her trust. As for Lord Arthur, it took him several days to recover from the crushing disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely shattered. Still, his excellent common sense soon reasserted itself, and his practical mind quickly settled on a course of action. Since poison had been a total failure, it was obvious that dynamite, or some other explosive, was the next thing to attempt.

He therefore went back over the list of his friends and relatives and, after careful consideration, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of notable culture and learning, was incredibly fond of clocks and possessed a remarkable collection of timepieces, from the fifteenth century to the present, and it seemed to Lord Arthur that this passion of the good Dean’s offered an ideal opportunity for carrying out his plan. Where to find an explosive device was, of course, another issue altogether. The London Directory could give him no help, and he felt it would be useless to go to Scotland Yard, since they never seemed to know anything about dynamite plots until after a blast, and even then had only a vague notion of what had occurred.

Suddenly he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with strong revolutionary leanings whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s that winter. Count Rouvaloff was supposed to be writing a biography of Peter the Great and to have come to England to study the documents relating to the Tsar’s time here as a shipwright; but it was generally suspected that he was a Nihilist agent, and there was no doubt the Russian Embassy viewed his presence in London with deep distrust. Lord Arthur was convinced that he was just the man for the job, and one morning he drove to Rouvaloff’s lodgings in Bloomsbury to seek his advice and help.

“So you’re getting serious about politics?” Count Rouvaloff asked when Lord Arthur had explained why he had come; but Lord Arthur, who despised any show of pretension, felt compelled to admit that he had not the slightest interest in social issues, and wanted the explosive device solely for a strictly family matter that concerned no one but himself."}

This left me no alternative but to regret that I had been “betrayed into a warmth which,” and generally to reject, as indefensible, the supposition that I was to be discovered anywhere. Drummle and I then sat snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove indulged in indiscriminate contradiction, and at last the advancement of good feeling was proclaimed to have proceeded at a prodigious pace.

I recount it lightly, but it was no light matter for me. For I cannot adequately relate what misery it brought me to imagine that Estella could display any favour toward a despicable, lumpish, sullen lout, so far beneath the average. To this instant, I believe it was owing to some pure blaze of generosity and selflessness in my love for her that I could not bear the idea of her bending to that cur. Certainly I should have been wretched whoever she had preferred; yet a worthier choice would have afflicted me with a different form and measure of suffering.

It was easy for me to ascertain, and I did soon ascertain, that Drummle had begun to dog her steps, and that she permitted it. Shortly, he was perpetually trailing after her, and he and I crossed paths daily. He clung on, in a dreary stubborn fashion, and Estella held him on; now encouraging, now discouraging, now almost flattering him, now openly scorning him, now knowing him intimately, now barely recalling who he might be.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers had dubbed him, was accustomed to lurking, however, and possessed the patience of his species. Added to this, he carried a blockheaded assurance in his wealth and family grandeur, which at times served him well—almost substituting for concentration and resolute aim. Thus, the Spider, doggedly surveilling Estella, outwatched many astuter creatures, and would often unwind himself and drop at the proper instant.

At a particular Assembly Ball at Richmond (Assembly Balls were held in most places then), where Estella had eclipsed every other beauty, that blundering Drummle hovered about her under such toleration from her that I determined to speak to her regarding him. I seized the next chance; it came when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to escort her home, and she sat apart among some flowers, ready to depart."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b50a60e11613de238863210c","rewritten_text":"He had truly been unaware of the influence he held. He followed her into the shrubs with no thought of using it. He came only out of concern to see how she was enduring Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no selfish purpose—no goal beyond trying, if she allowed a chance, to comfort or advise her. Everything else was spontaneous, the immediate effect of what he heard on his feelings. The joyful certainty that she felt nothing for Frank Churchill, that her heart was entirely free of him, sparked the hope that, in time, he might win her affection himself. But that hope was not for the present; in a brief moment when eagerness overruled judgment, he only dared to ask whether she would allow him to try to win her. And the higher hopes that unfolded afterward were even more enchanting. The love he had asked permission to create—if he could—was already his. Within half an hour, he went from utter distress to something so close to perfect happiness it deserved no other name.\n\nHer transformation matched his. That same half-hour gave them both the precious certainty that they were loved, removing from both the same amount of ignorance, jealousy, and distrust. His jealousy had been long-standing, dating back to Frank Churchill’s arrival—or even the expectation of it. He had loved Emma and envied Frank Churchill almost from the same moment, one feeling probably revealing the other. It was his jealousy of Frank Churchill that drove him from the country. The Box Hill gathering convinced him to leave. He would spare himself from seeing such welcomed, encouraged attentions again. He left to learn to be indifferent. But he went to the wrong place. There was too much domestic happiness in his brother’s home; womanhood appeared too kind there; Isabella was so like Emma—differing only in those notable inferiority that made Emma shine more brightly—that even more time would have accomplished little. Yet he stayed on determinedly, day after day, until that very morning’s post brought the news about Jane Fairfax. Then, with the happiness he could not deny—having never believed Frank Churchill remotely worthy of Emma—blended with such tender concern, such intense anxiety for her, he could stay no longer. He rode home through the rain, and walked up immediately after dinner to see how this sweetest and best of all women, flawless despite her faults, endured the revelation."}

{"request_id":"bb2db30857fa87840244ec51","rewritten_text":"But when I saw you become cherished by another; when I imagined that you might be adored as something other than a sacred emblem of beauty and virtue, or that you could return an affection more fervent than the one you felt for me, the demon stirred in my heart. I drove away your suitor, and from that moment peace deserted me. I chased sleep in vain; my eyelids would not close, and my blood boiled ceaselessly. I awakened to a new existence as a hopeful soul might wake in Hell. I will not tarnish your thoughts by recounting my battles, my fury at myself, my despair. Let a veil fall over the unthinkable impressions of a guilty father; such torments should not be made common. Everything was tumult, sin, remorse, and hatred, yet the softest love still survived. What first roused me to resolve that I would subdue this passion and restore her father to my child was witnessing your bitter, sympathetic grief. That is what brought me here: I believed that if I could stir again the sorrow I had felt at your mother’s death, and revive the memories associated with her that had slept for seventeen years, then all affection for her daughter would fade. In an effort at heroism I decided to come alone, to depart from you—the very life of my being—and not look upon you until I might do so without guilt. It failed; I misjudged my courage or underestimated my love. I should surely have died had you not hurried to me. Would that I truly had been snuffed out!" 

"And now, Mathilda, I must share my final confession. I was pitiably deluded to imagine I could overcome my love for you; I never shall. The sight of this dwelling, these fields and woods, once inhabited by my first love, has only increased it: in my frenzy I dared tell myself—Diana died to give her birth; her mother’s spirit passed into her, and she should be as Diana to me. However I strive to banish it, this attachment clings the tighter, this guilty feeling more unnatural than hatred, that blights your hopes and ruins me forever.

Better to have loved despair, and safer to have kissed her.

Neither distance nor time can tear from my soul what has become part of its essence. Since my arrival I have unceasingly endured the inferno of passion implanted in me, burning until all is cold, rigid, and lifeless."}

{"request_id":"6824ac4be1b6a6bd24e8bb23","rewritten_text":"But how was a confused village boy like me supposed to avoid that marvelous inconsistency the best and wisest people fall into every day?

“It may all be perfectly true,” I said to Biddy, “but I’m terribly taken with her.”

In short, I rolled onto my face when I got to that point, grabbed handfuls of hair on either side of my head, and yanked hard. All the while I knew my heart’s madness was so completely mad and misplaced that I was quite aware it would have served me right if I’d lifted my head by my hair and knocked it against the pebbles to punish my face for belonging to such a fool.

Biddy was the wisest of girls, and she didn’t try to argue with me anymore. She laid her hand, a comforting hand though roughened by work, on my hands one after the other and gently took them out of my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder in a soothing way while, with my face on my sleeve, I cried a little—just as I had in the brewery yard—and felt vaguely convinced I’d been badly treated by someone, or by everyone; I can’t say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” Biddy said, “which is that you felt you could trust me, Pip. And I’m glad of another thing, which is that of course you know you can count on me to keep it and always do my best to deserve it. If your first teacher (dear me! such a poor one, and so needing lessons herself!) were teaching you now, she thinks she knows what lesson she’d set. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you’ve outgrown her, and it’s no use anymore.” Then, with a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and said, changing her voice to a fresh, pleasant tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, standing up, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I’ll always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never will be, so that means always. Not that I ever need to tell you anything, because you already know everything I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” Biddy said, barely above a whisper, as she looked away at the ships. Then she repeated, with her earlier pleasant tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we’d walk a little farther, and we did, and the summer afternoon softened into a summer evening, and it was very beautiful."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b79315cd6024ab1e5aea524a","rewritten_text":"Smallpox! I rushed to the king and murmured in his ear, “Out the door at once, sire! That woman is dying of the sickness that swept Camelot two years ago.” He never moved. “Truly I shall stay—and help.” I whispered again, “King, you mustn’t. You have to go.” “You mean well,” he said, “and your words have sense. Yet it would shame a king to show fear, and shame a knight to hold back his hand when help is needed. Be at peace, I will not go. It is you who must leave. The Church’s ban is not on me, but it forbids you to stay here, and she will punish you harshly if word reaches her of this trespass.” It was a deadly place for him and could cost his life, but arguing was useless. Once he set his honor on the matter, nothing could move him; I knew that, so I said no more. The woman spoke: “Kind sir, will you climb the ladder and tell me what you see? Do not fear to tell the truth, for a mother’s heart can reach a point where it cannot break again—being already broken.” “Wait,” said the king, “feed the woman. I will go,” and he laid down the knapsack. I turned to go, yet the king was already on his way. He stopped and looked at a man lying in the dim light who had neither noticed nor spoken. “Is it your husband?” asked the king. “Yes.” “Is he asleep?” “Thank God for that mercy—yes, these three hours. Where can I turn to repay such gratitude? My heart is bursting with it for the sleep he sleeps now.” I said, “We will be careful. We will not wake him.” “No, you will not, for he is dead.” “Dead?” “Yes. What a victory to know it! No one can hurt or insult him anymore. He is in heaven now and happy; and if not there, then he stays in hell content, because in that place there is neither abbot nor bishop. We were boy and girl together; we were man and wife for five and twenty years, never apart until this day. Think how long it is to love and suffer together. This morning he lost his mind, and in his fancy we were children again wandering through bright fields; so in that innocent, joyful talk he strayed farther and farther, still smiling lightly, and went into those other fields we do not know and passed from mortal sight.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1a3269830916a8be260190b4","rewritten_text":"April 7th. I rose at dawn and, to my profound delight, at last saw what I could only conclude was the northern Pole itself. There it lay, unquestionably, immediately below my feet; yet, alas, I had risen to such an immense altitude that nothing could be observed with precision. Indeed, judging from the sequence of numbers marking my altitudes at different times between six in the morning on April second and twenty minutes to nine the same day (when the barometer fell), one might fairly deduce that at four o’clock on the morning of April seventh the balloon had attained no less than, certainly, 7,254 miles above sea level. Although this height may appear tremendous, the calculation likely gives a figure far beneath the reality. At any rate, I unquestionably surveyed the entire major diameter of the globe; the complete northern hemisphere spread below me like an orthographic chart, and the great equatorial circle itself traced the edge of my horizon. Your Excellencies may readily imagine that the tightly bounded territories never yet explored inside the Arctic circle, though lying directly under me and therefore presenting no foreshortening, were still, by their smallness and the immense remoteness of my vantage point, too minute to allow very exact scrutiny. Yet whatever was visible proved both singular and stirring. North of that colossal rim earlier mentioned, which, with slight qualification, may be termed the final boundary of human discovery in these latitudes, there stretched an unbroken—or nearly unbroken—expanse of ice. During its first degrees this surface appeared sensibly flattened, later depressed into a plane, and finally grew slightly concave, terminating at the Pole itself in a sharply defined circular nucleus whose apparent diameter formed at the balloon an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its dusky color, shifting in intensity, was always darker than any other point on the visible hemisphere, and at times deepened into an absolute and impenetrable black. Beyond this, little more could be determined. By noon the circular centre had notably shrunk in circumference, and by seven in the evening I had lost it altogether; the balloon crossed the western edge of the ice and sped swiftly off toward the equator.\n\nApril 8th. The earth’s apparent diameter exhibited a sensible decrease, along with a considerable change in its general hue and aspect."}

content.text: {"request_id":"05af7c503b97e71cf387f8c9","rewritten_text":"Even merely reading about the splendours of the dead seemed marvelous.\n\nNext he gave himself over to embroideries and to the tapestries that served as frescoes’ substitutes in the cold chambers of the northern European peoples. As he delved into the matter—with that remarkable gift he possessed of becoming wholly immersed for the moment in whatever occupied him—he felt almost desolate at the thought of time’s havoc on beautiful and wondrous things. He, at least, had been spared that fate. Summer succeeded summer, and yellow jonquils blossomed and withered again and again, and nights of terror retold their disgrace, yet he remained unaltered. No winter touched his face or dimmed his flowerlike radiance. How different it was with material creations! What had become of them? Where was the great robe, crocus in hue, showing gods battling giants, that brown maidens had fashioned to delight Athena? Where was the enormous velarium Nero stretched over the Colosseum, that Titanic purple sail depicting the starry heavens with Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white steeds harnessed with gilded reins? He yearned to behold the strange table-napery wrought for the Priest of the Sun, showing all the delicacies and dishes one could desire at a feast; the funeral cloth of King Chilperic with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastical garments that enraged the Bishop of Pontus and were ornamented with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—in fact, every subject a painter may copy from nature”; and the coat once worn by Charles of Orleans, whose sleeves were embroidered with the verses of a song beginning “Madame, je suis tout joyeux,” the musical accompaniment stitched in golden thread and every note, of the square form then in vogue, created with four pearls. He read of the chamber arranged in the palace at Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, broided and emblazoned with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, their wings similarly adorned with the queen’s arms, the whole executed in gold.” Catherine de Médicis had a mourning-bed fashioned for her from black velvet dusted with crescents and suns. Its curtains were damask, with leafy wreaths and garlands figured on a ground of gold and silver, edged with pearl embroidery, and it stood in a room hung with ranks of the queen’s emblems cut in black velvet upon cloth of silver. Louis XIV possessed gold-embroidered caryatids fifteen feet tall in his suite."}
