{"request_id":"6b8c7055ffe371c5ae98b8f5","rewritten_text":"“Yes, burglar’s tools. That seems to calm you a lot. But what did you expect we’d found?”

Huck was cornered with that sharp look on him. He would have given anything for a believable answer. Nothing came. The stare drilled deeper. A foolish reply surfaced. There was no time to judge it, so he blurted it out weakly: “Sunday-school books, maybe.”

Huck was too upset to smile, but the old man laughed loud and happy, his whole body shaking, and said such laughter was worth money because it cut down the doctor’s bill. Then he added, “Poor fellow, you’re pale and worn out—you’re not well at all, no wonder you’re a little light-headed. But you’ll be fine. Rest and sleep will set you right, I hope.”

Huck fumed at himself for being such a fool and showing so much nervous excitement, because he had already dropped the idea that the bundle from the tavern was the treasure as soon as he heard the talk at the widow’s stile. He had only thought it probably wasn’t the treasure—he hadn’t known for sure—and the hint of a captured bundle was too much for his self-control. Still, he felt glad the little scene had happened, because now he knew for certain that bundle was not the bundle, and his mind was calm and comfortable. Everything felt like it was moving the right way now. The treasure must still be in No. 2, the men would be arrested that day, and he and Tom could grab the gold that night without trouble or fear of being interrupted.

Just as breakfast ended there was a knock at the door. Huck jumped to hide, not wanting to be connected in any way with the recent event. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas, and saw groups of townsfolk climbing the hill to stare at the stile. So the word had gotten out. The Welshman had to tell the night’s story to the visitors. The widow spoke openly of her gratitude for being saved.

“Don’t say a word about it, ma’am. There’s someone else you owe more to than me and my boys, maybe, but he won’t let me tell his name. We wouldn’t have been there without him.”"}

{"request_id":"86882a14de5ed4d19ab9e90f","rewritten_text":"Mr. Elliot looking up with so much respect.”

“Absolutely delightful!” cried Mrs. Clay, though she didn’t dare turn her eyes toward Anne. “Exactly like a father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, may I call you father and son?”

“Oh, I don’t forbid anyone’s words. If you insist on such notions! But honestly, I barely notice his attentions being any more than other men’s.”

“My dear Miss Elliot!” exclaimed Mrs. Clay, raising her hands and eyes and letting the rest of her astonishment sink into a discreet silence.

“Well, my dear Penelope, you don’t have to be so concerned about him. I did invite him, you know. I sent him away smiling. When I found he was really going to spend the whole day tomorrow with his friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.”

Anne admired her friend’s skill in showing such pleasure at the expectation and actual arrival of the very person whose presence must truly interfere with her primary goal. It was impossible that Mrs. Clay didn’t hate the sight of Mr. Elliot; yet she could put on such a pleasant, calm face and seem perfectly satisfied with the shortened freedom of devoting only half as much attention to Sir Walter as she otherwise would.

For Anne, it was truly distressing to watch Mr. Elliot enter the room, and quite painful to have him approach and speak to her. She had already suspected he wasn’t always sincere, but now she saw nothing but insincerity. His respectful attention to her father, so at odds with his earlier remarks, was revolting; and when she thought of his cruel behavior toward Mrs. Smith, she could hardly tolerate the sight of his current smiles and gentleness, or the sound of his artificial pleasantries.

She meant to avoid any change in manner that might provoke a protest from him. It was vitally important to her to escape any questioning or commotion; but she intended to be as decidedly cool toward him as their relationship allowed, and to quietly retrace the few steps of unnecessary intimacy she had been gradually led into. She was accordingly more guarded and more distant than she had been the night before.

He wanted to rekindle her curiosity about how and where he’d once heard her praised; he wanted very much to enjoy more urging from her. But the spell was broken: he discovered that the heat and energy of a crowded room had been necessary to spark his modest cousin’s vanity; or at least, he found it couldn’t be done now, not with any of the efforts he dared make amid the stronger claims of the others."}

{"request_id":"0baa5a04830afae55c73bf57","rewritten_text":"But enough of that. I will begin my story: it is my last duty, and I hope I have the strength to finish it. I confess no crimes; my mistakes may be forgiven, for they came not from malice but from poor judgment, and I believe few would claim they could, with wiser choices, have avoided the misery that has claimed me. My fate has been ruled by necessity, a dreadful necessity. It would have taken hands stronger than mine—stronger than any human hands, I think—to break the thick, iron chain that has kept me, once full of joy and love of goodness, bound to a misery that ends only now, with death. But I wander; my story remains untold. I will pause, wipe my dim eyes, and try to trade this dull yet heavy sorrow for the sharper feelings of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank: he lost his father early and was raised by a weak mother who gave him all the indulgence she thought due a wealthy noble. He was sent to Eton and then to college, and from childhood he enjoyed the free use of large sums of money, gaining from the start the independence that a boy with such advantages always finds at a public school.

Under these conditions his passions found rich ground where they could take root and grow as flowers or weeds, depending on their nature. Always left to act for himself, his character became distinct very early, showing many facets where a sharp observer could see the seeds of both virtues and misfortunes. His careless extravagance, which made him waste immense sums to satisfy passing whims he glorified as passions, often showed itself in boundless generosity. Yet while he busied himself with the needs of others, his own desires were satisfied entirely. He gave his money, but no wish of his own was sacrificed for others; he gave his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was eager to have engaged in any way.

I do not claim that, had his own desires been set against those of others, he would have shown undue selfishness, but he never faced that test. Raised in prosperity and surrounded by its blessings, he was loved by everyone, and everyone wanted to please him."}

{"request_id":"04ef759e2728d299b470a7e9","rewritten_text":"His manner was stubborn to the extreme, and “dat deuced bug” were the only words he spoke along the way. I carried two dark lanterns, while Legrand made do with the scarab, which he had tied to the end of a bit of whip-cord. He swung it back and forth like a magician. Seeing this latest sign of his unbalanced mind, I could barely keep from tears. I decided it was best to indulge his whim for now, at least until I could find a better plan that might work. Meanwhile I tried, without success, to get him to talk about the point of the expedition. After persuading me to come, he refused to talk about anything less than essential, answering every question with “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the head of the island in a small skiff and climbed the high land on the mainland shore. Then we headed northwest through a stretch of country so wild and lonely that there was no sign any person had ever passed there. Legrand walked ahead with purpose, stopping only now and then to check what seemed to be landmarks he had set on some earlier trip.

In this way we traveled for about two hours, and the sun was just setting when we reached a region even more desolate than any we had seen. It was a kind of plateau near the top of an almost unreachable hill, thickly wooded from bottom to peak, broken by giant crags that seemed to rest loosely on the ground and, in many cases, were kept from sliding into the valleys only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines ran in several directions, giving the scene an even grimmer solemnity.

The natural platform we had climbed was choked with brambles. We soon learned we could not force our way through without a scythe, so Jupiter, on his master’s orders, cut a path for us to the base of an enormously tall tulip-tree. It stood on the level with eight or ten oaks, towering over them all and over any tree I had ever seen in the grace of its leaves and shape, the spread of its branches, and its general majesty."}

content.text: {"request_id":"adefe5397eee756bada6bbf2","rewritten_text":"“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped it, showing he thought Joseph was lacking. “But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be hungry, you must be tired. Sit down. Here’s a chicken from the Boar, here’s a tongue from the Boar, here are one or two other little things from the Boar, which I hope you won’t disdain. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, springing up again as soon as he sat, “see before me the one I always played with in his happy childhood? And may I—may I—?” He meant to ask if he could shake hands. I agreed, and he shook my hand warmly before sitting again. “Here is wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink, thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favourites wisely! And yet I cannot,” he said, rising yet again, “see before me someone—and drink to someone—without again asking—May I—may I—?” I said he could, and he shook my hand again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same, and the wine went straight to my head as if I had stood on it first. Mr. Pumblechook served me the liver wing and the best slice of tongue (none of those odd back streets of pork now), and took little for himself. “Ah! poultry, poultry! Little did you think,” he told the bird in the dish, “when you were a young chick, what awaited you. You never thought you would be refreshment under this humble roof for one who—Call it a weakness if you like,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? may I—?” It was soon pointless to keep saying he could, so he just did it. I wonder how he managed so many handshakes without cutting himself on my knife. “And your sister,” he went on after eating steadily, “who had the honour of raising you by hand! It’s a sad picture to think she can no longer fully understand that honour. May—” I saw he was coming at me again and stopped him. “We’ll drink her health,” I said. “Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, sinking back in his chair, limp with admiration, “that’s how you know them, sir!” (I don’t know who sir was, but it wasn’t me and there was no third person there.) “That’s how you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"87b379be38fbbda7f87349af","rewritten_text":"She suddenly felt a strong urge to go to the front door; she wanted to check if it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of another motive? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight by now. She left her seat—she would go. One half of her would not keep acting wiser than the other, always doubting its own intentions. She would see if it was raining. But she was sent back almost immediately when Captain Wentworth himself walked in with a group of men and women, clearly his acquaintances, whom he must have met a little way down Milsom Street. He was more obviously startled and unsettled by the sight of her than she had ever noticed before; his face flushed. For the first time since they had renewed their acquaintance, she felt she was the one showing the slightest emotion. She had the advantage of a few moments’ preparation. The overwhelming, blinding, bewildering first shock had already passed for her. Yet she still had plenty to feel—agitation, pain, pleasure, something between delight and misery.

He spoke to her and then turned away. His manner was marked by embarrassment. She could not have called it cold or friendly, only embarrassed.

After a short pause he returned and spoke again. They exchanged polite questions on ordinary topics: neither likely gained much from the answers, and Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than before. From being so constantly around each other, they had learned to speak with apparent calm and indifference, but he could not manage it now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. There was some kind of self-consciousness about him. He looked very well—not as if he had been suffering physically or emotionally—and he talked of Uppercross, of the Musgroves, even of Louisa, with a fleeting hint of his old mischievous expression as he mentioned her; but it was still Captain Wentworth uncomfortable, uneasy, unable to pretend otherwise.

It did not surprise Anne, but it pained her, that Elizabeth refused to acknowledge him. She saw that he saw Elizabeth, and that Elizabeth saw him, that there was perfect mutual recognition; she was certain he was ready to be recognized, expecting it, and she had the anguish of watching her sister turn away with unwavering coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was growing very impatient, now pulled up, and the servant entered to announce it."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5ec64e71663ecee1b0438345","rewritten_text":"“Oh, hang my hat! I want Virginia!” shouted the little Duke with a laugh, and they galloped on to the train station. There Mr. Otis asked the station master if anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but no one had. The station master telegraphed up and down the line and promised a strict watch for her; after Mr. Otis bought a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper closing his shop, he rode off to Bexley, a village about four miles away, said to be a favorite gypsy hangout because of the big common nearby. They woke the local policeman, but he knew nothing, and after riding all over the common they turned their horses toward home, reaching the Chase around eleven, exhausted and nearly heartbroken. Washington and the twins were waiting for them at the gatehouse with lanterns, since the avenue was very dark. There was no sign of Virginia. The gypsies had been caught on Brockley meadows, but she wasn’t with them; they explained their sudden departure by saying they had mistaken the date of Chorton Fair and rushed off for fear of being late. They were sincerely upset to hear Virginia was missing, grateful as they were to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of them had stayed behind to help search. The carp pond had been dredged, and the entire Chase thoroughly explored, but to no effect. Clearly, for that night at least, Virginia was lost to them, and in the deepest gloom Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, the groom following with the two horses and the pony. In the hall they found a cluster of terrified servants, and in the library poor Mrs. Otis lay on a sofa, nearly out of her mind with fear and worry, while the old housekeeper bathed her forehead with cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted she eat something and ordered supper for everyone. It was a mournful meal; hardly anyone spoke, and even the twins were hushed and subdued, being very fond of their sister. When they finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleading, sent everyone to bed, saying nothing more could be done that night and that he would telegraph Scotland Yard in the morning to send detectives at once."}

content.text: {"request_id":"698094160ac784eecbb48ccd","rewritten_text":"It was the opening of February; and Anne, having already spent a month in Bath, grew restless for tidings from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted far more than Mary’s scant report. Three weeks had gone by without any word. All she knew was that Henrietta had returned to the family home; that Louisa—though pronounced to be mending quickly—remained in Lyme; and she was thinking of them all very earnestly one evening when a thicker-than-usual letter from Mary was handed to her, enlivened further by Admiral and Mrs Croft’s compliments. The Crofts must be in Bath! That was something to engage her. They were people toward whom her heart readily turned. “What’s this?” exclaimed Sir Walter. “The Crofts are come to Bath? The very Crofts who lease Kellynch? What have they sent you?” “A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.” “Oh, such letters serve excellently as passports. They ensure one’s presentation. I should have called on Admiral Croft regardless. I am aware of what is due to my tenant.” Anne could not listen a moment longer; she would not even have known how the poor Admiral’s complexion fared; her letter had seized all her thoughts. It had been begun some days earlier. “February 1st. “MY DEAR ANNE, “I make no excuses for my silence, because I know how little people value letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too amused to care about Uppercross, which, as you well know, offers very little to set down. We have passed a wretchedly dull Christmas; Mr and Mrs Musgrove did not give a single dinner party the whole season. I do not count the Hayters as anybody. However, the holidays are finally ended: I do not believe any children ever had such lengthy ones. I know I never did. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be astonished to learn they have never gone home. Mrs Harville must be a queer sort of mother to part with them so long. I do not understand it. They are by no means pleasant children, to my mind; yet Mrs Musgrove seems to like them at least as well as, if not better than, her own grandchildren. What dreadful weather we have endured! It may not be felt in Bath, with your fine pavements; but in the country it matters a good deal. Not a soul has called on me since the second week of January, except Charles Hayter, who has been coming much more often than agreeable. Between ourselves, I think it is a great pity that Henrietta did not stay at Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little out of his path.”"}

{"request_id":"84af30a895bc81bc574b69bb","rewritten_text":"“Well, that’s how everyone does it, Huck.”

“Tom, it doesn’t matter. I ain’t everyone, and I can’t stand it. Being tied up like that is awful. And food comes too easy—I don’t care about eating when it’s like that. I have to ask if I want to go fishing; I have to ask if I want to go swimming—damn it if I don’t have to ask to do everything. And I’ve got to talk so polite it’s no comfort—I’ve got to sneak up to the attic and swear a while every day just to get a taste in my mouth, or I’d die, Tom. The widow wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me shout, she wouldn’t let me yawn, or stretch, or scratch in front of folks—” He flared with a fresh burst of irritation and hurt. “And blast it all, she prayed all the time! I never saw such a woman! I had to run, Tom—I just had to. Besides, school’s about to start, and I’d have had to go—well, I wouldn’t stand that, Tom. Look here, Tom, being rich isn’t what it’s cracked up to be. It’s nothing but worry and sweat and wishing you were dead all the time. These clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I ain’t ever giving them up. Tom, I wouldn’t have landed in all this trouble if it hadn’t been for that money; now you take my share along with yours, and give me a ten-cent piece once in a while—not too often, because I don’t care a lick for anything unless it’s hard to get—and go beg off with the widow for me.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It wouldn’t be right; and besides, if you’d try this a little longer, you’d come to like it.”

“Like it! Yeah—the way I’d like a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed stuffy houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick to them. Blame it! Just when we got guns, and a cave, and everything ready for robbing, this foolishness has to come up and ruin it!”

Tom saw his chance.

“Look, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good grief; are you dead serious, Tom?”

“Just as serious as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you join the gang if you ain’t respectable, you know.”

Huck’s joy was doused.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"386ae0736533763607b38cae","rewritten_text":"He let her know that Frank admired her greatly—thought her very beautiful and very charming; and with so much to recommend him overall, she felt she had no right to judge him harshly. As Mrs. Weston remarked, “all young people will have their little whims.”

There was one person among his new acquaintances in Surrey who was not so forgiving. Generally he was judged throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury with great fairness; people made generous allowances for the small excesses of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so often and bowed so well. But there was one mind among them that bows or smiles could not soften or distract from criticizing—Mr. Knightley. The news was brought to him at Hartfield; for a moment he was silent, but Emma heard him almost at once mutter to himself, over a newspaper he held, “Hum! Just the trifling, silly fellow I took him for.” She half thought of taking offense, but a quick look convinced her he said it only to ease his own feelings, not to provoke anyone; so she let it go.

Though in one instance they brought less pleasing news, Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit that morning was in another way especially well timed. Something occurred while they were at Hartfield that made Emma seek their advice; and, even better, she wanted exactly the guidance they offered.

This was the situation: The Coles had lived in Highbury for several years and were very decent people—friendly, generous, and unpretentious. Yet they were from a lower background, involved in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first came to the country, they lived within their income, quietly, entertaining little, and that modestly; but the past year or two had brought them a large increase of wealth. Their town business had yielded higher profits, and fortune in general had favored them. With their wealth, their ambitions grew: they wanted a larger house, more company. They enlarged their home, hired more servants, and increased their expenses in every area; by now they were, in fortune and style of living, second only to the family at Hartfield. Their love of society, along with their new dining room, prepared everyone to expect them to host dinner parties; a few gatherings, mostly of single men, had already happened. Emma could hardly imagine they would dare invite the regular and best families—neither Donwell, nor Hartfield, nor Randalls. Nothing would tempt her to go if they did; and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal carry less weight than she wished."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3d9d20123cf3472e2f7eb9fa","rewritten_text":"Once our friend was settled in his new office, we turned our attention toward Windsor. Its nearness to London eased the sting of leaving Raymond and Perdita. We said goodbye in the Protectoral Palace. It was amusing to watch my sister immerse herself in the part she had to play, trying to hold her new position with suitable dignity. Her pride and her modest demeanor clashed like never before. Her shyness was genuine, born from a fear of being misjudged and from her tendency to shrug off the world’s neglect, traits she shared with Raymond. Yet Perdita thought of others more than he did; some of her bashfulness came from wanting to spare the people around her from feeling inferior—an idea she never applied to herself. Idris, thanks to her birth and upbringing, would have fit more naturally into ceremonial rituals; but her habitual ease made such tasks dull, while Perdita enjoyed her new role despite its drawbacks. Filled with fresh ideas, she barely felt sorrow at our departure. She kissed us goodbye lovingly, promised to visit soon, and did not resent the necessity for our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless; he had no idea what to do with his newly gained power. His mind overflowed with plans, though none were settled yet. He promised himself, his friends, and the world that his time as Protector would be marked by some act of extraordinary glory. So we spoke of them and reflected as our diminished party returned to Windsor Castle. Glad to have escaped political turbulence, we hurried toward solitude with doubled enthusiasm. We had plenty to occupy us; my restless nature now expressed itself through sheer intellectual effort, and rigorous study proved a perfect remedy for the fevered energy that would have plagued me in idleness. Perdita allowed us to bring Clara back to Windsor; she and my two beautiful infants became endless sources of interest and joy.\n\nOnly one thing disturbed our peace: Adrian’s health. It clearly declined, yet no symptom revealed the disease, unless his shining eyes, animated features, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption. Still, he felt neither pain nor dread. He threw himself into books, and when he needed rest, he found it with those he loved best—his sister and me."}

{"request_id":"4406be45206009f468e4c1ac","rewritten_text":"Three or four months went by, and winter settled in. I had been in school most of that time and could spell, read, and write a little, and I could recite the times table up to six times seven is thirty-five. I don’t think I could ever go further, even if I lived forever. I never cared for arithmetic, anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I could stand it. Whenever I got extra tired I skipped, and the whipping I got the next day did me good and lifted my spirits. The longer I stayed in school, the easier it became. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they didn’t rub me so hard. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed still pressed on me, but before the weather turned cold I would slip out sometimes and sleep in the woods, and that gave me a rest. I liked the old ways best, but I was beginning to like the new ones a little, too. The widow said I was improving slow but steady and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I knocked over the salt cellar. I reached for some salt fast, wanting to toss it over my left shoulder to ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson got there first and stopped me. She said, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; you’re always making a mess!” The widow spoke up for me, but that couldn’t keep bad luck away, and I knew it. After breakfast I went out feeling worried and shaky, wondering where the trouble would land on me and what it would be. There are ways to keep off certain kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of them, so I didn’t try anything. I just walked along, low and watchful.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile that led through the tall board fence. An inch of fresh snow lay on the ground, and I saw someone’s tracks. They had come up from the quarry, lingered around the stile for a while, then gone on around the garden fence. It seemed strange that after waiting there they hadn’t come in. I couldn’t figure it out. It felt mighty odd, somehow. I meant to follow the track around, but first I crouched to study it."}

content.text: {"request_id":"54b2fec947e46fcb117f7a63","rewritten_text":"We both loved Adrian, though she was still too young to fully appreciate his gifts or share my sympathy for his pursuits and opinions. I spent all my time with him. His sensitivity and sweetness gave our conversations a tender, otherworldly quality. Then he could be as cheerful as a lark singing from its perch in the sky, his thoughts soaring like an eagle, as innocent as a gentle dove. He could shake Perdita out of her seriousness and soothe the restless drive that tormented me. I looked back on my own frustrated desires and harsh struggles with others like a troubled dream, and I felt as transformed as if I had moved into another body, whose fresh senses and nervous system showed the world differently in the mirror of the mind. Yet it wasn’t so; I was still the same in strength, in my hunger for sympathy, in my need for action. My manly virtues remained, for the sorceress Urania spared Samson’s hair while he slept at her feet; only everything was softened and humanized. Nor did Adrian teach me merely the dry facts of history and philosophy. As he used them to help me rein in my reckless, untamed spirit, he also opened the living page of his own heart and let me feel and understand its strange nature.\n\nThe former queen of England had tried, even when he was a child, to plant daring and ambitious plans in her son’s mind. She saw that he had genius and exceptional talent; she cultivated these so she could later use them to serve her own purposes. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even tolerated his untamed love of freedom, hoping it would, as so often happens, turn into a craving for power. She tried to raise him with a sense of grievance and a desire to avenge himself on those who had brought about his father’s abdication. In this she failed. Accounts—however distorted—of a great and wise people asserting their right to govern themselves stirred his admiration: from early on he became a republican by principle. Yet his mother didn’t lose hope. To her love of authority and proud sense of birth she added iron determination, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying her son’s temperament. By using praise, criticism, and exhortation, she tried to find and strike the right chords; and though the music she produced sounded like discord to her, she pinned her hopes on his abilities and remained convinced she would ultimately bend him to her will."}

{"request_id":"e8444f9f594987611ee3996f","rewritten_text":"“Heavens above!” the Duchess murmured to herself. “So he really is some kind of cheiropodist, after all. How utterly dreadful. I do hope he turns out to be a foreigner—at least that would soften it a little.”

“I simply must introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” exclaimed the Duchess. “You don’t mean he is actually here?” She began hunting for a little tortoise-shell fan and a very frayed lace shawl, so she could leave at a moment’s notice.

“Why, naturally he is here; I should never think of hosting a party without him. He assures me my hand is psychically pure, and that if my thumb had been the tiniest fraction shorter, I would have become a hopeless pessimist and entered a convent.”

“Oh, now I understand!” said the Duchess, greatly comforted. “He tells fortunes, does he?”

“And misfortunes, too,” replied Lady Windermere. “Some in abundance. Next year, for instance, I face terrible peril both on land and sea, so I plan to live in a balloon and hoist up my dinner in a basket every night. It is written on my little finger, or else on my palm—I forget which.”

“But surely that is tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence has learned to resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their palms read monthly, just to know what they ought not to do. Of course we go and do it anyway, but at least the warning is delightful. If someone doesn’t fetch Mr. Podgers this instant, I shall be forced to fetch him myself.”

“Allow me, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man who had been listening nearby with an amused smile.

“Thank you, Lord Arthur, but I fear you would not recognize him.”

“If he is as exceptional as you claim, Lady Windermere, I cannot fail to notice him. Tell me his appearance, and I’ll bring him straight to you.”

“Well, he doesn’t resemble a cheiromantist in the least. Not in the mysterious, esoteric, or romantic sense. He is a short, stout fellow, with a comical bald head and large gold spectacles; somewhere between a family physician and a village solicitor. I am truly sorry, but it isn’t my doing. People are so tiresome. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look just like pianists; and I recall last season inviting an appalling conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up ever so many people, wore a coat of mail, and kept a dagger up his sleeve—and would you believe that when he arrived he resembled a pleasant old clergyman and spent the evening telling jokes?”"}

{"request_id":"753e657a8f62df1f072141f1","rewritten_text":"One day while I was working on my studies with Mr. Pocket, a letter arrived by post, and just seeing the envelope set my heart racing; though I’d never seen the handwriting addressing it, I knew whose hand it was. It had no formal opening like Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, or anything of the kind, but simply read:

“I’m coming to London the day after tomorrow on the midday coach. I believe it was agreed you’d meet me? In any case Miss Havisham believes so, and I’m writing because she told me to. She sends her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If I’d had time, I probably would have ordered several new suits for the occasion; but since I didn’t, I had to make do with what I already owned. My appetite vanished on the spot, and I couldn’t find a moment’s peace until the day came. That didn’t make things any better; in fact, I was worse than ever, and I started haunting the coach office in Wood Street, Cheapside, long before the coach had even left the Blue Boar back home. Even though I knew this perfectly well, I still felt it would be unsafe to let the coach office out of my sight for more than five minutes at a time; and in this irrational state I had completed the first half-hour of a four or five-hour vigil when Wemmick bumped into me.

“Hello, Mr. Pip,” he said. “How are you? I wouldn’t have thought this was your usual territory.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and I asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both doing well, thank you,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He’s in splendid spirits. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I’m thinking of firing eighty-two rounds, if the neighbors don’t complain and that cannon of mine can handle the strain. Still, that’s not London talk. Where do you think I’m headed?”

“To the office?” I suggested, since he was headed that way.

“Close enough,” Wemmick replied. “I’m going to Newgate. We have a banker’s parcel case on right now, and I’ve been down the road having a look at the scene of the crime, and now I need a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Good heavens, no,” Wemmick replied very dryly. “But he’s accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us could be accused, you know.”"}

“Tell me why?”

“For one reason,” the girl said firmly, “because the lady knows everything and will support me. I have her promise. And another reason is that, bad as his life has been, mine has been bad too. Many of us have followed the same path together, and I won’t betray them. They could have betrayed me, but they didn’t, even though they’re bad.”

“Then,” said the gentleman quickly, as if this was what he had aimed for, “turn Monks over to me and let me handle him.”

“What if he betrays the others?”

“I promise you, if he is forced to tell the truth, that will be the end of it. There must be things in Oliver’s small history that would be painful to make public, and once the truth is out, they will go free.”

“And if it isn’t?” the girl asked.

“Then,” the gentleman continued, “Fagin will not be brought to justice without your consent. If that happens, I could show you reasons that would convince you.”

“Do I have the lady’s promise on that?” asked the girl.

“You do,” Rose replied. “My sincere and faithful pledge.”

“Monks would never learn how you found out what you know?” the girl asked after a brief pause.

“Never,” said the gentleman. “The information will be used against him in such a way that he could never guess.”

“I have been a liar among liars since I was a child,” the girl said after another pause. “But I’ll trust your words.”

After both assured her it was safe, she described, in a voice so low the listener often struggled to catch the meaning, the public house where she had been followed that night, including its name and location. From her pauses, it seemed the gentleman was making quick notes. Once she had explained the layout, the best place to watch without being noticed, and the night and hour when Monks most often visited, she paused a moment, trying to picture his face more clearly.

“He is tall,” the girl said, “a strong man but not heavy. He moves with a wary gait, always looking over his shoulder first to one side, then the other.”"}

{"request_id":"8b76f6d418759601c85af781","rewritten_text":"Just as they were leaving the dining-room, midnight commenced booming from the clock tower, and with the last stroke came a crash and a piercing scream; a terrible peal of thunder shook the house, uncanny music drifted through the air, a panel at the staircase’s summit flew open with a loud report, and onto the landing stepped Virginia, pale and white, holding a little casket. In an instant they all hurried toward her. Mrs. Otis clasped her fervently to her heart, the Duke covered her with frantic kisses, and the twins whirled around them in a wild war-dance.

“Good heavens! child, where have you been?” Mr. Otis demanded rather sharply, convinced she had been playing some foolish prank. “Cecil and I have been riding everywhere looking for you, and your mother has nearly died of fright. You must never try such practical jokes again.”

“Except on the Ghost! except on the Ghost!” cried the twins, dancing about.

“My darling, thank God you are found; you must never leave me again,” murmured Mrs. Otis, kissing the trembling girl and smoothing the tangled gold of her hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come and see him. He had been very wicked, but he was truly sorry for all he had done, and before he died he gave me this box of lovely jewels.”

The whole family stared at her in stunned silence, yet she remained solemn and composed; turning about, she led them through the gap in the wainscot along a narrow hidden passage, Washington following with a candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a heavy oak door studded with rusty nails. The moment Virginia touched it, it swung back on massive hinges, and they stepped into a small low chamber with a vaulted ceiling and a single tiny barred window. Set into the wall was a great iron ring, and fastened to it lay a gaunt skeleton, stretched full length on the stone floor, its long fleshless fingers seeming to reach for an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just beyond its grasp. The jug had clearly once held water, for green mould lined its interior. On the trencher there remained only a mound of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her little hands, and began to pray silently, while the rest of the company watched in awe the grim tragedy whose secret had now been revealed to them."}

{"request_id":"64ec9dfc9bd36b4b20e6f2f8","rewritten_text":"Had she known her sister wanted to pull her away from such hopes and circumstances, what would she have felt? Only her mother, who likely would have felt almost the same, could have understood. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was the only thing that eased her sorrowful certainty that her husband never meant to go there himself.

Yet none of them knew what had happened, and their excitement went on, with hardly a pause, until the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. She had often been in his company since her return, so her nerves were mostly calm; the feelings of earlier fondness were gone completely. She had even learned to see in the very gentleness that first charmed her a showiness and monotony that now annoyed and tired her. His current conduct toward her gave her fresh annoyance, because his quick desire to revive the attentions of their early acquaintance could now only irritate her. She lost all concern for him when she found herself picked out for such empty, trivial flirtation; and while she firmly discouraged him, she could not help feeling the rebuke in his believing that, after however long and for whatever reason his attentions had ceased, her vanity would still be pleased and her preference won at any time by their renewal.

On the regiment’s final day in Meryton, he dined with other officers at Longbourn; and Elizabeth was so unwilling to part on friendly terms that when he asked about her time at Hunsford, she told him Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked if he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, and alarmed; but after a brief pause and a returning smile, he answered that he used to see him often, and after noting that he was a very gentlemanlike man, asked how she had liked him. Her reply praised him warmly. With an air of indifference he then added, “How long did you say he stayed at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves once you know him.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, giving her a look she noticed. “And may I ask—” but stopping himself, he went on in a lighter tone, “Is it in his manner that he improves?”"}

{"request_id":"7361aa1d335136a8eac849f4","rewritten_text":"“But do not think I did not feel it was an evil in itself.”

“Depend on it, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I might not like them any better for that. So many women and children have no right to be comfortable on board.”

“My dear Frederick, you are talking nonsense. What would become of us sailors’ wives, who often need to be carried from one port to another after our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“My feelings, you see, did not stop me from taking Mrs Harville and her whole family to Plymouth.”

“But I cannot bear to hear you talking like a fine gentleman, as if women were all fine ladies instead of sensible creatures. None of us expect smooth water every day.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has a wife, he will sing another tune. Once he is married, if we live to see another war, we will see him doing what you and I, and many others, have done. He will be very grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Ay, that we shall.”

“Now I have done,” cried Captain Wentworth. “When married people start in on me with, ‘You will feel differently once you are married,’ I can only say, ‘No, I shall not.’ Then they say again, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that ends it.”

He rose and walked away.

“What a great traveler you must have been, ma’am!” said Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Pretty well, ma’am, in the fifteen years of my marriage, though many women have done more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times, and once went to the East Indies and back, besides visiting places nearer home—Cork, Lisbon, Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Straits, and never was in the West Indies. We do not call Bermuda or Bahama the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs Musgrove had nothing to say in disagreement; she could not remember ever calling them anything at all.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” continued Mrs Croft, “nothing can beat the accommodations of a man-of-war. I speak of the higher rates. In a frigate, of course, you are more confined, though any sensible woman can be perfectly happy there; and I can honestly say the happiest part of my life was spent on board ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.”"}

{"request_id":"730ae2abc8e1ffab6d24c597","rewritten_text":"Besides sailors, almost no one can tie this knot, and it seems to be unique to the Maltese. I picked the ribbon up at the base of the lightning rod. It couldn’t have belonged to either victim. Even if I am wrong in deducing from this ribbon that the Frenchman was a sailor serving on a Maltese ship, I did no harm by mentioning it in the advertisement. If I am mistaken, he’ll just think I was misled by some detail and won’t bother to look into it. But if I’m right, we gain a great advantage. The Frenchman, although aware of the crime yet innocent of it, will naturally hesitate before replying to the advertisement or demanding the orangutan. He will think, “I’m innocent; I’m poor; my orangutan is extremely valuable—practically a fortune for me. Why should I lose it because of needless fears? It’s here, within reach. It was found in the Bois de Boulogne, far from the scene of the slaughter. Who would ever suspect a mere animal of such a deed? The police are baffled—they haven’t found a single clue. Even if they track the animal, they can’t prove I knew about the murder or involve me because of that knowledge. Above all, I am known. The advertiser identifies me as the beast’s owner. I don’t know how much he really knows. If I avoid claiming my valuable property, which people know I possess, I’ll make the animal itself seem suspicious. It’s not wise to draw attention to myself or to the creature. I’ll answer the advertisement, recover the orangutan, and hide it until the fuss dies down.”

At that moment we heard a step on the stairs.

“Be ready,” said Dupin. “Have your pistols, but don’t use or show them until I give the signal.”

We had left the front door open, and the visitor entered without ringing and came several steps up the staircase. He seemed to hesitate, and soon we heard him going down again. Dupin was heading quickly to the door when we heard the man climbing back up. This time he didn’t retreat; he came up confidently and knocked on our chamber door.

“Come in,” said Dupin, cheerful and hearty.

A man entered. He was clearly a sailor—a tall, strong, muscular fellow with a daredevil look that was not entirely unattractive."}

{"request_id":"1e030f432742e41c27f08aad","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, one might have sworn that Nemesis had filched the shield of Pallas and displayed the Gorgon’s visage to him. He appeared turned to stone, his face marble-like in its sorrow. He had led the delicate, opulent existence of a young man of lineage and wealth, a life exquisite for its freedom from sordid anxieties, its charming boyish indifference; and now, for the first time, he became aware of Destiny’s dreadful mystery, of Doom’s alarming significance.

How insane and grotesque it all appeared! Could it be that inscribed upon his hand, in characters unreadable to himself yet legible to another, there lay some horrible secret of guilt, some scarlet sign of crime? Was there no possible escape? Were we nothing better than chess pieces, shifted by an invisible force, vessels shaped by the potter’s whim, for honour or for disgrace? His reason rebelled against the thought, yet he felt some catastrophe hovered above him, and that he had suddenly been summoned to bear an intolerable load. Actors are fortunate indeed. They can decide whether they will show themselves in tragedy or comedy, whether to suffer or make merry, to laugh or to weep. In real life it is not so. Most men and women must act roles for which they possess no fitness. Our Guildensterns perform Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets must jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, yet the casting is wretched.

Abruptly Mr. Podgers came into the room. At the sight of Lord Arthur he started, and his coarse, flabby face turned a sort of greenish yellow. The two men locked eyes, and for an instant there was silence.

“The Duchess has left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and has asked me to fetch it,” said Mr. Podgers at last. “Ah, there it is on the sofa! Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me a direct answer to a question I am about to ask.”

“Another time, Lord Arthur; the Duchess is uneasy. I fear I must depart.”

“You shall not go. The Duchess can wait.”

“Ladies should not be detained, Lord Arthur,” replied Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. “The fair sex is apt to grow impatient.”

Lord Arthur’s finely cut lips curled with petulant scorn. The poor Duchess seemed to him of no moment at all. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and put out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw there,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I must know it. I am not a child.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"6d3ffd68d9d73f493bda70eb","rewritten_text":"He couldn’t help it. It drove him crazy to think Becky Thatcher didn’t even suspect he was alive. But she saw, and she knew she was winning, and she was glad to watch him suffer as she had.  Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted that he had things to do, that time was short. It didn’t work—the girl kept chirping. Tom thought, “Oh, hang her, will I never get rid of her?” Finally he had to be off to those errands—and she innocently said she would be “around” when school let out. He hurried away, hating her for it.  “Any other boy!” Tom thought, grinding his teeth. “Any boy in town but that Saint Louis fop who thinks he dresses so fine and is high society! All right, I beat you the first day you ever saw this town, mister, and I’ll beat you again! Just wait till I catch you! I’ll just—”  He acted out a fight with an imaginary boy—pounding the air, kicking and gouging. “Oh, you do, do you? You yell enough, do you? There, let that teach you!” He finished the imaginary whipping to his satisfaction.  Tom bolted home at noon. His conscience couldn’t stand any more of Amy’s thankful cheer, and his jealousy couldn’t take any more of the other torment. Becky went back to looking at pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes crawled and no Tom showed up to suffer, her victory started to fade and she lost interest; she grew solemn and distracted, then sad. Two or three times she perked up at a footstep, but it was wishful thinking. No Tom came. At last she felt completely miserable and wished she hadn’t pushed things so far. When poor Alfred, seeing he was losing her and not knowing why, kept saying, “Oh, here’s a jolly one! Look at this!” she finally lost patience and cried, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care for them!” She burst into tears, stood up, and walked away.  Alfred caught up beside her and was about to try comforting her, but she cried, “Go away and leave me alone, can’t you! I hate you!”  So he stopped, not knowing what he had done—she had said she would look at pictures all through the noon break—and she walked on, crying. Then Alfred went pondering into the empty schoolhouse. He felt humiliated and angry. He easily guessed the truth—the girl had used him just to work out her spite on Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"431c32647584dc6ab6074f4e","rewritten_text":"Yet he had wronged no one, jailed no one; far from collecting what he was owed with harsh insistence, he had willingly given it up, casting himself into a world that offered him no favor, earning his own place there, and working for his own bread. Monsieur Gabelle had managed the bankrupt and tangled estate under written orders to spare the people, to give them what little could be given—whatever firewood the heavy creditors allowed in winter, and whatever produce could be rescued from their clutches in summer—and no doubt he had stated and proved this for his own protection, so it would inevitably come to light now.

This supported the desperate decision Charles Darnay had begun to form: he would go to Paris.

Yes. Like the sailor from the old tale, winds and currents had carried him within the pull of the Loadstone Rock, which now drew him irresistibly, and he had to go. Everything that rose in his mind pushed him onward, faster and faster, more steadily toward that terrible attraction. His buried unease had been that wicked purposes were being pursued in his unhappy homeland by wicked hands, and that he, who could not help but know he was better than they, was absent when he should have been trying to stop the bloodshed and uphold mercy and humanity. With that unease half suppressed and half accusing him, he had found himself contrasted with the brave old gentleman whose sense of duty was so strong; that comparison (damaging to himself) was immediately followed by the scorn of Monseigneur, which hurt him deeply, and by Stryver’s sneers, which were especially coarse and wounding for long-standing reasons. After those came Gabelle’s letter: the plea of an innocent prisoner, facing death, to his justice, honor, and good name.

His decision was made. He must go to Paris.

Yes. The Loadstone Rock was pulling him, and he had to keep sailing until he struck it. He knew of no rock; he barely saw any danger. The motive with which he had done what he had done, even if left unfinished, presented itself to him as something that would be gratefully recognized in France when he appeared to claim it. Then that shining vision of doing good, so often the hopeful mirage of generous minds, rose before him, and in that illusion he even saw himself wielding some influence to guide this ferocious Revolution that was spinning disastrously out of control."}

{"request_id":"7da602a5bb6cb33a4fd3d7eb","rewritten_text":"“Are you talking about Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I never imagined anyone else—and I thought you understood. When we discussed him, it seemed perfectly clear.”

“Not entirely,” Emma replied with forced calm. “Everything you said then seemed to refer to another man. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill. I remember you praising the service Mr. Frank Churchill did you when he protected you from the gipsies.”

“Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how you forget!”

“My dear Harriet, I clearly remember what I said. I told you I did not wonder at your attachment—that after what he had done for you, it was perfectly natural. You agreed, speaking warmly about that service, even describing how you felt when he stepped in to save you. That impression is vivid in my mind.”

“Oh dear,” cried Harriet, “now I remember what you mean; but I was thinking of something entirely different at the time. I did not mean the gipsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. No!”—her voice rose—“I was thinking of a much more precious moment—when Mr. Knightley came and asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused, when no one else would stand up with me. That was the kind act; that was the noble generosity; that was the service that made me realize how far above every other person he was.”

“Good God!” exclaimed Emma. “This is the most unfortunate, most dreadful mistake! What can be done?”

“You would not have encouraged me if you had understood me?” asked Harriet. “Still, I cannot be worse off than if the other gentleman had been the one—and now, it might be possible—”

She paused. Emma could not speak.

“I cannot blame you, Miss Woodhouse,” Harriet resumed, “for seeing a huge difference between the two, for me or anyone. You must think one far more beyond my reach than the other. But I hope, Miss Woodhouse, that supposing—if—strange as it seems—yet they were your own words, that stranger things have happened and matches of greater inequality than between Mr. Frank Churchill and me. So it appears such a thing as this may have happened before—and if I should be so extremely fortunate as to—if Mr. Knightley truly—if he is not troubled by the difference, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, you will not oppose it or try to create obstacles.”"}

{"request_id":"1cb3b0ba17384a50cd746361","rewritten_text":"Ever since we had taken him abroad at the stairs, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were suspected. I saw none. We certainly had not been suspected, and at that time we were certainly not being shadowed or followed by any boat. If a boat had waited on us, I would have steered toward shore and forced her to move on or reveal her intention. But we kept on without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and looked, as I have said, like a natural part of the setting. It was striking—though perhaps the miserable life he had led explained it—that he was the least anxious of all of us. He was not indifferent, for he told me he hoped to live long enough to see his gentleman become one of the finest men in a foreign land. He was not inclined to be passive or resigned, as I understood it, but he had no idea of meeting danger halfway. When it reached him, he faced it, yet he would not trouble himself until it did.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here with my dear boy and have my smoke after being day after day between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I understand the joys of freedom,” I replied.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head gravely. “But you don’t know it like I do. You’d have to be under lock and key, dear boy, to know it like I do—but I’m not going to be low.”

It struck me as inconsistent that for any overriding idea he would endanger his freedom and even his life. But I considered that perhaps freedom without danger was too far removed from all the habits of his existence to mean to him what it would to another man. I was not far wrong, for he said, after smoking a little:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, on the other side of the world, I was always looking over here, and it turned dull being there, even though I was growing rich. Everybody knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody’s mind would be troubled about him. They aren’t so easy about me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, at least, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” I said, “you will be perfectly free and safe again within a few hours.”

“Well,” he answered with a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And do you believe so?”"}

{"request_id":"1800113ecf8bb79e766e3df8","rewritten_text":"“Shucks, Tom,” I said, “you might tell a person. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he’s got to have it. All the nobles do.”

That was just how he was. If he didn’t feel like explaining something, he wouldn’t. You could question him for a week and it wouldn’t matter.

He’d already settled the coat of arms business, so now he started to finish the rest of that part of the work, which was planning a mournful inscription—said Jim had to have one, like they all did. He made up several, wrote them on a paper, and read them out:

1. Here a captive heart burst.

2. Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and friends, wore out his sorrowful life.

3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a worn spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity.

4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, perished a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV.

Tom’s voice shook as he read them, and he almost broke down. When he finished he couldn’t decide which one Jim should scratch onto the wall—they were all so good. Finally he said Jim could scratch them all. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch that much onto the logs with a nail, and he didn’t even know how to make letters; but Tom said he would outline them for him, and then Jim would only have to follow the lines. Then pretty soon he said:

“Come to think of it, the logs won’t do; they don’t have log walls in a dungeon. We have to carve the inscriptions into a rock. We’ll bring a rock.”

Jim said a rock was worse than logs. He said it would take him such an awfully long time to carve them into a rock he’d never get out. But Tom said he would let me help him. Then he checked how me and Jim were getting along with the pens. It was tediously hard, slow work, and it didn’t give my hands any chance to heal from the sores, and we hardly made any progress; so Tom said:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the mournful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"2c5666c4a4a7ad2a67c44710","rewritten_text":"“Listen carefully; I have learned the language of despair, know it by heart, because I am Despair—joyous, triumphant Despair. Yet those words are untrue, for the wave may be dark but it is not bitter. We lie down, close our eyes with a gentle good night, and when we wake we are free. Come now, no more delay, slow one! See the pleasant potion! Look, I am a spirit of good, not a mortal maid calling you, and with persuasive tones (oh, that they might persuade you!) I say, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I fixed my eyes on his face, and his exquisite beauty, the heavenly compassion shining from his eyes, his gentle yet earnest expression of pleading and wonder even before he spoke, changed my taut emotions, taking away the hardness of despair and filling me with the softest grief. I saw his eyes grow wet as he took both my hands in his; and sitting down beside me, he said:

“This is a sorrowful act into which you would lead me, dearest friend, and your torment must be deep indeed to fill you with such wretched thoughts. You long for death yet fear it, and you wish me to be your companion. But I have less courage than you, and even with you I dare not die. Listen to me, and then decide if you should convince me of your plan, even if with the overpowering eloquence of despair you could make black death so inviting that fair heaven would seem darkness. Listen, I beg you, to the words of one who has himself nurtured desperate thoughts, who longed impatiently for death, but at last crushed that phantom underfoot and blunted its sting. Come; as you have played Despair with me, I will play Una with you and lead you unharmed from his dark cavern. Listen to me, and let yourself be softened by words untouched by selfish passion.

“We cannot tell what this vast world means, with its strange mix of good and evil. Yet we have been placed here and ordered to live and hope. I do not know what we are meant to hope for, but there is some good beyond us that we must seek, and that search is our earthly duty. If misfortune strikes us, we must fight her; we must push her aside and still press on to find whatever it is in our nature to desire. Whether this glimpse of future good prepares us for another existence I do not know, or whether it simply means that we, as laborers in God’s vineyard, must lend a hand to smooth the way for those who come after us.”"}

{"request_id":"255269a4d4b5dedd1ee0db44","rewritten_text":"She would be settled among people who loved her and were wiser than she was; secluded enough to be safe, yet busy enough to stay cheerful. She would never be led into temptation, nor left exposed for it to find her. She would be respectable and happy; and Emma conceded she was the luckiest creature alive to have inspired such steady and persistent devotion in a man like that—or, if not quite the luckiest, second only to Emma herself.

Harriet, necessarily drawn away by her obligations to the Martins, spent less and less time at Hartfield, which was no cause for regret. The closeness between her and Emma had to diminish; their friendship needed to settle into a calmer goodwill, and, fortunately, what ought to happen and must happen already seemed to be unfolding in the most gradual, natural way.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church and watched her hand placed in Robert Martin’s with complete satisfaction, untouched even by memories connected with Mr. Elton standing before them. Perhaps, indeed, at that moment she could barely see Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might next be for herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were also in London, merely waiting for November.

Emma and Mr. Knightley chose the intervening month as boldly as they dared. They had decided their marriage should be completed while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so they could take the planned fortnight’s trip to the seaside. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed with the decision. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could they win his consent? He had never yet mentioned their marriage except as something far off.

When first approached on the subject, he was so miserable they nearly lost hope. A second reference, however, caused less pain. He began to think it would happen and that he could not prevent it—a very encouraging step in the mind’s journey toward acceptance. Still, he was not content. In fact, he seemed so unhappy that his daughter lost her nerve. She could not bear to see him suffering, to know he imagined himself neglected; and though her reason nearly accepted both Mr. Knightleys’ assurance that once the event was over his anguish would soon pass, she hesitated—she could not go on."}

content.text: {"request_id":"941778af1678c8061351f913","rewritten_text":"At last the narrow streets and alleys opened into a wide space dotted with pens for livestock and other signs of a cattle market. Sikes slowed down there, because the girl could no longer keep up with the brutal pace they had been forced to maintain. He turned to Oliver and harshly ordered him to grab Nancy’s hand. “Do you hear me?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and glanced around. They were in a dark corner, well away from other passersby. Oliver knew all too well that resisting would be useless. He held out his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly. “Give me the other,” said Sikes, snatching Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!” The dog looked up and growled. “Listen, boy,” said Sikes, pressing his other hand to Oliver’s throat. “If he so much as whispers, grab him. Understand?” The dog growled again and, licking his lips, stared at Oliver as though he couldn’t wait to clamp onto his throat. “He’s as eager as a Christian—may I go blind if he isn’t,” said Sikes, eyeing the animal with a grim, savage approval. “Now you know what’s coming, so scream all you like; the dog will soon put a stop to it. Get moving, kid!” Bull’s-Eye wagged his tail, pleased by this rare show of affection, and after another cautionary growl at Oliver, led the way onward. They were crossing Smithfield, though Oliver might just as well have believed it to be Grosvenor Square. The night was dark and foggy. The shop lights barely managed to pierce the thickening mist, which wrapped the streets and houses in gloom, making the unfamiliar place seem even more alien and intensifying Oliver’s bleak uncertainty. They had only hurried forward a few steps when a deep church bell struck the hour. At its first peal, his two escorts halted and looked toward the sound. “Eight o’clock, Bill,” said Nancy once the bell was silent. “What’s the point of telling me? I can hear, can’t I?” Sikes snapped. “I wonder if they can hear it,” Nancy said. “Of course they can,” Sikes shot back. “It was St. Bartholomew’s fair time when I was arrested, and there wasn’t a penny trumpet there I couldn’t hear squealing. Once they locked me up for the night, the racket outside made that thunderous old jail seem so quiet I could’ve bashed my brains out against the iron plates on the door.”"}

{"request_id":"a6f35142f4c80b66fd9428ad","rewritten_text":"After they joined in the general grief over the dreadful outcome Elizabeth saw as nearly certain, though Miss Bennet could not claim it was totally impossible, Elizabeth pressed on. “Tell me everything I have not yet heard. Give me more details. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they no warning before the elopement? They must have seen them together constantly.”

“Colonel Forster admitted he had often suspected a preference, especially from Lydia, but nothing that alarmed him. I feel so sorry for him. His manners were as attentive and kind as possible. He was on his way to us to express his concern before he imagined they had not gone to Scotland; when that fear began to spread, it sped his journey.”

“And was Denny sure Wickham would not marry? Did he know they meant to run off? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?”

“Yes; but when Colonel Forster questioned him, Denny denied knowing anything of their plan and would not share his real opinion. He did not repeat that he believed they would not marry, and from that I hope he might have been misunderstood earlier.”

“And until Colonel Forster appeared, none of you doubted that they were actually married?”

“How could such an idea enter our heads? I felt a little uneasy—somewhat afraid for my sister’s happiness with him in marriage, because I knew his conduct had not always been quite right. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only saw how imprudent the match must be. Kitty then claimed, with very natural pride at knowing more than the rest of us, that Lydia’s last letter had prepared her for such a step. It seems she had known of their being in love for many weeks.”

“But not before they went to Brighton?”

“No, I do not think so.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think badly of Wickham himself? Does he know his true character?”

“I must admit he no longer spoke as well of Wickham as he once did. He thought him imprudent and extravagant; and since this sad event, it is said he left Meryton heavily in debt, though I hope that is false.”

“Oh, Jane, if we had been less secret, if we had told what we knew about him, this could not have happened!”

“Perhaps it would have been better,” her sister replied.

“But to reveal someone’s past faults without knowing their present feelings seemed unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"c35895785c1680cab8132e48","rewritten_text":"Winters in the latitude of Sullivan’s Island seldom turn truly harsh, and in autumn it is an uncommon occurrence to think a fire necessary. Nevertheless, around the middle of October, 18—, there came a day of exceptional chill. Just before sunset I fought my way through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, a place I had neglected for several weeks—my home being then in Charleston, nine miles distant from the island, with the means of going back and forth far inferior to those of the present day. Reaching the hut, I knocked, as I usually did, and receiving no answer, hunted for the key in its usual hiding place, unlocked the door, and stepped in. A cheerful fire was roaring on the hearth, a rarity, yet a welcome one. I shed my overcoat, sank into an arm-chair beside the crackling logs, and waited serenely for my hosts to appear.

After nightfall they arrived, greeting me with the warmest hospitality. Jupiter, his smile stretching from ear to ear, bustled about preparing marsh-hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his moods—what else shall I call them?—of fervor. He had discovered an unfamiliar bivalve forming a new genus and, more than that, had tracked down and captured, with Jupiter’s help, a scarabæus he was convinced entirely novel, though he wished to hear my opinion on the morrow.

“And why not tonight?” I said, rubbing my hands over the blaze and consigning the whole tribe of scarabæi to perdition.

“Ah, if only I had known you were here!” replied Legrand. “But it’s been so long since last we met, and how could I guess you would visit me tonight of all nights? On my way home I encountered Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, quite foolishly, I lent him the insect; so you cannot see it until morning. Stay overnight, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It is the most beautiful thing on earth!”

“What? Sunrise?”

“Nonsense! No—the bug. It glows a brilliant gold, about the size of a large hickory-nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and another, somewhat longer, near the other. The antennæ are—”

“Dey aint no tin in him, Massa Will, I keep tellin you,” Jupiter broke in; “de bug a goole bug, solid, ebery part of him, inside and out, ceptin his wing—nebber felt so hebby a bug in all my born days.”"}

{"request_id":"03d361e63a972f5fe95fa144","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and grabbed his left, bending so low to study it that the gold rims of his spectacles nearly touched the palm. For an instant his face turned mask-white with horror, but he quickly regained his composure, and, looking up at Lady Windermere with a forced smile, said, “It is the hand of a charming young man.”

“Of course it is!” said Lady Windermere. “But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.”

“All charming young men are,” said Mr. Podgers.

“I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,” Lady Jedburgh murmured pensively. “It is so dangerous.”

“My dear, they never are too fascinating,” cried Lady Windermere. “But I want details. Details are the only things that interest me. What is going to happen to Lord Arthur?”

“Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—”

“Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!”

“And he will lose a relative.”

“Not his sister, I hope?” Lady Jedburgh said in a plaintive tone.

“Certainly not his sister,” replied Mr. Podgers with a placating wave of his hand, “just a distant relative.”

“Well, I’m horribly disappointed,” said Lady Windermere. “I have absolutely nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives anymore. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she had better keep a black silk dress handy; it always does for church, you know. And now let’s go have supper. They have probably eaten everything by now, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup, but he is so upset about politics at the moment that I never feel quite sure of him. I do wish General Boulanger would calm down. Duchess, you must be tired?”

“Not at all, dear Gladys,” said the Duchess, waddling toward the door. “I have enjoyed myself enormously, and the chiropodist—I mean the palm reader—is most interesting. Flora, where is my tortoiseshell fan? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, very kind of you, I’m sure.” And the good creature finally managed to get downstairs without dropping her scent bottle more than twice.

All this time Lord Arthur Savile had been standing by the fireplace, feeling the same dreadful foreboding, the same sickening sense of coming disaster. He smiled sadly at his sister as she swept past on Lord Plymdale’s arm, lovely in her pink brocade and pearls, and he barely heard Lady Windermere when she called for him to follow her. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the idea that anything could come between them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"05d5e0910d1d1d6f42d5c21d","rewritten_text":"Not everyone would have been so determined and kind as she was, refusing to accept Jane’s response; but she insisted she would not write that sort of refusal yesterday, as Jane wanted. She would wait—and sure enough, last evening it was settled that Jane would go. Quite a surprise to me! I had absolutely no idea. Jane pulled Mrs. Elton aside and told her outright that, after considering the benefits of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had decided to accept it. I did not know a word until it was all arranged.”

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?”

“Yes, all of us; Mrs. Elton insisted we come. It was arranged like that on the hill while we were strolling with Mr. Knightley. ‘You simply must all spend the evening with us,’ she said—‘I absolutely must have you all come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?”

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he declined from the start. Even though I thought he would attend, since Mrs. Elton said she wouldn’t let him off, he didn’t; but my mother and Jane and I were all there, and we had a very pleasant evening. With such kind friends, Miss Woodhouse, one must always have a good time, though everyone seemed rather worn out after the morning’s outing. Even fun, you know, can be tiring—and I cannot say any of them appeared to enjoy it very much. Still, I will always remember it as a very pleasant gathering and feel deeply grateful to the kind friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you didn’t realize it, had been making up her mind all day?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the moment comes, it must be unwelcome to her and to all her friends—but I hope her engagement will have every possible consolation—I mean regarding the family’s character and manners.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, everything that could make her happy is there. Besides the Sucklings and Bragges, there isn’t another nursery establishment so generous and elegant in all of Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance. Mrs. Smallridge is the most delightful woman—a lifestyle almost equal to Maple Grove—and as for the children, except for the little Sucklings and little Bragges, nowhere are there such sweet, well-bred children. Jane will be treated with such respect and kindness! It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary! I truly cannot bring myself to tell you her salary, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"385960babfc428358c4e25cc","rewritten_text":"You don’t know anything about me unless you’ve read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, but that doesn’t matter. That book was written by Mr. Mark Twain, and he mostly told the truth. He stretched a few things, but mostly it was true. That’s nothing special, though. I never met anybody who didn’t lie sooner or later, except Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly—and Mary and the Widow Douglas are all written about in that book, which is mostly true, with a few exaggerations like I said before.

Here’s how that book ends: Tom and I found the money the robbers hid in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars each—all gold. It was a fearful lot of money when it was piled up. Judge Thatcher took it and invested it, and it brought us a dollar a day each all year long—more than a person could figure what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me in as her son and said she would civilize me; but it was hard living in that house all the time, with the widow so solemn and proper in everything she did. When I couldn’t take it anymore, I ran off. I got back into my old rags and my sugar-hogshead again, and I was free and content. But Tom Sawyer tracked me down and said he was starting a band of robbers, and I could join if I went back to the widow and behaved. So I went back.

The widow cried over me and called me a poor lost lamb, and she called me a lot of other things too, but she didn’t mean any harm. She put me in those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and sweat and feel squeezed in. Then the old routine started over. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to show up on time. When you got to the table you couldn’t start eating right away; you had to wait for the widow to bow her head and mumble over the food, even though there wasn’t anything wrong with it—except everything was cooked separately. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different; things get mixed, the juices trade places, and the food tastes better.

After supper she took out her book and taught me about Moses and the bulrushes, and I was eager to learn all about him; but pretty soon she let slip that Moses had been dead a long time. After that I didn’t care about him anymore, because I don’t put much stock in dead people."}
