content.text: {"request_id":"5aa0a8780f7c427b1bc61acc","rewritten_text":"April 19th. This morning, around nine o’clock, to my great relief, the moon’s surface lying terribly close and my fear at its peak, the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs that the atmosphere was changing. By ten o’clock I had reason to believe the air had grown considerably denser. By eleven, the apparatus required almost no effort, and at noon, after some hesitation, I dared to unscrew the tourniquet. When nothing bad happened, I threw open the rubber chamber and detached it from the car. As expected, spasms and agonizing headaches struck immediately after such a rash, dangerous experiment. Yet since these and other breathing difficulties were not severe enough to threaten my life, I resolved to endure them as best I could, knowing I left them behind with every moment I descended toward the moon’s denser layers. Still, my descent remained violently fast, and it soon became terrifyingly clear that, although I was likely right about an atmosphere proportional in density to the satellite’s mass, I had been wrong in assuming this density, even at the surface, would support the heavy load inside my balloon car. It should have done so, in equal measure with Earth, given that actual weight on either world should match the degree of atmospheric compression. That it did not was evident from my precipitous plummet; why it failed must relate to those possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. Regardless, I was now extremely close to the planet and descending with dreadful velocity. I lost no time in throwing overboard my ballast, then my water kegs, then the condensing apparatus and rubber chamber, and finally every item in the car. It made no difference. I continued to fall with horrible speed and was now less than half a mile above the surface. As a last resort, after discarding my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car loose from the balloon—it weighed no small amount—and, clutching the net with both hands, I scarcely had time to note that the whole countryside was crowded with tiny dwellings before I plunged headlong into the very center of a fantastical-looking city and the midst of a vast crowd of ugly little people. None of them said a word or made the slightest effort to help me; they merely stood there like fools, grinning absurdly, staring sideways at me and my balloon with their arms akimbo."}

{"request_id":"766a94a16dffe5ec80bba469","rewritten_text":"“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and looked around, trying to figure out where I was. It was after sunrise, and I had been sleeping hard. Pap stood over me looking sour and sick. He said:

“What are you doing with this gun?”

I figured he didn’t remember anything about what he’d been up to, so I said:

“Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me?”

“Well, I tried, but I couldn’t move you.”

“All right. Don’t stand there jabbering all day; go see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll come in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I headed up the riverbank. I noticed pieces of branches and other trash floating by, and some loose bark; that told me the river was rising. I figured I’d be having a grand time if I were over in town. Every June rise brought luck for me, because as soon as the water starts rising, cordwood and logs come floating along—sometimes a dozen together. All you have to do is grab them and sell them to the wood-yards and sawmill.

I walked up the bank, one eye open for Pap and the other eye out for what the river might bring. Suddenly a canoe showed up—a real beauty, about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I dived headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam hard for the canoe. I half expected someone to be lying in it, because people liked to trick others that way: they’d play possum, and when someone pulled a skiff up close, they’d sit up and laugh at him. But not this time. It was really a drift canoe, and I climbed in and paddled her to shore. I figured the old man would be pleased—she was worth ten dollars. But when I reached land Pap still wasn’t in sight, and as I was pushing her into a little creek like a gully, covered with vines and willows, another idea came to me: I’d hide her well, and instead of running into the woods when I made my getaway, I’d go fifty miles downriver and settle in one spot, so I wouldn’t have such a hard time traveling on foot.

The creek was close to the shanty, and I kept thinking I could hear the old man coming, but I got the canoe hidden. Then I stepped out and looked past a clump of willows, and there he was, down the path a bit, taking aim at a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"3841c8505624befe1b414866","rewritten_text":"“Is that the whole of it? That is not much! Many stand under the Republic’s anger and must watch through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I am he. I must be, as I am the last.”

Jarvis Lorry has answered all the questions. He has stepped down and stands with his hand on the coach door, talking to a group of officials. They slowly stroll around the coach and slowly climb onto the box to inspect the few bags on the roof; peasants lingering nearby press closer to the doors and stare greedily inside. A small child in its mother’s arms has its short arm stretched out so it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has already gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.”

“May we depart, citizen?”

“You may depart. Forward, my postilions! Safe travels!”

“I salute you, citizens.—And the first danger is past!”

Jarvis Lorry says this again, clasping his hands and looking up. Terror fills the carriage; someone is sobbing; the unconscious traveler breathes heavily.

“Are we not going too slowly? Can they not be made to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would look like fleeing, my darling. I must not push them too hard; it would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see if we are pursued!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, no one follows us.”

Houses pass in twos and threes, lonely farms, ruined structures, dye-works, tanneries, open fields, rows of bare trees. Hard uneven pavement lies below us, deep soft mud on each side. Sometimes we veer into the bordering mud to avoid the stones that rattle and jolt us; sometimes we get stuck in ruts and sloughs there. Our impatience torments us so much that in our frantic fear we think of jumping out and running—hiding—doing anything but remaining still.

Out of the open land, back again among ruined buildings, lonely farms, dye-works, tanneries, cottages in twos and threes, avenues of bare trees. Have these men tricked us, leading us back by another route? Is this not the same place twice? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see if we are pursued! Quiet! The posting-house.

Our four horses are removed slowly; slowly, the coach sits in the narrow street, without horses and seemingly doomed to never move again; slowly, the new horses appear, one after another; slowly, the fresh postilions arrive, sucking and braiding their whip lashes; slowly, the old postilions count their money, make mistakes, and end up dissatisfied."}

content.text: {"request_id":"14d706ac7953da97431e7815","rewritten_text":"Early in the morning, slipping once more past my creditors, I hurried to the bookseller’s stall and spent the little cash I had on volumes about Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. I did it partly by selling some household furniture to cover half their claim, and partly by promising to pay the rest once I finished a small project I told them I was planning, for which I asked their help. Since they were ignorant men, they agreed easily.\n\nWith matters settled, I quietly arranged with my wife to sell what property we had left and to borrow small sums under various pretenses, not worrying about future repayment, until we had a good amount of ready money. Little by little I bought fine cambric muslin in twelve-yard pieces, twine, some caoutchouc varnish, and a large deep wicker basket made to order, along with everything else needed to build a balloon of unusual size. I told my wife to sew it as quickly as possible and instructed her exactly how to proceed. Meanwhile, I turned the twine into netting of the right size, fitted it with a hoop and the necessary cords, and bought a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, a barometer with important modifications, and two more obscure astronomical instruments. By night I moved to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam five iron-bound casks holding about fifty gallons each and one larger cask, six ten-foot tinned tubes three inches in diameter, a quantity of a certain metallic substance or semi-metal I will not name, and a dozen demijohns of a common acid. content.text: {"request_id":"6d6f542816adfb4fc16cf43d","rewritten_text":"Without stopping to think, and barely aware of her own emotions, Elizabeth finished this letter, grabbed the other, and with the greatest impatience opened it and read the following, written a day after the first had ended.\n\n“By now, my dearest sister, you will have received my hurried letter. I hope this one is clearer, but although I am not pressed for time, my head is so muddled that I cannot promise to be coherent. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what I mean to say, but I have bad news that cannot wait. Reckless as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now desperate to know it has happened, for we have far too much reason to fear they did not go to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the day before, only a few hours after the express. Though Lydia’s short letter to Mrs. F. led them to believe they were going to Gretna Green, Denny let something slip suggesting he believed W. never meant to go there or to marry Lydia at all. This was reported to Colonel F., who, immediately alarmed, set off from B. to follow their route. He followed them easily to Clapham, but no farther; for when they entered that town, they switched to a hackney coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All that is known after this is that they were seen continuing on the London road. I do not know what to think. After making every inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. went on to Hertfordshire, anxiously repeating his questions at every turnpike, and at the inns in Barnet and Hatfield, but with no success; no such people had been seen. With the warmest concern, he came to Longbourn and shared his fears with us in the kindest way. I am truly sorry for him and Mrs. F., yet no one can blame them. Our distress, dear Lizzy, is very great. My father and mother expect the worst, but I cannot think so poorly of him. Many circumstances might make it preferable for them to marry privately in town rather than pursue their first plan; and even if he could form such a scheme against a young woman of Lydia’s connections, which seems unlikely, can I think her so lost to all sense? Impossible! Yet I am distressed to find that Colonel F. will not count on their being married: he shook his head when I expressed hope and said he feared W. was not a man to be trusted.”"}

{"request_id":"e464506121388c0496543a03","rewritten_text":"He never tried again. The boys lay there counting the dragging minutes until it seemed time must be finished and eternity turning gray; then they were thankful to see the sun finally setting. 

One snore stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, gave a grim smile at his comrade whose head drooped on his knees, nudged him with his foot, and said: 

"Hey! You’re supposed to be on watch, aren’t you! It’s fine, though—nothing happened." 

"My! Was I asleep?" 

"Oh, partly. It’s almost time for us to get going, pard. What’ll we do with the little bit of loot we’ve got left?" 

"I don’t know—leave it here like always, I guess. No point in hauling it off till we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is quite a load." 

"Well, fine—we can swing by here one more time." 

"Sure—but I’d say come at night like we used to—it’s better." 

"Yes, but listen; it might be a long time before I get the right shot at that job; things could go wrong; it’s not in a very safe place. Let’s just bury it for real—and bury it deep." 

"Good plan," said the comrade. He walked across the room, knelt, pried up a hearthstone near the back, and took out a bag that jingled sweetly. He pulled twenty or thirty dollars for himself, the same for Injun Joe, then handed the bag over. Joe was in the corner now, kneeling and digging with his bowie knife. 

The boys forgot every fear and misery in a flash. With hungry eyes they watched each move. Luck!—the glory of it was beyond imagination! Six hundred dollars could make half a dozen boys rich! This was treasure-hunting under the best possible stars—no annoying guesswork about where to dig. They jabbed each other every moment—meaningful nudges easy to read: “Oh, aren’t you glad now that we’re here!” 

Joe’s knife hit something. 

"Hey!" he said. 

"What is it?" asked his comrade. 

"Half-rotten plank—no, I think it’s a box. Come give me a hand and we’ll find out why it’s here. Never mind, I’ve busted a hole." 

He reached in and pulled his hand back out— 

"Man, it’s money!" 

The two men studied the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were as excited and as thrilled as the men. 

Joe’s comrade said, 

"We’ll finish fast. There’s an old rusty pick over in the weeds on the other side of the fireplace—I spotted it a minute ago.""}

{"request_id":"a7ebff3a0693648c416646ff","rewritten_text":"I hasten now to the portion of my history most touching, for I am about to recount incidents that impressed me with emotions that transformed me from what I had been into what I have become.

Spring advanced swiftly; the days grew fine and the skies clear. It astonished me to see the region, formerly dreary and desolate, suddenly adorned with exquisite flowers and rich verdure. My senses were indulged and revived by a thousand delightful fragrances and an equal number of lovely sights.

One day when the cottagers paused from their labor—the old father playing his guitar while the children listened—I noticed that Felix’s face was sorrowful beyond expression. He sighed repeatedly, and once the old man stopped his music; by his gestures I assumed he was questioning the reason for his son’s melancholy. Felix answered in a cheerful tone, and the old man was about to resume his playing when a knock sounded at the door.

A lady appeared, mounted on horseback and attended by a countryman acting as her guide. She wore dark attire and a thick black veil. Agatha put a question to her, but the stranger simply responded by uttering, in a gentle voice, Felix’s name. Her accent was musical yet unlike any of my companions. Hearing his name, Felix hastened toward her; she threw back her veil as soon as she beheld him, revealing a face of celestial beauty and expression. Her hair, a lustrous raven hue, was intricately braided; her eyes were dark yet mild, though lively; her features were symmetrical, and her complexion marvelously fair, each cheek touched with a charming blush.

Felix seemed enraptured at the sight of her. Every trace of grief vanished, replaced by a rapture I could scarcely have imagined. His eyes shone, his cheeks flushed with joy, and in that moment I thought him almost as beautiful as the stranger. She seemed moved differently; brushing tears from her lovely eyes, she extended her hand to Felix, who pressed it ardently and called her, so far as I could discern, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand the words, yet smiled. He helped her dismount, dismissed the guide, and led her into the cottage. After some talk between Felix and his father, the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet and was about to kiss his hand, but he raised her and embraced her warmly.

It soon became clear that although the stranger spoke in articulate tones, possessing a language of her own, neither she nor the cottagers could understand the other."}

{"request_id":"99fff8feeb8aa6d9744a1653","rewritten_text":"It was Lady Windermere’s last reception before Easter, and Bentinck House was more crowded than ever. Six Cabinet Ministers had arrived straight from the Speaker’s Levée in their decorations, every beautiful woman wore her most fashionable gown, and at the end of the picture gallery stood Princess Sophia of Carlsruhe, a heavy, Tartar-looking lady with tiny black eyes and magnificent emeralds, speaking dreadful French at the top of her voice and laughing wildly at everything said to her. It was certainly a remarkable mix of people. Splendid peeresses chatted amiably with fiery Radicals, famous preachers brushed shoulders with noted skeptics, and a whole cluster of bishops kept trailing a portly prima donna from room to room; on the staircase several Royal Academicians, disguised as artists, were posted, and it was said that at one point the supper room was absolutely packed with geniuses. In truth, it was one of Lady Windermere’s finest nights, and the Princess remained until nearly half past eleven.

As soon as she left, Lady Windermere returned to the picture gallery, where a celebrated political economist was solemnly explaining the scientific theory of music to an indignant Hungarian virtuoso, and began talking to the Duchess of Paisley. She looked wonderfully beautiful with her elegant ivory throat, her large blue forget-me-not eyes, and her heavy coils of golden hair. They were real golden hair—not the pale straw shade that now steals the gracious name of gold, but the gold woven into sunbeams or hidden in strange amber; it gave her face the framing of a saint, yet with no small measure of a sinner’s allure. She was a fascinating study in psychology. Early in life she had discovered the important truth that nothing looks as much like innocence as indiscretion; and through a series of reckless escapades, half of them quite harmless, she had obtained all the privileges of a distinctive personality. She had more than once changed her husband—Debrett lists three marriages—but since she had never changed her lover, the world long ago stopped gossiping about her. She was now forty, childless, and possessed of that excessive passion for pleasure which is the secret to staying young.

Suddenly she looked around the room eagerly and said in her clear contralto voice, “Where is my palm reader?”

“Your what, Gladys?” exclaimed the Duchess, starting despite herself.

“My palm reader, Duchess; I can’t do without him just now.”

“Dear Gladys! You are always so original,” murmured the Duchess, trying to remember what exactly a palm reader was, and hoping it wasn’t the same thing as a chiropodist.

“He comes to examine my hand twice a week without fail,” Lady Windermere continued, “and he is endlessly fascinating about it.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"ccea7c0940e0817e187eba8f","rewritten_text":"There was in all this a peculiar charm that drew and entranced me. He seemed roused from a long, dreamlike slumber, feeling somewhat like one of the seven sleepers, or like Nourjahad in that delicate imitation of an eastern story: Diana was gone; his friends were altered or dead, and, on his awakening, I was the only being left for him to love on earth. How precious the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became now that I had so beloved a companion for my wanderings. With my father I sought every delightful nook, whether on the islands or beside the tree-sheltered cascades; each shaded lane or dell tangled with underwood and fern. His conversation expanded my ideas. I felt as though I had been remade and bore all the vigor and brightness of a new creature: his arrival seemed to transport me from a cramped spot of earth into a universe without bounds for imagination and intellect. My life had once resembled a pleasant country brook, never meant to leave its native meadows, but, when its course was done, to be quietly swallowed and leave no trace. Now it appeared a varied river winding through a fruitful, exquisite landscape, ever shifting, ever fair. Alas! I did not foresee the desert it was soon to meet; the rocks that would rend its waters, and the hideous prospect that would be mirrored yet more grotesquely in its waves. Life glittered then; I began to learn to hope, and what brings sharper despair than hope destroyed? Is it not marvelous that sorrow should so swiftly track such celestial joy? I tasted from an enchanted cup, yet gall lay at the bottom of its slow-drawn sweetness. My heart brimmed with deep affection, yet its very profundity and fullness kept it serene. I never imagined that misery could spring from love; the lesson that all must eventually take was taught me in a fashion few are forced to receive. I mourn still—must eternally mourn—those brief months of Edenic bliss; I broke no command, I ate no forbidden fruit, yet I was mercilessly expelled. Alas! my companion did, and I was hurled down in his ruin. But I stray from my tale—let sorrow arrive at its appointed moment; at this point in my narrative I may still speak of happiness. Three months slipped by in this enchanting communion when my aunt fell ill. I spent a whole month in her room tending her, yet her malady was mortal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. Death is so dreadful to the living; the chains of habit are so strong, even when affection does not forge them, that the heart must writhe when they snap."}

{"request_id":"06bc50034eae0427a07edcc2","rewritten_text":"Her colour altered, and she remained silent.

Mrs. Gardiner had stationed herself a little to the rear; and when Elizabeth paused, he asked Mrs. Gardiner if she would favour him with an introduction to her companions. This was a politeness she had not expected; and she almost had to smother a smile at his seeking the acquaintance of some of the very persons his pride had spurned when he addressed herself. “How astonished he will be,” she thought, “once he learns who they are! At present he assumes they belong to the fashionable world.”

Yet the introduction was made at once; and as Mrs. Gardiner explained their relationship to her, she allowed herself a covert glance at him, curious how he might take it, and half expecting him to flee at top speed from such degrading associates. That the connection startled him was unmistakable: nevertheless, he bore it with resolution; instead of withdrawing, he turned back with them and entered into conversation with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth could not help feeling satisfaction, could not help exulting. It soothed her that he should perceive she had relations who need inspire no shame. She listened with the greatest attention to every exchange between them, delighting in each remark, each phrase of her uncle that displayed his sense, his taste, or his good breeding.

Before long, the talk drifted to fishing; and she heard Mr. Darcy, with perfect courtesy, invite Mr. Gardiner to fish there whenever he pleased during his stay in the neighbourhood, offering also to provide him with tackle, and indicating the stretches of the stream where sport was generally best. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, cast her a look that spoke her astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but could not be more gratified; the compliment must be meant wholly for herself. Still, her amazement was extreme; over and over she asked herself, “Why is he so changed? What can be the cause? It cannot be on _my_ account, it cannot be for _my_ sake that his manners are thus softened. My reproaches at Hunsford could not produce an alteration like this. It is impossible that he should still cherish love for me.”

After they had proceeded some way thus, the two ladies leading, the two gentlemen following, upon returning to their former arrangement after descending to the river’s edge to examine more closely a curious aquatic plant, a small change occurred. It sprang from Mrs. Gardiner, who, wearied by the morning’s exertion, found Elizabeth’s support insufficient, and therefore chose to lean upon her husband instead."}

{"request_id":"871536fe366c1ac883e5cda1","rewritten_text":"“Do you come back often?”

“I haven’t been here since.”

“Nor have I.”

The moon started to rise, and I thought of that calm gaze at the white ceiling which was gone forever. The moon rose higher, and I remembered the pressure of his hand when I spoke the last words he ever heard.

Estella was the next to break the silence between us.

“I’ve often hoped and planned to come back, but I was kept away by so many circumstances. Poor, poor old place!”

The first rays of moonlight touched the silvery mist, and they shone on the tears falling from her eyes. Not realizing I saw them, and trying to control herself, she said quietly,

“Were you wondering, as you walked along, how it came to be left like this?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The land belongs to me. It’s the only thing I haven’t given up. Everything else has slipped away from me, little by little, but I kept this. It was the only thing I fought to keep through all those miserable years.”

“Is something going to be built here?”

“Finally, yes. I came to say goodbye before the change. And you,” she said with a touching interest in a wanderer, “you still live abroad?”

“I do.”

“And you’re doing well, I’m sure?”

“I work hard enough for a modest living, and so—yes, I’m doing well.”

“I’ve often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long, painful time when I pushed away the memory of what I threw aside when I didn’t know its worth. But once my duty no longer conflicted with remembering, I made room for it in my heart.”

“You’ve always had your place in my heart,” I replied.

We were silent again until she spoke.

“It never occurred to me,” Estella said, “that I’d say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place. I’m very glad to do both.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? Parting is painful for me. The memory of our last parting has always been sorrowful and painful.”

“But you said to me,” Estella returned earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ If you could say that then, you won’t hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has taught me more than anything else, and taught me to understand what your heart used to be. I’ve been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape.”"}

{"request_id":"4c499154e8aa99ef97104d08","rewritten_text":"I told myself right off I didn’t aim to get tangled up in any business like that.

Come morning, when I went downstairs, the parlor was closed tight and the watchers had cleared out. Nobody hung around but the family, the widow Bartley, and our lot. I studied their faces, trying to read if anything had taken place, but couldn’t make out a thing.

Around midday the undertaker arrived with his helper. They set the coffin in the center of the room on two chairs, arranged our chairs in rows, and borrowed extras from neighbors until the hall, the parlor, and the dining room were crammed. I noticed the coffin lid was fixed as before, but I didn’t dare peek underneath it with folks nearby.

Then people started pouring in. The beaters and the girls settled in the front row at the coffin’s head, and for half an hour the crowd filed by slow, single file, pausing to gaze on the dead man’s face, some shedding a tear. It stayed mighty still and solemn, except for the girls and the beaters holding their handkerchiefs to their eyes, heads bowed, sobbing a little. No other noise but shoes scraping the floor and noses blowing—the sort of thing that gets noisier at funerals, unless it’s church.

Once the place was packed, the undertaker slipped around in his black gloves with his smooth, soothing style, giving final touches, arranging folks and furniture so everything sat tidy and easy, and making no more racket than a cat. He never spoke a word; he shifted folks, squeezed in those arriving late, opened passageways, and did it all with nods and hand signs, then stationed himself against the wall. He was the softest, glidiest, stealthiest fellow I ever laid eyes on; there wasn’t any more grin to him than to a ham.

They’d borrowed a melodeon—a squeamish one—and once all was set a young woman sat down to play it. It screeched and whimpered, and everybody joined in the singing, and Peter was the only one who caught a break, if you ask me. Then Reverend Hobson started up, slow and solemn, and as soon as he did the wildest uproar bust loose down in the cellar you ever heard. It was just one dog, but he kicked up a powerful hullabaloo and kept at it steady; the parson stood there over the coffin waiting—you couldn’t even hear yourself think."}

“What do you think happened to Basil?” asked Dorian, holding his Burgundy up to the light and marveling at how calmly he could talk about it.

“I have no idea. If Basil wants to hide, that’s his business. If he’s dead, I don’t want to think about him. Death is the only thing that ever frightens me. I despise it.”

“Why?” the younger man asked wearily.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, raising the gilded trellis of an open vinaigrette box to his nose, “nowadays we can survive everything except death. Death and vulgarity are the only two facts in the nineteenth century that can’t be explained away. Let’s have our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran away with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house is rather lonely without her. Of course, marriage is merely a habit, a bad habit. But one feels the loss even of one’s worst habits. Perhaps we miss those the most. They become such an essential part of one’s character.”

Dorian said nothing, but rose from the table, went into the next room, sat at the piano, and let his fingers wander over the black and white ivory keys. After the coffee was brought in, he stopped and looked over at Lord Henry. “Harry, has it ever occurred to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was very popular and always carried a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn’t clever enough to have enemies. Of course, he had a brilliant talent for painting. A man can paint like Velázquez and still be terribly dull. Basil was rather dull. He only interested me once, when he told me years ago that he adored you and that you were the driving force of his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” said Dorian, sadness in his voice. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some newspapers do. It doesn’t seem at all likely to me. I know Paris has dreadful neighborhoods, but Basil wasn’t the kind of man who would go to them. He had no curiosity. That was his biggest flaw.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you I murdered Basil?” asked the younger man."}

{"request_id":"503fbafa2d28095e1987d5bb","rewritten_text":"“He was handed over to you. You see I know the circumstances?”

“That’s the truth, certainly,” said Defarge. A nudge from his wife’s elbow as she knitted and hummed had warned him to answer, but keep it short.

“It was to you,” said the spy, “that his daughter came; and it was from your care that his daughter took him, accompanied by a tidy brown gentleman—what was his name?—with a small wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—over to England.”

“That’s the truth,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Really?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much about them now?” asked the spy.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In fact,” Madame broke in, looking up from her work and her soft song, “we never hear about them. We got the news of their safe arrival, and maybe another letter, or maybe two; but since then they have gone their way in life—we ours—and we have had no correspondence.”

“Exactly so, madame,” replied the spy. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” echoed Madame. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English are cold, it seems to me.”

“Oh! You know I’m English.”

“I can tell from your tongue,” said Madame. “And what the tongue is, I suppose the person is.”

He did not take the comparison as flattering, but he made the best of it and laughed it off. After finishing his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman; to someone who, like herself, was born French. And speaking of Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!), it’s curious that she’s going to marry the nephew of the Marquis for whom Gaspard was lifted to that height of so many feet; in other words, the current Marquis. But he lives anonymously in England; he isn’t a Marquis there; he’s Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting, but the news had a clear effect on her husband. No matter how he busied himself behind the little counter, striking a light and lighting his pipe, he was unsettled, and his hand wasn’t steady. The spy wouldn’t have been much of a spy if he hadn’t noticed it, or stored it away.

Having scored at least this one point, whatever it might end up being worth, and with no customers coming in to help him to any other, Mr. Barsad paid for what he had drunk and took his leave, politely saying before he left that he looked forward to the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

{"request_id":"9fe222a241b7e595a7c55feb","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, gently resting his hand on the Doctor’s arm again after a brief silence, “what do you think caused this attack?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette replied, “that there was a powerful and extraordinary resurgence of the chain of thoughts and memories that first caused the illness. Some intense, deeply distressing associations were vividly brought back, I think. It’s likely he had long feared that those associations would resurface—perhaps under certain circumstances, perhaps at a particular moment. He tried in vain to prepare himself; maybe the attempt to prepare made him less able to endure it.”

“Will he remember what happened during the relapse?” asked Mr. Lorry, naturally hesitant.

The Doctor looked bleakly around the room, shook his head, and answered in a low voice, “Not at all.”

“Now, about the future,” Mr. Lorry hinted.

“As for the future,” the Doctor said, regaining his composure, “I would have great hope. Since Heaven in its mercy restored him so quickly, I would have great hope. He gave way under the pressure of something complicated, long feared and dimly anticipated and fought against, and after the storm had broken and passed, he recovered. I would hope the worst is over.”

“Well, well! That’s comforting. I’m thankful!” said Mr. Lorry.

“I am thankful,” the Doctor echoed, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two other points,” said Mr. Lorry, “on which I’m eager to be informed. May I continue?”

“You can’t do your friend a greater favor.” The Doctor offered him his hand.

“To the first, then. He’s studious and unusually energetic; he throws himself with great zeal into acquiring professional knowledge, running experiments, and many other pursuits. Now, does he overdo it?”

“I think not. It may be the nature of his mind to need constant occupation. That may be partly inherent, partly the result of suffering. The less it was engaged with healthy things, the more danger there was of it turning elsewhere. He may have noticed this in himself and realized it.”

“You’re sure he isn’t strained too far?”

“I’m sure of it.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked now—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that could happen easily. There’s been a violent strain in one direction, and it needs a counterbalance.”

“Forgive me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose, for a moment, he *was* overworked; would the disorder flare up again?”"}

{"request_id":"8917e044762640e700d51f54","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often mused on the old notion of the Bi-Part Soul and entertained myself with imagining a double Dupin—one creative, the other analytic.

Do not infer from this that I am unveiling some mystery or writing a romance. What I witnessed in the Frenchman was only the product of an excited, perhaps disordered intellect. Yet his comments at such times are best illustrated by an example.

One night we were wandering along a long, dirty street near the Palais Royal. We both seemed absorbed in thought and had not exchanged a word for at least fifteen minutes when Dupin suddenly burst out:

“He is a very little fellow, no doubt; he would suit the Théâtre des Variétés better.”

“Certainly,” I answered without thinking, not at first realizing—so wrapped up was I in my reflections—how uncannily he had echoed my musings. The next instant I recovered myself, and my amazement was immense.

“Dupin,” I said solemnly, “this passes my understanding. I confess I am astonished and can scarcely trust my senses. How could you know I was thinking of ——?” Here I halted, to make sure whether he really knew whom I had in mind.

“—— of Chantilly,” he said. “Why stop? You were observing inwardly that his tiny figure disqualified him for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been reflecting on. Chantilly was formerly a cobbler in the Rue St. Denis who, seized with stage-mania, had attempted the role of Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy and been famously lampooned for his trouble.

“Tell me, for Heaven’s sake,” I cried, “the method—if there is one—by which you have plumbed my mind in this matter.” In truth I was even more startled than I cared to admit.

“It was the fruiterer,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the mender of soles lacked sufficient stature for Xerxes et id genus omne.”

“The fruiterer! You amaze me—I know no fruiterer at all.”

“The man who jostled you as we entered this street—perhaps fifteen minutes ago.”

Then I remembered that a fruiterer, balancing a large basket of apples on his head, had nearly knocked me over by accident as we left the Rue C—— for the lane where we now stood; yet how that encounter connected with Chantilly remained utterly beyond me."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6dc629619f34f400eb91b04a","rewritten_text":"Now that he had nothing to hold, he pressed the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left into the hollow of his right, then ran a hand over his bearded chin, cycling through the motions without a pause. Bringing him back from the drift he always fell into after speaking was like calling a fragile person out of a faint, or trying, in hopes of some revelation, to hold the spirit of a dying man. “Did you ask me my name?” “Of course I did.” “One Hundred and Five, North Tower.” “Is that all?” “One Hundred and Five, North Tower.” He made a tired sound that was neither sigh nor groan and bent to work again, until the quiet was broken once more. “You’re not a shoemaker by trade?” Mr. Lorry asked, staring at him. His hollow eyes turned to Defarge, as if to pass the question to him; but when no help came, they dropped to the floor before returning to the questioner. “I’m not a shoemaker by trade? No, I wasn’t a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—” He slipped away again, for minutes, all the while repeating those measured movements with his hands. His eyes finally drifted back to the face they had left; when they focused on it, he jolted, as though waking from sleep and picking up last night’s conversation. “I asked permission to teach myself, and I gained it with great difficulty after a long time, and I’ve been making shoes ever since.” As he held out his hand for the shoe that had been taken from him, Mr. Lorry said, still watching his face: “Monsieur Manette, don’t you remember me at all?” The shoe fell to the floor, and he stared fixedly at the questioner. “Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry put a hand on Defarge’s arm—“don’t you remember this man? Look at him. Look at me. Isn’t there some old banker, old business, old servant, old time rising in your mind, Monsieur Manette?” The prisoner of many years stared in turn at Mr. Lorry and Defarge, and faint signs of sharp intelligence emerged at the center of his brow, forcing their way through the dark fog that had settled over him. They clouded again, they faded, they vanished—but they had been there."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6f7e3739d2dcd80709c8358e","rewritten_text":"About ten minutes later the tea bell rang, and when Virginia didn’t come down, Mrs. Otis sent a footman upstairs to fetch her. After a short while he returned and reported that he couldn’t find Miss Virginia anywhere. As she usually went out to the garden every evening to pick flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis wasn’t alarmed at first, but when six o’clock struck and Virginia still didn’t appear, she became genuinely agitated. She sent the boys out to look for her, while she and Mr. Otis searched every room in the house. At half past six the boys came back and said they couldn’t find any sign of their sister. All of them were now in a state of intense anxiety and didn’t know what to do, when Mr. Otis suddenly remembered that a few days earlier he had given a band of gypsies permission to camp in the park. He immediately set off for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they were staying, taking his eldest son and two farmhands with him. The little Duke of Cheshire, utterly frantic with worry, pleaded to be allowed to go along, but Mr. Otis refused because he was afraid there might be trouble. When they arrived, however, they found that the gypsies had already left, and it was clear their departure had been rather hurried, as the fire was still burning and plates lay scattered on the grass. After sending Washington and the two men to scour the area, he raced home and sent telegrams to every police inspector in the county, instructing them to look for a little girl who had been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He then ordered his horse to be brought around, and, after insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode off with a groom along the Ascot Road. He had only gone a couple of miles when he heard someone galloping behind him, and, looking back, saw the little Duke riding up on his pony, face flushed and bareheaded. “I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy gasped, “but I can’t eat dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry with me; if you’d let us get engaged last year, none of this would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!”\n\nThe Minister couldn’t help smiling at the handsome young rascal and was genuinely moved by his devotion to Virginia. Leaning down from his horse, he patted the boy kindly on the shoulders and said, “Well, Cecil, if you won’t go back, I suppose you’ll have to come with me, but I’ll need to get you a hat at Ascot.”"}

{"request_id":"8629bde30f61a374ed3a8cba","rewritten_text":"“No, no, that is to-morrow; and I especially wanted to see Knightley today for that very reason. Such a horribly broiling morning! I even walked across the fields”—she spoke as if deeply wronged—“which made everything worse. And then he was not at home! I assure you I am not pleased at all. No apology left, no message for me. The housekeeper insisted she knew nothing about my being expected. So strange! And no one could say where he had gone. Perhaps to Hartfield, perhaps to the Abbey Mill, perhaps into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this is not like our friend Knightley! Can you explain it?”

Emma entertained herself by agreeing that it was indeed very strange and that she had not a word to defend him.

“I cannot imagine,” said Mrs. Elton, feeling the insult as a wife ought to, “I cannot imagine how he could behave so to you, of all people! The very last person one would expect him to forget! My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message for you, I am sure he did. Even Knightley could not be so wildly careless; his servants must have forgotten. Depend on it, that was what happened. It is very likely with the Donwell servants; I have often noticed they are terribly awkward and negligent. I would not have such a creature as his Harry waiting at our sideboard for anything. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very poorly of her. She promised Wright a recipe and never sent it.”

“I met William Larkins,” continued Mr. Elton, “as I reached the house, and he told me I would not find his master at home, but I did not believe him. William seemed rather out of sorts. He said he could not imagine what was happening to his master lately, but he could hardly ever get a word with him. I have nothing to do with William’s troubles, yet it is very important that I see Knightley today; and it is therefore a serious annoyance that I took this hot walk for nothing.”

Emma felt she could do nothing better than go home at once. She was probably wanted there even now; and Mr. Knightley might be kept from falling further into offense with Mr. Elton, if not with William Larkins.

She was pleased, as she took her leave, to find Miss Fairfax determined to walk out of the room with her and even downstairs; it gave her the chance she instantly used, to say,"}

{"request_id":"6ec7244d6ff5880277c03738","rewritten_text":"“It’s just a tick.”

“Where’d you pick him up?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I’m not looking to sell.”

“Fine. It’s a pretty puny tick anyway.”

“Oh, anybody can put down a tick that isn’t theirs. I’m happy with it. It’s a good enough tick for me.”

“Sure, ticks are everywhere. I could have a thousand if I wanted.”

“Then why don’t you? Because you know you can’t. This one’s pretty early, I figure. It’s the first I’ve seen this year.”

“Hey, Huck—I’ll trade you my tooth for it.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom pulled out a slip of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry eyed it wistfully. The urge was strong. Finally he said:

“Is it real?”

Tom lifted his lip and showed the gap.

“All right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a deal.”

Tom tucked the tick into the percussion-cap box that had recently been the pinchbug’s cell, and the boys went their separate ways, each feeling richer.

When Tom reached the little isolated frame schoolhouse, he walked in briskly, as if he had hurried there as fast as he could. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike speed. The master, perched high in his big splint-bottom armchair, was dozing, lulled by the sleepy hum of study. The disturbance woke him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew his full name always meant trouble.

“Sir!”

“Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?”

Tom was about to take shelter in a lie when he saw two long braids of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized through the electric spark of love. Beside that figure was the only empty seat on the girls’ side of the room. Instantly he said:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The master’s pulse stopped; he stared helplessly. The hum of study ceased. The pupils wondered if this reckless boy had lost his senses. The master said:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

There was no mistaking it.

“Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astonishing admission I’ve ever heard. A simple ruler won’t do for this offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm swung until it was worn out and the supply of switches noticeably shrank. Then came the order:

“Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this be a lesson to you.”

The ripple of giggles around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but really it was caused more by his reverent awe of his unknown idol and the fearful pleasure in the good fortune that awaited him."}

{"request_id":"ca7c10e732e5dc1ae13d9f33","rewritten_text":"“If I can’t live on that, I won’t ask anyone to help me. Is that acceptable?”

A mighty roar of applause broke out, and through it rose the king’s voice: “Loose his bonds and set him free! Show him honor, high and low, rich and poor, for he has become the king’s right hand, invested with power and authority, and his seat is on the highest step of the throne! Now drive away this creeping night and bring back light and cheer, that the whole world may bless you.”

But I said, “It is nothing for a common man to be shamed before the world, but it would disgrace the king if anyone saw his minister naked without also seeing him freed from that shame. If I might ask for my clothes again—”

“They are not suitable,” the king interrupted. “Fetch garments of another kind; dress him like a prince!”

My plan was working. I needed things to stay as they were until the eclipse became total. Otherwise they would keep begging me to end the darkness, and of course I couldn’t do that. Sending for clothes bought me some time, but not enough. I had to find another excuse. I said it was natural for the king to rethink, to regret a little what he had done in excitement. So I would let the darkness deepen awhile, and if after a reasonable time the king still held the same decision, the darkness would be lifted. The king and everyone else disliked the idea, but I had to stand firm.

It grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I wrestled with those clumsy sixth-century clothes. Soon it was pitch-dark, and the crowd groaned in dread as cold uncanny night breezes moved through the place and stars flickered into view. When the eclipse finally became total I was relieved, but everyone else was miserable, which made sense. I said, “By his silence the king still accepts the terms.” Then I raised my hands, held them a moment, and said with the deepest solemnity, “Let the enchantment dissolve and pass harmless away!”

For a moment there was no answer in that thick dark and that graveyard hush. Then a silver edge of sun showed itself, and a moment later the assembly burst into a vast shout and surged toward me like a flood to overwhelm me with blessings and thanks; and Clarence was certainly among the last waves of that flood."}

{"request_id":"596e3b74d2b96202561b113d","rewritten_text":"I hurried along, and we soon reached my college. Then I remembered, with a shiver, that the creature I had left in my rooms might still be there, alive and roaming about. I dreaded seeing the monster, but I feared even more that Henry might see him. So I begged Henry to stay a few minutes at the bottom of the stairs while I ran up to my rooms. My hand was already on the lock before I came to my senses. I stopped, shaking with cold dread. I flung the door open, the way children do when they expect a ghost waiting on the other side, but nothing appeared. I stepped in with fear. The room was empty, and my bedroom was clear of its hideous visitor. I could hardly believe my luck, but once I was sure my enemy was gone, I clapped my hands for joy and ran back down to Clerval.

We went up to my room together, and the servant soon brought breakfast, but I could not control myself. It was not only joy that surged through me; my skin tingled with sharp sensitivity, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for a moment; I leaped over chairs, clapped my hands, and burst into wild laughter. At first Clerval thought my excitement came from delight at seeing him, but when he watched me more closely, he saw a strange madness in my eyes he could not explain, and my loud, unrestrained, almost cruel laughter alarmed and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what is wrong? Do not laugh like that. You are very ill! What is causing all this?”

“Do not ask me,” I shouted, covering my eyes, for I imagined the feared specter slipping into the room. “He can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I imagined the monster grabbing me; I struggled wildly and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had expected with such joy turned so strangely bitter. But I saw none of his grief, for I lay senseless and did not return to consciousness for a very long time.

This was the start of a nervous fever that kept me confined for many months. Through all of it Henry alone nursed me. Later I learned that, knowing my father was too old and frail for such a long journey and how unhappy my sickness would make Elizabeth, he spared them this sorrow by hiding how serious my illness was."}

{"request_id":"68bf848467991fa4b1a9360b","rewritten_text":"“I must go, unsure what awaits me, but I will come back here or join your group as soon as I can. A single word or look will decide whether I enter your father’s house tonight or never.”

Such a letter was not something she could recover from quickly. Half an hour alone to think might have calmed her, but the ten minutes she had before being interrupted, along with the constraints of her situation, did nothing to soothe her. Each moment only brought fresh excitement. It was overwhelming joy. Before she even moved past the first rush of feelings, Charles, Mary, and Henrietta all came in.

The urgent need to seem her usual self led to an immediate effort, but after a while she could do no more. She stopped understanding a word they were saying and had to claim she felt unwell and excuse herself. They could then see she looked very ill, were frightened and worried, and refused to leave her. This was awful. If they had only gone away and left her to enjoy the quiet of that room, she would have been cured; but having them all standing or hovering around her was maddening, and in desperation she said she would go home.

“Of course, my dear,” cried Mrs Musgrove, “go home at once and take care of yourself, so you can be well enough for the evening. I wish Sarah were here to treat you, but I am no doctor. Charles, ring and order a chair. She must not walk.”

But the chair was impossible. Worse than anything! To give up even the chance of saying two words to Captain Wentworth during her calm, solitary walk through town (and she was almost sure she would meet him) was unbearable. She protested against the chair, and Mrs Musgrove—who thought only of one kind of illness—after making sure, with some anxiety, that there had been no fall, that Anne had not slipped lately and hit her head, that she was certain she had had no fall, could let her go cheerfully and expect to find her better in the evening.

Determined to skip no possible precaution, Anne struggled and said—

“I am afraid, ma’am, that it is not perfectly clear. Please mention to the other gentlemen that we hope to see your whole party tonight. I fear there was some mistake, and I want you especially to assure Captain Harville and Captain Wentworth that we hope to see them both.”

“Oh, my dear, it is quite clear, I promise you.”"}

{"request_id":"dab4b59352614ec2b164ae55","rewritten_text":"“If you want one for home use, I can supply an excellent model, and I guarantee you’ll be satisfied with the result. May I ask who it’s meant for? If it’s for the police, or anyone connected with Scotland Yard, I’m afraid I can’t help you. The English detectives are really our best allies, and I’ve always found that by counting on their stupidity, we can do whatever we please. I couldn’t part with a single one of them.”

“I assure you,” said Lord Arthur, “it has nothing to do with the police. In fact, the clock is meant for the Dean of Chichester.”

“My word! I had no idea you felt so strongly about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do nowadays.”

“I’m afraid you give me too much credit, Herr Winckelkopf,” said Lord Arthur, blushing. “The truth is, I really know nothing about theology.”

“So it’s purely a private matter?”

“Purely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf shrugged and left the room, returning a few minutes later with a round cake of dynamite about the size of a penny, along with a charming little French clock topped by an ormolu figure of Liberty trampling the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face lit up when he saw it. “That’s exactly what I want,” he exclaimed, “and now tell me how it’s triggered.”

“Ah, that’s my secret,” replied Herr Winckelkopf, regarding his invention with understandable pride. “Let me know when you want it to explode, and I’ll set the mechanism to the exact moment.”

“Well, today is Tuesday, and if you could send it out at once—”

“That’s impossible; I have a great deal of important work underway for friends of mine in Moscow. Still, I might ship it tomorrow.”

“Oh, that will be quite soon enough,” said Lord Arthur politely. “If it’s delivered tomorrow night or Thursday morning, that’s fine. Time the explosion for Friday at noon exactly. The Dean is always at home then.”

“Friday, at noon,” repeated Herr Winckelkopf, making a note of it in a large ledger lying on a bureau near the fireplace.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising, “please let me know how much I owe you.”

“It’s such a small matter, Lord Arthur, that I’d rather not charge. The dynamite costs seven shillings and sixpence, the clock will be three pounds ten, and the shipping about five shillings. I’m only too happy to oblige a friend of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But what about your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"d88af1dd81262fe83858f511","rewritten_text":"It was well past noon when he woke. His valet had tiptoed in several times to see if he was moving and wondered why his young master slept so late. At last the bell rang, and Victor glided in with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sèvres china, then pulled back the olive satin curtains with their shimmering blue lining that covered the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” asked Dorian Gray drowsily.

“One fifteen, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, sipped some tea, and sorted through his letters. One had come by hand that morning from Lord Henry. He hesitated, then set it aside. The others he opened without interest. They held the usual mix of cards, dinner invitations, tickets for private views, programmes of charity concerts, and similar things that fashionable young men receive every morning during the season. There was a heavy bill for a chased silver Louis Quinze toilet set he still hadn’t dared send to his guardians, who were very old-fashioned and did not see that we live in an age where unnecessary things are our only needs; and there were several politely worded offers from Jermyn Street moneylenders willing to lend any amount at a moment’s notice at very reasonable interest.

After about ten minutes he rose, threw on an elaborate dressing gown of silk-embroidered cashmere, and went into the onyx-paved bathroom. The cool water revived him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had gone through. Now and then a faint sense of taking part in some odd tragedy returned, but it felt as unreal as a dream.

Once dressed, he went to the library and sat down to a light French breakfast set out for him on a small round table beside the open window. The day was exquisite. The warm air felt heavy with spice. A bee flew in and circled the blue-dragon bowl filled with sulphur-yellow roses in front of him. He felt completely happy.

Suddenly his eyes fell on the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he started.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” asked his valet, setting an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I’m not cold,” he murmured."}

{"request_id":"d0fd8e701beee5b33d0de1ef","rewritten_text":"And if he asked why I wanted it, and what right I thought I had to it, I would tell him, even though he cared little for such poor dreams, that I had loved Estella deeply and for a long time, and that although I had lost her and must live a mourning life, anything that affected her was still nearer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing Mr. Jaggers stand there completely still and silent, apparently unmoved by my appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you’re a man with a gentle heart. I’ve seen your pleasant home, and your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways with which you brighten up your business life. I beg you to say a word for me to Mr. Jaggers, and explain to him that, given all the circumstances, he should be more open with me!”

I have never seen two men look more strangely at each other than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this speech. At first I worried that Wemmick would be instantly fired, but that fear faded when I saw Mr. Jaggers relax into something like a smile, and Wemmick grow bolder.

“What’s all this?” asked Mr. Jaggers. “You with an old father, and you with pleasant, playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick replied. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, laying his hand on my arm and smiling broadly, “this man must be the most cunning impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” said Wemmick, growing bolder still. “I think you’re the impostor.”

Again they traded their earlier strange looks, each apparently still suspecting the other of trying to fool him.

“You with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“So long as it doesn’t interfere with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it be so. Now that I look at you, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you’re planning and contriving to have a pleasant home of your own one of these days, when you’re tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and actually sighed. “Pip,” he said, “let’s not talk about ‘poor dreams;’ you know more about such things than I do, having much fresher experience of that kind. But now about this other matter. I’ll put a scenario to you. Mind! I admit nothing.”

He paused, waiting for me to say that I fully understood he had expressly stated that he admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “consider this scenario. Suppose a woman, under circumstances like those you mentioned, kept her child hidden, and was forced to tell her lawyer, because he insisted that, in order to understand the full scope of his defense, he needed to know the truth about that child.”"}

{"request_id":"70bf128b684edbd6f000fc24","rewritten_text":"“So now I’m the owner of a few knights,” I said as we rode off. “Who would ever have thought I’d end up listing assets like that? I won’t know what to do with them unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, if it please you, sir, and their squires.”

“That’s a good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I didn’t understand you. I’ll tell you soon.” Then she mused softly, turning the words over her tongue with care: “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; yes, just so; where do they hang out. Truly the phrase has a fine and charming grace, and is prettily worded besides. I’ll repeat it again and again in my idle hours, so I may perhaps learn it. Where do they hang out. Indeed! Already it falls lightly from my tongue, and since—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes, the knights, you know. You were going to tell me about them. A while back, remember? Figuratively speaking, the game’s started.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Step up to the plate. I mean get to work on your statistics, and don’t waste so much tinder getting your fire going. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will gladly, and I’ll begin without delay. So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Good grief!”

You see, I realized my mistake right away. I’d set her machinery in motion; it was my fault; she’d take thirty days to get down to the actual facts. She usually began without an introduction and finished without a point. If you interrupted she either kept going as if nothing had happened or answered with a couple of words, then went back and repeated the sentence. So interruptions only made things worse; yet I had to interrupt, and pretty often, to save my own life—a person would die if he let her monotony drip on him all day.

“Good grief!” I cried in my distress. She went right back and started over:

“So the two of them departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. And so they came to an abbey of monks, where they were well lodged. In the morning they heard mass in the abbey, and then they rode on until they came to a great forest; then Sir Gawaine saw in a valley near a turret twelve lovely damsels and two knights in armor on great horses, and the damsels went back and forth by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"c4208723c0ed9a43bce37595","rewritten_text":"Mary never addressed Bath herself; the drudgery of a slow, frustrating correspondence with Elizabeth devolved entirely upon Anne.

Breakfast had scarcely ended when Captain and Mrs Harville, along with Captain Benwick, joined them for their final stroll through Lyme. They needed to leave for Uppercross by one o’clock, and until then were determined to remain together, outdoors as long as possible.

Anne soon found Captain Benwick drawing near her as they entered the street. Their talk the previous evening had not discouraged him from seeking her company again, and they walked awhile conversing once more of Mr Scott and Lord Byron, still unable, as any two readers might be, to align their opinions on either’s merits. Some incident, however, brought about an almost general reshuffling among their friends, and Anne found Captain Harville at her side in Benwick’s place.

“Miss Elliot,” he said, lowering his voice, “you have performed a kindness in coaxing that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he had such company more often. It does him harm, I believe, to be so shut up; but what can we do? We cannot part.”

“No,” Anne replied, “I can readily believe that to be impossible; yet in time perhaps—we know what time accomplishes in every sorrow, and you must remember, Captain Harville, your friend is still a young mourner—only last summer, I understand.”

“Ay, quite true,” he sighed deeply, “only June.”

“And perhaps not made known to him immediately.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, newly appointed to the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, dreading to hear of him; he sent letters inland, but the Grappler was ordered to Portsmouth. The news had to follow him there, yet who was to deliver it? not I. I would almost sooner have been run up to the yard-arm. No one could do it but that fine fellow” (gesturing to Captain Wentworth). “The Laconia had entered Plymouth the week before; no fear of her being sent out again. He chanced the rest; wrote for leave of absence, but without waiting for an answer, travelled night and day till he reached Portsmouth, hurried straight to the Grappler, and stayed with the poor man a whole week. That was what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. Judge, Miss Elliot, how dear he must be to us!”

Anne considered the question with complete conviction, and said as much as her own feeling, and Captain Harville’s composure, allowed; for he was too moved to pursue the topic further, and when he spoke again, it was on something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"157a452ef4ee71cfb31bd281","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. The perfect thing would be for all of us to ride on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and me—with my dear husband walking alongside. I really must talk to him about buying one. In the country it seems almost essential; no matter how many ways a woman has to occupy herself, she can’t stay shut indoors forever—and those long walks, you know—dust in summer, mud in winter.”

“You won’t find either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and right now it’s completely dry. Still, come on a donkey if that’s what you prefer. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I want everything to suit you in every possible way.”

“That I’m sure you do. I really must give you full credit, my good friend. Beneath that peculiar dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you’re the truest humorist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I completely appreciate your thoughtfulness in this whole plan. You’ve come up with exactly what will delight me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table set in the shade. He wanted to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the outing; and he knew that if any of them sat outdoors to eat, Mr. Woodhouse would inevitably fall ill. Under the harmless pretense of a morning drive and a couple of hours at Donwell, Mr. Woodhouse must not be lured into misery.

He was invited in good faith. No hidden horrors were to reproach him for his easy trust. He did agree to go. He had not visited Donwell in two years. “On some very fine morning, he and Emma and Harriet could go perfectly well; he could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls strolled around the gardens. He didn’t think they could be damp in the middle of the day. He would be very glad to see the old house again and very happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any other neighbor. He could see no objection at all to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there on some very fine morning. He considered it extremely well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—much cleverer than dining out. He did not care for dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was lucky in everyone’s ready agreement. The invitation was so well received everywhere that it seemed as if, like Mrs. Elton, each person took the plan as a personal compliment. Emma and Harriet declared themselves very eager for the pleasure it promised; and Mr. Weston, unprompted, promised to bring Frank over to join them if he could—a display of approval and gratitude that might have been done without. Mr. Knightley was then obliged to say he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston promised to write at once and spare no argument to persuade him to come."}

{"request_id":"1defa93a44570be6211f6b0b","rewritten_text":"He shivered and went back, closing the window behind him.

When he reached the door, he turned the key and opened it without even glancing at the murdered man. He felt that the key to the whole affair was not to let himself grasp what had happened. The friend who had painted the fatal portrait that had caused all his misery was gone from his life. That was enough.

Then he thought of the lamp. It was an unusual Moorish piece, dull silver worked with burnished steel arabesques and studded with rough turquoise. His servant might notice it was missing, and questions would follow. He hesitated, then turned back and took it from the table. He couldn’t avoid seeing the dead body. How still it was! How horribly white the long hands looked! It was like a dreadful wax figure.

After locking the door behind him, he crept quietly downstairs. The wood groaned and seemed to cry out in pain. He stopped several times and listened. No—everything was silent. It was only the sound of his own footsteps.

In the library he saw the bag and coat in the corner. They would have to be hidden. He unlocked a concealed cabinet in the wainscoting, where he kept his own strange disguises, and put them inside. He could burn them later. Then he checked his watch. Twenty minutes to two.

He sat down and began to think. Every year—almost every month—men were hanged in England for exactly what he had done. A fever of murder seemed to be in the air. Some blood-red star must have drifted too close to the earth... And yet, what evidence was there against him? Basil Hallward had left the house at eleven. No one had seen him return. Most of the servants were at Selby Royal. His valet had gone to bed... Paris! Yes, Basil had gone to Paris, and by the midnight train, just as he had intended. With his secretive ways, it would be months before anyone became suspicious. Months! Everything could be destroyed long before that.

Suddenly he had an idea. He put on his fur coat and hat and went out into the hall. There he paused, hearing the slow heavy tread of a policeman on the pavement outside and seeing the flash of the bull’s-eye lantern reflected in the window. He waited, holding his breath.

After a few moments he lifted the latch and slipped outside, closing the door very gently behind him. Then he started ringing the bell."}

{"request_id":"524f2fe42eb9e39981d29224","rewritten_text":"Other chances to study them were sure to come. Before long, Anne had seen the four together often enough to form an opinion, though she was too prudent to share it at home, where neither husband nor wife would be pleased. While she believed Louisa was the slight favorite, she also felt certain—so far as memory and experience allowed—that Captain Wentworth loved neither of them. They were more taken with him; yet even that feeling was not real love, only a brief fever of admiration that might, and likely must, slip into love for some of them. Charles Hayter seemed to know he was being overlooked, and still Henrietta sometimes looked torn between the two men. Anne wished she could point out to them all what they were doing, and warn them of the trouble they risked. She did not suspect anyone of deceit. Her greatest comfort was believing that Captain Wentworth had no idea of the pain he caused. There was no gloating, no petty triumph in him. He had probably never heard, and never considered, Charles Hayter’s claims. His only fault was in accepting the attentions (for “accepting” was the word) of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw. Three days passed without a single visit to Uppercross—a striking change. He even turned down a formal dinner invitation; and when Mr Musgrove found him surrounded by heavy books, both Mr and Mrs Musgrove were certain something was wrong, and gravely remarked that he was studying himself to death. Mary hoped and felt sure Henrietta had given him an outright dismissal, while her husband kept expecting to see him again tomorrow. Anne could only think Charles Hayter was being sensible.

One morning around this time, Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth had gone shooting together, and while the sisters at the Cottage sat quietly working, their visitors appeared at the window—the sisters from the Mansion-house.

It was a lovely November day, and the Miss Musgroves walked through the small grounds and paused solely to announce that they planned a long walk; therefore, they assumed Mary would not want to join them. When Mary instantly answered, a little jealous at being thought a poor walker, “Oh, yes, I should like that very much; I am very fond of a long walk,” Anne was sure, from the expression on the girls’ faces, that her company was exactly what they did not want. Again she marveled at the family habit that seemed to require everything to be shared and every plan to be communicated and carried out together, no matter how inconvenient or unwanted."}

{"request_id":"19f880fd04a3788c9e95ff48","rewritten_text":"If she had known that her sister meant to pull her away from such prospects and realities, what would she have felt? Only her mother could have understood, for she might have felt almost the same. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was her sole consolation for the bleak conviction that her husband never intended to go there himself.

Yet they were completely unaware of what had happened, and their giddy excitement lasted, with barely a pause, right up to the day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to see Mr. Wickham for the last time. Since she had often been in his company since coming back, her agitation was mostly gone; the turmoil of her earlier attraction had entirely vanished. She had even learned to perceive, in the very gentleness that had first charmed her, an affected sameness that disgusted and exhausted her. In his present behaviour toward her she found a new source of annoyance, because the inclination he soon showed to renew the attentions that had marked the beginning of their acquaintance could only, after all that had since occurred, provoke her. She lost all concern for him when she realized that he had singled her out as the target of such idle, frivolous flirtation; and while she firmly rebuffed him, she could not help but feel rebuked that he believed her vanity would be gratified and her preference secured at any moment by the return of his attentions, however long absent and for whatever reason.

On the very last day the regiment remained in Meryton, he dined with other officers at Longbourn; and Elizabeth was so little inclined to part from him on good terms that when he casually asked how she had spent her time at Hunsford, she mentioned that Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy had both spent three weeks at Rosings, and asked if he knew the former.

He looked surprised, displeased, even alarmed; but after a moment’s recovery and a returning smile, said he had once seen him often; then, noting that he was a very gentlemanlike man, he asked how she had liked him. Her reply praised him warmly. With an air of nonchalance, he soon added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him often?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners are very different from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves once you know him.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with a look she noticed. “And may I ask—” but stopping himself, he added more lightly, “Is it in his manners that he improves?”"}

{"request_id":"7b690377e207a03d5e6ea8a5","rewritten_text":"“Your father might let you stay, if your mother agrees. Fathers never think daughters as important. If you stay another full month, I can take one of you as far as London, for I am going there in early June for a week. Since Dawson has no objection to the barouche-box, there will be plenty of room for one of you—and if the weather is cool, I might even take both, as neither of you is large.”

“You are all kindness, madam; but we must follow our original plan.”

Lady Catherine looked resigned. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always speak plainly, and I cannot bear the idea of two young women traveling post alone. It is highly improper. You must find someone to send. I have the strongest dislike of such things. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended according to their station. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted she have two man-servants with her. Miss Darcy, daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not properly travel in any other way. I am very careful about these matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am glad I thought to mention it, for it would reflect badly on you to let them go alone.”

“My uncle will send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, does he? I am glad someone thinks of these things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you mention my name at the Bell, you will be well attended to.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions about their journey, and, since she did not answer all of them herself, Elizabeth had to pay attention—which she counted fortunate, for with her mind so full she might have forgotten where she was. Reflection had to be saved for solitary hours; whenever she was alone, she indulged in it as her greatest relief, and every day she took a solitary walk so she could enjoy the strange pleasure of painful memories.

Mr. Darcy’s letter was becoming something she would soon know by heart. She studied every sentence, and her feelings toward its writer varied greatly. When she remembered his manner of address, she still burned with indignation; but when she thought how wrongly she had judged and reproached him, her anger turned against herself, and his disappointed feelings became the object of her compassion."}
