{"request_id":"d938ab8f18913996ece57854","rewritten_text":"The studio was saturated with the lush scent of roses, and whenever the light summer breeze rustled the garden trees, the heavy fragrance of lilacs or the subtler perfume of pink-blossoming hawthorn drifted through the open door.

From the corner of the Persian saddlebag divan where he lounged, doing what he always did—smoking countless cigarettes—Lord Henry Wotton could just glimpse the honey-sweet, honey-colored laburnum blooms, their trembling branches barely able to carry such fiery beauty. Every so often, the fantastical silhouettes of birds crossing the long tussore silk curtains in front of the enormous window created a fleeting Japanese effect, reminding him of those pale, jade-faced Tokyo painters who try to suggest speed and motion through an art that must remain still. The low drone of bees forcing their way through the tall, unmown grass or circling over and over around the dusty gilt trumpets of the sprawling woodbine only made the stillness feel heavier. The faint roar of London sounded like the deep bourdon note of a distant organ.

In the center of the room, clamped to a tall easel, stood the full-length portrait of a young man of extraordinary beauty. Seated a little way in front of it was the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance years ago stirred so much public excitement and inspired so many strange theories.

As the painter studied the elegant, handsome figure he had so skillfully captured, a pleased smile crossed his face and seemed ready to stay. But he abruptly jumped up, shut his eyes, and pressed his fingers over his lids, as though he were trying to trap within his mind some elusive dream he feared waking from.

“It’s your finest work, Basil, the best thing you’ve ever done,” Lord Henry said lazily. “You must send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is too large and too vulgar. Every time I’ve gone, either there were so many people I couldn’t see the paintings—which was dreadful—or so many paintings I couldn’t see the people—which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only option.”

“I don’t think I’ll send it anywhere,” Basil replied, tossing back his head in that odd way that used to make his Oxford friends laugh."}

You’re the watchman, aren’t you! All right, though—nothing’s happened.” “My! Have I been sleeping?” “Only partly. Near time for us to be moving, pard. What’ll we do with what little plunder we’ve still got?” “I don’t know—leave it here as usual, I suppose. No reason to haul it off until we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver’s heavy to lug.” “Well—all right—it ain’t any trouble to come once more.” “No—but I’d rather come at night the way we used to—it’s safer.” “Yes; but listen, it might be a while before I get the right chance for that job; accidents could happen; it’s not in such a safe spot; we’ll just bury it properly—and bury it deep.” “Good notion,” said the comrade. He crossed the room, knelt, lifted one of the back hearth-stones, and fetched out a bag that clinked pleasantly. He took off twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same for Injun Joe, and handed the bag over. Joe was kneeling in the corner, digging with his bowie-knife. Instantly, the boys forgot every fear and misery. With greedy eyes they tracked every motion. Fortune!—its splendor was beyond imagining! Six hundred dollars could make half a dozen boys rich! Here was treasure-hunting under the best auspices—there’d be no vexing uncertainty about where to dig. They nudged each other at every turn—eloquent prods easily read, saying simply—“Oh, aren’t you glad now that we’re here!” Joe’s knife struck something. “Hey!” he said. “What is it?” asked his comrade. “Half-rotten plank—no, I think it’s a box. Here—lend a hand and we’ll find out what it’s doing here. No need, I’ve broken a hole.” He reached in and pulled his hand back out— “Man, it’s money!” The two examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were as thrilled and delighted as the men. Joe’s comrade said: “We’ll make short work of this. There’s a rusty old pick among the weeds in the corner on the far side of the fireplace—I spotted it a minute ago.”"}

{"request_id":"5c9cc3ece964336d5405a024","rewritten_text":"When I returned, I found this letter from my father:

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably been waiting impatiently for a letter setting the date of your return to us, and I was first tempted to write only a few lines telling you when to come home. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I dare not do it. How shocked you would be, my son, expecting a joyful welcome, only to find tears and misery. And how, Victor, am I to tell you of our disaster? Your time away cannot have dulled your feeling for our joys and sorrows, yet how can I cause my long-absent son such pain? I want to prepare you for the horrible news, yet it’s impossible. Even now I imagine your eyes running over this page, searching for the words that carry the dread news.

“William is dead—that sweet child whose smile warmed my heart, who was so gentle but so lively! Victor, he was murdered.

“I won’t try to console you, only to tell you what happened.

“Last Thursday (May 7th), my niece, your two brothers, and I walked at Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, and we stayed out longer than usual. It was already twilight when we thought of going back, and then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were missing. We sat on a bench to wait for their return. Soon Ernest arrived and asked if we had seen William. He said they had been playing, that William had run off to hide, and that he had searched in vain, then waited a long time, but William never came back.

“This report alarmed us, and we continued searching until night fell. Elizabeth suggested he might have gone home. He wasn’t there. We went back out with torches; I couldn’t rest, thinking my sweet boy was lost and exposed to the damp night air, and Elizabeth was in torment. Around five in the morning I found my lovely boy, whom I had last seen full of health the night before, lying on the grass, pale and still, the mark of the murderer’s fingers on his neck.

“We carried him home, and the anguish on my face gave the secret away to Elizabeth. She begged to see the body. I tried to stop her, but she insisted, and once in the room where he lay, she quickly examined the poor child’s neck and, clasping her hands, cried, ‘Oh God!’”"}

{"request_id":"915392e0f93084ebb69b2b87","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it and was about to start on the bureau when he was called in to get ready for Sunday school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a bar of soap, and he went outside, set the basin on the little bench, dipped the soap in the water and set it aside, rolled up his sleeves, poured the water out on the ground very carefully, then went back into the kitchen and started rubbing his face with the towel behind the door. But Mary took the towel away and said:

“Now aren’t you ashamed, Tom? You mustn’t be so bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was a bit thrown off. The basin was filled again, and this time he stood over it a moment, working up his nerve, took a deep breath, and began. When he came into the kitchen soon after, both eyes shut and hands searching for the towel, a respectable amount of suds and water was running from his face. But when he was done with the towel, he still wasn’t passable, because the clean patch stopped at his chin and jaw like a mask; below and beyond that line stretched a dark stretch of untouched dirt down his chest and around his neck. Mary took over, and when she finished he was a man and a brother without color lines, his soaked hair neatly brushed and the short curls arranged into a tidy, even look. [He privately flattened the curls with effort and plastered his hair close to his head; he thought curls were girlish, and his own made his life miserable.] Then Mary brought out the suit he had worn only on Sundays for two years—they were simply called his “other clothes,” which tells us how many he had. After he dressed, she straightened him up; she buttoned his neat jacket to his chin, turned his wide shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and topped him with his speckled straw hat. He now looked greatly improved—and just as uncomfortable. He felt as uncomfortable as he appeared, because whole clothes and cleanliness always cramped him. He hoped Mary would overlook his shoes, but that hope died; she smeared them well with tallow, as people did, and brought them out. He lost his temper and said he was always made to do everything he didn’t want to do."}

content.text: {"request_id":"143a00ea596a9f053adbe515","rewritten_text":"Weeks passed, and I became more and more absorbed in you. Then something new happened. I had painted you as Paris in delicate armour, and as Adonis with a huntsman’s cloak and polished boar-spear. You had sat crowned with heavy lotus blossoms on the prow of Adrian’s barge, looking out over the green, muddy Nile. You had bent over the still pool of a Greek woodland and seen in its silent silver the marvel of your own face. All of it had been what art should be—unconscious, ideal, distant. One day, a day I sometimes call fatal, I decided to paint a wonderful portrait of you as you really are, not in the clothes of past ages but in your own dress and in your own time. Whether it was the realism of that approach, or the simple wonder of your personality shown to me so directly, without mist or veil, I do not know. But as I worked, every small stroke of colour seemed to expose my secret. I grew afraid others would see my worship. I felt, Dorian, that I had said too much, that I had poured too much of myself into it. So I resolved never to let the picture be exhibited. You were a little annoyed, but you did not understand what it meant to me. Harry, who heard about it, laughed at me. I did not mind. When the picture was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt certain I was right. After a few days the piece left my studio, and once that unbearable fascination was gone, it seemed silly that I had ever believed it showed anything beyond your remarkable looks and my own skill. Even now I cannot help thinking it is wrong to believe the passion one feels while creating is ever truly shown in the work. Art is always more abstract than we like to think. Form and colour only tell us about form and colour—that is all. Often it seems art hides the artist far more than it reveals him. So when I got the offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the main piece in my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I see now you were right. The picture cannot be shown. Please do not be angry with me, Dorian, for what I have confessed."}

{"request_id":"9ae2e841639c0aed60f289bf","rewritten_text":"Emma felt no remorse for stooping to visit the Coles. The outing supplied her with many agreeable remembrances the following day; and whatever she might have sacrificed in the way of stately exclusiveness was more than compensated by the glimmer of popular approval. Doubtless she had enchanted the Coles—worthy souls deserving of delight—and she had left behind a reputation that would not quickly fade.

Complete happiness, even in recollection, is rare; and there were two matters on which she was not entirely at ease. She questioned whether she had violated the bond of woman to woman by betraying her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings to Frank Churchill. It was scarcely proper; yet the idea had been so powerful that it broke out in spite of her, and his ready acquiescence in all she said flattered her discernment so much that she could not be perfectly convinced she ought to have remained silent.

Her other regret likewise concerned Jane Fairfax, and here she entertained no uncertainty. She sincerely and plainly lamented the inferiority of her own playing and singing. She deeply lamented the idle hours of her childhood—and seated herself to practise with vigor for an hour and a half.

She was then interrupted by Harriet’s arrival; and if Harriet’s admiration could have soothed her, she would soon have been appeased.

“Oh! if only I could play like you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Do not couple us, Harriet. My playing resembles hers no more than a lamp resembles sunshine.”

“Oh, dear—I think you are the better performer of the two. I rate your playing quite as high as hers. I would much rather listen to you. Everyone last evening praised your performance.”

“Those who knew anything about it must have felt the difference. The fact is, Harriet, my playing is just good enough to earn praise, while Jane Fairfax’s far surpasses it.”

“Well, I shall always maintain you play quite as well as she does, or that, if there is any difference, nobody could ever detect it. Mr. Cole spoke of the elegance of your taste; and Mr. Frank Churchill went on and on about your taste, saying he valued taste far more than execution.”

“Ah! but Jane Fairfax possesses both, Harriet.”

“Can you be sure? I saw she had execution, but I did not know she had any taste. Nobody mentioned it. And I detest Italian singing.—One cannot make out a word of it. Besides, even if she does play so extremely well, it is merely what she is bound to do, since she will have to teach.”"}

{"request_id":"da9e48b5d56db2ebf218a36e","rewritten_text":"Even so, the boy kept growing paler, more downcast, and more depressed. She tried hot baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges. He stayed as solemn as a hearse. She added a thin oatmeal diet and blister plasters to back up the water treatment. She gauged his capacity like a jug and filled him every day with patent remedies.

By now Tom hardly noticed persecution. This stage terrified the old lady. That indifference had to be shattered no matter what. Then she heard about Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a large supply right away. She tasted it and felt profound gratitude. It was pure fire in liquid form. She gave up the water cures and everything else and put her faith entirely in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and waited anxiously. Her worries vanished instantly; her heart was calm again, because the “indifference” was gone. The boy couldn’t have shown more wild, eager interest if she’d lit a fire under him.

Tom decided it was time to snap out of it; this lifestyle might suit his tragic mood, but it was losing romance and gaining too much chaotic variety. He weighed several escape plans and settled on pretending to adore Pain-killer. He asked for it so often he became a pest, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop bothering her. If it had been Sid, she would have enjoyed it without a second thought; but since it was Tom, she kept secret watch on the bottle. She noticed the medicine really was disappearing, yet it never occurred to her that Tom was treating a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One day, as Tom was dosing the crack, his aunt’s yellow cat wandered up, purring, eyeing the teaspoon greedily, begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you mean it, Peter.”

But Peter insisted he wanted it.

“You’d better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“You’ve asked for it, so I’ll give it to you, because I’m not mean; but if you dislike it, you can’t blame anyone but yourself.”

Peter agreed. Tom pried the cat’s mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter shot two yards into the air, then let out a war whoop and tore around the room, slamming into furniture, toppling flowerpots, and creating general havoc."}

{"request_id":"0041859c7570ed4d03ab834a","rewritten_text":"“I suppose I may ask you two questions?”

“You can ask,” said Monks, with a hint of surprise. “Whether I answer is another matter.”

“That makes three questions,” remarked Mr. Bumble, trying to be witty.

“Is that what you expected to get from me?” the matron demanded.

“It is,” said Monks. “And the other question?”

“What do you plan to do with it? Could it be used against me?”

“Never,” Monks responded, “nor against me either. Look at this—but don’t step closer, or your life won’t be worth a rush.”

He suddenly shoved the table aside and, pulling an iron ring in the floorboards, threw back a large trapdoor right by Mr. Bumble’s feet. The shock sent Bumble stumbling several steps back.

“Look down,” said Monks, lowering the lantern into the darkness. “Don’t be afraid of me. I could have dropped you quietly enough while you sat over it, if that had been my plan.”

Encouraged, the matron moved to the edge; even Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, crept closer. The muddy water, swollen by heavy rain, rushed below. The roar of its splashing and swirling against the slimy green piles drowned every other sound. There had once been a mill underneath; the tide, foaming and chafing around the few rotting posts and scraps of machinery still left, seemed to leap forward with new force once free of the useless obstacles that had tried to block it.

“If you threw a man’s body down there, where would it be by morning?” asked Monks, swinging the lantern over the dark shaft.

“Twelve miles downriver, and chopped to bits as well,” Bumble answered, recoiling.

Monks pulled the small packet from his breast, where he had hastily hidden it. He tied it to a lead weight from an old pulley lying on the floor, then dropped it into the stream. It fell straight and true, slipping into the water with barely a splash, and vanished.

The three of them looked at one another and seemed to breathe easier.

“There,” Monks said, closing the trapdoor, which thudded back into place. “If the sea ever gives up the dead, like the books say, it will keep its gold and silver and that rubbish with it. We’re finished talking and can end this pleasant gathering.”

“By all means,” Mr. Bumble replied eagerly.

“You’ll keep your mouth shut, won’t you?” Monks said, with a threatening glare."}

{"request_id":"0507e8212fd6f6e46d2afdf3","rewritten_text":"“So you won’t, won’t you? Oh, you sweet little flat!”

“It’s wicked, ain’t it, Oliver?” Charley Bates asked. “He’ll end up scragged, won’t he?”

“I’ve no idea what you mean,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. With that, Master Bates snatched up the tail of his neckerchief; holding it upright, he let his head drop sideways and forced a queer sound through his teeth, presenting by this lively mime that scragging and hanging were one and the same.

“That’s the ticket,” Charley said. “See how he gapes, Jack! I never met such capital company as that boy there; he’ll finish me off, I’m certain.” Having laughed himself nearly silly again, Master Charley Bates resumed his pipe, tears standing in his eyes.

“You’ve been badly raised,” remarked the Dodger, inspecting his boots with immense satisfaction after Oliver had buffed them. “Still, Fagin will make something of you, or you’ll be the first he ever had that didn’t pay. You’d best start straightaway; you’ll be in the line long before you expect it, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates supported this counsel with sundry moral observations of his own; when these were spent, he and his companion Mr. Dawkins launched into a glowing account of the myriad delights belonging to their way of life, lacing the description with countless suggestions that the best course for Oliver was to win Fagin’s favour without delay, by the same methods they themselves had used.

“And always keep this in mind, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as the Jew’s key was heard rattling in the door overhead, “if you won’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the point of jawing like that?” Master Bates broke in; “he doesn’t understand.”

“If you won’t take pocket handkerchers and watches,” the Dodger continued, translating his speech to Oliver’s comprehension, “some other bloke will; then the coves who lose them will be worse off, and you’ll be worse off, too, and no soul a halfpenny the better except the chaps who nab them—and you’ve as good a claim to them as they have.”

“Certainly, certainly!” said the Jew, who had slipped in without Oliver noticing. “It’s all contained in a nutshell, my dear; in a nutshell, take the Dodger’s word. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old fellow rubbed his hands gleefully while he confirmed the Dodger’s logic in this fashion, chuckling with delight at his pupil’s skill.

The talk went no further just then, for the Jew had come home accompanied by Miss Betsy and a gentleman unfamiliar to Oliver, though the Dodger greeted him as Tom Chitling; after lingering on the stairs to swap a few compliments with the lady, he now entered the room."}

{"request_id":"6a307eb7d6ce145789f2c92b","rewritten_text":"He said that as he left home and passed through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke coming from the inn’s chimney. Thinking travelers might be gathered there, he knocked and was let in. Inside he found only Lucy and her mother. Her mother had lost the use of her limbs from rheumatism, so little by little all the other residents of the area had departed, leaving them alone. Lucy begged him to stay; in a week or two her mother would be better, and then they could set out, but if they were left abandoned like this they would surely die. The man said his wife and children were already among the emigrants, so he believed it impossible to remain. As a last resort, Lucy gave him a letter for Idris, to be delivered wherever he met us. At least he carried out this task, and Idris, deeply moved, received the following letter:—

“Honored lady,

“I know you will remember and pity me, and I dare to hope you will help me; what other hope do I have? Forgive my way of writing; I am so confused. A month ago my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already better, and in another month she would surely be able to travel, in the way you kindly offered to arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone. As each person left, they said perhaps my mother would be better before we were completely deserted. Three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who had stayed to the end because of his newborn child; since there were many of them, I thought I might convince them to wait a bit longer for us. But I found their house deserted. I hadn’t seen another soul until this good man arrived. What will become of us? My mother doesn’t know our situation; she is so ill that I’ve kept it from her.

“Won’t you send someone to us? I’m sure we will die miserably if things stay as they are. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road, and even if she were better and I somehow knew the roads and could travel the many miles to the sea, you would all be in France by then, and the great ocean would lie between us, which is terrifying even to sailors.”"}

{"request_id":"f72d296e45acccd8f081fdbf","rewritten_text":"Their arrival had lit a kind of fire in the heart of Saint Antoine, spreading fast as they moved along, flashing like flames across the faces at nearly every door and window. Still, no one followed them, and no one spoke when they stepped into the wine-shop, though every eye there fixed on them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

That seemed to loosen every tongue. A chorus of “Good day!” answered him.

“It is bad weather, gentlemen,” Defarge said, shaking his head.

At that, each man glanced at his neighbor, then everyone lowered their eyes and sat silent. One man alone rose and went out.

“My wife,” Defarge said aloud to Madame Defarge, “I have traveled several leagues with this good mender of roads, named Jacques. I met him by chance a day and a half outside Paris. He is a good child, this mender of roads named Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man rose and went out. Madame Defarge set wine before the mender of roads called Jacques, who lifted his blue cap to the others and drank. He carried coarse dark bread inside his blouse; he ate it now and then, munching and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter. A third man rose and went out.

Defarge took a draught of wine, though less than he had poured for the stranger, being himself used to it, and waited until the countryman had finished his breakfast. He looked at no one, and now no one looked at him; not even Madame Defarge, who had picked up her knitting again and was at work.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked when the time was right.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come, then! You shall see the room I told you you could use. It will suit you perfectly.”

They went out of the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, from the courtyard up a steep staircase, from the staircase into a garret—the same garret where once a white-haired man had sat on a low bench, stooping forward, busily making shoes.

No white-haired man waited there now; but the three men who had left the wine-shop one by one were there. And between them and that white-haired man far away, the only link was that they had once peered at him through cracks in the wall.

Defarge shut the door carefully and spoke in a low voice:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness I met as arranged, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"e9b2df15ea1f328a137a522b","rewritten_text":"But no, there was something flashier than even that. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future stretched before him, blazing with unimaginable splendor. His name would echo around the world and make people shudder. He pictured himself tearing across the dancing seas in his sleek, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with his grisly flag flying at the fore. At the height of his fame, he would stride into the old village church, sunburned and weather-beaten, dressed in a black velvet doublet and trunks, great jackboots, a crimson sash, a belt bristling with horse pistols, a crime-stained cutlass at his side, a slouch hat with trailing plumes, his black flag unfurled, skull and crossbones displayed, while the whispers rose in awed delight: “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—The Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was settled; his path was chosen. He would run away from home and set out. He would leave the very next morning. So he had to start preparing. He gathered his resources. He went to a rotting log nearby and began digging under one end with his Barlow knife. Soon he hit wood that sounded hollow. He slid his hand in and recited this incantation with solemn emphasis:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. Lifting it revealed a neat little cache with sides and bottom of shingles. Inside lay a marble. Tom’s astonishment was boundless. He scratched his head in perplexity and said, “Well, that beats anything!” Then he flung the marble away in irritation and stood thinking. The truth was, a superstition he and all his friends considered infallible had failed. If you buried a marble with the required spell, left it alone for two weeks, and then reopened the spot with the incantation he had just used, every marble you had ever lost would have gathered there, no matter how widely scattered. But this time, it had clearly failed. Tom’s whole structure of faith was shaken. He had heard of it succeeding many times and never of it failing. It never occurred to him that he himself had tried it several times but could never relocate the hiding places afterward. He pondered the mystery for a while and finally concluded that some witch had interfered and broken the charm."}

{"request_id":"1527b87dcfca684fe13794fd","rewritten_text":"All this, and even more—vastly more—would I most cheerfully relate. Yet, to be concise, I must insist on my recompense. I yearn to return to my family and my home; and as the condition of any further disclosures from me—in view of the illumination I can offer upon many most weighty branches of both physical and metaphysical science—I must entreat, through the good offices of your honorable body, forgiveness for the crime I committed in causing the deaths of the creditors at the time of my departure from Rotterdam. This, therefore, is the aim of the present communication. Its bearer, a native of the moon, whom I have persuaded and carefully coached to act as my envoy to earth, will await your Excellencies’ decision, and bring back the sought pardon to me, if it be obtainable in any fashion.

“I have the honor to remain, etc., your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

Upon finishing this remarkable manuscript, Professor Rub-a-dub, it is related, let his pipe tumble to the floor in sheer astonishment, and Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, having removed his spectacles, polished them, and returned them to his pocket, so far forgot propriety and his own dignity as to turn thrice upon his heel, in the pure essence of amazement and admiration. There could be no doubt—the pardon must be procured. Thus swore, with a hearty oath, Professor Rub-a-dub, and thus the illustrious Von Underduk ultimately concluded, as he took his fellow savant by the arm and, without uttering a syllable, set forth at full speed for home to ponder the measures to be pursued. Upon reaching the burgomaster’s threshold, however, the professor ventured to remark that since the messenger had seen fit to vanish—surely terrified to death by the ferocious looks of the Rotterdam burghers—the pardon would scarcely be of service, as no one save a lunar being would dare undertake so prodigious a voyage. The burgomaster concurred in this, and the matter was therefore dropped. Not so, however, the gossip and conjecture. Once published, the letter stirred a multitude of tales and views. Some ultra-wise souls even rendered themselves absurd by deriding the whole affair as nothing more than a hoax. Yet hoax, in the vocabulary of such people, seems a blanket term for everything beyond their understanding. For my own part, I cannot imagine on what grounds they have leveled such a charge. Let us examine their statements:"}

{"request_id":"236b19bb79c9e05b1815214c","rewritten_text":"Could not tell if the voice was a man’s or a woman’s. Could not catch the words, but believed the language was Spanish. This witness described the condition of the room and the bodies just as we reported yesterday.

“Henri Duval, a neighbor and silver-smith, testifies that he was among the first to enter the house. He generally agrees with Musèt’s account. As soon as they forced their way in, they shut the door again to keep out the quickly growing crowd, despite the late hour. This witness thought the high voice belonged to an Italian. He knew it was not French. Could not be certain it was a man’s voice; it might have been a woman’s. He did not know Italian. Could not make out the words, but the tone convinced him the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had spoken with both often. He was sure the high voice was neither of the two deceased women.

“Odenheimer, a restaurateur, offered his testimony. Because he does not speak French, he was questioned through an interpreter. He is from Amsterdam. He was passing the house when the screams began. They lasted several minutes—perhaps ten. They were long, loud, and terribly distressing. He was among those who entered the building. He confirmed the earlier evidence in every respect except one. He was sure the sharp voice was a man’s—a Frenchman’s. Could not make out the words. They were loud and quick, uneven, spoken as if the speaker were afraid and angry. The voice was rough—not really shrill but rough. He would not call it a shrill voice. The gruff voice said “sacré,” “diable,” and once “mon Dieu.”

“Jules Mignaud, banker of the firm Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the older Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She opened an account with his banking house in the spring—eight years before. She often deposited small sums. She drew nothing until the third day before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs. This amount was paid in gold, and a clerk escorted the money home.

“Adolphe Le Bon, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, states that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her home with the 4000 francs, packed in two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from him, while the old lady took the other.”"}

{"request_id":"9f44fb19eb77057fbf785f34","rewritten_text":"Such were the events that weighed on Felix’s heart and made him, when I first saw him, the unhappiest member of his family. He could have borne poverty, and while hardship was the reward of his virtue he took pride in it; but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were miseries far more bitter and beyond repair. The arrival of the Arabian woman revived his spirit.

When the news reached Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to think no more of her lover and to prepare to return to her native land. Safie’s generous nature was outraged by this command; she tried to reason with her father, but he left her in anger, repeating his tyrannical order.

A few days later, the Turk rushed into his daughter’s room and told her that he had reason to believe someone had revealed his stay in Leghorn, and that he would soon be handed over to the French government; he had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople, where he would sail in a few hours. He meant to leave his daughter in the care of a trusted servant to follow at her convenience with most of his property, which had not yet arrived in Leghorn.

Once alone, Safie considered what she ought to do in this sudden crisis. A life in Turkey filled her with loathing; both her faith and her feelings opposed it. From some papers of her father’s that came into her hands she learned of her lover’s exile and the name of the place where he was living. She hesitated for a while, but finally made up her mind. Taking some of her own jewels and a sum of money, she left Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who knew the common tongue of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

She reached a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage without trouble, but there her attendant fell dangerously ill. Safie tended her with devoted care, yet the poor girl died, and the Arabian was left alone, unable to speak the language of the country and entirely ignorant of the world’s customs. She was fortunate, though. The Italian had mentioned their destination, and after her death the mistress of the house where they had stayed ensured that Safie safely reached her lover’s cottage."}

{"request_id":"f1664524bdc1540cec4a6c90","rewritten_text":"Reading his letter again as she answered it softened her so much that she had to bolster herself with a few firm phrases, and she was so distressed at the thought of making him unhappy, so troubled over what his mother and sisters would think and say, so anxious that they not judge her ungrateful, that Emma believed if the young man had crossed her path at that moment, he would have been accepted after all.

Still, the letter was written and sealed and sent. The matter was settled and Harriet safe. She felt rather low all evening, but Emma could excuse her gentle regrets and sometimes eased them by speaking of her own affection, sometimes by mentioning Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” she said in a slightly mournful tone.

“And if you were, I could never bear to let you go, my Harriet. You are far too essential at Hartfield to be spared for Abbey-Mill.”

“And I’m sure I should never wish to go there, for I’m never happy anywhere but Hartfield.”

Later she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what happened. I am sure Miss Nash would—for Miss Nash thinks her own sister very well married, and he is only a linen-draper.”

“One would not want greater pride or polish in a schoolteacher, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you this chance of marriage; even this success would seem valuable to her. As for anything better for you, she is probably quite unaware. The attentions of a certain person can hardly have made it into Highbury gossip yet. So far I suspect you and I are the only ones his looks and manners have clued in.”

Harriet blushed, smiled, and remarked that it was odd anyone should like her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton certainly lifted her spirits; but before long she was tender-hearted again toward the rejected Mr. Martin.

“Now he has my letter,” she murmured. “I wonder what they are all doing—whether his sisters know—if he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he won’t take it too hard.”

“Let us think instead of our absent friends who are occupied more cheerfully,” cried Emma. “Perhaps at this very moment Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his mother and sisters, telling them how much lovelier the original is, and after being asked five or six times, finally letting them hear your name—your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"503dbb232b55c544d6fc6f5d","rewritten_text":"After I sent in the petitions, I could not keep away from the places where they were. I felt they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near. In that restless, aching state of mind, I walked the streets every evening, passing the offices and houses where I had left the petitions. To this day, the tired western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night—with their rows of stern, shut-up mansions and their endless lamps—remain bleak to me because of it.

I could not visit him as often now, and he was kept under tighter watch. Thinking they suspected me of trying to carry poison to him, I asked to be searched before sitting down at his bedside. I told the officer there that I would do anything to prove my intentions were pure. No one was cruel to him or to me. There was duty to do, and it was done without roughness. The officer always told me he was worse, and other sick prisoners in the room, along with prisoners acting as nurses—criminals, yet capable of kindness, thank God—always said the same.

As the days passed, I saw more often that he lay quietly looking at the white ceiling, his face empty of light until one of my words flashed across it for a moment before fading again. Sometimes he could hardly speak or not at all. Then he answered with slight pressures of his hand, and I learned to understand him.

On the tenth day, I saw a greater change than before. His eyes turned toward the door, brightening as I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said when I sat by his bed, “I thought you were late. But I knew you couldn’t be.”

“It’s exactly the time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always wait at the gate, don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. I don’t want to lose a moment.”

“Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand in silence, remembering how I had once meant to desert him.

“And best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable with me since I fell under a dark cloud than when the sun shone.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"e2174d44397ef27f80de6275","rewritten_text":"Week after week passed, and I became more and more obsessed with you. Then something new happened. I had painted you as Paris in delicate armor, and as Adonis with a hunter’s cloak and polished boar spear. You sat crowned with heavy lotus blossoms on the prow of Adrian’s barge, staring across the green, murky Nile. You leaned over a quiet pool in some Greek forest and saw the miracle of your own face in the silent silver of the water. All of it had been what art should be—unconscious, ideal, distant. One day—sometimes I think it was fatal—I decided to paint an extraordinary portrait of you as you really are, not in the costumes of dead ages but in your own clothes and in our own time. Whether it was the realism of the approach or simply the wonder of your personality shown to me so directly, without haze or veil, I can’t say. But as I worked on it, every layer of color seemed to reveal my secret. I grew afraid that others would discover my worship. I felt, Dorian, that I had confessed too much, that I had put too much of myself into it. That was when I resolved never to let the picture be exhibited. You were slightly irritated, but you didn’t understand what it meant to me. Harry, when I told him about it, laughed at me, but I didn’t care. When the picture was finished and I sat alone with it, I felt I was right... Well, after a few days it left my studio, and once I’d rid myself of the unbearable fascination of its presence, it seemed foolish to think I had seen anything in it beyond your remarkable beauty and my ability to paint. Even now I can’t help feeling it’s a mistake to believe that the passion we feel during creation ever truly shows in the work we produce. Art is always more abstract than we imagine. Form and color tell us only about form and color—that’s all. It often strikes me that art hides the artist far more completely than it ever reveals him. So when I got this offer from Paris, I decided to make your portrait the centerpiece of my exhibition. It never occurred to me that you would refuse. I understand now that you were right. The picture can’t be shown. Don’t be angry with me, Dorian, for what I’ve confessed to you."}

{"request_id":"4cfdb70d25de3425564ac116","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s feelings overpowered her ambition, and, for the young man’s sake, she gave up any further plotting for Sir Walter. Yet she has skill as well as emotion, and it now seems uncertain whose schemes will win in the end, his or hers. After stopping her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he may yet be coaxed and flattered into making her Lady William instead.

No one can doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and humiliated by losing their companion and discovering her deceit. They could turn to their important cousins for comfort, certainly, but they must feel keenly how empty it is to flatter and follow others without being flattered and followed in return.

Anne, reassured early that Lady Russell now meant to cherish Captain Wentworth as she should, found no shadow on her future happiness except the painful thought that she had no relations to give him whom a sensible man could value. In that, she felt her inferiority sharply. Their unequal fortunes did not disturb her for a moment; but having no family ready to welcome and appreciate him properly—nothing respectable, harmonious, or kindly to offer in return for the worth and eager welcome she received from his brothers and sisters—caused as much pain as her mind could feel amid such a joyful future. She could only add two friends to his list, Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. Yet he was quite willing to attach himself to them both. Lady Russell, despite all her former mistakes, he now truly esteemed. Though he could not pretend she had been right in separating them at first, he was ready to praise nearly everything else about her; and Mrs Smith had many reasons to win his quick and lasting regard.

Mrs Smith’s recent good deeds toward Anne were reason enough, and their marriage, instead of costing her a friend, gave her two. She was their first visitor when they settled, and Captain Wentworth repaid her kindness by helping her recover her late husband’s West Indian property. He wrote letters, handled business, and worked through every small difficulty with the energy and courage of a bold man and loyal friend, fully repaying all the services she had given or ever intended to give his wife."}

{"request_id":"b8e428fa4fcc23c4b7e31f0b","rewritten_text":"There was something so unusual in the way Mr. Wopsle’s eyes kept widening, as if he were turning over a hundred thoughts and getting more confused by the minute, that I could not make sense of it. Even after he’d floated up to the rafters in a giant watch case, I sat there thinking about it and still couldn’t figure it out. An hour later, when I left the theatre, I was still puzzling over it when I found him waiting for me near the door.

“How are you?” I said, shaking his hand as we walked down the street together. “I saw you had seen me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It’s the strangest thing,” Mr. Wopsle said, drifting back into that faraway stare, “and yet I could swear to him.”

Alarmed, I begged him to explain.

“Whether I would have noticed him at first if you hadn’t been there,” Mr. Wopsle went on in that same absent way, “I can’t say for sure; still, I think I would have.”

Without meaning to, I glanced around, like I had gotten used to doing when heading home, because his mysterious words sent a shiver through me.

“Oh! He can’t be in sight,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I came off the stage. I saw him go.”

Because I had reason to be suspicious, I even suspected this poor actor. I distrusted it as some plan to trap me into admitting something. So I studied him as we walked, but kept quiet.

“I had this ridiculous notion that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw you had no idea he was there, sitting behind you like a ghost.”

The chill returned, but I was determined not to speak yet, because everything he said could be part of an attempt to make me link his hints to Provis. Of course I was absolutely sure Provis hadn’t been there.

“I suppose you think I’m acting strangely, Mr. Pip; I can see you do. But it’s so very strange! You’ll hardly believe what I’m about to tell you. I could barely believe it myself if you were the one telling me.”

“Really?” I said.

“Indeed. Mr. Pip, do you remember the Christmas Day when you were a little child, and I dined at the Gargerys’, and some soldiers came to the door to get a pair of handcuffs fixed?”

“I remember it perfectly.”

“And you remember there was a chase after two convicts, and we took part, and Gargery carried you on his back, while I led the way and you kept up as best you could?”"}

{"request_id":"e2f9c6ec78b9b85324c1ee64","rewritten_text":"With no work in his hands, he pressed the knuckles of his right hand into the hollow of his left, then the knuckles of his left into the hollow of his right, then swept a hand across his bearded chin, over and over without a pause. Drawing him back from the wandering state he always fell into after he spoke was like trying to revive a frail person from a faint, or like trying, in hope of one last revelation, to hold back the spirit of a dying man.

“Did you ask me for my name?”

“I certainly did.”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

“Is that all?”

“One Hundred and Five, North Tower.”

With a tired sound that was neither sigh nor groan, he bent to work again until the silence broke once more.

“You are not a shoemaker by trade?” asked Mr. Lorry, staring steadily at him.

His gaunt eyes turned to Defarge as if to pass the question on; when no help came, they dropped to the ground and then crept back to Mr. Lorry.

“I am not a shoemaker by trade? No, I was not a shoemaker by trade. I—I learned it here. I taught myself. I asked permission to—”

He drifted away again, even for minutes, still repeating those measured motions with his hands. At last his gaze slowly returned to the face it had left; when it settled there, he started and spoke like a man waking suddenly, picking up a thought from the night before.

“I asked to teach myself, and after a long time I received permission with great difficulty, and I have made shoes ever since.”

When he held out his hand for the shoe taken from him, Mr. Lorry, still looking intently at his face, said:

“Monsieur Manette, do you remember nothing of me?”

The shoe fell to the floor, and he stared fixedly at the questioner.

“Monsieur Manette”—Mr. Lorry placed his hand on Defarge’s arm—“do you remember nothing of this man? Look at him. Look at me. Is there no old banker, no old business, no old servant, no old time rising in your mind, Monsieur Manette?”

The prisoner of many years sat staring in turn at Mr. Lorry and Defarge. Faint traces of a once keen intelligence on his forehead forced their way through the dark fog that enveloped him. They were quickly clouded again; they faded and vanished. But they had been there."}

{"request_id":"283991bf10d28c7b712583b9","rewritten_text":"I want to see you securely well connected, and for that reason it’s best to keep your circle as refined as possible; so, if you’re still in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope your friendship with his sisters won’t pull you into knowing his wife, who will probably be some farmer’s daughter with no education.”

“Of course. Yes. Not that I believe Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who hadn’t been educated and properly brought up. Still, I don’t want to set my opinion against yours—and I’m sure I won’t want to know his wife. I’ll always think highly of the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and I’d be very sorry to give them up, because they’re just as well educated as me. But if he marries a very ignorant, vulgar woman, then yes, I’d better keep away from her if possible.”

Emma watched her through the twists and turns of this speech and saw no worrying signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted there was no stronger bond, and that Harriet wouldn’t be a serious obstacle to any friendly plan of her own.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day while walking on the Donwell road. He was on foot; after a respectful glance at Emma, he looked with obvious happiness at Harriet. Emma was glad for the chance to inspect him, and by walking a few yards ahead while they talked, her sharp eye quickly became familiar with Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was neat, and he looked like a sensible young man, but he had no other advantages; once compared with gentlemen, she thought he would lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s affections. Harriet did care about manners; she had commented on her father’s gentleness with admiration and surprise. Mr. Martin looked as if he didn’t know what manners were.

They stayed together only a few minutes, because Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting; then Harriet came running to her with a smiling face and a flutter of excitement, which Miss Woodhouse hoped to calm soon.

“Just imagine our meeting him! How very odd! Pure chance, he said, that he hadn’t gone around by Randalls. He didn’t think we ever walked this road. He thought we walked toward Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"2498c69f5e9e5f19b3b706c3","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The omission fell back on the offender; for when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no condolence arrived at Kellynch, and there was every reason to fear that the Dalrymples now considered the connection ended. How to settle this anxious matter and be received as cousins again was the question: and it was one that, in a sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot thought trivial. Family connections were always worth keeping, good company always worth seeking; Lady Dalrymple had taken a house for three months in Laura Place and would be living in style. She had been in Bath the year before, and Lady Russell had heard her praised as a charming woman. It was very desirable to renew the connection, if it could be done without compromising the Elliots’ dignity.

Sir Walter, however, insisted on his own approach, and finally wrote a very polished letter full of explanation, regret, and entreaty to his right honorable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot admired the letter, but it accomplished its aim by producing three scrawled lines from the Dowager Viscountess. She was very much honored and would be happy to know them. The hard part was done, the rewards began. They called in Laura Place, and they received the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honorable Miss Carteret to be displayed wherever they would show best; and “Our cousins in Laura Place,” “Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret,” were repeated to everyone.

Anne felt ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been delightful, she would still have been embarrassed by the fuss they caused, but they were nothing special. They had no superior manners, accomplishments, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple was called a charming woman simply because she had a smile and a polite answer for all. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and awkward that she would never have been endured in Camden Place if not for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted she had expected something better; yet it was still “an acquaintance worth having.” When Anne expressed her opinion of them to Mr Elliot, he agreed that they were nothing in themselves, but insisted that, as family connections, as good company, as people who would draw other good company, they had their worth. Anne smiled and said, “My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people, who have a great deal of conversation; that is what I call good company.”"}

{"request_id":"b848201b4770a4fa91fc4e59","rewritten_text":"These reflections soothed me enough that by afternoon I fell into a deep slumber, though the fever burning in my veins denied me tranquil dreams. The ghastly scene of the preceding day continued to play relentlessly before my eyes; the women fleeing, and Felix, raging, wrenching me from his father’s feet. I woke drained, and realizing night had already fallen, I slipped out of my hiding-place to search for food.

When my need was satisfied, I turned onto the familiar path that led to the cottage. Everything there seemed peaceful. I crawled into my hovel and waited silently for the hour when the household typically arose. That time came and went, the sun climbed higher, yet the cottagers did not appear. A tremor seized me, fearing some terrible calamity. The cottage interior remained dark, and no sound met my ear; I cannot convey the torment of that suspense.

Soon two peasants went by, and stopping near the cottage, began discussing something with emphatic gestures; however, I could not comprehend their words, for they spoke the village dialect unlike that of my protectors. Shortly afterward Felix came with another man; I was astonished, as I knew he had not left the cottage that morning, and I waited anxiously to learn from their speech the cause of these strange proceedings.

“‘Have you considered,’ said his companion, ‘that you will have to pay three months’ rent and forfeit the produce of your garden? I wish to take no undue advantage, so I beg you to take a few days to settle your decision.’

“‘It avails nothing,’ Felix answered; ‘we can never again dwell in your cottage. My father’s life is in extreme peril because of the dreadful event I have described. My wife and sister will never shake off their terror. I implore you, do not argue further. Reclaim your dwelling and let me escape this place.’

Felix shook violently while speaking. He and the man went into the cottage, stayed only a few minutes, then departed. I beheld no member of the De Lacey family again.

For the rest of the day I lingered in my hovel, sunk in absolute, senseless despair. My protectors had gone, severing the single thread that tied me to the world. For the first time my heart filled with vengeance and hatred. I made no attempt to repress them; instead, letting myself be carried away by their current, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death."}

{"request_id":"911fabb4c543f0198c33c557","rewritten_text":"To glimpse a star by looking slightly away—using the outer parts of the retina, which are more sensitive to weak light—lets us see the star clearly. It gives the best sense of its glow, a glow that fades as soon as we stare straight at it. More rays strike the eye when we look directly, yet in the sidelong glance there is a finer ability to understand. Too much depth of scrutiny confuses and weakens thought; we can even make Venus disappear from the sky by staring too long, too hard, or too directly.

“As for these murders, let us make some inquiry for ourselves before forming an opinion. The investigation will amuse us,” (I found the word odd in that context but said nothing) “and besides, Le Bon once did me a service, and I am not ungrateful. We will go see the place with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and can easily get permission.”

Permission secured, we set off immediately for the Rue Morgue. It is one of those poor streets between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. Afternoon was far advanced when we arrived, as that district lies far from where we lived. The house was easy to spot, since many people still stood across the way, staring up at the closed shutters with idle curiosity. It was an ordinary Paris house, with a gateway and, on one side, a glassed-in watch-box with a sliding panel, showing it to be a concierge’s lodge. Before going inside we walked up the street, turned down an alley, and after another turn entered the rear of the building—Dupin examining the whole neighborhood and the house itself with a careful attention whose purpose I could not guess.

We retraced our steps, returned to the front door, rang, and, after showing our credentials, were admitted by the officers in charge. We went upstairs into the room where the body of Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been found, and where both victims still lay. The disorder in the room had, as usual, been left untouched. I saw nothing beyond what the “Gazette des Tribunaux” had reported. Dupin inspected everything, including the bodies themselves. We then went through the other rooms and out into the yard, a gendarme accompanying us the whole time."}

{"request_id":"ce1d65c49577286a816316f0","rewritten_text":"“She would be such a delightful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed, but added, “Our little friend Harriet Smith is also just such a charming young person. You will like Harriet. Emma could not have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am very glad to hear it—but Jane Fairfax, everyone knows, is so accomplished and so superior—and exactly Emma’s age.”

This topic was discussed pleasantly, and other subjects of similar importance followed and ended just as harmoniously. Yet the evening did not finish without a small return of agitation. The gruel arrived and prompted a great deal of conversation—praise and comments—firm opinions about how wholesome it was for everyone, and rather sharp criticisms of many houses that could never produce it properly; but unfortunately, among the failures her daughter could cite, the most recent, and so the most notable, was her own cook at South End, a temporary hire who never could understand what she meant by a basin of nice smooth gruel, thin but not too thin. She had asked for it many times, but never received anything acceptable. This opened a dangerous topic.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern. The sound murmured in Emma’s ear, “Ah! there is no end to the sad consequences of your visiting South End. It is too upsetting to discuss.” For a moment she hoped he would stay silent and think it over, enough to enjoy his own smooth gruel again. After a few minutes, however, he began, “I shall always regret that you went to the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you regret it, sir? I assure you, it did the children a great deal of good.”

“And besides, if you had to go to the sea, it should not have been South End. South End is unhealthy. Perry was surprised you chose South End.”

“I know many people think so, but it is really a mistake, sir. We were all perfectly healthy there and never had the slightest inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield says it is entirely wrong to consider the place unhealthy. I am sure he is reliable, for he thoroughly understands the nature of the air, and his own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry spent a week at Cromer once, and he considers it the best of all the sea-bathing places.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"66897e4cbb90d15e266d0556","rewritten_text":"On the morning set for Admiral and Mrs. Croft to see Kellynch Hall, Anne naturally took her usual walk to Lady Russell’s to stay out of the way until it was over; once it was, she immediately regretted missing the chance to see them. The meeting went wonderfully well and settled everything at once. Each lady had already been inclined to reach an agreement, so each saw only good manners in the other; as for the men, the Admiral’s hearty good humor and open, trusting generosity had to affect Sir Walter, who had also been coaxed into his most polished behavior by Mr. Shepherd telling him that, according to rumor, the Admiral knew him as the perfect example of a gentleman. The house, grounds, furniture, the Crofts themselves, the terms, the timing, everything and everyone met approval; and Mr. Shepherd’s clerks were set to work without a single preliminary clause needing alteration from “This indenture showeth.” Sir Walter, without hesitation, declared the Admiral the best-looking sailor he had ever seen, and even said that if his own valet could do the Admiral’s hair he would not be ashamed to be seen with him anywhere; while the Admiral, with matching warmth, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we’d make a deal quickly, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but there seems no harm in him.” Each set of compliments would have been considered about equal. The Crofts would take possession at Michaelmas; and since Sir Walter planned to leave for Bath during the previous month, they had no time to lose in making the necessary arrangements. Lady Russell, sure that Anne would not be allowed any influence or importance in choosing their new house, disliked seeing her rushed away so soon and wanted to find a way for her to stay until she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas. But because she had her own commitments that would bring her away from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not give the full invitation she wished. And though Anne dreaded Bath’s possible September heat in all its white glare and hated giving up the sweet yet mournful influence of the country in autumn, she decided that, all things considered, she did not wish to stay."}

{"request_id":"0dcb59df8ecf1ec4278784bf","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had elapsed since my father’s return, and the seasons were almost complete in their cycle—it was now late May; the woods were clad in their freshest green, and the sweet scent of new-cut grass floated over the fields. I believed the balmy air and fair visage of Nature might steady him with mild sensations, gifting him gentle feelings of peace and love so that I might gain the confidence I longed to draw from him.

I therefore chose the evening of one such day for my effort. Inviting him to walk, I guided him to a nearby beech wood whose light shade protected us from the slanting, piercing rays of the setting sun. After some time of silent walking, I seated myself with him upon a mossy knoll. It is strange, yet even now the spot seems present before me—the slender, smooth trunks were many of them entwined with ivy, whose shining darkest-green leaves contrasted with the pale bark and the light foliage of the young beech shoots springing from their parent stems. The short grass mingled with moss and was partly strewn with the dead leaves of the previous autumn which the wind had sometimes gathered into little heaps—there were a few moss-covered stumps near. The breeze stirred the leaves gently, and through their green canopy the bright blue sky was visible. As evening advanced, the distant trunks glowed red from the sun, the wind wholly ceased, and a few birds passed over us on their way to rest.

Here we sat together, and when you learn all that took place—all that tore our spirits in this tranquil spot, which save for wild passions might have been a paradise to us—you will not wonder that I recall it as I gazed upon it so its calm might lend me quiet and embolden me with persuasive words. I saw all this and idly noted each detail in my mind while striving to arrange my thoughts in proper order for my purpose. My heart beat quickly as I urged myself toward speech; I was resolved not to be refused, yet I trembled to imagine how my words might strike him. At last, with great hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the overwhelming affection—you bore me when you first returned will, I hope, excuse my daring to speak to you, though I do so with a daughter’s tenderness, yet also with the liberty of a friend and equal.”"}

{"request_id":"6e7220b911b0e5fee788271c","rewritten_text":"She would be settled among those who cherished her and possessed more judgment than she did; secluded enough for security, yet busy enough for spirits. She would neither be drawn into temptation nor left exposed to it. She would be proper and contented; and Emma acknowledged her to be the most fortunate creature alive, to have inspired so steady and enduring an attachment in such a man; or, if not quite the most fortunate, surpassed only by herself.

Harriet, inevitably occupied with the Martins, was less and less at Hartfield; which was unregretted. The closeness between her and Emma had to decline; their friendship must soften into a calmer benevolence; and, happily, what should happen, and must happen, appeared already to be beginning, in the most gentle and natural way.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church, and witnessed her hand placed in Robert Martin’s with a perfect contentment, which no recollections—even of Mr. Elton standing there—could diminish. Perhaps, indeed, at that moment she hardly regarded Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose benediction at the altar might shortly fall upon herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, though the last couple of the three to be engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved Campbells. The Mr. Churchills likewise were in town; and they only awaited November.

The intervening month was the period Emma and Mr. Knightley had fixed, as far as they dared. They resolved their marriage should take place while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, allowing them the planned fortnight away on a seaside tour. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed in approving it. But Mr. Woodhouse—how was Mr. Woodhouse to be persuaded? He had never yet mentioned their marriage except as a remote concern.

When first approached on the subject, he was so wretched that they nearly despaired. A second mention, in truth, caused less agony. He started to believe it would happen, and that he could not prevent it—a very encouraging step for a mind moving toward resignation. Still he was not content. Indeed he appeared so far from it that his daughter’s resolve failed. She could not endure seeing him in torment, aware he imagined himself forsaken; and though her reason almost yielded to the assurances of both Mr. Knightleys that once the event was past his agitation would soon subside, she faltered—she could not go on."}

{"request_id":"de52c3cb66a33efbf47ad96c","rewritten_text":"The oaks around us housed a tribe of nightingales—there I am now; Idris, in the prime of her youth, stands beside me—remember, I am just twenty-two, and the beloved of my heart has barely seen seventeen summers. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the lowlands, and Adrian, in his favorite boat, was occupied with the dangerous sport of snapping off the highest branch of a submerged oak. Are you so tired of life, Adrian, that you toy with danger like this?

He had taken his prize and was steering his boat through the torrent; we stared at him anxiously, but the current carried him away from us. He was forced to land far downstream and take a long detour before he could rejoin us. “He is safe!” said Idris when he sprang ashore and waved the bough over his head in triumph. “We will wait here for him.”

We were alone together; the sun had set; the nightingales began their song; the evening star shone clear in the lingering light of the west. My angelic girl’s blue eyes were fixed on this lovely emblem of herself: “How the light pulses,” she said, “which is the life of that star. Its wavering brilliance seems to tell that its state, like ours on earth, is unsteady and uncertain; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Do not gaze at the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Do not read love in its trembling rays; do not study distant worlds; do not speak of the fancied image of a sentiment. I have been silent so long; so long, even to illness, I have yearned to speak to you and surrender my soul, my life, my whole being to you. Do not look at the star, dear love—or do, and let that eternal spark plead for me; let it be my witness and advocate, shining silently—love is to me what light is to the star; as long as it remains untouched by annihilation, so long will I love you.”

The ecstasy of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s callous gaze. I still feel her graceful form pressed against my overflowing heart—still do sight, pulse, and breath falter at the memory of that first kiss. Slowly and quietly we went to meet Adrian, whose approach we heard.

I begged Adrian to return to me after he had taken his sister home. And that same evening, walking along the moonlit forest paths, I poured out my whole heart—its delight and its hope—to my friend. For a moment he looked troubled. “I might have foreseen this,” he said. “What conflict will now unfold!”"}

{"request_id":"002778e174c377d6aa1e9b3f","rewritten_text":"“So, what conclusion have you reached? What impression have I made on your imagination?”

I felt my skin crawl when Dupin asked this. “A madman,” I answered, “must have done it—some raving maniac who escaped from a nearby Maison de Santé.”

“In some ways,” he said, “your idea isn’t off the mark. But the voices of madmen, even in their wildest fits, never match the strange voice heard on those stairs. Madmen belong to some nation, and their language, however incoherent their words, still keeps the structure of syllables. Besides, a madman’s hair is not like what I’m holding. I pulled this little tuft out of Madame L’Espanaye’s tightly clenched fingers. Tell me what you make of it.”

“Dupin!” I cried, shaken to the core. “This hair is highly unusual—this is not human hair.”

“I never said it was,” he replied. “But before we settle that point, take a look at this sketch I’ve drawn on this paper. It’s an exact copy of what one witness described as ‘dark bruises and deep indentations of fingernails’ on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what Messrs. Dumas and Etienne called ‘a series of livid spots, clearly the impression of fingers.’

“You can see,” he went on, laying the paper on the table, “that the drawing shows a firm, steady grip. There’s no slipping. Each finger held on—likely until the victim died—with the same fierce grasp it first sank in with. Now try to place all your fingers at once into the impressions as you see them.”

I tried, but I couldn’t manage it.

“Maybe we aren’t testing this properly,” he said. “The paper is flat, but a human throat is round. Here’s a piece of wood about the same circumference as a throat. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.”

I followed his instructions, but the mismatch was even clearer. “These marks,” I said, “were not made by a human hand.”

“Now read this passage from Cuvier,” Dupin replied.

It was a detailed anatomical description of the large tawny orangutan of the East Indian islands. Its immense size, tremendous strength and agility, savage ferocity, and talent for mimicry are common knowledge. I grasped the full terror of this murder immediately.

“The description of the fingers,” I said when I finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”"}

{"request_id":"044f4a61afebe78862c25ee2","rewritten_text":"“Nothing but a tick.”

“Where’d you find him?”

“Out in the woods.”

“What’ll you take for him?”

“I don’t know. I’m not aiming to sell him.”

“All right. It’s a mighty small tick, anyhow.”

“Oh, anybody can run down a tick that isn’t theirs. I’m pleased with this one. It suits me.”

“Sho, ticks are thick as fleas. I could have a thousand if I wanted.”

“Well, why don’t you? Because you know you can’t. This must be an early tick. It’s the first I’ve seen this year.”

“Say, Huck—I’ll swap you my tooth for him.”

“Let’s see it.”

Tom pulled out a slip of paper and carefully unwrapped it. Huckleberry gazed with longing. The urge was mighty. At last he murmured:

“Is it genuine?”

Tom lifted his lip to show the gap.

“Well, all right,” Huckleberry said, “you’ve got a bargain.”

Tom tucked the tick into the percussion-cap box that lately held the pinchbug, and the boys parted, each feeling richer than before.

When Tom arrived at the little solitary frame schoolhouse, he strode in briskly, as though he had made all haste. He hung up his hat and dropped into his seat with businesslike dispatch. The master, enthroned in his grand splint-bottomed arm-chair, was napping, soothed by the sleepy drone of lessons. The interruption roused him.

“Thomas Sawyer!”

Tom knew his full name meant mischief.

“Sir!”

“Come here. Now, sir, why are you late again, same as always?”

Tom was about to retreat into a falsehood when he spotted two long tails of yellow hair down the back he knew by love’s electrical sympathy; and beside that form lay the only empty seat among the girls. He instantly declared:

“I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!”

The master’s pulse seemed to halt, and he stared in helpless astonishment. The study-drone ceased. The scholars wondered if this reckless boy had gone mad. The master demanded:

“You—you did what?”

“Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.”

No mistaking it.

“Thomas Sawyer, that is the most amazing admission I ever heard. No simple ferule suits such an offense. Take off your jacket.”

The master’s arm worked until it was weary and the pile of switches notably reduced. Then came the command:

“Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this teach you.”

The titter running round the room seemed to shame the boy, yet his blush sprang more from reverent awe of his unknown idol and the fearful delight in such grand good luck."}

The Widow Douglas’s generous hospitality was a tempting bait, and together with Tom’s urging it soon won. They decided not to tell anyone about the night’s plan. Then Tom realized Huck might arrive that very night and give the signal. The thought drained much of his excitement. Still, he couldn’t bear to give up the fun at Widow Douglas’s house. Why should he, he reasoned—the signal hadn’t come the night before, so why expect it tonight? The certain fun of the evening outweighed the uncertain treasure, and, like a typical boy, he chose to follow the stronger temptation and promised himself not to think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles below town the ferry stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the forest depths and rocky heights echoed far and near with shouts and laughter. They tried every possible way to get hot and tired, and after a while the wanderers straggled back to camp with serious appetites, and then the feast’s destruction began. Afterward came a cooling spell of rest and conversation beneath spreading oaks. Before long someone shouted:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. Bundles of candles were gathered, and immediately there was a mad scramble up the hill. The cave’s mouth was partway up the hillside, shaped like a giant letter A. The massive oak door stood unbarred. Inside lay a small chamber, as cold as an icehouse, walled by solid limestone that sweated with damp chill. It felt romantic and mysterious to stand there in the deep gloom and look out at the sunlit green valley. But the solemn mood soon faded and the roughhousing resumed. As soon as someone lit a candle, everyone rushed at its owner; a struggle and brave defense followed, but the candle was quickly knocked down or blown out, and then came a burst of laughter and another chase. But all things end. Soon the line of explorers filed down the steep slope of the main passage, their flickering row of lights just enough to reveal the lofty rock walls nearly meeting sixty feet overhead. This main passage was only eight or ten feet wide. Every few steps other tall and even narrower cracks branched off to either side—for McDougal’s Cave was a great maze of twisting aisles that ran into one another, split apart, and led nowhere."}

{"request_id":"c420969b852112d02cdc0ee3","rewritten_text":"I now arrive at the account of myself. Of the opening stages of my life there is little worth noting, so I will be concise; yet I must linger somewhat over my childhood, so it may be understood how, when one hope collapsed, existence became a void, and how, when the single affection allowed me was withered, my life perished along with it.

I have already mentioned that my aunt bore hardly any resemblance to my father. I am persuaded that, though guiltless of malice, she possessed the chilliest heart that ever beat in a human breast—entirely incapable of tenderness. She received me under her guardianship merely from a sense of obligation; but she had long been accustomed to solitude, undisturbed by childish noise and chatter, and would not permit me to ruffle her calm. She had never married, and for the past five years had lived completely alone upon an estate descending to her from her mother, on the banks of Loch Lomond in Scotland. My father had expressed, through his letters, a desire that she should live with me at his ancestral mansion situated in lovely country outside Richmond, Yorkshire. She refused this plan, but as soon as she had settled the business our father’s departure forced into her hands, she left England and carried me with her to her Scottish property.

The charge of me in infancy, and up to my eighth year, fell to a servant of my mother’s, who had joined us in our retreat for that duty. I occupied a secluded wing of the house and saw my aunt only at fixed intervals. Twice each day she appeared: near midday she visited my nursery, and after her dinner I was led to her. She never embraced me, and throughout my stay in the room she seemed afraid I would vex her with some childish whim. My devoted nurse coached me carefully before daring to bring me into the parlour—and the dread stirred by my aunt’s wintry glance and clipped words was so intense that I seldom brought shame upon her lessons or broke the exemplary stillness she bid me adopt during those brief audiences.

In my nurse’s kind supervision I roamed unchecked through our park and the neighbouring fields. Born of the sincerest love, I showed from earliest days a most sensitive nature. I cannot convey with what fervour I cherished everything—yes, even the lifeless objects that surrounded me."}
