content.text: {"request_id":"8c084ee90d0225eeda8b0bd5","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in amazement for a few moments, then, realizing he was completely serious, he wrote an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and slid it across the table. “Scotland Yard would pay dearly for this address, my dear fellow.” “They’re not getting it,” Lord Arthur said with a laugh; after shaking the young Russian’s hand warmly, he ran downstairs, checked the paper, and told the driver to head for Soho Square. There he dismissed the cab, wandered down Greek Street until he reached a place called Bayle’s Court, went through the archway, and found himself in a curious dead-end apparently taken over by a French laundry, as clotheslines crisscrossed between the houses and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked all the way to the end and knocked on a small green house. After a long wait—long enough for every window in the court to blur with curious faces—the door was opened by a rather rough-looking foreigner who, in very poor English, asked what business he had there. Lord Arthur handed him the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him; as soon as the man saw it, he bowed and showed him into a shabby front parlor on the ground floor. A moment later Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in with a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork in his left hand. “Count Rouvaloff has given me an introduction to you,” said Lord Arthur, bowing. “I would like a brief meeting with you on a business matter. My name is Smith—Robert Smith—and I want you to supply me with an explosive clock.” “Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” the cheerful little German said with a laugh. “Don’t look so frightened; it’s my job to know everyone, and I remember spotting you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. Is her ladyship well? Would you mind sitting with me while I finish my breakfast? The pâté is excellent, and my friends tell me my Rhine wine is better than anything they get at the German Embassy.” Before Lord Arthur had recovered from being recognized, he found himself in the back room, drinking exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock glass marked with the Imperial monogram and chatting like an old friend with the notorious conspirator. “Explosive clocks,” Herr Winckelkopf said, “don’t travel well for foreign delivery. Even if they slip through Customs, the train schedules are so erratic that they usually explode before they reach their intended destination.”"}

{"request_id":"2983ad183b7a64547e1dae0f","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what’s wrong now? How is your master?”

“To tell de truth, massa, he ain’t near so well as he could be.”

“Not well! I’m sorry to hear it. What does he complain of?”

“Dat’s just it! He never complains of anything—but he’s mighty sick all de same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you say so right away? Is he stuck in bed?”

“No, he ain’t! He ain’t stuck nowhere—that’s what makes de trouble. My mind is real heavy about poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I want to understand what you’re saying. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong?”

“Why, massa, no need to get vexed—Massa Will says nothing at all is wrong with him—but then why does he go around looking like this, with his head down and his shoulders up, and as pale as a goose? And he keeps a syphon all de time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a syphon with figures on de slate—the strangest figures I ever saw. I’m starting to get scared, I tell you. Got to keep a mighty close eye on his moves. T’other day he slipped off before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick ready cut to give him a real good whipping when he got back—but I’m such a fool I couldn’t do it after all—he looked so very poorly.”

“Eh? what? ah yes! On the whole, I think you’d better not be too hard on the poor fellow—don’t beat him, Jupiter—he isn’t fit for it. But can’t you guess what caused this illness—or rather this change in him? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, massa, nothing unpleasant since then—it was before then, I’m afraid—it was the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, massa, I mean the bug—there, now.”

“The what?”

“The bug. I’m certain Massa Will got bit somewhere ’round the head by that gold bug.”

“And what reason have you, Jupiter, for thinking so?”

“Claws enough, massa, and a mouth too. I never saw such a mean bug—he kicks and he bites everything that comes near him. Massa Will caught him first, but had to let him go mighty quick, I tell you—that must be when he got bit. I didn’t like the look of the bug’s mouth at all myself, so I wouldn’t touch him with my fingers, but I picked him up with a piece of paper I found.”"}

{"request_id":"15aa927f0897de1da3389327","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”

“Wire fence?”

“Yes. You hinted at it yourself two or three years ago.”

“Oh, I remember—the first time the Church tested its strength against us and then decided to wait for a better season. Well, how did you set up the fence?”

“I run twelve very strong wires—bare, not insulated—from a big dynamo in the cave, with only a positive and a negative brush.”

“Yes, that’s right.”

“The wires go out from the cave and enclose a flat circle a hundred yards across. They form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—so twelve circles inside each other—and their ends return to the cave.”

“Right; continue.”

“The wires are fixed to heavy oak posts set only three feet apart, sunk five feet into the ground.”

“That’s good and solid.”

“Yes. The wires have no ground connection outside the cave. They go out from the positive brush of the dynamo; there’s a ground connection through the negative brush; the other ends of the wires come back to the cave, and each one is grounded separately.”

“No, no, that won’t do!”

“Why not?”

“It’s too costly—wastes power. You need only one ground connection, through the negative brush. The other end of every wire must come back into the cave and be fastened separately without any ground connection. Now look at the savings. A cavalry charge slams into the fence; you’re using no power, spending nothing, because there’s only one ground connection until those horses hit the wire. The instant they touch it they complete the circuit with the negative brush through the ground and drop dead. Don’t you see? You use no energy until it’s needed; your lightning waits like a loaded gun, but it costs you nothing until you fire it. Yes, stick to the single ground connection—”

“Of course! I don’t know how I missed that. It’s not only cheaper but more effective, because broken or tangled wires cause no trouble.”

“No, especially if we have an indicator in the cave and disconnect any broken wire. Go on. The Gatlings?”

“Yes—that’s ready. In the center of the innermost circle, on a broad platform six feet high, I set up a battery of thirteen Gatling guns with plenty of ammunition.”

“That’s it. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights arrive, there’ll be music. The edge of the cliff above the cave—”

“I’ve put a wire fence there too, and a Gatling.”"}

{"request_id":"91df72af76c743beee198c5c","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had secured an excellent residence in Camden Place, a lofty, dignified spot befitting a man of importance; he and Elizabeth were installed there entirely to their liking. 

Anne crossed the threshold with a sinking spirit, bracing for a confinement of many months, and whispering to herself, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Yet an unexpected warmth in their greeting heartened her. Her father and sister were eager to display the new house and furnishings, and received her with real civility. Her presence making a fourth at dinner was even remarked upon as a benefit. 

Mrs Clay was all pleasantness and smiles, but, as always, her courtesies seemed automatic. Anne had anticipated that she would perform all that was proper at first meeting; what surprised her was the genuine complacency of the others. They were obviously in high spirits, and she was soon to hear the reasons. They had no desire to listen to her. Having positioned themselves for compliments about being lamented in their former neighbourhood—praise Anne could not offer—they put only a few mild questions before insisting the conversation be entirely theirs. Uppercross roused no interest, and Kellynch scarcely any; the subject was all Bath. 

They delighted in assuring her that Bath exceeded their expectations in every particular. Their house, beyond doubt, was the best in Camden Place; their drawing-rooms possessed advantages over every other they had seen or heard about, and the superiority extended equally to the arrangement and taste of the furnishings. Their acquaintance was highly coveted. Everyone wished to visit them. They had declined numerous introductions, yet still received cards from people wholly unknown to them. 

Here were abundant sources of enjoyment. Could Anne be surprised that her father and sister were content? She might refrain from surprise, yet she could only sigh that her father felt no disgrace in the alteration of his circumstances, saw nothing to lament in relinquishing the duties and dignity of a resident landowner, and found so much to be proud of in the trivialities of town life. She must sigh, and smile, and marvel too, when Elizabeth flung open the folding-doors and strode triumphantly from one drawing-room into the next, exulting in their size; marvel at the notion of that woman, who had once presided over Kellynch Hall, feeling pride in expanses bounded by walls scarce thirty feet apart. 

But their happiness had another ingredient. They possessed Mr Elliot as well."}

content.text: {"request_id":"bef1f6835d58b5ba6c5bfd99","rewritten_text":"I met the peculiar stranger I want to describe while touring Warwick Castle. Three traits drew me to him: his straightforward innocence, his astonishing knowledge of ancient armor, and how calming his presence was—probably because he did all the talking. As modest visitors do, we drifted toward the rear of the group being guided through, and he immediately began saying things that captivated me. As he spoke—softly, pleasantly, smoothly—he seemed to slip, almost without my noticing, out of the present day and into some distant era, some long-forgotten land; gradually he cast such a spell over me that I felt I was moving among the ghosts, shadows, dust, and mold of a gray antiquity, conversing with one of its relics. He talked about Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Lancelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and all the other great names of the Round Table just as I would talk about my closest friends, enemies, or neighbors—and the longer he went on, the older he seemed, impossibly old, faded, dry, musty, ancient. Finally he turned to me and said, as casually as someone might talk about the weather, “You know about transmigration of souls; do you know about the transposition of eras—and bodies?” I said I had never heard of it. He seemed so uninterested—exactly like someone making small talk about the weather—that he didn’t notice whether I answered or not. A brief silence followed, broken by the droning voice of the paid guide: “Ancient hauberk, sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramore the Desirous; note the round hole in the chain mail on the left breast; no known explanation; believed to have been made by a bullet after the invention of firearms—maybe vandalism by Cromwell’s soldiers.” My new acquaintance smiled—not a modern smile, but one that must have vanished from general use centuries ago—and muttered, apparently to himself, “Know this, I saw it happen.” Then, after a pause, he added, “I did it myself.” By the time I had recovered from the jolt of that remark, he was gone. All evening I sat by my fire at the Warwick Arms, wrapped in a dream of bygone days while the rain battered the windows and the wind howled around the eaves and corners. Now and then I opened old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book and feasted on its wonders and adventures, drank in the fragrance of its forgotten names, and drifted back into the dream."}

{"request_id":"e18dc8557b51220cadf63b3b","rewritten_text":"“This must have been that very period of Mr Elliot’s life,” observed Anne, “which has always stirred my particular curiosity. It must coincide with when he first became acquainted with my father and sister. I never met him myself; I only heard of him. Yet there was something in his behavior then, regarding my father and sister, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that I never could reconcile with the man we see now. It hinted at a different character.”

“I know the whole history, I know the whole history,” exclaimed Mrs Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I knew him, yet he talked of them endlessly. I know he received invitations and encouragement, and I know he refused to go. I can probably satisfy you on matters you would hardly expect; and as for his marriage, I was in full possession of the facts at the time. I knew all the pros and cons; I was the confidante to whom he revealed his hopes and schemes; and though I had not previously known his wife—her inferior rank, indeed, made that impossible—I knew her through all the rest of her life, or at least up to two years before her death, and can answer whatever you wish to ask.”

“No,” replied Anne, “I have no particular question about her. I have always understood they were not a happy couple. But I should like to learn why, at that stage of his life, he would slight my father’s acquaintance as he did. My father was certainly inclined to treat him with great and proper attention. Why did Mr Elliot withdraw?”

“Mr Elliot,” said Mrs Smith, “at that period of his life, had a single aim: to make his fortune, and by a somewhat quicker route than the law would allow. He resolved to secure it through marriage. He was determined, at least, not to ruin it through an unwise marriage; and I know he believed (whether rightly or wrongly I cannot say) that your father and sister, in their politeness and invitations, were plotting a match between the heir and the young lady, and such a match could never have fulfilled his notions of wealth and independence. That was the motive behind his withdrawal, I assure you. He told me everything. He never hid anything from me. It was odd, that having left you behind in Bath, the first and closest acquaintance I formed after marrying should be your cousin; and that, through him, I should be constantly hearing of your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"45c23b34676f762fd5f1384a","rewritten_text":"I repeated to myself that beautiful passage describing Dante entering the earthly Paradise, and I imagined how sweet it would be, when I walked along those lovely banks, to see the car of light descend bringing back my long-lost parent. While I waited for that moment, I pictured winding a garland from the flowers there and crowning myself in joy. I would sing sul margine d’un rio, my father’s favorite song, and my voice, gliding through the still air, would tell him in whatever bower he waited for our reunion that his daughter had come. Then the mark of misery would fade from my brow, and I would lift my eyes without fear to meet his, which always shone with the soft glow of innocent love. When I thought of the magic in those deep eyes, I wept softly, afraid that my sobs might disturb the fairy scene. 

I was so completely lost in this daydream that I walked on without noticing where I went, until I stooped to pick a flower for my wreath on that bleak plain where no flower grew. Then I woke from my dream and realized I had no idea where I was. 

The sun had set, and the rosy light that the clouds kept from his descent was nearly gone. A wind swept the plain. I looked around and saw nothing to tell me my location. I had lost my way and could not find the path. I wandered, but the growing darkness blurred every possible guide. At last the blackest night covered everything. I grew tired, and since my servant was to sleep in the nearby village and would not be alarmed by my absence, and since I was safe in this wild place from any intruder, I decided to spend the night there. I was too weary to walk farther. The air was cold, but I did not care about discomfort; I thought I was hardened to the weather after two years of solitude when no change of season stopped my constant wandering. 

I lay on the grass, wrapped in darkness without the faintest ray of light. Nothing made a sound, for the deep night had lulled the insects to sleep, and they were the only creatures living on that lonely spot where no tree or shrub offered shelter to anything else. A wondrous silence filled the air, calming my senses yet stirring my soul. My mind rushed from image to image and seemed to grasp eternity."}

{"request_id":"39b5381a89f54d38e538722e","rewritten_text":"There arrives a season in every properly fashioned boy’s life when he burns to run off somewhere and dig up buried treasure. That fever struck Tom one day. He set out to track down Joe Harper but came up empty. Then he went hunting for Ben Rogers; Ben had gone fishing. Before long he bumped into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom drew him aside to a secluded spot and laid the scheme before him. Huck was agreeable. Huck was always ready to join any undertaking that promised amusement and demanded no cash, for he possessed a vexing surplus of that kind of time that isn’t money. “Where we going to dig?” asked Huck.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is it planted all over?”

“No, sir, it ain’t. It’s hidden in mighty particular spots, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests buried under the tip of a limb of an old dead tree, right where the shadow falls at midnight; but mostly under the floors of ha’nted houses.”

“Who puts it there?”

“Why, robbers, of course—who else would you reckon? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it belonged to me I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and have fun.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t. They always tuck it away and leave it.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No, they aim to, but they generally forget the signs, or else they die. Anyway, it stays there for ages and gets rusty; and eventually somebody comes on an old yellow paper that tells how to track the marks—a paper you’ve got to puzzle over for about a week because it’s mainly signs and hy’roglyphics.”

“Hyro—what?”

“Hy’roglyphics—pictures and such, you know, that look like they don’t mean a thing.”

“Got one of them papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t want any marks. They always stash it under a ha’nted house or on an island, or beneath a dead tree with one branch sticking out. Well, we’ve worked on Jackson’s Island a bit and we can try it again sometime; and there’s the old ha’nted house up the Still-House branch, and there are scads of dead-limb trees—cartloads of ’em.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“Hear that! No!”

“Then how will you know which one to pick?”

“Go at all of ’em!”

“Why, Tom, that’ll eat up the whole summer.”

“Well, what if it does? Imagine you dig up a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest crammed with di’monds. How about that?”

Huck’s eyes blazed.

“That’s bully. Plenty bully for me. Just give me the hundred dollars and I don’t care a rap for di’monds.”"}

{"request_id":"6dd97c94b7602f7c322fdf79","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, in Somersetshire, never opened any book for pleasure except the Baronetage. In its pages he found something to fill idle hours and to soothe him when he was upset. There his mind stirred with admiration and respect as he studied the few remaining families with ancient patents; there any unwelcome feelings about his home life slipped into pity and contempt while he scanned the countless new creations of the last century. And if nothing else in the volume could hold him, he only had to read his own entry to feel constant interest. The book always fell open to this page:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park in the county of Gloucester, by whom (she died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

This was exactly how the printer had first set the paragraph; but Sir Walter improved it, as he thought, by adding for the benefit of himself and his family these words after Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross, in the county of Somerset,” and by carefully inserting the exact day of the month on which he lost his wife.

Then came the family history and rise, told in the usual terms: how they first settled in Cheshire; how they were noted in Dugdale; how they served as high sheriff, represented a borough in three parliaments, showed loyalty, and gained the dignity of a baronetcy in the first year of Charles II, along with all the Marys and Elizabeths they married. Altogether it formed two neat duodecimo pages and ended with the arms and motto: “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed by Sir Walter’s handwriting once more:—

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character, vanity about his looks and his status. He had been remarkably handsome in youth, and at fifty-four he was still a very fine-looking man. Few women thought more about their appearance than he did, and no valet to any newly made lord could take greater pleasure in the place he held in society. He ranked the blessing of beauty as second only to the blessing of a baronetcy; and the Sir Walter Elliot who possessed both was always the object of his sincerest admiration and devotion.

His good looks and his rank did earn one genuine attachment, for through them he had secured a wife whose character was far better than anything he himself deserved."}

{"request_id":"4dfdd3f1aef16e053b8fc7a0","rewritten_text":"After a while, midnight boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and with each strike of the deep bell the night seemed to shiver. Then the railway lights blinked out, leaving a single lamp glowing like a huge ruby on a towering mast, and the city’s roar faded.

At two o’clock he rose and wandered toward Blackfriars. How unreal everything appeared, like some strange dream! The houses across the river seemed built from darkness itself. It was as if silver and shadow had remade the world. The enormous dome of St. Paul’s loomed like a bubble in the dim air.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle he spotted a man leaning over the parapet, and when he came closer the man looked up, the gaslight shining directly on his face.

It was Mr. Podgers, the palm-reader! That fat, flabby face, the gold-rimmed glasses, the wan, weak smile, and the sensual mouth could belong to no one else.

Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea flashed through him, and he crept silently up from behind. In an instant he grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There was a crude curse, a heavy splash, and then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously over the edge but could see nothing of the palm-reader except a tall hat spinning in a whirl of moonlit water. Eventually it sank too, and no sign of Mr. Podgers remained. Once he thought he glimpsed the bulky misshapen figure swimming toward the staircase by the bridge, and a terrible feeling of failure swept over him, but it turned out to be just a reflection, and when the moon slid out from behind a cloud it vanished. At last he seemed to have fulfilled destiny’s decree. He let out a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

“Have you dropped something, sir?” a voice asked suddenly behind him.

He turned to see a policeman with a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing important, sergeant,” he replied with a smile, and hailing a passing hansom, he climbed in and told the driver to head to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swung between hope and fear. Sometimes he half expected Mr. Podgers to stroll into the room, yet at other moments he felt Fate couldn’t be so unjust. Twice he went to the palm-reader’s address in West Moon Street, but could not bring himself to ring the bell. He craved certainty and dreaded it.

At last it arrived. He was sitting in the club smoking-room, sipping tea, and listening with mild boredom to Surbiton’s account of the latest comic song at the Gaiety when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"eb4fddfa6bf241714a06a04b","rewritten_text":"I went from shop to shop, buying whatever was needed to change his appearance. Once that business was done, I headed on my own to Little Britain. Mr. Jaggers was at his desk, but when he saw me enter, he immediately got up and stood before his fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I replied. I had carefully considered what I intended to say on the way there.

“Don’t implicate yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t implicate anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything: I don’t want to know anything; I’m not curious.”

Of course I realized he knew the man had arrived.

“I merely want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to reassure myself that what I’ve been told is true. I don’t hope it’s untrue, but I can at least verify it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head and staring at the floor as if listening. “Told suggests spoken communication. You can’t have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I’ll say informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I’ve been informed by a man named Abel Magwitch that he is the long-unknown benefactor.”

“That’s the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And only him?” I asked.

“And only him,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I’m not unreasonable enough, sir, to consider you in any way responsible for my mistakes or false conclusions, but I always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” replied Mr. Jaggers, looking at me coolly and biting his forefinger, “I’m not responsible for that.”

“Yet it seemed so likely, sir,” I said with a heavy heart.

“Not a shred of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his coat. “Don’t trust appearances; rely on evidence. There’s no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I sighed after standing silent awhile. “I’ve confirmed the information, and that’s the end of it.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you can understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout all my dealings with you, I have kept to the exact facts. There hasn’t been the smallest deviation from the strict facts. You know that?”

“Completely, sir.”

“I warned Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must never expect me to stray from the strict facts.”"}

Tom kept whitewashing, completely ignoring the steamboat. Ben stared for a second and then said, “Hey-yi! You’re in a fix, aren’t you!”

No response. Tom examined his last stroke with an artist’s eye, gave the brush another light sweep, and looked at the effect again. Ben pulled up beside him. Tom’s mouth watered for the apple, but he stayed with his work. Ben said:

“Hey, old fellow, you stuck working, huh?”

Tom spun around and said:

“Oh, it’s you, Ben! Didn’t even notice.”

“Say—I’m heading out to swim, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But of course you’d rather be working—right? Sure you would!”

Tom studied him a moment and said:

“What do you call work?”

“Why, isn’t that work?”

Tom went back to painting and answered casually:

“Well, maybe it is, maybe it isn’t. All I know is, it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh come on, you’re not pretending you like it?”

The brush kept moving.

“Like it? I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get the chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That gave Ben a new perspective. He stopped nibbling the apple. Tom brushed delicately back and forth, stepped away to check the effect, added a touch here and there, evaluated it again—Ben watching every move, getting more and more interested, more and more absorbed. Soon he said:

“Hey, Tom, let me whitewash a little.”

Tom thought it over, was about to agree, then changed his mind:

“No—no—I don’t think that’ll do, Ben. See, Aunt Polly’s really particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it were the back fence I wouldn’t mind and neither would she. Yep, she’s real particular about this one; it has to be done very carefully. I guess there isn’t one boy in a thousand—maybe two thousand—who can do it the way it needs to be done.”

“No kidding? Oh come on—let me try. Just a bit—I’d let you if our places were switched, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest; but Aunt Polly—well, Jim wanted to do it, but she wouldn’t let him; Sid wanted to do it, and she wouldn’t let Sid.”"}

{"request_id":"421e615b0f977f3a9c4e8f06","rewritten_text":"Had she known her sister was intent on wrenching her from such prospects and realities, what feelings would have possessed her? Only her mother, who might have experienced nearly the same, could have understood. Lydia’s trip to Brighton was the sole comfort offsetting her sorrowful conviction that her husband never meant to go there himself.

Yet they remained wholly unaware of what had occurred; their delight went on, with scarcely a pause, until the very day Lydia left home.

Elizabeth was now to meet Mr. Wickham for the last time. As she had often been in his company since returning, her agitation had subsided; the emotions of past preference entirely so. She had even learned to discern, in the very gentleness that had once charmed her, an affectation and monotony that disgusted and fatigued. In his present conduct toward her, moreover, she found a new source of displeasure; for the inclination he soon displayed to revive the attentions that had marked the early stage of their acquaintance could now serve only to provoke. Discovering herself singled out by such idle, frivolous gallantry, she ceased to feel any concern for him; and while she resolutely checked it, she could not miss the implied reprimand in his supposing that, however long and for whatever reason his attentions had been suspended, her vanity would be pleased and her preference secured at any moment by their renewal.

On the very last day the regiment remained in Meryton, he dined, with other officers, at Longbourn; and Elizabeth was so little disposed to part from him affably that when he casually asked how her time had been spent at Hunsford, she mentioned Colonel Fitzwilliam and Mr. Darcy having both stayed three weeks at Rosings, and inquired whether he knew the former.

He looked astonished, displeased, alarmed; but with a moment’s recollection and a returning smile, said he had formerly seen him often; and after remarking that he was a very gentlemanlike man, asked how she had liked him. Her reply warmly favored him. With an air of indifference, he soon after added, “How long did you say he was at Rosings?”

“Nearly three weeks.”

“And you saw him frequently?”

“Yes, almost every day.”

“His manners differ greatly from his cousin’s.”

“Yes, very different; but I think Mr. Darcy improves on closer acquaintance.”

“Indeed!” cried Wickham, with a look she did not miss. “And may I ask—” but checking himself, he continued, in a lighter tone, “Is it in address that he improves?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"76e746752ce0fd3710167126","rewritten_text":"Mr. Elliot looked up with such deference.” “Perfectly charming!” exclaimed Mrs. Clay, though she dared not turn her gaze toward Anne. “Just like father and son! Dear Miss Elliot, am I not allowed to say father and son?” “Oh! I do not forbid anyone their expressions. If you must think so! But, upon my honour, I scarcely perceive his attentions surpassing those of other gentlemen.” “My dear Miss Elliot!” cried Mrs. Clay, raising hands and eyes, then suppressing the rest of her astonishment into a convenient silence. “Well, Penelope, you need not feel such alarm about him. Remember, I invited him. I dismissed him with smiles. When I discovered he truly meant to spend the entire day tomorrow with friends at Thornberry Park, I took pity on him.” Anne admired her friend’s skill in appearing so delighted by both expectation and actual arrival of the very person whose presence must interfere with her principal aim. Surely Mrs. Clay detested the sight of Mr. Elliot; yet she could adopt an obliging, tranquil expression, and appear perfectly content with having her licence to devote herself to Sir Walter reduced to only half the usual degree. To Anne, Mr. Elliot’s entrance proved exceedingly distressing, and his approaching to speak to her was painful. Previously she had suspected him of lacking complete sincerity; now she detected duplicity everywhere. His respectful deference to her father, set against his earlier commentary, was detestable; and thinking of his cruel behaviour toward Mrs. Smith, she could barely endure his smiles and gentle manner or the sound of his contrived good sentiments. She intended to avoid any change in demeanor that might provoke remonstrance from him. She sought to escape all questions or display; nonetheless she meant to be as unmistakably cool toward him as their kinship allowed, and to withdraw, quietly as possible, from those few steps of needless intimacy she had imperceptibly taken. Thus she was more guarded and colder than the evening before. He was eager to rekindle her curiosity about how and where he had heard her formerly praised; anxious to be gratified by renewed inquiry; but the spell had been broken: he discovered the bustle and excitement of a public room were necessary to arouse his modest cousin’s vanity; at least he found it could not now be achieved by any efforts he could attempt amid the authoritative claims of the others."}

Then, all at once, he’s flat on his back, and he can’t figure out how it happened. That’s how I handled Brother Dowley. I began talking in a lazy, easy way, as if I only wanted to pass the time; and the oldest man alive couldn’t have tracked where I started and guessed where I meant to end up.

“Boys, there are a lot of curious things about law, and custom, and use, and all that, once you look at them; yes, and about the flow and advance of human opinion and movement, too. There are written laws—they die; but there are unwritten laws—they are eternal. Take the unwritten law of wages: it says wages have to rise, little by little, down through the centuries. And see how it works. We know what wages are now, here and there and yonder; we take an average and call that today’s wage. We know what wages were a hundred years ago, and two hundred years ago; that’s as far back as we can go, but it’s enough to give us the law of progress, the rate of regular increase; and so, without a document to help, we can come close to figuring what wages were three, four, five hundred years ago. Good so far. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking back; we turn around and apply the law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what wages will be at any time you want, for hundreds and hundreds of years ahead.”

“What, goodman, what!”

“Yes. In seven hundred years wages will be six times what they are now in your region, and farmhands will get 3 cents a day, and mechanics 6.”

“I’d I might die now and live then!” broke in Smug the wheelwright, greed shining in his eye.

{"request_id":"2c2b71a4605721abcf138657","rewritten_text":"“One word more, Rose. Beloved Rose! just one more!” Harry burst out, placing himself before her. “Had I been less—less fortunate, as the world phrases it—had some quiet, hidden life been my lot—had I been poor, ailing, helpless—would you have turned away then? Or has this hesitation sprung up only because I seem destined for wealth and distinction?”

“Do not force me to answer,” Rose replied. “That situation never has existed and never will. It is unfair—almost unkind—to insist upon it.”

“If your reply is what I scarcely dare to hope,” Harry went on, “it will throw a ray of joy across my solitary path, and guide me onward. It is no small thing to do this by uttering a few short words to one who loves you beyond all else. Oh, Rose: in the name of my fervent, unfaltering devotion; in remembrance of all I have suffered for you, and all you condemn me yet to suffer; answer me this single question!”

“Then, had your fate been otherwise shaped,” Rose returned; “had you been even slightly, yet not so widely, above me; if I could have aided and cheered you in some modest, peaceful retreat, and not been a stain and hindrance amid ambitious, distinguished circles; I should have been spared this ordeal. I have every reason to be happy, very happy, now; but then, Harry, I admit I should have been happier.”

While she confessed it, busy memories of childhood’s hopes, treasured long ago, thronged Rose’s mind; but they came with tears, as old hopes do when they return blighted, and those tears brought relief.

“This weakness is beyond my control, yet it strengthens my resolve,” said Rose, reaching out her hand. “I must leave you now, indeed.”

“I ask but one pledge,” Harry said. “Once, only once again—say within a year, perhaps much sooner—let me speak of this once more, for the last time.”

“Not to urge me to forsake my just determination,” answered Rose, a sorrowful smile hovering on her lips; “it would be useless.”

“No,” said Harry; “merely to hear you repeat it, if you will—finally repeat it. I will lay before you whatever rank or fortune may be mine; and if you still hold to your present decision, I will not endeavor, by speech or deed, to alter it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose replied; “it is but one more pang, and perhaps by then I shall bear it better.”

She offered her hand again."}

You are far too needful at Hartfield to be lent to Abbey-Mill.” “And I am sure I should never wish to go; I am content only at Hartfield.” Later she said, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be vastly surprised if she knew what had passed. I am certain Miss Nash would be—for she considers her sister very well married, and it was only to a linen-draper.” “One would be sorry to see greater pride or delicacy in the mistress of a school, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would covet such a chance of marriage herself. Even this triumph would seem precious to her. As for anything higher for you, I imagine she is utterly ignorant. The attentions of a certain person can scarcely have entered the small talk of Highbury yet. Thus far, I suspect you and I alone have interpreted his looks and manners.” Harriet blushed, smiled, and murmured something about her amazement that people should be so partial to her. The idea of Mr. Elton was unquestionably heartening; yet before long she was tender once more towards the dismissed Mr. Martin. “Now he has received my letter,” she said softly. “I cannot help wondering what they are all about—whether his sisters know—if he is unhappy, they must be unhappy as well. I hope he will not feel it too deeply.” “Let us think of our absent friends who are more pleasantly occupied,” cried Emma. “Perhaps at this very moment Mr. Elton is displaying your portrait to his mother and sisters, declaring how much lovelier the original is, and after being begged for it five or six times, is at length consenting to let them hear your name—your own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"5d25ac14ec3fd64a34c18c62","rewritten_text":"April 12. The balloon suddenly changed direction in a way I had expected but which still thrilled me. It had been traveling along the twentieth parallel south when it sharply turned east and kept going that way through the day, staying almost perfectly within the plane of the moon’s ellipse. The car, however, began to sway noticeably because of this new course and continued to do so for many hours. 

April 13. I was again frightened by the loud crackling sound that had alarmed me on the tenth. I thought about it for a long time but could not find an explanation. The apparent size of the earth shrank dramatically and now filled an angle of only a little more than twenty-five degrees from the balloon. The moon was nearly at my zenith and could not be seen at all. I was still moving in the plane of the ellipse but gained very little ground toward the east. 

April 14. The apparent size of the earth dropped even more quickly. I became convinced that the balloon was traveling along the line of apsides toward perigee—in other words, following the exact path that would take me to the moon at the point where it comes closest to the earth. The moon was directly overhead and therefore out of sight. Condensing the air required long, exhausting labor. 

April 15. By now I could no longer make out even the faint outlines of continents or seas on the earth. Around midday I heard the terrifying noise for the third time. It lasted longer and grew louder as it went on. I stood stunned, expecting some horrible destruction, when the car shook violently and a huge burning mass, of a material I could not identify, roared past the balloon with the voice of a thousand thunders. After my fear eased, I decided it must have been a massive volcanic fragment thrown off by the world I was rapidly approaching, likely one of those strange objects that sometimes fall to earth and are called meteoric stones for lack of a better name. 

April 16. Today, by straining to look upward through each side window in turn, I was delighted to see a small part of the moon’s disk protruding on all sides beyond the balloon’s huge circumference."}

{"request_id":"b9587421074225753d5c7db8","rewritten_text":"It was then that both his gaze and mine settled upon a scrap of parchment, which I initially took for paper. It lay half hidden in the sand, one corner protruding. Close to that spot I noticed the remains of what seemed once to be the hull of a ship’s longboat. The wreck had clearly been there ages; scarcely anything in its frame still resembled boat timbers.

“Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon after we turned homeward and met Lieutenant G—— on the way. I showed him the insect, and he entreated me to let him take it to the fort. When I consented, he at once slipped it into his waistcoat pocket, leaving behind the parchment in which it had been enclosed, which I had continued to hold while he examined the beetle. Perhaps he feared I might reconsider and thought best to secure the treasure immediately—you know how fervent his interest is in everything touching Natural History. Meanwhile, without realizing it, I must have placed the parchment into my own pocket.

“You recollect that when I approached the table intending to sketch the beetle, I found no paper at its usual place. I opened the drawer and discovered none there either. I searched my pockets, hoping to find some old letter, when my hand encountered the parchment. I recount exactly how it came into my keeping, for the details struck me with unusual force.

“Doubtless you will think me fanciful, but I had already formed a sort of linkage. I had connected two links of a long chain. There was a boat along a sea-coast, and near that boat lay a parchment—no mere paper—bearing the image of a skull. You will naturally ask, ‘what is the relationship?’ I answer that the skull, the death’s-head, is the familiar emblem of the pirate. The banner of the death’s-head flies in every engagement.

“I mentioned that the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment endures—almost indestructible. Matters of little significance are seldom committed to parchment; for the routine needs of drawing or writing it serves far less well than paper. This thought hinted at some meaning—some relevance—behind the death’s-head. I also took note of the parchment’s shape. Though one corner had been destroyed by some mishap, the original form was plainly oblong.”"}

{"request_id":"351807a5d5d3d91c65871f8c","rewritten_text":"But when I saw someone else fall in love with you—when I imagined you being loved as anything less than a sacred emblem of beauty and virtue—or when I imagined you loving someone else more passionately than you loved me, a demon woke inside me. I drove your lover away, and from that moment I have known no peace. I have searched in vain for sleep and rest; my eyelids refused to close, and my blood was forever raging. I woke into a new life the way someone dying in hope might wake in Hell. I will not tarnish your imagination by describing my battles, my rage at myself, and my despair. Let a veil fall over the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father; the secrets of such a tormented heart must not be made common. Everything was upheaval, crime, remorse, and hate, and yet still the softest love; and what first inspired me to resolve to conquer my passion and to restore my child to her father was the sight of your bitter and sympathetic grief. That is what brought me here: I thought if I could awaken again the sorrow I felt at your mother’s death, if I could revive the memories of her that had lain dormant for seventeen years, then any love for her child would die out. In a fit of heroism I decided to go alone, to leave you—the life of my life—and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it failed: I overestimated my strength, or underestimated my love. I would certainly have died if you hadn’t hurried to me. I almost wish I had been extinguished.

And now, Mathilda, I must confess one last thing. I was tragically wrong to think I could defeat my love for you; I never can. Seeing this house, these fields, and woods where my first love lived has made it stronger. In my madness I dared tell myself—Diana died to give her child life; her spirit was passed into her daughter, and so the daughter should be as Diana to me. The more I try to tear it out, the tighter it grips: this guilty love more unnatural than hate, which ruins your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to have loved despair itself, and safer to have kissed her.

No time or distance can rip from my soul what has become part of it. Since I arrived here, not for a moment have I been free of the hellish passion planted in me to burn until everything is cold, rigid, lifeless."}

{"request_id":"3e96d32f0a446cecdb095317","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced back at him, without success, as he headed for the door.

“Good night!” the uncle said. “I look forward to the pleasure of seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Show my nephew to his room there!—And burn my nephew in his bed, if you like,” he muttered to himself before ringing his little bell again and summoning his valet to his own chamber.

Once the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis paced in his loose robe to ease himself gently toward sleep on that hot, still night. Rustling around the room, his soft slippers silent on the floor, he moved like a cultivated tiger—looked like some unrepentantly wicked marquis from a tale, at the moment when his periodic change into a tiger was either just ending or just beginning.

He walked from end to end of his luxurious bedroom, reviewing the fragments of the day’s journey that rose unbidden in his mind: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the setting sun itself, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the little village in the hollow, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender in his blue cap pointing out the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain reminded him of the Paris fountain, the small bundle lying on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, shouting, “Dead!”

“I’m calm now,” Monsieur the Marquis said, “and can go to bed.”

Leaving only one light burning on the wide hearth, he let his thin gauze curtains fall around him and heard the night break its silence with a long sigh as he settled himself to sleep.

The stone faces on the outer walls stared blindly into the black night for three heavy hours; for three heavy hours, the horses in the stables rattled their harness, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound with very little resemblance to the noise poets say the owl makes. But creatures like that are stubborn about saying what is written for them.

For three heavy hours, the stone faces of the chateau, lion and human, stared blindly into the night. Dead darkness covered the landscape, and dead darkness laid its own hush over the hushed dust on every road. The burial ground had reached the point where its small mounds of poor grass were indistinguishable from one another; the figure on the Cross might have stepped down, for all anyone could see. In the village, taxer and taxed slept soundly. Dreaming, perhaps, of feasts—as the starving often do—and of comfort and rest, as a driven slave or yoked ox might, its gaunt inhabitants slept deeply, fed and freed in their dreams."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0afa2d049a88728e5adf85af","rewritten_text":"I told myself I wasn’t about to get tangled up in anything like that. When I went downstairs in the morning, the parlor was closed and the watchers were gone. Only the family, Widow Bartley, and our crew were around. I studied their faces to see if anything had happened, but I couldn’t tell. Around midday the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They set the coffin on two chairs in the middle of the room, arranged our chairs in rows, and borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were packed. The coffin lid looked as it had before, but I didn’t dare peek underneath with everyone around. Soon people started pouring in. The frauds and the girls sat in the front row at the head of the coffin, and for half an hour the guests filed past slowly in a single line, gazing at the dead man’s face for a moment. Some shed a tear, and everything was hushed and solemn, except for the girls and the con men holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, heads bowed, sniffling a little. There was no other sound beyond shuffling feet and people blowing their noses—folks always do that more at a funeral than anywhere except church. When the place was full, the undertaker glided around in his black gloves with quiet, comforting efficiency, putting on the final touches and getting people and things tidy and orderly without making more noise than a cat. He never spoke; he just shifted people around, squeezed in latecomers, opened passageways, all with nods and hand signals. Then he took his place against the wall. He was the softest, smoothest, stealthiest man I’d ever seen, and his face wasn’t any more cheerful than a slab of ham. They’d borrowed a wheezy melodeon, and once everything was ready a young woman sat down to play it. It screeched and wheezed, but everybody joined in singing, and in my opinion Peter was the only one with a good thing going on. Then Reverend Hobson began, slow and solemn, and right away the most outrageous commotion erupted in the cellar that anyone had ever heard. It was just one dog, but he made an awful racket and kept at it nonstop. The preacher had to stand there over the coffin and wait—you couldn’t even hear yourself think."}

{"request_id":"cbbbb1010584678f3eaafb7e","rewritten_text":"My heart thudded wildly and with an unaccountable dread I dismissed the servant, locked the door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were its contents.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed the trust you placed in me; I have tried to stain your mind and acquainted your innocent heart with the gaze and speech of unlawful, monstrous desire. I must atone for these crimes, and should attempt to match my punishment to my guilt. You must already anticipate what I am about to declare: we must separate, and forever part.

“I rob you of your parent and only friend. I cast you, unprotected, upon the world: your hopes are shattered; the peace and security of your untainted mind ruined; memory will bring before you ghastly images of guilt and the torment of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who draw all this misery down upon you; I, who cast you out and without mercy have stamped distrust and anguish on the heart and brow of my own child, who with fiendish frivolity tried to steal her loveliness to replace it with the foul deformity of sin; I, in the overflowing agony of my soul, implore you to pardon me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must and do abhor me: yet pardon me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts pursue me in my exile with unforgiving anger. I must never see you again; never hear your voice; yet the soft murmur of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning in my distraught brain and heart; I am sure I would feel it even within my grave. And I dare urge this plea by telling how miserably I was ensnared in this fiery torment and of my every struggle to free myself: truly, had your soul been less pure and radiant I would not attempt to justify myself to you; I would fear that by making you view me with less abhorrence you might likewise loathe vice less. But in speaking to you I feel I appeal to an angelic judge. I cannot depart without your pardon and must strive to wrest it from you, or else plunge into despair. I implore you therefore to listen to me, and if in the virtuous, guilt may in some measure be lessened by keen suffering and remorse that shatters the brain like madness, perhaps you may believe—though I dare not—that I possess some claim to your compassion.

“I beseech you to recall our first happy days beside the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned after a weary wandering of sixteen years, during which, though I had endured many perils and sorrows, my affections had been utterly blank.”"}

{"request_id":"428a3579108ca847f7a1ca9d","rewritten_text":"P.S.—Please tell me about the bows. Jennings insists they are in fashion.

Lord Arthur looked so grave and miserable over the letter that the Duchess burst into peals of laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she cried, “I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what shall I say about the clock? I think it is a marvelous invention, and I should like to have one myself.”

“I don’t care much for them,” said Lord Arthur with a sad smile, and after kissing his mother he left the room.

When he reached his room, he threw himself onto a sofa, and tears filled his eyes. He had done everything he could to carry out this murder, yet both times he had failed, and through no fault of his own. He had tried to fulfill his duty, but it seemed as though Destiny itself had betrayed him. He felt weighed down by the emptiness of good intentions and the uselessness of trying to be noble. Perhaps it would be better to break off the marriage altogether. Sybil would suffer, yes, but suffering could never truly spoil a nature as noble as hers. As for himself, what did it matter? There is always some war in which a man can die, some cause to which he can give his life, and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny shape his fate. He would not lift a finger to aid her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he felt obliged to dine with them. Their empty talk and idle jokes did not interest him, and as soon as the coffee arrived he left them, inventing an engagement so he could escape. As he was leaving the club, the hall-porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, asking him to come the next evening and examine an explosive umbrella that went off as soon as it was opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. He tore the letter into shreds. He had decided he would try no more experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat for hours by the river. The moon peered through a mane of tawny clouds like a lion’s eye, and countless stars dotted the hollow sky like gold dust scattered on a purple dome. Now and then a barge drifted into the murky current and floated away with the tide, and the railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as the trains shrieked across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"7687cf6b4adc327af0d3085f","rewritten_text":"“Unless you call Miss Havisham a he. And even you wouldn’t go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, uptown?” Joe asked.

“Is there another Miss Havisham downtown?” my sister shot back.

“She wants this boy to go and play there. Of course he’s going. And he had better play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me in warning to be as lively as possible, “or I’ll make sure he does.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham uptown—everyone for miles had heard of her—as an extremely rich and stern lady who lived in a huge, gloomy house barricaded against thieves, and who kept to herself.

“Well, I’ll be!” Joe exclaimed, stunned. “How did she ever hear of Pip?”

“Fool!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Because someone,” Joe hinted politely, “said she wanted him to go and play there.”

“Couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew a boy who could go and play there? Isn’t it possible that Uncle Pumblechook might be her tenant, and that he sometimes—we won’t say every quarter or half-year, because that would be expecting too much of you—but sometimes goes there to pay his rent? Couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, always so considerate and thoughtful for us—though you may not see it, Joseph,” she added with the deepest reproach, as if he were the most unfeeling of nephews, “then mention this boy, standing prancing here”—which I swear I was not doing—“that I have always been a willing slave to?”

“Good again!” cried Uncle Pumblechook. “Well said! Nicely pointed! Excellent! Now, Joseph, you understand the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister said, still reproachful, while Joe sheepishly rubbed the back of his hand across his nose again and again, “you do not—though you may think you do—understand the situation. You may believe you do, but you do not, Joseph. Because you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, realizing that for all we know this boy’s fortune might be made by going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, to keep him there tonight, and to take him himself to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lord have mercy!” my sister cried, ripping off her bonnet in sudden desperation, “here I am talking to a pair of mooncalves, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the mare catches cold at the door, and the boy is smeared with grime from the hair on his head to the soles of his feet!”"}

{"request_id":"3d1e2fb09187ba4976cec59a","rewritten_text":"Emma had no later cause to recant her poor estimation of Mrs. Elton. Her observations had been tolerably accurate. Just as Mrs. Elton struck her at their second encounter, so she remained whenever they met thereafter—self-satisfied, overbearing, free and easy, uninformed, and ill-mannered. She possessed a touch of beauty and a trace of accomplishment, yet so little judgment that she fancied herself entering with superior worldly knowledge to enliven and refine a rural neighbourhood; and imagined Miss Hawkins to have held a position in society that only Mrs. Elton’s own consequence could surpass.

There was no sign that Mr. Elton held any opinion different from his wife’s. He appeared not only content with her, but proud. He seemed to congratulate himself on bringing to Highbury a woman whom even Miss Woodhouse could not rival; and most of her new acquaintances, inclined to praise, or unaccustomed to judge, guided by Miss Bates’s kind intentions, or assuming that the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she asserted, were perfectly satisfied; so Mrs. Elton’s commendation passed from mouth to mouth as it should, unhampered by Miss Woodhouse, who readily maintained her initial offering and spoke with good grace of her being “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one regard Mrs. Elton became even worse than at first. Her feelings shifted toward Emma. Probably affronted by the scant encouragement her overtures of intimacy received, she retreated in her turn and gradually grew much colder and more distant; and although the result was welcome, the ill will that prompted it necessarily heightened Emma’s dislike. Her manners, and Mr. Elton’s as well, were disagreeable toward Harriet. They were sneering and careless. Emma trusted it must quickly effect Harriet’s cure; but the sentiments that could inspire such conduct lowered them both considerably. It could not be doubted that poor Harriet’s attachment had been laid before conjugal confidence, and Emma’s own part in the affair, under colouring least favourable to her and most soothing to him, had likely been supplied also. Harriet was, of course, the object of their mutual dislike. When conversation flagged, they could readily begin abusing Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they dared not show by open disrespect toward her took a wider outlet in scornful treatment of Harriet.

Mrs. Elton conceived a great notion of Jane Fairfax, and from the start. Not merely when one might suppose a feud with one young woman would recommend another, but from the earliest moment; and she was not content with a natural and reasonable admiration—rather, without invitation, claim, or excuse, she must needs be anxious to aid and advocate her. Before Emma had forfeited her trust, and about their third meeting, she heard the whole of Mrs. Elton’s knight-errantry on the subject."}

{"request_id":"6f61ac7b841143b252135af0","rewritten_text":"You wouldn’t know about me unless you’d read a book called The Adventures of Tom Sawyer; but that doesn’t make any difference. That book was written by Mr. Mark Twain, and he mostly told the truth. There were some things he stretched, but for the most part it was the truth. That’s nothing. I never met anybody who hadn’t lied one time or another, unless it was Aunt Polly, or the widow, or maybe Mary. Aunt Polly—Tom’s Aunt Polly, she is—and Mary, and the Widow Douglas are all set down in that book, which is mostly true, with a few stretchers, like I mentioned. 

Now the way that book finishes is like this: Tom and me came across the money the robbers hid in the cave, and it made us rich. We got six thousand dollars apiece—in gold. It looked like a powerful heap when you stacked it. Judge Thatcher took it and put it out at interest, and it brought in a dollar a day each, right through the year—more than anyone could think what to do with. The Widow Douglas took me for her son and said she’d civilize me; but it was tough staying in the house steady, considering how mournful proper and tidy the widow was in every way; and after I couldn’t bear it no more I took off. I got into my old rags and my sugar-hogshead again, and felt free and content. But Tom Sawyer found me and said he was fixing to start a band of robbers, and I could join if I’d go back to the widow and be respectable. So I went back.

The widow cried over me, called me a poor lost lamb, and a batch of other names, too, though she never meant harm. She dressed me in those new clothes again, and all I could do was sweat and sweat, feeling squeezed and stiff. Well, then it all started over. The widow rang a bell for supper, and you had to be on time. When you got to the table you couldn’t begin eating right away; you had to wait for the widow to bow her head and mumble something over the victuals, though nothing was wrong with them—only everything was cooked separate. In a barrel of odds and ends it’s different; things mix, the juices trade around, and the food goes down better.

After supper she fetched out her book and taught me about Moses and the Bulrushers, and I was in a hurry to hear the whole of it; but after a while she let slip that Moses had been dead a good long while; so then I didn’t care any further, because I don’t take stock in dead folks."}

{"request_id":"ede2758194e86535b48fb252","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke warmly about his sister’s skill.

“I am very pleased to hear such a good report of her,” said Lady Catherine. “Please tell her from me that she cannot expect to excel unless she practices a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he answered, “that she does not need that advice. She practices very regularly.”

“So much the better. One can never practice too much. When I next write to her, I will insist she never neglect it. I often tell young ladies that no one can become excellent at music without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play truly well unless she practices more. And though Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is perfectly welcome, as I have often told her, to come to Rosings every day and play the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. In that part of the house she would be in no one’s way.”

Mr. Darcy looked slightly ashamed of his aunt’s lack of manners and stayed silent.

When coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth she had promised to play for him, and she sat down at once at the instrument. He moved a chair close to her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then began talking again to her other nephew, until he walked away from her and, with his usual calm, positioned himself by the pianoforte so he could watch the performer’s face clearly. Elizabeth saw what he was about and, at the first pause, turned to him with a playful smile.

“You mean to scare me, Mr. Darcy, by coming in all this state to hear me. But I will not be frightened, even if your sister does play so well. I have a stubborn streak that will never let others frighten me. My courage grows every time someone tries to intimidate me.”

“I shall not say you are wrong,” he replied, “because you could not truly believe I would try to frighten you. And I have known you long enough to see that you take great pleasure in occasionally claiming opinions that are not really yours.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this description of herself and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin is giving you a very fine idea of me and teaching you not to believe a single word I say. I am especially unlucky to meet someone so capable of revealing my true character in a place where I had hoped to pass myself off with some credit.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"206309966162fcfa6b601fae","rewritten_text":"The storm raged violently all night, but nothing particularly noteworthy happened. The next morning, however, when they came down to breakfast, they found the terrible bloodstain on the floor once more. “I can’t blame Paragon Detergent,” said Washington, “because I’ve tried it with every cleaner imaginable. It must be the ghost.” He scrubbed the stain away again, yet on the following morning it reappeared. It was there again on the third morning, even though Mr. Otis himself had locked the library the night before and taken the key upstairs. The whole family was now thoroughly intrigued; Mr. Otis began to suspect he had been too dismissive in denying ghosts existed, Mrs. Otis announced she intended to join the Psychical Society, and Washington prepared a long letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the persistence of bloodstains associated with crime. That night all doubts about the tangible reality of phantoms vanished forever.\n\nThe day had been warm and sunny, and in the cool of the evening the entire family went out for a drive. They did not return until nine o’clock, when they ate a light supper. The conversation never once touched on ghosts, so there were not even the basic conditions of receptive expectation that so often precede psychic phenomena. The topics discussed, as I have since heard from Mr. Otis, were simply what cultured, upper-class Americans usually talk about: the overwhelming superiority of Miss Fanny Davenport over Sarah Bernhardt as an actress; the difficulty of obtaining green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the finest English homes; Boston’s crucial role in the development of the world-soul; the benefits of the baggage check system in railroad travel; and the sweetness of the New York accent compared to the London drawl. Nothing supernatural was mentioned, nor was Sir Simon de Canterville referenced at all. At eleven o’clock the family retired, and by half-past the lights were out. Some time later Mr. Otis awoke to a strange sound in the corridor outside his room. It sounded like metal clanking, drawing closer with every moment. He rose immediately, struck a match, and checked the time. It was exactly one o’clock. He remained completely calm and felt his pulse, which was steady. The odd noise continued, accompanied now by clearly audible footsteps. He slipped on his slippers, took a small oblong vial from his dressing case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"51dcba4e37f41d3cb8a8e38c","rewritten_text":"“Why, we could build quite a thrilling superstition on that idea. I suppose you plan to call the bug scarabaeus caput hominis, or something similar—Natural Histories have plenty of those names. But where are the antennae you mentioned?”

“The antennae!” Legrand exclaimed, growing strangely heated. “Surely you see them. I drew them as clearly as they appear on the real insect, and that should be enough.”

“Well, well,” I replied, “maybe you did—but I don’t see them.” I handed the paper back without further comment, hoping not to upset him. Still, the situation surprised me; his irritability made no sense, and the drawing absolutely showed no antennae. It really did resemble the usual illustrations of a death’s-head.

He snatched the paper peevishly and was about to crumple it and toss it into the fire when a quick glance at the sketch suddenly fixed his attention. His face turned bright red, and in the next moment deathly pale. For several minutes he sat there poring over the drawing. Then he got up, took a candle from the table, and sat on a sea chest in the far corner. He studied the paper again, rotating it in every direction. He stayed silent, and his behavior astonished me; yet I thought it wiser not to irritate his growing moodiness with a remark. Soon he pulled a wallet from his coat, slipped the paper carefully inside, and placed both in a writing desk, which he locked. His manner became calmer, though the earlier enthusiasm was gone. He seemed not exactly sullen, but rather lost in thought. As the evening passed he sank deeper into his reverie, and nothing I said could rouse him. I had planned to spend the night at the hut, as I often had, but seeing him in this state, I decided to leave. He did not urge me to stay, yet as I departed he shook my hand with more than his usual warmth.

About a month later—during which I saw nothing of Legrand—his servant Jupiter came to visit me in Charleston. I had never seen the good old man look so downcast, and I feared some serious trouble had befallen my friend."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a8c5d802f9491d9af0143ea3","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, with his face pale from terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, forcing his way through the ring of fur-coated footmen around the big striped awning, seeming blind and deaf to everything. The night was bitter cold, and the gas-lamps around the square flared and flickered in the sharp wind, yet his hands burned with fever and his forehead felt ablaze. He stumbled on, almost like a drunk. A policeman gave him a curious glance as he passed, and a beggar who shuffled out of an archway to ask for alms shrank back, frightened by a misery greater than his own. Once he stopped under a lamp and stared at his hands. He thought he already saw blood staining them, and a faint cry slipped from his shaking lips. Murder! That was what the palm-reader had foreseen. Murder! The night itself seemed aware of it, and the desolate wind howled it in his ears. The dark corners of the streets were filled with it. It leered at him from the rooftops. First he reached the Park, whose somber woods seemed to draw him in. He leaned wearily against the railings, cooling his forehead on the wet metal and listening to the trembling silence of the trees. “Murder! Murder!” he kept repeating, as if repetition could dull the horror of the word. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he almost hoped Echo might hear him and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. He felt a mad urge to stop any passer-by and confess everything. Then he wandered across Oxford Street into narrow, sordid alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he went by. From a dark courtyard came curses and blows, followed by shrill screams, and on a damp doorstep he saw the hunched shapes of the poor and old. A strange pity swept over him. Were these children of sin and misery doomed to their end, just as he was? Were they, like him, mere puppets in a monstrous show? Yet it was not the mystery but the grotesque comedy of suffering that struck him: its uselessness, its absurd lack of meaning. How jumbled everything seemed! How empty of harmony! He marveled at the clash between the shallow optimism of the day and the real facts of life. He was still very young. After a while he found himself standing before Marylebone Church. The silent road looked like a long ribbon of polished silver, streaked here and there with the dark, waving arabesques of shadows."}

{"request_id":"128432ca652d79d46d1b707d","rewritten_text":"Mr. Darcy spoke warmly about his sister’s skill. 

“I’m very glad to hear such a good report of her,” said Lady Catherine. “And please tell her from me that she cannot expect to excel unless she practices a great deal.”

“I assure you, madam,” he replied, “she does not need that advice. She practices very regularly.”

“So much the better. One cannot practice too much; and when I next write to her, I shall insist she does not neglect it under any circumstances. I often tell young ladies that no real excellence in music can be attained without constant practice. I have told Miss Bennet several times that she will never play truly well unless she works harder; and though Mrs. Collins has no instrument, she is very welcome—as I have often told her—to come to Rosings every day and play the pianoforte in Mrs. Jenkinson’s room. She wouldn’t impede anyone there, you know.”

Mr. Darcy looked somewhat embarrassed by his aunt’s lack of tact and said nothing.

When the coffee was finished, Colonel Fitzwilliam reminded Elizabeth of her promise to play for him, so she sat down at the instrument at once. He pulled a chair close beside her. Lady Catherine listened to half a song, then began talking again to her other nephew, until he walked away from her and, moving with his usual deliberation toward the piano, positioned himself to have a full view of the lovely performer’s face. Elizabeth noticed what he was doing and, at the first convenient pause, turned to him with a mischievous smile and said,

“You intend to intimidate me, Mr. Darcy, by coming with such ceremony to listen. But I will not be frightened, even though your sister plays so well. There is a stubbornness in me that cannot bear to be frightened by others’ wills. My courage always rises when someone tries to intimidate me.”

“I won’t declare that you are mistaken,” he replied, “because you cannot really suppose I meant to frighten you; and I have known you long enough to recognize that you greatly enjoy occasionally claiming opinions that are not actually yours.”

Elizabeth laughed heartily at this portrait of herself and said to Colonel Fitzwilliam, “Your cousin will give you a very charming impression of me and teach you not to believe a word I say. I am particularly unlucky to meet someone so capable of exposing my true character in a part of the world where I hoped to pass myself off with some degree of credit.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"671f3b25c0c180fbb476cabc","rewritten_text":"Yet now she wished the whole thing had never happened. Convinced he had indulged too freely in Mr. Weston’s superior wine, she felt certain he would insist on spouting foolishness. Determined to rein him in as much as her own behaviour could manage, she was already arranging to speak with composed serenity and solemnity about the weather and the night; but she had barely begun, barely had they cleared the sweep-gate and rejoined the other carriage, before her chosen topic was dashed to pieces—her hand seized—her attention claimed—and Mr. Elton, seizing the opportune moment, was outright declaring fervent love to her. He professed feelings he assumed must already be known, hopeful, fearful, worshipful, ready to perish if she spurned him; yet confident his burning devotion, unmatched affection, and unprecedented passion must make some impression, in short firmly determined to be accepted in earnest without delay. So it truly was. Without hesitation—without excuse—without even a show of timidity, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s suitor, proclaimed himself _her_ suitor. She attempted to silence him; but in vain; he persisted and poured out the entire speech. Furious as she felt, she determined in the moment to master herself before replying. She sensed that half this foolishness must be wine-inspired, and thus hoped it might be limited to the present hour. Therefore, blending seriousness with playfulness, which she trusted would fit his half-and-half condition, she answered, “I am quite amazed, Mr. Elton. This—addressed to _me_! You are forgetting yourself—you take me for my friend—any message to Miss Smith I will gladly deliver; but no more of this directed at _me_, if you please.” “Miss Smith!—message to Miss Smith!—What could she possibly intend!” He echoed her words with such confident emphasis, such swaggering pretence of astonishment, that she could not help replying sharply, “Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behaviour! I can explain it only one way; you are not yourself, or you could not speak to me, or about Harriet, in this manner. Control yourself enough to say no more, and I shall try to forget it.” Yet Mr. Elton had taken only sufficient wine to lift his spirits, not to muddle his faculties. He entirely understood his own intentions; and, after vehemently insisting her suspicion was grossly unjust, and briefly touching upon his regard for Miss Smith purely as her friend—while admitting his surprise that Miss Smith should be mentioned at all—he returned to expounding his own passion and pressed earnestly for a favourable reply."}
