{"request_id":"f710c619081431a5221cc934","rewritten_text":"“Farewell, Uncle George. If I linger, I’ll never reach luncheon on time. Thank you for giving me what I wanted. Nothing delights me more than learning everything about new acquaintances and nothing about old ones.”

“Where are you dining, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I’ve invited myself and Mr. Gray along. He’s her latest protégé.”

“Humph! tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, to stop pestering me with her charitable schemes. I’m weary of them. The good soul acts as though I have no occupation but signing cheques for her whims.”

“As you wish, Uncle George, though it will do no good. Philanthropists lose every trace of humanity. That’s their defining trait.”

The elder man grumbled assent and summoned his servant with the bell. Lord Henry walked up the low arcade into Burlington Street and headed toward Berkeley Square.

So this was how Dorian Gray’s lineage ran. Baldly told though it was, the tale evoked a strange, almost modern romance. A lovely woman risking everything for a mad devotion, a handful of wild weeks of bliss, abruptly broken by some hideous, treacherous act; months of voiceless anguish, then a child born in torment; the mother taken by death, the boy consigned to loneliness and the rule of an aged, loveless guardian. Yes, it made an intriguing background. It gave the youth a setting, rendered him closer to perfection. Behind every exquisite thing lay something tragic. Worlds must labour that even the meanest blossom might unfold.... And how entrancing he had been at dinner the previous evening, when he sat across from him at the club, eyes startled, lips parted in tremulous delight, the crimson shades deepening the awakening wonder of his expression. Speaking to him felt like playing a superb violin. He responded to every touch and vibration of the bow.... The act of influence held something horribly fascinating. Nothing else resembled it. To project one’s soul into a gracious shape and let it rest there briefly; to hear one’s intellectual notions returned, now with the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another as though it were some subtle essence or peculiar fragrance—there was genuine joy in that—perhaps the richest joy that remained to us in an age so cramped and vulgar, grossly sensuous in its pleasures and grossly common in its ambitions.... He was a remarkable specimen, this youth he had met so curiously in Basil’s studio, or could, at least, be moulded into one."}

{"request_id":"b0da1f7be21d707737a5a5b0","rewritten_text":"“Mark my words; I’ve mastered the language of despair. I know it by heart, because I am Despair—a strange creature, jubilant, triumphant Despair. Yet those words ring false, for the wave may be dark, but it isn’t bitter. We lie down, close our eyes with a soft good night, and when we wake, we are free. Come then, no more delays, you slow one! See the pleasant draught! Look, I am a spirit of goodness, not a mortal girl who invites you, and with pleading tones (oh, that they might win you!) says, Come and drink.”

As I spoke, I fastened my gaze on his face, and his unearthly beauty, the divine compassion shining in his eyes, his gentle yet earnest look of disapproval and amazement—even before he spoke—changed my strained mood, stripped away my harsh despair, and left me with the gentlest sorrow. I saw tears in his eyes too as he took both my hands in his; sitting down beside me, he said:

“This is a grievous act you would lead me to, dearest friend, and your sorrow must be deep indeed to fill you with these miserable thoughts. You long for death and yet you fear it, and wish me to share it with you. But I have less courage than you, and even with you beside me, I dare not die. Listen to me, then decide if you should win me to your plan, even if the overwhelming eloquence of despair could make death so tempting that heaven itself seemed dark. Listen, I beg you, to one who has nurtured his own desperate thoughts and longed impatiently for death, but who at last has trampled the phantom underfoot and crushed its sting. Come, since you have played Despair with me, I will play Una with you and lead you unhurt from his dark cavern. Listen, and let yourself be softened by words free of selfish passion.

“We don’t know what this vast world means; its strange blend of good and evil. Yet we have been placed here, told to live and to hope. I know not what we are to hope for, but there is some good beyond us that we must seek, and that is our task on earth. If misfortune comes against us, we must fight her off, throw her aside, and press forward to find what our nature requires. Whether this vision of future good prepares us for another existence, I cannot say; or whether we, as laborers in God’s vineyard, must lend a hand to clear the way for our descendants.”"}

{"request_id":"0024158a9fa9062334bc4e2e","rewritten_text":"The examination detained us until nightfall, when we withdrew. As we returned, my companion paused briefly to drop into the office of one of the daily journals.

I have remarked that my friend’s caprices were numerous, and that I humored them—_Je les ménageais_; there is no English phrase for it. Just now he chose to refuse any discussion of the murder until about midday on the morrow. At that hour he suddenly asked whether I had noticed anything _peculiar_ at the site of the deed.

Something in the way he stressed the word “peculiar” made me shiver without knowing the cause.

“No, nothing _peculiar_,” I replied; “nothing, at least, beyond what was reported in the paper.”

“The ‘Gazette,’” he said, “has failed, I fear, to convey the extraordinary horror of the affair. But put aside the idle comments of that print. It seems to me that this enigma is judged insoluble precisely because of that which ought to render it easy to solve—I mean the _outré_ nature of its features. The police are bewildered by the apparent lack of motive—not for the murder as such—but for the hideousness of the murder. They are also perplexed by the supposed impossibility of reconciling the voices overheard in dispute with the facts that no one was found above stairs except the slain Mademoiselle L’Espanaye, and that there was no avenue of escape without attracting the attention of those on the stair. The ferocious confusion of the chamber; the corpse wedged head downward in the chimney; the dreadful mangling of the old lady’s body; these facts, with those already stated and others I need not detail, have sufficed to benumb the faculties and wholly baffle the vaunted _acumen_ of the government officers. They have fallen into the crude yet common mistake of confusing the uncommon with the recondite. Yet it is through such departures from the ordinary plane that reason gropes its way, if at all, toward the truth. In inquiries such as the one now before us, the proper question is not so much ‘what has occurred,’ as ‘what has occurred that never happened before.’ Indeed, the readiness with which I shall reach, or have reached, the key to this mystery is directly proportional to the appearance of its insolubility in the eyes of the police.”

I gazed at the speaker in silent wonder.

“I am now waiting,” he went on, glancing toward our chamber door—“I am now expecting a person who, though possibly not the actual author of these butcheries, must have been in some degree involved in their execution.”"}

{"request_id":"ec9ec6ffb1bf53415fe9953a","rewritten_text":"“I am very ignorant, and it troubles me—only a little.”

“Tell me what is on your mind.”

“I have a cousin, my sole relative and an orphan like myself, whom I love dearly. She is five years younger than I, living in a farmer’s house in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has become of me—for I cannot write—and if I could, how should I explain it? It is better left so.”

“Yes, yes: better as it stands.”

“What I was thinking as we came along, and still think now as I look into your kind, strong face that gives me so much courage, is this:—If the Republic truly benefits the poor, if they grow less hungry and suffer less in every way, she might live many years; she might even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you suppose”—the patient eyes, so full of endurance, brim with tears, the lips part more and tremble—“that it will feel long to me, waiting for her in that better land where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot, my child; there is no Time there, no hardship there.”

“You comfort me so deeply! I am so ignorant. Should I kiss you now? Has the moment arrived?”

“Yes.”

She touches his lips; he touches hers; they bless each other solemnly. The slender hand is steady as he lets it go; nothing but a sweet, bright constancy shows in the patient face. She steps forward ahead of him—then she is gone; the knitting women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.”

The murmur of countless voices, countless faces turning upward, the surge of many footsteps along the crowd’s edge, until it swells forward in one mass, like a single great heave of water, all vanish in a flash. Twenty-Three.

{"request_id":"775a446284d617feac3dd621","rewritten_text":"“In English, the letter that appears most often is e. After that, the order is a o i d h n r s t u y c f g l m w b k p q x z. E is so dominant that you rarely see a sentence of any real length where it isn’t the most common letter.

“We already have the basis for something more than a mere guess. The general use of this table is obvious, but with this particular cipher we’ll need it only in a limited way. Since 8 is the character that shows up most frequently, we’ll begin by assuming it stands for the letter e. To test that, let’s see whether 8 appears often in pairs, because e is doubled very frequently in English—think of words like ‘meet,’ ‘fleet,’ ‘speed,’ ‘seen,’ ‘been,’ ‘agree,’ and so on. In this cryptogram, we find it doubled five times, even though the text is short.

“So let’s take 8 as e. Now, of all words in English, ‘the’ is the most common; so let’s check whether any three-character sequences repeat with an 8 at the end. If they do, those sequences most likely stand for ‘the.’ Sure enough, there are seven repetitions of the sequence ;48. We can therefore take ; as t, 4 as h, and 8 as e—the last of which is now firmly confirmed. That’s a major step forward.

“Once we know a single word, we can identify beginnings and endings of several others. Look at the next-to-last time the sequence ;48 appears, near the end of the cipher. We know the semicolon right afterward begins a word, and of the six characters following that ‘the,’ we already know five. Let’s write them down using the letters we have, leaving a blank for the unknown one—

 t eeth.

“At once we see that the ending ‘th’ cannot belong to the word starting with the first t; if we run through the entire alphabet trying letters in the blank, no word can be formed with that th there. That leaves t ee, and if we go through the alphabet again, we find the only possible solution is the word ‘tree.’”"}

{"request_id":"3248d2a49194af55ab40ac26","rewritten_text":"“I know she would!”

Widow Douglas’s generous hospitality was a tempting lure. Between that and Tom’s arguments the plan soon won out. They agreed to keep the evening’s scheme to themselves. Then it struck Tom that Huck might show up that very night and give the signal. The idea drained much of the excitement from his plans. Still, he couldn’t stand the thought of missing the fun at Widow Douglas’s place. Why should he give it up, he asked himself—there had been no signal the night before, so why would it be more likely tonight? The guaranteed amusement outweighed the uncertain treasure, and like the boy he was, he chose the stronger urge and refused to think about the box of money again that day.

Three miles downstream the ferry stopped at the mouth of a wooded hollow and tied up. The crowd poured ashore, and soon the forest depths and rocky heights rang with shouts and laughter. They tried every possible way to get hot and tired, and after a while the wanderers straggled back to camp with hearty appetites; then they set about demolishing the good food. After the feast came a pleasant spell of rest and conversation in the shade of broad oaks. After a while someone called out:

“Who’s ready for the cave?”

Everyone was. They gathered bundles of candles, and immediately there was a mad dash up the hill. The cave entrance was partway up the slope, shaped like a capital A. Its heavy oak door stood unbarred. Inside lay a small chamber, as cold as an icehouse, lined by nature with solid limestone slick with chill dampness. Standing there in the gloom and looking out at the sunlit green valley felt both romantic and mysterious. But that solemn feeling faded fast, and the horseplay resumed. As soon as someone lit a candle, everyone piled onto the owner; after a brief scuffle and spirited defense, the candle was knocked down or blown out, prompting cheers of laughter and another chase. But everything ends. Eventually the group filed down the steep slope of the main passage, a wavering row of lights barely revealing the high stone walls rising almost to their meeting point sixty feet above. This main corridor was only eight or ten feet across. Every few steps, other lofty but narrower openings branched away on either side—for McDougal’s Cave was nothing but a sprawling maze of twisting passages that looped into each other, then out again, and led nowhere."}

{"request_id":"264ed9bb6b3ec14de4aee131","rewritten_text":"“But that hardly matters.”

“I might as well ask,” she replied, “why, clearly hoping to insult me, you told me you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character. Wasn’t that some excuse for my rudeness, if I was rude? But I have other reasons. You know I do. Even if my feelings hadn’t already been against you, even if they had been neutral or even favorable, do you think anything could make me accept the man who has perhaps ruined forever the happiness of a dearly loved sister?”

As she spoke, Mr. Darcy changed colour, but the feeling passed quickly, and he listened without interrupting her while she went on—

“I have every reason to think the worst of you. Nothing can excuse the unfair and ungenerous part you played there. You dare not, you cannot deny that you were the main, if not the only, cause of separating them, of exposing one to the world’s censure for fickleness, the other to its scorn for disappointed hopes, and dragging them both into the cruelest misery.”

She paused, and with sharp indignation saw that he listened with an expression that showed he felt no regret. He even looked at her with a smile that feigned disbelief.

“Can you deny it?” she demanded again.

With forced calm he replied, “I do not wish to deny that I did everything in my power to separate my friend from your sister, or that I am pleased with my success. Toward him I have shown more kindness than toward myself.”

Elizabeth refused to acknowledge this polite remark, though she understood its meaning, and it did nothing to win her over.

“But my dislike does not rest on this alone,” she continued. “Long before that happened, my opinion of you was fixed. Your character was revealed to me in the account I heard many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On that subject, what can you say? With what imagined act of friendship can you defend yourself? Under what false story can you deceive anyone now?”

“You take a keen interest in that gentleman’s affairs,” said Darcy, less calmly, his colour rising.

“Who, knowing what his misfortunes have been, could help feeling for him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated scornfully. “Yes, his misfortunes have been very great indeed.”

“And caused by you,” cried Elizabeth, fervently. “You have reduced him to his current state of poverty—relative poverty.”"}

{"request_id":"6e0e92c293e55c376276af72","rewritten_text":"How could I, a bewildered village boy, escape the strange contradictions that even the best and wisest fall into every day?

“It may all be true,” I told Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

After that, I rolled onto my face, grabbed the hair on each side of my head, and pulled hard. I knew how foolish my heart was—all wild and out of place—and I felt it would serve me right if I yanked my face up by my hair and knocked it against the pebbles to punish it for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy, ever the wisest girl, stopped trying to argue. She put her work-roughened but comforting hand over mine, one after another, and gently drew them out of my hair. Then she lightly patted my shoulder in a soothing way, while I cried into my sleeve, just as I had in the brewery yard, and felt a vague conviction that someone—or everyone—had treated me unfairly.

“I’m glad of one thing,” Biddy said, “and that is that you felt you could trust me, Pip. I’m glad of another thing too: you know you can rely on me to keep your secret and try to deserve your confidence. If your first teacher—poor thing, so in need of learning herself—were teaching you now, she thinks she knows the lesson she would set. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you’ve moved beyond her, so it’s useless now.” With a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and added in a fresh, pleasant tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, jumping up, putting my arm around her neck, and kissing her, “I will always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” Biddy said.

“You know I never will be, so that means always. Not that I need to tell you anything, because you know all I know—as I told you at home the other night.”

“Ah!” Biddy breathed, almost whispering, as she looked out at the ships. Then she repeated, in her earlier cheerful tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told her we would walk a little farther, and we did, as the summer afternoon softened into summer evening—so beautiful to see."}

content.text: {"request_id":"da1518119e3b9fd696507a26","rewritten_text":"Thus I spent two years. Day after day hundreds passed; nothing outward changed, yet some days quietly worked on my mind as I slid toward death. I studied more; I connected more with other people’s thoughts in books; I read history and felt my own identity fade among the crowd who had lived before me. Perhaps as the sting of immediate suffering eased, I became more human. Solitude also lost some of its charm: I began to want sympathy again; not that I wished to seek a crowd, but I longed for one friend to love me. You may say I was slowly becoming ready to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure, so free of outer influence, that in the world I would surely be thwarted by the coarse elements that mix even with its best feelings. Believe me, I was then less fit for any communion with other people than before. When I left them, they tormented me, but only as pain and sickness torment: something outside the mind that hurts it, and that I wanted to cast away. But now I would have wished for sympathy; I would have tried to bind my soul to someone else’s, and so I would have prepared for myself deep drafts of disappointment and suffering; for I was as tender as the sensitive plant, nothing but nerve. I did not seek sympathy and help in ambition or wisdom, but sweet and mutual affection; smiles to cheer me and gentle words of comfort. I wanted one heart into which I could pour my complaints without restraint, and from whose heavenly nature blessed fruit might grow from such poor seed. Yet how could I find this? The love that is the soul of friendship is a gentle spirit seldom found except when two kind beings are joined from early youth, or when bound by shared suffering and pursuits; it comes to a few chosen ones unsought and unaware; it descends as gentle dew on selected spots which, however barren before, grow under its kind influence into gardens of sweet plants; but when desired it flies; it mocks the prayers of those who worship it; it will bestow itself, but will not be sought.\n\nI knew all this and did not go out to seek sympathy; yet there on my solitary heath, under my low roof with desert all around, it came to me like a sunbeam in winter that adorns while it melts the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone on ruined fruit; I did not revive under its light, for I was too utterly undone to feel its kindly power."}

{"request_id":"8855edd8ce992e7fab075964","rewritten_text":"“I wrapped him up in the paper and stuffed part of it in his mouth—that was how I did it.”

“And you think your master was actually bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him sick?”

“I don’t think anything about it—I know it. Why would he keep dreaming about the gold so much if it isn’t because he was bitten by the gold-bug? I’ve heard about those gold-bugs before now.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How do I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how I know.”

“Well, Jup, maybe you’re right; but to what good fortune do I owe the honor of a visit from you today?”

“What’s the matter, master?”

“Did you bring any message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, master, I brought this pistol;” and here Jupiter handed me a note which read as follows:

“MY DEAR —— Why haven’t I seen you for so long? I hope you haven’t been foolish enough to take offense at any small brusqueness of mine; but no, that seems unlikely. Since I saw you I’ve had great cause for anxiety. I have something to tell you, yet hardly know how to tell it, or whether I should tell it at all.

“I haven’t been quite well for some days, and poor old Jup annoys me almost beyond bearing with his well-meant attentions. Would you believe it? The other day he prepared a huge stick to chastise me for slipping away and spending the day alone among the hills on the mainland. I truly believe my sickly appearance was the only thing that spared me a whipping.

“I’ve made no additions to my collection since we met.

“If you can make it convenient, come over with Jupiter. Do come. I want to see you tonight, on business of importance. I assure you it is of the highest importance.

“Ever yours,
“WILLIAM LEGRAND.”

Something in the tone of this note filled me with unease. The whole style was markedly different from Legrand’s usual manner. What was he imagining now? What new notion had seized his excitable brain? What “business of the highest importance” could he possibly have? Jupiter’s account of him promised nothing good. I feared that the ongoing weight of misfortune had finally unsettled my friend’s mind. Without hesitation, therefore, I made ready to go with the man.

When we reached the wharf, I noticed a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat we were to take.

“What does all this mean, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"e0db27bc3c801c2f752023b0","rewritten_text":"It is peculiar, but everyone who vanishes is reported to have been seen in San Francisco. It must be a charming city and contain all the attractions of the next world.”

“What do you suppose has become of Basil?” asked Dorian, raising his Burgundy toward the light and marveling at his own composure in discussing it.

“I have not the faintest notion. If Basil chooses to hide, it is no concern of mine. If he is dead, I prefer not to think about him. Death is the sole thing that ever frightens me. I loathe it.”

“Why?” murmured the younger man, tiredly.

“Because,” replied Lord Henry, drawing beneath his nose the gilt lattice of an open vinaigrette, “one can endure everything nowadays save that. Death and vulgarity are the only two realities in the nineteenth century that cannot be explained away. Let us take our coffee in the music-room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran off with played Chopin divinely. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house feels rather desolate without her. Naturally, marriage is only a habit, a bad one. Still, one regrets the loss even of one’s most wretched habits. Perhaps one regrets them most of all. They are so integral to one’s personality.”

Dorian remained silent, but left the table, moved into the adjoining room, sat at the piano, and let his fingers wander over the black and white ivory of the keys. When the coffee had been brought, he paused, and glancing at Lord Henry, said, “Harry, did it ever cross your mind that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was popular and always wore a Waterbury watch. Why should anyone murder him? He was not brilliant enough to make enemies. Of course, he had extraordinary talent for painting. But a man may paint like Velasquez and still be perfectly dull. Basil was decidedly dull. He interested me only once, and that was when he confessed, years ago, that he idolized you and that you were the governing motive of his art.”

“I was deeply attached to Basil,” said Dorian with a sad note in his voice. “But don’t people claim he was murdered?”

“Oh, certain papers do. It strikes me as highly improbable. I know there are terrible quarters in Paris, but Basil was not the type to frequent them. He lacked curiosity. It was his principal failing.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you that I had murdered Basil?” asked the younger man."}

{"request_id":"6b70f9fb4848841b4d5adb0f","rewritten_text":"He was dressed for the role of “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” one of his most famous disguises and the very cause of the Cantervilles’ quarrel with their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and as far as he could tell, everyone was asleep. He was heading toward the library to see whether any trace of the bloodstain remained when two figures suddenly sprang out of a dark corner, waved their arms wildly over their heads, and shouted “BOO!” in his ear.

Panic seized him, understandable enough under the circumstances, and he ran for the staircase, only to find Washington Otis waiting there with the big garden syringe. Trapped on all sides by his enemies and driven almost to desperation, he fled into the great iron stove, which luckily was unlit, and had to crawl home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his room filthy, disordered, and in despair.

After that night he made no more attempts at nocturnal outings. The twins set ambushes for him several times and scattered nutshells all over the hallways every night, to the great irritation of their parents and the servants, but it was useless. It was clear his feelings were so hurt that he would not show himself. Mr. Otis went back to his massive history of the Democratic Party, a project he had been working on for years; Mrs. Otis organized a spectacular clam-bake that astonished the whole county; the boys devoted themselves to lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American games; and Virginia rode through the lanes on her pony with the young Duke of Cheshire, who was spending the last week of his holiday at Canterville Chase. Everyone assumed the ghost had left, and indeed Mr. Otis wrote to Lord Canterville saying so. Lord Canterville replied with great pleasure at the news and sent his congratulations to the Minister’s excellent wife.

But the Otises were mistaken. The ghost was still in the house, though now nearly a wreck, and he had no intention of giving up, especially after learning that the young Duke of Cheshire was among the guests. The Duke’s great-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered Colonel Carbury a hundred guineas that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost, and he was found the next morning on the card-room floor, paralyzed so completely that, though he lived to an old age, he could never say anything again but “Double Sixes.”"}

{"request_id":"74bf6ef5b601b9d4da6b7d04","rewritten_text":"His story went thus: traveling from home and passing through Datchet, he was startled to see smoke curling from the inn’s chimney. Supposing he might find fellow travelers gathered there, he knocked and was let in. He discovered no one inside but Lucy and her mother; the latter, disabled by rheumatism, had lost the use of her limbs, and so, one after another, every remaining inhabitant had departed, leaving the two alone. Lucy begged him to stay; within a week or two her mother would improve, and they could then set forth, but they would surely die if abandoned helpless and desolate. The man replied that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, so in his view it was impossible to remain. As a desperate measure, Lucy entrusted him with a letter for Idris, to be delivered wherever he should meet us. This duty at least he performed, and Idris, moved, received the following letter:—

“HONOURED LADY,

“I know you will remember me and take pity, and I dare hope you will help me; what other hope exists? Forgive my manner of writing; I am utterly bewildered. A month ago my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already improving, and in another month I am sure she could travel, in the way you kindly promised to arrange. But now everyone is gone—everyone. As they departed, each said perhaps my mother would recover before we were entirely deserted. Three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who, because of his newborn child, remained behind till the end; the family being large, I thought I might persuade them to wait a little longer for us. Instead I found their house empty. Since then I have not seen a single soul until this good man arrived. What will become of us? My mother does not know our condition; she is so sick that I have concealed it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? We must surely perish miserably as we are. Were I to attempt to move my mother now, she would die on the road; and even if, once she improves, I could somehow learn the roads and travel so many miles to the sea, you would all be in France, and the vast ocean would separate us—a terror even to sailors.”"}

{"request_id":"c041b89e11f6aa0ba77b6d77","rewritten_text":"Her situation was truly one of uncommon trial and difficulty. Though she was consumed with eager determination to uncover the mystery surrounding Oliver’s past, she knew she had to honor the trust placed in her by the wretched woman she had just spoken with, as the young and innocent girl that she was. The woman’s words and manner had touched Rose Maylie deeply; alongside her love for her young charge, and nearly as intense in its devotion, burned her tender hope of guiding the outcast back toward repentance and hope.

They planned to remain in London only three days before leaving for several weeks on a distant stretch of coast. Midnight of the first day had come. What plan could she devise that could be carried out within forty-eight hours? And how could she delay the journey without rousing suspicion?

Mr. Losberne was with them and would remain for the next two days; but Rose knew the excellent gentleman’s impetuosity too well and could too clearly envision the fury with which he would, in the first burst of anger, condemn the young woman responsible for Oliver’s capture. She could not confide in him when there was no experienced voice to back her plea for the girl. All this demanded extreme caution and careful behavior when telling Mrs. Maylie, whose first instinct would surely be to consult the good doctor. As for turning to any legal adviser, even if she had known where to begin, it was scarcely conceivable for the same reason. She briefly thought of seeking help from Harry, but this immediately brought back the memory of their last parting, and she felt it unworthy to summon him when—tears rising as she followed the thought—he might by now have learned to forget her and found greater happiness away.

Torn by these conflicting reflections, leaning now toward one course and then another, and shrinking back from all of them as each new consideration rose before her, Rose passed a sleepless, anxious night. After further wrestling with herself the next day, she reached the desperate decision to consult Harry.

“If it pains him to come back here,” she thought, “how much it will pain me! Yet perhaps he won’t come; he may write, or he may come and carefully avoid meeting me—he did when he left. I hardly believed he would, but it was better for us both.” With that, Rose set down the pen and turned away, unwilling even to let the paper that would carry her message witness her tears."}

Quite a surprise to me! I had no idea! Jane took Mrs. Elton aside and told her immediately that, after thinking over the advantages of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had decided to accept it. I did not know a thing until it was finished. 

“You spent the evening with Mrs. Elton?” 

“Yes, all of us; Mrs. Elton insisted we come. The plan was made on the hill while we were walking with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend your evening with us,’ she said—‘I absolutely must have you all come.’” 

“Mr. Knightley was there too, was he?” 

“No, not Mr. Knightley; he refused from the start; and though I thought he would come, since Mrs. Elton said she would not let him off, he did not. But my mother, Jane, and I were all there, and we had a very pleasant evening. Such kind friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, are always pleasant, though everyone seemed rather tired after the morning party. Even pleasure is tiring—and I cannot say any of them seemed to have enjoyed it much. However, I will always think it a very pleasant gathering, and feel very grateful to the kind friends who included me.” 

“Miss Fairfax, I suppose, though you did not notice, had been making up her mind all day?” 

“I dare say she had.” 

“Whenever it happens, it must be unwelcome to her and to every friend—but I hope her position will have every comfort possible—I mean, in the character and manners of the family.” 

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Yes, indeed, everything that could make her happy is there. Except the Sucklings and Bragges, there is not another nursery in Mrs. Elton’s circle so generous and elegant. Mrs. Smallridge is the most delightful woman! Her style of living almost equals Maple Grove—and as for the children, except for the little Sucklings and Bragges, there are no sweeter, more elegant children anywhere. Jane will be treated with such respect and kindness! It will be nothing but pleasure, a life of pleasure. And her salary! I really cannot even bring myself to tell you the amount, Miss Woodhouse.”"}

{"request_id":"8770f155e85b531d687e7d2b","rewritten_text":"I passed several funeral processions; few mourners joined them, and the onlookers treated them as omens of disaster. Some watched with fierce eagerness, others ran off in fear, and a few cried aloud. 

After helping those who were already ill, Adrian had focused on hiding the plague’s symptoms and spread from London’s people. He knew that fear and dark expectations fed disease, that hopelessness and constant worry made bodies more open to infection. So no disturbing sights were allowed: shops mostly stayed open, and there were still some people in the streets. Even so, since I had not seen the city since the plague began, London looked changed enough to me. No carriages rolled by, grass grew tall between the paving stones, the houses seemed abandoned, and most shutters were closed. Everyone I passed wore a ghastly, frightened look, nothing like the usual brisk manner of Londoners. My lone carriage drew stares as it clattered toward the Protectoral Palace, and the fashionable streets around it were even bleaker and emptier. 

Adrian’s antechamber was crowded when I arrived; it was his scheduled hour for audiences. Not wishing to interrupt him, I waited and watched people come and go. They were merchants and tradespeople, their income gone with the halt of commerce and the pause in Britain’s usual money-making bustle. A new arrival often showed anxiety or outright terror, yet those who left after being heard looked calm, even content. I could see my friend’s influence in their quicker steps and brighter faces. When the clock struck two, no one else was admitted; the disappointed went away sullen or sorrowful while I entered the audience chamber. 

Adrian’s improved health struck me at once. He was no longer bent like an over-tended spring flower that grows too fast for its strength and droops under its own crown of blossoms. His eyes were clear, his face composed, and a concentrated energy showed in every movement—so different from his earlier languor. He sat at a table with several secretaries who sorted petitions or recorded notes from that day’s meetings, and two or three petitioners still waited nearby. I admired his fairness and patience. Anyone who could afford to live outside London he advised to leave at once, and he gave them the means to do so."}

I instructed my wife to sew it together as quickly as she could and provided her with all the detailed directions she would need. Meanwhile, I fashioned the twine into netting of proper extent, fitted it with a hoop and the required cords, and purchased a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, a common barometer with certain important alterations, and two astronomical instruments seldom seen. The outermost edges—the parts of the drawing nearest the margin of the vellum—stood out far more clearly than the rest. It was evident the heat had acted imperfectly or unevenly. I immediately lit a fire and exposed every inch of the parchment to a glowing warmth. At first, the sole result was the sharpening of the faint skull-lines; but by persisting, I saw appear, at the corner of the slip opposite the death’s-head, the figure I initially took for a goat. A closer look convinced me it was meant for a kid.

“Ha! ha!” I cried. “Truly, I’ve no right to laugh—a million and a half is no laughing matter—but you surely cannot forge a third link for your chain; you will find no special tie between your pirates and a goat. Pirates, you know, are no cattle-dealers.”

“I have already told you, the figure was not a goat.”

“Well then, a kid—much the same.”

“Nearly, yet not quite,” Legrand said. “You may have heard of Captain Kidd. I instantly regarded the creature as a punning or hieroglyphic signature. I use ‘signature’ because its place on the vellum implied as much. The death’s-head in the opposite corner wore the appearance of a stamp or seal. Still, I was vexed by the lack of all else—no body to my supposed instrument—no text to accompany my context.”

“I suppose you expected a letter between stamp and signature.”

“Something of that nature. The truth is, I felt an irresistible presentiment of great fortune at hand. I hardly know why. Perhaps it was more yearning than belief; yet Jupiter’s foolish talk about the bug being pure gold strangely fired my imagination. And then all those accidents and coincidences—so singular! Notice how purely accidental it was that every event happened on the only day in the year cool enough for a fire; and without the fire—or the dog’s timely intrusion—I should never have discovered the death’s-head, and thus never become master of the treasure.”"}

{"request_id":"513c51c05a7607f8c71d06d5","rewritten_text":"While events unfolded at the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the same old den from which the girl had taken Oliver, brooding over a dull, smoky fire. He rested a pair of bellows on his knee, as if he had been trying to coax the flames into livelier action. But he had sunk into deep thought; his arms folded over the bellows, his chin on his thumbs, his gaze fixed absently on the rusty bars.

Behind him, the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling sat at a table, intent on a game of whist. The Dodger played dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The sharp face of the Dodger, intelligent even in idleness, seemed even keener as he studied the game and carefully read Mr. Chitling’s hand. From time to time he cast intent glances, adjusting his own play according to what he saw in his neighbor’s cards. The night was cold, and the Dodger wore his hat indoors, as he often did. He clenched a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he needed a sip from the quart pot on the table, filled with gin-and-water for the group.

Master Bates watched the play closely, but being more excitable than his polished friend, he reached for the gin-and-water more often. He also tossed out jokes and stray remarks, all quite improper during a serious rubber. The Dodger, relying on their close friendship, took the liberty of scolding him more than once for these slip-ups. Master Bates took the lectures in good humor, merely telling his friend to be “blowed,” to stick his head in a sack, or responding with some equally tidy joke that won praise from Mr. Chitling. It was noteworthy that Mr. Chitling and his partner always lost, yet this never angered Master Bates. Instead it delighted him. At the close of every deal he roared with laughter, insisting he had never seen such a merry game in all his life.

“That makes two doubles and the rub,” Mr. Chitling said, face drawn, as he pulled a half-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw a fellow like you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

{"request_id":"88b29f82aad1efdd261d5a14","rewritten_text":"There was something so remarkable in the growing shine of Mr. Wopsle’s eye, and he seemed to be turning so many thoughts over and getting so confused, that I could not understand it. I kept thinking about it long after he had risen into the clouds in a large watch-case, and still I could not understand. I was still thinking about it when I left the theatre an hour later and found him waiting for me near the door.

“How are you?” I said, shaking hands with him as we headed down the street together. “I saw that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he answered. “Yes, of course I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who else?”

“It’s the strangest thing,” said Mr. Wopsle, slipping back into that dazed look. “And yet I could swear to him.”

Growing alarmed, I begged Mr. Wopsle to explain his meaning.

“Whether I would have noticed him at first if you hadn’t been there,” he said, still in that far-off way, “I can’t say for sure; but I think I would have.”

Without meaning to, I looked around me, as I often did when returning home; his mysterious words gave me a chill.

“Oh! He can’t be in sight,” said Mr. Wopsle. “He left before I went off. I saw him go.”

Because I had my reasons for being wary, I even suspected this poor actor. I feared he meant to trick me into admitting something. So I glanced at him as we walked, but kept silent.

“I had a foolish notion he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw you were entirely unaware of him, sitting behind you like a ghost.”

The chill crept over me again, yet I was set on staying quiet, for his words could easily be a plan to make me link these hints to Provis. Of course, I knew for certain Provis had not been there.

“I dare say you find me strange, Mr. Pip; indeed, I see you do. But it is so odd! You’ll hardly believe what I’m about to tell you. I could hardly believe it myself if you told me.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you remember long ago, on a certain Christmas Day, when you were a small child and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs fixed?”

“I remember it very well.”

“And you recall there was a chase after two convicts, and we joined it, and Gargery carried you on his back, and I led the way, and you kept up with me as best you could?”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"0dec973f7ed9baa973235529","rewritten_text":"We declared with such volume and conviction that we were free men that the liberty-spouting orator and his patriotic crowd grew interested. They gathered around us, taking on a very firm posture. The orator said: “If you truly are freemen, you have nothing to fear—Britain’s God-given liberties shield and protect you! (Applause.) You shall soon see. Produce your proof.” “What proof?” “Proof that you are freemen.” Ah—now I remembered! I came to my senses and said nothing. But the king burst out: “You’re mad, man. It would be better and more reasonable for this thief and scoundrel here to prove that we are not freemen.” You see, he knew his own laws the way many people do—by words, not by consequences. They take on real meaning and become vivid when you apply them to yourself. Everyone shook their heads and looked disappointed; some walked off, no longer interested. The orator spoke again, this time in a businesslike tone instead of sentiment: “If you do not know your country’s laws, it is time you learned them. You are strangers to us; you won’t deny that. You may be freemen; we don’t deny that; but you may also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove you are slaves—it requires you to prove you are not.” I said: “Dear sir, just give us time to send to Astolat; or give us time to send to the Valley of Holiness—” “Peace, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and you cannot hope to have them granted. It would take much time and inconvenience your master unjustifiably—” “Master, you idiot!” the king raged. “I have no master, I myself am the k—” “Silence, for God’s sake!” I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in trouble enough; it would only make things worse to let these people think we were lunatics. There’s no point in dragging out the details. The earl put us up for sale and auctioned us off. This same infernal law had existed in our own South in my era over thirteen hundred years later, and under it hundreds of freemen who couldn’t prove their status had been sold into lifelong slavery without it making any particular impression on me—but the moment the law and the auction block entered my personal experience, something that had merely seemed improper suddenly became hellish. That’s just how we are built. Yes, we were sold at auction, like pigs. In a large town with an active market we might have fetched a good price, but this place was utterly stagnant, so we sold for a sum that makes me feel ashamed every time I think of it."}

{"request_id":"e2fec8a6ddcde466854baad0","rewritten_text":"The studio was filled with the rich scent of roses, and when the light summer wind moved through the garden trees, it carried in through the open door the heavy smell of lilac or the lighter perfume of pink-flowering thorn.

From the corner of the divan made of Persian saddle-bags where he lay smoking endless cigarettes, as he always did, Lord Henry Wotton could just see the glow of the honey-sweet, golden blossoms of a laburnum, whose shaking branches seemed barely strong enough to support such fiery beauty. Every so often the fanciful shadows of birds in flight flickered across the long tussore-silk curtains stretched before the wide window, creating a brief Japanese effect and making him think of those pale, jade-faced painters of Tokyo who, through an art that must remain still, try to suggest speed and motion. The low buzzing of bees forcing their way through the tall unmown grass, or circling insistently around the dusty gilt horns of the wild woodbine, only seemed to make the silence heavier. The faint roar of London sounded like the deep drone of a distant organ.

In the center of the room, secured to an upright easel, stood a full-length portrait of a young man of extraordinary beauty, and in front of it, a little distance away, sat the artist himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance some years before had caused so much public excitement and so many strange rumors.

As the painter studied the graceful, handsome figure he had captured so well, a pleased smile passed over his face and seemed about to remain. But he suddenly jumped up and, closing his eyes, pressed his fingers to his eyelids as if he were trying to lock inside his mind some strange dream from which he dreaded waking.

“It is your best work, Basil, the best thing you have ever done,” said Lord Henry lazily. “You must absolutely send it next year to the Grosvenor. The Academy is too large and too vulgar. Whenever I have gone there, there have been either so many people that I could not see the pictures, which was dreadful, or so many pictures that I could not see the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is really the only place.”

“I don’t think I will send it anywhere,” Basil replied, throwing his head back in that odd way that used to make his friends laugh at him at Oxford."}

{"request_id":"1e7e1d5850866406a9dd3d5a","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a very respectable-looking old gentleman and a good-looking younger one whose right arm was in a sling. And, my goodness, how the crowd hollered and laughed and wouldn’t stop. I couldn’t see the joke in it, and figured the duke and king couldn’t either. I expected them to turn pale. But no, not even a hint of pale. The duke never let on he knew anything was wrong; he just wandered around smiling and contented, like a jug gently bubbling over with buttermilk. And the king stared down mournfully at the newcomers, as if it hurt his heart to think there were such frauds and scoundrels in this world. He played it perfectly. Many of the leading people gathered around the king to show they were on his side. The old gentleman who had just arrived looked baffled out of his wits. Soon he began to speak, and I saw right away he sounded like an Englishman—not exactly like the king, though the king’s imitation was pretty good. I can’t give his exact words or imitate his way of talking, but he turned to the crowd and said something like this:

“This is a surprise I wasn’t expecting. I’ll admit, plain and honest, I’m not in the best shape to handle it. My brother and I have had bad luck: he broke his arm, and our luggage was mistakenly taken off at a town upriver last night. I am Peter Wilks’s brother Harvey, and this is his brother William, who can’t hear or speak, and now can’t even make useful signs since he only has one hand to do it with. We are who we say we are, and in a day or two, when I get our baggage, I can prove it. But until then I’ll say nothing more and head to the hotel to wait.”

So he and the new dummy left. The king laughed and blustered:

“Broke his arm—very likely, isn’t it?—and so convenient for a fraud who has to make signs and doesn’t know how. Lost their baggage! That’s really good—and mighty clever under the circumstances!”

He laughed again, and so did everyone else except maybe three or four people, or maybe half a dozen. One was that doctor. Another was a sharp-looking gentleman with an old-style carpetbag made of carpet material, who had just come off the steamboat and was whispering with the doctor while glancing over at the king and nodding. That was Levi Bell, the lawyer who had gone up to Louisville. Another was a big rough fellow who had come up, listened to all the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

{"request_id":"dd92adb6030ea9854247a2e5","rewritten_text":"His character and temperament, though different from hers, would have satisfied all her hopes. Their marriage would have benefited them both: her ease and liveliness could have softened his mind and refined his manners, while his judgment, experience, and knowledge of the world would have offered her far greater advantages.

But no such happy marriage would now show the admiring public what true marital happiness looked like. Another engagement, very different and preventing the first, was about to take place in their family.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would be supported in even modest independence. Yet she could easily imagine how little lasting happiness awaited a couple brought together only because their passion outweighed their virtue.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. In reply to Mr. Bennet’s thanks, he briefly assured him of his eagerness to promote the welfare of any member of the family, and ended by begging that the subject never be mentioned to him again. The main purpose of his letter was to tell them that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

“It has long been my wish that he should do so,” he added, “as soon as his marriage was settled. And I think you will agree that removing him from that corps is highly advisable for both himself and my niece. Mr. Wickham intends to enter the Regulars; among his old friends, there are still some willing and able to help him in the army. He has been promised an ensigncy in General ----’s regiment, now stationed in the north. It is good that it lies so far from this part of the country. He makes fair promises; and I hope that among different company, where each will have a reputation to maintain, they will both behave more prudently. I have written to Colonel Forster to inform him of our plans and to ask him to reassure Mr. Wickham’s various creditors in and near Brighton with promises of quick payment, for which I have pledged myself. Will you take the trouble to offer the same assurances to his creditors in Meryton? I will include a list, based on his information. He has listed all his debts; I hope at least he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything should be settled in a week. They will then join his regiment unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and Mrs. Gardiner tells me my niece very much wishes to see you all before she leaves the south.”"}

{"request_id":"7a66cce410df3f0fb3b4abd2","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said, when we stood at the tree’s base, “come here! Was that skull tacked to the branch with the face outward, or turned inward against the wood?”

“De face turned out, massa, so de crows could peck de eyes easy, widout no bother.”

“Very well—was it this eye or that one through which you dropped the beetle?” Legrand tapped each of Jupiter’s eyes in turn.

“Dis one, massa—the left eye—jis same as you telled me,” he answered, pointing, however, to his right eye.

“That suffices—we’ll try once more.”

Now my friend, in whose madness I fancied I detected a certain method, shifted the peg that marked the beetle’s fall to a position about three inches west of where it had been. As before, he measured from the trunk to this peg and then prolonged the line straight out to fifty feet, which brought us to a spot several yards away from the site of our previous digging.

Around this new point he traced a circle, somewhat broader than the earlier one, and we set to with our spades again. I was desperately tired, yet, scarcely aware what had transformed my mood, I no longer felt such distaste for the toil he demanded. Indeed, I had grown inexplicably absorbed—nay, even animated. Perhaps there was something in Legrand’s wild behavior—an air of planning, of cool calculation—that impressed me. I dug zealously, and once or twice I caught myself actually peering, with something strikingly like anticipation, for the imaginary treasure whose image had crazed my poor companion. When these wandering thoughts held me most strongly, and after we had labored perhaps an hour and a half, the dog again broke out in fierce howls. His earlier agitation had been, clearly, mere play or whim; now he sounded fierce and earnest. When Jupiter tried once more to muzzle him, the animal fought savagely, sprang into the pit, and raked away the soil in a frenzy. Within moments he had laid bare a heap of human bones—two complete skeletons tangled together—mixed with several metal buttons, and what seemed the powdery remains of rotted woollen cloth. A couple of strokes of a spade brought up the blade of a large Spanish knife, and, as we dug deeper, three or four loose coins of gold and silver came into view."}

{"request_id":"b190b05d8c61119f0170713b","rewritten_text":"I longed to feign my death; my satisfied heirs would lay claim to my fortune, and I should buy my liberty. Yet the stratagem must be artfully wrought; I could not be left penniless, some funds must be secured. Alas, to what vile expedients must I stoop? Still, an entire existence steeped in falsehood was otherwise my lot: and whenever shame at plotting any deceit made me recoil from my intention, some aunt or cousin would come, and their visit irresistibly drew me back and fixed me in my scheme. They would remind me that death is every person’s destiny; then insist my father had surely lost his senses since my mother died, that he was deranged and that I was fortunate—for in one frenzy he might have slain me instead of ending his own wild life. All this, of course, was gently expressed; not bluntly, lest my feelings suffer, but

murmured thus and thus, in cautious hints soft and low,

with lowered lashes and sympathetic smiles or whimpers; and I listened with a composed face though every nerve quivered; I who dared not murmur yea or nay to such profanity. Oh, what a delectable life, entirely without guile! I with my dove’s visage and fox’s heart: for in truth I felt only the abasement of lying, without any sacred sense of conscious innocence to redeem it. I, who had formerly been clothed in the radiant robe of sincerity, must now borrow a coat of many colours: it would seem ill-fitted at first, but habit would teach me to drape it in graceful folds, to practice deception with elegance. Aye, I might dye my spirit with falsehood until its native hue was wholly concealed. Oh, beloved father! Receive the pure heart of your wretched daughter; allow me to join you as stainless as I once was, else you will fail to know my altered form. As sorrow might transform Constance, so would deceit transform me until in heaven you would exclaim, “This is not my child”—My father, to be happy now and when we meet again I must flee from this entire existence, which is mockery to one such as I. Only in solitude shall I remain myself; in solitude I shall remain yours.

Alas! Even now I look back with loathing on my devices and contrivances by which, after many painful struggles, I secured my escape. I might detail, at great length, the methods I employed—first to obtain a modest support for the rest of my years, and next to assure the belief of my demise: I might, but I refuse."}

{"request_id":"a9b5c3cff607de63f72e92d2","rewritten_text":"“There wasn’t any tender nurturing by hand back then. Not at all!”

Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to accept.

“He was no end of trouble to you, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble in sympathy with my sister.

“Trouble?” my sister repeated. “Trouble?” Then she launched into a terrifying list of every illness I had caused, every night I had kept her awake, every high place I had fallen from, every low place I had fallen into, every injury I had inflicted on myself, and all the times she had wished me dead and I had stubbornly refused to oblige her.

I think the Romans must have driven each other crazy with their noses. Maybe that’s why they were so restless. Whatever the reason, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose aggravated me so much during the recounting of my offenses that I wanted to yank it until he yelped. Still, everything I had suffered so far was nothing compared to the horror that seized me when the silence after my sister’s tirade finally broke, during which everyone, as I painfully knew, had been looking at me with disgust and outrage.

“Still,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently steering the conversation back to its original topic, “pork—boiled—is rich, isn’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, Uncle,” said my sister.

Oh heavens, the moment had arrived! He would find it weak, call it weak, and I would be undone. I clutched the table leg under the cloth with both hands and waited for the verdict.

My sister fetched the stone bottle, came back with it, and poured his brandy: no one else had any. The wretched man toyed with his glass—picked it up, held it to the light, set it down—stretching out my agony. Meanwhile Mrs. Joe and Joe were busily clearing the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the miserable creature play with his glass, pick it up, smile, throw his head back, and drain the brandy. Immediately afterward, everyone was struck with unspeakable panic as he leaped to his feet, spun around several times in a horrifying coughing fit like a mad dance, and bolted outside; then we saw him through the window, violently spitting and making the ugliest faces, clearly out of his senses.

I kept holding on while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran after him."}

{"request_id":"3ae877afe4026916ba8cb137","rewritten_text":"Their arrival kindled a sort of blaze in Saint Antoine’s bosom, spreading swiftly as they passed, flickering in fiery faces at most doorways and windows. Still, none trailed behind them, and no man spoke when they stepped into the wine-shop, though every eye there fixed on them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

If it was a cue to loosen tongues, it worked, bringing forth an echoed “Good day!”

“The weather is poor, gentlemen,” Defarge added, shaking his head.

At that, each man glanced at his neighbour, then every gaze dropped and they sat mute. Only one man rose and departed.

“My wife,” Defarge called aloud to Madame Defarge, “I have travelled certain leagues with this worthy mender of roads, named Jacques. I met him—by chance—one day and a half from Paris. He is a fine fellow, this mender of roads named Jacques. Give him beverage, my wife!”

Another man stood and left. Madame Defarge placed wine before the road-mender called Jacques, who lifted his blue cap to the room and drank. Tucked inside his blouse he carried coarse dark bread; between sips he ate, sitting there chewing and drinking near Madame Defarge’s counter. A third man got up and went out.

Defarge refreshed himself with a swallow of wine—but he took less than was poured for the newcomer, being himself a man to whom wine was no rarity—and waited until the countryman finished his meal. He looked at no one present, and now no one regarded him; not even Madame Defarge, who had picked up her knitting and was at it.

“Have you finished your meal, friend?” he asked when it was timely.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come then! You shall see the lodging I told you you might occupy. It will fit you wonderfully.”

Out of the wine-shop into the street, from the street into a courtyard, out of the courtyard up a steep stair, off the stair into a garret—once the garret where a white-haired man sat on a low bench, bent forward and intensely busy, making shoes.

No white-haired man sat there now; yet the three men were present who had individually left the wine-shop. And between them and the distant white-haired man remained the single small link that they had once peered in at him through wall chinks.

Defarge shut the door with care and spoke in a subdued tone:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! Here stands the witness encountered by arrangement, by me, Jacques Four.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"bee351d032295486b9832ec0","rewritten_text":"Right in front of him, in the weak moonlight, he saw an old man with a terrifying look. The stranger’s eyes glowed like red coals, long gray hair hung in tangled coils over his shoulders, and his antique clothes were dirty and torn. Heavy manacles and rusty chains dangled from his wrists and ankles.  “My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains. I’ve brought you a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that purpose. It is supposed to work perfectly with one application, and the wrapper carries several testimonials from our most respected clergymen. I’ll leave it here by the bedroom candles, and I will gladly supply more if you need it.” With these words, the United States Minister set the bottle on a marble table, shut his door, and went to bed.  For a moment the Canterville ghost stood completely still, outraged. Then, hurling the bottle down on the polished floor, he fled down the corridor, moaning hollowly and shining with a ghastly green light. Just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open, two small figures in white robes appeared, and a large pillow whizzed past his head. There was clearly no time to lose, so he quickly slipped into the Fourth Dimension as his escape route, vanished through the wainscoting, and the house quieted down.  When he reached a small secret room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to grasp what had happened. Never, in his brilliant three-hundred-year career, had he been so insulted. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had frightened into a faint as she stood before her mirror in lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids who had gone into hysterics when he merely grinned at them from behind the curtains of a spare room; of the parish rector, whose candle he had blown out as the man came late one night from the library, and who had since been under Sir William Gull’s care, a true martyr to nervous disorders; and of old Madame de Tremouillac, who had woken early one morning to see a skeleton sitting in an armchair by the fire reading her diary, then spent six weeks bedridden with brain fever, only to convert to the Church and break off her connection with that notorious skeptic Monsieur de Voltaire once she recovered."}

{"request_id":"0fb3a889354a57688ee309f0","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often pondered on the old idea of the split soul and privately amused myself with imagining two Dupins—the one who invented and the one who solved.

Let no one suppose from this that I’m revealing a mystery or writing a romance. What I’ve described about the Frenchman was simply the result of an excited, perhaps even unhealthy, intelligence. But the best way to explain the nature of his remarks at such times is to offer an example.

One night we were walking down a long, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Both of us seemed deep in thought, and we hadn’t spoken for at least fifteen minutes. All at once Dupin broke out with these words:

“He’s a very small fellow, that’s true, and he’d be better suited for the Théâtre des Variétés.”

“There’s no doubt about that,” I answered automatically, not at first realizing—so engrossed was I in my own reflections—how perfectly he’d matched my thoughts. A second later I came to my senses, and my amazement was immense.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “this is beyond me. I admit I’m stunned and can hardly trust my senses. How could you possibly know I was thinking of ——?” I stopped to make absolutely sure he knew whom I had in mind.

“—— of Chantilly,” he said. “Why pause? You were telling yourself his tiny frame made him unfit for tragedy.”

That was exactly the subject of my thoughts. Chantilly was once a cobbler in the Rue St. Denis who, crazed for the stage, had taken on the role of Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy of the same name and had been publicly ridiculed for it.

“For heaven’s sake,” I cried, “tell me how—if there’s any method at all—you managed to read my mind like this.” In truth I was even more shaken than I cared to show.

“It was the fruit seller,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the mender of soles lacked the height for Xerxes and the rest of that sort.”

“The fruit seller? You astound me—I don’t know any fruit seller at all.”

“The man who ran into you when we entered the street—maybe fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that a fruit seller carrying a large basket of apples on his head had nearly knocked me over by accident as we left the Rue C—— and stepped into the street where we now stood; but how that connected to Chantilly was beyond me."}

{"request_id":"756665a26514768094c558e4","rewritten_text":"No letter of condolence had been sent to Ireland. The neglect had fallen on the offender’s own head; when poor Lady Elliot died, no letter of condolence reached Kellynch, and there was every reason to fear that the Dalrymples now viewed the relationship as ended. How to settle this anxious business properly and be accepted as cousins again was the question, and it was a question that neither Lady Russell nor Mr. Elliot, in their sensible way, considered unimportant. “Family connections are always worth preserving; good company is always worth seeking. Lady Dalrymple has taken a house in Laura Place for three months and will be living in style. She was in Bath last year, and Lady Russell heard her praised as a delightful woman. It would be very desirable to renew the connection, if it could be done without the Elliots compromising their propriety.”

Sir Walter, however, insisted on his own approach, and finally wrote a very elegant letter full of explanation, regret, and entreaty to his right honorable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr. Elliot admired the letter, but it accomplished its purpose by eliciting three scrawled lines from the Dowager Viscountess. “She was very much honored, and would be happy to make their acquaintance.” The toil of the business was over, and the rewards began. They visited at Laura Place, they possessed the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honorable Miss Carteret, displayed wherever they would be most conspicuous; and “Our cousins in Laura Place,” “Our cousin Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret,” were mentioned to everyone.

Anne was ashamed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been exceptionally agreeable, she would still have been ashamed of the excitement they inspired, but they were nothing. There was no superiority of manners, accomplishments, or understanding. Lady Dalrymple had earned the name of “a charming woman” merely because she had a smile and a polite answer for everyone. Miss Carteret, with even less to say, was so plain and awkward that she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place but for her birth.

Lady Russell admitted she had expected something better; still, “it was an acquaintance worth having.” And when Anne ventured to share her opinion of them with Mr. Elliot, he agreed they were insignificant in themselves, but maintained that, as family connections, as good company, as people who would gather good company around them, they had value. Anne smiled and said,

“My idea of good company, Mr. Elliot, is the company of clever, well-informed people who have a lot to say; that is what I call good company.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"8c6c00631ccbb5f970299638","rewritten_text":"I don't rush him out of the blue and risk bungling halfway; instead, I slip off to one side and edge in on him bit by bit, so he never dreams I'm about to clip him; then, suddenly, he's flat on his back without the faintest notion how it came about. That’s just how I went after brother Dowley. I began talking slow and easy, as though I were merely idling away the time; and the oldest soul alive couldn’t have taken the compass of where I set out and guessed where I meant to land: “Boys, there’s plenty that’s curious in law, and custom, and usage, and all that, once you come to studying it; yes, and in the course and growth of human thought and movement, too. Written laws wear out; but unwritten laws—they endure forever. Take the unwritten law of wages: it decrees they must creep upward, bit by bit, through the centuries. Mark the workings of it. We know what wages are now, here and there and elsewhere; we strike an average and call that the pay of to-day. We know what wages stood at a hundred years since, and two hundred; that’s as far back as we can get, yet it’s enough to show the law of progress, the measure and rate of the regular increase; and so, though we have no documents, we can come close to deciding what wages were three and four and five hundred years ago. Good, so far. Do we halt there? No. We quit peering backward; we swing around and apply the law to what lies ahead. Friends, I can name what people will earn at any date in the future you please, for centuries on. “What, goodman, what!” “Yes. In seven hundred years wages will have risen to six times what they are now in your parts, with farm laborers getting 3 cents a day, and mechanics 6.” “I would I might die now and live then!” broke in Smug the wheelwright, his eyes shining greedily. “And that’s not the whole of it; they’ll get their board besides—such as it is: it won’t puff them up. Two hundred and fifty years after that—now keep your ears open—a mechanic’s wages will be—remember, we’re talking law here, not guesswork; a mechanic’s wages will be twenty cents a day!” A hushed gasp of wonder ran through them, and Dickon the mason whispered, eyes and hands uplifted:"}

{"request_id":"66c4f5c5dd1ec99a62406f6f","rewritten_text":"Emma never had any later reason to revise her low opinion of Mrs. Elton; her first impression was all too accurate. However Mrs. Elton struck her on their second meeting was exactly how she appeared at every meeting afterward—full of self-importance, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and ill-mannered. She had a little beauty and a few accomplishments, yet so little judgment that she believed she arrived armed with superior worldly knowledge to enliven and improve a country neighborhood, convinced that Miss Hawkins had held a social standing only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could surpass.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton saw her any differently. He seemed not only happy with her but proud, wearing the look of a man congratulating himself on having brought to Highbury a woman even Miss Woodhouse could not rival. Most of Mrs. Elton’s new acquaintances, inclined to praise or unused to judging, followed Miss Bates’s good humor or simply assumed the bride must be as clever and agreeable as she claimed. Thus compliments on Mrs. Elton passed from person to person as they naturally would, unhindered by Miss Woodhouse, who cheerfully continued her initial contribution by speaking pleasantly of Mrs. Elton’s being “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect Mrs. Elton became even worse than she seemed at first: her feelings toward Emma shifted. Probably offended by how little Emma encouraged her offers of friendship, she pulled back and gradually grew much colder and more distant. Although Emma welcomed the cooler behavior, the malice causing it only increased her dislike. Mrs. Elton’s manners toward Harriet—and Mr. Elton’s as well—were equally disagreeable: sneering and dismissive. Emma hoped such treatment would quickly cure Harriet’s attachment, yet the feelings that fueled it lowered the Eltons considerably in her eyes. Clearly, Harriet’s affection had been offered up to marital confidences, and Emma’s own part in the story, painted in the harshest colors for her and the most flattering for him, had likely been shared as well. Naturally, Harriet became the object of their shared resentment. Whenever conversation lagged, it must have been effortless to fall into criticizing Miss Woodhouse; and the hostility they dared not show Emma through open disrespect found freer expression in the contemptuous way they treated Harriet.

Mrs. Elton instantly developed a strong interest in Jane Fairfax—right from the start. It was not merely that a quarrel with one young woman made the other more appealing; from the very beginning she indulged in excessive admiration, and without invitation or justification insisted she was there to help and protect Jane. Before Emma had lost her confidence and on about their third meeting, she heard the full extent of Mrs. Elton’s self-appointed knight-errantry on the subject."}

{"request_id":"6a74c7349590361f9beca7c4","rewritten_text":"After supper the whole gang trooped out to the bar to go turtle-egg hunting. They prodded the sand with sticks, and whenever the ground felt loose they dropped to their knees and dug with their hands. Often a single pit yielded fifty or sixty eggs. They were flawless white globes, just a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they devoured a celebrated fried-egg supper, and repeated the feast on Friday morning.

Once breakfast was over, they charged out whooping across the bar, chasing one another round and round and shedding their clothes as they ran until they were bare. Then they carried on their romp far up the shallow bar against the strong current, which every so often swept their legs out from under them and made the game all the more amusing. Now and again they huddled together and slapped water into each other’s faces with their palms, edging closer with turned faces to dodge the choking spray, until they grappled and wrestled, the victor ducking his mate, and the whole knot went under in a whirl of pale arms and legs, rising again all at once, puffing, spluttering, laughing, and gasping for air.

When fatigue set in, they dashed ashore, sprawled on the dry blazing sand, and buried themselves in it, only to bolt back into the river and repeat the first act over again. At last it dawned on them that their bare hides imitated flesh-colored “tights” well enough, so they traced a ring in the sand and staged a circus—with three clowns in the ring, since none would resign that finest rank to another.

Afterward they produced their marbles and played “knucks,” “ringtaw,” and “keeps” until the sport went dull. Joe and Huck plunged in for another dip, but Tom kept out, having discovered that when he kicked off his trousers he had flung his string of rattlesnake rattles from his ankle, and he marveled that he had eluded cramp so long without that mystic amulet. He held back until he found it, and by then the other boys were weary and wanted a rest. Bit by bit they drifted apart, slipped into the “dumps,” and stared wistfully across the broad river toward the village napping in the sun. Tom caught himself tracing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe; he scratched it away and scolded himself for his frailty. Yet he wrote it anew despite himself; he could not resist. He rubbed it out once more and saved himself by herding the other boys together and joining their company."}
