{"request_id":"8b59c5f23fb5c552b0142d84","rewritten_text":"“Starve you to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my case. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you, I never eat anything now; but it is very kind of you, all the same, and you are far nicer than the rest of your dreadful, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” cried Virginia, stamping her foot. “It is you who are rude and vulgar and dreadful, and as for dishonesty, you know you stole the paints from my box to touch up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, including the vermilion, so I couldn’t finish any sunsets. Then you took the emerald-green and the chrome-yellow, and finally I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white, so I could only paint moonlight scenes, which are always depressing to look at and very hard to paint. I never told on you, though I was extremely annoyed, and the whole thing was absurd; who ever heard of emerald-green blood?”

“Well, really,” said the Ghost rather meekly, “what else could I do? It is very difficult to get real blood nowadays, and since your brother started it all with his Paragon Detergent, I certainly saw no reason why I shouldn’t take your paints. As for color, that is always a matter of taste: the Cantervilles have blue blood, for example, the very bluest in England; but I know you Americans don’t care about such details.”

“You know nothing about it, and the best thing you can do is emigrate and improve your mind. My father will be delighted to give you a free passage, and though there is a heavy duty on spirits of every kind, there will be no trouble at the Custom House, as the officers are all Democrats. Once in New York, you are sure to be a great success. I know lots of people there who would give a hundred thousand dollars to have a grandfather, and much more to have a family ghost.”

“I don’t think I should like America.”

“I suppose because we have no ruins and no curiosities,” said Virginia sarcastically.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” answered the Ghost. “You have your navy and your manners.”

“Good evening; I’ll go ask Papa to get the twins an extra week’s holiday.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I am so lonely and unhappy, and I truly don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep and I cannot.”

“That’s quite absurd! You only have to go to bed and blow out the candle.”"}

{"request_id":"11a9b5915a998ce162152dc6","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue vault of heaven, and by the fire of love consuming my heart, that if you grant my prayer, so long as they live you shall never look upon me again. Return home and begin your labours; I shall watch their progress with unspeakable anxiety; be assured that when you are prepared I will appear.”

With these words he abruptly left me, fearing, perhaps, any change in my resolve. I watched him descend the mountain swifter than an eagle’s flight, until he vanished among the ridges of the frozen sea.

His story had filled the entire day, and the sun hung on the edge of the horizon when he departed. I knew I ought to hurry down into the valley, lest darkness should enclose me, yet my heart felt heavy and my pace lagged. The toil of threading the narrow paths and planting my feet firmly as I went bewildered me, absorbed as I was in the emotions born of that day’s events. Night was well advanced when I reached the midway resting place and sat beside the fountain. The stars shone fitfully as clouds swept past them; dark pines rose before me, and here and there a shattered tree lay upon the earth; the scene held a solemn grandeur that stirred strange reflections. I wept bitterly, and clasping my hands in torment, cried, “O stars and clouds and winds, you are all poised to mock me; if you truly pity me, crush sensation and memory: let me be nothing; but if you refuse, depart, depart, and leave me in darkness.”

Wild and wretched thoughts indeed, yet I cannot describe how the unending twinkle of the stars oppressed me, nor how I bent my ear to each gust of wind as though it were some dull, hideous siroc sweeping to devour me.

Dawn broke before I reached the village of Chamounix; without rest I turned directly back to Geneva. Even within my own heart I could not give voice to my sensations—they burdened me like a mountain and their sheer weight smothered my agony. Thus I returned home and, entering the house, presented myself to my family. My gaunt and disordered aspect provoked great alarm, yet I answered no question, scarcely spoke at all. I felt as if I were under a curse—no longer entitled to their sympathy—as though I might never again take part in their fellowship."}

content.text: {"request_id":"14ebdab48afb43c9cce1134f","rewritten_text":"Once, though, the lieutenant inquired why he had ventured so far over the ice in such an unusual conveyance. His face immediately darkened with profound melancholy, and he answered, “To find one who escaped from me.” “And did the man you pursued travel in the same way?” “He did.” “Then likely we have seen him, for the day before we took you aboard we witnessed a span of dogs pulling a sledge, with a man inside, crossing the ice.” This stirred the stranger’s attention, and he asked numerous questions about the path the dæmon, as he named him, had taken. Shortly afterward, when he and I were alone, he said, “I have no doubt roused your curiosity, along with that of these good people; but you are too considerate to press me with questions.” “Certainly; it would indeed be most impertinent and unkind for me to trouble you with any curiosity of mine.” “And yet you saved me from a situation both strange and perilous; you compassionately restored me to life.” Soon after, he asked whether I believed the breaking of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I responded that I could not say with any certainty, for the ice did not give way until near midnight, and the traveller might have reached a safe place before then; but I had no means to judge. From that moment, a fresh vigor animated the stranger’s waning frame. He displayed fierce eagerness to stand upon the deck to look out for the sledge that had appeared before; but I have convinced him to stay in the cabin, for he is far too frail to brave the raw air. I have promised that someone will keep watch on his behalf and notify him at once should any new sight come into view. Such is my journal regarding this singular episode up to the present day. The stranger has slowly recovered his strength yet remains very quiet and seems uncomfortable when anyone besides myself enters his cabin. Nevertheless, his manners are so winning and gentle that the sailors all take an interest in him, even though they have had minimal dealings together. For my own part, I begin to love him like a brother, and his persistent, profound sorrow moves me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble being in happier times, since even in ruin he remains so engaging and amiable. I told you once in a letter, dear Margaret, that I expected no friend upon the open sea; yet I have found a man whom, before grief broke his spirit, I would have been proud to call the brother of my heart."}

{"request_id":"eb3b0aaaa9e5df687e9d9c0f","rewritten_text":"To her credit, the young lady didn’t actually say she wouldn’t go; she only declared, with great emphasis and sincerity, that she’d be “blessed” if she did. It was a polite, delicate way of sidestepping the request, proving she had that natural good breeding which can’t bring itself to cause a fellow creature the sting of a blunt refusal.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned away from the young lady—who was gaily, even flamboyantly dressed in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers—to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” the Jew said gently, “what do you say?”

“That it won’t work, so there’s no point trying it, Fagin,” Nancy answered.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes demanded, looking up with a scowl.

“Exactly what I said, Bill,” the woman replied calmly.

“You’re exactly the right person for it,” Mr. Sikes argued. “Nobody around here knows anything about you.”

“And I’d like to keep it that way,” Nancy responded with the same composure. “So it’s more a no than a yes from me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” Nancy shot back.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” insisted Sikes.

And Mr. Sikes turned out to be right. Through a mix of threats, promises, and bribes, the lady in question was eventually persuaded to take on the task. She wasn’t held back by the same concerns as her charming friend; having recently moved to the Field Lane neighborhood from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she wasn’t as afraid of being recognized by her many acquaintances.

So, after tying a clean white apron over her dress and tucking her curl-papers up under a straw bonnet—both items supplied from the Jew’s endless stock—Miss Nancy made ready to head out on her mission.

“Hold on a minute, my dear,” the Jew said, pulling out a small covered basket. “Carry this in one hand. It makes you look more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key to hold in the other, Fagin,” suggested Sikes. “Looks real and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, it really does,” said the Jew, hanging a large street door key on the forefinger of Nancy’s right hand. “There—very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he added, rubbing his palms together.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy suddenly cried, bursting into tears and wringing the little basket and the door key in utter anguish. “What’s happened to him? Where have they taken him? Oh, please have mercy and tell me what’s been done with the dear boy, gentlemen—please, gentlemen, if you would, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"db931afb5fd79041cad62757","rewritten_text":"“Come on, Tom,” I said. “You could tell a guy. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, I don’t know. But he’s got to have it. All nobles do.”

That was just how he operated. If he didn’t feel like explaining something, he simply wouldn’t. You could keep at him for a week and it wouldn’t matter.

He had all that coat-of-arms stuff settled, so now he moved on to the rest of it, which was to come up with a sorrowful inscription—said Jim had to have one, same as the rest. He came up with a bunch, wrote them on a sheet of paper, and read them out loud:

1. Here a captive heart burst.

2. Here a poor prisoner, abandoned by the world and friends, wore out his sorrowful life.

3. Here a lonely heart broke, and a tired spirit went to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity.

4. Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, died a noble stranger, natural son of Louis XIV.

Tom’s voice shook as he read, and he nearly lost it. When he was finished he couldn’t decide which of them Jim should scratch on the wall, they were all so good; finally he figured he’d let him scratch every one of them. Jim said it would take him a year to scratch that much stuff onto the logs with a nail, and besides he didn’t know how to make letters; but Tom said he would draw them out for him, and all Jim had to do was follow the lines. Then pretty soon he said:

“Come to think of it, the logs won’t work; dungeons don’t have log walls. We’ve got to carve the inscriptions in a rock. We’ll bring in a rock.”

Jim said a rock was worse than the logs; it would take him such a terribly long time to carve them into stone he would never get out. But Tom said I could help him. Then he checked how Jim and I were doing with the pens. It was awful hard work, real slow, and it wouldn’t let my hands heal up from the blisters, and we were hardly making any progress at all; so Tom said:

“I know how to fix it. We need a rock for the coat of arms and the sad inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that same rock.”"}

{"request_id":"8290e26e9fb143ec5ab61389","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” finally stood arraigned. The judges wore feathered hats on the Bench, yet the coarse red cap with its tricolour cockade ruled upon other heads. Surveying Jury and raucous spectators, he could imagine the established order overturned, as though criminals were judging the innocent. The vilest rabble of the city—ever equipped with its share of base, cruel souls—governed the spectacle, voicing noisy comments, cheers, hisses, predictions, and rushes toward the verdict, unchecked. Most of the men carried arms of one kind or another; among the women some wielded knives or daggers, others ate and drank as they watched, many knitted. Among these last sat one woman with spare knitting tucked beneath her arm, working steadily. She occupied the front row beside a man Darnay had not glimpsed since reaching the Barrier, yet instantly identified as Defarge. He noticed her lean once or twice to whisper in his ear, and judged her to be his wife; still, what most struck him was that though the pair had stationed themselves as close to him as possible, they never once turned his way. They appeared to await something with stubborn resolve, fixing their attention on the Jury and nothing else. Beneath the President took his seat Doctor Manette in his customary neat attire. So far as the prisoner could discern, only he and Mr. Lorry among those unconnected with the Tribunal kept their ordinary garments, refusing the coarse Carmagnole dress.

Charles Evrémonde, styled Darnay, faced the public prosecutor’s charge as an emigrant whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree outlawing all emigrants upon pain of death. The decree’s date after his return to France mattered not. There he stood, and there stood the decree: seized within France, his head was demanded.

“Take off his head!” roared the crowd. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang for silence and asked whether the prisoner had not lived many years in England. Certainly he had.

Was he then an emigrant? How did he classify himself?

Not an emigrant, he hoped, in the spirit and meaning of the law.

Why not, the President inquired.

Because he had voluntarily given up a title and station that repelled him, and had left his country—he submitted, before the present Tribunal’s sense of the word emigrant came into use—to live by his own labour in England rather than feed upon the labour of France’s overburdened people."}

{"request_id":"aa6858adc9203722dc227704","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thanks for the information. I like to know everything about my new friends and nothing about my old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I invited myself and Mr. Gray. He’s her latest protégé.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha, Harry, to stop bothering me with her charity requests. I’m sick of them. The woman thinks I have nothing to do but write checks for her ridiculous projects.”

“All right, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, though it won’t make any difference. Philanthropic people completely lose their sense of humanity. That’s their defining trait.”

The old man grunted in approval and rang the bell for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low arcade into Burlington Street and turned toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s birth. Even though it had been told crudely, it still struck him with the suggestion of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a wild passion. A few mad weeks of happiness cut short by a vicious, treacherous crime. Months of silent agony, then a child born in pain. The mother carried off by death, the boy left to loneliness and the rule of an old, loveless man. Yes, it was an intriguing background. It framed the boy, made him more perfect, in a way. Behind every exquisite thing that exists, there’s something tragic. Worlds have to suffer so that even the humblest flower may bloom. And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, sitting across from him at the club, eyes wide and lips parted in anxious delight, the red candle shades deepening the dawning wonder of his face to a richer rose. Talking to him was like playing a fine violin. He responded to every touch and shiver of the bow. There was something terrifyingly captivating in wielding influence. Nothing else was like it. To project one’s soul into a graceful form and let it rest there for a moment; to hear one’s own ideas echoed back with all the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another as if it were a subtle liquid or strange perfume—there was real pleasure in that, perhaps the most satisfying pleasure left to us in an era so limited and vulgar, so crudely sensual in its pleasures and coarse in its aims. He was a remarkable type, this boy he had met by such a curious chance in Basil’s studio—or at least he could be shaped into a remarkable type."}

{"request_id":"d96e2b8ba33f644d419582a0","rewritten_text":"“Are you talking about Mr. Knightley?”

“Of course I am. I never imagined you’d think of anyone else—and I assumed you understood. When we discussed it, I thought it was as clear as it could be.”

“Not quite,” Emma replied, struggling to stay composed. “Everything you said seemed to point to someone else. I could almost swear you mentioned Mr. Frank Churchill by name. I know you talked about how he protected you from the gypsies.”

“Oh, Miss Woodhouse, how forgetful you are!”

“My dear Harriet, I remember exactly what I said. I told you I wasn’t surprised by your attachment; that given what he’d done for you, it was completely natural. You agreed, spoke passionately about how grateful you were, and even described what you felt when he stepped forward to save you. That’s burned into my memory.”

“Oh, dear,” Harriet cried, “now I remember what you’re referring to; but at the time I was thinking of something else entirely. It wasn’t the gypsies or Mr. Frank Churchill. No!”—with a lift of her head—“I was thinking of a far more precious moment—when Mr. Knightley came and asked me to dance after Mr. Elton refused to and no one else was available. That was the kind act, the noble generosity, the moment that made me realize how far above everyone else he was.”

“Good God!” exclaimed Emma. “This has been the most disastrous, most heartbreaking misunderstanding! What can be done now?”

“You wouldn’t have encouraged me if you’d understood? At least I can’t be worse off than I would have been if the other man had truly been the one—and now there is a chance—”

She stopped for a few seconds. Emma couldn’t speak.

“I don’t blame you, Miss Woodhouse,” she went on, “for seeing a big difference between the two, whether for me or anyone. You must think one of them is five hundred million times too good for me compared to the other. Still, I hope that if—however unlikely it may seem—but they were your own words, that stranger matches than between Mr. Frank Churchill and me had happened; so perhaps even something like this has happened before. And if I should be so extraordinarily lucky—if Mr. Knightley actually—if he doesn’t care about the disparity, I hope, dear Miss Woodhouse, that you won’t oppose it or try to create obstacles.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"8053217a0dbb68cecc2dbf5d","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke up in the morning, he couldn’t remember where he was. He sat up, rubbed his eyes, and looked around. Then he remembered. Dawn was cool and gray, and the whole forest was wrapped in a deep, peaceful stillness. Not a leaf stirred; nothing disturbed nature’s quiet meditation. Dew-beaded leaves and grass glistened. A white layer of ash covered the fire, and a thin blue thread of smoke climbed straight into the air. Joe and Huck were still asleep.\n\nFar away in the forest a bird called, and another answered. Soon the tapping of a woodpecker echoed nearby. Slowly, the dim gray morning brightened, and sounds gathered as life began to stir. Nature shaking off sleep and getting down to work unfolded before Tom’s thoughtful eyes. A tiny green worm crawled along a dewy leaf, raising most of its body to “sniff around,” then moving again—measuring, Tom said. When the worm headed toward him, he froze, hope rising and falling as the creature advanced or veered away. When it paused, body arched in midair, then settled decisively onto Tom’s leg and started exploring, his heart soared—for that meant he would get a new suit of clothes—surely a flashy pirate outfit. Then a column of ants appeared from nowhere, busy at their chores; one marched along hauling a dead spider five times its size up a tree trunk. A brown, spotted ladybug climbed to the top of a grass blade, and Tom leaned close and whispered, “Ladybug, ladybug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children are alone,” and she sprang into the air to check—which didn’t surprise him, since he already knew how easily fooled she was by tales of fires and had taken advantage of it before. A dung beetle rolled up next, straining at its ball, and Tom touched it just to see it snap its legs tight and play dead. By now the birds were in full celebration. A catbird, the northern mimic, landed in a tree over his head and poured out imitations of her neighbors in pure delight; then a sharp-voiced jay dropped down like a streak of blue flame, perched on a twig within arm’s reach, cocked its head, and stared at the strangers with burning curiosity. A gray squirrel and a bigger “fox” squirrel dashed past, sitting up now and then to study and chatter at the boys, for these wild creatures had probably never seen human beings before and didn’t quite know whether to be afraid."}

{"request_id":"82ecf0040293883244afbfaa","rewritten_text":"But it is truly remarkable that she always hears Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she will find her grandmother no deafer than she was two years ago—which is saying a lot at my mother’s age—and it really has been a full two years, you know, since she was here. We have never gone so long without seeing her before, and as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we will hardly know how to make enough fuss over her now.”

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Really! That must be a great pleasure.”

“Thank you; you are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says the same kind things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends in Highbury as they will be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell will want the carriage himself one of those days. So good of them to send her the whole way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, Friday or Saturday next. That is what she writes about. That is why she wrote outside the usual schedule, as we call it; because ordinarily we would not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, so I thought. I feared there was little chance of hearing anything about Miss Fairfax today.”

“So obliging of you! No, we would not have heard, except for this particular circumstance of her coming so soon. My mother is thrilled—she is to stay with us for at least three months. Three months, she says positively, as I am about to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is, you see, that the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon persuaded her parents to come and see her immediately. They had not planned to go until summer, but she is so eager to see them again—for until she married last October, she had never been away from them for more than a week, which must make it very strange to be in different kingdoms—I was going to say, but anyway different countries—and so she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I truly do not know which, but we shall see soon in Jane’s letter—wrote in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own to urge them to come immediately. They were going to meet them in Dublin and bring them back to their estate, Bally-craig, a beautiful place, I imagine."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ab4d8b212c67c8e17df8faa5","rewritten_text":"Once, though, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far over the ice in such a strange vehicle. The man’s expression at once sank into deepest gloom, and he answered, “To chase one who ran from me.” “And did the man you chased travel the same way?” “Yes.” “Then I think we saw him, for the day before we found you we saw dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice.” This roused the stranger, and he asked countless questions about the path the demon, as he called him, had taken. Soon after, when we were alone, he said, “I have surely stirred your curiosity, as well as that of these kind people; but you are too considerate to ask.” “Of course; it would be very rude and cruel of me to press you with questions.” “And yet you saved me from a strange and dangerous situation; you have kindly brought me back to life.” Soon after, he asked whether I thought the breaking ice had destroyed the other sledge. I replied I could not say with any certainty, since the ice did not break up until near midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety before then; but I could not judge. From then on a new energy seemed to animate the stranger’s failing body. He showed great eagerness to be on deck to watch for the sledge that had passed before; but I persuaded him to stay in the cabin, for he was far too weak to endure the raw air. I promised that someone would keep watch for him and alert him at once if any new object appeared. Such is my journal of this strange event up to now. The stranger has slowly regained health but remains very quiet and grows uneasy when anyone but me enters his cabin. Yet his manners are so agreeable and gentle that all the sailors take an interest in him, though they have spoken with him very little. For my part, I begin to love him like a brother, and his constant, deep sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble being in his better days, since even now, in ruin, he is still so appealing and kind. I once wrote to you, dear Margaret, that I would find no friend on the vast ocean; yet I have found a man who, before misery broke his spirit, I would have been proud to call the brother of my heart."}

{"request_id":"c23c012c8c7f3245f3336243","rewritten_text":"“Men marry because they are weary; women marry out of curiosity. Both end up disillusioned.”

“I doubt I shall ever marry, Harry. I am far too in love. That is one of your own little sayings, and I am putting it into practice, as I do everything you advise.”

“And who is it you adore?” Lord Henry asked after a moment.

“An actress,” Dorian Gray answered, colouring.

Lord Henry lifted his shoulders. “That is an exceedingly ordinary beginning.”

“You would never call it ordinary if you saw her, Harry.”

“What is her name?”

“Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard the name.”

“No one has. Yet the day will come when everyone will. She is a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women belong to the decorative sex. They never have anything to say, though they manage to say it delightfully. Women stand for matter triumphant over mind, just as men stand for mind prevailing over morals.”

“Harry, how can you talk like that?”

“My dear Dorian, it is simply true. I am dissecting women just now, so I should know. The subject is far less complex than I supposed. In the end, women divide into two groups, the plain and the painted. Plain women are extremely serviceable: if you want to acquire a reputation for propriety, just take them down to supper. The other women are exceptionally delightful. They fall into one error, though, painting themselves to seem youthful. Our grandmothers painted so that they might speak brilliantly. Rouge and esprit once went hand in hand. That has finished. So long as a woman can appear ten years younger than her own daughter, she feels entirely content. As for talk, there are not more than five women in London worth listening to, and two of those can’t be received in respectable circles. But tell me about this prodigy of yours. How long have you known her?”

“Ah! Harry, your opinions make me shudder.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“Not quite three weeks.”

“And where did you encounter her?”

“I shall tell you, Harry, only you must not be unkind over it. After all, none of it would have occurred if I had not met you. You infected me with a fierce craving to learn every secret of life. For days after our first meeting, something seemed to pulse through my veins. As I lounged in the park or sauntered along Piccadilly, I would look at everyone who passed me and wonder, with a crazed curiosity, what manner of existence they led. Some enthralled me. Others filled me with dread. The very air seemed laden with some exquisite poison. I longed for sensations…”"}

{"request_id":"c6bf33ed5ff816086b1a21d7","rewritten_text":"Well, three or four months slid by, and it was deep into winter now. I’d been at school almost steady and could spell and read and write a little, and knew the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five, and I don’t reckon I could ever go any further even if I lived forever. I don’t set much store by arithmetic, anyhow.

At the start I despised the school, but after a spell I found I could put up with it. When I got mighty tired I’d play hookey, and the whipping I’d catch the next day seemed to do me good and hearten me. So the longer I attended school the easier it grew. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they weren’t so sharp on me. Staying in a house and sleeping in a bed mostly weighed on me, but before the cold weather I used to slip out and sleep in the woods sometimes, and that rested me. I liked the old ways best, yet I was getting so I kind of liked the new ones a little bit. The widow said I was coming along slow but sure, and doing very satisfactory. She claimed she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning I happened to upset the saltcellar at breakfast. I reached for some as quick as I could to toss over my left shoulder and head off bad luck, but Miss Watson was ahead of me and brushed me aside. She says, “Take your hands away, Huckleberry; what a mess you’re always making!” The widow spoke a good word for me, but that wasn’t going to fend off the bad luck, I knew that well enough. I went out after breakfast feeling anxious and shaky, wondering where it would hit me and what it would be. There are ways to dodge some kinds of bad luck, but this wasn’t one of them, so I didn’t try anything, just prowled along down in the mouth and on the lookout.

I headed down to the front garden and climbed over the stile where you pass through the tall board fence. A new inch of snow lay on the ground, and I spotted somebody’s tracks. They’d come up from the quarry, lingered around the stile a while, then went on circling the garden fence. It was strange they hadn’t come in after standing around so. I couldn’t figure it. It seemed mighty peculiar. I was fixing to follow the trail, but I bent down to study the tracks first."}

{"request_id":"e1685a58580d4db1536133d4","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats; every now and then you’d see one stick his nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she had to keep things close at hand to throw at them when she was alone, or they’d never let her rest. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot, saying she was usually a good shot with it, but she’d wrenched her arm a day or two back and wasn’t sure she could throw straight now. Still, she watched for a chance, and right away she threw at a rat, missed him by a mile, and cried “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so badly. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to leave before the old man got back, but of course I didn’t show it. I took the thing, and the first rat that showed his nose I let fly, and if he’d stayed where he was he’d have been a very sick rat. She said that was first-rate and figured I’d get the next one. She fetched the lump of lead and brought back a hank of yarn she wanted help with. I held up both hands while she slipped the hank over them and went on talking about her own and her husband’s affairs. But she broke off long enough to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You’d better have the lead in your lap, ready.”

So she dropped the lump into my lap right then, and I clamped my legs over it while she kept talking. But only for a minute. Then she took off the hank, looked me straight in the face, very pleasantly, and said:

“Come on now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob?—or what is it?”

I guess I shook like a leaf and hardly knew what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay right where you are. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you either. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it, and what’s more, I’ll help you. My old man will too if you want him to. You see, you’re a runaway apprentice, that’s all. That’s nothing. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been treated badly and decided to run. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"394572b453e9146edaa2aeab","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall in Somersetshire was a man who, for his own amusement, never opened any book except the Baronetage. There he found occupation for an idle hour and comfort when troubled, there his mind was stirred to admiration and respect by studying the dwindling traces of the earliest patents, there any unpleasant feelings caused by domestic matters turned naturally into pity and contempt as he flipped through the almost endless creations of the last century, and there, if every other page failed him, he could read his own history with an interest that never faded. This was the page his favorite volume always fell open to:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park in the county of Gloucester; by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a stillborn son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

This was exactly how the paragraph had first left the printer’s hands, but Sir Walter had improved it for his own and his family’s information by adding, after Mary’s birth date, the words, “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross in the county of Somerset,” and by inserting, with great precision, the day of the month on which he lost his wife.

Afterward came the history and rise of the ancient, respectable family, in the usual terms: how it first settled in Cheshire, how it was mentioned in Dugdale, how it served as high sheriff, represented a borough in three consecutive parliaments, displayed loyal zeal, and obtained the dignity of baronet in the first year of Charles II, along with all the Marys and Elizabeths they had married. Altogether it filled two handsome duodecimo pages and ended with the arms and motto—“Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset”—with Sir Walter’s handwriting again in the finale:

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great-grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity was the beginning and the end of Sir Walter Elliot’s character: vanity about his looks and his position. He had been remarkably handsome in his youth, and at fifty-four he was still a very fine man. Few women thought more about their own appearance than he did, and the valet of any newly made lord could not be more pleased with his social standing. He considered the blessing of beauty second only to the blessing of a baronetcy, and the Sir Walter Elliot who possessed both gifts was constantly the object of his warmest respect and devotion.

His good looks and his rank did have one honest claim on his affection, since thanks to them he had secured a wife of far better character than he himself could ever have deserved."}

content.text: {"request_id":"de83375722ed1199233dd969","rewritten_text":"He slipped quietly out of the wainscoting, an evil smile on his cruel, wrinkled mouth, and the moon withdrew behind a cloud as he crept past the great oriel window where his own arms and those of his murdered wife gleamed in azure and gold. On he slid like a dark shadow, the very night seeming to hate him as he went. Once he thought he heard someone call and stopped, but it was only a dog baying from the Red Farm, so he continued, muttering strange sixteenth-century curses and now and then waving his rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the passage leading to luckless Washington’s room. For a moment he stood there, the wind blowing his long gray hair around his head and twisting the unnamed horror of the dead man’s shroud into grotesque folds. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he knew the moment had come. He chuckled and turned the corner, but immediately gave a pitiful wail, stumbled backward, and covered his pale face with his long bony hands. Right before him stood a horrible specter, still as a carved statue and monstrous as a madman’s dream. Its head was bald and polished, its face round, fat, and white, and hideous laughter had twisted its features into an eternal grin. Scarlet rays shot from its eyes, the mouth was a wide pit of fire, and a hideous garment like his own wrapped its monumental body in silent snow. On its chest hung a placard with strange writing in antique letters, some scroll of shame, some record of wild sins, some dreadful calendar of crime, and in its right hand it held high a gleaming steel falchion.\n\nHaving never seen another ghost before, he was naturally terrified, and after a quick second glance at the awful phantom, he fled back to his room, tripping over his long winding-sheet as he raced down the corridor and dropping the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jack-boots, where the butler found it in the morning. Once in his own apartment he threw himself on a small pallet-bed and buried his face under the covers. After a time, though, the brave old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to speak to the other ghost as soon as daylight came. So, just as dawn touched the hills with silver, he returned to the spot where he had first seen the grisly phantom, thinking that two ghosts were better than one and that, with the help of his new ally, he might safely deal with the twins."}

{"request_id":"7e617f0fa2ae248da16614d7","rewritten_text":"“Yeah, it is—and I could’ve had it if I’d been big enough; I saw him first. Who caught him?”

“It was some old guy—a stranger—and he sold his claim on him for forty dollars because he has to head up the river and can’t stick around. Imagine that! You better believe I’d wait, even if it took seven years.”

“That’s me, every time,” I said. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth more than that if he’s willing to sell it so cheap. Maybe something’s not right about it.”

“But it is—straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells everything about him, down to the last detail—describes him like a picture, and even names the plantation he’s from, down below New Orleans. No sir, there’s no trouble with that deal, you can bet on it. Hey, give me a chew of tobacco, will you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went to the raft and sat in the wigwam to think. But I couldn’t figure anything out. I thought until my head was sore, but I couldn’t see any way out of the mess. After this whole long trip, after everything we’d done for those scoundrels, it had all come to nothing, everything smashed and ruined, because they had the heart to play a trick like that on Jim and make him a slave again, for life, among strangers, for forty filthy dollars.

Once I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home where his family was, if he had to be a slave, so I might as well write a letter to Tom Sawyer and ask him to tell Miss Watson where Jim was. But I dropped that idea for two reasons: she’d be furious and disgusted at his running off and being ungrateful, and she’d sell him straight down the river again; and if she didn’t, everybody naturally despises an ungrateful black man, and they’d make Jim feel it all the time, so he’d feel low and disgraced. And then think of me! Word would get around that Huck Finn helped a black man get free, and if I ever met anyone from that town again I’d be ready to drop down and lick his boots from shame. That’s how it is: a person does a lowdown thing and then doesn’t want to face the consequences. Thinks that as long as he can hide it, it’s no disgrace. That was exactly my situation. The more I thought about it, the more my conscience gnawed at me, and the more wicked, low, and worthless I felt."}

{"request_id":"30945653735f6d2a1740e283","rewritten_text":"The elegant gentlemen of the finest breeding wore dangling trinkets that chimed as they moved; those golden chains rang like tiny bells. Along with that chiming, and the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, there was a flutter in the air that kept Saint Antoine and its ravenous hunger far away.

Clothing was the unfailing spell used to keep everything in its place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that would never end. From the Palace of the Tuileries, through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals of Justice, and all society (except the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball even reached the Common Executioner, who had to perform “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was rare—Monsieur Paris, as his fellow professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest called him in the churchly style, presided in this dainty outfit. And who among the guests at Monseigneur’s reception in that seventeen hundred and eightieth year of our Lord could doubt that a system rooted in a frizzled, powdered, gold-laced, pump-wearing, white-silk-stockinged hangman would outlast the stars!

After Monseigneur relieved his four men of their burdens and drank his chocolate, he ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holies opened and came out. Then came submission, cringing, fawning, servility, and utter humiliation. There was no bowing left for Heaven—which might be one reason why Monseigneur’s worshippers never bothered with it.

Dropping a promise here and a smile there, a whisper for one lucky servant and a wave of the hand for another, Monseigneur graciously passed through his rooms to the distant region of the Circumference of Truth. There, Monseigneur turned and came back again, and in due time was shut up in his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites, and was seen no more.

When the show ended, the flutter in the air became a little storm, and the precious little bells rang down the stairs. Soon only one person remained, and he, with his hat under his arm and his snuffbox in his hand, slowly passed the mirrors on his way out.

“I devote you,” said this person, stopping at the last door and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

With that, he shook the snuff from his fingers as if shaking dust from his feet, and quietly walked downstairs."}

{"request_id":"7afde4905d180757be092d6e","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired escort went riding in Brockley Meadows, where she ripped her riding skirt badly squeezing through a hedge. When she returned home, she decided to slip up the back stairs so no one would see her. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door happened to be open, she thought she saw someone inside, and assuming it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes brought her sewing there, she looked in to ask for help mending her skirt. To her huge surprise, it was the Canterville Ghost himself! He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees flying through the air, and the red leaves spinning wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, his whole posture radiating deep despair. He looked so wretched, so worn out, that Virginia—who at first thought of running away and locking herself in her room—felt overwhelmed with compassion and decided to try to comfort him. Her tread was so light, and his sorrow so deep, that he didn’t even notice her until she spoke.

“I’m so sorry for you,” she said, “but my brothers are going back to Eton tomorrow, and then, if you behave yourself, no one will bother you.”

“It’s ridiculous to ask me to behave,” he answered, turning in astonishment to the pretty little girl who had dared to address him. “Utterly ridiculous. I have to rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and roam around at night, if that’s what you mean. It’s my only reason for existing.”

“It’s no reason at all for existing, and you know you’ve been terribly wicked. Mrs. Umney told us the first day we got here that you killed your wife.”

“Well, I freely admit it,” the Ghost replied peevishly, “but it was purely a family affair and nobody else’s concern.”

“It’s terribly wrong to kill anyone,” said Virginia, whose voice sometimes held a gentle Puritan solemnity inherited from some old New England ancestor.

“Oh, I can’t stand the cheap severity of abstract morals! My wife was very plain, never starched my ruffs properly, and had no idea how to cook. Why, there was a stag I shot in Hogley Woods—a magnificent pricket—and do you know how she sent it up to the table? Still, it doesn’t matter now, because it’s all over, and I don’t think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death, even if I did kill her.”"}

{"request_id":"6be3e977aed83eb32b65ddb8","rewritten_text":"I now examined the skull drawing carefully. Its outer edges—the parts closest to the edge of the parchment—were much sharper than the rest. It was clear the heat had worked unevenly. I immediately lit a fire and held every portion of the parchment to the intense heat. At first, the only result was that the faint lines of the skull grew darker; but when I kept at it, a figure appeared at the corner of the slip, diagonally opposite the skull. At first I thought it was a goat. After looking more closely, though, I realized it was meant to be a kid.

“Ha! ha!” I said. “Granted, I have no business laughing—a million and a half is too serious for jokes—but you’re not going to build a third link in your chain. You won’t find any special connection between pirates and goats. Pirates have nothing to do with goats; they belong to the farming crowd.”

“But I just told you the figure wasn’t a goat.”

“Well then, a kid—almost the same thing.”

“Almost, but not entirely,” Legrand replied. “You’ve probably heard of Captain Kidd. I immediately saw the animal figure as a kind of punning or hieroglyphic signature. I call it a signature because its position on the parchment gave me that idea. The skull at the opposite corner had the look of a stamp or seal. But I was badly bothered by what was missing—the body of the instrument I imagined, the text that would match my context.”

“I assume you expected a letter between the stamp and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I couldn’t shake the feeling that some great fortune was coming. I can hardly explain why. Maybe it was more desire than belief. But you know, Jupiter’s foolish claim that the bug was solid gold really fired my imagination. And then the string of accidents and coincidences—those were so extraordinary. Do you see how mere chance made these things happen on the one day of the year cool enough for a fire? And without that fire, or without the dog showing up at just that moment, I would never have discovered the skull, and never become the owner of the treasure.”"}

{"request_id":"54d95a5d8645dbebe13d10ca","rewritten_text":"As they were leaving the dining room, the clock tower began to strike midnight, and at the final stroke they heard a crash and a piercing cry; a terrible clap of thunder shook the house, an eerie strain of music drifted through the air, a panel at the top of the staircase sprang open with a bang, and Virginia stepped out onto the landing, pale and white, a small casket in her hand. In an instant they all rushed toward her. Mrs. Otis seized her in a fierce embrace, the Duke covered her with frantic kisses, and the twins performed a wild war dance around them.

“Good heavens, child, where have you been?” said Mr. Otis, rather sharply, convinced she had played some foolish prank on them. “Cecil and I have ridden all over the countryside searching for you, and your mother has been scared to death. You must never pull these practical jokes again.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” screamed the twins as they hopped around.

“My own darling, thank heaven you’re safe; you must never leave my side again,” murmured Mrs. Otis, kissing the trembling child and smoothing the tangled gold of her hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I’ve been with the Ghost. He’s dead, and you have to come see him. He had done terrible things, but he truly regretted them all, and before he died he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The entire family stared at her in stunned silence, but she was sober and earnest, and turning around she led them through the opening in the paneling and down a narrow secret passage, Washington following with the lit candle he had snatched from the table. At last they reached a massive oak door studded with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung back on its heavy hinges, revealing a small low chamber with a vaulted ceiling and a single tiny barred window. Set into the wall was a huge iron ring, and chained to it lay a gaunt skeleton stretched full length on the stone floor, its long fleshless fingers straining toward an old-fashioned trencher and ewer placed just beyond reach. The jug had clearly once held water, as green mold coated its interior. The trencher held nothing but a pile of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her little hands, and began to pray in silence, while the rest of the group watched in awe at the terrible tragedy now revealed to them."}

content.text: {"request_id":"693fa24e922a1aff8ef1d2c5","rewritten_text":"We both agreed in loving Adrian. She was still a child and could not yet appreciate his full merit or share my sympathy with his pursuits and opinions. I was always with him. His sensitivity and sweetness gave our conversations a tender, almost otherworldly tone. Then he would be merry as a lark singing from the sky, his thoughts soaring like an eagle, his innocence gentle as a dove. He could lighten Perdita’s seriousness and ease the biting restlessness in me. Looking back on my own restless desires and painful struggles with other people felt like remembering a troubled dream, and I felt as changed as if I had been reborn into another body with new senses and nerves that altered how the world reflected in my mind. Yet I was still the same in strength, in my deep need for companionship, in my hunger for action. My manly virtues did not leave me; it was as if the muse Urania spared Samson’s hair while he slept at her feet, for everything was softened and made more humane. Adrian did not limit himself to teaching me the dry truths of history and philosophy. While using them to help me master my wild, uncultured spirit, he also opened to me the living page of his own heart and let me feel and understand its astonishing nature.\n\nThe ex-queen of England had tried since his infancy to plant daring and ambitious designs in her son’s mind. She saw he possessed genius and rare talent, and she nurtured these gifts so she could later use them to promote her own plans. She encouraged his thirst for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even tolerated his fierce love of freedom, hoping it would, as often happens, turn into a passion for power. She tried to raise him feeling resentful and eager to take revenge on those who had helped force his father’s abdication. In this she failed. Even distorted accounts of a great and wise nation claiming its right to govern itself stirred his admiration, and early on he became a republican by conviction. Still, his mother did not lose hope. Alongside love of authority and proud noble birth, she possessed firm ambition, patience, and self-control. She devoted herself to studying her son’s temper. By praising, scolding, and exhorting him, she tried to find and strike the right chords; and though the music her efforts produced sounded discordant to her, she built her hopes on his talents and felt sure she would eventually prevail."}

{"request_id":"a7ebcf66e4b5d8420f3259bc","rewritten_text":"They rode past deserted brickfields. The fog thinned there, and he could make out the odd bottle-shaped kilns with orange tongues of fire fanning out. A dog barked as they passed, and somewhere far off a stray sea-gull screamed in the dark. The horse stumbled in a rut, then swerved and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled again over rough, paved streets. Most windows were dark, but here and there wild shadows showed against a blind lit from behind. He watched them with interest. They moved like giant puppets and gestured as if alive, and he hated them. A dull rage filled his heart. When they turned a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open door, and two men ran after the hansom for nearly a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

People say passion makes the mind move in circles. Certainly, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips silently repeated those subtle words about soul and sense until he felt they gave complete voice to his mood, granting intellectual approval to passions that would have ruled him even without it. The same thought crept from one corner of his mind to another, and the fierce desire to live, the most terrible of man’s hungers, sent energy racing through every shaking nerve and fiber. Ugliness that once repelled him for its harsh reality became precious to him now for that very truth. Ugliness was the lone reality. Coarse fights, filthy dens, the brutal chaos of disordered life, the sheer vileness of thieves and exiles, struck him as more vivid, in their raw immediacy, than all the graceful forms of art or the dreamy echoes of music. They were what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the man halted with a jerk at the top of a dark lane. Beyond the low roofs and jagged chimney-stacks, the black masts of ships rose up. White mist curled like ghostly sails around the yards.

“Somewhere around here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started and looked around. “This will do,” he said, and after jumping out and giving the driver the promised extra fare, he hurried toward the quay. A lantern glowed now and then at the stern of a huge merchant ship. The light shivered and splintered in the puddles. A red glare poured from a steamer ready to depart that was taking on coal. The slimy pavement shone like wet oilskin."}

{"request_id":"ad6061d15fb91916651de743","rewritten_text":"Accordingly, I determined to jump down the instant we reached the town and remove myself from his hearing. I carried out this plan without difficulty. My small portmanteau lay in the boot beneath my feet; a twist of the hinge freed it; I dropped it in front of me, followed it out, and found myself under the first lamp upon the initial stones of the town pavement. The convicts proceeded with the coach, and I knew precisely where they would be spirited away to the river. In imagination, I saw their boat with its crew of prisoners waiting at the slime-coated steps, heard once more the gruff “Give way, you!” as if to hounds, and again beheld the sinister Noah’s Ark riding on the black water.

I could not have declared what alarmed me, for my dread was utterly shapeless and obscure, yet it weighed heavily upon me. While I walked toward the hotel, I felt a terror far beyond the apprehension of an unpleasant or awkward recognition, and it set me quivering. I am sure it took no distinct outline, but was the momentary revival of the fright of childhood.

The Blue Boar’s coffee-room stood empty, and I had ordered and even begun my dinner there before the waiter recognized me. When he had apologized for his forgetfulness, he asked if he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I answered, “decidedly not.”

The waiter—he who had carried up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials the day I was bound—looked astonished, and soon contrived to place a grimy old local newspaper directly before me so that I picked it up and read the following paragraph:

Our readers will learn, not without a degree of interest, concerning the late romantic rise in fortune of a young iron artificer from this neighbourhood (and what a topic, indeed, for the wand of our not yet universally celebrated fellow citizen TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and confidant was a most respectable personage not entirely disconnected from the corn and seed business, whose most convenient and spacious premises stand within a hundred miles of the High Street. It is not quite apart from our own personal feeling that we chronicle HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is satisfying to know that our town produced the originator of the latter’s fortune."}

content.text: {"request_id":"4ea3768709c1ed97e07a5b14","rewritten_text":"The storm roared furiously throughout the night, yet nothing noteworthy transpired. At breakfast next morning they discovered the dreadful bloodstain once more on the floor. “It cannot be the fault of Paragon Detergent,” Washington declared. “I have used it with every adjunct imaginable. It must be the ghost.” He erased the stain again, only for it to reappear on the second morning. On the third morning it was present yet again, although Mr. Otis had himself locked the library overnight and carried the key upstairs. Now the whole household grew genuinely absorbed; Mr. Otis suspected he had been overly dogmatic in denying ghosts, Mrs. Otis announced she would join the Psychical Society, and Washington drafted a lengthy letter to Messrs. Myers and Podmore about the Persistence of Sanguineous Stains in connection with Crime. That night all hesitation about the objective reality of phantasmata was finally dispelled.\n\nThe day had been warm and bright, and in the cool evening the entire family went driving. They did not return until nine, when they ate a light supper. Their talk never once touched on spirits, so even those preliminary conditions of receptive anticipation that often prelude psychical phenomena were absent. According to Mr. Otis, their subjects were only those common in the conversation of cultivated Americans of the higher type: the incomparable superiority of Miss Fanny Davenport over Sarah Bernhardt on the stage; the difficulty of procuring green corn, buckwheat cakes, and hominy even in the finest English homes; Boston’s role in shaping the world-soul; the merits of the baggage-check system in railway travel; and the sweetness of the New York accent compared with the London drawl. No reference at all was made to anything supernatural, nor was Sir Simon de Canterville mentioned. At eleven the family retired, and by half past the house lay dark. Some time later Mr. Otis was roused by an odd sound in the corridor outside his room, a clanking as of metal that drew closer every moment. He was immediately on his feet, struck a match, and checked the time: exactly one o’clock. He remained perfectly composed and took his pulse, which was entirely normal. The peculiar noise continued, and together with it he clearly heard footsteps. He slipped into his slippers, removed a small oblong vial from his dressing-case, and opened the door."}

{"request_id":"06b10f04749075dbfcb6af34","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” Duff answered. 

“And to interpret ‘yokel’ for the ladies, you mean the attempt wasn’t made by a countryman?” Mr. Losberne asked with a smile.

“That’s right, sir,” Blathers replied. “This is all about the robbery, then?”

“All,” said the doctor.

“And what’s this about the boy the servants keep talking about?” Blathers asked.

“Nothing at all,” the doctor answered. “One of the scared servants decided he had something to do with the break-in, but it’s nonsense.”

“Very easily settled, if so,” Duff remarked.

“He’s quite right,” Blathers said, nodding and idly clicking the handcuffs as if they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What does he say about himself? Where did he come from? He didn’t fall out of the clouds, did he, sir?”

“Of course not,” the doctor replied, glancing nervously at the two ladies. “I know his whole history, but we can talk about that later. You’d like to see where the thieves tried to get in first, I suppose?”

“Certainly,” Mr. Blathers said. “We should inspect the place first and question the servants afterward. That’s the usual procedure.”

They got lights, and Blathers and Duff, followed by the town constable, Brittles, Giles, and everyone else, went into the small room at the end of the hall to look out the window. Then they went across the lawn to look in through the window; then someone handed out a candle so they could examine the shutter; then a lantern so they could trace footprints; then a pitchfork to probe the bushes. All this was done with everyone looking on in breathless suspense. They came back in, and Mr. Giles and Brittles acted out their part in the previous night’s adventure, performing it about six times over: disagreeing the first time in only one important point, and by the last time in perhaps a dozen. Once they finished, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held a long meeting together which, for secrecy and gravity, would make the most serious medical consultation seem like child’s play.

Meanwhile the doctor paced the next room in great anxiety, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with worried faces.

“Honestly,” he said, stopping after many quick turns, “I hardly know what to do.”"}

{"request_id":"c40ec1c4d47e5b5614addffe","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said as we reached the base, “come here! Was the skull nailed to the branch with the face outward or pressed against the wood?”

“The face was outward, massa, so the crows could get at the eyes easily, without trouble.”

“Then was it this eye or that one you dropped the beetle through?” Legrand tapped each of Jupiter’s eyes as he spoke.

“It was this eye, massa—the left eye—just like you told me,” he answered, indicating his right eye.

“That settles it—we have to try again.”

Now my friend, whose madness I was beginning to see, or thought I saw, showed signs of having a method. He moved the peg marking where the beetle had fallen about three inches west of its original spot. Then, measuring from the trunk to the new peg and extending the line fifty feet straight ahead as before, he pointed out a place several yards from where we had been digging.

We drew a circle around this new position, larger than the previous one, and started digging again with the spades. I was exhausted, yet without quite knowing why, my feelings changed; I no longer felt much aversion to the work. I had become inexplicably fascinated—no, even excited. Perhaps something in Legrand’s wild behavior—a hint of planning or deliberation—impressed me. I dug with enthusiasm, and every now and then I caught myself actually looking with something like expectation for the imagined treasure that had driven my unfortunate friend mad. At the height of these wandering thoughts, after we had worked for about ninety minutes, we were interrupted again by the dog’s fierce howling. At first his restlessness had been clearly playful or impulsive, but now it took on a harsh, serious tone. When Jupiter tried to muzzle him again, the dog fought furiously, leaped into the hole, and clawed wildly at the dirt. In moments he uncovered a pile of human bones—two complete skeletons—mixed with several metal buttons and what looked like decayed wool dust. A few blows of a spade unearthed the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug deeper, three or four loose gold and silver coins appeared."}

{"request_id":"0979034977e8bd4eecce25b8","rewritten_text":"“She and the children might remain quite comfortably.”

“Ah! papa—that is precisely what you have never managed, nor do I imagine you ever will. Isabella is never happy apart from her husband.”

The fact was too clear for debate. Distasteful as it proved, Mr. Woodhouse could only let out a resigned sigh; and seeing his spirits damped by the notion of his daughter’s devotion to her husband, Emma quickly shifted to a topic certain to raise them.

“Harriet must allow us as much of her company as possible while my brother and sister are here. I know she will like the children. We are exceedingly proud of the children, are we not, papa? I wonder which she will find the handsomest, Henry or John?”

“Aye, I wonder which indeed. Poor little souls, how delighted they will be to come. They love being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they do, sir. Truly, I know not who does not.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John is the very picture of his mama. Henry is the eldest, named after me, not his father. John, the second, takes his father’s name. Some folks wonder, I believe, that the eldest was not called after his father; yet Isabella insisted on Henry, and I thought it exceedingly lovely of her. And he is remarkably clever. They are all very clever, and have so many charming ways. They will come and plant themselves by my chair, and say, ‘Grandpapa, might we have a length of string?’ and once Henry asked for a knife, but I told him knives were made only for grandpapas. I think their father is often too rough with them.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you are yourself so extremely gentle; but could you compare him with other fathers, you would not call him rough. He desires his boys to be lively and hardy; and if they misbehave, he can give a sharp word now and then; yet he is a tender father—Mr. John Knightley is certainly an affectionate father. The children all adore him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and flings them up to the ceiling in a most alarming manner!”

“But they enjoy it, papa; nothing pleases them more. It is such delight that, if their uncle did not enforce turns, whichever child began would never yield to the other.”

“Why, I cannot comprehend it.”

“That is how it is with all of us, papa. Half the world cannot comprehend the pleasures of the other half.”"}

{"request_id":"399e19277932158cff1dc20c","rewritten_text":"“Then hear me! You there!” Monks answered. “His father, stricken with illness in Rome, was joined by his wife—my mother—whom he had long been apart from. She traveled from Paris, taking me along, to oversee his affairs, I suppose, for neither she nor he in truth cared much for each other. He lay unaware of us, his senses gone, and slept until the following day, when he died. In his desk were two papers, written the evening his sickness began, addressed to you,” he said to Mr. Brownlow, “wrapped in a few short lines, with a note on the cover stating they were not to be sent till after his death. One was a letter to that girl Agnes; the other, a will.”

“What of the letter?” Mr. Brownlow asked.

“The letter? A sheet covered, crossed and re-crossed, full of repentant confession and pleads to God for aid. He had fooled the girl with a tale of some secret—one day to be revealed—that hindered their marriage for the time; and she waited, patient and trusting, until her trust carried her too far and she lost what couldn’t be restored. She was then only months from her confinement. He detailed what measures he had intended, had he lived, to shield her disgrace, and begged her, should he die, not to curse his memory or imagine the weight of their sin would fall on her or their child; the blame, he said, was solely his. He recalled the day he gave her the small locket and the ring bearing her Christian name, leaving the other side blank for the name he hoped to share with her one day—beseeched her to keep it still, wearing it next her heart as before—and wandered on, wildly repeating the same words again and again, as if driven mad. I believe he was.”

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow prompted while Oliver’s tears dropped fast.

Monks made no reply.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “matched the tone of the letter. He spoke of misery his wife had laid upon him; of the rebellious disposition, vice, malice, and untimely evil passions of you, his only son, schooled to despise him; and he left to you and your mother annuities of eight hundred pounds each. The greater share of his estate he divided into two halves—one portion for Agnes Fleming, and the other for their child, should it be born alive and reach maturity.”"}

{"request_id":"6108cf13b9edcdb8a2a47a1f","rewritten_text":"Mrs Clay’s affections got the better of her prudence, and for the young gentleman’s sake she relinquished any further plotting for Sir Walter. Yet she possesses ability as well as feeling; and it remains uncertain whether his craft or hers will ultimately prevail, whether, after he has hindered her from becoming Sir Walter’s wife, he might not, after all the coaxing and fond attention, be brought to make her Lady William instead.

No one could doubt that Sir Walter and Elizabeth were shocked and mortified at losing their companion and having her duplicity exposed. They could, of course, retreat to their grand cousins for solace; but for a long time they must taste how incomplete the pleasure is when one flatters and trails after others without being flattered and followed in return.

Anne, having soon perceived Lady Russell’s intention of loving Captain Wentworth as she ought, had only one alloy upon the happiness of her hopes: the awareness that she had no relations to present to him whom a sensible man could prize. In that respect she felt her inferiority acutely. The disparity in fortune mattered nothing; it never cost her a regret. But possessing no family to welcome and value him properly, nothing respectable, harmonious, or kindly to offer in exchange for all the merit and hearty reception awaiting her in his brothers and sisters, produced as piercing a pain as her mind could feel amid otherwise high felicity. Only two friends remained for her to add to his circle, Lady Russell and Mrs Smith. Towards both, however, he was very willing to attach himself. Lady Russell, despite all her past offences, he could now sincerely admire. Though he need not declare that she was justified in separating them originally, he was prepared to say nearly every other favourable thing of her. As for Mrs Smith, her claims were manifold and secured a quick, lasting esteem.

Mrs Smith’s recent kind offices for Anne were merit enough, and their marriage, rather than costing her one friend, secured her two. She became their earliest visitor in their established home; and Captain Wentworth, by guiding her towards the recovery of her husband’s property in the West Indies—writing on her behalf, acting for her, and with all the spirited diligence of a bold man and faithful friend seeing her through every petty complication of the affair—fully repaid the benefits she had bestowed, or intended to bestow, upon his wife."}

{"request_id":"5ce7b37d09590c6c6f65c53c","rewritten_text":"It is strange, but everyone who vanishes is said to have been seen in San Francisco. It must be a charming city, with all the appeal of the next world.”

“What do you think happened to Basil?” asked Dorian, holding his Burgundy up to the light and wondering how he could talk about it so calmly.

“I have no idea. If Basil wants to hide, that’s his affair. If he’s dead, I’d rather not think about him. Death is the only thing that frightens me. I hate it.”

“Why?” asked the younger man tiredly.

“Because,” said Lord Henry, touching his nose with the gilt grille of an open vinaigrette, “nowadays you can survive everything but that. Death and vulgarity are the only facts in the nineteenth century you can’t explain away. Let’s have our coffee in the music room, Dorian. You must play Chopin for me. The man my wife ran off with played Chopin beautifully. Poor Victoria! I was very fond of her. The house is rather lonely without her. Of course marriage is just a habit, a bad habit. But one still misses even one’s worst habits. Perhaps those are the ones we miss most. They are such an essential part of one’s personality.”

Dorian said nothing, but rose from the table, went into the next room, sat at the piano, and let his fingers wander over the ivory keys. After the coffee arrived, he stopped and looked over at Lord Henry. “Harry, did it ever occur to you that Basil was murdered?”

Lord Henry yawned. “Basil was very popular and always wore a Waterbury watch. Why would anyone murder him? He wasn’t clever enough to have enemies. He had a wonderful talent for painting, of course. But a man can paint like Velázquez and still be dull. Basil was really rather dull. He only interested me once, when he told me years ago that he adored you and that you were the driving force of his art.”

“I was very fond of Basil,” said Dorian, his voice sad. “But don’t people say he was murdered?”

“Oh, some papers do. It doesn’t seem likely. I know there are horrible places in Paris, but Basil wasn’t the sort to go to them. He had no curiosity. That was his main failing.”

“What would you say, Harry, if I told you I murdered Basil?” asked the younger man."}

“Henri Duval, a neighbor and a silversmith by trade, testifies that he was among the first to enter the house. He confirms Musèt’s account in general. As soon as they broke in, they shut the door again to keep out the crowd, which grew quickly despite the late hour. He thinks the sharp voice belonged to an Italian. He was sure it wasn’t French. He couldn’t tell if it was a man’s voice. It might have been a woman’s. He didn’t know Italian. He couldn’t make out the words, but was convinced from the tone that the speaker was Italian. He knew Madame L. and her daughter and had often spoken with both. He was certain the sharp voice wasn’t either of the deceased.

“Odenheimer, a restaurateur, gave his testimony voluntarily. Since he didn’t speak French, he was examined through an interpreter. He’s a native of Amsterdam. He was passing the house at the time of the screams. They lasted several minutes—probably ten. They were long, loud, and terribly distressing. He was one of those who entered the building. He confirmed the earlier evidence in every respect but one. He was sure the sharp voice belonged to a man—a Frenchman. He couldn’t make out the words. They were loud and rapid, uneven, spoken in fear as well as anger. The voice was harsh, rather than shrill. He wouldn’t call it shrill. The gruff voice kept repeating “sacré,” “diable,” and once “mon Dieu.”

“Jules Mignaud, banker of the firm Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. He is the elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye had some property. She opened an account with his bank in the spring of the year—eight years earlier. She made frequent deposits in small amounts. She hadn’t drawn anything until three days before her death, when she personally withdrew 4000 francs. This sum was paid in gold, and a clerk escorted her home with the money.

“Adolphe Le Bon, clerk to Mignaud et Fils, testifies that on the day in question, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her residence with the 4000 francs, divided into two bags. When the door was opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from his hands, while the elderly lady relieved him of the other.”"}

And then he was not at home! I assure you I am thoroughly displeased. No apology left, no message for me. The housekeeper declared she had no notion I was expected.—Most extraordinary!—No one had any idea where he had gone. Possibly to Hartfield, or to the Abbey Mill, or perhaps into his woods.—Miss Woodhouse, this is not what one expects from our friend Knightley!—Can you account for it?”

Emma diverted herself by insisting that it was indeed exceedingly extraordinary, and that she had not a word to offer in his defence.

“I cannot conceive,” said Mrs. Elton (suffering the affront as a wife ought), “I cannot conceive how he could behave so to you, of all people! The very last person one could imagine being forgotten!—My dear Mr. E., he must have left a message for you; he surely must.—Even Knightley could not be so capricious;—the servants must have overlooked it. Depend upon that: and it is very likely with the Donwell servants, who, I have often observed, are astonishingly clumsy and negligent.—I would not, for any inducement, allow that fellow Harry to stand at our sideboard. And with respect to Mrs. Hodges, Wright holds her in the poorest estimation.—She promised Wright a recipe and never forwarded it.”

“I met William Larkins,” continued Mr. Elton, “as I approached the house, and he told me I would not find his master within, but I paid him no heed.—William seemed somewhat out of sorts. He did not know what had come over his master lately, he said, but he could scarcely ever get a word with him. I care nothing for William’s complaints, yet it truly is of the highest consequence that *I* see Knightley today; and therefore it is a matter of serious inconvenience that I should have taken this hot walk for nothing.”

Emma felt she could do no better than make straight for home. In all likelihood she was expected there at that very moment; and Mr. Knightley might be spared from sinking deeper into offence with Mr. Elton, if not with William Larkins.
