{"request_id":"13e12aeed61ab0aa8265f3f0","rewritten_text":"For years Dorian Gray could not shake the hold this book had on him—or rather, he never even tried. He ordered no fewer than nine large-paper first editions from Paris and had each one bound in a different color to match his moods and the shifting whims of a nature he sometimes felt he had almost lost control of. The hero, a marvelous young Parisian whose romantic and scientific sides were oddly united, became a kind of preview of himself. Indeed, the whole book seemed to contain the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic hero. He never knew—never even had reason to know—the strange fear of mirrors, polished metal, and still water that seized the young Parisian early on, brought about by the sudden decay of beauty that had once been extraordinary. With almost cruel delight—and perhaps cruelty hides in nearly every joy, certainly in every pleasure—he would read the book’s final section, where the sorrow and despair of someone who had lost what he valued most in others and in the world was told in tragic, if slightly exaggerated, detail.

For the magnificent beauty that had captivated Basil Hallward and many others never seemed to leave Dorian. Even those who heard the worst rumors about his way of life—and now and then strange whispers spread through London and became club gossip—could not believe anything dishonorable about him when they saw him. He always looked like someone unstained by the world. Men who spoke crudely fell silent when Dorian Gray entered. The purity of his face seemed to rebuke them. His presence alone made them remember the innocence they had ruined. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have avoided the corruption of an age both sordid and sensual.

Often, when he returned from those mysterious, lengthy absences that stirred so much speculation among those who were his friends—or thought they were—he would creep upstairs to the locked room, open the door with the key he always kept, and stand with a mirror before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him, looking from the wicked, aging face on the canvas to the fair young face smiling back at him from the polished glass."}

{"request_id":"5fd68852bc0b076ffd45b57f","rewritten_text":"Great God! If I had guessed even for a moment what my fiendish enemy truly intended, I would have exiled myself forever and wandered the world alone rather than consent to this wretched marriage. Yet the monster, as if using magic, hid his real purpose from me; and while I thought I was preparing only for my own death, I hurried the fate of someone far dearer.

As the wedding day drew closer, whether from cowardice or some prophetic feeling, my heart sank. I hid my unease behind a show of cheerfulness that brought smiles to my father but hardly fooled the watchful eyes of Elizabeth. She looked toward our union with calm contentment, tinged with fear born from past misfortunes, that what seemed solid happiness might dissolve into nothing and leave only lasting regret.

Plans were made, guests offered congratulations, and everything appeared joyful. I tried to lock the torment inside my heart and joined in my father’s designs, though they might only serve as decorations for my tragedy. Through his efforts, part of Elizabeth’s inheritance had been restored by the Austrian government, including a small estate on the shores of Como. We agreed that immediately after our wedding we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness beside the beautiful lake.

Meanwhile I took every precaution to defend myself if the fiend attacked. I carried pistols and a dagger everywhere and stayed alert against trickery, which gave me a measure of calm. Indeed, as the time approached, the threat seemed like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing my peace, while the happiness I expected in my marriage became more certain as the date was spoken of constantly as something no accident could prevent.

Elizabeth appeared content; my calm behavior helped steady her. Yet on the day that was to fulfill my wishes and determine my fate, she grew sorrowful, filled with a strong sense of looming evil, and likely she also remembered the dreadful secret I had promised to reveal to her the next day."}

He dealt the same to King Uriens of the land of Gore. After that came Sir Bagdemagus, and Gareth sent him crashing to the ground, horse and man. {"request_id":"185e5cfc834a0f04254004ec","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so satisfied with their conversation that he never again troubled himself or bothered his dear sister Elizabeth by mentioning it; she was glad to know she had said enough to keep him silent.

The day came for him and Lydia to leave, and Mrs. Bennet had to accept the separation, which, since her husband had no intention of joining her scheme of taking them all to Newcastle, was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when will we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I don’t know. Maybe not for two or three years.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They will have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s farewells were much warmer than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said many charming things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they were out of the house, “as ever I saw. He simpers, smirks, and makes love to us all. I am extremely proud of him. I defy even Sir William Lucas to show a more valuable son-in-law.”

The loss of her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very low for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “there is nothing worse than parting with friends. One feels so forlorn without them.”

“This is what comes, you see, madam, of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It should make you more content that your other four are single.”

“It is no such thing. Lydia is not leaving me because she is married, but only because her husband’s regiment is so far away. If it had been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.”

But the dull mood this event threw her into was soon relieved, and her spirits stirred again with hopeful excitement, by a piece of news just being spread. The housekeeper at Netherfield had orders to prepare for her master’s arrival; he was coming in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet could hardly sit still. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head by turns.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for Mrs. Philips first brought her the news). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, though. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never want to see him again. But still, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield if he likes.”"}

{"request_id":"2dc7e84391a46f9b6ff80795","rewritten_text":"It was well past noon when he finally woke up. His valet had tiptoed into the room several times to check if he was stirring, puzzled by how long his young master was sleeping. At last the bell rang, and Victor came in quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters on a small tray of old Sèvres porcelain, then drew back the olive satin curtains with their shimmering blue lining that hung before the three tall windows.

“Monsieur slept well this morning,” he said with a smile.

“What time is it, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked groggily.

“One fifteen, Monsieur.”

How late it was! He sat up, sipped some tea, and began sorting through his letters. One was from Lord Henry, delivered by hand that morning. He hesitated before setting it aside. He opened the others without much interest. They held the usual assortment of calling cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private previews, programs for charity concerts, and similar things that pour in on fashionable young men every morning during the season. There was a rather steep bill for a chased silver Louis XV dressing set that he still hadn’t had the nerve to send to his guardians, who were terribly old-fashioned and couldn’t grasp that we live in an age when unnecessary things are our only necessities; there were also several very polite letters from Jermyn Street moneylenders offering to advance any amount of cash instantly at the most reasonable interest rates.

After about ten minutes he got up, pulled on an ornate silk-embroidered cashmere dressing gown, and went into the onyx-floored bathroom. The cool water revived him after his long sleep. He seemed to have forgotten everything he had gone through. Now and then a faint sense of having taken part in some strange tragedy came over him, but it felt as unreal as a dream.

Once he was dressed, he went into the library and sat down to the light French breakfast set out on a small round table beside the open window. The day was exquisite. The warm air seemed scented with spices. A bee flew in and buzzed around the blue dragon bowl filled with sulfur-yellow roses that stood in front of him. He felt completely happy.

Suddenly his gaze fell on the screen he had placed in front of the portrait, and he started.

“Too chilly for Monsieur?” asked his valet, setting an omelet on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I’m not cold,” he murmured."}

content.text: {"request_id":"febed9f1075903e894f20b85","rewritten_text":"Colonel Grangerford was a gentleman, through and through, and so was his whole family. He was well born, as they say, and the Widow Douglas claimed that was just as valuable in a man as in a racehorse, and nobody ever denied she was top aristocracy in our town. Even Pap said so, though he was no more fancy than a mudcat. Colonel Grangerford was very tall and very slim, with a dark, pale complexion and not a trace of redness anywhere. He shaved his thin face clean every morning. His lips were the thinnest kind, so were his nostrils, and he had a high nose, heavy eyebrows, and the darkest eyes, set so deep they seemed to stare at you from caverns. His forehead was high, his hair black and straight, hanging to his shoulders. His hands were long and thin, and every day he wore a fresh shirt and a full linen suit so white it almost hurt to look at. On Sundays he put on a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane with a silver head. There wasn’t anything frivolous about him, and he never raised his voice. He was as kind as could be—you could feel it, and it made you trust him. Sometimes he smiled, and it was something to see. But when he straightened up like a flagpole and the lightning started flashing from under his eyebrows, you wanted to climb a tree first and ask questions later. He never needed to tell anyone to mind their manners; everybody behaved around him. People loved having him around; he felt like sunshine most of the time, like he made the weather good. If he turned into a storm cloud, it got dark for half a minute, but that was enough—nothing went wrong for a week after that.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family stood up and wished them good day, and didn’t sit again until they did. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter sat, mixed a glass of bitters, and handed it to him. He held it until Tom’s and Bob’s were ready, and then they bowed and said, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam.” The colonel and the old lady bowed just the slightest bit and said thank you, and then all three drank. Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and that dash of whiskey or apple brandy in the bottom of their glasses and gave it to me and Buck, and we drank to the old folks, too."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ba188f77ce5873030aa3698d","rewritten_text":"Each person compared it—not to the voice of someone from any nation whose language he knew—but to the opposite. The Frenchman thought it was a Spaniard’s voice and “might have made out some words if he had known Spanish.” The Dutchman insisted it was a Frenchman, yet it is recorded that “not understanding French, this witness was examined through an interpreter.” The Englishman believed it was German and “does not understand German.” The Spaniard “is sure” it was English, but “judges solely by the tone,” since “he has no knowledge of English.” The Italian thought it was Russian, though “he has never spoken with a native of Russia.” Another Frenchman disagreed with the first and was certain the voice was Italian; however, “not being familiar with that language,” he, like the Spaniard, was “convinced by the tone.” How extraordinarily strange that voice must have been to draw such testimony! In its very tones, people from five great European regions could recognize nothing familiar. You might say it could have been Asian or African. Neither Asians nor Africans are plentiful in Paris; but without rejecting that idea, I’ll just highlight three points. One witness called the voice “harsh rather than shrill.” Two others said it was “rapid and uneven.” No words—or even word-like sounds—were identified by any witness. “I don’t know,” Dupin continued, “what impression I’ve made on you so far, but I don’t hesitate to say that legitimate deductions from even this part of the testimony—the part about the rough and shrill voices—are enough to create a suspicion that should guide every further step in investigating the mystery. I said ‘legitimate deductions,’ though that doesn’t fully express my meaning. I intend to say these deductions are the only proper ones, and that the suspicion arises inevitably from them as the sole outcome. What that suspicion is, however, I won’t say yet. I only ask you to remember that, for me, it was forceful enough to shape and direct my inquiries in the chamber. “Now let us imagine ourselves inside that room. What should we look for first? The escape route the murderers used. It’s no exaggeration to say that neither of us believes in supernatural events.”"}

{"request_id":"d19fc7f7301ad0a8f592261b","rewritten_text":"“I trust I shall shortly enjoy the pleasure of presenting my son to you,” observed Mr. Weston.

Mrs. Elton, perfectly ready to imagine a special compliment meant for herself in this hope, returned the most gracious of smiles.

“You have heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I suppose,” he went on, “and know that he is my son, though he does not carry my name.”

“Oh! certainly, and I shall be delighted to make his acquaintance. I am sure Mr. Elton will hasten to call on him, and we shall both find much pleasure in receiving him at the Vicarage.”

“You are exceedingly kind.—Frank will be quite happy, I know.—He is expected in town next week, if not earlier. We had notice of it in a letter today. I came upon the letters in my walk this morning, and seeing my son’s handwriting, ventured to open it—although it was not addressed to me—it was meant for Mrs. Weston. She is his chief correspondent, I assure you. I scarcely ever get a letter.”

“And so you actually broke the seal of what was directed to her! Oh! Mr. Weston—(laughing with affected reproach) I must protest.—A truly dangerous precedent!—Pray do not allow your neighbours to adopt such conduct.—Upon my word, if this is what is before us, we married women must put forth our energies!—Oh! Mr. Weston, I could never have credited it of you!”

“Ay, we men are sad creatures. You must beware, Mrs. Elton.—This letter informs us—it is a brief note—penned in haste merely to supply the tidings—it informs us they are all coming up to town immediately, on Mrs. Churchill’s account—she has been unwell all winter, and finds Enscombe too cold—so they are to shift southward without delay.”

“Indeed!—from Yorkshire, if I remember. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, about one hundred and ninety miles from London—a long journey.”

“Yes, truly, very long. Sixty-five miles further than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of ample fortune?—You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, dashes about. You will scarcely credit me—but twice within one week he and Mr. Bragge traveled to London and back with four horses.”

“The difficulty about the distance from Enscombe,” remarked Mr. Weston, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we understand, has not been able to leave the sofa for a full week at a time. In Frank’s latest letter she declared, he said, that she was too feeble to reach her conservatory without the support of both his arm and his uncle’s!”"}

{"request_id":"913dfa6a2f19b1552803186b","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, the force of gravitation would steadily wane in proportion to the squares of the increasing distances, and thus, with velocity swelling to a prodigious acceleration, I should ultimately reach those remote tracts where Earth’s attraction yields to the moon’s. In keeping with this view, I deemed it unnecessary to burden myself with more provisions than would suffice for forty days.

“There was, nevertheless, another obstacle that gave me a measure of uneasiness. It has been noted that in balloon ascents of considerable elevation, apart from the discomfort of breathing, intense distress arises in head and body, often with bleeding at the nose and other alarming symptoms, all of which become more oppressive as altitude increases. This reflection was somewhat disquieting. Was it not likely these symptoms would augment without limit, or at least until life itself ended? I ultimately decided otherwise. Their source was to be found in the gradual removal of the usual atmospheric pressure upon the body’s surface and the resulting distention of the superficial blood-vessels—not in any actual disorganization of the animal system, as happens with respiratory difficulty, where insufficient atmospheric density fails to chemically renovate the blood within a heart ventricle. Absent this failure of renovation, I could discern no reason life might not continue even in a vacuum; for the chest’s expansion and contraction, commonly termed breathing, is a purely muscular effort and cause, not consequence, of respiration. In short, I concluded that as the frame grew accustomed to lacking atmospheric pressure, the painful sensations would steadily lessen—and while they lasted, I trusted in the iron hardness of my constitution to bear them.

“Thus, if it please your Excellencies, I have set forth some, though not all, of the reflections that induced me to devise the project of a lunar voyage. I shall now proceed to bring before you the outcome of a venture seemingly so bold in theory, and certainly so utterly without precedent in human annals.

“Having reached the altitude already specified—three miles and three-quarters—I flung from the car a quantity of feathers and perceived that I still rose with ample speed; consequently, there was no occasion to release ballast. This pleased me, for I wished to retain as much weight as possible, for reasons I shall elucidate later.”"}

{"request_id":"9a223fc4101cf4863041467c","rewritten_text":"She suddenly longed to reach the outer door; she wished to know whether it rained. Why should she accuse herself of any hidden motive? Captain Wentworth must already be gone from sight. She rose and resolved to go; she would not permit one half of herself to be forever reputed wiser than the other, or to suspect the other of being worse than it was. She would see about the rain. Yet she was immediately driven back when Captain Wentworth himself entered, accompanied by a set of ladies and gentlemen clearly of his acquaintance, whom he must have met a short way below Milsom Street. He appeared more visibly struck and flustered at seeing her than she had ever before witnessed; he flushed deeply. For the first time since they had renewed their acquaintance, she felt she betrayed the lesser composure of the two. In the few moments preceding his appearance she had gained the advantage of preparation. The overwhelming, dazzling, confusing first shock was past for her. Still, there was much to endure! Agitation, distress, joy—something between rapture and despair—filled her.

He spoke, then turned aside. His whole manner bespoke confusion. She could not have named it either cold or cordial—nothing so precise as embarrassed.

After a brief pause, he again approached and addressed her. Mutual inquiries on ordinary topics followed: neither likely became wiser from their conversation, and she remained fully aware of his being less at ease than he once had been. Simply by the necessity of constant meetings they had learned to speak to one another with apparent calmness and indifference; yet he could not manage it now. Time had altered him, or Louisa had altered him. Some sort of consciousness hung upon him. He looked exceedingly well, not as one suffering either in health or spirits, and he talked of Uppercross, the Musgroves, indeed even of Louisa, catching for an instant his old arch expression as he pronounced her name; nevertheless, it was Captain Wentworth ill at ease, uncomfortable, unable to pretend the contrary.

Anne felt no surprise, though she was pained, to observe Elizabeth refuse to recognize him. She saw that he noticed Elizabeth, that Elizabeth noticed him, that there was perfect internal recognition on both sides; she felt certain he stood ready to be acknowledged, expecting it, and she suffered to watch her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot was becoming quite impatient, now stopped at the door; the servant entered to announce it."}

{"request_id":"a8c60b802993b286e2f73464","rewritten_text":"“You must adopt a portion of my philosophy: dwell on the past only when its recollection yields delight.”

“I cannot credit you with such a philosophy. _Your_ reflections must be so free from reproach that the calm they bring is ignorance, not philosophy. It is otherwise with _me_. Painful memories force themselves forward, and they cannot, should not, be dismissed. I have been selfish all my life in conduct, though not in creed. Childhood instructed me in what was _right_, yet no one taught me to master my temper. I received sound principles, but was left to follow them with pride and conceit. Sadly, as an only son (and for years an only _child_), I was indulged by my parents, who, though virtuous themselves—my father especially, so kindly and amiable—allowed, encouraged, nearly instructed me to be self-centered and domineering, to care for no one beyond my own household, to think poorly of everyone else, to _wish_ to think poorly of their sense and worth compared with mine. Thus I was from eight to eight-and-twenty; and thus I might have remained, but for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you? You taught me a lesson, severe at the outset, yet most profitable. You humbled me as I deserved. I sought you with no doubt of a welcome. You proved how insufficient were all my claims to charm a woman deserving to be charmed.”

“Had you persuaded yourself that I should?”

“Indeed I had. What say you to my presumption? I fancied you wished, anticipated my attentions.”

“Then my manners were at fault, though unintentionally, I assure you. I never meant to mislead, though my spirits might often betray me. How you must have despised me after _that_ evening!”

“Despise you! I was angry at first, perhaps; but very soon my anger turned where it ought.”

“I hardly dare ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, indeed; surprise was all I felt.”

“Your surprise could not exceed _mine_ at being treated with attention. My conscience told me I deserved no unusual politeness, and I admit I did not expect _more_ than was due.”

“My intention _then_,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, by every civility I possessed, that I was not so base as to resent the past; and I hoped to win your pardon, to soften your bad opinion, by convincing you your rebukes had been observed.”"}

{"request_id":"7ea0e83328ed658f241199e6","rewritten_text":"I have already said he was a poet. At twenty-three he brought out his first poem, and the whole nation greeted it with enthusiasm. Fortune shone on him without pause; never had fame grown so quickly, and it was complete. The crowd praised the very verses that scholars admired in their studies; not a single voice disagreed.

During this peak of glory he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of exquisite beauty, living with her guardian; from the moment people saw them together, they seemed made for each other. Elinor lacked Woodville’s genius, yet she was generous and noble, lifted by her youth and the love she inspired above any knowledge but that of virtue and goodness. She was lovely, her manners frank and simple; her deep blue eyes shone with a light born of sensibility joined with wisdom.

They were made for each other, and soon they loved. Woodville felt love’s delight for the first time, and Elinor was thrilled to win the heart of one so beautiful and glorious among his fellows. Could anything but pure joy come from such a union?

Woodville was a poet, sought by every society, every eye fixed on him when he appeared; yet he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was rich. Her guardian did not oppose their affection: Woodville’s merit was too great for anyone to object to his lack of wealth. But her father’s dying will forbade her to marry before reaching the age of twenty-one, and her fortune depended on her obeying this command. She had just turned twenty, so she and her lover had to accept the delay. Still, they were always together, their happiness like Paradise. They studied side by side, planned their future work, and, drinking love and joy from each other’s eyes and words, they barely resented the wait for their complete union. Woodville’s glory kept growing, and Elinor became even lovelier and wiser under the guidance of her accomplished lover.

In two months Elinor would be twenty-one; everything was ready for their marriage. How can I tell the catastrophe that struck such joy? But the earth would no longer be the earth, covered with blight and sorrow, if one such pair of angelic beings had been allowed to live only for one another. Search the world and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have given them. For such supreme joy to exist, the whole order of things among us miserable earth-dwellers would have had to change."}

{"request_id":"1b97f794a9a5816db24cc5f5","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man—a very nice, kindly looking old man when I woke him. I told him my brother and I were over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and we camped on part of a raft we found. Around midnight he must have kicked his gun while dreaming, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go there, fix him up, and keep quiet about it so we could go home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who are your folks?” he says.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. After a minute he says:

“How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I say, “and it shot him.”

“Strange dream,” he says.

So he lit his lantern, grabbed his saddle-bags, and we headed out. But when he saw the canoe, he didn’t like the looks of it—said it was big enough for one but didn’t seem safe for two. I say:

“Oh, you don’t have to be afraid, sir; she carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

But he stepped on the gunwale, rocked her, shook his head, and said he reckoned he’d look around for a bigger one. But they were all locked and chained, so he took my canoe and told me to wait till he came back, or I could keep looking, or maybe go home to get them ready for the surprise if I wanted. I said I didn’t. So I told him exactly how to find the raft, and he left.

Pretty soon an idea struck me. I says to myself, suppose he can’t fix that leg in no time flat, like the saying goes? Suppose it takes him three or four days? What are we going to do—hang around until he spills the secret? No, sir; I know what I’ll do. I’ll wait, and if he comes back saying he has to go again, I’ll get down there too, even if I have to swim. We’ll tie him up, keep him, and shove off down the river; and when Tom’s done with him we’ll pay him what it’s worth, or everything we got, then let him back on shore.

So I crawled into a lumber pile to sleep, and next time I woke, the sun was high overhead! I jumped up and ran to the doctor’s house, but they told me he’d left sometime in the night and hadn’t come back yet."}

content.text: {"request_id":"1d692ab5565a98e87102abc2","rewritten_text":"I rose early the next morning, slipped past my creditors once more, and hurried to the bookseller’s stall, where I spent the little cash I had on books about Mechanics and Practical Astronomy. After getting home safely with them, I poured all my spare time into studying and quickly made the progress I believed necessary to carry out my plan. During this period I did everything I could to win over the three creditors who had been tormenting me. I eventually succeeded—partly by selling enough household furniture to cover half of what I owed, and partly by promising to pay the remainder after completing a small project I claimed to be planning, for which I asked their help. They were uneducated men, so it wasn’t hard to bring them around to my purpose.\n\n“Once everything was arranged, my wife and I, with great secrecy and care, sold what little property we still owned, and borrowed various small sums under different pretenses, never worrying about how we would repay them later. With the funds I gathered this way, I gradually purchased fine cambric muslin in twelve-yard lengths; twine; a supply of caoutchouc varnish; a large, deep, custom-made wicker basket; and several other items necessary to build and outfit an unusually large balloon. I instructed my wife to sew it together as quickly as possible, giving her all the directions she needed for the exact method to follow. Meanwhile, I wove the twine into a net of sufficient size, fitted it with a hoop and the required lines, and acquired a quadrant, a compass, a spyglass, a modified barometer, and two less common astronomical instruments. I then seized chances to move by night, to a secluded spot east of Rotterdam, five iron-bound casks holding about fifty gallons each and one larger cask; six tinned tubes, each three inches across, properly shaped, ten feet long; some of a particular metallic or semi-metallic substance whose name I won’t reveal; and a dozen demijohns of a very common acid. The gas to be produced from these materials had never been generated by anyone else—or at least never used for such a purpose. I would gladly disclose the secret if it were mine to share, but it belongs to a citizen of Nantes, France, who told it to me under certain conditions.”"}

{"request_id":"84925cb84376a7fb5c779fb2","rewritten_text":"“This must have been the very time in Mr Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “that has always stirred my special curiosity. It must have been when he first met my father and sister. I never met him myself; I only heard about him; but there was something in how he behaved toward them then, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that I have never been able to match with what he is now. It suggested a different sort of man.”

“I know it all, I know it all,” cried Mrs Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I met him, but he talked of them endlessly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I can satisfy you, perhaps, on points you would hardly expect; and as for his marriage, I knew every detail at the time. I knew every reason for and against it; I was the friend he trusted with his hopes and plans; and though I had not known his wife before, her lower place in society made that impossible, I knew her all the rest of her life, or at least until the last two years, and can answer any question you like.”

“No,” said Anne, “I have no particular question about her. I always understood they were not a happy couple. But I want to know why, at that time, he slighted my father’s acquaintance the way he did. My father was certainly ready to show him all the kindness and attention that was proper. Why did Mr Elliot hold back?”

“Mr Elliot,” replied Mrs Smith, “at that point in his life, had one goal: to make his fortune, and by a quicker route than the law. He was determined to make it through marriage. He was determined, at least, not to ruin it with an imprudent marriage; and I know he believed—rightly or wrongly, I cannot say—that your father and sister, in their politeness and invitations, were planning a match between the heir and the young lady. Such a match could never have met his ideas of wealth and independence. That was why he drew back, I assure you. He told me the whole story. He hid nothing from me. It was curious that, after leaving you behind me in Bath, the first and closest acquaintance I made on marrying should be your cousin; and that, through him, I should keep hearing of your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"b276a7e05f54c7b3809e42b0","rewritten_text":"“If you wish for one for domestic purposes, I can furnish an excellent piece and assure you that you will be satisfied with the effect. Might I enquire for whom it is meant? Should it be for the police, or for anyone associated with Scotland Yard, I fear I cannot accommodate you. The English detectives are truly our greatest allies, and by trusting in their folly, we may accomplish exactly what we desire. I could not spare even one of them.”

“I promise you,” declared Lord Arthur, “it bears no reference to the police whatsoever. In truth, the clock is designed for the Dean of Chichester.”

“Dear me! I was unaware that you felt so passionately about religion, Lord Arthur. Few young men do at present.”

“I fear you credit me with too much, Herr Winckelkopf,” said Lord Arthur, colouring. “In fact, I am quite ignorant of theology.”

“It is then a strictly private business?”

“Entirely private.”

Herr Winckelkopf lifted his shoulders and withdrew, returning shortly with a round cake of dynamite about the size of a penny, and a charming little French clock, topped with an ormolu Liberty trampling the hydra of Despotism.

Lord Arthur’s face lit up at the sight. “That is precisely what I require,” he exclaimed, “and now explain how it is set off.”

“Ah! that is my mystery,” replied Herr Winckelkopf, surveying his creation with justified pride; “let me know the exact moment you wish it to explode, and I will adjust the mechanism accordingly.”

“Well, today is Tuesday, and if you could dispatch it at once—”

“That cannot be; I have a great deal of pressing work to manage for some acquaintances in Moscow. Yet I might send it away tomorrow.”

“Oh, that will be perfectly timely!” said Lord Arthur courteously, “if it arrives tomorrow night or Thursday morning. As for the explosion, let us say Friday at noon on the dot. The Dean is invariably at home then.”

“Friday, at noon,” Herr Winckelkopf repeated, jotting the detail into a large ledger that rested on a bureau near the hearth.

“And now,” said Lord Arthur, rising, “pray inform me how much I owe you.”

“It is such a trifling affair, Lord Arthur, that I hesitate to exact payment. The dynamite costs seven and sixpence, the clock three pounds ten, and the carriage roughly five shillings. I am delighted to oblige any companion of Count Rouvaloff’s.”

“But your trouble, Herr Winckelkopf?”"}

{"request_id":"3c9f07f81a53d5cf97916979","rewritten_text":"There was a strange, enchanting quality in all of this that drew me in. It was as if he had finally woken from a long, dreamlike sleep, feeling like one of the seven sleepers or like Nourjahad from that charming imitation of an eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends were altered or dead, and on his awakening I was all he had left to love on earth.

How dear the waters, mountains, and woods of Loch Lomond became now that I had such a beloved companion for my wanderings. With my father I visited every delightful spot, whether on the islands or near the tree-sheltered waterfalls, every shady path or hollow tangled with underwood and fern. His conversation widened my mind. I felt renewed, with the freshness and vigor of a new being. His arrival seemed to lift me from a narrow patch of earth into a universe boundless to imagination and understanding. My life before had resembled a pleasant country rill, destined never to leave its native fields but to fade quietly when its course was done. Now it seemed a varied river flowing through a rich and lovely landscape, ever changing and ever beautiful. Alas! I did not foresee the desert it was about to reach, the rocks that would tear its waters, and the hideous scene that would return its image in a more twisted form. Life was bright then; I was learning to hope, and what brings more bitter despair than hope destroyed?

Is it not strange that grief should so quickly follow such heavenly happiness? I drank from an enchanted cup, yet gall lay at the bottom of its long sweetness. My heart overflowed with affection, yet it was calm because of its great depth and richness. I never imagined that misery could arise from love, and the lesson we all must learn eventually was forced on me in a way few ever endure. I mourn now, I must always mourn, those few short months of paradise; I broke no command, I tasted no apple, yet I was mercilessly driven out. Alas! my companion did, and I was cast down in his fall. But I stray from my tale—let sorrow come when its time arrives; here I may still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this joyful companionship when my aunt fell ill. I spent an entire month in her chamber nursing her, but her disease was mortal and she died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. Death is so terrible to the living; the chains of habit are so strong even when love does not bind them, and the heart must agonize when they break."}

{"request_id":"71be402630c49fcbe4fc62dc","rewritten_text":"During the meal, Mr. Bennet hardly spoke; but once the servants had departed, he deemed it fitting to converse with his visitor, and opened a topic where he anticipated Mr. Collins would excel. He remarked upon Mr. Collins’s fortunate patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and her concern for his comfort seemed quite extraordinary. Mr. Bennet could not have selected a better subject. Mr. Collins waxed eloquent in her commendation. The theme raised him to an even more solemn demeanour, and with the gravest expression he declared he had never witnessed such conduct in a person of rank—such affability and condescension as those he himself had received from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both the sermons he had had the honour to deliver before her. She had invited him twice to dine at Rosings and had summoned him only the previous Saturday to complete her quadrille table that evening. He knew many regarded Lady Catherine as proud, yet he himself had seen nothing but affability in her. She had always addressed him as she would any other gentleman; she raised no objection to his mingling with the neighbourhood’s society, nor to his leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as he could, provided he chose wisely; and had once called upon him in his modest parsonage, where she fully approved the alterations he had made and even stooped to propose some additional ones—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all exceedingly proper and polite, I am sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very agreeable woman. It is a pity great ladies in general are not more like her. Does she reside near you, sir?”

“The garden of my humble dwelling is parted only by a lane from Rosings Park, her ladyship’s residence.”

“I think you mentioned she was a widow, sir? Has she a family?”

“She has but one daughter, the heiress of Rosings and of very large property.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better off than many girls. And what sort of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is an exceedingly delightful young lady. Lady Catherine herself asserts that, in genuine beauty, Miss de Bourgh surpasses the most handsome of her sex, for there is in her features the mark of a young woman of distinguished birth.”"}

{"request_id":"6785f587b6b739f86492080e","rewritten_text":"I wanted to feign death; then my contented heirs would grab my wealth, and I could buy freedom. But I had to plan carefully. I would not be left penniless, so I had to secure some money. Alas, to what loathsome shifts must I resort? Yet a whole life of falsehood was otherwise my fate, and any time remorse over being the author of a deception made me shrink, I was irresistibly pushed back into it by another visit from some aunt or cousin. They would tell me death is the end of all people, and then declare that my father had surely lost his senses since my mother’s death; that he was mad and I was fortunate, because in one of his fits he might have killed me instead of destroying his own crazed life. And all this, to be sure, was delicately worded; not in coarse language that might hurt my feelings but

whispered so and so
in dark hint soft and low

with their eyes downcast, and sympathizing smiles or whimpers; and I listened with a calm face while every nerve trembled. I dared not say yes or no to any of this blasphemy. Oh, what a delightful life without guile! I with my dove’s look and fox’s heart; for I felt only the degradation of lying, and none of the sacred sense of conscious innocence that might atone for it. I, who once clothed myself in the bright garment of sincerity, now had to borrow many-colored garments. They might fit awkwardly at first, but practice would let me arrange them in elegant folds, to lie with grace. Yes, I might dye my soul with lies until I had completely hidden its native color. Oh, beloved father! Accept the pure heart of your unhappy daughter; let me join you unspotted as before, or you will not recognize my altered appearance. As grief might change Constance, so would deceit change me until in heaven you would say, “This is not my child.” My father, to be happy now and when we meet again, I must flee this life that is mere mockery for someone like me. Only in solitude shall I be myself; in solitude I shall be yours.

Alas! Even now I look back with disgust at the tricks and schemes by which, after many painful struggles, I carried out my retreat. I could describe at length the steps I took, first to secure a slight maintenance for the rest of my life, and then to make everyone believe I was dead. I could, but I will not."}

{"request_id":"46a55f2f6f28c35e5e4ba6bf","rewritten_text":"Dear me, she was a consummate talker. It would not have suited me to hint that it was quite late, that I was worn out, drowsy, and eager for sleep. I wished I had taken myself off to bed when I had the opportunity. Now I had to see it through; nothing else to be done. So she tinkled on and on, while the castle slumbered in profound, eerie stillness, until after a time there rose, as though from far beneath, a faint sound like a muffled scream—with such pain in it that my skin prickled. The queen paused, eyes gleaming with delight; she cocked her slender head the way a bird does when it listens. The sound tunneled up through the quiet once more.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is indeed a stubborn spirit that suffereth long. Many hours hath it been now.”

“Suffereth what?”

“The rack. Come—ye shall behold a merry sight. If he will not yield his secret even now, ye shall watch him rent in twain.”

What an exquisitely smooth she-devil she was; so calm and self-possessed, while every nerve down my legs twinged in sympathy with that man’s torment. Escorted by armored guards carrying blazing torches, we clattered through echoing hallways, descended stone staircases clammy and dripping, smelling of damp and centuries of captive darkness—a chilly, uncanny trek, a long one, not the more pleasant or shorter for the sorceress’s chatter, which dwelt on the victim and his offense. He had been accused by an unknown informer of slaying a stag in the royal preserve. I said:

“Anonymous testimony is hardly the right thing, your Highness. It were fairer to bring the accused face to face with the accuser.”

“I had not bethought me of that, it being but a small matter. Yet even an I would, I could not, for that the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, and straightway departed, so the forester knoweth him not.”

“Then this Unknown is the only witness who saw the stag killed?”

“Marry, _no_ man _saw_ the slaying; this Unknown observed the bold varlet near the spot where the stag lay, and came with right loyal fervor to betray him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown, too, was near the dead stag? Might it not be he himself who did the killing? His loyal zeal—behind a mask—seems a trifle suspicious. But what does your Highness expect to gain by racking the prisoner? Where lies the advantage?”

“He will not confess otherwise; without confession his soul were lost. For his crime the law forfeits his life—and of a surety will I see that he pay it!—yet it were peril to my own soul to let him perish unconfessed and unabsolved.”"}

{"request_id":"5b77accd9b1e378298e75672","rewritten_text":"It is quite striking that she always hears Jane better than she hears me. Jane speaks so clearly! Still, she will not find her grandmother any deafer than she was two years ago, which says a lot for someone my mother’s age—and it really has been a full two years since she was here. We have never gone so long without seeing her before, and as I was telling Mrs. Cole, we will hardly know how to pay her enough attention now.

“Are you expecting Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed! That must be a great pleasure.”

“Thank you. You are very kind. Yes, next week. Everyone is so surprised, and everyone says such nice things. I am sure she will be as happy to see her friends at Highbury as they will be to see her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot say which, because Colonel Campbell wants the carriage for one of those days. So kind of them to send her the whole way! But they always do, you know. Oh yes, Friday or Saturday next. That is what she writes about. That is why she wrote sooner than usual, as we call it; normally we would not have heard from her before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, so I imagined. I was afraid there was little chance of hearing anything of Miss Fairfax today.”

“So kind of you! No, we would not have heard, if it had not been for this particular reason—her coming here so soon. My mother is delighted! She is to stay with us for at least three months. Three months, she says so positively, as I am going to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation is that the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon persuaded her father and mother to come over and see her immediately. They had not meant to go until the summer, but she is so impatient to see them again—for until she married last October, she was never away from them for more than a week, which must make it very odd to be in different countries, I was going to say in different kingdoms. So she wrote a very urgent letter to her mother—or her father, I honestly do not know which, but we shall see in Jane’s letter—wrote in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, urging them to come right away, and they would meet them in Dublin and take them back to their country estate, Balycraig, which I imagine is a beautiful place."}

{"request_id":"90bf9dc41f2e7530baf6036e","rewritten_text":"“Well, then,” he pressed on, “what conclusion have we drawn? What manner of impression have I fixed upon your imagination?”

Dupin’s question sent a chill crawling over me. “A madman,” I answered, “must have committed this act—some crazed maniac who broke loose from a nearby Maison de Santé.”

“In certain points,” he returned, “your notion bears relevance. Yet the voices of lunatics, even in their wildest fits, never correspond to that singular voice heard upon the stairs. However erratic a madman may be, he belongs to some nation, and his tongue, despite disjointed words, keeps regular syllables. Moreover, the hair of a madman is nothing like what I now hold. I unwound this little tuft from the stiffly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Consider what you can make of it.”

“Dupin!” I cried, thoroughly shaken; “this hair is extraordinary—it is not human.”

“I have not claimed it is,” he replied. “But before we pronounce on that, look at this slight sketch I have drawn. It reproduces exactly what part of the testimony described as ‘dark bruises and deep indentations of fingernails’ upon Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what Messrs. Dumas and Etienne called a ‘row of livid spots, plainly finger marks.’

“You will observe,” he continued, laying the paper on the table, “that the sketch conveys the idea of a firm, unmoving grip. There is no trace of slipping. Each finger seems to have maintained—perhaps up to the instant of death—the dreadful hold with which it first sank in. Try now to place all your fingers simultaneously within the respective impressions as shown here.”

I tried, and could not manage it.

“Perhaps we are not testing properly,” he said. “The sheet lies on a flat plane; a human throat is cylindrical. Here is a billet of wood, roughly equal in circumference. Wrap the drawing around it and repeat the experiment.”

I complied, but the impossibility stood out even clearer. “This,” I declared, “cannot be the mark of a human hand.”

“Then read,” said Dupin, “this passage from Cuvier.”

It was an exact anatomical and general description of the grand fulvous Orang-Outang of the East Indian islands. Everyone knows well the enormous size, immense strength and agility, savage ferocity, and mimicking instincts of those animals. At once I grasped the full horror of the murder.

“The description of the digits,” I said, finishing the reading, “corresponds perfectly with this drawing.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"29b0d7747a5580ee03fe929e","rewritten_text":"How long I lingered in that condition no human arithmetic could determine. It must, nevertheless, have been a substantial interval, for when I partially regained some consciousness of being, dawn was breaking, the balloon towering at an immense altitude over a desert of sea, and not the faintest hint of land could be detected anywhere within the sweeping circle of the horizon. Yet the sensations that greeted my recovery were far less agonizing than might be expected. In truth, there was a certain budding insanity in the tranquil inspection I began to make of my predicament. I raised each hand, one at a time, to my eyes, marveling at what incident could have produced the bulging veins and the ghastly blackness staining my fingernails. Next I scrutinized my head, shaking it again and again, and feeling it with meticulous care until I was satisfied it was not, as I had been more than half suspecting, larger than my balloon. Then, with an air of sagacity, I thrust my fingers into both breeches pockets, and, missing a notebook and a toothpick case, tried to account for their loss; as no explanation offered itself, I experienced a sting of vexation. Only then did it occur to me that the joint of my left ankle was suffering great uneasiness, and a dim comprehension of my situation began to flicker through my brain. But, strangely enough, I felt neither amazement nor terror. If any emotion stirred at all, it was a kind of inward chuckle at the ingenuity I was ready to display in escaping this scrape; never did I for a moment treat my final safety as a matter open to doubt. For several minutes I lay plunged in the deepest contemplation. I clearly remember frequently compressing my lips, placing my forefinger beside my nose, and employing other gestures and grimaces familiar to men who, seated comfortably in their chairs, ponder affairs of intricacy or consequence. When I believed my thoughts sufficiently marshaled, I carefully and deliberately slipped my hands behind me and unfastened the large iron buckle attached to the waistband of my inexpressibles. The buckle had three teeth which, being somewhat rusty, rotated on their pivots only with great difficulty. After some labor I managed to turn them to a right angle from the buckle’s body and was pleased to see they held firm in that pose. Clamping the makeshift instrument between my teeth, I then set about untying the knot of my cravat. Several times I was obliged to pause before the maneuver could be accomplished, yet accomplished it was at last."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a4e32c3a46ea809790fe6a34","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water to conclude the feast. After a while Becky proposed they move on. Tom fell silent a moment before saying, “Becky, can you stand it if I tell you something?” Becky’s face went white, but she believed she could. “Well, Becky, we have to stay here where there’s water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!” Becky broke into tears and laments. Tom tried to soothe her, but with little success. Presently Becky said, “Tom!” “What is it, Becky?” “They’ll miss us and search for us!” “Yes, they will! Of course they will!” “Maybe they’re searching already, Tom.” “I suppose maybe they are. I hope so.” “When would they miss us, Tom?” “When they return to the boat, I guess.” “Tom, it might be dark then—would they see we weren’t there?” “I don’t know. But your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.” Becky’s frightened expression brought Tom to his senses and he realized his blunder. Becky hadn’t been expected home that night! The children fell silent and reflective. Soon Becky’s renewed sobs told Tom that what he feared had struck her too—Sabbath morning might be half gone before Mrs. Thatcher found out Becky was not at Mrs. Harper’s. They fixed their gaze on their little candle, watching it waste away without mercy; saw the half-inch wick stand alone at last; watched the weak flame flutter, climb a thin trail of smoke, pause a moment at the top, and then—the terror of total darkness! Becky later slowly realized she was crying in Tom’s arms; neither knew how long it had taken. All they remembered was that after what felt an endless stretch of time, both awoke from a heavy stupor of sleep and took up their misery once more. Tom said it might already be Sunday—perhaps even Monday. He tried to get Becky talking, but her anguish was overwhelming—every hope crushed. Tom insisted they must have been missed long ago and someone surely sought them. He shouted in case someone might hear, but the echo in the darkness sounded so ghastly he dared not try again. Hours crept by, and hunger came to plague them. Tom still had part of his half of the cake; they split it and ate. Yet they only felt more ravenous than before."}

content.text: {"request_id":"83ba598c55e05de38ad17650","rewritten_text":"After a while, midnight boomed from the tall tower at Westminster, and with each deep stroke the night seemed to quiver. Then the railway lights went out, leaving one lamp glowing like a large ruby on a giant mast, and the city’s roar faded. At two o’clock he got up and wandered toward Blackfriars. Everything looked unreal, as if in a strange dream. The houses across the river seemed built from darkness. It was as if silver and shadow had remade the world. The huge dome of St. Paul’s loomed like a bubble in the dim air. As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle he saw a man leaning over the parapet, and when he drew closer the man looked up, the gaslight shining on his face. It was Mr. Podgers, the palm reader. No one could mistake the fat, loose face, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the weak smile, the sensual mouth. Lord Arthur stopped. A brilliant idea flashed through him, and he crept quietly forward. In a moment he grabbed Mr. Podgers by the legs and threw him into the Thames. There was a coarse oath, a heavy splash, and silence. Lord Arthur peered over but saw nothing of the palm reader except a tall hat spinning in a swirl of moonlit water. After a while it too sank, and Mr. Podgers vanished. At one point he thought he saw the bulky misshapen figure swimming toward the bridge stairs, and dread of failure swept over him, but it was only a reflection, and when the moon came out from the clouds it disappeared. At last he seemed to have fulfilled the decree of fate. He let out a deep sigh of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips. “Have you dropped anything, sir?” asked a voice behind him suddenly. He turned and saw a policeman with a bull’s-eye lantern. “Nothing important, sergeant,” he replied with a smile, hailed a passing hansom, jumped in, and told the driver to go to Belgrave Square. For the next few days he wavered between hope and fear. At times he almost expected Mr. Podgers to walk in, yet at other moments he felt Fate could not be so unfair to him. Twice he went to the palm reader’s address on West Moon Street, but he could not bring himself to ring. He longed for certainty yet feared it. At last it came. He was in the club smoking-room having tea, listening wearily to Surbiton describe the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

{"request_id":"36fc510063cce81b8c9c0918","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, face ashen with terror and eyes blazing with grief, pushing through the ring of fur-clad footmen about the striped awning, apparently blind and deaf to everything. The night was piercingly cold; the gas-lamps around the square flared and sputtered in the sharp wind, yet his hands burned with fever and his brow felt aflame. He forged on, with the unsteady pace of a drunken man. A policeman eyed him curiously as he passed, and a beggar who slunk from an archway to plead for coins shrank back, frightened by a wretchedness deeper than his own. Once he halted beneath a lamp and stared at his hands. He fancied he already saw the blot of blood there, and a faint cry slipped from his shaking lips.

Murder! That was what the cheiromantist had discerned in his palm. Murder! The very night seemed aware of it, and the desolate wind shrieked it in his ear. The shadowed corners of the streets teemed with it. It grinned down from the roofs.

His first stop was the Park, its sombre grove exerting a strange spell. He leaned, exhausted, against the railings, pressing his brow to the damp metal, listening to the quivering hush among the trees. “Murder! murder!” he kept muttering, as if sheer repetition might dull the horror of the word. The sound of his own voice made him quake, yet he almost wished Echo would catch it and rouse the sleeping city. He felt an insane impulse to halt any passer-by and pour out everything.

Next he drifted over Oxford Street into cramped, sordid lanes. Two painted women jeered at him as he went past. From a dark courtyard came oaths and blows, followed by piercing screams, and on a wet doorstep he glimpsed the hunched shapes of poverty and age. A strange compassion seized him. Were these children of vice and want destined for their fate, just as he was for his? Were they, like him, no more than puppets in some monstrous spectacle?

Yet it was not the enigma of suffering but its comedy that struck him, its utter futility, its grotesque lack of meaning. How incoherent everything appeared! How bereft of harmony! He marvelled at the clash between the day’s shallow optimism and the true facts of life. He was still very young.

Eventually he found himself before Marylebone Church. The mute roadway stretched like a long ribbon of polished silver, marked here and there by the dark arabesques of wavering shadows."}

{"request_id":"4bd6bb859cb5cb9357ba1d1d","rewritten_text":"She wasn’t mistaken about the rats. Every so often one would poke its snout out of a hole in the corner. She kept things close at hand to fling at them whenever she was by herself, or else they’d torment her without cease. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot and said she usually could hit with it, but she’d strained her arm a day or two before and wasn’t sure she could throw straight now. Still, she watched for her chance and soon let fly at a rat; she missed badly and cried “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to get away before the old man returned, but naturally I didn’t let that show. I took the lead, and the first rat that poked out, I let go; if he’d stayed put he’d have been a mighty sick rat. She called it fine work and figured I’d bag the next. She retrieved the lead and brought a hank of yarn she wanted me to help with. I held up my hands while she draped the hank over them, talking about her own affairs and her husband’s. But she broke off to say:

“Keep watch for the rats. You better keep the lead in your lap, ready.”

So she dropped the lump into my lap then and there, and I squeezed my knees together on it while she kept on. But only for a minute. Then she took the hank away, looked me straight in the eye, friendly-like, and said:

“Come now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob?—or which?”

I reckon I trembled like a leaf, not knowing what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make sport of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m a bother here, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit right where you are. I won’t hurt you, and I won’t inform on you, neither. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it; and more than that, I’ll help you. My old man will too if you want him. See, you’re just a runaway apprentice, that’s all. It’s nothing. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been mistreated, and you decided to light out. Bless you, child, I’d never tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"557c43c177659ed80cf53728","rewritten_text":"They know how sharp the lad is; he’ll get sent down for life. They won’t settle for anything less than making the Artful a lifer.”

“What d’ye mean by lagging and a lifer?” Mr. Bolter demanded. “What’s the sense of talking to me like that? Why don’t yer speak so’s I can understand?”

Fagin was about to translate these mysterious phrases into plain talk; had he done so, Mr. Bolter would have learned they meant “transportation for life.” But the conversation was interrupted by Master Bates, hands buried in his breeches-pockets and his face twisted into a half-comic distress.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” Charley declared, after he and the newcomer were introduced.

“What’s that supposed to mean?”

“They’ve tracked down the gent the box belongs to; two or three others are coming to ’dentify him; and the Artful’s booked for the long voyage,” said Master Bates. “I’ll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband, to visit him before he starts his travels. To think Jack Dawkins—flash Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—should be deported over a cheap twopenny-halfpenny snuff-box! Never thought he’d be nabbed for less than a gold watch with chain and seals, at the very least. Oh, why didn’t he clean out some wealthy old gent of all his valubles, and sail off like a gentleman, instead of like any common prig, with no honour nor glory!”

Having voiced his sympathy for his unlucky friend, Master Bates dropped onto the nearest chair, wearing an air of gloom and disappointment.

“What do you mean by saying he’s no honour nor glory?” Fagin cried, turning a furious look on his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the top-sawyer among you? Any of you ever match him or get near him on any scent, eh?”

“Not one,” Master Bates answered, his voice thick with remorse. “Not a soul.”

“Then what’s this talk? What are you bawling about?” Fagin snapped.

“’Cause it isn’t entered on the record, is it?” Charley shot back, stung into full defiance by his grief. “’Cause it won’t show in the indictment; ’cause nobody’ll ever know half of what he could do. How’ll he be listed in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe not there at all. Oh, my eye, my eye, what a blow!”

“Ha! ha!” Fagin crowed, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter in a fit of mirth that shook him as though he had the palsy. “See the pride they take in their trade, my dear.”"}

{"request_id":"6383945c9cfa65697765182e","rewritten_text":"He carefully drove a peg into the exact spot where the beetle had fallen. Then he pulled a tape measure from his pocket. He fixed one end to the nearest part of the tree trunk, ran the tape down to the peg, and extended it farther along the line already set by the tree and peg for fifty feet, while Jupiter cleared the brambles with a scythe. At that point he drove another peg. Using that second peg as the center, he marked a rough circle about four feet wide. He took up a spade, gave one to Jupiter and another to me, and urged us to start digging at once.

To be honest, digging held no charm for me, and at that time I would gladly have refused. Evening was approaching, and I was worn out from the day’s exertions. Yet I saw no way to avoid it and dreaded upsetting my poor friend by refusing. If I could have counted on Jupiter’s help, I would have tried to drag the madman home by force, but I knew too well the old servant’s loyalty to hope he would ever oppose his master. I felt sure my friend had fallen for one of those Southern tales about buried treasure, and that finding the beetle—or Jupiter’s claim that it was “a real gold bug”—had convinced him. A mind already leaning toward madness could easily latch onto such ideas, especially when they fit its favorite notions. I remembered, too, how he had called the beetle “the key to his fortune.” Altogether, I was frustrated and bewildered, but finally decided to make the best of it, dig willingly, and end the fantasy sooner by showing him the truth with my own eyes.

Once we lit the lanterns, we attacked the ground with a zeal that would have suited a saner purpose. As the light shone on our bodies and tools, I could not help thinking what a striking group we made, and how odd and suspicious our work would have seemed to any wanderer who might have come upon us.

We dug steadily for two hours."}

content.text: {"request_id":"52ea3f955f4c6e90b1d97f67","rewritten_text":"On the morning fixed for Admiral and Mrs Croft to inspect Kellynch Hall, Anne felt it most natural to make her nearly daily visit to Lady Russell’s, keeping out of the way until the whole matter was settled, and then felt it most natural to regret missing the chance of seeing them. The meeting of the parties turned out extremely satisfactory, and settled the affair immediately. Each lady had been predisposed toward agreement, and therefore perceived nothing but courtesy in the other; and regarding the gentlemen, there was such thorough good humour, such frank, trusting generosity in the Admiral, that Sir Walter could not help responding—especially as Mr Shepherd had flattered him with reports that the Admiral already knew him as a paragon of manners, leading him to his very finest, most polished behaviour. House, grounds, furniture, all met approval, the Crofts were approved, terms, timing, every aspect was right, and Mr Shepherd’s clerks were set to work without a single preliminary point to adjust of all that “This indenture sheweth.” Sir Walter promptly declared the Admiral the handsomest sailor he had ever encountered, and even said that if his own valet might regulate the Admiral’s hair, he would never feel embarrassed to appear anywhere in his company; and the Admiral, with equal warmth, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I imagined we should come quickly to terms, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, yet there seems no harm in him”—a pair of mutual compliments that would have been reckoned nearly equivalent. The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas; and as Sir Walter intended to move to Bath during the preceding month, no time could be lost in arranging every dependent detail. Lady Russell, convinced Anne would not be permitted any usefulness or importance in selecting the house they were to secure, was most unwilling to have her rushed off so soon, and hoped to contrive that she might remain behind until she herself could escort her to Bath after Christmas; but having commitments that would take her away from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not extend the invitation she wished, and Anne, though apprehensive of possible September heat in the white glare of Bath and deeply sorry to forfeit the influence, so sweet and so melancholy, of autumn in the countryside, still did not feel, all things considered, that she desired to stay."}

content.text: {"request_id":"2e9c7ab899260f81c276cf12","rewritten_text":"“Never!” the girl retorted. “Tell me why?” “For one reason,” she answered with steady resolve, “for one reason alone: the lady is aware and will stand beside me; I know she will, for she has pledged as much. Besides, for this other reason—though he has lived wickedly, I have lived wickedly too. Many of us have trod the same paths together, and I will not betray them, when any one of them—bad as they are—might have betrayed me, yet didn’t.” “Then,” said the gentleman swiftly, as if this were the point he had strained to reach, “place Monks in my hands and leave him for me to manage.” “What if he betrays the others?” “In that event,” he replied, “if the truth must be forced from him, there the matter will end. There must be passages in Oliver’s little story which it would be painful to drag into public view; and once the truth is laid bare, the others shall go unscathed.” “And if it is not?” the girl suggested. “Then,” continued the gentleman, “Fagin shall not be surrendered to justice without your consent. In such a situation I believe I could show you reasons that would prevail upon you to grant it.” “Do I have the lady’s promise to that effect?” the girl asked. “You do,” Rose answered. “My faithful pledge.” “Monks would never discover how you learned what you know?” the girl said after a brief pause. “Never,” declared the gentleman. “The information would be applied in such a manner that he could not even conjecture.” “I have been a liar, and among liars since my earliest days,” she said after another silence, “but I will accept your word.” Receiving reassurance from both that she could safely do so, she continued—in such a low tone that the listener often struggled to grasp even the general sense of her words—to describe, by name and situation, the public-house where she had been shadowed that night. From her occasional pauses it seemed the gentleman was hurriedly noting the details she furnished. When she had precisely laid out the location of the building, the best point from which to observe it without attracting attention, and the night and hour when Monks most frequently visited, she fell silent for a few moments, apparently to summon his features and bearing more vividly to mind. “He is tall,” she said, “a powerfully built man, though not fleshy. He has a stealthy gait; and as he walks he constantly glances over his shoulder, first on one side, then the other.”"}

He entered the Temple and revived himself by pacing King’s Bench Walk and Paper Buildings twice before heading to Stryver’s chambers. Stryver’s clerk, who never joined these meetings, had gone home, so Stryver opened the door himself. He wore slippers, a loose dressing gown, and left his throat bare for comfort. His eyes showed the wild, strained lines common to heavy drinkers of his kind, marks you can trace through portraits of every drinking age, from Jeffries onward. “You’re a little late, Memory,” Stryver said. “About the usual time; maybe fifteen minutes later.” They went into a shabby room lined with books and strewn with papers, warmed by a roaring fire. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the chaos of papers a table gleamed with plenty of wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons. “You’ve had your bottle, I see, Sydney.” “Two tonight, I think. I’ve been dining with the client—or watching him dine—it’s all the same!” “That was a sharp point you used in the identification, Sydney. How did you hit on it? When did it occur to you?” “I thought he was a handsome fellow, and that I might have been much like him, if I’d had any luck.” Mr. Stryver laughed until his early paunch shook. “You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.” With a sullen air, the jackal loosened his clothes, went into the next room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. Soaking the towels and partially wringing them out, he folded them onto his head in a way dreadful to see, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!” “Not much boiling down tonight, Memory,” Stryver said cheerfully as he sorted through his papers. “How much?” “Only two sets.” “Give me the worst first.” “There they are, Sydney. Fire away!” The lion stretched out on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking table, while the jackal sat at his own littered table on the other side, bottles and glasses within easy reach."}

{"request_id":"cbfb9ed1197cc21b93945883","rewritten_text":"We finally agreed to live together while I stayed in the city; and since my finances were less strained than his, I paid to rent and furnish a place whose style matched the rather theatrical gloom we both shared—a timeworn, grotesque mansion, long abandoned thanks to superstitions we didn’t bother to investigate, and now tottering toward collapse in a secluded, desolate corner of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had anyone known how we spent our days in that house, we would have been thought mad—though likely harmlessly so. We were completely secluded. We let no visitors in. I had kept our address secret from all my former acquaintances, and it had been many years since Dupin had either known or been known in Paris. We existed entirely within ourselves.

It was one of Dupin’s whims (what else can I call it?) to adore the night for its own sake; and, as with all his eccentricities, I quietly indulged him, surrendering myself to his wild fancies without reserve. The dark goddess could not stay with us always, but we could imitate her presence. At the first hint of dawn we shut all the grimy shutters of our old house, lighting a couple of tapers that were heavily perfumed yet gave off only the palest, ghastliest light. By their glimmer we occupied our minds in dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the arrival of real Darkness. Then we went out arm in arm, continuing the day’s discussions or wandering far and wide until late, seeking in the wild lights and shadows of the crowded city that endless mental stimulation which quiet observation can offer.

During these nights I couldn’t help noticing, and admiring (though I should have expected it from his vivid imagination), Dupin’s peculiar gift for analysis. He seemed eager to practice it—if not exactly to show it off—and freely admitted how much pleasure it gave him. He told me, with a low, amused laugh, that most men were transparent to him, and he liked to follow such claims with direct, startling displays of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. In those moments his manner was cold and distant; his eyes looked blank; and his voice, usually a warm tenor, climbed to a treble that might have sounded petulant were it not for the deliberateness and clarity of his speech."}

{"request_id":"79a59c39732d0c16ea327705","rewritten_text":"“You’ve encouraged an artificial sense of soul and spirit in him, ma’am, unfit for someone of his station—just as the board, Mrs. Sowerberry, who are practical philosophers, would tell you. What business have paupers with souls or spirits? It’s enough that we let them have living bodies. If you had kept the boy on gruel, ma’am, this would never have happened.”

“Dear, dear!” cried Mrs. Sowerberry, lifting her eyes devoutly to the kitchen ceiling. “This is what comes of being generous!”

Mrs. Sowerberry’s generosity to Oliver had amounted to bestowing upon him all the filthy scraps no one else would touch; so there was considerable meekness and self-sacrifice in her taking Mr. Bumble’s heavy accusation to heart, although, to do her justice, she was entirely innocent in thought, word, or deed.

“Ah!” said Mr. Bumble, when the lady lowered her gaze, “the only thing left to do now, that I can think of, is to keep him in the cellar for a day or two, until he’s starved down a bit; then bring him out and keep him on gruel throughout the apprenticeship. He comes from bad blood. Highly excitable temperaments, Mrs. Sowerberry! Both the nurse and the doctor said that his mother forced her way here despite agony and obstacles that would have killed any well-disposed woman weeks sooner.”

At this point in Mr. Bumble’s speech, Oliver, catching just enough to know his mother was being mentioned, resumed kicking with such ferocity that every other sound was drowned out. Mr. Sowerberry returned at that moment. Oliver’s offense was explained to him with the embellishments the ladies thought best to inflame his anger, and he unlocked the cellar door in an instant, dragging his rebellious apprentice out by the collar.

Oliver’s clothes had been torn during the beating he’d taken; his face was bruised and scratched, and his hair hung in wild strands over his forehead. The fiery flush still burned, however; and when he was hauled from his prison, he scowled boldly at Noah, looking quite undaunted.

“Now, you’re a fine young fellow, aren’t you?” said Sowerberry, shaking Oliver and boxing his ear.

“He called my mother names,” Oliver said.

“Well, what if he did, you ungrateful brat?” said Mrs. Sowerberry. “She deserved what he said, and worse.”

“She didn’t,” said Oliver.
