content.text: {"request_id":"ddb01af606556b2c8289cb52","rewritten_text":"“But, in fact, when we ascend to any given altitude, the mass of air we leave beneath us in any further ascent is by no means proportional to the extra height climbed (as is clear from what I explained earlier), but steadily decreases. It is therefore clear that, no matter how high we go, we cannot literally reach a boundary beyond which there is no atmosphere. I argued it must exist, even if it exists in a state of infinite thinness. “On the other hand, I knew that many arguments attempt to prove a real and definable limit to the atmosphere, beyond which there is absolutely no air. Yet a consideration overlooked by those who defend such a limit seemed to me, though not a definitive refutation of their belief, a point worth very serious investigation. When we compare the intervals between Encke’s comet’s successive arrivals at perihelion, after accounting with utmost precision for all disturbances caused by planetary attraction, we find the periods gradually shortening; that is, the major axis of the comet’s ellipse shrinks, slowly but with perfect regularity. This is exactly what should occur if the comet experiences resistance from an extremely rare ethereal medium pervading the region of its orbit. For it is clear that such a medium, by slowing the comet’s speed, would increase its centripetal force by weakening its centrifugal force. In other words, the sun’s attraction would constantly gain strength, drawing the comet closer with each revolution. Indeed, there is no other way to explain this variation. Yet again: the actual diameter of the comet’s nebulosity contracts rapidly as it approaches the sun and expands just as rapidly as it heads toward aphelion. Was I not justified in agreeing with M. Valz that this apparent decrease in volume originates from compression by the same ethereal medium I just mentioned, which is only denser the nearer it lies to the sun? The lens-shaped phenomenon called the zodiacal light also deserved careful thought. This glow, so striking in the tropics and impossible to mistake for any meteoric brightness, rises obliquely from the horizon and generally follows the sun’s equator. It seemed to me clearly a kind of rare atmosphere extending outward from the sun, beyond at least the orbit of Venus, and, I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not suppose this medium was limited to the comet’s orbital path or to the sun’s immediate surroundings.”"}

{"request_id":"f8fd088e55006be2ac8a2644","rewritten_text":"The party separated into two adjoining benches, Anne seated among those in front, while Mr Elliot, aided by his ally Colonel Wallis, managed to secure the spot beside her. Miss Elliot, encircled by her cousins and the central recipient of Colonel Wallis’s attentions, felt perfectly satisfied.

Anne’s spirits were well suited for an evening’s amusement; it occupied her mind just enough. She could indulge the tender, laugh at the lively, heed the learned, and endure the tedious, and she had never enjoyed a concert more, at least through the first act. Near its end, during the pause after an Italian song, she explained its words to Mr Elliot. They shared a concert bill between them.

“This,” she said, “captures nearly the sense—or really the meaning—of the lines, for surely the sense of an Italian love-song is not to be discussed; yet it is as close as I can render it, since I make no claim to knowing the language. My Italian is very poor.”

“Yes, yes, I see it,” he replied. “You clearly know nothing about it. You possess only enough Italian to turn these inverted, rearranged, clipped lines into plain, intelligible, polished English at first sight. There is no need to protest your ignorance further. The evidence is before us.”

“I cannot argue against such gracious praise; but I should dread undergoing a real scholar’s scrutiny.”

“I have not enjoyed the privilege of visiting Camden Place so long,” he rejoined, “without learning something of Miss Anne Elliot; and I consider her as one whose modesty prevents the world from recognizing half her talents, and whose talents are more than modesty would allow any other woman naturally to possess.”

“For shame, for shame! Such flattery is excessive. I forget what comes next,” she said, turning back to the bill.

“Perhaps,” Mr Elliot murmured, “I have known your character longer than you suppose.”

“Indeed! In what way? You could only know of me since my arrival in Bath, unless you heard of me earlier through my own relations.”

“I was acquainted with you by report long before you reached Bath. I had listened to those who knew you well describe you. I have been familiar with your character for many years. Your person, your mind, accomplishments, demeanor—they were all known to me.”

Mr Elliot achieved the effect he sought. No one can resist the allure of such mystery."}

After a short interval he returned, saying he could not find Miss Virginia anywhere. Since she usually went out into the garden each evening to gather flowers for the dinner table, Mrs. Otis felt no concern at first; but when six o’clock struck and there was still no sign of Virginia, she grew genuinely distressed. She dispatched the boys to search the grounds while she and Mr. Otis went through every room in the house. By half-past six the boys were back, reporting they could discover no trace of their sister. Everyone was now in a state of extreme agitation, uncertain how to proceed, when Mr. Otis suddenly recollected that a few days earlier he had granted a band of gypsies permission to camp in the park. He immediately set off for Blackfell Hollow, where he knew they had been, taking his eldest son and two farm-servants. The little Duke of Cheshire, nearly beside himself with worry, entreated to accompany them, but Mr. Otis refused, fearing there might be some disturbance. On reaching the clearing, he found the gypsies gone, and their departure plainly abrupt, for the fire still burned and plates lay scattered on the grass. After sending Washington and the two men to comb the neighbourhood, he hurried home and wired every police inspector in the county, instructing them to watch for a little girl said to have been abducted by tramps or gypsies. He then ordered his horse and, insisting that his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, rode off along the Ascot road with a groom. He had scarcely covered a couple of miles when he heard a horse pounding behind him. Turning, he saw the little Duke racing up on his pony, flushed and bareheaded. “I’m dreadfully sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy panted, “but I can’t touch dinner while Virginia is lost. Pray don’t be cross with me. If you had let us become engaged last year, all this trouble would never have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! I won’t go!” The Minister could not help smiling at the handsome young rogue, and was deeply moved by his devotion to Virginia, so he leaned from his saddle, clapped him affectionately on the shoulders, and said, “Very well, Cecil, if you refuse to return, I suppose you must ride with me. {"request_id":"bc70aca7e53160b6587acc29","rewritten_text":"When we got back to the raft and he started counting, he saw he had collected eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also walked off with a three-gallon jug of whiskey he found under a wagon on his way home through the woods. The king said that, all things considered, it beat any day he’d ever had in the missionary business. He said there was no point pretending otherwise—heathens were nothing compared to pirates when you wanted to work a camp meeting.

The duke had thought he was doing pretty well until the king showed up, but after that he wasn’t nearly as impressed with himself. He had set up and printed two small jobs for farmers at that printing office—horse bills—and pocketed four dollars. He had also taken in ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper, which he promised to run for four dollars if they paid upfront—so they did. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he sold three subscriptions at half a dollar each on the condition they pay in advance; they were planning to pay with cordwood and onions like usual, but he claimed he’d just bought the business, cut the price as low as he could, and was going to run it for cash. He set up a little poem he made himself—three verses—kind of sweet and sad, called “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart”—and he left it all set up ready to print without charging a cent. All told, he took in nine dollars and a half and said he’d earned it with a decent day’s work.

Then he showed us another little job he’d printed and hadn’t charged for because it was for us. It showed a picture of a runaway Black man with a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” underneath. The text was all about Jim and described him exactly. It said he ran away from St. Jacques’ plantation forty miles below New Orleans last winter, and probably headed north, and that anyone who caught him and sent him back would get the reward plus expenses.

“Now,” says the duke, “after tonight we can travel in daylight if we want. Whenever we see anyone coming we can tie Jim hand and foot with a rope, lay him in the wigwam, show this handbill, and say we caught him up the river. We can say we were too poor to ride a steamboat, so we got this little raft on credit from friends and are heading down to collect the reward.”"}

{"request_id":"75ef2a008355e5e7891400dc","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by heaven’s blue sky, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you will never see me again as long as they live. Go home and begin your work; I will watch their progress with indescribable anxiety. Do not fear, for when you are ready, I will appear.”

With those words he suddenly left me, perhaps afraid my feelings might change. I watched him descend the mountain faster than an eagle, and soon he was lost among the waves of ice.

His story had filled the entire day, and the sun was touching the horizon when he departed. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness overtook me, but my heart was heavy and my steps slow. The effort of winding along the narrow mountain paths and placing my feet securely with each slow step burdened me, while my mind was consumed with the day’s events. It was well into night when I reached the halfway resting place and sat beside the fountain. The stars shone only now and then as clouds drifted past them; dark pines rose before me, and here and there a fallen tree lay on the ground. The scene was solemn and roused unsettling thoughts. I wept bitterly, and clasping my hands in agony, cried out, “Oh stars, clouds, and winds, you are all about to mock me; if you truly pity me, crush sensation and memory, let me become nothing. Otherwise, leave me, depart, and let me stay in darkness.”

These thoughts were wild and miserable, yet I cannot describe how the endless flicker of the stars oppressed me or how I listened to every gust of wind as though it were some dull, hideous sirocco coming to consume me.

Morning broke before I reached the village of Chamounix. I took no rest but returned straight to Geneva. Even within my own heart I could not express what I felt—my emotions weighed on me like a mountain, and their sheer force crushed my agony beneath them. So I returned home, and when I entered the house, I appeared before my family. My gaunt, frenzied look filled them with alarm, but I answered no questions; I hardly spoke. I felt banished, as if I no longer had any right to their sympathy, as if I could never again share their company."}

{"request_id":"fe77ae486ec250448ec8132f","rewritten_text":"Lady Windermere was giving her final reception before Easter, and Bentinck House seemed more thronged than ever. Six Cabinet Ministers had drifted over from the Speaker’s Levée wearing their stars and ribbons, every pretty woman displayed her most stylish gown, and at the far end of the picture-gallery stood the Princess Sophia of Carlsrühe, a stout Tartar-like figure with minute black eyes and superb emeralds, shouting dreadful French and laughing uproariously at every remark addressed to her. The assembly was certainly a remarkable mixture. Resplendent peeresses chatted amiably with fierce Radicals, popular preachers brushed shoulders with celebrated sceptics, a whole cluster of bishops endlessly pursued a plump prima-donna from room to room, several Royal Academicians lingered on the staircase disguised as artists, and rumor insisted that for a time the supper-room was completely overflowing with geniuses. Indeed, it ranked among Lady Windermere’s finest evenings, and the Princess did not depart till close upon half-past eleven.

When the Princess left, Lady Windermere went back to the picture-gallery, where a renowned political economist was earnestly expounding the scientific basis of music to an outraged Hungarian virtuoso, and began chatting with the Duchess of Paisley. She looked marvelously lovely, with her stately ivory throat, her large forget-me-not blue eyes, and the weighty masses of her golden hair. True _or pur_ it was—not that pale straw shade which now presumes to claim the graceful name of gold, but the very gold woven into sunbeams or concealed within rare amber; it bestowed upon her face something of the halo of a saint, mingled with no small measure of a sinner’s allure. She presented a curious psychological puzzle. Early on she had grasped the significant truth that nothing so closely resembles innocence as a misstep; through a succession of daring escapades, half of them entirely harmless, she had won all the privileges of having a personality. More than once she had changed her husband—Debrett actually credits her with three marriages—but as she never changed her lover, society long ago stopped whispering scandal. She was now forty, without children, and possessed of that insatiable hunger for pleasure which is the secret to perpetual youth.

Suddenly she scanned the room with bright eagerness and exclaimed, in her clear contralto, “Where is my cheiromantist?”

“Your what, Gladys?” cried the Duchess, giving a startled jump.

“My cheiromantist, Duchess; I cannot exist without him at the moment.”

“Dear Gladys! you are perpetually so inventive,” murmured the Duchess, striving to remember what exactly a cheiromantist might be, and praying it was not identical with a chiropodist.

“He comes to inspect my hand twice every week without fail,” Lady Windermere went on, “and he is endlessly fascinating about it.”"}

{"request_id":"1520025e7128cfd9f52bdfed","rewritten_text":"“He was handed over to you. You see I know the circumstances?”

“Such is the fact, assuredly,” Defarge replied. His wife, still knitting and trilling, had brushed his elbow to remind him to respond, but always briefly.

“It was to you,” the spy went on, “that his daughter came; and it was from your keeping that she took him, attended by a trim brown gentleman—what is his name?—with the little wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—to England.”

“Such is the fact,” Defarge repeated.

“Most interesting recollections!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Indeed?” said Defarge.

“You hear little of them now?” he asked.

“No,” Defarge answered.

“In truth,” Madame interposed, glancing up from her handiwork and her soft tune, “we hear nothing of them. We learned they arrived safely, and perhaps received one letter, perhaps two; but since then they have pursued their path in life—we, ours—and there has been no correspondence.”

“Exactly so, madame,” the spy returned. “She is about to be married.”

“About to be?” Madame echoed. “She was pretty enough to have married long before. You English are cold, I think.”

“Oh! You know I am English.”

“I see your tongue is,” she answered; “and what the tongue is, I presume the man is.”

He did not appreciate the comparison; still, he let it pass with a laugh. Finishing his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is to be married. But not to an Englishman; to one who, like herself, is French by birth. And speaking of Gaspard—ah, poor Gaspard! It was savage, savage!—it is curious that she is going to wed the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was lifted to that lofty height of so many feet; in short, the current Marquis. But he lives concealed in England; there he is no Marquis, but Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge knitted unruffled, yet the news visibly unnerved her husband. Behind the little counter, try as he might with striking a light and kindling his pipe, he was unsettled, and his hand failed him. The spy would not have earned his name if he had not noticed and fixed the fact in his mind.

Having at least scored this single point, whatever value it might hold, and no new patrons arriving to offer fresh opportunity, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and withdrew; taking care, before departing, to remark with courtesy that he anticipated the pleasure of meeting Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ebfdaa804bebdebb38467e79","rewritten_text":"My father had lived, and his memory sustained my very existence. I might feel gratitude to others, but I could never again love or hope as I once had; everything was suffering; even my pleasures were merely endured, never enjoyed. I was like a solitary hollow among mountains, enclosed on every side by steep, black cliffs where no warmth could reach and from which there was no escape to brighter fields. So it happened that although friendship’s spirit soothed me for a moment, it could not restore me. It came like some gentle visitation; it departed and I hardly felt the loss. The spirit of life was dead within me; do not be surprised, then, that when it arrived I did not welcome the best gift of heaven—a friend—more gladly, or grieve more bitterly when it left. My friend’s name was Woodville. I will briefly tell his story so you may judge how cold my heart must have been not to be revived by his eloquence and tender sympathy; and how, since he too was profoundly unhappy, we might have been a comfort to each other had I not been hardened to stone by the Medusa head of Misery. Woodville’s misfortunes did not pierce the heart as mine did; his grief was natural, meant not to destroy but to purify the heart, and once its shadow moved past him, he might shine brighter and happier than before. Woodville was the son of a poor clergyman and had received a classical education. He was one of those rare souls whom fortune favors from birth, on whom she lavishes every gift of intellect and appearance without limit, and whom she guards so closely that no flaw, however slight, nor disappointment, however brief, can touch them. She seemed to fashion his mind with an excellence no dross could tarnish, and his understanding was such that no error could corrupt it. His genius was transcendent, and when it rose like a brilliant star in the east, all eyes turned toward it in admiration. He was a poet—a word so often degraded that it fails to convey his greatness. He resembled one of the ancient poets crowned by the muses in their cradle and fed with honey by bees. As he moved among other men he seemed wrapped in a heavenly halo that set him apart and raised him above them. His surpassing beauty, the dazzling fire of his eyes, and his words, whose rich tones enveloped the listener in silent and ecstatic wonder, set him above everyone else, so that in his presence they seemed born only to serve his superior brilliance."}

{"request_id":"0f998559129ca9398697f35f","rewritten_text":"He let her know that Frank admired her greatly—thought her very beautiful and very charming; and with so much to recommend him overall, she felt she ought not to judge him too harshly. As Mrs. Weston remarked, “all young people will have their little whims.”

There was one person among his new acquaintances in Surrey who was not so forgiving. Throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury he was generally judged with considerable generosity; people made allowances for the small excesses of such a handsome young man—one who smiled so frequently and bowed so gracefully; but there was one spirit among them that could not be softened from its critical stance by bows or smiles—Mr. Knightley. The incident was reported to him at Hartfield; for a moment he said nothing, but Emma almost immediately heard him mutter to himself over the newspaper in his hand, “Hum! exactly the trivial, foolish fellow I always thought him.” She was half inclined to take offense; but a moment’s observation convinced her he spoke only to relieve his own feelings and not to provoke anyone, so she let it pass.

Even though they were, in one respect, bearers of unwelcome news, Mr. and Mrs. Weston’s visit that morning was particularly timely in another. Something happened while they were at Hartfield that made Emma seek their advice; and, even luckier, she wanted exactly the advice they offered.

This was the situation: The Coles had been settled in Highbury for some years and were very decent people—friendly, generous, and unpretentious; yet they were of low origins, engaged in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first moved to the country they lived within their means, quietly, entertaining little company and that very modestly; but over the past year or two their finances had improved considerably—their town business had produced greater profits, and fortune in general had favored them. With their wealth, their ambitions grew: they wanted a larger house and more society. They enlarged their house, increased their household staff, and expanded their expenses in every direction; and by now, in wealth and lifestyle, they were second only to the family at Hartfield. Their passion for company and their new dining room prepared everyone for their entertaining dinner guests; several parties, mostly involving single men, had already been held. Emma could scarcely imagine they would presume to invite the most established families—neither Donwell, nor Hartfield, nor Randalls. Nothing could induce her to go if they did; and she regretted that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal less meaningful than she wished."}

“My dear Victor,

“You have likely been impatient for a letter fixing the date of your homecoming, and at first I intended to send only a few lines naming the day I expected you. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I cannot do it. How great would be your shock, my son, if, anticipating a joyful welcome, you instead met tears and misery? And how, Victor, can I recount our calamity? Distance cannot have dulled your sense of our happiness and sorrow; how shall I inflict such pain on my long-absent child? I long to prepare you for the dreadful news, yet I know it is impossible; even now your eyes fly over the page in search of the words that bear the horrific message.

“William is dead!—that dear little boy whose smiles enlivened and warmed my heart, so gentle yet so merry! Victor, he has been murdered!

“I will not attempt consolation, but merely describe the circumstances.

“Last Thursday (May 7th), my niece, your two brothers, and I walked in Plainpalais. The evening was mild and tranquil, and we extended our stroll farther than usual. It had already grown dusk before we considered returning, and then we realized William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were missing. We sat down to wait for them. Presently Ernest came and asked if we had seen his brother; he said they had been playing together, that William had darted off to hide, that he searched in vain and afterward waited a long time, but William did not return.

“This tale alarmed us, and we continued searching until darkness, when Elizabeth guessed he might have gone home. He was not there. We set out again with torches; I could not rest while imagining my darling boy lost and subject to the night’s damps and dews; Elizabeth suffered torment as well. Around five in the morning I found my lovely child, whom I had seen the evening before full of life and health, lying on the grass pale and motionless; the mark of the murderer’s fingers was on his neck.

“He was carried home, and the anguish plain on my face revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She was desperate to view the body. At first I tried to hold her back, but she insisted, and entering the room where he lay, she quickly examined the victim’s throat, then wrung her hands and cried, ‘O God!’”}"}

{"request_id":"0e19f6468d2928c1dd375161","rewritten_text":"“Ah, I mistook your meaning. I imagined you said ‘anybody,’ therefore I supposed that meant—well, anybody; in other words, everybody.”

“It doth—so long as the party be of exalted lineage; all the better if he be royal.”

“In sooth, that seemeth reasonable,” replied the abbot, spying his chance to smooth matters and stave off disaster, “for it were scarce likely that so marvelous a boon should be granted for the unveiling of the affairs of folk of mean degree, rather than for those born hard by the summits of greatness. Our Arthur the king—”

“Wouldst thou hear of him?” the enchanter cut in.

“Most joyfully, yea, and with thanks.”

Instantly everyone was steeped in awe and curiosity once more, the hopeless simpletons. They gloated over the charms and turned toward me with a “Well then, what have you to answer to that?” expression, once the pronouncement came:

“The king, worn out with the chase, lies these two hours in his palace, tasting dreamless sleep.”

“Heaven’s blessing rest upon him!” murmured the abbot, crossing himself; “may that slumber renew both flesh and spirit.”

“And so it might, were he indeed sleeping,” said I, “but the king is not asleep; he is in the saddle.”

Fresh trouble—clashing authorities once more. None knew which of us deserved credence; my name yet held some weight. The wizard’s contempt awoke, and he declared:

“Lo, I have met many marvelous seers and prophets and magicians in my days, yet never one who could sit idle and descry the heart of things without an incantation.”

“You have dwelt in forests and have missed much. I myself employ charms, as these brethren can attest—but only when the matter is worth it.”

When it comes to dealing out satire, I fancy I can hold my side up. That thrust made the fellow writhe. The abbot inquired concerning the queen and the court, and received this answer:

“They, too, lie asleep, their bodies spent even as the king’s.”

I retorted:

“That is just another falsehood. Half of them are busy with their diversions, and the queen with the rest are not asleep—they ride. Very well, perhaps now you can spread your talents somewhat and inform us whither the king and queen, and all riding with them, are bound at this moment.”

“They sleep now, as I have declared; but on the morrow they shall ride, for they start a journey toward the sea.”

“And by vespers of the day after tomorrow, where shall they be?”

“Far to the north of Camelot, with the half of their way accomplished.”

“That is yet another lie, erring by the measure of a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"a9c66b8149664585c8c6b5a4","rewritten_text":"“Good heavens!” the Duchess muttered to herself. “He really is some sort of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I do hope he’s a foreigner, at least. It wouldn’t seem quite so awful then.”

“I simply must introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” cried the Duchess. “You can’t mean he’s here?” She began hunting for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very worn lace shawl so she could slip away at a moment’s notice.

“Of course he’s here. I would never dream of having a party without him. He says I have a perfect psychic hand, and that if my thumb had been the tiniest bit shorter, I would have been a hopeless pessimist and retired to a convent.”

“Oh, I see!” said the Duchess in obvious relief. “He’s a fortune-teller, I take it?”

“And a misfortune-teller too,” Lady Windermere replied. “A whole heap of them. Next year, for example, I am in deadly danger both on land and at sea, so I’m going to live in a balloon and haul up my dinner in a basket every evening. It’s all written there on my little finger—or on the palm of my hand—I forget which.”

“But surely that’s tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone ought to have their hands read once a month, just to know what not to do. Naturally one goes ahead and does it anyway, but it’s delightful to be warned. Now, if someone doesn’t go fetch Mr. Podgers at once, I’ll have to go myself.”

“Allow me, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man who had been standing nearby, listening with an amused smile.

“Thank you so much, Lord Arthur, but I’m afraid you would never recognize him.”

“If he’s as remarkable as you claim, Lady Windermere, I can hardly miss him. Describe him to me, and I’ll bring him to you at once.”

“Well, he’s not in the least like a chiromantist. I mean, he isn’t mysterious, or esoteric, or romantic-looking. He’s a short, stout little man with a comical bald head and large gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country solicitor. I’m terribly sorry, but it isn’t my fault. People are so exasperating. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. Last season I even invited a notorious conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up any number of people, always wore a coat of mail, and kept a dagger up his sleeve—and do you know, when he arrived he looked just like a kindly old clergyman and cracked jokes all evening?”"}

{"request_id":"b465aba66c944613d42ac7fa","rewritten_text":"He was short but held himself very straight, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He began his lecture by summing up the history of chemistry and the improvements made by learned men, speaking with passion as he named the most famous discoverers. Then he briefly described the current state of the science and explained many basic terms. After a few introductory experiments, he ended with a tribute to modern chemistry, words I will never forget:

“The ancient teachers of this science,” he said, “promised impossibilities and achieved nothing. The modern masters promise little; they know metals cannot be transformed and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem made only to handle dirt, and whose eyes peer endlessly into microscopes and crucibles, have performed miracles. They reach into nature’s hidden places and show how she works in secret. They climb to the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new, almost unlimited powers; they can command the thunder, imitate the earthquake, and even mock the invisible world with its own shadows.”

Such were the professor’s words—rather, the words of fate—spoken to destroy me. As he continued I felt as if my soul were wrestling a solid enemy; each key that formed the mechanism of my being was struck; chord after chord sounded, until my mind filled with one thought, one idea, one purpose. So much has been done, cried the soul of Frankenstein—more, far more, will I achieve; following the steps already marked, I will pioneer a new path, reveal unknown powers, and uncover for the world the deepest mysteries of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in rebellion and turmoil; I felt that order would eventually rise from it, but I lacked the power to bring it about. Gradually, after dawn, sleep came. When I awoke, my thoughts from the previous night seemed like a dream. What remained was a resolve to return to my former studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural talent. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private his manners were even gentler and more appealing than in public, for the dignity he showed in the lecture hall was at home replaced by warmth and kindness."}

{"request_id":"a2a999154277b44dfa52d1d1","rewritten_text":"Knights and fully armored horses couldn’t move very fast. They would do the best they could, and now that the ground was firm, with no snow or mud, they would probably keep up a seven-mile pace. They would have to switch horses twice, and they’d arrive around six, or a little after; there’d still be plenty of daylight. They would spot the white cloth I planned to tie around my right arm, and I would take charge. We’d surround the prison and have the king out in no time. It would look dramatic and picturesque enough, all things considered, though I would have preferred noon for its more theatrical flair.

Next, to add to my options, I figured I’d track down some of the people I once recognized and reveal myself to them. That could get us out of this mess without involving the knights. But I had to be cautious; it was risky. I needed luxurious clothing, and I couldn’t just leap into it. I had to work up to it gradually, buying suit after suit from shops far apart, choosing something a little finer each time, until I finally reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I set out.

But the plan collapsed instantly. The first corner I turned, I ran smack into one of our slaves, poking around with a watchman. I coughed right then, and he shot me a look that cut to my core. I’m pretty sure he thought he’d heard that cough before. I ducked into a shop immediately and moved along the counter, asking prices while keeping an eye on them. They had stopped, talking together and peering in through the doorway. I decided to slip out the back way, if there was one, and asked the shopwoman if I could go back there to search for the escaped slave rumored to be hiding somewhere behind the shop. I told her I was an officer in disguise, and my partner was out front with one of the murderers in custody; would she be kind enough to tell him he didn’t need to wait, but should hurry down to the far end of the back alley so he could block the fugitive when I flushed him out.

She was burning with excitement to see one of those already famous murderers, and she set off on the errand at once."}

{"request_id":"c626d3461415ca9e8f70381c","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and offered my apology. He replied, “Not in the least,” and continued. 

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you can imagine she was pursued as a splendid match. Her half-brother once more had plenty of resources, yet through debt and a fresh madness squandered them miserably all over again. The quarrel between him and her was more intense than the quarrel between him and his father, and it is suspected he nurtured a deadly grudge against her for having provoked their father’s anger. Now I reach the cruel part of this tale—only pausing, dear Handel, to point out that a dinner-napkin is not meant to be inserted into a tumbler.” 

Why I was trying to stuff mine into my tumbler I cannot conceive. I only know that with a determination worthy of a nobler cause, I was straining every effort to fold it within those boundaries. Once more I thanked him and expressed regret, and once more he said in the brightest tone, “Not at all, I assure you!” before going on. 

“There appeared in the picture—at the races, or the assemblies, or any place you choose—a certain man who wooed Miss Havisham. I never saw him (for this occurred five-and-twenty years ago, before our day, Handel), yet I heard my father say he was a flashy figure, well suited for the part. But that he wasn’t to be confused, even by ignorance or prejudice, with a gentleman, my father stoutly insists; because his principle is that no man who isn’t a gentleman at heart has ever been, since the world began, a gentleman in manner. He says no polish can conceal the wood’s grain, and the more polish you add, the more the grain insists on showing. Well then! This man chased Miss Havisham diligently and professed utter devotion to her. I believe she had not displayed much warmth before that time; but whatever warmth she possessed blazed forth then, and she adored him. She unquestionably idolized him. He worked upon her love so methodically that he obtained great sums of money from her, and persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery—which weak kindness had left him at their father’s death—at an enormous price, using the argument that once he became her husband he must possess and administer the whole concern. Your guardian had no part in Miss Havisham’s counsels at that time, and she was too proud and too much enamoured to take advice from anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"8e29c415d7ef788a87c3b2c8","rewritten_text":"Hearing Jim say that made me sorry for him, it felt like such a come-down. My conscience began riling me up worse than ever till finally I told it, “Quit riding me—it ain’t too late yet—I’ll paddle ashore at first light and confess.” Right away I felt relieved, pleased, light as a feather. Every bit of worry dropped off. I kept sharp watch for a light, half humming to myself. After a bit, one showed, and Jim hollers:

“We’s safe, Huck, we’s safe! Jump up en crack yo’ heels! Dat’s good ole Cairo at las’, I jis knows it!”

I says:

“I’ll take the canoe over and see, Jim. Might not be, you know.”

He sprang up, readied the canoe, spread his old coat in the bottom for me to sit, handed me the paddle; and as I shoved off, he says:

“Pooty soon I’ll be shout’n for joy, en I’ll say it’s all cause o’ Huck; I’s a free man, en couldn’ never ben free if it hadn’ ben for Huck; Huck done it. Jim ain’t ever gwine forgit you, Huck; you’s de best fren’ Jim ever had; en you’s de only fren’ ole Jim’s got now.”

I was paddling away, sweating to betray him; but when he said that, it just knocked the stuffing out of me. I drifted slower then and couldn’t say for sure if I was glad I’d started or not. When I was thirty yards off, Jim says:

“Dah you goes, de ole true Huck; de on’y white genlman dat ever kep’ his promise to ole Jim.”

That made me feel downright sick. Still, I told myself I had to go through with it—no backing out. Just then along comes a skiff with two men carrying guns; they drew up and so did I. One asks:

“What’s that out there?”

“Piece of a raft,” says I.

“You belong on it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men aboard?”

“Just one, sir.”

“Well, five niggers lit out tonight from up yonder above the head of the bend. Is your man white or black?”

I didn’t answer quick. I tried, but couldn’t get the words past my throat. I spent a second or two mustering up the grit, but I warn’t man enough—didn’t have the nerve of a rabbit. I felt myself giving way; so I let it go and blurted:

“He’s white.”

“I reckon we’ll go see for ourselves.”

“I’d be obliged if you would,” says I, “cause it’s pap out there, and maybe you’ll help me tow the raft in to where that light is.”"}

{"request_id":"3760b5c5e0175745280146a3","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was quite upset when Lord Canterville refused, and asked him to change his mind, but the kindly peer was firm. At last he convinced the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her, and when the young Duchess of Cheshire was introduced at the Queen’s first drawing-room after her marriage in the spring of 1890, her jewels drew universal admiration. Virginia received the coronet that rewards all good little American girls, and married her childhood sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming and so in love that everyone was pleased with the match, except the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had hosted no fewer than three costly dinner parties to that end, and, strangely, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis was very fond of the young Duke personally, but in theory he disliked titles, and, as he said, “was not without fear that, under the weakening influence of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true principles of republican simplicity might be forgotten.” His objections were completely overruled, however, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter on his arm, there was not a prouder man in all England.

After the honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went down to Canterville Chase, and the day after they arrived they walked in the afternoon to the lonely churchyard by the pine woods. There had been much trouble at first about the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but at last they decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some lovely roses, which she scattered on the grave, and after standing there awhile they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up at her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he tossed away the cigarette, took her hand, and said, “Virginia, a wife should have no secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you do,” he replied with a smile. “You have never told me what happened when you were shut up with the ghost.”

“I have never told anyone, Cecil,” Virginia said gravely."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d27c3d6835e259081fb29253","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, gravity would keep decreasing with the squares of the distances, and with my speed increasing greatly, I would eventually reach regions where the moon’s pull would replace the earth’s. With this in mind, I decided it was not worth carrying more supplies than would last forty days. During another moment of worry, I recalled accounts from balloon ascents at great heights. Aside from painful breathing, travelers felt severe discomfort in their heads and bodies, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms that worsened the higher they went. Would these symptoms keep increasing, perhaps until death? I finally decided they would not. They came from the gradual loss of normal atmospheric pressure on the body, which swelled the surface blood vessels, rather than from any true disorder of the organs, as with breathing trouble when the air grows too thin to refresh the blood in the heart. Unless the blood failed to renew, I saw no reason life could not continue even in a vacuum, since the expansion and contraction of the chest, commonly called breathing, is a purely muscular action and the cause, not the result, of respiration. In short, I believed the body would adjust to the lack of air pressure and the pain would slowly fade; while it lasted, I trusted in my strong constitution to endure it. Thus, your Excellencies, I have shared some, though not all, of the reasons that led me to plan a journey to the moon. I will now tell you the outcome of an effort so bold in idea and so entirely unmatched in human history. When I reached the altitude already mentioned—three miles and three quarters—I tossed a handful of feathers from the car and saw that I still rose quickly enough, so I did not need to throw off ballast. I was glad, because I wanted to keep as much weight as possible with me, for reasons I will explain later."}

content.text: {"request_id":"88fa4ab2b8de96b206f3fc18","rewritten_text":"April 19th. This morning, to my great relief, around nine o’clock, the moon’s surface lay terrifyingly close, and my fears were at their peak, when the pump of my condenser finally showed clear signs that the atmosphere was changing. By ten I believed the air had grown much denser. By eleven, the apparatus needed very little attention, and at noon, though nervous, I dared to unscrew the tourniquet. Finding I suffered no harm, I opened the gum-elastic chamber and detached it from the car. As expected, the rash danger of this experiment brought on spasms and fierce headache. Yet these breathing difficulties were not severe enough to threaten my life, and I chose to bear them, knowing I was leaving them behind as I moved toward the denser layers near the moon. Still, my descent stayed violently swift, and I soon realized with alarm that, although I had likely been right about finding an atmosphere dense enough for the moon’s mass, I was wrong to think even the surface air could support the heavy load in my balloon’s car. It should have matched Earth’s surface, with gravity on each body balancing the compressed atmosphere. My headlong fall proved it did not; the cause could only be those possible geological disturbances I mentioned earlier. Whatever the reason, I was now almost on the planet and dropping with dreadful force. I wasted no time: over went the ballast, then the water-kegs, then the condensing gear and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every object inside the car. It made no difference. I still plunged down at an awful speed and was no more than half a mile above the ground. As a last hope, after tossing away my coat, hat, and boots, I cut the car loose, since it weighed a good deal, and clung with both hands to the netting. I barely had time to see that the landscape for as far as I could look was dotted thickly with tiny houses before I crashed headlong into the center of a fantastical city and into a huge crowd of ugly little people. Not one of them said a single word or tried in the least to help me. They simply stood like a bunch of fools, grinning ridiculously, staring sideways at me and my balloon, arms planted on their hips."}

{"request_id":"641dd706bc3396ca81fb0068","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted she was a little surprised by the match, but she spoke more about how sincerely she wished them happiness than about her astonishment, and Elizabeth could not convince her to see it as unlikely. Kitty and Lydia felt no envy of Miss Lucas, because Mr. Collins was only a clergyman; the news mattered to them only as gossip to share in Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant at having a daughter well married, something she could now throw back at Mrs. Bennet, and she visited Longbourn more often than usual to say how happy she was, even though Mrs. Bennet’s sour expressions and spiteful remarks might have been enough to chase happiness away.

There was a reserve between Elizabeth and Charlotte that kept them both silent on the subject, and Elizabeth was convinced that real trust could never exist between them again. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her turn with greater affection to her sister, whose integrity and grace she was sure she could never doubt, and for whose happiness she grew more worried by the day, because Bingley had been gone a week with no word of returning.

Jane had replied to Caroline’s letter right away and was counting the days until she might reasonably expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father and written with all the solemn formality that a year’s stay in the family might have inspired. Having eased his conscience on that matter, he went on to declare with abundant enthusiasm how happy he was to have secured the affection of their charming neighbor, Miss Lucas, and then explained that he had been so ready to accept their invitation to Longbourn solely in hopes of enjoying her company; he hoped to return on Monday fortnight. Lady Catherine, he added, so wholeheartedly approved of his marriage that she wanted it to happen as soon as possible, which he trusted would surely persuade his dear Charlotte to set an early date and make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer a pleasure for Mrs. Bennet. Instead, she was just as inclined to complain about it as her husband. It was very odd that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge; it was also extremely inconvenient and troublesome. She hated having visitors in the house when her health was so delicate, and lovers were the most disagreeable company of all."}

{"request_id":"a48f493c957779d7ac435b18","rewritten_text":"“Do you often return?”

“I have not set foot here since then.”

“Nor have I.”

As the moon rose, I remembered the calm gaze fixed on the white ceiling that was gone. As the moon rose, I recalled the pressure of his hand when I spoke the final words he heard in life.

Estella next broke the quiet stretching between us.

“I have often wished and meant to come back, but many things have held me away. Poor, poor old place!”

The silvery mist caught the first glint of moonlight, and the same light rested on the tears slipping from her eyes. Unaware that I noticed, and trying to master them, she quietly asked,

“Were you wondering, as you walked, how it came to be left like this?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The land is mine. It is the one possession I have not given up. Everything else has fallen from me bit by bit, but I held this. It was the only firm resistance I made through all those miserable years.”

“Is it to be built on?”

“At last it is. I came to bid it farewell before it changes. And you,” she added with a tone that touched a wanderer, “you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And you prosper, I know?”

“I labor hard for a decent living, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Indeed?”

“Lately, very often. There was a long harsh season when I kept far from me the memory of what I discarded when I knew nothing of its value. But since my duty has not clashed with admitting that remembrance, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have never lost your place in mine,” I replied.

We fell silent again until she spoke.

“I never imagined,” said Estella, “that in taking leave of this place I should also take leave of you. I am very glad of it.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? To me, parting is sorrowful. The memory of our last parting has always been sad and painful to me.”

“But you said to me,” Estella returned with great earnestness, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ And if you could say that then, you will not hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has outweighed all other lessons and taught me what your heart used to be. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into something better.”"}

{"request_id":"e4675014d2f6e274e327292a","rewritten_text":"Then I murmured over to myself that enchanting passage that recounts Dante’s entrance into the earthly Paradise, imagining how blissful it would be, when I wandered along those lovely banks, to watch the chariot of light descend bearing my long-lost parent back to me. While I waited with that expectation, I imagined twisting a garland from the flowers growing there and crowning myself in delight: I would sing sul margine d’un rio, my father’s favourite song, and believed my voice drifting through the still air would carry to whatever bower he occupied, awaiting our reunion, the news that his daughter had come. The traces of sorrow would vanish from my brow, and I should lift my eyes without fear to meet his, always radiant with the gentle light of innocent affection. When I recalled the spell of those deep eyes I began to weep, though softly, lest my sobs should mar the fairy vision.

So completely was I absorbed in that dream that I walked on heedless until I bent to pluck a bloom for my wreath on that desolate plain where no flowers grew, and then I woke from the reverie to find myself I knew not where.

The sun had already gone down, and the rosy light the clouds had borrowed from his setting had all but faded. A wind swept the plain; I looked around and saw nothing by which to gauge my location; I was lost, and my efforts to recover the path were fruitless. I continued wandering, while the advancing dusk blurred any trace that might have guided me. Soon everything was draped in the profound shadow of the darkest night; I grew tired, and since my servant would sleep that night at the neighboring village, so no one would be alarmed at my absence, and I knew I was safe from intruders in that solitary region, I resolved to remain where I was. Truly I was too exhausted to go further: the air was cold, but bodily discomfort was nothing to me, and I fancied I had grown used to changes of weather during two years of solitude, when no shift of season interrupted my ceaseless wanderings.

I stretched upon the grass, encircled by a darkness into which not the faintest ray of light broke. No sound reached me, for the deep night had lulled the insects—the only creatures that inhabited that lonely waste where no tree or shrub offered shelter to any other being. There was a marvelous stillness in the air that soothed my senses yet quickened my spirit, and my thoughts raced from vision to vision, seeming to clasp eternity."}

{"request_id":"aa61f2e2776ed04cbc05e7bf","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water to end the feast with. After a while Becky suggested that they move on again. Tom was quiet for a moment. Then he said:

“Becky, can you bear it if I tell you something?”

Becky’s face grew pale, but she thought she could.

“Well then, Becky, we have to stay here, where there’s water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!”

Becky broke into tears and wailing. Tom tried to comfort her, but it hardly helped. At last Becky said:

“Tom!”

“Well, Becky?”

“They’ll miss us and hunt for us!”

“Yes, they will! Of course they will!”

“Maybe they’re hunting for us now, Tom.”

“Why, I reckon maybe they are. I hope so.”

“When would they miss us, Tom?”

“When they get back to the boat, I guess.”

“Tom, it might be dark then—would they notice we hadn’t come?”

“I don’t know. But anyway, your mother would miss you as soon as they got home.”

A frightened look on Becky’s face brought Tom to his senses, and he knew he had made a mistake. Becky wasn’t supposed to go home that night. The children fell silent and thoughtful. A moment later Becky burst into tears again, and Tom knew she was thinking the same thing he was—that Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher realized that Becky wasn’t at Mrs. Harper’s.

The children fixed their eyes on their small candle and watched it melt slowly and mercilessly away, saw the half inch of wick stand alone at last, watched the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, linger at its top a moment, and then—utter darkness took over.

Neither knew how long it was before Becky slowly realized she was crying in Tom’s arms. All they knew was that, after what felt like a huge stretch of time, both awoke from a dead stupor of sleep and took up their misery again. Tom said it might be Sunday now—maybe Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but her grief was too heavy, and all her hopes were gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago, and that the search was surely underway. He would shout and maybe someone would come. He tried it, but in the darkness the distant echoes sounded so horrible that he didn’t try again.

The hours slipped away, and hunger returned to torment the captives. Some of Tom’s half of the cake was left; they shared it and ate it. But they felt hungrier than before."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3947bcad42f5ac3934741dd0","rewritten_text":"I remembered how things were during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. Up North a carpenter made three dollars a day at gold value; down South he earned fifty—paid in Confederate shinplasters that were worth about a dollar a bushel. In the North a pair of overalls cost three dollars, a single day’s pay; in the South they cost seventy-five, equal to two days’ wages. Everything else scaled the same way. So wages in the North were effectively twice as high as in the South, because Northern paychecks bought twice as much.\n\nI got to know various people in the village, and I was pleased to see our new coins circulating everywhere—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, lots of nickels, some silver; all among the artisans and common folk; and even some gold, though that was in the bank, meaning the goldsmith’s shop. I stopped in while Marco, son of Marco, was arguing with a shopkeeper over a quarter-pound of salt, and I asked for change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They obliged—after they’d bitten the coin, rung it on the counter, tested it with acid, and interrogated me about where I got it, who I was, where I’d come from, where I was headed, when I expected to arrive, and maybe a couple hundred more questions. When they ran out, I kept right on volunteering information: told them I owned a dog named Watch, that my first wife was a Free Will Baptist, her grandfather was a Prohibitionist, I once knew a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip who died trusting in a glorious resurrection, and on and on until even that ravenous village busybody started looking satisfied and maybe a little annoyed. Still, he had to respect a man with my financial clout, so he didn’t mouth off to me, though I noticed he took it out on his underlings, which was only natural. Yes, they broke my twenty, but I could tell it strained the bank, as you’d expect—it was like walking into a tiny nineteenth-century general store and suddenly asking the owner to change a two-thousand-dollar bill. He might manage it, but he’d be wondering why a small farmer was carrying that much cash, and I suspect the goldsmith thought the same. He followed me to the door and stood there watching me leave with reverent admiration."}

{"request_id":"bddc81bd7738829b2f4ffc10","rewritten_text":"The two ladies rejoiced at seeing their dear friend once more, declared it an age since their last meeting, and again and again inquired how she had been occupying herself during their absence. The rest of the family received little notice; they shunned Mrs. Bennet as much as possible, spoke scarcely to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. They soon departed, springing up with an alacrity that astonished their brother, and hastening off as though to flee Mrs. Bennet’s civilities.

The prospect of the Netherfield ball was exceedingly pleasing to every female in the house. Mrs. Bennet chose to regard it as a tribute to her eldest daughter and felt especially gratified that Mr. Bingley, rather than a formal card, delivered the invitation himself. Jane imagined a cheerful evening among her two friends and the attentions of their brother; Elizabeth anticipated dancing much with Mr. Wickham, and observing in Mr. Darcy’s looks and conduct the confirmation of all she believed. The happiness Catherine and Lydia envisioned was less tied to any single circumstance or person; for though each, like Elizabeth, intended to dance half the night with Mr. Wickham, he by no means was the only partner capable of pleasing them, and, after all, a ball was simply a ball. Even Mary could tell her family that she felt no reluctance toward it.

“So long as I may have my mornings to myself,” she said, “that suffices. I do not think it any sacrifice to join occasionally in evening engagements. Society lays claims upon us all; and I count myself among those who deem intervals of diversion and amusement desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so lively on the occasion, that although she seldom addressed Mr. Collins without necessity, she could not resist asking whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation, and, if so, whether he considered it proper to share in the evening’s entertainments. She was somewhat astonished to discover he harbored no hesitation about it, and was far from fearing any reprimand, whether from the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh, for daring to dance.

“I by no means imagine, I assure you,” said he, “that a ball of this nature, offered by a young man of character to respectable company, can carry the least ill effect; and so far from objecting to dance myself, I shall hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins during the evening; and I seize this moment to solicit yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances in particular; a preference which I trust my cousin Jane will ascribe to the proper motive, and not to any want of regard for her.”"}

{"request_id":"e585ab91486b00b84d0e2cf3","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, uncertain where to head next. “At Tellson’s bank at nine,” he murmured thoughtfully. “Should I show myself in the meantime? I think so. These people ought to know that I’m here; it’s sensible, and might be necessary preparation. But caution—caution—caution! Let me think this through!”

Reining in the steps that had started toward one destination, he paced the darkening street and followed the thought to its possible outcomes. His first instinct held firm. “It’s best,” he said, firmly decided, “for these people to know there’s such a man as me here.” He turned his face toward Saint Antoine.

Defarge had described himself that day as the proprietor of a wine-shop in the Saint Antoine suburb. Someone who knew the city, as Carton did, could find the place without asking. Once he confirmed its location, Carton left those cramped streets, ate at a small restaurant, and fell fast asleep after dinner. For the first time in years, he had no strong liquor. Since the previous night he had taken nothing stronger than a little thin wine, and the night before he had poured the brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth like a man who was done with it.

It was as late as seven when he woke refreshed and went back into the streets. On his way to Saint Antoine he paused at a shop window with a mirror and made slight adjustments to his loose cravat, his coat collar, and his unruly hair. That done, he went straight to Defarge’s and stepped inside.

Only one customer was in the shop: Jacques Three, the man with nervous fingers and a rasping voice. Carton had seen him on the Jury. He stood drinking at the small counter, talking with the Defarges, husband and wife, while The Vengeance joined the conversation like an equal partner in the business.

Carton walked in, took a seat, and requested—in halting French—a small measure of wine. Madame Defarge gave him a casual glance, then a sharper one, and another sharper still. She approached him herself and asked what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” Madame Defarge asked, lifting her dark brows inquisitively.

He looked at her as if even a single French word took effort to form, then replied in the same strongly foreign accent as before."}

{"request_id":"79498714a2ade3ad22932efa","rewritten_text":"“Tom!”

No answer.

“TOM!”

No answer.

“What’s become of that boy, I wonder? You, TOM!”

No answer.

The old lady slid her spectacles down and peered over them around the room; then she pushed them up and peered beneath them. She hardly ever looked through them for something as small as a boy; they were her formal pair, her pride, built for “style,” not service—she could have seen just as well through a couple of stove lids. She looked puzzled for a moment, then said, not angrily but still loud enough for the furniture to hear:

“Well now, if I get my hands on you I’ll—”

She didn’t finish, because by then she was bending down and jabbing the broom under the bed, and she needed her breath for the jabs. All she turned up was the cat.

“I never saw the like of that boy!”

She went to the open door, stood there, and looked out over the tomato vines and jimson weeds that passed for a garden. No Tom. So she pitched her voice at a distance-setting and shouted:

“Y-o-u-u, TOM!”

There was a rustle behind her, and she turned just in time to grab a small boy by the back of his jacket and stop his escape.

“There! I could’ve guessed that closet. What were you doing in there?”

“Nothing.”

“Nothing! Look at your hands. And look at your mouth. What is that mess?”

“I don’t know, Aunt.”

“Well, I do. It’s jam—that’s what it is. Forty times I’ve told you if you didn’t leave that jam alone I’d tan your hide. Hand me that switch.”

The switch hovered in the air—the danger was critical—

“Hey! Look behind you, Aunt!”

The old lady spun around and snatched her skirts out of harm’s way. The boy bolted instantly, scrambled up the high board fence, and vanished over it.

His Aunt Polly stood surprised a moment, then broke into a gentle laugh.

“Confound that boy, can’t I ever learn? Hasn’t he fooled me like that enough times that I ought to be ready for him by now? But old fools are the biggest fools of all. Can’t teach an old dog new tricks, they say. But heavens, he never plays them the same way twice, and how’s a body to know what’s coming? He seems to know just how long he can tease me before I blow, and he knows if he can stall me for a minute or make me laugh, it’s all over again and I can’t land a lick on him.”"}

{"request_id":"4d0e7f595a1331df9d436625","rewritten_text":"“Why, surely you don’t mean—” my sister began.

“Yes, I do, Mum,” replied Pumblechook; “but hold on a moment. Go on, Joseph. Good man! Continue!”

“What would folks present say,” Joe went on, “to twenty pound?”

“Handsome is the word,” my sister answered.

“Well then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pound.”

That abject hypocrite Pumblechook bobbed again, and remarked with a patronizing chuckle, “It’s beyond that, Mum. Fine! Keep it up, Joseph!”

“Then, to wind it up,” Joe said, cheerfully handing my sister the bag, “it’s five-and-twenty pound.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pound, Mum,” echoed that meanest of cheats, Pumblechook, standing to shake her hand; “and it’s only what you deserve (as I declared when they asked my opinion), and I wish you joy of it!”

Had the scoundrel stopped there, his offense would have been dreadful enough, but he darkened his guilt by proceeding to arrest me, assuming a patronage that cast all his earlier wrongdoing in the shade.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, gripping my arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always carry through what they start. This lad must be bound, without delay. That’s my way. Bound without delay.”

“Goodness knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said (clutching the money), “we’re greatly obliged.”

“Don’t mind me, Mum,” returned the infernal cornchandler. “A pleasure’s a pleasure everywhere. But this boy, you understand; we must have him bound. I said I’d attend to it—in honest truth.”

The Justices sat in the nearby Town Hall, and we immediately crossed over to have me bound apprentice to Joe before their Magisterial honors. I say we crossed over, but Pumblechook shoved me across as though I had just picked a pocket or set a rick ablaze; indeed, the general notion in Court was that I’d been caught in the act; for as Pumblechook hustled me along through the crowd, I heard some ask, “What has he done?” and others, “He’s a youngster, but looks bad, doesn’t he?” A gentleman of gentle and kindly face even pressed on me a tract with a woodcut featuring a scowling youth tricked out with a whole sausage-shop of irons, titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall struck me as a curious place, with higher pews than a church and people leaning over them to stare, and with mighty Justices (one with a powdered head) leaning back in their chairs, arms folded, or taking snuff, or nodding off, or writing, or reading the papers, and with a few glossy black portraits along the walls, which my untutored eye took for a mixture of hardbake and sticking plaster."}

{"request_id":"3d13cab6e31c64c5d2fd7e4e","rewritten_text":"His face, deeply sunburned, was more than half hidden by whiskers and a thick mustache. He carried a massive oak cudgel, but seemed otherwise unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and greeted us with a “good evening” in French, the accent somewhat Neuchâtel, yet still clearly indicating Parisian roots.

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I assume you’re here about the orangutan. Honestly, I almost envy you owning him; a remarkably fine and undoubtedly valuable animal. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew a long breath, like a man relieved of an unbearable weight, and then replied in a confident tone:

“I can’t say for sure—but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no, we had nowhere to keep him here. He’s at a livery stable on Rue Dubourg, just nearby. You can fetch him in the morning. Naturally you’re prepared to prove ownership?”

“Of course I am, sir.”

“I’ll be sorry to give him up,” Dupin said.

“I don’t expect you to go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the man said. “Wouldn’t expect it. I’m quite willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, anything reasonable.”

“Well,” my friend replied, “that’s entirely fair, certainly. Let me think! What should I take? Oh! I’ll tell you. My reward will be this: you’ll give me every bit of information you can about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke those last words very softly, very calmly. Just as calmly, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from his coat and laid it on the table without the slightest fuss.

The sailor’s face flared up as if he were suffocating. He jumped up and clutched his cudgel, but the next moment he fell back into his seat, shaking violently, pale as death. He said nothing. I pitied him from the bottom of my heart.

“My friend,” said Dupin gently, “you’re frightening yourself needlessly—you truly are. We mean you no harm at all. I give you the honor of a gentleman, and of a Frenchman, that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you’re innocent of the atrocities in the Rue Morgue. However, it won’t do to deny that you’re somewhat involved in them.”"}

{"request_id":"7d8e27bd044365065834821f","rewritten_text":"To be fair to the young lady, she never flatly said she wouldn’t do it; she only strongly wished to be damned if she would. It was a polite, delicate way of refusing and showed she had the kind of natural good manners that hates causing anyone the pain of a blunt rejection.

The Jew’s face fell. He turned from this young lady—who was dressed cheerfully, even flamboyantly, in a red gown, green boots, and yellow curlers—to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” the Jew said gently, “what do you say?”

“That it’s no good, so don’t bother trying, Fagin,” Nancy replied.

“What do you mean by that?” Mr. Sikes demanded with a nasty look.

“What I said, Bill,” the woman answered calmly.

“Why, you’re the perfect person for it,” Sikes argued. “No one around here knows you.”

“And I’d like to keep it that way,” Nancy answered in the same calm tone. “So it’s more no than yes for me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” said Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” said Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” said Sikes.

And Sikes was right. With a mix of threats, promises, and bribes, they finally got the lady to take the job. Unlike her smartly dressed friend, she had recently moved from the distant but respectable suburb of Ratcliffe to Field Lane, so she wasn’t worried about being recognized by any of her many acquaintances.

With a clean white apron tied over her dress and her curlers tucked under a straw bonnet—both supplied from the Jew’s endless stock—Miss Nancy prepared to set out on her errand.

“Wait a moment, my dear,” said the Jew, pulling out a small covered basket. “Carry this in one hand. It looks more respectable, my dear.”

“Give her a door key for the other hand, Fagin,” Sikes suggested. “Makes it look proper and genuine.”

“Yes, yes, my dear, so it does,” said the Jew, hanging a big front-door key on the forefinger of her right hand. “There; very good! Very good indeed, my dear!” he said, rubbing his hands.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” Nancy cried, bursting into tears and clutching the basket and key in agony. “What’s become of him? Where have they taken him? Please pity me and tell me what’s happened to the dear boy, gentlemen; please, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d041902c22976f83da88d538","rewritten_text":"Dawn had come when I set the manuscript aside. The rain had mostly stopped, leaving the world gray and sad, and the worn-out storm was sighing itself to rest. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his door, which was slightly open. I heard his voice, so I knocked. There was no answer, though he kept speaking. I peered in. He lay on his back in bed, talking in broken but lively bursts, his arms thrashing restlessly the way delirious patients do. I slipped in quietly and leaned over him. He kept muttering exclamations. I spoke a single word to get his attention. His glassy eyes and ashen face lit at once with pleasure, gratitude, joy, and welcome.\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you’re here at last—how I’ve longed for you! Sit by me—don’t go—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where’s your hand?—give it to me, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is right, all is peaceful, and I’m happy again—we’re happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You’re so dim, so vague, like a mist, a cloud, but you’re here, and that’s blessing enough; and I have your hand; don’t take it away—it’s only for a little while, I won’t need it long…. Was that the child?… Hello—Central!… she doesn’t answer. Asleep, maybe? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and say goodbye…. Sandy! Yes, you’re there. I drifted for a moment, and thought you were gone…. Have I been sick long? It must be so; it feels like months. And such dreams! such strange, terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as waking—delirium, of course, yet so real! I thought the king had died, I thought you were in Gaul and couldn’t get home, I thought there was a revolution; in the wild frenzy of those dreams I thought Clarence and I and a handful of my cadets fought and wiped out the whole chivalry of England! But even that wasn’t the strangest. I seemed to be a creature from a far future age, centuries away, and even that felt real! Yes, I seemed to have flown back from that age into this one, then forward again, and was dropped, a stranger and alone in that strange England, with thirteen centuries yawning between me and you! between me and my home and my friends! between me and everything dear to me, everything that could make life worth living!”"}

{"request_id":"989926f6c471ce365c6bf263","rewritten_text":"There was something so extraordinary in the growing brightness of Mr. Wopsle’s eye, and he appeared to be balancing so many notions and becoming so muddled, that I could not interpret it. I sat pondering over it long after he had risen to the clouds in a large watch-case, and still I could make nothing of it. I was yet reflecting on it when I stepped out of the theatre an hour later and discovered him lingering near the entrance for me.

“How are you?” I said, shaking his hand as we turned down the street together. “I noticed that you saw me.”

“Saw you, Mr. Pip!” he replied. “Certainly I saw you. But who else was there?”

“Who besides?”

“It is the oddest thing,” Mr. Wopsle said, drifting back into that absent expression, “and yet I could swear to him.”

Growing uneasy, I implored Mr. Wopsle to make his meaning clear.

“Whether I should have observed him at first without your being there,” Mr. Wopsle went on in the same absent manner, “I can’t say for sure; but I think I should.”

Unconsciously I glanced about, as was my habit when going home; for these enigmatic words sent a cold shiver through me.

“Oh! He can’t be within sight,” Mr. Wopsle said. “He left before I went off. I watched him go.”

Because of my reason for suspicion, I even doubted this poor player. I feared some scheme to lure me into an admission. So I watched him as we walked together, but kept silent.

“I had an absurd idea that he must be with you, Mr. Pip, until I saw you were wholly unaware of him, sitting behind you there like a spirit.”

The earlier chill crawled over me once more, but I was determined not to speak yet, for his words easily allowed that he might be trying to prompt me to link these allusions with Provis. Naturally, I was entirely certain and secure that Provis had not been present.

“I dare say you are astonished at me, Mr. Pip; in fact, I can see you are. But it is so very surprising! You’ll scarcely credit what I am about to tell you. I could scarcely credit it myself, if you said it.”

“Indeed?” I said.

“No, indeed. Mr. Pip, you recall, in bygone days, a particular Christmas Day when you were a mere child, and I dined at Gargery’s, and some soldiers came to the door to have a pair of handcuffs repaired?”

“I remember it perfectly.”

“And you recollect that there was a pursuit of two convicts, and that we joined it, and Gargery carried you on his back, and I took the lead, and you stayed with me as best you could?”"}

{"request_id":"64de09cf5414364e20f0b1ad","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” I said, “what’s the matter now? How is your master?”

“To tell the truth, sir, he’s not as well as he should be.”

“Not well! I’m truly sorry to hear it. What does he complain of?”

“That’s just it! He never complains about anything, but he’s very sick all the same.”

“Very sick, Jupiter! Why didn’t you just say so? Is he confined to bed?”

“No, he’s not! He isn’t shut up anywhere—that’s exactly what bothers me. My mind feels very heavy about poor Master Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to understand what you’re talking about. You say your master is sick. Hasn’t he told you what’s wrong?”

“Why, sir, it’s not worth getting angry over. Master Will keeps saying nothing’s the matter with him—but then why does he go around like this, with his head down and his shoulders up, and as pale as a goose? And he keeps a siphon all the time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a siphon with the figures on the slate—the strangest figures I ever saw. I’m starting to get scared, I tell you. I’ve got to keep a very close eye on his moves. The other day he slipped away before sunrise and was gone the whole blessed day. I had a big stick cut and ready to give him a good beating when he came back—but I’m such a fool I couldn’t go through with it after all—he looked so very poor.”

“Eh? What? Ah yes—on the whole, I think you’d better not be too harsh with the poor fellow. Don’t flog him, Jupiter—he really couldn’t stand it. But can’t you imagine what has caused this illness, or rather this change in his behavior? Has anything unpleasant happened since I saw you?”

“No, sir, nothing unpleasant has happened since then—it was before that, I’m afraid—it was the very day you were there.”

“How? What do you mean?”

“Why, sir, I mean the bug—there it is.”

“The what?”

“The bug—I’m certain Master Will was bitten somewhere around the head by that gold bug.”

“And what makes you think that, Jupiter?”

“Plenty of reason, sir, and a mouth too. I never saw such a devilish bug—it kicks and bites everything that comes near it. Master Will caught it first, but had to let it go again very quickly, I’ll tell you—then must have been when he got the bite. I didn’t like the look of the bug’s mouth myself, not at all, so I wouldn’t hold it with my fingers. I picked it up with a piece of paper I found.”"}
