{"request_id":"7e444a1e2b2fc98215e4328c","rewritten_text":"The day slipped by much as the previous one had. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several morning hours with the invalid, who kept improving, though gradually; and when evening came, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing-room. Yet the loo table was absent. Mr. Darcy sat writing, while Miss Bingley, placed close beside him, watched the evolution of his letter, constantly distracting him with messages intended for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were engaged at piquet, with Mrs. Hurst observing their play.

Elizabeth took up some needlework and found sufficient diversion in listening to the exchange between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant compliments—on his penmanship, the straightness of his lines, or the length of his letter—paired with the utter indifference with which he received them, made a curious conversational duet, fully matching Elizabeth’s view of both participants.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to get such a letter!”

He offered no reply.

“You write amazingly fast.”

“You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must need to write in a year! Business letters, too! I should think them dreadful!”

“It is lucky, then, that they fall to me rather than to you.”

“Please tell your sister I long to see her.”

“I have already conveyed that, at your request.”

“I fear you dislike your pen. Let me mend it. I mend pens astonishingly well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How can you manage to write so evenly?”

He stayed silent.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her progress on the harp, and pray let her know I am entirely enraptured with her lovely little design for a table; I find it infinitely superior to Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to postpone your raptures until my next letter? At the moment I have no space to treat them properly.”

“Oh, it does not signify. I shall see her in January. But do you always send her such charming long letters, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are generally long; whether always charming is not mine to judge.”

“It is my rule that anyone who can write a long letter easily cannot write ill.”

“That will never do as a compliment for Darcy, Caroline,” her brother exclaimed, “because he does not write with ease. He searches too hard for words of four syllables. Do you not, Darcy?”

“My style differs very much from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless fashion imaginable.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"30f45e7d790a378e8cba9d83","rewritten_text":"Back home in my own era, that money was raised through tariffs, and people liked to imagine some foreign importer paid them; it soothed their minds to believe it. In reality Americans paid the duty themselves, and it was spread so evenly that a man worth a hundred million and the newborn child of a day laborer each shouldered exactly the same yearly burden—six dollars apiece. I doubt anything could be fairer than that. Now, Scotland and Ireland both paid tribute to Arthur, and all the British Isles together held a little under a million souls. A mechanic earned about three cents a day when he covered his own food and lodging. Under that standard the national budget ran to ninety thousand dollars a year, or two hundred fifty a day. Therefore, by swapping gold for nickels during a king’s-evil ceremony, I harmed no one, displeased nobody, and satisfied everyone, while slicing four-fifths off that day’s public expense—a savings equal to eight hundred thousand dollars in my America. I learned that move at a very distant source—the wisdom of my boyhood—because a true statesman never scorns wisdom however humble its beginnings. As a kid I saved my pennies and sent buttons to foreign missions. The button served the uninformed native just as well as coin, while the coin served me better than the button; everyone came out happy and no one got hurt.\n\nMarinel handled the patients as they showed up. He examined each applicant; if the fellow couldn’t meet the requirement he was warned away, and if he could, he was ushered on to the king. A priest intoned, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king stroked the infected sores while the scripture continued, and at the end the patient graduated with his nickel—the king hung it around his neck personally—and off he went. Does that sound like it would heal anyone? Yet it did. Any ritual will work if the patient’s faith in it is strong enough. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin was said to have appeared to a goose-herding girl—the girl herself swore it—and they built the chapel on the spot and hung up a painting of the vision, a picture you’d imagine would scare an invalid away. Instead, thousands of the infirm and the halt visited it every year, prayed before it, and departed cured; even the healthy could gaze on it without harm."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a3bf955b67ccf35ebf5b734d","rewritten_text":"You’d rouse up after a while and peer around to see what stirred you, and maybe catch a steamboat hacking her way upstream, so far over toward the opposite bank you couldn’t make out a thing about her except whether she carried a stern-wheel or a side-wheel; then for near an hour there’d be nothing to spy and nothing to hear—just pure lonesomeness. Next a raft would glide past, way off in the distance, and likely there’d be some fellow on it chopping, because that’s near about all they ever do on a raft; you’d see the axe glitter and drop—you didn’t hear a sound; you’d watch it lift again, and by the time it was above his head you’d catch the _k’chunk!_—the sound had taken that whole stretch of time to cross the water. That’s how we’d spend a day, loafing around, listening to the hush. One time a heavy fog settled in, and every raft or scow drifting by was bashing on tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t plow into them. A scow or raft crept near enough we could hear their talk and swearing and laughing—plain as anything; yet there was not a trace to see; it gave you the crawls, like ghosts fooling around in the air. Jim reckoned it truly was spirits; but I told him:  “No; spirits ain’t going to say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’” As soon as it turned night we pushed off; once we steered her to midstream we let her be, letting the current choose where she drifted; then we lit up our pipes, let our legs trail in the water, and jawed about all sorts of matters—we stayed naked night and day whenever the skeeters allowed it—the new clothes Buck’s family fixed for me were too fine for comfort, and besides I never had much use for clothes anyhow. Sometimes we’d have the whole river to ourselves for an age. Over yonder lay the banks and islands, across the water; and every so often a spark glowed—that’d be a candle in some cabin window; and at times you’d see a spark or two on the water—belonging to a raft or scow, you know; maybe a fiddle tune or a song would float across from one of those crafts. Living on a raft is a beautiful thing. We had the heavens above, all sprinkled with stars, and we’d lie flat on our backs and stare up at them, arguing whether they’d been made or merely happened. Jim insisted they were made, but I claimed they just happened; it seemed to me it would have taken too long to _make_ such a multitude."}

{"request_id":"e200cfc1a3eea04525ef01a5","rewritten_text":"At the sight of it, the Ourang-Outang immediately leaped through the chamber door, ran down the stairs, and then, through a window that happened to be open, jumped into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair. The ape, still clutching the razor, sometimes stopped to look back and make frantic gestures at him, waiting until he nearly caught up before bolting away again. The chase went on like this for a long time. The streets were silent, nearly three o’clock in the morning. Passing down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive caught sight of a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s room on the fourth floor. Rushing to the building, it saw the lightning rod, climbed with unbelievable speed, grabbed the shutter flung flat against the wall, and swung itself straight onto the headboard of the bed. The whole maneuver took less than a minute. As it entered, the Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile the sailor was both relieved and alarmed. He hoped he could finally recapture the animal, since it could barely get out of the trap it had entered except by climbing down the rod, where he might catch it. Yet he worried about what it might do inside the house. This fear pushed him to keep following. A lightning rod is easy to climb, especially for a sailor, but when he reached the level of the window, far to his left, he could do no more than lean over for a glimpse inside. That glance nearly made him lose his grip in horror. The night split with the terrible cries that had woken everyone on the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, wearing their nightclothes, seemed to have been sorting papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been wheeled into the middle of the room. It stood open, its contents scattered on the floor. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window, and from the delay between the beast’s entrance and the screams, it likely went unnoticed at first. The slam of the shutter would have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked in, the huge creature had grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by her loose hair and was waving the razor near her face, mimicking a barber’s motions."}

content.text: {"request_id":"1192b43f8bec9e0620b415ae","rewritten_text":"“I must take leave to observe, Sir Walter,” Mr Shepherd remarked one morning at Kellynch Hall as he set the newspaper aside, “that the present moment is much in our favour. Peace will be sending all our wealthy naval officers ashore. They will all be searching for homes. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, for selecting tenants— tenants of the most responsible kind. Many a handsome fortune has been amassed during the war. Should a rich admiral fall in our way, Sir Walter—” “He would be an exceedingly lucky man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter returned; “I have nothing more to say. Kellynch Hall would be a positive treasure to him— the greatest prize of all, though he had captured ever so many already— hey, Shepherd?” Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he ought, at this sally, and then continued— “In a business light, Sir Walter, naval officers are easy to transact with. I have some acquaintance with their mode of conducting affairs; and I freely confess they entertain very generous views, and are as likely to prove acceptable tenants as any class one could meet. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would take leave to propose is, that if, in consequence of any rumours spreading regarding your purpose— which must be considered possible, for we know how hard it is to keep the affairs and intentions of one part of the world from the notice and curiosity of another; rank has its price; I, John Shepherd, might conceal any family matters I pleased, since no one would consider me worth observation; but Sir Walter Elliot has watchers he may find hard to evade— and thus I merely warn you that it will not greatly surprise me if, with all our discretion, some rumour of the truth should escape; in which case, as I was going to say, since applications will undoubtedly follow, I should judge any from wealthy naval commanders especially worth attention; and I beg to add that two hours will bring me over at any time to spare you the trouble of answering.” Sir Walter only nodded. But soon after, rising and walking across the room, he observed with sarcasm— “There are few among the gentlemen of the navy, I fancy, who would not be astonished to find themselves in a house of this class.” “They would survey their surroundings, no doubt, and bless their luck,” said Mrs Clay— who was present; her father had brought her over, nothing being so beneficial to Mrs Clay’s health as a drive to Kellynch— “but I perfectly agree with my father that a sailor might prove an exceedingly desirable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"2d7c48fd7f92ff7029963b92","rewritten_text":"But enough of that. I will commence my tale: it is my final duty, and I trust I have strength enough to accomplish it. I chronicle no crimes; my errors may readily be excused, for they sprang not from wicked intent but from lack of judgement; and I believe few would assert that, through different conduct and loftier wisdom, they could have escaped the misfortunes that have made me their victim. My destiny has been ruled by necessity, a monstrous necessity. It demanded hands stronger than mine—stronger, I am convinced, than any human power—to shatter the thick, adamantine chain that held me, once breathing nothing but joy and wholly possessed by a fervent love of goodness, yet driven to misery that could only end, and is now about to end, in death. But I am losing the thread; my story is still untold. I will rest a moment, wipe my dimmed eyes, and strive to forget the present obscure yet heavy sorrow in the sharper feelings of the past.

I drew my first breath in England. My father belonged to the nobility: he had been bereft of his own father early and was reared by a weak mother with all the indulgence she deemed fitting for a wealthy lord. He was sent to Eton and later to college, and from childhood was allowed free command of large sums of money, thus enjoying from his earliest youth the independence that a boy with such advantages inevitably acquires at a public school.

Under such influences his passions found a rich soil wherein they might strike roots and grow either as flowers or weeds according to their nature. Being always permitted to act for himself, his character became quickly and strongly defined, presenting a varied surface on which a keen observer might discern the seeds of both virtue and misfortune. His heedless extravagance, which led him to squander vast amounts to satisfy passing whims that he, because of their apparent energy, dignified with the name of passions, often manifested itself in unbounded generosity. Yet while he busied himself with the needs of others, his own desires were indulged to the fullest. He bestowed his money, but none of his own wishes were sacrificed to his gifts; he gave his time, which he set little value on, and his affections, which he rejoiced to have awakened in any fashion.

I do not assert that, had his own desires been placed in opposition to those of others, he would have proved unduly selfish, but this trial never occurred. He was nurtured in prosperity and attended by all its benefits; everyone loved him and sought to please him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a079e04d1a094ee93527da57","rewritten_text":"On the morning set for Admiral and Mrs Croft to view Kellynch Hall, Anne found it best to take her nearly daily walk to Lady Russell’s and stay away until the visit was finished; afterward she regretted missing the chance to see them. The meeting between the parties pleased everyone and settled the matter immediately. Each lady already inclined toward an agreement and therefore saw only good manners in the other; and among the gentlemen, the Admiral’s cheerful humor and open, trusting generosity impressed Sir Walter, who had also been coaxed into his most polished behavior by Mr Shepherd mentioning that the Admiral had heard of him as a model of good breeding. They approved the house, grounds, furniture, terms, timing—everything and everyone—and Mr Shepherd’s clerks were set to work without any preliminary dispute about what “This indenture sheweth.” Sir Walter quickly declared the Admiral the best-looking sailor he had ever met and even said that if his own servant had arranged the Admiral’s hair, he would not be ashamed to be seen with him anywhere; and the Admiral, equally cordial, remarked to his wife as they drove back through the park, “I thought we would soon reach a deal, my dear, despite what they told us at Taunton. The Baronet will never set the Thames on fire, but he seems harmless”—reciprocal compliments considered much the same. The Crofts were to take possession at Michaelmas, and since Sir Walter planned to move to Bath during the previous month, there was no time to lose in arranging everything. Lady Russell, convinced that Anne would not be allowed any role or importance in choosing their new house in Bath, was reluctant to have her hurried away so soon and wished to find a way for her to stay behind so she could take her to Bath herself after Christmas; but with her own commitments taking her away from Kellynch for several weeks, she could not extend the full invitation she wanted, and Anne, though dreading possible September heat in Bath’s glaring whiteness and grieving to miss the bittersweet influence of autumn in the country, did not think she truly wanted to remain under the circumstances."}

{"request_id":"a0af57e62eaa9693bf6e5925","rewritten_text":"I now turn to my own story. There is little to tell about the early part of my life, and I will be brief; still, I must linger over my childhood so it may be clear how, when one hope deserted me, all life became empty, and how, when the only affection I was allowed to nurture was destroyed, my existence went out with it.

I have already said my aunt was very unlike my father. Without the slightest trace of malice, she possessed the coldest heart that ever beat in a human chest, utterly incapable of affection. She took me in because she saw it as a duty, but she had lived alone too long, undisturbed by children’s noise and chatter, to let me disrupt her peace. She had never married, and for the last five years she had lived entirely alone on an estate inherited from her mother on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. My father had written asking her to live with me at his ancestral home, which stood in lovely country near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused, but as soon as she settled the matters left in her care by her brother’s departure, she left England and took me with her to her Scottish estate.

The charge of me as an infant, and later until I turned eight, fell to a servant of my mother’s who came with us for that purpose. I lived in a secluded part of the house and saw my aunt only at set times. Twice a day she appeared: once around noon she would come to my nursery, and once after dinner I was brought to her. She never embraced me and seemed afraid the whole time I was in the room that I might irritate her with some childish mischief. My good nurse carefully drilled me before she dared lead me into the parlor, and the awe inspired by my aunt’s cold gaze and stiff words was so intense that I rarely forgot her lessons or failed to maintain the exemplary stillness expected of me during those brief visits.

Under my nurse’s care I roamed free through our park and the nearby fields. Born of the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years a most sensitive nature. I cannot describe with what passion I loved everything, even the lifeless objects around me."}

The condition of the room and of the bodies was described by this witness exactly as we detailed yesterday.

“Henri Duval, neighbor and silversmith, states that he was among the first group to enter the home. He confirms Musèt’s account overall. After forcing entry, they shut the door again to keep out the rapidly growing crowd, despite the late hour. The high-pitched voice, he believes, was that of an Italian. Was certain it was not French. Could not state with confidence that it was a man’s voice; it may have been a woman’s. Did not understand Italian. Could not make out the words, yet felt sure from the tone that the speaker was Italian. Knew Madame L. and her daughter well, having conversed with both often. Was sure the piercing voice did not belong to either of the victims.

“Odenheimer, restaurateur. This witness came forward of his own accord. He does not speak French and was questioned through an interpreter. A native of Amsterdam. Was passing the house when the screams were heard. They continued several minutes—perhaps ten. They were prolonged, loud, terribly appalling. He was among those who entered the building and confirmed all earlier testimony except on one point. He insists the shrill voice was male—French. Could not decipher the words. They came fast and loud, uneven, apparently spoken in fear as well as wrath. The voice was harsh—more rough than shrill. Could hardly call it a shrill voice. The gruff voice repeated “sacré,” “diable,” and once “mon Dieu.”

“Jules Mignaud, banker of the firm Mignaud et Fils, Rue Deloraine. The elder Mignaud. Madame L’Espanaye possessed some property and opened an account at his bank in the spring of the year—eight years prior. She frequently deposited small sums. She drew nothing until three days before her death, when she withdrew in person 4000 francs. The sum was paid in gold, and a clerk escorted her home with it.

“Adolphe Le Bon, clerk at Mignaud et Fils, attests that on that day, around noon, he accompanied Madame L’Espanaye to her house carrying the 4000 francs divided between two bags. When the door opened, Mademoiselle L. appeared and took one bag from him, while the elderly lady took the other.”"}

{"request_id":"7c9efedfe3111b2975fa7652","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scratch up the cupboard with it and was getting ready to start on the bureau when he was summoned to get dressed for Sunday school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a bar of soap, and he stepped outside, setting the basin on a little bench. He dipped the soap in the water and set it aside, rolled up his sleeves, poured the water out gently onto the ground, and then slipped back into the kitchen to scrub his face vigorously on the towel behind the door. But Mary snatched the towel away and said:

“Now aren’t you ashamed, Tom? You can’t be that bad. Water won’t hurt you.”

Tom was slightly unsettled. She refilled the basin, and this time he hovered over it for a moment, summoning courage; he took a deep breath and began. When he came back into the kitchen with both eyes squeezed shut, feeling for the towel with his hands, a respectable mix of suds and water was streaming off his face. Yet after he finished with the towel, he still wasn’t acceptable; the clean patch ended abruptly at his chin and jaw like a mask, and below that stretched a dark field of untouched dirt spreading across his chest and circling his neck. Mary took over, and when she finished he looked like a man and a brother without any distinction of color, his soaked hair neatly brushed and its short curls arranged into a tidy, symmetrical pattern. [He secretly flattened the curls with a lot of effort, plastering his hair down, because he considered curls effeminate and his own tormented him endlessly.] Then Mary produced a suit he had worn only on Sundays for two years—they were simply referred to as his “other clothes”—and that tells us the size of his wardrobe. After he dressed, she put him in order; she buttoned his snug roundabout up to his chin, flipped his enormous shirt collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and set his speckled straw hat on his head. He now looked greatly improved and decidedly miserable. He felt exactly as miserable as he looked, because whole clothes and cleanliness chafed him. He hoped Mary would forget his shoes, but that wish died quickly; she coated them thoroughly with tallow, as was customary, and brought them out. He lost his temper and complained that he was always forced to do everything he didn’t want to do."}

{"request_id":"d32fef5aa99eccfda4ee5e00","rewritten_text":"She studied me closely for a moment, then said quietly, “What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I answered, “that you won’t mix them up with the others. They may share the same blood, but believe me, they are not of the same nature.”

Still watching me, Miss Havisham repeated, “What do you want for them?”

“I’m not so sly,” I admitted, feeling myself blush, “that I could hide from you—even if I wanted to—that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would give the money to do my friend Herbert a lasting service in life, a service that must be done without him knowing, I could show you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowledge?” she asked, settling her hands on her stick so she could study me more closely.

“Because,” I said, “I began helping him over two years ago without his knowing, and I don’t want that secret betrayed. Why I can’t finish it myself, I can’t explain. That part of the secret belongs to someone else, not me.”

She slowly turned her eyes from me to the fire. After watching it in silence for what seemed a long time by the light of the slowly burning candles, she was roused when some of the red coals collapsed. She looked back at me—first blankly, then with growing focus. All the while Estella kept knitting. Once Miss Havisham had fixed her attention on me again, she spoke as if our talk had never paused: “What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her and trying to steady my shaking voice, “you know I love you. You know I have loved you for a long time, and dearly.”

She raised her eyes to my face when I spoke, her fingers kept working, and she looked at me without expression. I saw Miss Havisham glance from me to her and back again.

“I would have said this sooner, except for the mistake I made so long. It led me to hope that Miss Havisham meant us for each other. While I believed you could not help yourself, in a way, I kept silent. But I have to say it now.”

Still expressionless, and with her fingers moving, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said to that gesture. “I know. I have no hope of ever being able to call you mine, Estella.”"}

{"request_id":"f90941750fe8f03507db8fa0","rewritten_text":"As they were leaving the dining room, the clock tower began striking midnight. When the last stroke echoed, they heard a crash and a sharp scream; a terrible thunderclap rattled the house, eerie music drifted through the air, a hidden panel at the top of the stairs flew open with a bang, and onto the landing stepped Virginia, pale and wan, holding a small casket. In an instant everyone rushed to her. Mrs. Otis wrapped her in a fierce embrace, the Duke covered her with frantic kisses, and the twins whirled around them in a wild war dance.

“Good heavens, child, where have you been?” Mr. Otis demanded angrily, convinced she had been playing another trick. “Cecil and I have ridden all over the countryside hunting for you, and your mother has been terrified. You must never play these practical jokes again.”

“Except on the Ghost! Except on the Ghost!” screamed the twins as they spun around.

“My darling, thank God you’re safe; you must never leave my side again,” whispered Mrs. Otis while she kissed the shaking girl and smoothed her tangled golden hair.

“Papa,” Virginia said quietly, “I have been with the Ghost. He is dead, and you must come see him. He was very wicked, but he was truly sorry for what he had done, and before he died he gave me this box of beautiful jewels.”

The whole family stared at her in stunned silence, but she was calm and serious. She turned and led them through the opening in the paneling down a narrow hidden corridor, Washington following with a candle he had snatched from the table. Eventually they reached a heavy oak door studded with rusty nails. When Virginia touched it, it swung open on creaking hinges, and they entered a small low room with a vaulted ceiling and one tiny barred window. Set into the wall was a massive iron ring, and chained to it lay a gaunt skeleton stretched out on the stone floor, its long bony fingers straining toward an old trencher and jug placed just beyond reach. The jug had once held water, but now its interior was green with mold. Nothing lay on the trencher except a drift of dust. Virginia knelt beside the skeleton, folded her hands, and prayed silently, while the others watched in awe at the terrible tragedy whose secret now stood revealed."}

{"request_id":"b5dfd0adf22b003d0b85dc9f","rewritten_text":"Countrymen, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and vagabonds of every low sort were mixed together in one mass. Drovers whistled, dogs barked, oxen bellowed and plunged, sheep bleated, pigs grunted and squealed, hawkers shouted, people swore and fought. Bells rang and loud voices poured from every public-house. The crowd pressed, shoved, drove, beat, whooped, and yelled; horrible clamor rose from every corner of the market; unwashed, unshaven, filthy figures ran back and forth, thrusting themselves in and out of the crush. It overwhelmed the senses.

Mr. Sikes, dragging Oliver, forced his way through the thickest part of the crowd and paid little attention to the sights and sounds that astonished the boy. He nodded once or twice to passing friends and turned down invitations to take a morning dram, pushing forward until they left the chaos and reached Holborn through Hosier Lane.

“Now, young’un!” said Sikes, looking up at St. Andrew’s clock. “Almost seven! You have to keep up. Come on, don’t lag already, Lazy-legs!”

He jerked Oliver’s wrist as he spoke, and Oliver broke into a half-trot to match the housebreaker’s long strides as best he could.

They kept up this pace until they passed Hyde Park Corner and headed toward Kensington. Sikes slowed then, waiting for an empty cart approaching from behind. Seeing “Hounslow” painted on it, he asked the driver as politely as he could to give them a ride to Isleworth.

“Jump in,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes; he’s my boy,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver and sliding his hand into the pocket where he kept his pistol.

“Your father walks a bit too fast for you, eh?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver’s short breath.

“Not at all,” said Sikes quickly. “He’s used to it. Here, hold my hand, Ned. Get in!”

He lifted Oliver into the cart, and the driver pointed to a pile of sacks, telling him to lie down there and rest.

As they passed each milestone, Oliver wondered more and more where Sikes meant to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, Brentford—each slipped behind them—and still they moved on as steadily as if the journey had only just begun."}

{"request_id":"075b25118598e48a4ce5e08f","rewritten_text":"“We have been to your residence,” said the first man. “Not finding you there, and being told you were likely walking this way, we followed in hopes of overtaking you. Will you please get into the carriage?”

Both men were commanding. As they spoke, they shifted to place me between them and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“Gentlemen,” I said, “forgive me, but I usually ask who seeks my help and what sort of case I am being called to.”

The second man answered. “Doctor, your clients are people of rank. As for the case itself, our faith in your skill assures us you will figure it out better than we can explain it. Enough. Will you please enter the carriage?”

I had no choice but to obey, and I stepped inside without another word. They both followed—one leaping in after raising the steps. The carriage turned around and resumed its former speed.

I repeat this conversation exactly as it happened. I am sure every word is the same. I describe everything as it took place, forcing my mind not to stray from the job. Whenever I mark the breaks that follow, I stop for the moment and hide these pages.

*****

The carriage left the city streets, passed the North Barrier, and entered the country road. Two-thirds of a league from the Barrier—it was only afterward, when I retraced the route, that I measured the distance—it left the main avenue and soon stopped at a solitary house. All three of us got out and walked along a damp, soft path in a garden where a neglected fountain had overflowed, until we reached the door. It did not open at once after the bell rang, and one of my escorts struck the man who finally opened it across the face with his heavy riding glove.

This did not especially strike me; I had seen common folk beaten more often than dogs. But the other man, also angry, hit him in the same way. Their appearance and manner were now so identical that I realized for the first time they were twin brothers.

From the moment we stepped through the outer gate—which we found locked and which one brother opened for us and relocked—I had heard cries coming from an upper room."}

content.text: {"request_id":"162037f8bec0a856b12b13b1","rewritten_text":"There was plenty of cold water to end the meal with. After a while Becky suggested they move on again. Tom stayed quiet a moment before he said, “Becky, can you handle it if I tell you something?” Becky’s face went pale, but she thought she could. “Well then, Becky, we have to stay here where there’s water to drink. That little piece is our last candle!” Becky burst into tears and cried uncontrollably. Tom did his best to comfort her, but not much came of it. Finally Becky said, “Tom!” “Well, Becky?” “They’ll miss us and look for us!” “Yes, they will! Of course they will!” “Maybe they’re already looking for us, Tom.” “Well, I guess they might be. I hope they are.” “When would they notice we’re gone, Tom?” “When they get back to the boat, I suppose.” “Tom, it could be dark by then—would they notice we hadn’t come back?” “I don’t know. But anyway, your mother would notice as soon as they got home.” The frightened look on Becky’s face made Tom realize he’d made a mistake. Becky wasn’t even supposed to go home that night! The children fell silent and thoughtful. In a moment Becky broke into fresh sobs, which showed Tom that she had the same thought he did—that Sunday morning might be half over before Mrs. Thatcher realized Becky wasn’t at Mrs. Harper’s. The children fixed their eyes on the tiny candle and watched it melt away, slow and merciless; they watched the half inch of wick stand alone at last; watched the weak flame rise and fall, climb the thin column of smoke, linger at the top a moment, and then—utter darkness took over! Neither of them knew how much time passed before Becky slowly realized she was crying in Tom’s arms. All they knew was that after what felt like a vast stretch of time, both woke from a deathlike stupor of sleep and sank back into their misery. Tom said it might be Sunday now—maybe even Monday. He tried to get Becky to talk, but her grief was too heavy, all her hope gone. Tom said they must have been missed long ago and the search was surely underway. He’d shout, maybe someone would hear. He tried, but in the darkness the distant echoes sounded so terrifying that he wouldn’t try again. The hours dragged by, and hunger returned to torment them. Part of Tom’s half of the cake was left; they divided it and ate, but they only felt hungrier afterward."}

{"request_id":"847718667cbca6c2bcdcbf1a","rewritten_text":"Yet the little town knew no mirth that tranquil Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s household were being dressed in mourning, weighed down with sorrow and tears. An unaccustomed hush settled over the village, though it was commonly quiet enough. The villagers went about their business distractedly and spoke rarely, though long sighs escaped them. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children; they lacked spirit for their games and soon abandoned them.

That afternoon Becky Thatcher roamed the empty schoolyard, sunk in gloom. Though she lingered there, she found no comfort. She murmured to herself:

“Oh, if only I had a brass andiron knob again! But I’ve nothing now to remember him by.” A little sob caught in her throat.

After a moment she halted and said inwardly:

“It happened right here. Oh, if only it could be done over, I would never say that—not for the entire world. But he’s gone; I’ll never, never, never see him again.”

That thought broke her down, and she drifted away, tears slipping over her cheeks. Soon a knot of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s companions—came along, leaned on the picket fence, and spoke in reverent whispers of how Tom did this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe mentioned some small detail (brimful of dreadful forewarning, as they now clearly perceived). Each pointed out the exact place where the missing lads had stood, adding, “and I was standing just so—just as I am now, and pretend you’re him—I was this close—and he smiled exactly like this—and then something ran all over me, like—awful, you know—and I never guessed what it signified then, but I can see it now!”

Next they quarreled over who had last seen the dead boys alive. Many asserted that melancholy honor and produced proofs, somewhat embellished by each witness. When they finally agreed who actually exchanged the last words with the departed, the fortunate ones assumed a sort of solemn significance, and the rest stared at them, full of envy. One poor youngster, having nothing else to boast of, reminded them with a rather obvious pride:

“Well, Tom Sawyer licked me once.”

But that attempt at glory sank; nearly every boy could claim the same, which made the distinction meaningless. The cluster drifted away, still recounting memories of their lost heroes in hushed tones."}

content.text: {"request_id":"1a081040ca922d78640a2866","rewritten_text":"When Tom woke in the morning, he puzzled over his whereabouts. He pushed himself upright, rubbed his eyes, and gazed around. Then awareness dawned. The dawn lay cool and gray, and the woods lay steeped in a delectable sense of rest, hushed and serene with the deep pervasive calm. Not a leaf moved; not a whisper intruded upon Nature’s vast reverie. Dewdrops beaded every leaf and blade. A white sheet of ashes blanketed the fire, from which a thin blue thread of smoke climbed straight up. Joe and Huck still slept. \n\nFar off, a bird called; another responded; soon the tapping of a woodpecker took hold. The cool dim gray slowly paled, and sound by sound life quickened. The miracle of Nature rousing herself and setting to work unfolded before the meditative boy. A little green worm crawled over a dewy leaf, lifting two-thirds of its form into the air now and then to “sniff around,” then moved on again—for it was measuring, Tom declared. As the worm neared him of its own accord, he kept as motionless as stone, his hopes rising and falling in turn as the creature approached or seemed bent elsewhere; and when it paused with its curved body raised, pondered a painful moment, and then decisively dropped onto Tom’s leg to begin a journey across him, his heart rejoiced—for that meant, without a doubt, he was to get a new suit of clothes, a gaudy pirate uniform. Then a parade of ants emerged from no particular spot and busied themselves; one wrestled heroically with a dead spider five times its size and hauled it straight up a tree trunk. A brown-spotted ladybug scaled the dizzy summit of a blade of grass, and Tom bent near and murmured, “Lady-bug, lady-bug, fly away home, your house is on fire, your children’s alone,” and she took wing and flew off to look after it—no shock to the boy, for he already knew this insect was gullible about conflagrations, and he had exploited its innocence before. Next came a tumblebug, sturdily shoving its ball, and Tom touched it just to watch it clamp its legs tight and feign death. By now the birds were in full riot. A catbird, the northern mimic, settled in a tree above Tom’s head and poured out her neighbors’ songs in transported delight; then a sharp-voiced jay swooped down, a streak of blue flame, and perched on a twig almost within the boy’s reach, cocked his head, and scrutinized the strangers with devouring curiosity; a gray squirrel and a big “fox” squirrel scurried along, sitting up every so often to inspect and chatter at the boys, for the wild things likely had never seen human beings before and scarcely knew whether fear was warranted."}

{"request_id":"46545cc6dcd889216079f9f2","rewritten_text":"“What’s the matter?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What do you mean? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. Your honour told me to wake you.”

“Oh! I remember. Very good, very good.”

After a few sluggish attempts to fall asleep again, which the man cleverly thwarted by poking the fire steadily for five minutes, he rose, flung on his hat, and went out. He turned into the Temple and, having revived himself by twice pacing the pavements of King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings, went into Stryver’s chambers.

The Stryver clerk, who never attended these conferences, had gone home, and Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing-gown, with his throat left bare for comfort. He bore that somewhat wild, strained, scarred look about the eyes that may be seen in all free livers of his sort, from the portrait of Jeffries downward, and which can be traced, in varying artistic guises, through the portraits of every Drinking Age.

“You’re a little late, Memory,” said Stryver.

“About the usual hour; perhaps a quarter of an hour behind.”

They moved into a dingy room lined with books and strewn with papers, with a roaring fire. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the litter a table gleamed with plenty of wine, and brandy, and rum, and sugar, and lemons.

“You’ve had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I have been dining with the day’s client; or watching him dine—it comes to the same!”

“That was a rare point, Sydney, that you brought to bear upon the identification. How did you hit upon it? When did it occur to you?”

“I thought he was rather a handsome fellow, and I fancied I should have been much the same sort of fellow, if I had ever had any fortune.”

Mr. Stryver laughed until his precocious paunch quivered.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Set to work, set to work.”

Sullenly, the jackal loosened his dress, went into an adjoining room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. Soaking the towels and partially wringing them, he folded them over his head in a fashion hideous to see, sat down at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down to do tonight, Memory,” said Mr. Stryver cheerily, looking through his documents.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There you are, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion then settled himself on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking-table, while the jackal sat at his own paperscattered table opposite, with bottles and glasses within easy reach."}

{"request_id":"184bb896093c44b3594df5ff","rewritten_text":"Tom joined the new chapter of the Cadets of Temperance because he liked their flashy regalia. He promised to avoid smoking, chewing, and swearing as long as he belonged. Soon he discovered something new—that promising not to do something is the quickest way to make a person want to do exactly that. Tom was soon tormented by the urge to drink and curse; it grew so strong that only the hope of showing off his red sash kept him from quitting the order. Fourth of July was approaching; but he gave up that plan—abandoned it before he had worn his shackles for forty-eight hours—and set his hopes on old Judge Frazer, the justice of the peace, who seemed to be on his deathbed and would certainly have a grand public funeral, being such an important figure. For three days Tom was deeply worried about the Judge’s health and starved for updates. Sometimes his hopes soared—so high that he dared to take out his regalia and practice in front of the mirror. But the Judge had an infuriating habit of wavering. At last he was declared on the mend—and then recovering. Tom was disgusted and felt cheated. He turned in his resignation at once—and that night the Judge relapsed and died. Tom decided he would never rely on a man like that again.

The funeral was splendid. The Cadets marched in a manner designed to torment the ex-member with jealousy. Yet Tom was a free boy again, and there was some comfort in that. He could drink and swear now—but to his surprise he did not want to. Simply knowing he could do it removed the desire and the thrill.

Soon Tom was surprised to find that his longed-for vacation was starting to feel a bit dull.

He tried keeping a diary—but nothing happened for three days, so he gave it up.

The first traveling troupe of blackface minstrels came to town and caused a stir. Tom and Joe Harper organised a troupe of their own and enjoyed two happy days.

Even the Glorious Fourth turned out something of a failure, because it rained hard, no parade was held, and the greatest man in the world (in Tom’s mind), Mr. Benton, a real United States Senator, was a crushing disappointment—for he was not twenty-five feet tall or even close to it.

A circus arrived."}

{"request_id":"5654082dc5c4a9d8cd6aa734","rewritten_text":"“But that matters little.”

“I might as well ask,” she retorted, “why, with such an obvious intention to offend and insult me, you chose to tell me that you liked me against your inclination, against your judgment, and even against your character? Was that not justification enough for any incivility on my part, if I _was_ uncivil? Yet I have other grievances, as you well know. Even had my own feelings not already condemned you—had they been neutral, or even favourable—do you imagine any persuasion could induce me to accept the man who has been the cause of wrecking, perhaps forever, the happiness of a dearly loved sister?”

At these words, Mr. Darcy’s colour changed; but the feeling was brief, and he listened without attempting to interrupt while she went on,—

“I have every reason imaginable to think poorly of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous conduct you displayed _there_. You dare not, you cannot deny that you were the chief, if not the sole instrument of dividing them; that you exposed one to the world’s censure for fickleness and whim, the other to its mockery for hopes defeated, and plunged the pair of them into the cruellest misery.”

She paused, and with rising indignation observed that he listened with an expression implying he was entirely untouched by remorse. He even regarded her with a smile of feigned disbelief.

“Can you deny you have done this?” she reiterated.

Assuming composure, he replied, “I have no desire to deny that I used every effort to part my friend from your sister, or that I take satisfaction in having succeeded. Towards _him_ I have acted with more kindness than towards myself.”

Elizabeth disdained to acknowledge this courteous comment, though its import did not escape her, nor was it likely to appease her.

“But it is not solely this business,” she continued, “on which my aversion rests. Long before it occurred, my opinion of you was fixed. Your character was unfolded in the account I received many months ago from Mr. Wickham. On that subject, what defence can you offer? Under what imaginary act of friendship could you justify yourself? Or by what misrepresentation could you impose upon others?”

“You take a fervent interest in that gentleman’s concerns,” said Darcy, in a less composed tone and with deepened colour.

“Who that knows his misfortunes could help being interested in him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy echoed contemptuously,—“yes, his misfortunes have indeed been heavy.”

“And inflicted by you,” Elizabeth cried passionately. “You reduced him to his present condition—comparative poverty.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cc523f696061267aa81511bf","rewritten_text":"Mrs. Otis, who I may add is a sound judge of Art since she spent several winters in Boston when she was young, has told me that these jewels are very valuable and would sell for a high price. In these circumstances, Lord Canterville, I trust you see why I cannot let them stay with anyone in my family; all such showy ornaments, however fitting they may be for the British aristocracy, would be completely out of place for people raised on the stern—indeed, I believe eternal—principles of republican simplicity. I should mention that Virginia is very eager for you to let her keep the box as a keepsake of your unfortunate but misguided ancestor. As it is extremely old and quite damaged, you might consider agreeing to her request. For my part, I am rather surprised to hear one of my children express sympathy with anything medieval, and I can only explain it by noting that Virginia was born in one of your London suburbs shortly after Mrs. Otis returned from a visit to Athens.’\n\nLord Canterville listened very soberly to the worthy Minister’s words, occasionally tugging at his grey moustache to hide a reluctant smile, and when Mr. Otis finished, he shook him warmly by the hand and said, ‘My dear sir, your delightful little daughter did my unlucky ancestor, Sir Simon, a very great service, and my family and I owe her much for her extraordinary courage and spirit. The jewels are clearly hers, and by heavens, if I were cruel enough to take them from her, the old rogue would be out of his grave in a fortnight, making my life a perfect torment. As for their being heirlooms, nothing is an heirloom unless it is named as such in a will or legal paper, and no one even knew these jewels existed. I assure you I have no more claim on them than your butler does, and when Miss Virginia grows up I imagine she will enjoy having pretty things to wear. Besides, you forget, Mr. Otis, that you bought the furniture and the ghost as a single lot, and anything that belonged to the ghost became yours at once, since whatever trouble Sir Simon caused in the corridor at night, in law he was quite dead, and you acquired his property by purchase.’"}

{"request_id":"f2d2aed55b79f168715ab535","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how mysterious they were! There was something animal in the soul, and the body had its own moments of spirituality. The senses could become refined, and the intellect could become debased. Who could say where the physical impulse stopped or the psychic impulse began? How shallow were the arbitrary definitions of everyday psychologists! And yet how hard it was to decide between the claims of the different schools! Was the soul a shadow sitting in the house of sin? Or was the body actually inside the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? Separating spirit from matter was a mystery, and joining spirit to matter was a mystery as well.

He began to wonder whether psychology could ever become such a precise science that every small spring of life would be revealed to us. As it stood, we always misunderstood ourselves and rarely understood others. Experience had no moral value. It was only the name people gave to their mistakes. Moralists usually treated it as a kind of warning, credited it with a certain ethical power in shaping character, praised it as something that taught us what to follow and showed us what to avoid. But there was no driving force in experience. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly showed was that our future would mirror our past, and that the sin we once committed with disgust we would commit many times with pleasure.

It was obvious to him that the experimental method was the only way to reach any scientific analysis of the passions; and Dorian Gray was certainly a subject ready-made for him and seemed to promise rich, fruitful results. His sudden wild love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological phenomenon of considerable interest. There was no denying that curiosity played a large part in it—curiosity and the craving for new experiences—yet it was not straightforward but deeply complex. Whatever there was in it of the purely sensual instinct of youth had been reshaped by the imagination, turned into something that seemed to the boy himself to be removed from the senses, and was therefore all the more dangerous. The passions whose origins we lied to ourselves about were the ones that ruled us most tyrannically. Our weakest motives were the ones we recognized clearly. It often happened that while we thought we were experimenting on others we were really experimenting on ourselves.

While Lord Henry sat brooding on these matters, there was a knock at the door, and his valet entered to remind him it was time to dress for dinner."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c0c10a3f45bf305e32da1a17","rewritten_text":"Dawn had just broken when I put the Manuscript away. The rain had nearly stopped, the world lay gray and sorrowful, and the worn-out storm was sighing and sobbing as it drifted into rest. I went to the stranger’s chamber and listened at his slightly open door. I caught the sound of his voice, so I knocked. He did not answer, yet he kept speaking. I looked inside. The man lay on his back in the bed, muttering in fragments yet with spirit, his arms lashing about in that uneasy way fevered people have. I slipped in quietly and leaned over him. His murmurs and exclamations continued. I spoke a single word to draw his notice. Instantly his glazed eyes and ashen features shone with delight, gratitude, joy, welcome.\n\n“Oh, Sandy, at last you are here—you cannot know how I yearned for you! Sit close—don’t abandon me—never go away again, Sandy, never. Where is your hand?—give it, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is right, all is peace, and I am happy once more—we are both happy, aren’t we, Sandy? You are so dim, so shapeless, merely a mist, a cloud, but you are here, and that is blessing enough; and I have your hand; do not take it back—it will be only for a brief space, I shall not ask it long.... Was that the child?... Hello-Central!... she makes no response. Sleeping, perhaps? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and bid her farewell.... Sandy! Yes, you are still there. I wandered for an instant, thought you had gone.... Have I been ill long? I suppose so; it feels like months. And such dreams! such strange and dreadful dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality itself—delirium, surely, yet so real! Why, I believed the king was dead, believed you were in Gaul unable to return, believed there was a revolution; in that wild chaos of dreams I thought Clarence and I and a mere handful of my cadets fought and annihilated all the chivalry of England! Yet even that was not the strangest. I seemed to become some being from a far unborn age, centuries away, and even that felt as real as the rest! Yes, I thought I had flown back out of that era into ours, and then forward to it once more, and was left, a stranger and desolate, in that uncanny England, with a gulf of thirteen centuries yawning between me and you! between me and my home and my comrades! between me and everything beloved, everything that could make life worth the living!”"}

{"request_id":"f2bd506228f166e8bc332d2c","rewritten_text":"His features, much scorched by the sun, were more than half concealed beneath whiskers and mustachios. He carried a massive oaken cudgel, yet seemed otherwise without weapons. He gave an awkward bow and greeted us with a “good evening” in French accents which, though a bit Neufchâtel in flavor, still betrayed unmistakable Parisian roots.

“Take a seat, my friend,” said Dupin. “I assume you’ve come about the Ourang-Outang. Truly, I almost grudge you his possession; he’s a remarkably fine creature, and doubtless of great value. How old would you judge him to be?”

The sailor drew a deep breath, like a man unburdened of a grievous weight, and answered with confidence:

“I’ve no means of knowing—but he cannot be more than four or five years old. Have you got him here?”

“Oh no, we’re unfitted to keep him here. He’s lodged at a livery stable in the Rue Dubourg, close by. You may take him in the morning. You are, of course, ready to prove your ownership?”

“Certainly I am, sir.”

“I shall regret parting with him,” Dupin added.

“I don’t expect you to take all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the fellow replied. “Wouldn’t be reasonable. I’m quite willing to pay a reward for recovering the animal—in reason, of course.”

“Well,” returned my companion, “that is quite fair. Let me see!—what should the reward be? Ah! I have it. You shall give me every scrap of information you possess about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin uttered these last words in a very subdued voice, very calmly. Just as calmly he strolled to the door, locked it, and slipped the key into his pocket. He then drew a pistol from his breast and laid it on the table without the slightest perturbation.

The sailor’s visage flushed as though he were on the verge of suffocation. He sprang up and clutched his cudgel, but the next instant sank back into his chair, shaking uncontrollably and looking like death itself. He did not utter a syllable. I pitied him with all my heart.

“My good fellow,” said Dupin gently, “you are frightening yourself needlessly—you truly are. We intend you no harm whatever. I give you the pledge of my honor as a gentleman and a Frenchman that we mean you no injury. I am perfectly aware that you are innocent of the butchery in the Rue Morgue. Still, it will not do to deny that you are, in some degree, involved.”"}

{"request_id":"ec32a36102ffee205df5eced","rewritten_text":"Nearly a year had passed since my father’s return, and the seasons had almost completed their circle. It was late May; the woods were wrapped in fresh green, and the fields carried the sweet scent of newly cut grass. I believed the warm air and the gentle beauty of nature might help me inspire him with softer feelings and prepare him for the trust I was determined to win.

I chose an evening on one of those days for my attempt. I asked him to walk with me and guided him to a nearby beech wood whose light shade shielded us from the slanting, dazzling beams of the setting sun. After we walked silently for some time, I sat with him on a mound of moss. It is strange, but I still seem to see that place now: the slim, smooth trunks wrapped in ivy whose glossy dark leaves contrasted with the white bark and the light leaves of the young beech shoots sprouting from the parent trunks. Short grass mingled with moss, partly covered by dead leaves from the last autumn that the winds had piled into small mounds here and there. A few moss-covered stumps stood around. The leaves stirred gently in the breeze, and through their green canopy the bright blue sky showed through. As evening arrived, the distant trunks glowed red in the sunlight, the wind died away, and a few birds flew past us on their way to rest.

There we sat together, and when you hear all that passed—how terrible events tore at our souls in this calm spot, which could have been a paradise if not for strange passions—you will understand why I remember it so clearly, hoping its peace might give me courage and persuasive words. I saw all these details and noted them blankly in my mind while I tried to arrange my thoughts for what I meant to do. My heart pounded as I prepared to speak to him, for I was determined not to be turned away, yet I trembled at what my words might do to him. At last, with great hesitation, I began:

“Your kindness to me, my dearest father, and the affection—the overwhelming affection—you showed when you first returned will, I hope, excuse me in your eyes as I dare to speak to you, not only with the tender love of a daughter but also with the freedom of a friend and equal.”"}

{"request_id":"1c44b124a29dfde4773d7372","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself, so the tiresome task of keeping up a slow, disappointing correspondence with Elizabeth fell entirely on Anne.

Breakfast had barely finished when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick arrived; they had arranged one last walk around Lyme together. They were supposed to start for Uppercross by one o’clock, and meant to stay together and outdoors as long as possible until then.

As soon as they were all in the street, Anne noticed Captain Benwick drawing near her. Their talk the night before clearly had not discouraged him, and they walked together for some time, speaking again of Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, still as unable as any other two readers to agree about either author’s merits, until something caused a general rearrangement in the group and she suddenly found Captain Harville at her side instead of Captain Benwick.

“Miss Elliot,” he said quietly, “you have done something good in getting that poor fellow to talk so much. I wish he could have such company more often. It’s bad for him to be shut up the way he is, but what can we do? We cannot separate.”

“No,” said Anne, “I can easily believe that to be impossible; but in time, perhaps—we know what time does for every sorrow, and you must remember, Captain Harville, that your friend can still be called a young mourner—only last summer, I understand.”

“Yes, true enough,” he replied with a deep sigh, “only June.”

“And perhaps he did not know of it so soon.”

“Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, just made first lieutenant of the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, dreading to hear of him; he sent letters ahead, but the Grappler was ordered to Portsmouth. The news had to meet him there, but who was to tell him? Not I. I would as soon have been hoisted to the yardarm. No one could do it but that good man,” he said, pointing to Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had come into Plymouth the week before, with no danger of being ordered back to sea. He took his chance with the rest, sent up a request for leave, but without waiting for the reply, traveled night and day until he reached Portsmouth, rowed straight out to the Grappler, and never left the poor fellow for a week. That is what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. Judge for yourself, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us!”

Anne mentally answered the question without hesitation and said all that her feelings allowed or that Captain Harville’s emotions could endure, for he was too moved to continue the topic, and when he spoke again it was of something entirely different."}

{"request_id":"27d406520c8b8d69fc6c5350","rewritten_text":"“We went to your home,” said the first man, “but you weren’t there, and when we learned you were likely walking this way, we followed in hopes of catching up with you. Please get into the carriage.”

“Their manner was commanding, and as they spoke they positioned themselves so that I stood between them and the carriage door. They were armed. I was not.

“‘Gentlemen,’ I said, ‘forgive me, but I usually ask who seeks my help, and what sort of case I am being called to.’

“The second man answered. ‘Doctor, your clients are people of rank. As for the nature of the case, we trust your skill to understand it better than we could explain it. That’s enough. Please get into the carriage.’

“I had no choice but to comply, and I stepped in without a word. Both of them followed—the last jumped in after raising the steps. The carriage turned around and sped off at its previous pace.

“I repeat this conversation exactly as it happened. I’m sure this is word for word. I’m recording everything precisely as it occurred, forcing my mind to stay fixed on the task. Where I insert the dashed lines that follow, I pause for the moment and hide my notes.

*****

“The carriage left the city streets, passed through the North Barrier, and rolled onto the country road. Two-thirds of a league from the Barrier—though I only calculated that later—we turned off the main avenue and soon stopped at an isolated house. All three of us got out and walked along a damp, soft path through a garden, where an unattended fountain had overflowed, until we reached the door. It didn’t open immediately when we rang, and one of my escorts hit the servant who opened it with his heavy riding glove across the face.

“There was nothing unusual to me in that gesture; I had seen ordinary people struck more often than dogs. But the other man, also angry, struck him the same way with his arm, and their expressions and posture were so identical at that moment that I realized they were twin brothers.

“From the time we’d arrived at the outer gate—which was locked until one brother opened it for us and then locked it again—I had heard cries coming from an upstairs room.”"}

{"request_id":"50332f0a227aa593bf5ff06d","rewritten_text":"I went from shop to shop, buying whatever was needed to change his appearance. When that business was done, I headed to Little Britain on my own errand. Mr. Jaggers sat at his desk, but as soon as he saw me enter, he rose and stood before his fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be careful.”

“I will, sir,” I answered, for I had planned what I meant to say on my way there.

“Don’t condemn yourself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “and don’t condemn anyone else. You understand—anyone. Don’t tell me anything: I don’t want to know anything; I’m not curious.”

Of course I realized he knew the man had come.

“I only want, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to assure myself that what I have been told is true. I don’t hope it is false, but at least I can confirm it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he asked, tilting his head and looking not at me but thoughtfully at the floor. “‘Told’ would suggest spoken communication. You can’t have spoken communication with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person named Abel Magwitch that he is the long-unknown benefactor to me.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And only he?” I said.

“And only he,” said Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to hold you in any way responsible for my mistakes and wrong conclusions, but I always believed it was Miss Havisham.”

“As you say, Pip,” returned Mr. Jaggers, turning his eyes on me coolly and biting his forefinger, “I am not responsible for that at all.”

“And yet it seemed so likely, sir,” I pleaded, downcast.

“Not a speck of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and gathering up his skirts. “Take nothing on appearances; take everything on evidence. There’s no better rule.”

“I have nothing more to say,” I answered with a sigh after a short silence. “I have confirmed my information, and that is the end of it.”

“And with Magwitch—in New South Wales—having finally revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will understand, Pip, how strictly, throughout my dealings with you, I have kept to the exact line of fact. There has never been the least deviation from the exact line of fact. You know that?”

“Quite, sir.”

“I informed Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must never expect me to deviate from the exact line of fact.”"}

{"request_id":"8d5c630a22a2eea34fe2c013","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is astonishing! I must meet Dorian Gray.”

Hallward rose from the seat and paced along the garden path. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “to me, Dorian Gray is purely an artistic impulse. You might find nothing remarkable in him. I see everything there is. He is most present in my work when no likeness of him appears. He is, as I have told you, the hint of a new style. I discover him in the sweep of certain lines, in the delicacy and grace of certain colours. That is all.”

“Then why refuse to exhibit his portrait?” Lord Henry asked.

“Because, without meaning to, I have breathed into it a hint of this strange artistic worship, of which I have never cared to speak to him. He knows nothing of it. He never shall. But the world might suspect, and I refuse to lay my soul before their barren, inquisitive eyes. I will not have my heart placed beneath their microscope. There is far too much of myself in that painting, Harry—far too much!”

“Poets are less particular than you. They know how convenient passion can be for print. Nowadays a broken heart yields countless editions.”

“I detest them for it,” Hallward exclaimed. “An artist ought to make lovely things, yet leave nothing of his own life within them. We live in a time when people treat art as though it were meant to be memoir. We have lost the pure idea of beauty. Someday I shall show the world what it truly is; and for that reason, the world shall never look upon my portrait of Dorian Gray.”

“I think you are mistaken, Basil, but I will not dispute it. Only the intellectually adrift ever argue. Tell me, does Dorian Gray care greatly for you?”

The painter pondered a moment. “He is fond of me,” he replied after a pause; “I know he is. Naturally I flatter him outrageously. I take a strange delight in saying things to him that I know I shall regret. Usually he is delightful to me, and we sit in the studio and speak of countless matters. Yet now and again he grows horribly inconsiderate and seems to take a definite pleasure in hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, as though I have handed over my entire soul to someone who treats it like a blossom for his lapel, a little adornment to gratify his vanity, a ornament suited to a summer’s day.”"}

{"request_id":"37d760d6a3a5129023ecd5be","rewritten_text":"“And only think, ma’am,” pleaded Oliver, tears forcing their way despite his struggle to hold them back, “pray think how young she is, and how much kindness she gives, and the joy and comfort she brings to everyone near her. I’m sure—really sure—quite persuaded—that, for your sake, as good as you are; and for her own; and for the sake of all those she makes so happy; she will not die. Heaven will never suffer her to die so young.”

“Hush!” replied Mrs. Maylie, resting her hand upon Oliver’s head. “You speak like a child, poor boy. Yet you remind me of my duty, all the same. I let it slip for a moment, Oliver, but I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old, and have witnessed enough of sickness and death to understand the torment of parting from those we love. I have seen sufficient, too, to know it isn’t always the youngest and best who are kept to those that cherish them; but that should console us in our grief; for Heaven is just; and such scenes teach us vividly that there exists a brighter world than this, and that the way to it is swift. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how dearly!”

Oliver was amazed to find that, as Mrs. Maylie uttered these words, she checked her lamenting as if by sheer resolve; and, drawing herself erect while she spoke, grew calm and steadfast. He was even more astonished to observe that this steadiness endured; and that, amid all the subsequent care and vigil, Mrs. Maylie remained ever ready and self-possessed: fulfilling every duty that had fallen on her, steadily, and, outwardly at least, even with cheerfulness. But he was young, and was ignorant of what strong minds can do in moments of trial. How should he know, when even those who possess such minds are seldom aware themselves?

A fearful night followed. As morning broke, Mrs. Maylie’s forebodings were only too sadly realized. Rose had entered the earliest stage of a high, dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not yield to idle grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, placing her finger on her lips while she looked steadily into his face; “this letter must go, with the utmost speed, to Mr. Losberne. It has to be carried to the market-town, no more than four miles away, by the footpath across the meadows: and from there dispatched by special messenger on horseback, direct to Chertsey. The people at the inn will see to it: and I am certain I can trust you to have it done.”

Oliver could say nothing, but let his eager expression show how ready he was to be off at once."}

{"request_id":"d5504d93455982b4e82aa782","rewritten_text":"“On that topic I shall remain consistently silent; you may rely upon my never uttering an ungenerous reproach when once we are married.”

She was compelled to cut him short at this point.

“You are much too precipitate, sir,” she exclaimed. “You seem to forget I have returned no answer. Let me do so without further delay. I am obliged by the compliment you intend me. I fully acknowledge the honour of your proposals, yet I am compelled to decline them.”

“I am perfectly aware,” Mr. Collins rejoined, giving a ceremonious wave of his hand, “that young ladies commonly reject the man whom in secret they resolve to accept when he first sues for their favour; and that at times the refusal is repeated twice, even thrice. I am therefore in no way discouraged by what you have said, and still hope soon to conduct you to the altar.”

“Upon my word, sir,” cried Elizabeth, “that hope is astonishing after my declaration. Believe me, I am not one of those ladies (if such ladies exist) so bold as to stake their happiness on the chance of a second proposal. My refusal is in the utmost earnest. You could never make me happy, and I am convinced I should be the last woman on earth to render you so. Indeed, were your friend Lady Catherine acquainted with me, she would perceive I am unfit in every respect for that station.”

“If it were certain Lady Catherine would think so,” said Mr. Collins very solemnly, “but I cannot suppose her ladyship would in the least disapprove of you. Be assured, moreover, that when next I have the honour of seeing her, I shall extol your modesty, prudence, and other amiable qualities.”

“Believe me, Mr. Collins, any commendation of me is needless. Allow me to judge for myself, and favour me so far as to credit my words. I sincerely wish you both happy and prosperous, and by refusing your hand do all within my power to preserve you so. In offering it, you have, I think, fully satisfied your sense of delicacy toward my family, and may claim Longbourn estate when it descends, without the slightest self-reproach. The matter, therefore, may be considered definitively settled.” Rising as she spoke, she would have left the room but for Mr. Collins, who resumed,

“When next I have the honour to address you on this subject, I trust to obtain a more agreeable reply than you have now afforded me; though I acquit you of cruelty for the present, as I know it is the established practice of your sex to reject a gentleman on his first application, and perhaps you have already said as much to encourage my suit as is compatible with the strict delicacy of the female character.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"328b6737602cad6a28c40c04","rewritten_text":"The mental traits commonly discussed under the label of analytical scarcely admit of dissection themselves. We recognize them solely through their manifestations. Among other things we know that, when they exist in excess, they are to their owner a source of keenest pleasure. As the muscular man rejoices in his bodily prowess, savoring any exertion that sets his sinews to work, so does the analyst revel in that moral activity which disentangles. He finds delight even in the slightest occupation that brings his gift into play. Riddles, puzzles, hieroglyphs are his favorites; in resolving each he displays a shrewdness that to ordinary minds seems almost supernatural. Though his conclusions result from the pure essence of method, they wear, in fact, the entire aspect of intuition.\n\nThe power of solving may perhaps be greatly strengthened by mathematical study, particularly by that highest branch which, unjustly and simply because its procedures retreat, has been styled, as if preeminent, analysis. Yet computation, in itself, is not analysis. The chess player, for instance, may perform the former without exerting the latter. Hence the influence of chess upon intellectual character is seriously misconceived. I am not composing a treatise, merely introducing a rather singular tale with scattered remarks; I shall therefore assert that the more refined and more practical exercise of the reflective intellect is demanded by the modest game of draughts than by all the laborious trifling of chess. In chess, where each piece has eccentric movements with varying and changeable values, mere complexity is mistaken—an error not uncommon—for depth. Here the attention is summoned with force. Let it droop for a moment, and an oversight follows, bringing harm or defeat. Since the possible moves are not only numerous but intricate, the hazards of such mistakes multiply; in nine instances out of ten it is the player of steadier concentration, rather than sharper penetration, who wins. In draughts, conversely, where the moves are uniform and scarcely vary, chances of inadvertence are reduced, and, the attention being comparatively unoccupied, any advantage gained by a player springs from superior acumen. To be less abstract, envision a draughts match with the pieces reduced to four kings, where naturally no oversight is to be anticipated. Plainly, victory can then be secured (the players being nearly equal) only through some recherché maneuver, born of a vigorous exertion of intellect."}

{"request_id":"eae5aec142e522711717db72","rewritten_text":"With everything thus harmoniously settled, the agreement was sealed by another teacup of peppermint cordial, the more needful because of the lady’s fluttered nerves. While she sipped, she informed Mr. Bumble of the old woman’s passing.

“Very good,” said he, tasting his peppermint. “I’ll stop by Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send in the morning. Was that what startled you, love?”

“It was nothing particular, dear,” she replied evasively.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble insisted. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” the lady answered. “One day. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” cried Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any impertinence from those male paupers as—”

“No, no, love!” the lady cried quickly.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble went on, “if I believed any of them had dared to lift their wulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” she returned.

“They had better not!” he declared, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, parochial or extra-parochial, who would presume it, and I’ll tell him he wouldn’t do so twice!”

Lacking any energetic gestures, the speech might not have flattered the lady’s beauty; but, as Mr. Bumble accompanied it with many martial motions, she was deeply affected, and fervently declared he was indeed a dove.

The dove then flipped up his coat-collar, donned his cocked hat, and, after a lingering and affectionate embrace with his future partner, once more faced the night wind: pausing briefly in the male paupers’ ward to scold them, just to assure himself he possessed the necessary sharpness to be master of the workhouse. Satisfied of his fitness, Mr. Bumble departed with a buoyant heart and bright dreams of advancement that occupied him until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

As Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry were out to tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never inclined to exert himself beyond what was necessary for eating and drinking, the shop remained open, though it was past closing time. Mr. Bumble rapped his cane on the counter several times; receiving no answer, and seeing a light shining through the glass of the little parlour window behind the shop, he ventured to peep in—and was considerably astonished by what met his eyes."}
