{"request_id":"2f22b6c4eafd059c5a3197f3","rewritten_text":"Yet he had oppressed no man, imprisoned no man; so far was he from harshly exacting what was owing that he had surrendered his rights willingly, hurled himself upon a world offering him no favour, carved out a private station within it, and earned his own sustenance. Monsieur Gabelle had kept the bankrupt and tangled estate under written orders to spare the villagers, to give them the scraps available—fuel the rapacious creditors grudged them in winter, produce that could be rescued from the same clutch in summer—and doubtless he had urged this in his defence, so it could not fail to be evident now.

This inclined Charles Darnay to the desperate resolve he had begun to form: that he must go to Paris.

Indeed. Like the sailor in the old tale, winds and currents had borne him into the sphere of the Loadstone Rock, it drew him, and he must yield. Everything that rose before his thoughts impelled him faster, more steadily, toward that formidable magnet. His suppressed uneasiness had been that wicked purposes were being enacted in his suffering country by evil agents, and that he, who knew himself better than they, was absent, not striving to stem the slaughter or uphold mercy and humanity. With this disquiet half smothered and half reproachful, he had been driven to compare himself with the gallant old gentleman whose sense of duty was so unshakable; at once there followed the sneers of Monseigneur, keenly wounding him, and those of Stryver, which most of all were coarse and exasperating, for reasons of long standing. Upon these came Gabelle’s letter: the plea of a guiltless captive, in peril of death, appealing to his justice, honour, and reputation.

His mind was fixed. He had to go to Paris.

Indeed. The Loadstone Rock was hauling him, and he must sail onward, even to the crash. He knew of no reef; he scarcely perceived danger. The purpose with which he had acted, though the work was unfinished, presented itself to him in a shape that must win grateful recognition in France when he came to affirm it. Then arose that glorious dream of doing good, so often the hopeful mirage of many worthy spirits, and he even beheld himself within that illusion exerting some sway to guide this raging Revolution that was rushing so dreadfully wild."}

{"request_id":"ea850289a554cb2632ed5372","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was deeply upset by the second delay of the wedding, and Lady Julia, who had already ordered her gown, did everything she could to make Sybil call off the match. Yet Sybil loved her mother dearly and had given her whole life to Lord Arthur, so nothing Lady Julia said could shake her trust. As for Lord Arthur, it took him days to recover from his awful disappointment, and for a while his nerves were completely shattered. Still, his good common sense soon returned, and his sound, practical mind did not leave him uncertain for long. Since poison had been a total failure, explosives—dynamite or something similar—seemed the obvious next attempt. 

He went back over the list of his friends and relatives and, after careful thought, decided to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of great culture and learning, loved clocks and kept a remarkable collection of timepieces from the fifteenth century to the present. Lord Arthur decided this passion offered a perfect chance to carry out his plan. Finding an explosive device, however, was quite another issue. The London Directory gave him no help, and he felt there was no point in going to Scotland Yard, as they never seemed to know anything about dynamiters until after the blast, and not much even then. 

Suddenly he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with very revolutionary leanings whom he had met at Lady Windermere’s that winter. Count Rouvaloff claimed to be writing a life of Peter the Great and said he had come to England to study documents about the Tsar’s time here working as a ship carpenter, but it was widely suspected he was a Nihilist agent, and the Russian Embassy clearly disapproved of his presence in London. Lord Arthur felt he was exactly the man he needed and drove one morning to Rouvaloff’s lodgings in Bloomsbury to ask for his advice and help. 

“So you are taking up politics seriously?” said Count Rouvaloff after Lord Arthur explained why he had come. But Lord Arthur, who disliked any show of pretension, admitted that he had no interest in social issues at all and wanted the explosive device for a purely family matter that concerned no one but himself."}

{"request_id":"27691e9b09344c159b097774","rewritten_text":"The exquisite gentlemen of the highest breeding wore small dangling trinkets that chimed as they moved with languid grace; these golden chains rang like delicate little bells, and with that tinkling, along with the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, there was a flutter in the air that swept Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger far away.

Clothing was the unfailing talisman, the charm that kept everything in its place. Everyone was dressed for a Fancy Ball that would never end. From the Tuileries Palace, through Monseigneur and all the Court, through the Chambers, the courts of justice, and the whole of society (save for the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball extended all the way to the common executioner, who, under the spell, was required to perform his duties “curled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe was a rarity—Monsieur Paris, for so his brother professors in the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest called him in keeping with episcopal custom, presided in this dainty attire. And who among the guests at Monseigneur’s reception in that seventeen-hundred-and-eightieth year of our Lord could possibly doubt that a system rooted in a frizzled hangman, powdered, gold-laced, in pumps and white silk stockings, would outlast the stars themselves?

After Monseigneur relieved his four bearers of their burdens and took his chocolate, he ordered the doors of the Holiest of Holies thrown open and emerged. Then came such submission, such fawning and groveling, such servility, such abject humiliation! When it came to bowing in body and spirit, nothing was left for Heaven—which may have been one among other reasons why Monseigneur’s worshippers never concerned themselves with it.

Handing out a promise here and a smile there, a whisper to one fortunate slave and a wave of the hand to another, Monseigneur graciously moved through his rooms to the distant region of the Circumference of Truth. There, he turned around and came back again, and so, in due time, he had himself shut up in his sanctuary by the chocolate sprites and was seen no more.

Once the spectacle was done, the flutter in the air grew into quite a little storm, and the tiny precious bells went ringing down the stairs. Soon, only one person remained from all the crowd, and he, with his hat under his arm and his snuffbox in hand, slowly passed the mirrors on his way out.

“I dedicate you,” he said, stopping at the last door on his way and turning toward the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

With that, he flicked the snuff from his fingers as though shaking the dust from his feet, and calmly walked downstairs."}

{"request_id":"028527eb473e2171d606c929","rewritten_text":"The day unfolded much the same as the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several hours of the morning with the patient, who was still recovering, though slowly; in the evening, Elizabeth joined them in the drawing room. The loo table, however, was nowhere in sight. Mr. Darcy was writing, while Miss Bingley sat nearby, watching him compose his letter and repeatedly distracting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, and Mrs. Hurst was studying their game.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and was more than entertained by the exchange between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praise—whether of his handwriting, the straightness of his lines, or the length of his letter—and his complete indifference to her compliments made for an amusing dialogue that matched Elizabeth’s opinion of them both.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to receive such a letter!”

He gave no answer.

“You write unusually fast.”

“You’re mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“You must have so many letters to write in a year! Business letters, too! How dreadful I would find them!”

“Then it is fortunate that they fall to me instead of to you.”

“Please tell your sister that I am eager to see her.”

“I have already told her so once, at your request.”

“I’m afraid you don’t like your pen. Let me fix it for you. I am exceptionally good at sharpening pens.”

“Thank you—but I always take care of my own.”

“How do you manage to write so evenly?”

He remained silent.

“Tell your sister I’m delighted to hear about her progress on the harp, and please inform her that I’m absolutely thrilled with her beautiful little table design; I consider it far superior to Miss Grantley’s.”

“May I postpone your raptures until I write again? At the moment I lack the space to do them justice.”

“Oh, it doesn’t matter. I’ll see her in January. But do you always write such charmingly long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are generally long; but whether they are always charming is not for me to say.”

“It is my rule that anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write poorly.”

“That won’t do as a compliment for Darcy, Caroline,” her brother interjected, “because he does not write with ease. He searches too carefully for words of four syllables. Isn’t that so, Darcy?”

“My style of writing is quite different from yours.”

“Oh,” Miss Bingley exclaimed, “Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.”"}

{"request_id":"547b05ebedbe98c8c7ce2f4e","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” exclaimed the old lady as he came in, “why have you stayed away from me so long?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I have not a moment to myself,” Lord Arthur replied with a smile.

“I suppose that means you traipse about all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense? I cannot conceive why people make such a to-do about getting married. In my day we never dreamt of billing and cooing—neither in public nor in private.”

“I assure you I have not seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.”

“Of course; that is the only reason you visit an ugly old creature like me. I wonder you men don’t take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and now look—nothing but a rheumatic wretch with a false front and a sour temper. If it weren’t for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can ferret out, I do not believe I could get through the day. Doctors are worthless—good only for collecting fees. They cannot even mend my heartburn.”

“I have brought you a remedy for that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur seriously. “It is a marvelous thing, invented by an American.”

“I don’t fancy American inventions, Arthur. I am positive I don’t. I read several American novels lately, and they were utter rubbish.”

“Oh, but there is no rubbish about this at all, Lady Clem! I guarantee it is an infallible cure. You must promise to try it.” Lord Arthur drew a small box from his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is delightful, Arthur. Is it truly a gift? How very kind. And is this the famous medicine? It resembles a bonbon. I shall take it immediately.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem!” cried Lord Arthur, seizing her hand. “You must not do anything of the sort. It is a homoeopathic remedy, and if you swallow it without an attack of heartburn, it may do you no end of damage. Wait until the pain begins, and then take it. You will be amazed at the result.”

“I should like to swallow it now,” said Lady Clementina, holding the tiny transparent capsule up to the light, its bubble of liquid aconitine floating inside. “I am sure it is delicious. Truth be told, though I hate doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I shall save it for my next attack.”

“And when is that to be?” asked Lord Arthur eagerly."}

{"request_id":"66d5cb1b58c4c5eb64265235","rewritten_text":"I repeated to myself that beautiful passage about Dante entering the earthly Paradise, and imagined how wonderful it would be to walk along those lovely banks and see the chariot of light descend with my long-lost parent to return him to me. While I waited for that imagined moment, I pictured myself weaving a wreath from those beautiful flowers and crowning myself out of happiness: I would sing _sul margine d’un rio_, my father’s favorite song, so that my voice floating through the still air would tell him, wherever he sat anticipating our reunion, that his daughter had arrived. Then the mark of misery would fade from my forehead, and I would lift my gaze without fear to meet his eyes, which always shone with the gentle light of innocent love. Thinking of the enchantment in those deep eyes brought me to tears, though I wept softly so my sobs would not disturb the enchanted scene.

I was so completely lost in this daydream that I kept walking without noticing where I went until I bent to pick a flower for my wreath on that barren plain where no flower grew, and then I woke from my reverie and realized I had no idea where I was.

The sun had already set and the rosy glow that the clouds had taken from it on its way down had almost faded. A wind swept over the plain; I looked around but nothing showed me where I might be. I was lost, and my effort to find the path was useless. I wandered on, and the approaching darkness erased every trace that might guide me. Soon everything was shrouded in the pitch blackness of night; I grew tired, and knowing that my servant was spending the night in the nearby village, so my absence would alarm no one, and feeling sure I was safe from intruders in this desolate place, I decided to spend the night there. Truly I was too weary to walk farther: the air was cold, but I cared little for physical discomfort, and I thought of how well I had learned to endure the weather during my two years of solitude, when no change of season had ever stopped my constant wandering.

I lay down on the grass, surrounded by darkness untouched by even the faintest glimmer of light. No sound broke the stillness, for the deep night had lulled to sleep the insects—the only living creatures in that lonely spot where not a tree or shrub could shelter anything else. There was a marvelous silence in the air that soothed my senses yet quickened my spirit; my mind leapt from one image to another and seemed to embrace eternity."}

{"request_id":"5a8b4d33e0fd38d99385f5e6","rewritten_text":"Winters at the latitude of Sullivan’s Island are rarely very harsh, and during autumn a fire is almost never needed. Around mid-October, 18—, however, there was an unusually cold day. Just before sunset I pushed through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, which I hadn’t visited for several weeks—at the time I lived in Charleston, nine miles from the island, and the travel back and forth was nothing like it is today. When I reached the hut I knocked, as usual, and when no one answered, I looked for the key where I knew it was hidden, unlocked the door, and went inside. A fine fire was blazing on the hearth. It was something different, and most welcome. I shed my overcoat, settled into an armchair by the crackling logs, and waited patiently for my hosts to return.

Soon after dark they arrived and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, grinning from ear to ear, hurried around preparing marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his—what else should I call them?—fits of enthusiasm. He had found a previously unknown bivalve, representing a new genus, and, beyond that, with Jupiter’s help he had tracked down and captured a scarab he believed to be completely new, though he wanted my opinion on it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands over the fire, wishing the whole tribe of scarabs to the devil.

“Ah, if only I’d known you were here!” said Legrand. “But it’s been so long since I’ve seen you, and how could I predict you’d visit me tonight of all nights? On my way home I ran into Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and, very foolishly, I lent him the bug; so you won’t be able to see it until morning. Stay tonight, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest thing in creation!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Don’t be absurd! No—the bug. It’s a brilliant gold color, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and another, somewhat longer, at the other end. The antennae are—”

“Ain’t no tin in him, Master Will, I keep tellin’ you,” Jupiter cut in. “The bug is a gold bug, solid, all the way through, ’cept for his wings—I never felt a bug so heavy in my life.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"322b811db30e09814aac8616","rewritten_text":"“I wrapped him in de paper and shoved a scrap of it in his mouf—that’s how it went.” “And you are persuaded your master truly was bitten by the beetle, that the bite put him out of sorts?” “I ain’t tinkin’ nuttin’—I’s knowin’. What else make him dream ’bout de goole constant, if it ain’t ’cause de goole-bug bit him? I done heerd tell o’ dem goole-bugs afore now.” “But how can you be sure he dreams of gold?” “How I know? ’Cause he mutter ’bout it in his sleep—that’s how I knows.” “Well, Jup, perhaps you may be right; but to what lucky circumstance do I owe the pleasure of seeing you today?” “What’s de trouble, massa?” “Did you bring any word from Mr. Legrand?” “No, massa, I tote dis here pissel;” with that, Jupiter passed me a note which read: “MY DEAR ——Why have you been absent so long? I trust you have not been silly enough to take offence at any little brusquerie of mine; yet no—that seems unlikely. Since last we met I have had grave cause for disquiet. I have something to impart, yet scarcely know how to frame it, or if I ought to tell it at all. I have not been altogether well for some days, and poor old Jup torments me, almost past endurance, with his well-meant fussing. Could you credit it?—he got ready a tremendous cudgel, the other day, meaning to punish me for slipping away from him and passing the day, solus, among the mainland hills. I truly believe my haggard look alone kept me from a whipping. I have added nothing to my cabinet since you last saw it. If there is any way you can possibly manage it, come over with Jupiter. Do come. I desire to see you to-night on business of weight. I assure you it is of the highest weight. Ever yours, WILLIAM LEGRAND.” A certain tone in this message troubled me greatly. The whole manner of it was markedly unlike Legrand’s usual style. What could he be brooding over? What new whim had seized that ardent brain? What “business of the highest importance” could he have? Jupiter’s report promised nothing favorable. I feared the steady strain of hardship might at last have truly disturbed my friend’s mind. So without the least delay I got ready to go with the negro. When we reached the wharf, I remarked a scythe and three spades, all seemingly fresh from the shop, lying at the bottom of the boat in which we were to set out. “What does all this mean, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"73a7bc63e7cdf4bcb28d968f","rewritten_text":"During dinner, Mr. Bennet barely spoke; but once the servants left, he decided it was time to converse with his guest. He chose a topic on which he expected Mr. Collins to excel, remarking that Mr. Collins seemed very fortunate in his benefactor. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to his wishes and concern for his comfort were truly remarkable. Mr. Bennet could not have selected a better subject. Mr. Collins grew eloquent in her praise. The topic lifted him to an even more solemn manner, and with the utmost seriousness he protested that never in his life had he witnessed such behavior in a person of rank—such graciousness and condescension—as he had experienced from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both sermons he had already had the honor of preaching before her. She had invited him twice to dine at Rosings and had even sent for him just the previous Saturday to complete her quadrille table in the evening. Many considered Lady Catherine proud, he knew, but he himself had never seen anything but friendliness in her. She always spoke to him as she would to any other gentleman; she made no objection to his joining in the neighborhood’s society, nor to his leaving his parish for a week or two to visit relatives. She had even advised him to marry as soon as he could, provided he chose carefully, and had once honored him with a visit at his modest parsonage, where she fully approved the alterations he had been making and even condescended to suggest some herself—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and polite, I’m sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very agreeable woman. It’s a pity more great ladies are not like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden in which my humble home stands is separated from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s residence, by only a lane.”

“I think you said she was a widow, sir? Does she have any family?”

“She has only one daughter, the heiress of Rosings and of very considerable property.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better off than many girls. And what sort of young lady is she? Is she pretty?”

“She is a truly charming young lady. Lady Catherine herself says that, for genuine beauty, Miss de Bourgh far surpasses the most attractive of her sex, because there is something in her features that signifies a young woman of distinguished birth.”"}

{"request_id":"5382f1a1e4cbfa5d2dd8558a","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay,” was finally brought to trial.

His judges sat on the Bench in feathered hats, but everywhere else rough red caps with tricolor cockades were the common headwear. Looking at the Jury and the restless crowd, he might have thought the world had turned upside down and that criminals were judging honest men. The poorest and most vicious people in the city, always present in some number, ruled the scene: loudly commenting, cheering, jeering, guessing, and trying to hurry the verdict with no restraint. Most of the men were armed in one way or another; among the women, some had knives, some had daggers, some ate and drank while watching, and many knitted. Among the knitters was one who carried an extra piece of knitting under her arm. She sat in a front row, next to a man Darnay had not seen since arriving at the Barrier, yet recognized immediately as Defarge. He noticed she whispered in his ear once or twice and seemed to be his wife; but what struck him most about them was that, although they had placed themselves as close to him as possible, they never looked his way. They seemed to wait for something with stubborn resolve, staring at the Jury and nowhere else. Doctor Manette sat below the President, wearing his usual quiet clothes. As far as the prisoner could tell, he and Mr. Lorry were the only men not connected with the Tribunal who still wore their ordinary dress and had not put on the coarse Carmagnole costume.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was charged by the prosecutor as an emigrant whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants on pain of death. It did not matter that the decree was dated after his return to France. He was there, and the decree was there; he had been taken in France, and his head was demanded.

“Take off his head!” shouted the crowd. “An enemy to the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to silence them and asked the prisoner if it was true he had lived many years in England.

He admitted it was.

Was he not then an emigrant? How did he describe himself?

He hoped he was not an emigrant in the meaning and spirit of the law.

Why not? the President asked.

Because he had willingly given up a title he detested and a position he detested. He had left his country—he said this was before the Tribunal used the word emigrant in its current sense—to support himself by his own work in England, rather than live in France on the labor of an already overburdened people."}

Maybe to Hartfield, maybe to Abbey Mill, maybe into his woods. Miss Woodhouse, this isn’t how our friend Knightley behaves! Can you explain it?” Emma joked that it really was extraordinary and she didn’t have a word to say in his defense. “I can’t imagine,” Mrs. Elton said—feeling the slight as any wife should—“I cannot imagine how he could treat you like this, of all people! The last person anyone would expect him to forget! My dear Mr. E., he must have left you a message, I’m sure he did. Not even Knightley could be so eccentric; his servants must have forgotten it. You can depend on that being the case, and it’s very likely with the Donwell servants, who are all, as I’ve often noticed, extremely clumsy and negligent. I wouldn’t have someone like his Harry at our sideboard for any price. And as for Mrs. Hodges, Wright thinks very little of her. content.text: {"request_id":"8e051a5fb0f01aa81f6bd2d3","rewritten_text":"“But, in sober truth, when an ascension has been made to any altitude, the mass of atmosphere overcome by any further rise is far from proportional to the additional height (as should be clear from earlier remarks), and instead decreases in a continually diminishing ratio. Hence it is plain that, climb as far as we will, we cannot, strictly speaking, reach a boundary beyond which no air exists. The atmosphere must be there, I reasoned, though perhaps in a condition of immeasurable tenuity.\n\n“Conversely, I knew that many arguments had been advanced to establish a fixed and absolute limit to the atmosphere, beyond which air is wholly wanting. Yet a fact disregarded by those who advocate such a boundary seemed to me, if not a direct overthrow of their doctrine, at least a matter for weighty inquiry. When the intervals between Encke’s comet’s successive returns to perihelion are compared, after allowing with utmost precision for every disturbance from planetary attraction, we find the periods gradually lessening; that is, the major axis of its ellipse steadily shortens in a slow but perfectly regular contraction. This is exactly what must happen if the comet encounters resistance from an exceedingly tenuous ethereal substance filling the regions of its orbit. For such a medium, by slackening the comet’s speed, would strengthen its centripetal while weakening its centrifugal force. In simpler terms, the sun’s pull would be constantly gaining the advantage, drawing the comet closer at each revolution. In fact, no other explanation presents itself for the change observed. Furthermore—the actual diameter of the comet’s nebulous envelope shrinks swiftly as it nears the sun, and expands as rapidly as it heads toward aphelion. Was it not reasonable for me, with M. Valz, to suppose that this apparent contraction of bulk springs from the pressure of the same ethereal medium mentioned above, which becomes denser the nearer it lies to the sun? The lenticular phenomenon dubbed the zodiacal light likewise deserved study. This glow, so obvious in tropical latitudes and unmistakable for meteoric brilliance, climbs obliquely from the horizon and loosely follows the sun’s equatorial line. It struck me as nothing less than a sparse atmosphere stretched outward from the sun, reaching beyond Venus’s track at least, and, so I believed, indefinitely farther. Indeed, I could not imagine this medium limited to the comet’s orbit or restricted solely to the immediate precincts of the sun.”"}

{"request_id":"ed21831ef877f064755edcc3","rewritten_text":"But I wonder how long you would have continued on your own. When would you have spoken if I had not asked? My plan to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had a strong effect. Too strong, I fear; what becomes of the moral if our happiness comes from my breaking my promise, since I ought not to have mentioned it? This will never do.”

“You need not worry. The moral stays intact. Lady Catherine’s unjust attempts to separate us removed all my doubts. I do not owe my current happiness to your urgent wish to thank me. I was not in the mood to wait for you to begin. My aunt’s news gave me hope, and I was determined to learn everything at once.”

“Lady Catherine has been of immense use, which should make her happy, since she loves being useful. But tell me, why did you come down to Netherfield? Was it only to ride to Longbourn and feel embarrassed, or did you plan something more serious?”

“My true purpose was to see you and judge, if I could, whether I might ever hope you would love me. My stated purpose, or what I told myself, was to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and if she did, to confess to him what I have since confessed.”

“Will you ever have the nerve to tell Lady Catherine what is coming?”

“I am more likely to lack time than bravery, Elizabeth. But it must be done; and if you give me a sheet of paper, I will do it at once.”

“And if I did not have a letter to write, I might sit beside you and admire how steady your handwriting is, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt too, and she must not be neglected any longer.”

Elizabeth had not yet answered Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter, because she was reluctant to admit how she had overestimated her closeness with Mr. Darcy. Now that she had news she knew would delight her aunt, she felt almost guilty that her uncle and aunt had already missed three days of happiness, and she wrote at once:

“I would have thanked you sooner, dear aunt, as I ought to have done, for your long, kind, satisfying account; but to tell the truth, I was too out of spirits to write. You assumed more than truly existed. But now assume as much as you like; let your imagination run free in every direction the subject allows, and unless you believe me already married, you cannot be far wrong.”"}

{"request_id":"2c95cee67e8175cf2a577fac","rewritten_text":"“He was delivered to you. You see I know the circumstances?”

“That is the fact,” Defarge replied. His wife had brushed his elbow as she knitted and hummed, signaling that he should answer, but keep it brief.

“It was to you,” the spy continued, “that his daughter came; and from your care she took him, with that neat brown gentleman—what is his name?—the one with the small wig—Lorry—of Tellson and Company’s bank—and carried him over to England.”

“That is the fact,” Defarge repeated.

“Very interesting memories!” said the spy. “I have known Doctor Manette and his daughter in England.”

“Yes?” said Defarge.

“You don’t hear much about them now?” the spy asked.

“No,” said Defarge.

“In truth,” Madame broke in, looking up from her work and her little song, “we never hear about them. We received word of their safe arrival, and perhaps one more letter, or perhaps two; but since then they have gone their way in life, we ours, and we have kept no correspondence.”

“Precisely so, madame,” the spy replied. “She is going to be married.”

“Going?” Madame echoed. “She was pretty enough to have been married long ago. You English must be cold.”

“Oh! You know I am English.”

“I notice your tongue is,” Madame returned; “and as the tongue is, I suppose the man is.”

He did not take that as a compliment, but he handled it as well as he could and laughed it off. After finishing his cognac, he added:

“Yes, Miss Manette is going to be married. But not to an Englishman; to someone who, like her, was born French. Speaking of Gaspard (ah, poor Gaspard! It was cruel, cruel!), it is curious that she is going to marry the nephew of Monsieur the Marquis, for whom Gaspard was lifted to that height of so many feet—meaning, the present Marquis. Yet he lives unknown in England; he has no title there. He is Mr. Charles Darnay. D’Aulnais is his mother’s family name.”

Madame Defarge kept knitting steadily, but the news had a clear effect on her husband. No matter how he tried behind the little counter, striking a light and lighting his pipe, he was unsettled, and his hand was unsteady. The spy would not have been a spy if he had failed to notice or to remember it.

Having made at least this one score, whatever it might be worth, and with no customers coming in to help him with any other, Mr. Barsad paid for his drink and left, taking care to say politely before departing that he hoped to enjoy the pleasure of seeing Monsieur and Madame Defarge again."}

{"request_id":"a9a6a933903deeb37a0b3684","rewritten_text":"Were our proud dreams meant to fade like this? We had written our name just a little lower than the angels, and now we were no better than mayflies. We called ourselves the paragon of animals, and yet we proved to be the quintessence of dust. We complained that the pyramids had outlasted the embalmed bodies of their builders. Alas, the simple shepherd’s straw hut we passed on the road held within it the principle of greater longevity than the entire human race. How could we reconcile this grim change with our former ambitions and our seeming powers?

Suddenly an inner voice, clear and articulate, seemed to say: From eternity it was decreed this way. The steeds that carry Time forward have had this hour and this fulfillment chained to them since the void first bore its burden. Would you seek to unwrite the unchangeable laws of Necessity?

Mother of the world, servant of the Omnipotent, eternal and changeless Necessity, who sits with busy fingers ever weaving the unbreakable chain of events—I will not complain of your acts. If my human mind cannot accept that everything that exists is right, still, since what is must be, I will sit among the ruins and smile. Truly we were not born to enjoy, but to submit and to hope.

Will the reader tire if I describe in detail our long journey from Paris to Geneva? If day after day I recorded in journal form the pressing miseries of our fate, could my hand write, or language provide words to express, the variety of our woe, the jostling of one deplorable event upon another? Have patience, reader—whoever you are, wherever you dwell. Whether spirit or descendant of some surviving pair, your nature will be human, your home the earth. You will read here of the acts of the extinct race and will wonder if those who endured what you find recorded were made of frail flesh and soft substance like your own. Indeed they were—weep then; for surely, solitary being, you must be of gentle disposition. Shed compassionate tears, yet lend your attention to the tale and learn the deeds and sufferings of your forerunners.

Still, the final events that marked our passage through France were so filled with unsettling horror and gloomy misery that I should not linger too long over them. If I dissected each incident, every fragment of a second would hold a harrowing story, whose smallest word would curdle the blood in your young veins. It is right that I raise this monument to instruct you about the race that has passed, but not that I drag you through hospital wards or the hidden chambers of a charnel house."}

{"request_id":"8b8ae259d3eb5bd3ccbc4868","rewritten_text":"“Well, your father might let you go, if your mother can spare you. Daughters never matter as much to a father. And if you stay one more full month, I’ll be able to take one of you all the way to London, because I’m going there in early June for a week. Since Dawson has no objection to the barouche-box, there will be plenty of room for one of you—and if the weather happens to be cool, I wouldn’t mind taking both, as neither of you is large.”

“You are all kindness, madam, but I think we must stick to our original plan.”

Lady Catherine seemed reconciled. “Mrs. Collins, you must send a servant with them. You know I always say exactly what I think, and I cannot stand the idea of two young women traveling by post alone. It is highly improper. You must find a way to send someone. I detest that kind of thing. Young women should always be properly guarded and attended, in keeping with their station in life. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted she take two footmen with her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not have shown herself with propriety any other way. I am extremely attentive to such matters. You must send John with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I’m glad it occurred to me to mention it, because it would truly reflect poorly on you to let them travel alone.”

“My uncle is sending a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a valet, does he? I’m glad there is someone who thinks of such things. Where will you change horses? Oh, Bromley, of course. If you give them my name at the Bell, you will be well taken care of.”

Lady Catherine had many more questions about their trip, and since she did not answer all of them herself, attention was required—something Elizabeth considered fortunate; with her mind so preoccupied, she might have forgotten where she was. Reflection would have to be reserved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she surrendered to it as her greatest relief, and not a day passed without a solitary walk in which she could relish all the bleak pleasure of painful memories.

She was well on her way to knowing Mr. Darcy’s letter by heart. She pored over every sentence, and her feelings toward its writer shifted wildly. When she recalled the tone of his address, indignation still burned. But when she considered how unjustly she had condemned and rebuked him, her anger turned on herself, and his wounded feelings stirred her compassion."}

Not the least!” Joe offered me another spoonful of gravy, which I dared not accept. “He’s been a world of bother to you, ma’am,” remarked Mrs. Hubble, sympathizing with my sister. “Bother?” echoed my sister; “bother?” and she plunged into a dreadful inventory of every illness I’d indulged in, every night I’d kept her awake, each height I’d toppled off, every depth I’d tumbled into, each injury I’d inflicted on myself, and all the times she’d wished me in my grave, while I obstinately declined the invitation. I suspect the Romans must have provoked each other terribly with their noses; perhaps that accounts for their restlessness. At any rate, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose so exasperated me during the account of my misdeeds, I felt I could have pulled it till he roared. Yet all I had borne so far was nothing compared to the dreadful sensations that seized me when the silence following my sister’s recital was broken—during which, as I was painfully aware, everyone had turned their eyes on me in indignation and disgust. “Still,” observed Mr. Pumblechook, gently steering the company back to the matter from which they had strayed, “Pork—when viewed as biled—is rich, eh?” “Take a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister. O heavens, the moment had arrived! He would discover its weakness; he would pronounce it weak, and it would be all over with me! I clung fast to the table leg beneath the cloth, grasping it with both hands, and awaited doom. My sister fetched the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured him his brandy. None of the others touched any. The unhappy man dallied with his glass—lifted it, examined it against the light, replaced it—prolonging my torment. Meanwhile Mrs. Joe and Joe were lively in clearing the table for pie and pudding. I couldn’t remove my gaze from him. Still gripping the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the poor soul toy with his glass, lift it, smile, toss back his head, and swallow the brandy. Immediately afterward, the company was struck with unspeakable consternation when he sprang to his feet, whirled round several times in a horrifying, spasmodic, whooping-cough dance, and dashed out of the door; he then appeared through the window, violently plunging and spitting, contorting his face hideously, and seemingly deranged. I held tightly while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran after him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"dad82b9bc7304a9409ec150f","rewritten_text":"I rushed forward, gathered her into my arms, showered kisses on her, and pleaded, “Speak, dear heart—tell me what it is!” Her head drooped weakly against my chest, and she breathed, barely audible, “HELLO-CENTRAL!” “Make haste!” I cried to Clarence. “Telephone the king’s homeopath to come at once!” Two minutes later I was kneeling beside the child’s crib, while Sandy was sending servants scurrying through every corridor of the palace. One glance told me the truth—membranous croup. I bent close and murmured, “Wake up, darling! Hello-Central.” Her soft eyes fluttered open slowly, and she managed a faint, “Papa.” That was some relief; she was still a long way from death. I ordered sulphur remedies, fetched the croup-kettle myself; I never wait for physicians when either Sandy or the child falls ill. I understood how to care for both of them from experience. This little lad had spent much of its brief life cradled in my arms, and often I could smooth away its troubles and coax a laugh glistening through tears when even its mother failed. Sir Launcelot, clad in his finest armor, came striding through the grand hall on his way to the stock-board. He presided over that board and had taken the Siege Perilous off Sir Galahad’s hands, since the stock-board was now made up of the Knights of the Round Table using the Round Table for commercial matters. Seats there were worth figures you would never credit, so I won’t attempt to quote them. Sir Launcelot was a bear; he had run a corner in one of the new enterprises and was ready today to squeeze the shorts. But no matter—he remained the same old Launcelot, and one glance through the doorway, one glimpse of his little favorite lying ill, was enough. Bulls could gore bears and bears maul bulls to their hearts’ content; he would be in here standing guard over Hello-Central with all the loyalty he possessed. And that’s precisely what happened. He pitched his helmet into a corner, and within half a minute he was adjusting a fresh wick in the alcohol lamp and had the croup-kettle heating. Sandy by then had rigged a blanket canopy over the crib, so the arrangements were perfect. Sir Launcelot stoked the fire until the steam was up; together we packed the kettle with unslaked lime and carbolic acid, adding a dash of lactic acid besides, then filled it with water and slipped the steam nozzle underneath the canopy. Everything was in order at last, and we took our positions on opposite sides of the crib to keep watch."}

{"request_id":"9842007917f038a1981f7de2","rewritten_text":"Well, I said, I needed the watermelon. But he said I didn’t need it to break out of prison with; that was the difference. He said if I’d wanted it to hide a knife and sneak it to Jim to kill the seneskal, that would’ve been fine. So I let it go at that, though I couldn’t see any point in acting like a lawyer if I had to sit around and chew over gold-leaf distinctions every time I saw a chance to grab a watermelon.

Anyway, we waited that morning until everybody was busy and no one was around the yard; then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood off a ways to keep watch. After a while he came out, and we sat on the woodpile to talk. He says:

“Everything’s all set now except tools; that’s easy fixed.”

“Tools?” I said.

“Yeah.”

“Tools for what?”

“To dig with. We ain’t going to gnaw him out, are we?”

“Ain’t those old busted picks in there good enough to dig a nigger out with?” I said.

He turned on me, looking so pitying it could make you cry, and says:

“Huck Finn, did you ever hear of a prisoner having picks and shovels and all the modern conveniences in his closet to dig himself out with? Now I ask you—if you’ve got any sense at all—what chance would that give him to be a hero? They might as well lend him the key. Picks and shovels—they wouldn’t give them to a king.”

“Well then,” I said, “if we don’t want the picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of case-knives.”

“To dig the foundations out from under that cabin with?”

“Yes.”

“Confound it, it’s foolish, Tom.”

“It don’t matter how foolish it is, it’s the right way—and the regular way. And there isn’t any other way that I ever heard of, and I’ve read all the books that tell about these things. They always dig out with a case-knife—and not through dirt, either; usually it’s solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever. Why, look at one of those prisoners in the bottom dungeon of the Castle Deef, in the harbor of Marseilles, that dug himself out that way; how long was he at it, do you think?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don’t know. A month and a half.”"}

{"request_id":"4adafc527971266edab5ae33","rewritten_text":"Hearing Jim talk like that really hurt me; it dragged him down in my eyes. My conscience started nagging me harder than ever, until finally I said to it, “Back off—it’s not too late yet. I’ll paddle to shore at first light and confess.” Right away I felt calm and happy and light as air. All my worries vanished. I began watching hard for a light and humming to myself. After a while one appeared. Jim called out:

“We’re safe, Huck, we’re safe! Jump up and click your heels! That’s good old Cairo at last, I just know it!”

I said:

“I’ll take the canoe and go check, Jim. It might not be, you know.”

He jumped up, got the canoe ready, laid his old coat in the bottom for me to sit on, and handed me the paddle; and as I shoved off, he said:

“Pretty soon I’ll be shouting for joy, and I’ll say it’s all thanks to Huck. I’m a free man, and I never could’ve been free if it hadn’t been for Huck; Huck made it happen. Jim won’t ever forget you, Huck; you’re the best friend Jim’s ever had, and you’re the only friend old Jim’s got now.”

I was paddling away, sweating to turn him in; but when he said that, it knocked all the wind out of me. I went slower after that, and I wasn’t sure anymore whether I was glad I’d started or not. When I was fifty yards out, Jim said:

“There you go, the true Huck—the only white gentleman who ever kept his word to old Jim.”

I felt downright sick. But I said to myself, I have to do it—I can’t back out. Right then a skiff came along with two men holding guns. They stopped, and I stopped. One of them said:

“What’s that over there?”

“A piece of a raft,” I said.

“You belong on it?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Any men on it?”

“Only one, sir.”

“Well, five slaves ran off tonight up the river, above the head of the bend. Is your man white or Black?”

I didn’t answer right away. I tried, but the words wouldn’t come. I tried for a couple of seconds to brace myself and say it, but I wasn’t man enough—didn’t have the nerve of a rabbit. I felt myself giving in; so I quit trying, and finally said:

“He’s white.”

“I guess we’ll go see for ourselves.”

“I wish you would,” I said, “because my pap is the one there, and maybe you could help me tow the raft ashore where the light is.”"}

{"request_id":"03bde4b8c7ed19b9068e7b68","rewritten_text":"Yet how could I, a bewildered village boy, escape that delicious inconsistency that even the greatest and wisest fall into daily?

“It may all be perfectly true,” I said to Biddy, “but I admire her terribly.”

So I rolled onto my face at that thought, clutched the hair on both sides of my head, and gave it a hearty wrench. All the while I knew my heart’s folly to be so outrageously foolish and misdirected that I felt it would have served my face right if I had hoisted it up by the hair and banged it against the pebbles for belonging to such an idiot.

Biddy, being the wisest of girls, tried to argue no further with me. She laid her hand, a comforting hand though roughened by work, on my hands one after the other, and gently drew them from my hair. Then she softly patted my shoulder in a quieting way, while with my face buried on my sleeve I cried a little—just as I had done in the brewery yard—and felt dimly persuaded that I was much wronged by somebody, or by everybody; I can’t say which.

“I’m glad of one thing,” said Biddy, “and that is, that you have felt you could trust me, Pip. And I’m glad of another, and that is, that you know you may rely on my keeping your trust and always, so far, deserving it. If your first teacher (dear me! such a poor one, and so much in need of instruction herself!) were your teacher now, she thinks she knows what lesson she would give. But it would be a hard one to learn, and you have passed beyond her, and so it is no use now.” Then, with a quiet sigh for me, Biddy rose from the bank and asked, with a fresh and cheerful change of tone, “Shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

“Biddy,” I cried, getting up, slipping my arm round her neck, and giving her a kiss, “I shall always tell you everything.”

“Until you’re a gentleman,” said Biddy.

“You know I never shall be, so that’s forever. Not that I need tell you anything, for you know everything I know—as I said at home the other evening.”

“Ah!” said Biddy, in a mere whisper, while she looked away toward the ships. Then, repeating her pleasant question, “shall we walk a little farther, or go home?”

I told Biddy we would walk a little farther, and we did, and the summer afternoon mellowed into the summer evening, and it was very lovely."}

content.text: {"request_id":"85fbc91ef5c34427c3871ded","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was disproportionately broad, giving him a very round and ridiculous shape. His feet were invisible, though a suspicious horn-like substance would sometimes poke out through a tear in the bottom of the car—or more accurately, the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair was very gray and tied in a queue at the back. His nose was long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes were full, bright, and sharp; his chin and cheeks, though wrinkled with age, were broad, puffy, and doubled. There was not the slightest sign of ears anywhere on his head. This odd little gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin surtout with tight breeches to match, secured by silver buckles at the knees. His vest was a bright yellow fabric; a white taffeta cap was cocked jauntily to one side; and, to finish his outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his neck and fell onto his chest in a dainty bow of immense size.\n\nWhen he had descended, as I noted before, to about a hundred feet above the ground, the little old gentleman suddenly took fright and seemed unwilling to come any closer to the earth. He dumped out some sand from a canvas bag he could barely lift and immediately stopped in place. Then, in a hurried and nervous way, he pulled a large morocco pocketbook from a side pocket of his surtout. He balanced it suspiciously in his hand, stared at it in astonishment, and was clearly surprised by how heavy it was. He finally opened it, took out a huge letter sealed with red wax and tied carefully with red tape, and let it fall right at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent down to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still extremely agitated and apparently having no more business in Rotterdam, began at once to prepare for his departure. Because he needed to release ballast to rise again, he tossed out six bags in succession without bothering to empty them. Every one of them landed squarely on the burgomaster’s back, rolling him over twenty-one times in front of all the citizens of Rotterdam. Of course the great Underduk did not allow such insolence from the little old man to go unpunished."}

content.text: {"request_id":"65b5b4b0d6ef07909dec0328","rewritten_text":"“Basil, this is incredible! I have to meet Dorian Gray.” Hallward rose from the bench and paced the garden. After a while he returned. “Harry,” he said, “Dorian Gray is nothing more than a source of inspiration to me. You might see nothing in him. I see everything. He is most powerful in my work when he isn’t depicted at all. He is the hint of a new style. I find him in the sweep of certain lines, in the beauty and nuance of certain colors. That’s it.” “Then why won’t you show his portrait?” Lord Henry asked. “Because, without meaning to, I poured all this strange artistic devotion into it, and of course I never wanted to tell him that. He doesn’t know. He will never know. But the world might suspect, and I refuse to expose my soul to their shallow scrutiny. They won’t put my heart under a microscope. There’s too much of me in that painting, Harry—too much!” “Poets aren’t so careful. They know how marketable passion is. These days a broken heart gets a dozen editions.” “I despise them for that,” Hallward exclaimed. “An artist should create beautiful things without putting his life into them. Today people treat art as if it were autobiography. We’ve lost any sense of abstract beauty. One day I’ll show the world what it is; and that is exactly why they will never see my portrait of Dorian Gray.” “I think you’re wrong, Basil, but I won’t argue. Only the intellectually lost ever argue. Tell me, does Dorian Gray care for you?” The painter thought for a moment. “He likes me,” he answered after a pause. “I know he does. Of course I flatter him terribly. I take a strange pleasure in saying things to him that I know I’ll regret. Generally he’s wonderful to me, and we sit in the studio talking about a thousand topics. Every now and then, though, he’s terribly inconsiderate, and seems to enjoy hurting me. Then I feel, Harry, that I’ve handed over my entire soul to someone who treats it like a flower for his lapel, a decoration to feed his vanity, an ornament for a summer day.”"}

{"request_id":"ae08ce52dc1f0afdde10289c","rewritten_text":"While these events were happening in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old den—the same place from which the girl had spirited Oliver away—brooding over a dull, smoky fire. He had a pair of bellows on his knees, with which he had evidently been trying to coax the fire into better spirits; but he had fallen into deep thought, and with his arms folded over them and his chin resting on his thumbs, he stared absently at the rusty bars.

At a table behind him sat the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling, all absorbed in a game of whist, the Artful playing dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The face of the first-named gentleman, intelligent at all times, gained even greater interest from his close attention to the game and his careful reading of Mr. Chitling’s hand; upon which, from time to time, as opportunity allowed, he cast various intent glances, prudently regulating his own play according to what he observed in his neighbor’s cards. As it was a cold night, the Dodger wore his hat, as he often did indoors. He also held a clay pipe between his teeth, which he only removed briefly when he felt it necessary to reach for the quart mug on the table, filled with gin-and-water for everyone’s use.

Master Bates was attentive to the play as well; but being more excitable than his skilled friend, he resorted more often to the gin-and-water, and also indulged in many jokes and irrelevant comments, all quite improper for a serious rubber. Indeed, the Artful, relying on their close friendship, more than once took it upon himself to lecture his companion seriously on these improprieties; all of which warnings Master Bates accepted in excellent spirits, merely asking his friend to “be blowed,” or to stick his head in a sack, or replying with some other neatly turned quip of the same sort, whose clever timing impressed Mr. Chitling greatly. It was notable that the latter gentleman and his partner always lost, and that this fact, far from angering Master Bates, seemed to amuse him greatly, since he laughed uproariously at the end of every deal and swore he had never seen such a fun game in all his born days.

“That’s two doubles and the rub,” said Mr. Chitling, wearing a very long face as he pulled half a crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never saw such a fellow as you, Jack; you win everything.”"}

{"request_id":"62b814e47fe199155a7f6946","rewritten_text":"Reading his letter again while answering it softened her so much that she felt she had to steady herself with a few firm phrases; and she was so upset at the thought of making him unhappy, so concerned about what his mother and sisters would think and say, so worried they might see her as ungrateful, that Emma believed if the young man had appeared at that moment, he would have won her after all.

Still, the letter was written, sealed, and sent. The matter was settled, and Harriet was safe. She felt rather low all evening, but Emma understood her kindhearted regrets, easing them at times by speaking of her own affection, at times by bringing up Mr. Elton.

“I shall never be invited to Abbey-Mill again,” she said in a mournful tone.

“Nor could I ever bear to let you go, my Harriet. You are far too essential at Hartfield to be lent to Abbey-Mill.”

“And I am sure I should never want to go anywhere else; I am happy only at Hartfield.”

Later she added, “I think Mrs. Goddard would be very surprised if she knew what had happened. I am sure Miss Nash would—Miss Nash thinks her own sister very well married, and he is only a linen-draper.”

“One would not wish for more pride or refinement in the teacher of a school, Harriet. I dare say Miss Nash would envy you the chance of such a marriage. Even this triumph would seem valuable to her. As for anything better for you, I suppose she has no idea. The attentions of a certain person can hardly be gossip yet in Highbury. So far, I imagine you and I are the only ones whose eyes and ears have caught the meaning of his looks and manners.”

Harriet blushed and smiled, murmuring that she did not understand why people should like her so much. The thought of Mr. Elton certainly brightened her; but before long, her heart softened again toward the dismissed Mr. Martin.

“Now he has my letter,” she said softly. “I wonder what they are all doing—if his sisters know—if he is unhappy, they will be unhappy too. I hope he will not feel it too deeply.”

“Let us think of friends away from us who are more cheerfully occupied,” cried Emma. “Perhaps at this moment Mr. Elton is showing your portrait to his mother and sisters, telling them how much more beautiful the original is, and after being asked five or six times, finally letting them hear your name, your very own dear name.”"}

{"request_id":"2f80db871310e847c886b045","rewritten_text":"She cast everything aside, save for the memory that such things had once existed.

Since leaving Lady Russell’s home in September, Anne had never set foot in Kellynch. There had been no need, and on the few occasions when visiting the Hall might have been possible, she contrived to avoid it. Her first return was to take up her position again in the refined modern rooms of the Lodge, and to brighten its mistress’s sight.

Lady Russell’s happiness at their reunion held a shade of unease. She knew who had been staying at Uppercross. Yet, fortunately, either Anne had truly filled out and looked better, or Lady Russell imagined it; and while Anne received the compliments, she could not help linking them to her cousin’s quiet admiration, and relish the hope of enjoying another springtime of youth and allure.

When conversation began, she quickly felt a shift in herself. The topics that had so filled her heart when leaving Kellynch, which she believed neglected and had had to suppress among the Musgroves, were now only of lesser importance. Of late she had scarcely thought of her father, sister, and Bath. Their concerns had been overshadowed by Uppercross affairs; and when Lady Russell returned to former hopes and anxieties, expressing satisfaction in the house secured in Camden Place and regret that Mrs Clay remained with them, Anne would have blushed to confess that Lyme, Louisa Musgrove, and all her acquaintances there occupied her thoughts far more; that the household and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick interested her beyond her own father’s residence in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness with Mrs Clay. She had literally to labour at matching Lady Russell’s apparent concern for matters that ought by nature to have had the foremost claim on her attention.

Their talk on another subject involved a touch of discomfort at first. They had to discuss the Lyme accident. Lady Russell had not been in the house five minutes the previous day before the entire story poured over her; still, it had to be spoken of. She must inquire, deplore the imprudence, lament the outcome, and Captain Wentworth’s name had to pass both their lips. Anne felt she managed it less adeptly than Lady Russell. She could not utter the name while looking directly into Lady Russell’s face until she resorted to the stratagem of briefly explaining what she believed of his attachment to Louisa."}

{"request_id":"138719ff3972e2c6fabc34a1","rewritten_text":"Those aged and fragile figures were always witnessed by the public bowing, and rumor had it that once they bowed a customer out, they continued bowing in the vacant office until they bowed the next customer in.

The barrister was shrewd enough to realize that the banker would never have gone so far in expressing his opinion without a foundation of moral certainty. Though he was unprepared for the large dose he had to swallow, he forced it down. “And now,” said Mr. Stryver, brandishing his forensic forefinger toward the Temple at large when he had done so, “my way out of this is to put you all in the wrong.”

It was a specimen of Old Bailey tactics, which gave him considerable consolation. “You shall not put me in the wrong, young lady,” Mr. Stryver declared; “I will take care of that myself.”

Thus, when Mr. Lorry arrived that night as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, amid a clutter of books and papers spread out for effect, appeared to have nothing less on his mind than the morning’s issue. He even feigned surprise at sight of Mr. Lorry and seemed wholly abstracted and preoccupied.

“Well!” exclaimed that good-humored emissary after a full half hour of fruitless efforts to lead him back to the topic. “I have been to Soho.”

“To Soho?” echoed Mr. Stryver in a chill tone. “Oh, of course! What can I be thinking of!”

“And I am entirely satisfied,” said Mr. Lorry, “that I was correct in the talk we had. My view stands confirmed, and I repeat my counsel.”

“I give you my word,” replied Mr. Stryver with cordial politeness, “I am sorry for it on your account, and sorry for it on the poor father’s. I know this must always remain a tender point with the family; let us drop the subject.”

“I do not follow you,” Mr. Lorry said.

“I dare say you do not,” answered Stryver, nodding in a soothing yet conclusive manner; “no matter, no matter.”

“But it does matter,” urged Mr. Lorry.

“No, it does not; believe me, it does not. Having imagined there was sense where there is none, and a worthy ambition where none exists, I am well rid of my blunder, and no harm ensues. Plenty of young women have played similar foolish tricks before now, and repented in poverty and obscurity often enough. Viewed unselfishly, I regret the termination, because it would have been unfortunate for me in the worldly sense; viewed selfishly, I am glad it is over, because it would have been unfortunate for me in the worldly sense—it hardly needs stating that I could have gained nothing by it.”"}

{"request_id":"13b847c5f9eb862659be726b","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone said he was making a terrible mistake, since the place was undeniably haunted. Lord Canterville himself, an impeccably honorable man, felt it was his duty to bring up that point when they discussed terms.

“We haven’t cared to live there ourselves,” Lord Canterville said, “ever since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was terrified into a seizure she never truly recovered from, when two skeleton hands were laid on her shoulders as she dressed for dinner. I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family have seen the ghost, as has the parish rector, the Reverend Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the poor Duchess’s mishap, none of our younger servants would stay, and Lady Canterville barely slept because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” replied the Minister, “I’ll pay for the furniture and the ghost. I come from a modern country where money can buy anything, and with our lively young men painting the Old World red and carrying off your best actresses and prima donnas, I figure that if there really were such a thing as a ghost in Europe, we’d have it at home in one of our public museums, or touring as a show.”

“I’m afraid the ghost does exist,” Lord Canterville said with a smile, “even if it has ignored the offers of your ambitious impresarios. It’s been notorious for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always appears before any member of our family dies.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, Lord Canterville. But there’s no such thing as a ghost, sir, and I don’t believe the laws of nature are going to be suspended for the British aristocracy.”

“You certainly keep things natural in America,” Lord Canterville answered, not entirely understanding Mr. Otis’s last remark. “If you don’t mind having a ghost in the house, that’s fine. Just remember I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the sale was finalized, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family moved into Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis, formerly Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street and once a celebrated New York beauty, was now a striking, middle-aged woman with fine eyes and a magnificent profile."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3f38d6ca63900dcfd6313241","rewritten_text":"I have said he was a poet: at twenty-three he published his first poem, and the entire nation greeted it with excitement and delight. Fortune never stopped smiling on him; no reputation had ever risen so quickly, and soon everyone knew his name. The masses praised the very poems that amazed scholars in their studies, and not a single voice dissented.   It was at the height of this glory that he met Elinor. She was a young heiress of extraordinary beauty living under the care of her guardian, and the moment they were seen together it was clear they belonged to each other. Elinor lacked Woodville’s genius, but she was generous and noble, lifted by her youth and the love she inspired everywhere into a state where she knew nothing but virtue and excellence. She was lovely, her manner open and simple, her deep blue eyes glowing with a light that only sensitivity combined with wisdom could produce.   They were made for each other, and soon they loved. Woodville felt the joy of love for the first time, and Elinor was ecstatic to hold the heart of someone so splendid and admired among men. How could anything but pure happiness come from such a union?   Woodville was a poet—every society sought him, and whenever he appeared all eyes turned to him. Yet he was the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor was a rich heiress. Her guardian did not oppose their mutual affection; Woodville’s worth was too great for anyone to object to his lack of wealth. But her father’s dying will forbade her to marry before she came of age, and her fortune depended on obeying that command. She had just turned twenty, and she and her lover had to accept the delay. Still they were constantly together, living in what felt like Paradise: studying side by side, laying out future plans, and drinking in love and joy from each other’s eyes and words. They barely complained about postponing their final union. Woodville kept rising in fame, and Elinor grew lovelier and wiser under the guidance of her accomplished lover.   In two months, Elinor would turn twenty-one, and everything was ready for their marriage. How can I describe the catastrophe that struck such joy? Yet the earth would not be what it is—covered with blight and sorrow—if even one pair of angelic beings had been allowed to exist solely for each other. Search the world and you will not find the perfect happiness their marriage would have given them; everything in our miserable mortal order would have had to change to allow such complete joy."}

{"request_id":"789cd2522c552d16ddc3692d","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper whom Mrs. Otis had agreed, at Lady Canterville’s earnest plea, to retain in her old post. As they stepped down, she made each a low curtsey and, in a quaint, old-fashioned tone, said, ‘I bid you welcome to Canterville Chase.’ They followed her through the stately Tudor hall into the library, a long, low chamber paneled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at its far end. Tea was set out for them there, and after shedding their wraps they took their seats and began to glance around, while Mrs. Umney attended to them.

Mrs. Otis suddenly noticed a dull red mark on the floor near the hearth and, unaware of its true meaning, remarked to Mrs. Umney, ‘I fear something has been spilled there.’

‘Yes, madam,’ the aged housekeeper replied softly, ‘blood was spilled on that spot.’

‘How dreadful,’ Mrs. Otis exclaimed; ‘I do not like blood-stains in a sitting-room. It must be removed immediately.’

The old woman smiled and, in the same low, mysterious tone, said, ‘It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was slain on that very spot by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine years longer, then vanished under very strange conditions. His body was never found, but his guilty spirit still roams the Chase. The stain has been admired by tourists and others and cannot be taken away.’

‘Ridiculous,’ Washington Otis declared; ‘Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it in no time,’ and before the frightened housekeeper could stop him he was on his knees, briskly scrubbing the floor with what looked like a black cosmetic stick. Within minutes no sign of the blood-stain remained.

‘I knew Pinkerton would handle it,’ he cried with triumph, looking over at his admiring family; yet scarcely had he spoken when a terrible flash of lightning lit the gloomy room, a thunderous crash made them leap to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

‘What an outrageous climate!’ the American Minister observed calmly, lighting a long cheroot. ‘I reckon the old country is so overpopulated there isn’t enough decent weather to go around. I have always believed emigration is the only solution for England.’

‘My dear Hiram,’ Mrs. Otis cried, ‘what shall we do with a woman who faints?’

‘Charge it to her like breakages,’ the Minister replied; ‘she won’t faint again after that’; and within a few moments Mrs. Umney indeed revived."}

{"request_id":"d771017744909ca06acaadb7","rewritten_text":"He carefully drove a peg into the ground exactly where the beetle had fallen, then pulled a tape measure from his pocket. Fastening one end to the part of the tree trunk closest to the peg, he unrolled it to that peg, and, following the line established by the two points, continued another fifty feet—Jupiter hacking away the brambles with the scythe. At the spot reached, he drove a second peg and scratched out a rough circle about four feet wide around it. Taking up a spade himself and handing one to Jupiter and one to me, Legrand asked us to start digging as quickly as possible.

To be honest, I had no taste for such entertainment at any time, and in that moment I would gladly have declined; night was approaching, and I was very tired from the day’s exertions. Still, I saw no way out and feared upsetting my poor friend by refusing. If I could have counted on Jupiter’s help, I would have had no qualms about trying to drag the madman home by force; but I knew the old Black man’s temperament too well to expect him to assist me against his master. I was convinced Legrand had been infected by some Southern superstition about buried treasure and that the discovery of the scarab—or perhaps Jupiter insisting it was “a bug of real gold”—had bolstered his fantasy. A mind tilting toward madness could easily be carried away by such notions, especially when they encouraged cherished beliefs; I remembered his remark about the beetle being “the index of his fortune.” Altogether, I was upset and baffled, but finally I decided to make a virtue of necessity—to dig with good will so we could quickly prove to the dreamer, with plain evidence, that his ideas were false.

Once we lit the lanterns, we went to work with a zeal deserving a more sensible cause; and as the glare fell on our bodies and tools, I couldn’t help thinking what a picturesque group we made, and how strange and suspicious our labors would have seemed to any passerby who might have stumbled upon us.

We dug steadily for two hours."}

{"request_id":"0bf73006d9dfdc6ca6371720","rewritten_text":"The place looked like a maze of back lanes, ditches, and tiny gardens, and gave the impression of a rather dull retreat. Wemmick’s house was a small wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, and its roof was cut and painted to resemble a battery with cannons.

“My own work,” said Wemmick. “Looks nice, doesn’t it?”

I praised it highly. It was the smallest house I had ever seen, with the strangest gothic windows—most of them fakes—and a gothic door almost too small to get through.

“That’s a real flagstaff,” Wemmick continued, “and on Sundays I raise a real flag. Now look. After I cross this bridge, I pull it up—like this—and cut off the connection.”

The bridge was a plank spanning a gap about four feet wide and two feet deep. It was delightful to watch him lift it up and secure it, smiling as he did so with real enjoyment instead of just habit.

“At nine every night, Greenwich time,” Wemmick said, “the gun fires. There it is, you see! And when you hear it, you’ll admit it’s a Stinger.”

The mentioned cannon stood in a separate little fortress made of lattice-work. It was shielded from the weather by a clever tarpaulin setup like an umbrella.

“Then, at the back,” said Wemmick, “out of sight so it doesn’t spoil the idea of fortifications—because my rule is, if you have an idea, carry it through and keep it up—I don’t know if you agree—”

I said I certainly did.

“At the back there’s a pig, and there are chickens and rabbits; then I build my own little frames, you see, and grow cucumbers; and at supper you’ll see what kind of salad I can produce. So, sir,” Wemmick added, smiling again but with seriousness as he shook his head, “if you imagine the place under siege, it could hold out wonderfully for supplies.”

Then he led me to a bower about twelve yards away, reached by such clever twists in the path that it took a long while to get there, and in this hideaway our glasses were already set. Our punch was chilling in an ornamental lake, on the bank of which the bower stood. This body of water—with an island in the middle that might have been the salad for supper—was circular, and he had built a fountain in it which, when you started a small mill and pulled a cork from a pipe, played so vigorously it made the back of your hand quite wet."}

{"request_id":"b2a7575d24057d5d96ba9ba3","rewritten_text":"“All right, I’m agreed. It’s the best plan. Would you just clasp hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, that ain’t fit for this. That’ll do for small, trifling matters—’specially with girls, cuz they’ll double-cross you anyway and chatter if they take offense—but a big business like this needs writing. And blood.”

Tom’s whole spirit exulted in the notion. It was grim, shadowy, and ominous; the hour, the situation, the setting all matched. He stooped for a clean pine shingle lying in the moonlight, fished a bit of “red keel” from his pocket, set his work so the moon shone on it, and painfully scratched the words, pressing down each slow stroke with his tongue clamped between his teeth and easing up on the way back.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swears they will keep mum about This and They wish They may Drop down dead in Their Tracks if They ever Tell and Rot.”

Huckleberry admired Tom’s easy penmanship and the grandeur of his speech. He immediately plucked a pin from his lapel to prick himself, but Tom interrupted:

“Hold up! Don’t. A pin’s brass—it might have verdigrease on it.”

“What’s verdigrease?”

“It’s poison, that’s what. Just swallow a little once—you’ll find out.”

So Tom unwound the thread off one of his needles, and each boy pricked the pad of his thumb, squeezing out a bead of blood. After much squeezing, Tom managed to write his initials, using his littlest finger’s ball as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to shape an H and an F, and the vow was done. They buried the shingle near the wall with gloomy rites and mutterings, and the chains on their tongues were held to be locked and the key flung away.

A shape crept quietly through a gap at the opposite end of the wrecked building just then, but they didn’t notice.

“Tom,” whispered Huckleberry, “does this stop us from ever telling—always?”

“Of course. No matter what happens, we have to keep quiet. We’d fall dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yes, I reckon that’s true.”

They kept whispering for quite a while. Soon a dog lifted a long, deathly howl just outside—within ten feet. The boys grabbed each other, stricken with terror.

“Which of us is he after?” panted Huckleberry.

“I dunno—look out the crack. Hurry!”

“No, you, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”"}
