{"request_id":"94b5b766aa9a943469567f08","rewritten_text":"After dinner the whole gang headed out to the sandbar to hunt for turtle eggs. They jabbed sticks into the sand, and when they hit a soft spot they knelt and dug with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from a single hole. They looked like perfectly round white balls, just a bit smaller than an English walnut. That night they gorged on fried eggs, and they did it again Friday morning.

After breakfast they raced out onto the bar, shouting and skipping around, tossing clothes aside until they were naked, then kept up the chase far along the shallow water, pushing against the strong current that kept knocking their legs out from under them and made things even more fun. Every so often they crouched together and slapped water into one another’s faces with their palms, edging closer with their heads turned so the splash wouldn’t choke them, and finally locking arms in a wrestling match until the winner dunked his opponent, then everybody sank into a jumble of pale legs and arms and surfaced all at once, blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping.

Once they were worn out, they ran ashore, sprawled on the hot dry sand, and covered themselves with it, only to dash back into the water and repeat the whole show. Eventually it struck them that their bare skin looked a lot like flesh-colored tights, so they drew a ring in the sand and staged a circus—with three clowns, because none of them would surrender the top job.

Then they grabbed their marbles and played knucks and ringtaw and keeps until it got boring. Joe and Huck went for another swim, but Tom stayed put; when he kicked off his pants he had also kicked the string of rattlesnake rattles off his ankle, and he couldn’t believe he’d gone so long without cramping up when the charm wasn’t protecting him. He refused to swim again until he found it, and by then the other boys were tired and ready to lounge. Gradually they drifted apart, sank into gloomy moods, and stared longingly across the wide river toward the village dozing in the sun. Tom caught himself tracing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe; he scraped it away, furious with himself for being soft. Yet he wrote it again; he couldn’t stop. He wiped it out once more, then escaped the temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"745877c2d81d5163e8b2e9c6","rewritten_text":"To regard a star by mere sidelong glances—to look at it obliquely, employing the outer zones of the retina (more receptive of faint impressions than the central)—is to see the star clearly, to grasp its lustre most fully; that same lustre fades in exact ratio as we direct our gaze straight upon it. In the latter case a larger number of rays indeed enter the eye, yet, in the former, the faculty of apprehension is more delicate. Excessive profundity bewilders and weakens thought; even Venus herself can be banished from the heavens by an examination too prolonged, too intense, too direct.

“As to these murders, let us conduct our own investigations before forming any conclusion concerning them. Such an inquiry will amuse us,” [I deemed this an odd expression under the circumstances, but held my tongue] “and, besides, Le Bon once did me a kindness, for which I remain grateful. We will go inspect the premises personally. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and shall readily secure the necessary authorization.”

The authorization was secured, and we set out immediately for the Rue Morgue—one of those wretched streets lying between the Rue Richelieu and the Rue St. Roch. It was late in the afternoon when we arrived, this district being at a considerable remove from our usual haunts. The house was easy to discover, many persons still standing across the way, staring up at the shuttered windows with idle curiosity. It was an ordinary Parisian dwelling, having a gateway, and, on one side, a glazed porter’s lodge with a sliding panel in the window, denoting a loge de concierge. Before entering we walked up the street, turned down an alley, and then, doubling back, passed along the rear of the building—Dupin all the while examining both the house and the surrounding neighborhood with a minuteness of scrutiny for which I could imagine no motive.

Retracing our way, we returned to the front door, rang, and, after presenting our credentials, gained admission from the officials in charge. We ascended to the chamber where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye had been discovered, and where both corpses still lay. The disorder in the room, as usual, had been allowed to remain. I observed nothing beyond what had already been reported in the “Gazette des Tribunaux.” Dupin inspected everything—even the bodies of the victims. Afterwards we visited the other rooms and the yard, a gendarme escorting us throughout."}

{"request_id":"997c78f1dc074032067c541b","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?”

“Ten o’clock, sir.”

“What are you talking about? Ten o’clock at night?”

“Yes, sir. You told me to wake you.”

“Oh! Right. All right, all right.”

After a few sluggish attempts to fall asleep again—efforts the servant expertly thwarted by poking the fire for several minutes—he got up, threw on his hat, and went out. He turned into the Temple, and after restoring himself by pacing the pavement of King’s Bench Walk and Paper Buildings twice, he headed to Stryver’s chambers.

Stryver’s clerk, who never attended these meetings, had gone home, so Stryver himself opened the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing gown, his throat bare for comfort. His eyes bore that wild, strained, scarred look common to every hard drinker of his type, from Jeffries’s portrait onward, visible under every artistic disguise in the portraits of every drinking era.

“You’re a bit late, Memory,” Stryver said.

“Just about on time; perhaps fifteen minutes behind.”

They entered a dingy room lined with books and littered with papers, where a fire roared. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the chaos of papers, a table gleamed with ample wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

“You’ve had your bottle, I see, Sydney.”

“Two tonight, I think. I’ve been dining with the client—or watching him dine, which is the same thing!”

“That was a remarkable point you made about the identification, Sydney. How did you come up with it? When did it hit you?”

“I thought he was rather handsome, and I figured I’d have turned out about the same if I’d had any luck.”

Stryver laughed until his precocious paunch shook.

“You and your luck, Sydney! Get to work, get to work.”

Grudgingly, the jackal loosened his clothes, went to the next room, and returned with a large jug of cold water, a basin, and a couple of towels. Dipping the towels in the water and partially wringing them out, he folded them around his head in a hideous fashion, sat at the table, and said, “Now I’m ready!”

“Not much boiling down tonight, Memory,” Stryver said cheerfully as he sorted through his papers.

“How much?”

“Only two sets.”

“Give me the worst first.”

“There you go, Sydney. Fire away!”

The lion settled on his back on a sofa on one side of the drinking table, while the jackal took his seat at his own cluttered table on the other side, bottles and glasses within easy reach."}

{"request_id":"916a2b6245ceef780667c1d2","rewritten_text":"His face, burned dark by the sun, was more than half hidden by whiskers and a mustache. He carried a huge oak cudgel, but seemed otherwise unarmed. He bowed awkwardly and gave us a “good evening” in French accents that, though a bit Neufchâtel-like, still showed he came from Paris. 

“Sit down, my friend,” said Dupin. “I suppose you’ve come about the Ourang-Outang. Honestly, I almost envy you owning him; he’s a remarkably fine and surely valuable animal. How old do you think he is?”

The sailor drew a long breath, like a man freed from a terrible weight, then answered steadily:

“I can’t say exactly—but he can’t be more than four or five years old. Do you have him here?”

“Oh no, we had no way to keep him at the house. He’s at a livery stable on the Rue Dubourg, just nearby. You can collect him in the morning. You’re ready, of course, to prove he’s yours?”

“Certainly I am, sir.”

“I’ll be sorry to let him go,” said Dupin.

“I don’t expect you to go to all this trouble for nothing, sir,” the man replied. “Wouldn’t be right. I’m very willing to pay a reward for finding the animal—that is, any reasonable sum.”

“Well,” my friend replied, “that’s fair enough. Let me think!—what should I want? Oh! I know. My reward will be this. You will give me all the information you can about the murders in the Rue Morgue.”

Dupin spoke the last words in a very low, calm voice. Just as calmly, he walked to the door, locked it, and put the key in his pocket. Then he drew a pistol from his coat and set it on the table without the slightest fuss.

The sailor’s face went red, as if he were choking. He sprang to his feet and grabbed his cudgel, but the next moment he dropped back into his seat, shaking violently, his face pale as death. He said nothing. I felt deep pity for him.

“My friend,” said Dupin gently, “you’re frightening yourself for no reason—you truly are. We mean you no harm. I give you my honor as a gentleman and as a Frenchman that we intend you no injury. I know perfectly well that you are innocent of the crimes in the Rue Morgue. Still, you can’t deny that you’re involved to some degree.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"7b2e82bac1c3e527d5023af2","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner before them, though young, had long been steeped in the treason that now threatened his life. This correspondence with the public enemy did not begin today, or yesterday, or even last year or the year before. It was certain the prisoner had for a longer time been coming and going between France and England on secret business he could not honestly explain. If treason ever prospered—which fortunately it never did—the true wickedness of his schemes might have stayed hidden. Providence, however, moved someone beyond fear and reproach to uncover the prisoner’s plans and, horrified, report them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and the most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would appear before them. His position and bearing were, altogether, sublime. He had been the prisoner’s friend, but in an hour both fortunate and disastrous, the moment he detected his infamy he resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer cherish in his own heart on the sacred altar of his country. If statues were awarded in Britain, as in ancient Greece and Rome, to public benefactors, this shining citizen would surely have one. Since no such statues were decreed, he probably would not. Virtue, as the poets had observed (in countless passages which the jury, he felt certain, could recite word for word—at which the jury’s faces showed they knew nothing about those passages), is somewhat contagious, especially the radiant virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The high example of this flawless, unimpeachable witness for the Crown—merely to mention whom, however unworthy the speaker, was an honour—inspired the prisoner’s servant and filled him with a holy resolve to inspect his master’s desk drawers and pockets and to hide away his papers. Mr. Attorney-General expected attempts to disparage this admirable servant; but generally speaking, he preferred him over his own brothers and sisters, and esteemed him more than his own father and mother. He confidently invited the jury to follow his example. The testimony of these two witnesses, supported by the documents they would produce, would show that the prisoner had been supplied with lists of His Majesty’s forces and their deployment and readiness by sea and land, leaving no doubt that he had routinely passed that intelligence to a hostile power."}

{"request_id":"eb2ae4477f81e7dad5de7d25","rewritten_text":"Furthermore, hardly anyone outside the sea-going profession can fashion this knot, and it is particularly Maltese. I retrieved the ribbon at the base of the lightning-rod, and it could not have belonged to either of the victims. Even if my deduction from the ribbon—that the Frenchman served on a Maltese ship—proves mistaken, nothing is lost by what I stated in the advertisement. If I err, he will imagine I was misdirected by some circumstance and will not bother to look into it. Yet if I am correct, we have gained a great advantage. Though aware of the crime, yet guiltless, the Frenchman will naturally hesitate to respond to the notice—to claim the Ourang-Outang. He will reason: “I am innocent, impoverished, and my Ourang-Outang is exceedingly valuable—a fortune for a man in my position. Why should I forfeit it because of idle fears? It is within my reach. It was discovered in the Bois de Boulogne, far removed from that slaughter. How could anyone suspect a brute creature was responsible? The police are completely baffled—they have not obtained the smallest clue. Even if they could track the animal, they could never prove I knew of the murder, or involve me in guilt through that knowledge. Above all, I am known. The advertiser points me out as the owner of the animal. I cannot be sure how much he actually knows. If I do not claim property so valuable, known to be mine, I will, at the very least, render the creature itself subject to suspicion. Drawing attention to myself or to it is not wise. I shall answer the advertisement, recover the Ourang-Outang, and keep it hidden until the affair has blown over.”

Just then footsteps sounded on the stairs.

“Be ready,” Dupin told me, “keep your pistols at hand, but do not display or use them until I give the signal.”

The front door had been left open, so the visitor entered without ringing and had already taken several steps on the staircase. But now he seemed to falter. Soon we heard him going back down. Dupin was heading swiftly to the door when the footsteps ascended once more. This time the visitor did not retreat but climbed firmly to the top and knocked on our chamber door.

“Come in,” Dupin called, in a bright and cordial voice.

A man walked in. He was plainly a sailor—a tall, brawny figure with a certain reckless look about him, though not without a degree of rough attractiveness."}

{"request_id":"dac49af5f7ed4104c6a81166","rewritten_text":"“Should I call them in? Or Miss Bates? She is even closer—and I suspect Miss Bates is as able as anyone to guess what the others want. I believe we do need a larger council. What if I invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you please,” Mrs. Weston answered, hesitating. “If you think she will be of any use.”

“You will learn nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She will be full of delight and gratitude, yet she will tell you nothing. She will not even listen to your questions. I can see no benefit in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she is so entertaining, so very entertaining! I enjoy hearing Miss Bates talk. And I need not bring the entire family, you know.”

Mr. Weston joined them then, and when he heard the plan, he gave it his firm approval.

“Aye, do, Frank—go fetch Miss Bates and let us settle the matter at once. She will love the scheme, I am sure; and I do not know a fitter person to show us how to remove difficulties. Fetch Miss Bates. We are becoming a bit too particular. She is a constant lesson in how to be happy. But fetch them both. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady?…”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I shall think you a great simpleton, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I beg your pardon, sir. I did not recall it at once. Certainly, if you wish it, I will try to persuade them both.” And he ran off.

Long before he reappeared, escorting the short, neat, quick-moving aunt and her elegant niece, Mrs. Weston—like a kind-tempered woman and a good wife—had inspected the passage again and found its flaws far less than she had believed before, truly trifling; and thus the hard part of the decision ended. Everything else, at least in planning, was perfectly smooth. All the minor arrangements of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper, fell into place by themselves or were left as mere trifles to settle at any time between Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes. Everyone invited was certain to come; Frank had already written to Enscombe to ask for a few days beyond his fortnight, which could not possibly be denied. And it was sure to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she agreed heartily it must be so. They did not need her as an adviser, but as an approver (a much safer role) she was sincerely welcome. Her approval—both general and detailed, warm and unceasing—could not help but please; and for another half-hour they all walked back and forth between the rooms, some suggesting, some listening, all happily enjoying the future."}

{"request_id":"dd0b2ffc368a813991ba32ea","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in astonishment for several seconds, and then, perceiving he was perfectly in earnest, wrote an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and slid it across the table.  

“Scotland Yard would pay handsomely for that address, my dear friend.”  

“They shan’t get it,” laughed Lord Arthur; and after shaking the young Russian’s hand warmly, he ran downstairs, inspected the paper, and instructed the coachman to drive to Soho Square.  

There he dismissed his driver and wandered down Greek Street until he reached a passage called Bayle’s Court. Passing under the archway, he found himself in a curious cul-de-sac apparently devoted to a French laundry, for clothes-lines crisscrossed from house to house and white linen fluttered in the morning air. He walked to the far end and knocked at a tiny green house. After some delay—during which every window in the court became a blurred patch of prying faces—the door opened to reveal a rather rough-looking foreigner, who asked in dreadful English what his business might be. Lord Arthur produced the paper Count Rouvaloff had given him. Seeing it, the man bowed and invited him into a very shabby front parlour on the ground floor; a few moments later Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, hurried into the room with a wine-stained napkin around his neck and a fork clutched in his left hand.  

“Count Rouvaloff has sent me to you,” said Lord Arthur, bowing, “and I wish to have a short interview on a matter of business. My name is Smith—Robert Smith—and I want you to provide me with an explosive clock.”  

“Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” replied the jovial little German, laughing. “Pray don’t look so shocked; it is my duty to know everyone, and I remember catching sight of you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I trust her ladyship is in perfect health. Would you mind sitting with me while I finish breakfast? There is an excellent pâté, and my friends insist my Rhine wine surpasses anything at the German Embassy.” And before Lord Arthur had recovered from the surprise of being recognized, he found himself in the back room, sipping exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock-glass bearing the Imperial monogram and chatting in the most amiable fashion imaginable with the notorious conspirator.  

“Explosive clocks,” observed Herr Winckelkopf, “are seldom satisfactory for foreign shipment; even if they slip past the Custom House, the trains run so erratically that they usually explode long before arriving at their intended destination.”"}

{"request_id":"dc1f92aa3cb2781e89fdc3b1","rewritten_text":"A shade past noon the boys borrowed a small skiff from a townsman who happened to be away, and pushed off right then. Once they were several miles below Cave Hollow, Tom remarked:

“Now you notice how this bluff looks the same the whole stretch from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood-yards, bushes all alike. But do you spy that white patch up ahead where a landslide happened? That’s one of my signs. We’ll land there.”

They pulled ashore.

“Now, Huck, from where we stand you could touch that hole I escaped by with a fishing pole. Try to find it.”

Huck poked around everywhere but saw nothing. Tom strutted into a thick clutch of sumach and announced:

“Here she is! Look at it, Huck; it’s the coziest hideout in this country. You just keep still about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I needed a place like this, and finding it was the tough part. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers know—because of course there’s got to be a gang, or there’s no style in it. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds grand, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“It sure does, Tom. Who are we going to rob?”

“Oh, near anybody. Waylay folks—that’s the chief way.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not every time. Pen them in the cave till they fetch a ransom.”

“What’s a ransom?”

“Money. You make them wring all they can out of their friends; and after you’ve held them a year, if it ain’t paid, then you kill them. That’s the usual rule. Only you don’t kill the women. You lock up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich and scared half to death. You take their watches and things, but you always lift your hat and talk proper. Nobody’s as polite as robbers—you’ll find that in any book. Well, the women fall in love with you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two they quit crying, and then you couldn’t chase them away. If you drove them off they’d whirl around and come back. That’s how it goes in all the books.”

“Why, that’s real bully, Tom. I reckon it beats being a pirate.”

“Yes, it’s better in some fashions, because it keeps you near home and circuses and such.”

By then everything was set and the boys slipped into the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the tunnel’s far end, made their spliced kite-string fast, and continued on."}

{"request_id":"a33102db2de47ab5b31a16e9","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had never happened. She was sure he had been drinking too much of Mr. Weston’s good wine and that he would want to talk nonsense.

To keep him in check as much as possible, she was preparing to speak about the weather and the night with perfect calm and seriousness. Yet hardly had she begun, hardly had they passed through the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, when her topic was cut short—her hand was seized, her attention demanded, and Mr. Elton was suddenly pouring out intense declarations of love. He took advantage of the moment, insisting that his feelings must already be obvious, hoping and fearing and worshipping, ready to die if she rejected him, yet convinced that his passionate devotion and unmatched love could not fail to win her. He was determined to be accepted quickly. It was truly happening. Without hesitation, apology, or any sign of doubt, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s admirer, was claiming to be her suitor. She tried to stop him, but without success; he insisted on saying it all. Angry as she was, she decided to keep her temper when she finally spoke. She believed that half this foolishness came from drunkenness and hoped it might last only for the night. So, using a mix of seriousness and playfulness that she thought might suit his half-sober state, she answered,

“I am very much astonished, Mr. Elton. This to me! You are forgetting yourself—you mistake me for my friend. Any message for Miss Smith I will gladly deliver; but no more of this to me, if you please.”

“Miss Smith! A message to Miss Smith! What could she mean!” he cried, repeating her words with such confident and triumphant astonishment that she could not help replying quickly,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behaviour! I can explain it only one way; you are not yourself, or you could not speak of either me or Harriet like this. Control yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough to heighten his spirits, not to confuse his mind. He knew exactly what he meant; and after insisting that her suspicion was very unfair, briefly touching on his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—though expressing surprise that Miss Smith should be mentioned at all—he returned to his declaration of love and pressed hard for a favourable reply."}

{"request_id":"48e6820adbe805e6632f871d","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, unsure where to go. “At Tellson’s bank at nine,” he murmured thoughtfully. “Should I show myself in the meantime? I think so. These people should know I am here; it’s a sensible precaution and might be necessary. But careful, careful! Let me think this through.”

He stopped moving toward his first impulse, paced the darkening street a few times, and followed the idea to its possible outcomes. His first instinct held. “It is best,” he decided, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” He turned toward Saint Antoine.

Defarge had described himself that day as a wine-shop keeper in the Saint Antoine suburb. Someone who knew the city well could find his shop without asking directions. After locating it, Carton left the narrow streets, ate at a small restaurant, and fell sound asleep after the meal. For the first time in years, he had no strong liquor. Since the previous night he had taken only a little thin wine, and the night before he had poured the brandy onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth as if he were finished with it.

It was around seven when he woke refreshed and went out again. On his way back toward Saint Antoine, he paused at a shop window with a mirror, straightened his loose cravat and coat collar, and smoothed his unkempt hair. Then he went straight to Defarge’s and entered.

There were no customers except Jacques Three, with his restless fingers and croaking voice. This man, whom Carton had seen on the Jury, stood drinking at the counter, talking with Monsieur and Madame Defarge. The Vengeance joined in the conversation like one of the household.

Carton walked in, sat down, and asked in indifferent French for a small measure of wine. Madame Defarge glanced at him carelessly, then more sharply, then walked over herself to ask what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” asked Madame Defarge, raising her dark eyebrows inquisitively.

He looked at her, as if even a single French word took time to form, then replied in his former strong foreign accent."}

{"request_id":"39d78ca2711c7c48f718d083","rewritten_text":"If you choose otherwise, and look to my leniency and the mercy of those you have grievously wronged, take that chair in silence. It has been awaiting you for two whole days.”

Monks muttered some indistinct words, yet still faltered.

“You shall act quickly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “Should I utter a word, the other course will be lost forever.”

The man remained undecided.

“I have neither temper for argument,” said Mr. Brownlow, “nor any right to indulge it while I champion the dearest concerns of others.”

“Is there—” stammered Monks, his voice unsteady,—“is there—no compromise?”

“None whatever.”

Monks eyed the old gentleman anxiously; but discovering in his face only stern resolve, he stepped inside, and with a shrug, took his seat.

“Secure the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow instructed the attendants, “and return when I ring.”

They complied, leaving the pair by themselves.

“This is gracious usage, sir,” said Monks, casting down his hat and cloak, “from the oldest friend my father had.”

“It is precisely because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow; “because the dreams and wishes of young and joyful days were entwined with him, and with that fair being of his blood and kin who met her God in early life, leaving me here a solitary, desolate man. It is because he knelt beside me at his only sister’s death-bed when he was still a boy, on the morning which—save for Heaven’s decree—would have made her my young bride; because my scarred heart clung to him from then on, through all his struggles and misdeeds, until his death; because ancient memories and ties surged within me, and even the sight of you calls up old impressions of him; for all these reasons I am driven to deal tenderly with you now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and blush for the disgrace of your bearing that name.”

“What does the name matter?” demanded the other, after regarding, half silently and half in stubborn astonishment, his companion’s agitation. “What is the name to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow, “nothing to you. But it was _hers_, and even after so long it calls back to me—the aged man I am now—the warmth and thrill I once felt merely to hear it spoken by a stranger. I am truly glad you cast it off—truly—truly.”

“This is all very fine,” said Monks (keeping his assumed title) after a considerable pause, during which he had flung himself back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face hidden by his hand."}

{"request_id":"0253e486df3e375808c08163","rewritten_text":"Knights and horses in heavy armor couldn’t travel very fast. They would go as quickly as they could, and now that the ground was dry with no snow or mud, they would probably move at seven miles an hour. They would have to change horses a couple of times and would arrive around six, or a little later. It would still be light, and they would see the white cloth I planned to tie around my right arm so they could recognize me. Then I would take command. We would surround the prison and get the king out quickly. The whole scene would be dramatic and impressive, although I would have preferred noon for the more theatrical effect it would give.

To add more options, I thought I would look up some people I had known before and reveal myself to them. That might help us out of our trouble without needing the knights. But I had to be careful, because it was risky. I needed to dress richly, and I couldn’t just rush into it. I would build up to it slowly by buying several suits in shops far apart, each one a little finer than the last, until I reached silk and velvet and was ready for my plan. So I set out.

But the scheme collapsed immediately! At the first corner I ran into one of our slaves who was sneaking around with a watchman. I coughed at that moment, and he shot me a look that tore right through me. I think he believed he had heard that cough before. I stepped into a shop right away and moved along the counter, pricing things and watching them from the corner of my eye. They had stopped and were talking while staring in through the door. I decided to escape through the back, if there was a back way. I asked the shopwoman if I could step out there to search for the escaped slave, who was thought to be hiding somewhere in back, and said I was an officer in disguise. I told her my partner was at the door with one of the murderers in custody, and asked if she would kindly tell him not to wait but to go to the far end of the back alley and be ready to cut the slave off when I flushed him out.

She was burning with curiosity to see one of those already famous murderers and hurried off on the errand at once."}

{"request_id":"839df7a991e6521c2ef6f133","rewritten_text":"Just then both his gaze and mine landed on the scrap of parchment, which I had first taken for paper. It lay half buried in the sand with one corner sticking up. Nearby I noticed the remains of what looked like the hull of a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have been there for ages, because it barely still resembled boat timbers.

“Well, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon after, we started home and met Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he begged me to let him take it to the fort. When I agreed, he promptly slipped it into his waistcoat pocket, without the parchment it had been wrapped in, which I’d kept in my hand while he examined the beetle. Perhaps he feared I might change my mind and figured he should secure his prize at once—you know how fervent he is about anything related to Natural History. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have tucked the parchment into my own pocket.

“You remember when I sat down at the table to sketch the beetle, I couldn’t find any paper where I usually kept it. I looked in the drawer and found none there. I searched my pockets, hoping for an old letter, when my hand touched the parchment. That’s the exact way it came into my possession; the whole incident stuck with me vividly.

“No doubt you’ll think me imaginative—but I’d already made a sort of connection. I had linked two pieces of a larger chain. There was a boat on a shore, and not far from it, a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn on it. Naturally you’ll ask, ‘What’s the connection?’ I answer that a skull, or death’s-head, is the recognized symbol of pirates. The death’s-head flag flies in every engagement.

“I’ve said the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment is durable—almost indestructible. Trivial matters are rarely recorded on parchment; for simple drawing or writing, it’s far less handy than paper. That thought hinted at some purpose, some significance, in the death’s-head. I also noticed the parchment’s shape. Though one corner had been damaged by some accident, it was clear the original had been oblong.”"}

{"request_id":"f86d1d4fc16f0c9e3bec8b36","rewritten_text":"It seemed a maze of back alleys, drains, and tiny gardens, having the look of a somewhat dreary retreat. Wemmick’s dwelling was a small wooden cottage amid garden plots, its roof trimmed and painted like a gun battery.

“All my own work,” said Wemmick. “Pretty, isn’t it?”

I praised it heartily; it must have been the tiniest house I’d ever seen, with the oddest Gothic windows (most of them mere make-believe) and a Gothic door hardly large enough to squeeze through.

“That’s a genuine flagstaff, you observe,” Wemmick continued, “and on Sundays I send up an actual flag. Now look. Once I cross this bridge, I haul it up—so—and break the connection.”

The bridge was just a plank over a trench about four feet wide and two deep. But it was delightful to watch him raising it and securing it in place, smiling with relish, not just as a rote performance.

“At nine each evening, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun fires. There he stands, you know! And when you hear him go, I believe you’ll admit he’s a real Stinger.”

The artillery in question was set up in a separate little fort of lattice-work, shielded from the weather by an ingenious tarpaulin gadget resembling an umbrella.

“Then, behind,” Wemmick went on, “out of sight, so the notion of fortifications isn’t spoiled—because my rule is, if you have a notion, carry it through and maintain it—I’m not sure if you agree—”

I assured him I did.

“—Behind, there’s a pig, and there are chickens and rabbits; then I knock together a small frame, you see, and raise cucumbers; and at supper you’ll decide what manner of salad I can provide. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling yet grave as he shook his head, “if you can imagine the little place under siege, it would hold out an extraordinary while for provisions.”

He then led me to a bower about twelve yards away, though the path was so cleverly wound that it took quite a while to reach; there our glasses stood ready. Our punch cooled in an ornamental pool beside which the bower was built. This circular piece of water—with an island in the midst that might have supplied the evening salad—held a fountain he had devised, which, when you set a small mill spinning and pulled a cork from a pipe, spouted so vigorously it dampened the back of one’s hand."}

content.text: {"request_id":"2555d8324b87efadf188fe0f","rewritten_text":"After seeing our friend settled in his new office, we turned back toward Windsor. The nearness of the place to London softened the thought of parting from Raymond and Perdita. We said goodbye in the Protectoral Palace. It was pleasant to watch my sister take on her role, trying to carry it with suitable dignity. Her inner pride and outward humility were still at odds. Her shyness was genuine, born from fear of being misunderstood and from the slight sting of neglect that also troubled Raymond. Yet Perdita was more mindful of others; part of her bashfulness came from wanting to spare those around her any feeling of inferiority, a feeling she never aimed to evoke. Given her birth and education, Idris would have handled every ceremonial form better; but her ease, built on habit, made such tasks tedious. Perdita, despite the difficulties, clearly enjoyed her place. Filled with new thoughts, she felt little sorrow when we left; she kissed us affectionately and promised to visit soon, yet she did not regret the cause of our separation. Raymond’s spirits were boundless; unsure how to wield his fresh power, his head brimmed with plans without a single decision—still, he promised himself, his friends, and the world that his Protectorship would shine through some act of supreme glory. Talking of them and drawing moral lessons, we returned with smaller numbers to Windsor Castle. We rejoiced in our escape from political upheaval and embraced solitude with renewed pleasure. Work was plentiful, yet my restless nature now aimed at intellectual effort alone, and serious study proved an excellent cure for the fever of spirit that would have overtaken me in idleness. Perdita let us bring Clara back to Windsor; she and my two beautiful infants were constant sources of delight and amusement.\n\nOnly one thing disturbed our peace: Adrian’s health. It clearly declined, though no symptoms revealed the cause, unless his bright eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption; yet he felt neither pain nor dread. He threw himself eagerly into his books and rested from study in the company he cherished most, that of his sister and myself."}

content.text: {"request_id":"9e6b0e2228d409c53c06c58f","rewritten_text":"We shouted and insisted so loudly that we were free men that the liberty-spouting orator and his patriotic crowd paid attention, gathered around us, and took on a very stern air. The orator said, “If you truly are freemen, you have nothing to fear—the God-given liberties of Britain surround you like a shield and shelter! (Applause.) You shall soon see. Bring forth your proof.” “What proof?” “Proof that you are freemen.” Then I remembered and kept quiet. But the king burst out, “You are mad, man. It is more reasonable that this thief and scoundrel prove that we are not freemen.” He knew his own laws the way most people do—by words, not by consequences. The words take on a vivid meaning when you must apply them to yourself. Everyone shook their heads, looking disappointed; some walked away, uninterested. The orator spoke again, now in a businesslike tone, not a sentimental one: “If you do not know your country’s laws, it is time you learned them. You are strangers to us; you cannot deny it. You may be freemen; we do not deny that. But you may also be slaves. The law is clear: it does not require the claimant to prove you are slaves; it requires you to prove you are not.” I said, “Dear sir, give us time to send to Astolat; or give us time to send to the Valley of Holiness—” “Peace, good man. Those requests are extraordinary, and you cannot expect them to be granted. It would take much time and cause undue trouble to your master—” “Master, idiot!” the king shouted. “I have no master, I myself am the m—” “Silence, for God’s sake!” I got the words out in time to stop the king. We were already in enough trouble; nothing could be gained by convincing these people we were lunatics. There’s no use drawing it out. The earl put us up and sold us at auction. This same infernal law existed in America’s South in my own time, thirteen hundred years later. Under it, hundreds of freemen who couldn’t prove their freedom were sold into lifelong slavery, and it never made much impression on me; but when the law and the auction block touched my own life, what had merely seemed improper before suddenly became hellish. That’s how we are made. Yes, we were sold at auction like swine. In a big town with a busy market we would have brought a good price, but this place was utterly stagnant, so we sold for a sum that shames me every time I think of it."}

{"request_id":"a444bd4718ed5f8252d2852e","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced angrily up and down the room. I stood ready to receive and answer his accusations. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is utterly ridiculous,” he said. “You couldn’t behave more unreasonably if you were schoolboys.”

“You don’t understand,” said Raymond. “This is just one part of a whole system—a plan of tyranny I’ll never submit to. Because I’m Protector of England, am I supposed to be the only slave in the empire? My privacy invaded, my actions criticized, my friends insulted? No, I’ll rid myself of all of it. Bear witness.” He removed the star, the badge of his office, from his chest and threw it on the table. “I renounce my office. I give up my power—let anyone else take it!”

“Let him take it,” Adrian cried, “if he can claim—and if the world will acknowledge—that he’s your superior. There isn’t a man in England presumptuous enough. Know yourself, Raymond, and your anger will end; your calm will return. A few months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country or ourselves, we simultaneously prayed for the life and well-being of the Protector, inseparably tied to us. Your hours were dedicated to our benefit, your ambition was to win our approval. You adorned our towns with public buildings, bestowed useful institutions, and gave the land abundant fertility. The powerful and unjust shrank from judgment at your tribunal, and the poor and oppressed rose like morning flowers in the sunlight of your protection.

“Can you wonder that we’re all shocked and sorrowful when this seems changed? But come, this splenetic mood has already passed; resume your duties. Your supporters will cheer you, your enemies will be silenced, and our love, honour, and loyalty will be shown to you again. Master yourself, Raymond, and the world will be yours.”

“All this would make perfect sense if you were talking to someone else,” Raymond replied sullenly. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first noble in the land, might become its ruler. You, the good, wise, and just, could command every heart. But I see too soon for my own happiness, and too late for England’s good, that I took on a task beyond me. I can’t control myself. My passions are my masters; even my smallest impulse tyrannises over me. Do you think I renounced the Protectorate—and I have renounced it—in a fit of bad temper? By the living God, I swear never to take up that bauble again, never again to burden myself with the weight of care and misery represented by that symbol.”"}

{"request_id":"66ec2d4561ab23aed01c6c72","rewritten_text":"With everything settled so pleasantly, they sealed the agreement with another teacup of peppermint drink; the lady needed it, as her nerves were fluttering. While they sipped, she told Mr. Bumble that the old woman had died.

“Very good,” said Mr. Bumble, tasting the peppermint. “I’ll stop at Sowerberry’s on my way home, and tell him to send first thing tomorrow. Was that the thing that frightened you, my love?”

“It wasn’t anything specific, dear,” the lady answered, dodging the question.

“It must have been something, love,” Mr. Bumble insisted. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” she replied. “One day. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” cried Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any rudeness from any of the male paupers—”

“No, no, love!” she cut in quickly.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble went on, “if I thought any of them dared to raise their coarse eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” the lady answered.

“They’d better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fist. “Let me see any man, parish or not, who would dare, and I promise he wouldn’t try twice!”

Without his energetic gestures, this might not have sounded like much of a compliment, but as Mr. Bumble acted out his threat with a bold display, she was deeply moved by this proof of his devotion and declared, admiringly, that he was a dove.

The dove then flipped up his coat collar and set his cocked hat on his head. After he and his future wife shared a long and loving embrace, he faced the cold night again, pausing only a few minutes in the male paupers’ ward to scold them, satisfying himself that he had the right sharpness to be workhouse-master. Confident in his fitness, Mr. Bumble left the building lighthearted, filled with bright dreams of his future rise, and these thoughts carried him along until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry had gone out for tea and supper, and Noah Claypole was never eager to exert himself beyond what was needed for eating and drinking, so the shop remained open even though it was past closing time. Mr. Bumble rapped his cane on the counter several times; getting no response, and seeing a light glowing through the glass window of the little parlor behind the shop, he boldly peeked in to see what was happening, and what he saw surprised him greatly."}

content.text: {"request_id":"de72aaa7f09b1ca14320dd69","rewritten_text":"“Never,” the girl replied. “Why not?” “For one reason,” she answered firmly, “because that lady knows and will stand by me—I know she will, because she promised me she would. And also, because although he’s lived a wicked life, I’ve led a wicked life too. There are plenty of us who’ve walked the same paths together, and I won’t betray them. Any one of them could have turned on me but didn’t, bad as they may be.” “Then,” said the gentleman quickly, as if this was what he’d been hoping for, “hand Monks over to me and let me deal with him.” “What if he turns on the others?” “I promise you, if the truth is forced out of him, that’s where it ends. There must be parts of Oliver’s story that would be painful to expose publicly, and if the truth comes out, the rest will go free.” “And if it doesn’t?” the girl asked. “Then,” the gentleman continued, “Fagin won’t be brought to justice without your consent. In that case I could give you reasons that I believe would persuade you.” “Do I have the lady’s promise on that?” the girl asked. “You do,” Rose replied. “My true and faithful pledge.” “Monks would never find out how you learned what you know?” the girl asked after a brief pause. “Never,” said the gentleman. “The information would be used so that he could never even suspect.” “I’ve been a liar, and among liars since I was a child,” said the girl after another quiet moment, “but I’ll take you at your word.” After both assured her she could, she spoke in a voice so low it was often hard for the listener to catch the meaning, describing by name and location the tavern she’d been followed from that night. From her occasional pauses, it seemed the gentleman was making quick notes of what she was sharing. When she had explained the layout, the best place to watch without being noticed, and the night and hour Monks usually went there, she stopped to think, trying to bring his features and manner more clearly to mind. “He’s tall,” said the girl, “strongly built but not heavy. He has a stealthy way of walking, and as he walks, he keeps looking over his shoulder, first one way, then the other.”"}

{"request_id":"462eecc5f1aa4993e4df6738","rewritten_text":"In the morning she was found dead in her bed, apparently without having felt any pain. Sir Mathew Reid had been called at once, but naturally there was nothing he could do, and she was to be buried on the twenty-second at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death she had written her will, leaving Lord Arthur her little house in Curzon Street along with all her furniture, personal belongings, and paintings, except for her collection of miniatures, which was to go to her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to have. The estate was not worth very much, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was extremely eager for Lord Arthur to come back immediately, if possible, since there were many bills to settle, and Lady Clementina had never kept any proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s thoughtful remembrance of him, and he felt that Mr. Podgers had a great deal to answer for. Still, his love for Sybil overshadowed every other feeling, and the knowledge that he had done his duty brought him peace and comfort. When he reached Charing Cross, he felt perfectly content.

The Mertons welcomed him warmly. Sybil made him promise he would never again let anything come between them, and the wedding was set for the seventh of June. Life seemed bright and beautiful to him once more, and all his former happiness returned.

One day, however, while he was going through the house on Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of faded letters and emptying drawers full of odds and ends, the young woman suddenly gave a small cry of delight.

“What have you found, Sybil?” asked Lord Arthur, looking up from his work with a smile.

“This lovely little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it charming and Dutch? Please give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m well over eighty.”

It was the box that had contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint blush touched his cheeks. He had almost completely forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil—for whose sake he had endured all that terrible anxiety—should be the first to remind him of it.

“Of course you can have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh! thank you, Arthur; and may I have the bonbon too? I had no idea Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a horrifying thought flashed through his mind."}

{"request_id":"5223fda249d46bf4eb297408","rewritten_text":"There comes a moment in every well-made boy’s life when he’s hit with a fierce urge to go somewhere and dig for buried treasure. That feeling hit Tom one day. He headed out to find Joe Harper, but had no luck. Next he looked for Ben Rogers; he’d gone fishing. Before long he ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a private spot and laid out the plan in confidence. Huck was up for it. Huck was always willing to jump into anything that promised fun and cost nothing, because he had a steady surplus of the kind of time that isn’t money. “Where are we going to dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is it hidden everywhere?”

“No, of course not. It’s hidden in very particular places, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the tip of a branch of an old dead tree, right where the shadow falls at midnight; but mostly under the floor in haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Robbers, naturally—who else? Sunday school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it were mine I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and have fun.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t do things that way. They always hide it and leave it there.”

“Don’t they ever come back for it?”

“No, they mean to, but they usually forget the landmarks, or else they die. Anyway, it sits there for ages and gets rusty; and eventually somebody finds an old yellow paper that tells how to find the signs—a paper you have to puzzle over for about a week because it’s mostly symbols and hieroglyphics.”

“Hyro-what?”

“Hieroglyphics—pictures and stuff, you know, that don’t look like they mean anything.”

“Do you have one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how are you going to find the marks?”

“I don’t need any marks. They always bury it under a haunted house or on an island, or under a dead tree with one branch sticking out. We tried Jackson’s Island a little, and we can try it again sometime; and there’s the old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and there are plenty of dead-limb trees—loads of them.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“What a question! No!”

“Then how are you going to know which one to dig at?”

“Dig at all of them!”

“Tom, that’ll take all summer.”

“Well, so what? Suppose you find a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and gray, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How would that be?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s great. More than great to me. Just give me the hundred dollars and I don’t need any diamonds.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1116389df85fa9fe7f380efc","rewritten_text":"Smallpox! I leaped to the king and murmured in his ear: “Sire, out with you at once! The woman is dying of that same plague that swept Camelot two years past.” He did not stir. “Verily, I will remain—and render aid.” I bent close again: “Your Majesty, you must not. You must depart.” “You mean kindly, and your words have weight. Yet it were shame for a king to show fear, and shame for a belted knight to hold back his hand when succor is due. Enough, I refuse. It is you who need to withdraw. The Church’s ban spares me, but it forbids you this place, and should she learn of your trespass she will visit you harshly.” It was peril for him, and could well cost his life, yet there was no moving him. If he deemed his knightly honor engaged, debate was wasted; he would remain, come what might. I recognized that and let the matter drop. The poor woman spoke up: “Kind sir, of your charity climb yonder ladder and bring me tidings of what you see? Fear not to tell the whole, for sometimes a mother’s heart can break no further—being already broken.” “Stay,” said the king, “and give her food. I will go.” He set down the knapsack. I turned to start, but the king was already on the way. He paused over a man lying in the dimness, unnoticed till now. “Is that your husband?” he asked. “Yes.” “Is he asleep?” “Thanks be to God for that mercy, yes—these three hours. Where can I find coin enough to pay my gratitude? My heart overflows for the rest he rests in now.” I said: “We shall take care. We will not wake him.” “Ah no, you cannot, for he is dead.” “Dead?” “Indeed—and what triumph it is to know it! No one can harm or insult him any more. He is in heaven now and joyful; or if not there, he waits in hell, content, for there he will meet no abbot and no bishop. We were boy and girl together; we have been man and wife five and twenty years, never parted till now. Think how long that is to love and suffer side by side. This morning his mind wandered, and in his fancy we were children again roaming the happy fields; and so, in that innocent, cheerful talk, he rambled farther and farther, still lightly chatting, until he stepped into those other meadows we know naught of, and vanished from mortal sight.”"}

{"request_id":"e4e54eb63db32fe478057091","rewritten_text":"“Men marry because they are tired; women because they are curious, and both end up disappointed.”

“I doubt I will ever marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your sayings. I’m simply following it, the way I follow everything you tell me.”

“Who is it you’re in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“With an actress,” Dorian Gray said, blushing.

Lord Henry shrugged. “That’s a rather ordinary beginning.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard of her.”

“No one has—yet. People will someday. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are the decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they say that nothing charmingly. Women are the triumph of matter over mind, just as men are the triumph of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you talk like that?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s the truth. I’m analyzing women right now, so I ought to know. The subject is not as complex as I thought. In the end, there are only two kinds of women: the plain and the colorful. Plain women are very useful. If you want a reputation for respectability, just take them down to supper. The other women are delightful, but they make one mistake. They paint their faces to look young. Our grandmothers painted so they could talk brilliantly. Rouge and wit used to go together. That is finished now. As long as a woman can look ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s perfectly content. As for conversation, there are only five women in London worth talking to, and two of them can’t be invited into decent society. But tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah, Harry, your views frighten me.”

“Never mind that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you meet her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but don’t be unsympathetic about it. None of it would have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild urge to know everything about life. For days after I met you, something seemed to beat in my veins. As I lounged in the park or strolled down Piccadilly, I looked at everyone who passed and wondered, with a fierce curiosity, what kind of lives they led. Some of them fascinated me. Others terrified me. There was a sweet poison in the air. I craved every sensation..."}

{"request_id":"7b1aa08574ec777864075a30","rewritten_text":"Shall I be carried to the skies on soft flowered beds of ease, while others fight for the prize and sail through bloody seas? He was considered a remarkable reader. At church socials he was always asked to read poetry, and when he finished, the ladies would lift their hands and let them fall limp in their laps, roll their eyes, and shake their heads, as if to say, “Words can’t express it; it’s too beautiful—too beautiful for this mortal world.”

After the hymn was sung, Reverend Mr. Sprague turned himself into a bulletin board, reading off notices of meetings, societies, and other matters until it seemed the list would stretch to Judgment Day—a peculiar custom that still persists in America, even in cities, in this age of plentiful newspapers. Often, the less reason there is to keep a tradition, the harder it is to discard it.

Then the minister prayed. It was a generous, detailed prayer: for the church and its children; for the other churches in town; for the village; the county; the state; the state officials; the United States; the churches of the United States; Congress; the President; the government officers; poor sailors tossed by stormy seas; the oppressed millions groaning under European monarchs and Eastern despots; those who have the light and good news yet lack eyes to see or ears to hear; the heathen in far-off islands; and finally a plea that the words he was about to speak would find grace and favor, like seed sown in fertile soil, yielding in time a thankful harvest of good. Amen.

There was a rustle of skirts, and the standing congregation sat down. The boy whose story this book tells did not enjoy the prayer; he merely endured it—if that. He was restless throughout; he unconsciously kept count of the prayer’s details, for he wasn’t really listening, but he knew the familiar territory and the clergyman’s usual route. When a bit of new material slipped in, his ear caught it and his whole being rebelled; he considered additions unfair and downright wicked. In the middle of the prayer a fly landed on the back of the pew in front of him and tormented his spirit by calmly rubbing its hands together, wrapping its head with its arms, and polishing it so vigorously it seemed almost to detach from its body, exposing the thin thread of a neck; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them to its body as though they were coat tails; going through its entire grooming routine as serenely as if it knew it was perfectly safe."}

{"request_id":"d78c40b776adb48492ff1207","rewritten_text":"After I had sent in the petitions, I couldn’t stay away from the places where they were lodged. I felt as if they were more hopeful and less desperate when I was near. In that unreasonable restlessness and mental pain, I roamed the streets in the evenings, wandering past the offices and houses where I had left the requests. To this day, the weary western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night—with their rows of stern, shuttered mansions and their long lines of lamps—are melancholy to me because of those memories.

The daily visits I could make to him were shorter now, and he was more strictly guarded. Seeing—or believing—that I was suspected of trying to smuggle poison to him, I asked to be searched before I sat down at his bedside. I told the officer stationed there that I was willing to do anything to reassure him of my honest intentions. No one was hard on him or me. Duty had to be done, and it was done, but not cruelly. The officer always told me he was worse, and the other sick prisoners in the room, along with the prisoners who cared for them as nurses—criminals, yet not incapable of kindness, thank God!—always gave the same report.

As the days passed, I saw more and more how he would lie quietly staring at the white ceiling, his face empty of light until some word of mine brightened it for a moment before it faded again. Sometimes he was almost—or completely—unable to speak. Then he answered me with light pressures of his hand, and I came to understand him very well.

The days had reached ten when I noticed a greater change in him than ever before. His eyes were turned toward the door and lit up as I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said as I sat down by his bed, “I thought you were late. But I knew you couldn’t be.”

“It’s exactly the time,” I said. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always wait at the gate, don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So I don’t lose a moment of the time.”

“Thank you, dear boy, thank you. God bless you! You’ve never deserted me, dear boy.”

I pressed his hand silently, unable to forget that I had once meant to desert him.

“And what’s best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more comfortable with me since I was under a dark cloud than when the sun was shining.”"}

{"request_id":"b9a50d0fd6e708789e80cf09","rewritten_text":"“So now I own some knights,” I said as we rode off. “Who would have thought I’d live to count assets like that? I’ve no idea what to do with them unless I raffle them off. How many are there, Sandy?”

“Seven, please you, sir, and their squires.”

“A good haul. Who are they? Where do they hang out?”

“Where do they hang out?”

“Yes, where do they live?”

“Ah, I understood thee not. I will tell thee soon.” Then she murmured softly, tasting the words like they were sweets. “Hang they out—hang they out—where hang—where do they hang out; yes, just so; where do they hang out. Truly the phrase has a pleasing grace and is prettily turned. I will repeat it again and again in my idleness, and perhaps I shall learn it. Where do they hang out. Indeed! it already slips lightly from my tongue, and since—”

“Don’t forget the cowboys, Sandy.”

“Cowboys?”

“Yes, the knights, remember? You were going to tell me about them a moment ago. Figuratively speaking, play ball.”

“Game—”

“Yes, yes, yes! Step up to the plate. I mean get to work on the facts, and don’t waste so much kindling to start the fire. Tell me about the knights.”

“I will, and lightly begin. So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Great Scott!”

You see, I saw my mistake at once. I had set her machinery going; it was my fault; she would take thirty days to reach the point. She usually started without any introduction and stopped without giving the result. If you interrupted, she either kept going as if nothing happened or answered with a couple of words and then backed up and repeated the sentence. So interruptions only made it worse; yet I had to interrupt, and fairly often, to save my life; a person would die if that monotony dripped on him all day.

“Great Scott!” I said, miserable. She merely went back and began again:

“So they two departed and rode into a great forest. And—”

“Which two?”

“Sir Gawaine and Sir Uwaine. So they came to an abbey of monks and were well lodged there. In the morning they heard mass in the abbey, and then they rode on till they came to a great forest; then Sir Gawaine saw in a valley near a tower twelve fair damsels and two knights armed on great horses, and the damsels moved to and fro by a tree.”"}

{"request_id":"83ea6df1c8a41e7266670ef7","rewritten_text":"“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped it, showing how disappointed he was in Joseph.

“But my dear young friend,” Mr. Pumblechook said, “you must be hungry, you must be exhausted. Sit down. Here’s a chicken sent over from the Boar, here’s a tongue from the Boar, here are one or two other things from the Boar that I hope you won’t turn up your nose at. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, springing up again the moment he had sat down, “see before me him with whom I once sported in the happy days of his infancy? And may I—may I—?”

This ‘May I?’ meant could he shake hands. I agreed, and he did so fervently, then sat down again.

“Here is wine,” Mr. Pumblechook said. “Let us drink. Thanks to Fortune, and may she always choose her favorites with the same good judgment! And yet I cannot,” he added, rising again, “look upon One—and also drink to One—without again asking—May I—may I—?”

I said he could, he shook hands with me again, emptied his glass, and turned it upside down. I did the same, and if I had stood on my head before drinking, the wine couldn’t have gone to it faster.

Mr. Pumblechook served me the liver wing and the best slice of tongue (none of those obscure dead-ends of pork now) and, comparatively speaking, barely looked after himself at all. “Ah! poultry, poultry! You never guessed,” Mr. Pumblechook said, addressing the bird on the platter, “when you were a little fledgling, what lay ahead for you. You never thought you’d be refreshment beneath this humble roof for someone who—Call it a weakness if you like,” he said, getting up yet again, “but may I? may I—?”

It soon became useless to keep repeating that he could, so he just went ahead. How he managed to do it so often without stabbing himself on my knife, I can’t imagine.

“And your sister,” he continued after a steady bout of eating, “who had the honor of raising you by hand! It’s a sad picture to think she’s no longer capable of fully understanding the honor. May—”

I saw he was about to lunge at me again, so I stopped him.

“We’ll drink to her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, limp with admiration, “that’s how you recognize them, sir!” (I don’t know who Sir was supposed to be, but it certainly wasn’t me, and there was no third person present.) “That’s how you know the noble-minded, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"0dbbc22d5d0e2eb012d32225","rewritten_text":"With my heart racing and fear rising—I could not say why—I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were its words.

“My dear Child,

“I have betrayed your trust, tried to poison your mind, and forced your innocent heart to see and hear the expressions of forbidden, monstrous desire. I must atone for these crimes and try to match my punishment to my guilt. You are, I fear, prepared for what I must say: we must separate and remain apart forever.

“I rob you of your parent and only friend. You are cast out, without shelter, into the world; your hopes are ruined; the peace and safety of your clear mind destroyed. Memory will bring you terrifying images of guilt and the torment of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who bring all this misery upon you; I, who cast you out and have stamped distrust and agony on the heart and brow of my own child; I, who with devilish carelessness tried to steal her loveliness to replace it with the foul deformity of sin—I, in the overflowing pain of my heart, beg you to forgive me.

“I do not ask for your pity; you must hate me, and rightly so. But forgive me, Mathilda, and do not let your thoughts follow me into exile with relentless anger. I must never see you again; never hear your voice; yet the gentle whisper of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning in my disordered mind and heart; I am sure I would feel it even in my grave. I dare insist on this plea by telling you how I was horribly trapped in this web of fiery anguish and how I struggled to free myself. If your soul were less pure and bright I would never try to excuse myself to you; I would fear that if I made you despise me less you might also hate vice less. But in speaking to you I feel as if I appeal to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness, and I must try to win it or despair. I beg you to listen, and if guilt mixed with intense suffering and madness-like remorse can earn any mercy, perhaps you may think—you, if not I—that I have some claim on your compassion.

“I urge you to remember our first happy days on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen weary years of wandering, during which, though I faced many dangers and misfortunes, my heart had remained entirely empty.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"6170fd62fc5117227653356a","rewritten_text":"Poor Jack was later killed in a duel by Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara died of a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended, so in every way it had been counted a great success. Still, it was an extremely difficult disguise, if I may use such a stage term for one of the greatest supernatural mysteries, or, to speak more scientifically, a marvel of the higher-natural world, and he needed a full three hours to prepare. At last everything was ready, and he was pleased with his appearance. The tall leather riding-boots that went with the outfit were a bit too large, and he could find only one of the two horse-pistols, but overall he was satisfied, and at quarter past one he slipped out of the wainscoting and crept down the corridor. When he reached the twins’ room, called the Blue Bed Chamber because of the color of its hangings, he found the door slightly open. Wanting to make a dramatic entrance, he flung it wide, and a heavy jug of water dropped straight on him, soaking him to the skin and missing his left shoulder by only a couple of inches. At the same moment he heard muffled bursts of laughter coming from the four-poster bed. The shock to his nerves was such that he ran back to his room as fast as he could, and the next day he was laid up with a severe cold. The only thing that comforted him at all was that he had not brought his head with him, for if he had, the consequences could have been very serious.\n\nHe now abandoned all hope of frightening this insolent American family, and usually contented himself with creeping through the passages in soft slippers, with a thick red muffler around his throat to guard against drafts, and a small arquebuse in case the twins attacked him. The final insult he suffered came on the nineteenth of September. He had gone downstairs to the great entrance hall, certain that there, at least, he would be left in peace, and was amusing himself by making sarcastic comments on the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which now hung where the Canterville family portraits once did. He was simply but neatly dressed in a long shroud spotted with graveyard mold, had his jaw tied up with a strip of yellow linen, and carried a small lantern and a sexton’s spade."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d99279f517b91706a428c3df","rewritten_text":"Raymond was energized by the vivid sensations of restored health. As commander of the Athenians, he felt he now held a position worthy of his ambition, and in his dreams of taking Constantinople he anticipated an event that would stand as a landmark through the ages—an accomplishment unmatched in human history. A city celebrated for its majestic associations, admired worldwide for the beauty of its setting, and for hundreds of years the stronghold of the Ottomans, was to be freed from bondage and barbarism and returned to a people renowned for genius, civilization, and a spirit of liberty. Perdita relied on his renewed companionship, his love, his hopes and fame, the way a sybarite rests on a luxurious couch; every thought brought rapture, each emotion seemed to bathe in a congenial, soothing element.\n\nWe reached Kishan on the seventh of July. The weather during our journey had been clear. Each day, before dawn, we left our night’s camp to watch the shadows draw back from hill and valley, and to see the golden blaze of the rising sun. The soldiers with us, full of national spirit, took delight in the sight of nature’s beauty. Sunrise was greeted with triumphant music, while birdsong, catching our ears now and then, filled the pauses between the notes. At midday, we pitched our tents in some shady valley or leafy woodland among the mountains, while a stream, murmuring over pebbles, coaxed us into grateful sleep. Our evening marches, calmer, were even more pleasing than the restless energy of the morning. If the band played, they instinctively chose melodies of restrained feeling; the farewell of love or the melancholy of absence would give way to a solemn hymn, perfect for the peaceful loveliness of evening and raising the spirit toward grand, reverent thoughts. Often all sound fell silent so we could listen to the nightingales, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to travelers. When we crossed a valley, we were wrapped in gentle shadows and saw rocks tinted with beautiful colors. Crossing a mountain, we saw Greece laid out below like a living map, its famous peaks slicing the sky, its rivers threading the fertile land in silver lines. Barely daring to breathe, we English travelers gazed in awe at this splendid landscape, so unlike the muted tones and wistful charm of our own homeland. After we left Macedonia, the fertile but low plains of Thrace offered fewer attractions, yet our journey remained engaging. An advance guard announced our approach, and the local people quickly stirred to show honor to Lord Raymond."}

{"request_id":"1f673b961b847589e22c8f0a","rewritten_text":"Everything about this carried a strangeness that pulled me in and fascinated me. It was as though he had awakened from a long, dream-filled sleep, feeling like one of the seven sleepers or Nourjahad in that lovely imitation of an Eastern tale. Diana was gone; his friends were altered or dead, and when he opened his eyes again, I was all that was left on earth for him to love.

How precious the waters, mountains, and forests of Loch Lomond became now that I had such a beloved companion for my wanderings. I visited with my father every delightful spot, whether on the islands or along the tree-sheltered waterfalls, every shaded path or hollow tangled with undergrowth and fern. His conversation broadened my thoughts. I felt remade, filled with the freshness and vitality of a new existence: since his arrival, I seemed transported from a narrow patch of ground to a universe limitless to imagination and understanding. My life had previously been like a pleasant country stream, never meant to leave its native fields, destined to disappear quietly when its task was done and leave no trace. Now it seemed to me a varied river running through a fertile, beautiful landscape, always changing and always lovely. Alas, I did not know the desert it was soon to reach, the rocks that would tear its waters, and the hideous scene that would mirror itself in their distorted reflections. Life was brilliant then; I was beginning to learn hope—and what brings the heart more bitter despair than shattered hope?

Is it not strange that grief should follow such divine happiness so quickly? I drank from an enchanted cup, but bitterness lay at the bottom of its long sweetness. My heart was full of deep affection, yet it was calm because of that depth and fullness. I had no notion that misery could spring from love, and that lesson, which everyone must learn eventually, was given to me in a way few are forced to endure. I mourn now, and will always mourn, those few short months of paradisiacal bliss. I broke no command, I tasted no forbidden fruit, yet I was mercilessly driven out. Alas, my companion did, and I was cast down in his fall. But I stray from my account—let sorrow arrive when its time is set; at this point in my story I can still speak of happiness.

Three months passed in this delightful companionship before my aunt fell ill. I spent a whole month in her room nursing her, but her sickness was fatal, and she died, leaving me inconsolable for a time. Death is so terrible to the living; the chains of habit are so strong, even when affection does not bind them, that the heart must writhe in agony when they break."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5df40fd469223720d83d9ed8","rewritten_text":"We proclaimed our freedom so loudly and earnestly that the liberty-spouting orator and his patriotic crowd took an eager interest, gathered around us, and assumed a very resolute stance. The orator spoke: “If indeed ye are freemen, ye need fear nothing—the God-given liberties of Britain surround ye as shield and shelter! (Applause.) Ye shall quickly see. Produce your proofs.” “What proofs?” “Proof that ye are freemen.” Ah—then I remembered! I recovered my wits and kept quiet. But the king burst out: “Thou’rt mad, man. Reason would better say that this thief and knave prove we are not freemen.” You see, he knew his own laws the way people commonly do—by words, not by consequences. The meaning grows vivid enough when it applies to oneself. Everyone shook their heads and looked let down; some drifted away, uninterested. The orator remarked—this time with businesslike tones rather than sentimental ones: “If ye know not your country’s laws, ‘tis time ye learned. Ye are strangers to us; that ye will not deny. Ye may be freemen—we grant it; yet ye may also be slaves. The law is plain: it demandeth not that the claimant prove ye slaves, but that ye prove ye are not.” I said: “Dear sir, grant us only time to send to Astolat; or grant only time to send to the Valley of Holiness—” “Peace, good man. These are extraordinary requests, and ye cannot hope they will be granted. ‘Twould consume much time and unwarrantably inconvenience your master—” “Master, fool!” the king stormed. “I have no master; I myself am the m—” “Silence, for God’s sake!” I choked the words out in time to stop the king. We had troubles enough already; letting them think us lunatics could only harm us. No use spinning out the details. The earl took us in hand and sold us at auction. This same infernal law had prevailed in our own South in my day—more than thirteen centuries later—and under it hundreds of freemen unable to prove their status had been sold into lifelong bondage without stirring any special emotion in me; but the instant law and auction block crossed my personal path, what had been merely wrong became suddenly infernal. That’s how we’re built. Yes, we were sold at auction, like hogs. In a large city with brisk trade we’d have fetched a handsome sum; but this place was dead stagnant, and so we went for a price that shames me every time I recall it."}
