{"request_id":"f20e633ef6def86a9e083f21","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was busy with my books and Mr. Pocket, I received a note by post. Just seeing the outside sent me into a great flutter, for even though I had never seen the handwriting before, I guessed whose it was. It had no opening like Dear Mr. Pip, or Dear Pip, or Dear Sir, or Dear anything, but simply ran thus:—

“I am to come to London the day after to-morrow by the midday coach. I believe it was settled you should meet me? At all events Miss Havisham thinks so, and I write to obey her. She sends you her regard.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

If there had been time, I probably would have ordered several suits of clothes for the occasion; but since there was not, I had to be content with what I owned. My appetite disappeared at once, and I knew no peace or rest until the day arrived. Yet its arrival brought me no relief; instead, I grew worse and began haunting the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, even before the coach had left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew perfectly well when it would start, I could not bear to let the coach-office out of my sight for more than five minutes. In this unreasonable state I had finished the first half-hour of what would be a four or five hour watch when Wemmick bumped into me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” he said; “how do you do? I would hardly have thought this was your beat.”

I explained that I was waiting to meet someone arriving by coach, and I asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both flourishing, thank you,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He’s in wonderful spirits. He will be eighty-two next birthday. I’m thinking of firing eighty-two times, if the neighborhood doesn’t complain and that cannon of mine can stand the strain. But that’s not London talk. Where do you think I’m going?”

“To the office?” said I, since he was heading that way.

“Next thing to it,” Wemmick answered. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re dealing with a banker’s parcel case just now, and I’ve been down the road taking a look at the scene of action. Now I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I asked.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” answered Wemmick, very dryly. “But he is accused of it. So might you or I be. Either of us could be accused of it, you know.”"}

{"request_id":"1b2f2bdb15923b37ad817d08","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-haired cavalier rode across Brockley meadows. She tore her riding habit badly squeezing through a hedge, so when she returned home she decided to take the back staircase to avoid being seen. As she ran past the Tapestry Chamber, whose door stood open, she thought she saw someone inside. Believing it was her mother’s maid, who sometimes worked there, she stepped in to ask her to mend the torn habit. To her great surprise, it was the Canterville Ghost himself. He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees blown through the air and the red leaves whirling wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, and his whole posture showed deep depression. He looked so forlorn and shabby that little Virginia, who had first thought of running away and locking herself in her room, felt pity instead and decided to comfort him. Her step was so light, and his sorrow so deep, that he did not notice her until she spoke. 

“I’m so sorry for you,” she said, “but my brothers go back to Eton tomorrow, and then, if you behave, no one will bother you.” 

“It is ridiculous to ask me to behave,” he answered, looking round in astonishment at the pretty little girl who had dared speak to him. “Quite ridiculous. I must rattle my chains, groan through keyholes, and walk about at night, if that’s what you mean. It’s my only reason for existing.” 

“That is no reason to exist, and you know you have been very wicked. Mrs. Umney told us, the first day we arrived, that you killed your wife.” 

“Well, I admit it,” said the Ghost crossly, “but it was purely a family matter and concerned no one else.” 

“It is very wrong to kill anyone,” said Virginia, who sometimes had a sweet Puritan seriousness from some old New England ancestor. 

“Oh, I hate the cheap severity of abstract morals! My wife was very plain, never starched my ruffs right, and knew nothing about cooking. Once I shot a buck in Hogley Woods, a magnificent pricket, and do you know how she had it sent up to the table? Anyway, it doesn’t matter now. It is all over, and I don’t think it was very nice of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.”"}

{"request_id":"26ea72bf004d889c844e0d6a","rewritten_text":"The next day was set for the proof (lest our honor catch cold from delay), and the next day Drummle arrived with a polite little note in Estella’s hand, saying she had had the honor of dancing with him several times. This left me no choice but to regret that I had been “carried away into a warmth which,” and overall to reject, as unsustainable, the idea that I could be found anywhere. Drummle and I sat there snorting at each other for an hour, while the Grove took up indiscriminate contradiction, and finally it was announced that good feeling had advanced at a remarkable rate.

I talk about it lightly, but it was no light matter to me. I can’t describe the pain it caused me to think that Estella would show any favor to such a contemptible, clumsy, sullen fool, so far below the average. Even now, I believe it sprang from some pure fire of generosity and unselfishness in my love for her that I couldn’t bear the thought of her lowering herself to that brute. No doubt I would have been miserable no matter whom she favored; but a worthier rival would have brought a different kind and degree of distress.

It was easy for me to find out, and I soon did, that Drummle had begun to follow her closely, and that she allowed it. Soon he was always pursuing her, and he and I crossed paths every day. He persisted in his dull, stubborn way, and Estella kept him going; sometimes encouraging, sometimes discouraging him, sometimes almost flattering him, sometimes openly despising him, sometimes knowing him very well, sometimes barely remembering who he was.

The Spider, as Mr. Jaggers called him, was used to lying in wait and had the patience of his kind. On top of that, he had a blockheaded confidence in his money and family greatness, which sometimes served him well—almost replacing focus and firm resolve. So the Spider, doggedly watching Estella, outlasted many brighter insects, and would often unwind himself and drop at just the right moment.

At an Assembly Ball in Richmond (most places had Assembly Balls then), where Estella outshone all other beauties, this blundering Drummle hung around her so persistently, with so much tolerance from her, that I decided to speak to her about him. I seized the next chance, when she was waiting for Mrs. Blandley to take her home, sitting apart among some flowers, ready to leave."}

{"request_id":"cc8a9bbc00c9f8010ecc6e42","rewritten_text":"For that reason, I decided to hop out as soon as we reached the town and get away from his hearing. I pulled it off without trouble. My small portmanteau was in the boot under my feet; I only had to turn a hinge to take it out. I dropped it before me, climbed down after it, and was left standing at the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement. The convicts went on with the coach, and I knew where they would be whisked away to the river. In my imagination, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting for them at the slime-slicked stairs—heard again the rough “Give way, you!” like an order barked at dogs—and saw once more the villainous Noah’s Ark lying on the black water.

I could not have said what I was afraid of, for my fear was completely undefined and vague, but it was strong within me. As I walked toward the hotel, I felt a dread far worse than simply being worried about an unpleasant recognition, and it made me shake. I’m certain it never took any clear shape, and that it was a brief return of the childhood terror.

The coffee room at the Blue Boar was empty, and I had not only ordered dinner there, but begun eating it before the waiter recognized me. As soon as he apologized for forgetting me, he asked if he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said, “certainly not.”

The waiter—the same one who had once brought up the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was bound—looked surprised, and soon took the first chance to place a dirty old copy of a local newspaper so directly in my path that I picked it up and read this paragraph:

Our readers will be interested to learn, in connection with the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young ironworker from our area (what a subject, by the way, for the magical pen of our still not universally celebrated townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!) that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend was a highly respected figure with some connection to the corn and seed trade, whose very convenient and spacious business premises lie within a hundred miles of High Street. It is not entirely without pride that we note this gentleman as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is gratifying to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes."}

content.text: {"request_id":"8a17961ef4e693bfc538fb2c","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had rented an excellent house in Camden Place, an elevated and dignified address suited to a man of importance, and both he and Elizabeth had settled there very much to their liking. Anne entered with a sinking heart, dreading a months-long imprisonment and silently asking herself, “Oh, when will I get away again?” Yet the unexpectedly warm welcome helped her spirits. Her father and sister were genuinely pleased to show her the house and furnishings and greeted her kindly. Her being a fourth at dinner was mentioned as an advantage. Mrs. Clay was agreeable and smiling, but her courtesies and smiles felt routine. Anne had always expected her to play the part upon her arrival, but she had not expected real warmth from the others. They were clearly in excellent moods, and Anne soon heard their reasons. They had no wish to listen to hers. After setting up the chance to compliment themselves on how sorely they were missed in their old neighborhood—which Anne could not do—they asked only a few half-hearted questions before taking over the conversation entirely. Uppercross did not interest them, Kellynch hardly more; it was all about Bath. They assured her Bath exceeded their expectations in every way. Their house was undeniably the best in Camden Place, and their drawing rooms had many definite advantages over any others they had seen or heard about, with fitting-up and furniture just as superior. Their acquaintance was highly sought after. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had declined many introductions, yet cards were constantly being left by people they did not know. They had endless sources of enjoyment. Could Anne be surprised that her father and sister were pleased? She might not be surprised, but she had to sigh that her father felt no humiliation in his change, saw nothing to miss in the duties and dignity of the resident landowner, and could take so much pride in the trivialities of town. She had to sigh, and smile, and wonder too, as Elizabeth threw open the double doors and strode triumphantly from one drawing room to the other, boasting of the space, at the idea that a woman who had been mistress of Kellynch Hall could take pride in an expanse confined by two walls perhaps thirty feet apart. But that was not all that kept them content; they had Mr. Elliot as well."}

content.text: {"request_id":"2ba6910b9024a9bfbcd03f3a","rewritten_text":"The narrow streets and courtyards finally opened into a wide square dotted with pens for animals and other signs of a cattle market. Sikes slowed down once they reached this spot because the girl could no longer keep up with the fast pace. He turned to Oliver and ordered him to hold Nancy’s hand. “Do you hear?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated and looked around. They stood in a dark corner, well away from any passersby. Oliver knew resistance was useless. He held out his hand, and Nancy gripped it tightly. “Give me the other,” said Sikes, grabbing Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!” The dog looked up and growled. “See here, boy!” said Sikes, placing his other hand on Oliver’s throat. “If he so much as whispers, hold him. Do you understand?” The dog growled again, and licking his lips, stared at Oliver as if eager to sink his teeth into his neck. “He’s as willing as a Christian, strike me blind if he isn’t!” said Sikes, watching the dog with grim approval. “Now you know what to expect, so shout all you like; the dog will soon stop you. Move along, youngster!” Bull’s-eye wagged his tail in response to this rare endearment and, after another warning growl at Oliver, led the way. They were crossing Smithfield, although Oliver would not have known it from any other city square. The night was dark and foggy. Lights from the shops barely pierced the thickening mist, which covered the streets and houses in gloom, making the strange surroundings even more unfamiliar and deepening Oliver’s despair. They had gone only a few steps when the deep toll of a church bell sounded. At the first stroke, his two companions halted and turned toward the source of the sound. “Eight o’clock, Bill,” said Nancy when the bell stopped. “What’s the point of telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes snapped. “I wonder if they can hear it,” said Nancy. “Of course they can,” Sikes replied. “It was St. Bartholomew’s Fair when I got arrested, and there wasn’t a penny trumpet in the fair I couldn’t hear squeaking. After they locked me up for the night, the noise outside made the old prison seem so quiet I almost bashed my brains out against the iron plates on the door.”"}

{"request_id":"9cc0648a1bdab5e75b598da5","rewritten_text":"And if he pressed me for the reason I wanted it, and questioned my right to it, I would tell him—however little he valued such meagre visions—that I had loved Estella devotedly and for a long time, and that though I had lost her and must go on in bereavement, anything touching her was still dearer and nearer to me than all else on earth. Seeing Mr. Jaggers remain motionless, mute, and seemingly implacable before this appeal, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you for a man of kindly heart. I have seen your cheerful house, your aged father, and all the innocent, lively, playful ways with which you lighten your business existence. I beg you to speak for me to Mr. Jaggers, and tell him that, given every circumstance, he ought to be more open with me!”

Never had I witnessed two men stare at each other more strangely than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after that invocation. For an instant I feared Wemmick would be dismissed on the spot; but the fear faded as I observed Mr. Jaggers relax into the semblance of a smile, while Wemmick gained courage.

“What is all this?” demanded Mr. Jaggers. “You with an aged father, and you with pleasant, playful ways?”

“Well!” Wemmick answered. “If I don’t bring them here, where is the harm?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, laying his hand on my arm and smiling outright, “this fellow must be the craftiest impostor in London.”

“Not in the least,” retorted Wemmick, growing more valiant. “I think you’re the impostor.”

Again they traded those former odd looks, each seemingly still unsure whether the other was deceiving him.

“You, with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“So long as it doesn’t meddle with business,” Wemmick replied, “let it remain. Now that I study you, sir, I shouldn’t be surprised if you were scheming to secure a comfortable home of your own one of these days, when you’ve had enough of all this toil.”

Mr. Jaggers tilted his head backward two or three times, as though in review, and even drew a sigh. “Pip,” he said, “let’s leave off talking of ‘poor dreams;’ you know more about such matters than I do, having much fresher dealings with them. But now, concerning this other business. I’ll put a case to you. Mind! I admit nothing.”

He paused for me to assure him that I thoroughly understood he expressly admitted nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “take this case. Imagine that a woman, under the circumstances you have described, concealed her child, and was obliged to disclose the fact to her legal adviser, after he insisted he must know, in view of the latitude of his defence, exactly how the fact stood regarding that child.”"}

{"request_id":"1cc7ad0724fab9c3ff83c263","rewritten_text":"“No bringing up by hand then. Not a bit of it!”

Joe offered me more gravy, which I was afraid to take.

“He was a world of trouble to you, ma’am,” said Mrs. Hubble, sympathizing with my sister.

“Trouble?” echoed my sister; “trouble?” She launched into a terrifying list of every illness I had caused, every sleepless night I had given her, every high place I had fallen from, every low place I had fallen into, every injury I had inflicted on myself, and all the times she had wished me dead while I stubbornly refused to die.

I think the Romans must have annoyed each other terribly with their noses. Perhaps that was why they were such a restless people. In any case, Mr. Wopsle’s Roman nose irritated me so much during this recital of my misconduct that I wanted to pull it until he howled. But everything I had suffered so far was nothing compared with the awful feeling that seized me when the silence following my sister’s speech was broken, during which everyone had looked at me, as I felt painfully aware, with indignation and disgust.

“Yet,” said Mr. Pumblechook, gently steering the company back to the earlier topic, “pork—considered as boiled—is rich, too, isn’t it?”

“Have a little brandy, uncle,” said my sister.

O Heavens, it had come at last! He would find it weak, he would say it was weak, and I was doomed! I clutched the leg of the table under the cloth with both hands and waited for my fate.

My sister went for the stone bottle, returned with it, and poured his brandy, no one else taking any. The wretched man toyed with his glass—picked it up, held it to the light, set it down—dragging out my torment. Meanwhile Mrs. Joe and Joe briskly cleared the table for the pie and pudding.

I couldn’t take my eyes off him. Still gripping the table leg with hands and feet, I watched the miserable man play with his glass, lift it, smile, tilt back his head, and drink the brandy. Immediately after, the company was seized with indescribable alarm as he sprang to his feet, spun around several times in a terrifying, spasmodic whooping-cough dance, and bolted out the door; then he appeared through the window, violently spluttering and spitting, making the most hideous faces, and seeming completely out of his senses.

I held on tight while Mrs. Joe and Joe ran after him."}

{"request_id":"337e0c550bccab9faceac077","rewritten_text":"And he always pretended Peter supplied him with the talk, but that was false—he squeezed every last bit out of that young numbskull we ferried up to the steamboat.

Then Mary Jane brought the letter her father left, and the king read it aloud and blubbered over it. It left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls; it left the tanyard (doing brisk trade) with some other houses and land (worth about seven thousand) and three thousand in gold to Harvey and William, and told how the six thousand cash was hidden down cellar. So the two frauds said they’d fetch it up and keep everything square and above-board, and told me to bring a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the sack they emptied it on the floor, and it was a pretty sight, all them yaller-boys. Land, how the king’s eyes sparkled! He claps the duke on the shoulder and says:

“Oh, this ain’t bully nor noth’n! Oh, no, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, don’t it?”

The duke said it did. They pawed the yaller-boys, sifting them through their fingers and letting them jingle to the floor; and the king says:

“There ain’t no use talkin’; being brothers to a rich dead man and spokesmen of foreign heirs that’s got left is the trade for you and me, Bilge. This comes of relyin’ on Providence. It’s the best course, in the long run. I’ve tried ’em all, and there ain’t no better.”

Most anyone would’ve been pleased with the heap and taken it on faith; but no, they had to count it. So they counted, and it came up four hundred and fifteen dollars shy. Says the king:

“Dern him, what did he do with that four hundred and fifteen?”

They fretted over it awhile and hunted around for it. Then the duke says:

“Well, he was mighty sick, and likely he made a slip—I reckon that’s it. Best let it go and keep still. We can spare it.”

“Oh, shucks, sure we can spare it. I don’t care noth’n about that—it’s the count I’m dwellin’ on. We got to be powerful square and open and above-board here, mind. We got to lug this here money upstairs and count it before everybody—then there ain’t noth’n fishy. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"29490f76761e4b9dc2f9fe25","rewritten_text":"With my heart pounding and afraid though I didn’t know why, I sent the servant away, locked my door, and sat down to read my father’s letter. These were its words.  “My dear child,  “I have betrayed your trust; I tried to corrupt your mind and forced your innocent heart to witness the looks and language of unlawful, monstrous desire. I must atone for these crimes and try to make my punishment match my guilt. You are, I’m sure, prepared for what I must announce: we must separate and be parted forever.  “I am taking from you your parent and only friend. You are cast out into the world without shelter; your hopes are destroyed; the peace and safety of your pure mind ruined; memory will bring you terrifying images of guilt and the agony of innocent love betrayed. Yet I, who bring all this misery down on you; I, who cast you out and have pressed the seal of distrust and agony onto the heart and brow of my own child; I, who with devilish carelessness tried to steal away your loveliness and replace it with the foul deformity of sin—I beg you, in the overflowing anguish of my heart, to forgive me.  “I do not ask for your pity; you must and do loathe me. But forgive me, Mathilda, and don’t let your thoughts follow me into exile with unrelenting anger. I must never see you again, never hear your voice, but the soft murmurs of your forgiveness will reach me and cool the burning of my disordered brain and heart; I’m sure I would feel it even in my grave. And I dare back this request by telling you how miserably I was trapped in this fiery torment and how I fought to free myself. Truly, if your soul were less pure and bright I wouldn’t try to defend myself to you; I would fear that if I made you feel less disgust for me you might hate vice less. But in speaking to you, I feel as though I’m appealing to an angelic judge. I cannot leave without your forgiveness; I must try to earn it or I must despair. I implore you, then, to listen to my words, and if guilt can in any measure be lessened by sharp agony and remorse that tears at the mind like madness, perhaps you may believe, though I dare not, that I have some claim to your compassion.  “I ask you to remember our first happy life on the shores of Loch Lomond. I had returned from sixteen weary years of wandering, during which, though I faced many dangers and misfortunes, my heart had remained completely empty."}

content.text: {"request_id":"5eddd1d71cfa566df9ce57f3","rewritten_text":"“Nothing but a tick.” “Where’d you get him?” “Out in the woods.” “What’ll you take for him?” “I don’t know. I don’t want to sell him.” “All right. It’s a mighty small tick, anyway.” “Oh, anybody can run down a tick that isn’t theirs. I’m satisfied with it. It’s a good enough tick for me.” “Shoot, there’s plenty of ticks. I could have a thousand if I wanted.” “Well, why don’t you? Because you know you can’t. This is a pretty early tick, I guess. It’s the first one I’ve seen this year.” “Say, Huck—I’ll give you my tooth for him.” “Let’s see it.” Tom took out a bit of paper and carefully unrolled it. Huckleberry stared at it wistfully. The temptation hit hard. At last he said, “Is it real?” Tom lifted his lip and showed the gap. “Well, all right,” said Huckleberry. “It’s a trade.” Tom shut the tick in the percussion-cap box that had recently held the pinchbug, and the boys left, each feeling richer than before. When Tom reached the little isolated frame schoolhouse, he walked in briskly like someone who had come as fast as he could. He hung his hat on a peg and dropped into his seat with businesslike quickness. The master, perched high in his big splint-bottom armchair, was dozing, lulled by the sleepy buzz of study. The interruption woke him. “Thomas Sawyer!” Tom knew that when his full name was called, it meant trouble. “Sir!” “Come up here. Now, sir, why are you late again, as usual?” Tom was about to hide behind a lie when he saw two long tails of yellow hair hanging down a back he recognized by the spark of love; and by that figure was the only empty seat on the girls’ side. He instantly said, “I stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn!” The master’s pulse froze, and he stared helplessly. The buzz of study stopped. The pupils wondered if this reckless boy had lost his mind. The master said, “You—you did what?” “Stopped to talk with Huckleberry Finn.” There was no mistaking it. “Thomas Sawyer, this is the most astounding confession I’ve ever heard. No simple ferule will do for this offense. Take off your jacket.” The master’s arm worked until it was tired and the supply of switches was notably smaller. Then came the order: “Now, sir, go sit with the girls! And let this be a warning to you.” The giggle that rippled around the room seemed to embarrass the boy, but in truth the effect came more from his worshipful awe of his unknown idol and the fearful pleasure in his great good luck."}

{"request_id":"25d5d64ebea596668d4f4cee","rewritten_text":"My father stayed beside me to comfort me and to banish the sharp memories with bright hopes: I almost felt it sweet to weep because he could dry my tears.

Again he drew my thoughts away from sorrow by comparing it with his despair when he lost my mother. Even then I shuddered at the picture he painted of his own passions: he had a poet’s imagination, and when he described the storm that tore his feelings he gave his words such vivid life that I believed them even while trembling. I wondered how he had ever returned to daily duties after those wild thoughts seemed to give him kinship with the supernatural; as he spoke, his ideas were so immense that it seemed the human heart was too narrow to hold them. His emotions sounded more suited to a spirit whose home is the earthquake and volcano than to someone bound to a mortal body and human features. Yet these visions belonged to the past; he had changed since then. Now he was all affection, all gentleness; when I lifted my eyes to him in wonder as he spoke, the smile on his lips showed me his heart was filled with the kindest feelings.

Two months after my aunt’s death we moved to London, where my father led me to study more deeply than ever before. My progress was his joy; he stayed with me through every lesson, helping or working alongside me. We mixed often with society, and not a day passed without my father trying to adorn it with some new pleasure. The tender devotion he felt for me, and the love and respect with which I answered it, cast a charm over every hour. The hours seemed slow only because each minute was put to use; we lived more in a single week than many do in several months, and the variety and novelty of our delights gave flavor to them all.

We constantly went on outings together. Whether we visited beautiful scenes, admired fine paintings, or sometimes set out with no plan but to let amusement arise as it might, I was always happy when near my father. I felt regret whenever a third person joined us, yet if I turned to my father with a troubled expression, his eyes fixed on me and filled with tenderness at once restored joy to my heart. Oh, hours of intense delight! Brief as they were, they stretch as long as a lifetime when I look back through the mist of grief that soon rose afterward, as if to hide them from my sight."}

{"request_id":"9e844e9ef884c8df9b100041","rewritten_text":"“Oh, your father may release you, naturally, if only your mother can bear it. Daughters never weigh so heavily with their fathers. And should you remain another entire month, I could convey one of you as far as London, for I am to be there early in June for a week; and as Dawson makes no objection to the barouche-box, there would be excellent room for one of you—and indeed, should the weather prove cool, I should not hesitate to take you both, since neither of you takes up much space.”

“You are all generosity, madam; yet I think we must adhere to our original scheme.”

Lady Catherine appeared satisfied. “Mrs. Collins, you must dispatch a servant with them. You know I always speak plainly, and I cannot endure the notion of two young women travelling post alone. It is exceedingly improper. You must manage to send someone. Nothing displeases me more than that kind of thing. Young women ought invariably to be fitly protected and attended, according to their rank. When my niece Georgiana went to Ramsgate last summer, I insisted on two men-servants attending her. Miss Darcy, the daughter of Mr. Darcy of Pemberley and Lady Anne, could not have appeared suitably otherwise. I am remarkably scrupulous about such matters. Send John along with the young ladies, Mrs. Collins. I am thankful it entered my head to mention it; for it would truly reflect poorly on you to let them go unescorted.”

“My uncle intends to send a servant for us.”

“Oh! Your uncle! He keeps a man-servant, then? I am delighted someone is attentive to those matters. Where will you change horses? Oh, at Bromley, certainly. If you give my name at the Bell, you will receive proper attention.”

Lady Catherine had numerous further inquiries concerning their trip; and as she did not respond to them all herself, attentiveness was necessary—a circumstance Elizabeth considered fortunate; for with her mind so preoccupied she might otherwise have forgotten her surroundings. Reflection had to be saved for solitary hours: whenever she was alone, she indulged it as the greatest solace; and not a day passed without a solitary walk, in which she gave herself over to the wistful pleasure of painful memories.

Mr. Darcy’s letter she was on the verge of learning by heart. She scrutinized every line; and her sentiments toward its author were at times sharply opposed. When she recalled the tone of his address, she still burned with resentment; but when she reflected how unfairly she had condemned and reproached him, her anger turned inward; and his wounded feelings became objects of pity."}

content.text: {"request_id":"fc690caafcca16f7655c7a36","rewritten_text":"No one can imagine how awe-inspiring a similar sight would be if it happened in the full darkness of night. Hell itself might serve as a fitting picture. Even in daylight my hair stood on end as I looked down into the yawning pits, letting my mind roam through the strange vaulted halls, the glowing gulfs, and the red, ghastly chasms of that hideous and bottomless fire. I had escaped only by a hair’s breadth. If the balloon had stayed in the cloud a little longer—if getting drenched had not pushed me to drop the ballast—the result would have been certain ruin. Dangers like these, though rarely thought about, may be the most serious faced in ballooning. By now, however, I had risen high enough that this threat no longer worried me.\n\n“I was rising fast, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of nine and a half miles. It was growing very hard to breathe. My head throbbed violently; and, after feeling dampness on my cheeks for some time, I finally realized it was blood oozing quickly from my eardrums. My eyes also troubled me. When I passed my hand over them they seemed to bulge noticeably from their sockets, and everything in the car, even the balloon itself, looked warped to my sight. These symptoms were worse than I had expected, and they alarmed me. At that moment, foolishly and without thinking, I tossed overboard three five-pound bags of ballast. The increased rate of ascent carried me far too quickly into air that was extremely thin, and the result almost ended both the expedition and my life. I was suddenly gripped by a spasm that lasted more than five minutes, and even after it eased slightly, I could draw breath only at long intervals, gasping while bleeding heavily from nose and ears, and even a little from my eyes. The pigeons were in terrible distress and fought to escape, while the cat meowed miserably and staggered back and forth in the car, tongue hanging out, as if she had been poisoned. I realized too late how reckless it was to dump the ballast, and I was overwhelmed with panic. I expected nothing less than death, and death within minutes.”"}

{"request_id":"52a76ae427cf2d7bc5af3f1d","rewritten_text":"He couldn’t help himself. It infuriated him to think Becky Thatcher never even suspected he was still among the living. Yet she actually noticed, and knew she was winning her skirmish, delighted to watch him suffer as she had. 

Amy’s cheerful chatter became unbearable. Tom hinted at duties pressing on him, tasks needing attention, and the minutes slipping away. Useless—the girl kept chirping. Tom fumed, “Oh, plague the girl, will I ever shake her?” At last he decreed he must tend to those tasks—and she said guilelessly she would be “around” when school let out. He hurried off, hating her for it. 

“Any other boy!” Tom thought, teeth grinding. “Any other lad in the whole village except that Saint Louis loafer who thinks he dresses so fine and is aristocracy! All right, I drubbed you the first day you ever saw this place, mister, and I’ll drub you again! Just wait till I catch you! I’ll simply take and—” 

He acted out the thrashing of an invisible opponent—pummeling empty air, kicking, gouging. “Oh, you do, do you? You holler `nough, do you? There, let that teach you!” and the imaginary whipping ended to his liking. 

Tom bolted home at noon. He could not stand any more of Amy’s grateful bliss, and his jealousy could endure no more of the other torment. Becky resumed studying pictures with Alfred, but as the minutes crawled and no suffering Tom appeared, her triumph dimmed and she lost interest; solemnity and distraction came, then gloom. Twice or thrice she pricked up her ear at footsteps, but each time was vain hope; Tom never came. At last she was altogether wretched and wished she hadn’t pushed it so far. When poor Alfred, puzzled because he felt her slipping and couldn’t tell why, kept crying, “Oh, here’s a jolly one! see this!” she lost patience and said, “Oh, don’t bother me! I don’t care for them!” burst into tears, rose, and walked away. 

Alfred moved up beside her to offer comfort, but she snapped: 

“Go away and leave me alone, can’t you! I hate you!” 

So he stopped, wondering what offense he’d given—for she had promised to look at pictures all through the noon hour—and she walked on, weeping. Then Alfred wandered into the empty schoolhouse. Mortified and angry, he quickly hit upon the truth—the girl had only used him as a handy tool to vent her malice against Tom Sawyer."}

{"request_id":"c40ab4cece89d2611ee55551","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I misunderstood you. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ and of course I figured ‘anybody’ meant—well, anybody; basically, everyone.”

“It does—anyone of noble birth, and especially if he is royal.”

“That seems reasonable,” said the abbot, seeing his chance to calm things down and avoid a disaster, “because it would hardly make sense that such a marvelous gift would be granted to reveal matters concerning people less exalted than those born close to greatness. Our Arthur the king—”

“Would you know of him?” interrupted the enchanter.

“Most gladly, yes, and gratefully.”

Everyone was awestruck and fascinated again right away, the hopeless fools. They watched the spells intently, and looked at me with a “Well, what do you say to that?” expression when the announcement came:

“The king is tired from the hunt and has lain in his palace for two hours, sleeping dreamlessly.”

“God bless him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep refresh his body and soul.”

“And so it might, if he were sleeping,” I said, “but the king is not sleeping; the king rides.”

Here was trouble again—a clash of authorities. No one knew which of us to believe; I still had a bit of reputation left. The magician’s scorn rose, and he said:

“Lo, I have seen many marvelous seers and prophets and magicians in my life, but never one before who could sit idle and see into things without any incantation to aid him.”

“You have lived in the woods and missed much because of it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood knows—but only on truly important occasions.”

When it comes to sarcasm, I can handle my end. That jab made him squirm. The abbot asked about the queen and the court, and got this answer:

“They all sleep, being exhausted, like the king.”

I said:

“That is just another lie. Half of them are busy with their entertainments, the queen and the rest are not sleeping; they ride. Now maybe you can show off a bit more and tell us where the king and queen and everyone riding with them are headed this moment?”

“They sleep now, as I said; but tomorrow they will ride, for they go on a journey toward the sea.”

“And where will they be the day after tomorrow at vespers?”

“Far north of Camelot, with half their journey done.”

“That is another lie, out by a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"2129d22cd236796b8ca14880","rewritten_text":"The cramped streets and alleys finally opened upon a broad square; pens for livestock and other signs of a cattle-market stood scattered about. Sikes slackened his stride here, for the girl could no longer keep up the swift pace they had maintained. He swung toward Oliver and harshly ordered him to take Nancy’s hand.

“D’ye hear?” Sikes growled when Oliver hesitated, glancing around.

They had drawn into a shadowed corner, far from passers-by.

Oliver understood with painful clarity that resistance was useless. He extended his hand, which Nancy gripped tightly in hers.

“Give me t’other,” said Sikes, catching Oliver’s free hand. “Here, Bull’s-Eye!”

The dog lifted his head and gave a growl.

“Look here, lad!” said Sikes, placing his remaining hand at Oliver’s throat. “If he speaks the least soft word, hold him! D’ye hear?”

The dog responded with another growl and, licking his chops, stared at Oliver as though itching to fasten on his windpipe without delay.

“He’s as ready as any Christian, strike me blind if he ain’t!” Sikes muttered, gazing at the beast with grim, savage approval. “Now you know what’s coming to you, my lad, so sing out as fast as you please; the dog’ll soon stop that trick. March, youngster!”

Bull’s-eye wagged his tail, gratified by this rare affectionate remark; then, uttering another warning growl for Oliver’s benefit, trotted ahead.

They were crossing Smithfield, though it might as well have been Grosvenor Square for all Oliver knew. The night lay dark and fog-laden. The shop lights could scarcely pierce the thickening mist, which every moment grew heavier, cloaking streets and houses in murk, making the strange place stranger still to Oliver, and deepening his misery and dread.

They had hurried but a few steps more when a deep church bell tolled the hour. At its first stroke both companions halted and turned toward the sound.

“Eight o’clock, Bill,” Nancy murmured when the bell fell silent.

“What’s the use o’ telling me? I can hear it, can’t I?” Sikes snapped.

“I wonder if they hear it,” said Nancy.

“Course they do,” Sikes replied. “It was Bartlemy time when I was shopped; there warn’t a penny trumpet in the fair I couldn’t catch the squeal of. After they locked me up for the night, the riot outside made the old thundering jail so quiet, I almost felt like banging my brains out against the iron plates of the door.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9f5003e53fc7e922306688c2","rewritten_text":"“You must care, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his good name. You can’t want people to talk about you as if you were vile and ruined. Of course, you have status and wealth and all that. But status and wealth are not everything. Believe me, I don’t credit these rumours at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin writes itself on a man’s face. It cannot be hidden. People speak of secret vices, but there are none. If a miserable man has one, it shows in the lines of his mouth, the droop of his eyelids, even in the shape of his hands. Someone—I won’t give his name, though you know him—came to me last year for a portrait. I had never seen him before and knew nothing about him then, though I have learned plenty since. He offered an enormous price. I refused. There was something in the shape of his fingers that repelled me. I now know I was right to suspect him. His life is dreadful. But you, Dorian, with your clear, bright, innocent face and your astonishing, untouched youth—I cannot believe any accusation against you. Yet I hardly see you now. You never come to the studio, and when I am away from you and hear all the vile things people whisper, I don’t know how to respond. Why is it that a man like the Duke of Berwick leaves a club room when you enter? Why do so many London gentlemen refuse to go to your house or invite you to theirs? You were once a friend of Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name arose over the miniatures you lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley curled his lip and said that you might have the most refined tastes, but you were someone no pure-minded girl should ever meet, and no chaste woman should share a room with. I reminded him I was your friend and asked what he meant. He told me. He said it plainly before everyone. It was awful! Why is your friendship so deadly to young men? There was that wretched boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were his closest friend. There was Sir Henry Ashton, forced to leave England with a stained name.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"5e23bbb7f20a6d4ae6b02955","rewritten_text":"Soon his voice rang out in a kind of halloo. “How much fudder is got for go?” “How high up are you?” asked Legrand. “Ever so far,” the negro replied. “Can see the sky through the top of the tree.” “Forget the sky—listen to me. Look down the trunk and count the limbs below you on this side. How many have you passed?” “One, two, three, four, five—I passed five big limbs, massa, on dis side.” “Then go one limb higher.” In a few minutes the voice told us the seventh limb was reached. “Now, Jup,” cried Legrand, clearly very excited, “work your way out along that limb as far as you can. If you see anything odd, tell me.” At this point any lingering doubt about my poor friend’s madness vanished. I could only conclude he was truly deranged, and I grew very anxious to get him home. While I wondered what to do next, Jupiter spoke again. “Most scared to go much further on this limb—it dead limb pretty much all the way.” “Did you say it was a dead limb, Jupiter?” asked Legrand in a shaky voice. “Yes, massa, dead as a door-nail—done for sure—done left this life.” “What in heaven’s name shall I do?” asked Legrand, sounding desperate. “Do?” said I, glad for a chance to speak. “Why, come home and go to bed. Come on—be sensible. It’s getting late, and remember your promise.” “Jupiter,” he shouted, ignoring me, “do you hear me?” “Yes, Massa Will, hear you clear enough.” “Test the wood well with your knife and see if it’s very rotten.” “It rotten, massa, sure enough,” the negro answered after a moment, “but not so very rotten. Could go a little way out on the limb by myself, that’s true.” “By yourself! What do you mean?” “Mean the bug. It mighty heavy bug. Suppose I drop him first, then the limb won’t break with just one nigger.” “You infernal scoundrel!” cried Legrand, suddenly relieved. “How dare you talk such nonsense? If you drop that beetle I’ll break your neck. Look here, Jupiter, you hear me?” “Yes, massa, no need to holler so at poor nigger.” “Good—now listen. If you go out on that limb as far as you think safe, and don’t let go of the beetle, I’ll give you a silver dollar as soon as you come down.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"20764c4f40a0b931466efa45","rewritten_text":"“Hang my hat, I want Virginia!” cried the little Duke with a laugh, and they spurred on to the railway station. Mr. Otis questioned the station-master whether anyone matching Virginia’s description had been seen on the platform, but no word of her came. The station-master telegraphed up and down the line and promised strict watchfulness, and after Mr. Otis purchased a hat for the little Duke from a linen-draper who was closing his shutters, he rode on to Bexley, a village four miles off said to be a favorite gypsy resort because of the broad common nearby. There they woke the local policeman, yet he could give them no news, and after traversing the common they turned their horses homeward, reaching the Chase around eleven, exhausted and nearly broken-hearted. Washington and the twins met them at the gate-house with lanterns, for the avenue lay in deep darkness. Not the faintest sign of Virginia had been found. The gypsies had been intercepted on Brockley meadows, but she was not among them, and they explained their abrupt departure by saying they had misjudged the date of Chorton Fair and had hurried off lest they arrive late. In fact, they were quite troubled at Virginia’s disappearance, feeling grateful to Mr. Otis for letting them camp in his park, and four of them had remained to aid the search. The carp-pond had been dragged, and the entire Chase combed, yet nothing came of it. Clearly for that night Virginia was lost to them, and in profound gloom Mr. Otis and the boys walked up to the house, the groom trailing behind with both horses and the pony. In the hall they encountered a cluster of trembling servants, and poor Mrs. Otis lay on a library sofa, nearly distracted with fear and anxiety, the old housekeeper bathing her brow with eau-de-cologne. Mr. Otis immediately insisted she take some food and ordered supper for everyone. It proved a dismal meal, scarcely a word spoken, and even the twins, fond as they were of their sister, sat hushed and subdued. When they had finished, Mr. Otis, despite the little Duke’s pleadings, sent them all to bed, declaring nothing more could be done that night and that he would telegraph Scotland Yard in the morning for detectives to be dispatched at once."}

{"request_id":"3f978168c3dc5677a1d409fd","rewritten_text":"If not for me, he would never have escaped at all. Morgan le Fay despised him with her entire being and would never have relented toward him. Still, his offense came from thoughtlessness more than from deliberate wickedness. He had remarked that she had red hair. Indeed she did; yet that was no way to describe it. When people of a certain station have red hair it is called auburn.

Think of it: among these forty-seven prisoners were five whose names, crimes, and dates of imprisonment were no longer known! One woman and four men—each stooped, wrinkled, and mind-dulled relics. They had long since forgotten those particulars themselves; in any case they held only vague notions about them, never the same twice. The line of priests whose duty it was to pray daily with the captives, to remind them that God had shut them in for some inscrutable reason, and to teach them that patience, humility, and submission to oppression were the virtues He liked to see in those of lesser rank, possessed traditions about these poor human ruins but nothing beyond that. Those traditions reached only so far as recording the length of confinement, not the offenses. And even with tradition’s help, the sole fact provable was that none of the five had glimpsed daylight for thirty-five years; how much longer their deprivation stretched no one could conjecture. The king and queen knew nothing of these wretches except that they were heirlooms, assets passed down with the throne from the previous dynasty. Nothing of their story came with their persons, so the inheriting owners deemed them worthless and felt no curiosity about them. I asked the queen:

“Then why on earth didn’t you set them at liberty?”

The question was a stumper. She had no idea why it never occurred to her, the thought had simply never arisen. Thus she was forecasting the actual future of the prisoners of the Castle d’If without realizing it. It stood plain to me now that, owing to her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were merely property to her—no more, no less. And when we inherit property, we do not think to throw it away, even when we see no value in it.

When I led my procession of human bats out into the upper world and the blaze of the afternoon sun—after blindfolding them, mercy for eyes so long spared light—they made a spectacle. Skeletons, scarecrows, hobgoblins, pitiful terrors every one; the most legitimate offspring imaginable of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"e781f0b30e58faf0f0de01f8","rewritten_text":"When we got back to the raft and he counted up, he saw he had gathered eighty-seven dollars and seventy-five cents. He had also grabbed a three-gallon jug of whiskey he’d found under a wagon when he was starting home through the woods. The king said that, all things considered, it beat any day he’d ever had in the missionary line. He claimed it was no use arguing—heathens weren’t worth a thing next to pirates when it came to working a camp meeting.

The duke had thought he was doing pretty well until the king showed his haul, and then he didn’t feel so proud. He had set up and printed two small jobs for farmers in that printing office—horse bills—and got four dollars for them. He had also taken in ten dollars’ worth of advertisements for the paper, which he offered to run for four dollars if they paid in advance—and they did. The paper cost two dollars a year, but he took three subscriptions at half a dollar each on the condition they pay in advance. They wanted to pay in cordwood and onions as usual, but he said he had just bought the business, cut prices as much as he could, and was going to run it for cash. He set up a little poem of his own—three verses, kind of sweet and sad—titled “Yes, crush, cold world, this breaking heart,” and left it ready to print without charging anything. He took in nine dollars and a half and said he’d done a pretty fair day’s work for it.

Then he showed us another little job he’d printed and hadn’t charged for because it was for us. It had a picture of a runaway black man carrying a bundle on a stick over his shoulder, with “$200 reward” under it. The writing was all about Jim, describing him exactly. It said he’d run away from St. Jacques’ plantation, forty miles below New Orleans, last winter, and probably headed north; anyone who caught him and sent him back would get the reward and expenses.

“Now,” said the duke, “after tonight we can travel in daylight if we want. Whenever we see anyone coming, we can tie Jim hand and foot with a rope, lay him in the wigwam, and show this handbill. We’ll say we captured him up the river, and since we’re too poor to ride a steamboat, we got this little raft on credit from friends and are going down to collect the reward.”"}

{"request_id":"e48dbbcfd9122894dbf3b36f","rewritten_text":"The exquisitely bred gentlemen wore dainty pendants that chimed as they languished along; these gilded shackles tinkled like delicate bells; and with that chiming, along with the rustle of silk, brocade, and fine linen, a light commotion stirred the air that wafted Saint Antoine and his ravenous hunger to a distance.

Attire served as the unfailing charm that held everything in its appointed slot. Everyone was outfitted for a perpetual Fancy Ball. From the Tuileries Palace through Monseigneur and the entire Court, through the Chambers, the Tribunals, and all society (save for the scarecrows), the Fancy Ball extended even to the Common Executioner: who, maintaining the spell, had to perform “frizzled, powdered, in a gold-laced coat, pumps, and white silk stockings.” At the gallows and the wheel—the axe being seldom used—Monsieur Paris, so styled by his episcopal peers across the provinces, Monsieur Orleans, and the rest, officiated in this delicate attire. And who at Monseigneur’s levee in that seventeen hundred and eightieth year could harbor any doubt that a system rooted in a frizzled hangman, powdered, gold-trimmed, shod in pumps and white silk stockings, would endure until the stars expired!

Monseigneur, having relieved his four servants of their burdens and consumed his chocolate, ordered the portals of the Holiest of Holies flung wide, and stepped out. Then, such servility, such cringing and flattery, such abject submission! As for bending in body and soul, nothing remained for Heaven—which might have been one among other reasons why Monseigneur’s supplicants never troubled it.

Distributing a word of promise here and a smile there, a whisper for one delighted lackey and a wave of the hand for another, Monseigneur graciously moved through his chambers to the far-off precinct termed the Circumference of Truth. There he turned about, retraced his course, and eventually let the chocolate sprites seal him back inside his sanctuary, where he vanished from view.

With the spectacle concluded, the faint flutter became quite a brisk squall, and the dainty little bells jingled down the stairs. Soon only one figure remained of the throng, and he, hat tucked beneath his arm and snuffbox in hand, slowly paced past the mirrors toward the exit.

“I consign you,” said this figure, halting at the final door on his way and facing the direction of the sanctuary, “to the Devil!”

With that declaration, he flicked the snuff from his fingers as though brushing dust from his feet, and calmly descended the stairs."}

{"request_id":"28ab978de5d751faa7f90caf","rewritten_text":"Yet for all her efforts, the boy grew gloomier, paler, and more downcast. She tried hot baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges. The boy stayed as mournful as a hearse. She added a thin oatmeal diet and blister plasters to help the water cures. She measured his capacity like a jug’s and filled him daily with bogus remedies.

Tom had grown numb to her punishments. This stage terrified the old lady. She had to break this indifference at any cost. When she first heard of Pain-killer, she ordered a supply. She tasted it and felt grateful; it was fire in liquid form. She abandoned water treatments and everything else, and put all her faith in Pain-killer. She gave Tom a teaspoonful and waited anxiously. Her worries vanished and her soul relaxed, because the indifference was gone. The boy could not have shown more wild interest if she had lit a fire under him.

Tom realized it was time to stir things up. Life in his supposedly delicate state might seem dramatic, but it was growing drearily busy and chaotic. He considered many plans and settled on pretending to love Pain-killer. He asked for it so often that he became a pest, and his aunt finally told him to help himself and stop pestering her. If it had been Sid, she would have been joyful without doubt; but because it was Tom, she watched the bottle in secret. She noticed the medicine really was disappearing, but never guessed he was doctoring a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One day Tom was pouring a dose into the crack when his aunt’s yellow cat strolled up, purring, eyeing the spoon greedily, and begging for a taste. Tom said:

“Don’t ask if you don’t want it, Peter.”

But Peter insisted he did want it.

“You better be sure.”

Peter was sure.

“Now you’ve asked for it, and I’ll give it to you, because I’m not mean; but if you don’t like it, don’t blame anyone but yourself.”

Peter agreed. Tom pried his mouth open and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter leaped two yards into the air, let out a war whoop, and tore around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and causing general destruction."}

{"request_id":"468538d6a90f6f561446a667","rewritten_text":"The party sat divided on two benches that touched each other. Anne was on the front one, and Mr. Elliot, helped by his friend Colonel Wallis, managed to sit beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by her cousins and enjoying Colonel Wallis’s gallant attention, was perfectly content.

Anne’s mind was well-tuned to the evening’s entertainment; it occupied her just enough. She had feeling for the tender moments, liveliness for the cheerful, focus for the technical parts, and patience for the dull ones, and she had never enjoyed a concert more—at least during the first act. Near its end, during the pause after an Italian song, she explained the words to Mr. Elliot. They shared a concert program between them.

“This,” she said, “is almost the sense—the meaning of the words. I suppose the sense of an Italian love song is not to be discussed, but this is as close as I can manage. I do not claim to know the language. I am a very poor Italian scholar.”

“Yes, yes, I see that. You clearly know nothing about it. You can only turn these jumbled, shortened Italian lines into clear, graceful English at sight. Please say no more of your ignorance. Here is proof to the contrary.”

“I will not argue with such kind politeness, but I would be sorry to face a true expert.”

“I have not visited in Camden Place so long,” he said, “without learning something of Miss Anne Elliot; and I consider her too modest for the world to recognize half her talents, and too accomplished for such modesty to seem natural in any other woman.”

“For shame! This is too much flattery. I forget what comes next,” she said, turning back to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot whispered, “I have known your character longer than you think.”

“Indeed? How? You only could have known it since I came to Bath, except for what you might have heard from my family.”

“I knew of you long before you came to Bath. I heard you described by those who knew you well. I have been acquainted with you, in reputation, for years. Your person, your nature, your talents, your manner—they were all familiar to me.”

Mr. Elliot gained the interest he wanted. No one could resist the allure of such mystery."}

The jewels are clearly hers, and, honestly, I suspect that if I were heartless enough to take them back, the wicked old fellow would rise from his grave within a fortnight and make my life a misery. It’s just worry and sweat, and wishing you were dead all the time. These clothes suit me, and this barrel suits me, and I’m never letting them go again. Tom, I wouldn’t have got into all this trouble if it wasn’t for that money; now you take my share along with yours, and give me a dime now and then—not too often, because I don’t care for anything unless it’s kind of hard to get—and you go beg off for me with the widow.” “Oh, Huck, you know I can’t do that. It isn’t fair; besides, if you try this just a little longer you’ll come to like it.” “Like it! Sure—as if I’d like sitting on a hot stove long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cursed stuffy houses. I like the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick to them. Confound it! Just when we had guns, and a cave, and everything ready for robbing, this foolishness had to mess it all up!” Tom saw his chance. “Look here, Huck, being rich isn’t going to stop me from turning robber.” “No! Oh, good gracious! Are you serious, Tom?” “Just as serious as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang if you aren’t respectable, you know.” Huck’s joy died out. “You can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"c7bdac9ea0d7840d115ea7d9","rewritten_text":"I now come to my own story. The early part of my life holds little to tell, and I will be brief; but I must pause over my childhood so it is clear how, when a single hope failed, life became empty, and how, when the only affection I was allowed was destroyed, my existence ended with it.

I have said my aunt was very different from my father. Without a trace of malice she possessed the coldest heart I have ever known: it could not feel any affection. She took me in because she felt it was her duty, yet she had spent too many years alone, undisturbed by children, to let me disrupt her peace. She had never married, and for the last five years had lived entirely alone on an estate she inherited through her mother on the shores of Loch Lomond in Scotland. My father wrote, asking her to live with me at his family mansion in the lovely country near Richmond in Yorkshire. She refused this plan, but once she settled the matters left to her care after her brother departed, she left England and took me to her estate in Scotland.

A servant who had been my mother’s took charge of me as a baby and stayed with us to care for me until I was eight. I lived in a remote part of the house and only saw my aunt at set times. Twice a day she appeared: around noon she came to my nursery, and after dinner I was taken to her. She never embraced me, and the whole time I sat in her room she seemed afraid I would annoy her with some childish whim. My good nurse drilled me carefully before we dared enter the parlor—and the awe my aunt’s cold looks and stiff words inspired kept me from disobeying her lessons or breaking the exemplary stillness required during these brief visits.

Under my nurse’s watch I roamed freely through our park and the nearby fields. Born from the deepest love, I showed from my earliest years the highest sensibility. I cannot tell how intensely I loved everything around me, even inanimate objects."}

{"request_id":"cd8e3dfc9455ae6bc8da20bc","rewritten_text":"I examined the skull drawing closely. The outer lines, the ones nearest the edge of the vellum, were much clearer than the rest. It was obvious the heat had affected the parchment unevenly. I quickly lit a fire and held every part of the parchment over the flames. At first, only the faint lines of the skull grew darker, but after I kept at it, a figure appeared in the corner opposite the skull. At first I thought it was a goat, but on closer inspection I saw it was meant to be a kid.

“Ha! ha!” I said. “I shouldn’t laugh—a million and a half is no laughing matter—but you can’t add a third link to your chain. You won’t find any real connection between pirates and a goat. Pirates have nothing to do with goats; they’re for farmers.”

“But I just said the figure was not a goat.”

“Well, a kid then—almost the same thing.”

“Almost, but not quite,” said Legrand. “You may have heard of Captain Kidd. I saw the animal figure as a pun or a symbolic signature. I call it a signature because its position suggested that idea. The skull in the opposite corner had the appearance of a stamp or seal. Still, I was annoyed by the lack of everything else—the body of my imagined instrument—the text for my context.”

“I suppose you expected to find a letter between the seal and the signature.”

“Something like that. The truth is, I had a strong feeling that some great fortune was coming. I can hardly explain why. Maybe it was more desire than belief. Still, do you know that Jupiter’s foolish claim that the bug was solid gold had a surprising effect on my imagination? And then there were all the strange accidents and coincidences. Consider how accidental it was that everything happened on the only day cool enough for a fire, and that without the fire, or without the dog showing up exactly when he did, I never would have noticed the skull, and thus never found the treasure.”"}

{"request_id":"b182c691c4b219683fcc264a","rewritten_text":"Directly before him, under the pallid glow of the moon, stood an aged figure of dreadful countenance. The eyes flamed like smoldering embers; tangled coils of long grey hair draped over the shoulders; the attire, fashioned in an old style, hung filthy and in tatters, and from both wrists and ankles dangled ponderous fetters and corroded shackles.

“My dear sir,” Mr. Otis remarked, “I must really urge you to oil those chains, and I have brought, expressly for that purpose, a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator. One application is reputed completely effective, and the wrapper carries testimonials attesting to this from several of our most distinguished native clergymen. I shall leave it by the bedroom candles for you, and will gladly furnish more if you should need it.” With that, the United States Minister set the bottle on a marble table and, after shutting his door, went back to bed.

For an instant the Canterville ghost remained stock-still in sheer outrage; then, hurling the bottle furiously upon the gleaming floor, he raced down the passageway, groaning hollowly and shedding a ghastly green glow. Yet as he came to the head of the broad oak staircase, a door swung open, two little white-clad figures appeared, and a substantial pillow shot past his skull! Clearly there was not a moment to waste, and choosing the Fourth Dimension of Space for his flight, he slipped through the wainscot, leaving the household in sudden calm.

Upon arriving at a tiny secret room in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to grasp the situation. In an illustrious and unbroken stretch of three centuries he had never endured such an insult. He recalled the Dowager Duchess, whom he had terrified into a fit as she stood before her mirror in lace and diamonds; the four housemaids who fell into hysterics when he merely grinned at them from behind the curtains of one of the spare chambers; the parish rector, whose candle he had puffed out as the man returned late from the library, and who had needed Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a complete martyr to nervous complaints; and old Madame de Tremouillac, who, waking early one morning to see a skeleton seated in an armchair by the hearth reading her diary, had been confined to bed six weeks with brain fever and, upon recovery, had reconciled herself to the Church and severed connections with that notorious sceptic Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"c9eb9008c95dae253da747af","rewritten_text":"“Then I may put two questions to you?”

“You may inquire,” returned Monks, with a faint touch of surprise, “but whether I choose to respond is another question altogether.”

“Which brings the total to three,” remarked Mr. Bumble, attempting a little wit.

“Is this what you expected from me?” asked the matron.

“It is,” Monks answered. “And the second?”

“What do you intend to do with it? Could it be used to injure me?”

“Never,” said Monks, “nor to harm me. Now watch! But stir not an inch, or your life isn’t worth a rush.”

With that warning, he abruptly shoved the table aside, tugged an iron ring set in the planks, and flung back a broad trap that yawned at Mr. Bumble’s toes, sending the beadle scrambling several paces in alarm.

“Peer below,” said Monks, lowering the lantern into the void. “Have no fear of me. If I had meant mischief, I’d have let you slip quietly when you were sitting above it.”

Thus reassured, the matron crept to the edge; Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, joined her. The muddy flood, swollen by the downpour, raced beneath, drowning every other sound with the splash and whirl where it struck the slimy, green-stained piles. A mill had once stood there; the tide, foaming and fretting around the decayed stakes and the fragments of machinery still clinging, appeared to leap forward more fiercely now that the vain impediments to its headlong rush were swept aside.

“If a man’s corpse were thrown in there, where would it be by morning?” asked Monks, swinging the lantern in the dark shaft.

“Twelve miles downstream, and hacked to bits as well,” replied Bumble, shuddering at the notion.

Monks drew out the small packet he had hastily hidden in his breast, tied it to a lump of lead that had once belonged to a pulley lying on the floor, and dropped it into the torrent. It plunged cleanly, slicing the water with scarce a splash, and vanished.

As they gazed at one another, the three seemed finally able to draw easier breaths.

“There!” Monks exclaimed, letting the trap fall shut with a heavy clang that restored it to its place. “If the sea ever yields its dead, as the books promise, it will keep the gold, silver, and that rubbish among them. Our pleasant gathering is now concluded.”

“Most gladly,” said Mr. Bumble, eager to be gone.

“You’ll keep that tongue of yours still, won’t you?” Monks warned, fixing him with a menacing stare."}

{"request_id":"c7827da7f5bfbf0be41a52fa","rewritten_text":"At last we decided to live together during my stay in the city. Since my finances were a little better than his, I took on the cost of renting and furnishing, to match the strange dark mood we shared, a decrepit, grotesque house. It had long been abandoned because of superstitions we chose to ignore, and it leaned toward collapse in a lonely part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had anyone known our routine there, they would have thought us mad—though perhaps harmlessly so. We were completely shut away. No one visited us. Even my old acquaintances had no idea where I had gone, and Dupin had not had contact with anyone in Paris for many years. We lived entirely within our own world.

My friend had the odd fancy—what else could I call it?—of loving the night for its own sake, and I gave myself over to this eccentricity as I did to all his others. The dark goddess did not always stay with us, but we could recreate her. At the first light of day we closed all the dusty shutters of our ancient building and lit two heavily scented tapers that cast only the faintest, ghastliest glow. By that dim light we surrendered our minds to dreams—reading, writing, or talking—until the clock announced the real night. Then we went out into the streets, arm in arm, pursuing the conversations of the day or wandering far until late, searching through the wild lights and shadows of the crowded city for the endless mental stimulation that careful observation can bring.

During these outings I could not avoid noticing, and admiring, Dupin’s remarkable talent for analysis, though his vivid imagination had already led me to expect something of the sort. He seemed to take a sharp pleasure in exercising it, if not exactly in displaying it, and spoke openly of how much he enjoyed it. He told me, with a quiet chuckle, that most men, compared to him, carried windows in their chests, and he would back up that claim with direct and startling proof of how well he knew my own thoughts. At such moments he was cool and distant; his gaze seemed empty, and his voice, usually a rich tenor, rose into a thin treble that might have sounded peevish if not for the slow precision of his words."}

Mr. Otis sent Washington and the two men to comb the district, then ran home and sent telegrams to every police inspector in the county, warning them to watch for a young girl who might have been kidnapped by tramps or gypsies. He ordered his horse, insisted his wife and the three boys sit down to dinner, and rode off down the Ascot Road with a groom. He had scarcely gone two miles when he heard someone galloping behind him. Looking back, he saw the little Duke riding up on his pony, face flushed and bareheaded. “I’m terribly sorry, Mr. Otis,” the boy gasped, “but I can’t eat any dinner while Virginia is missing. Please don’t be angry; if you had let us be engaged last year, none of this would have happened. You won’t send me back, will you? I can’t go! content.text: {"request_id":"da74a08cec581c1e66f12a09","rewritten_text":"This brief conversation with Mr. Knightley afforded Emma much satisfaction. It ranked among the pleasant memories of the ball, which she revisited while strolling over the lawn the next morning. She was delighted that they had reached such a perfect understanding about the Eltons, their judgments of both husband and wife aligning so closely; and his commendation of Harriet, his willingness to yield in her favour, was especially pleasing. The Eltons’ insolence, which had seemed on the point of spoiling the rest of her evening, had yielded some of its greatest pleasures; and she anticipated another agreeable consequence—the ending of Harriet’s infatuation. From the way Harriet spoke of the matter before they left the ballroom, Emma was very hopeful. It was as if Harriet’s eyes had suddenly opened, revealing that Mr. Elton was not the exalted being she had imagined. The fever had passed, and Emma could scarcely fear its returning through harmful politeness. She relied on the Eltons’ ill temper to supply any further necessary discipline of pointed neglect. Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not too much enamoured, and Mr. Knightley not inclined to quarrel with her—what an exceedingly happy summer must lie ahead! She was not to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her that he could not allow himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, needing to be at home by noon. She did not lament it. Having settled all these reflections, reviewed them, and set them to rights, she was just turning back to the house, spirits revived for the demands of the two little boys and their grandpapa alike, when the broad iron swing-gate opened, and two people entered whom she had never more expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet on his arm—Harriet herself! One instant convinced her that something out of the ordinary had occurred. Harriet appeared pale and terrified, and he was trying to reassure her. The iron gates and the front door were not twenty yards apart; in another moment all three were in the hall, and Harriet, sinking instantly into a chair, swooned. A young lady who faints must be revived; questions need answering, and surprises explained. Such incidents are highly engaging, but their suspense cannot last long. In a few minutes Emma knew the whole. Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had likewise attended the ball, had gone out together, taking the Richmond road, which, though seemingly public enough for safety, had led them into alarm. About half a mile beyond Highbury, the road made a sharp turn and, thickly shaded by elms on both sides, grew very secluded for some distance; and when the young ladies had proceeded some way along it, they suddenly observed, a little ahead on a broader strip of turf beside the road, a group of gipsies."}

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, this gentleman came from Beauvais. Like your father, he was respected in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our dealings were business, but confidential. I was working in our French branch then, and had been for twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask, when exactly, sir?”

“I’m speaking of twenty years ago. He married—an English lady—and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many French gentlemen and families, were entirely in Tellson’s hands. In the same way, I am, or have been, trustee in one form or another for dozens of our customers. These are purely business ties, miss; there’s no friendship in them, no special interest, no sentiment. I move from one customer to another in my business life just as I move from one appointment to another in my working day. In short, I have no feelings; I’m a mere machine. To continue—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir, and I am beginning to think”—her oddly furrowed forehead fixed on him—“that when I was left an orphan because my mother lived only two years after my father, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the hesitant little hand held out to him, put it ceremoniously to his lips, then led the young lady back to her chair. Holding the chair-back with his left hand and using his right by turns to rub his chin, tug at his wig, or stress his points, he stood looking down into her face while she sat looking up into his.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will understand how truthful I was just now—saying I have no feelings, that all my dealings with other people are mere business—when you remember that I have never seen you since that day. No, you have been a ward of Tellson’s since then, and I have been occupied with other Tellson business. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning an enormous money mangle.”"}

{"request_id":"21722e3cc87e7aaa847f00ed","rewritten_text":"“Yes, it is—and I could have had it if I’d been big enough. I saw him first. Who caught him?”

“It was an old stranger, and he sold his claim for forty dollars because he has to go up the river and can’t wait. Think of that! I’d wait seven years if I had to.”

“That’s me every time,” I said. “But maybe his claim isn’t worth more than that if he’d sell it so cheap. Maybe something isn’t right.”

“But it is, straight as a string. I saw the handbill myself. It tells every detail—describes him like a picture and names the plantation he’s from below New Orleans. No trouble with that deal, you can bet. Say, give me a chew of tobacco, will you?”

I didn’t have any, so he left. I went to the raft and sat down in the wigwam to think, but I couldn’t figure anything out. I thought till my head hurt, yet I couldn’t see a way out of the mess. After this long trip, and after all we’d done for those scoundrels, everything was ruined. They had the heart to trick Jim like that and make him a slave for life among strangers, for forty dirty dollars.

Once I told myself it would be a thousand times better for Jim to be a slave at home with his family, if he had to be one, and I ought to write Tom Sawyer to tell Miss Watson where he was. But I dropped that notion for two reasons: she’d be furious at his rascality and ungratefulness in running off, and she’d sell him down the river again; and even if she didn’t, everyone naturally despises an ungrateful slave, and they’d make Jim feel it till he felt mean and ashamed. And then think of me! Word would spread that Huck Finn helped a slave to get his freedom, and if I ever saw anyone from that town again I’d be ready to kneel and lick his boots from shame. That’s how it goes: a person does a low-down thing and doesn’t want the consequences. Figures if he can hide it, it isn’t a disgrace. That was exactly my fix. The more I studied on it, the more my conscience ground me, and the more wicked and low and mean I felt."}
