{"request_id":"83d00f0a6df161207c4e9c75","rewritten_text":"“What’s going on?” Oliver demanded.

“Quiet!” the Dodger whispered. “Do you see that old fellow at the bookstall?”

“The old gentleman across the way?” said Oliver. “Yes, I see him.”

“He’ll do,” said the Dodger.

“A perfect setup,” added Master Charley Bates.

Oliver looked from one to the other in utter astonishment, but he had no chance to ask anything; the two boys slipped silently across the street and crept up behind the old gentleman who had caught Oliver’s attention. Oliver followed a few steps, uncertain whether to go forward or back, and stood there, watching in stunned silence.

The old gentleman looked thoroughly respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar, white trousers, and carried a stylish bamboo cane under his arm. He had picked up a book at the stall and stood there reading as intently as if he were in his own study chair. He might well have imagined himself there, for from his deep absorption it was obvious he noticed neither the stall, nor the street, nor the boys—nothing but the book. He read straight on, turning the page when he reached the bottom, starting at the top of the next, proceeding steadily with keen interest.

Imagine Oliver’s horror and panic, standing a few paces away with eyes stretched wide, when he saw the Dodger plunge his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! He saw him pass it to Charley Bates; then, to cap it all, watched them both tear away around the corner at full speed.

In a flash, the entire secret of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew crashed into Oliver’s mind.

For a moment he stood frozen, blood surging through his veins in terror until he felt as if he were being scorched. Then, dazed and frightened, he bolted, running as fast as his legs could carry him without any idea of what he was doing.

It all happened in a single minute. Just as Oliver began to run, the old gentleman, reaching for his pocket and missing his handkerchief, spun around. Seeing Oliver sprinting away at such a pace, he naturally assumed the boy was the thief; shouting “Stop thief!” with all his strength, he sprinted after him, book still in hand."}

{"request_id":"ce2169e53c12e9ff83acbb39","rewritten_text":"“You must learn some of my philosophy. Think of the past only when remembering it brings you pleasure.”

“I cannot believe you have that kind of philosophy. Your memories must be so free from blame that your satisfaction comes not from wisdom but, even better, from ignorance. For me it is different. Painful memories intrude when they should not and cannot be pushed away. I have been selfish all my life in practice, though not in intention. As a child I was taught what was right, but no one taught me to control my temper. I was given good principles, yet allowed to follow them in pride and arrogance. As the only son, and for many years the only child, I was spoiled by parents who, though good and especially my benevolent father, allowed and almost taught me to be selfish and domineering, to care for no one beyond my own family, to think poorly of everyone else, to wish to undervalue their judgment and worth compared to mine. That was who I was from eight to twenty-eight, and I might still be the same if not for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you? You taught me an important lesson, hard at first but most beneficial. You properly humbled me. I approached you without a doubt that you would accept me. You showed me how insufficient all my claims were to win a woman worthy of being won.”

“Had you truly convinced yourself that I would?”

“Yes, I had. What must you think of my vanity? I believed you were hoping for and expecting my proposal.”

“My manners must have misled you, though not on purpose, I assure you. I never meant to deceive you, but my spirits often carried me too far. You must have hated me after that evening!”

“Hate you! I might have been angry at first, but my anger soon turned in the right direction.”

“I hardly dare ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, not at all. I felt only surprise.”

“Your surprise could not have been greater than mine at being noticed by you. My conscience told me I deserved no special politeness, and I admit I did not expect more than what was due.”

“At that time,” Darcy replied, “I only wished to show you, by every courtesy I could offer, that I was not so petty as to resent the past. I hoped to win your forgiveness and lessen your poor opinion of me by proving that I had taken your reproofs to heart.”"}

{"request_id":"a6a5ad601cff80b859caf55f","rewritten_text":"But I wonder how long you would have gone on if left alone. I wonder when you would have spoken if I hadn’t asked you! My resolution to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had great effect. Too much, I’m afraid; for what becomes of the moral if our happiness comes from breaking a promise? I shouldn’t have brought up the subject. This will never do.”

“You don’t need to worry. The moral will be perfectly intact. Lady Catherine’s unjustified attempts to separate us removed all my doubts. I don’t owe my present happiness to your eagerness to show gratitude. I wasn’t in the mood to wait for you to broach anything. My aunt’s information had given me hope, and I was determined to learn everything right away.”

“Lady Catherine has been tremendously useful, which ought to make her happy, since she loves to be useful. But tell me, why did you come down to Netherfield? Was it just to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward? Or did you intend something more serious?”

“My true purpose was to see you and gauge, if possible, whether I could ever hope to make you love me. What I claimed, even to myself, was that I wanted to see if your sister still cared for Bingley, and, if she did, to confess everything to him as I later did.”

“Will you ever have the courage to tell Lady Catherine what’s about to happen to her?”

“I’m more likely to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. But it must be done; give me a sheet of paper and I’ll do it at once.”

“And if I didn’t have a letter of my own to write, I might sit beside you and admire how even your handwriting is, as another young lady once did. But I have an aunt too, who mustn’t be neglected any longer.”

Because she was unwilling to admit how much she had misjudged her relationship with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth still hadn’t answered Mrs. Gardiner’s long letter; but now, with something to share that she knew would be most welcome, she was almost ashamed to find her uncle and aunt had been deprived of three days of happiness, and she wrote immediately as follows:

“I would have thanked you sooner, my dear aunt, as I should have done, for your long, kind, satisfying account; but to tell the truth, I was too out of sorts to write. You assumed more than truly existed. But now imagine as much as you like; let your fancy run loose, indulge your imagination in every possible flight the subject allows, and unless you picture me already married, you cannot be very wrong.”"}

{"request_id":"1701c8ae600ade4ca15bf174","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think,” said the spy in his humblest tone as he turned to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness to ask this other gentleman, much younger than you, how he can under any circumstances justify playing that Ace he mentioned. I admit that I am a spy, and that it is seen as a shameful job—though someone must do it. But this gentleman is no spy, so why should he lower himself to become one?”

“I play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking the answer himself and glancing at his watch, “without hesitation, in just a few minutes.”

“I had hoped, gentlemen both,” said the spy, still trying to pull Mr. Lorry into the talk, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I could show no greater respect for your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“I am completely sure of it.”

The spy’s smooth manner, oddly at odds with his showy rough clothes and probably with his usual behavior, met such a barrier in Carton’s unreadable face—so puzzling even to wiser and more honest men than he—that it faltered and failed him. While he hesitated, Carton said, returning to his earlier air of studying cards:

“And now that I think of it again, I strongly suspect I have another good card here, not yet mentioned. That friend and fellow-Sheep who said he was grazing in the country prisons; who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” said the spy quickly.

“French, eh?” repeated Carton, thinking, seeming not to notice him, though he echoed the word. “Well, he may be.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy; “though it doesn’t matter.”

“‘Though it doesn’t matter,’” repeated Carton in the same mechanical tone—“‘though it doesn’t matter’—No, it doesn’t matter. No. Yet I know the face.”

“I think not. I’m sure not. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“It can’t be,” muttered Sydney Carton, looking back and idly turning his glass (which, fortunately, was a small one) again. “Can’t be. Spoke good French. Yet like a foreigner, I thought?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” cried Carton, striking his open hand on the table as a clear idea broke in his mind. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had him before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now there you are hasty, sir,” said Barsad, with a smile that pushed his aquiline nose even more to one side; “there you really give me an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"6b6ed8a958e30a2e88c566fd","rewritten_text":"“Why, you don’t mean—” my sister began.

“Yes I do, Mum,” said Pumblechook. “But hold on. Go on, Joseph. Good man! Keep going!”

“What would everyone here say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?”

“Generous would be the word,” my sister replied.

“Well then,” Joe said, “it’s more than twenty pounds.”

That miserable hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and said with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Very good! Stay with it, Joseph!”

“So, to finish it,” Joe said, happily handing the bag to my sister, “it’s five-and-twenty pounds.”

“It’s five-and-twenty pounds, Mum,” echoed that foul swindler Pumblechook, standing to shake her hand. “It’s no more than you deserve (as I said when they asked my opinion), and I wish you joy of the money!”

If the villain had stopped there, he would already have been bad enough, but he made it worse by seizing me like he had authority over me.

“Now you see, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, gripping my arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who finish what they start. This boy must be bound this instant. That’s my way. Bound at once.”

“Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” my sister said, clutching the money, “we’re deeply grateful to you.”

“Never mind me, Mum,” answered that evil corn dealer. “A pleasure is a pleasure all over the world. But this boy, you know; we must have him bound. I promised I’d handle it—for truth’s sake.”

The Justices were sitting in the nearby Town Hall, and we went at once so I could be bound apprentice to Joe before them. I say we went, but Pumblechook pushed me there as if I had just picked a pocket or set fire to a stack; the Court seemed sure I’d been caught in the act. As Pumblechook shoved me through the crowd, I heard some people ask, “What’s he done?” and others say, “He’s young, too, but he looks bad, doesn’t he?” One kindly looking person even gave me a tract decorated with a woodcut of a hateful young man decked out in chains like a sausage string, and titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL.

The Hall struck me as odd, with higher pews than a church and people hanging over them to watch. Mighty Justices (one with powdered hair) leaned back in chairs with folded arms, or took snuff, or napped, or wrote, or read newspapers. There were also glossy black portraits on the walls, which my untrained eye thought looked like hard candy mixed with sticking plaster."}

{"request_id":"49cf4d77a1ca368882012087","rewritten_text":"“If I can’t live on that, I won’t ask anyone to help me. Is that good enough?”

There was an enormous roar of applause, and above it the king’s voice rang out:

“Unbind him and set him free! Give him homage, high and low, rich and poor, for he has become the king’s right hand, clothed with power and authority, seated on the highest step of the throne! Now sweep away this creeping night and bring back light and cheer, so the whole world may bless you.”

But I answered:

“It is nothing for a common man to be shamed in front of the world; but it would dishonor the king if those who saw his minister stripped did not also see him restored from that shame. If I may ask for my clothes to be brought back—”

“They’re not fit,” the king interrupted. “Fetch other garments; dress him like a prince!”

My plan was working. I needed everything to remain as it was until the eclipse was total, otherwise they would press me again to chase away the darkness, and of course I couldn’t. Sending for clothes bought some time, but not enough. So I had to come up with another excuse. I said it would be natural if the king regretted, even a little, what he had done in his excitement; therefore I would let the darkness deepen a while, and if, after a reasonable time, the king held to his decision, the darkness would be lifted. Neither the king nor anyone else liked that, but I had to stand my ground.

It grew darker and darker, blacker and blacker, while I fought with those clumsy sixth-century clothes. Finally it was pitch black, and the crowd groaned in horror as the cold, otherworldly night breeze swept through and the stars came out and flickered in the sky. At last the eclipse was total, and I was very glad, though everyone else was miserable, which made perfect sense. I said:

“The king, by his silence, still agrees to the terms.” Then I raised my hands—held them that way a moment—and said with the gravest solemnity, “Let the enchantment dissolve and fade away without harm!”

There was no response, at first, in that deep darkness and that graveyard hush. But when the silver rim of the sun slid out a moment later, the crowd erupted with a massive shout and surged down like a flood to bury me in blessings and gratitude—and Clarence was certainly not last in that tide."}

content.text: {"request_id":"56c5d05227bddd7a3ead26b6","rewritten_text":"No fancy could figure the sublimity that might have been shown had a similar spectacle occurred amid the night’s darkness. Hell itself might have furnished an apt likeness. Even so, my hair bristled while I peered far down into the open gulfs, letting imagination descend, as it were, and pace the novel arched halls, the glowing pits, the crimson hideous fissures of the monstrous and measureless fire. I had indeed escaped by a hair. Had the balloon lingered even a very little longer within the cloud—in other words, had not the simple discomfort of being drenched driven me to throw out the ballast, certain destruction must have followed. Such hazards, though rarely noted, are perhaps the gravest that aeronauts must encounter. By this time, however, I had reached too lofty an elevation to remain troubled on that score.\n\n“I was now shooting upward fast, and by seven o’clock the barometer registered an altitude of not less than nine miles and a half. I began to suffer great difficulty in drawing breath. My head, likewise, ached violently; and, having long felt a dampness on my cheeks, I finally perceived it was blood, oozing rather freely from the drums of my ears. My eyes also tormented me. When I passed a hand across them they seemed to have bulged from their sockets in no trifling degree; every object in the car, and even the balloon itself, appeared distorted to my sight. These indications exceeded what I had anticipated and gave me some alarm. At that moment, very rashly and without reflection, I flung from the car three five-pound parcels of ballast. The increased speed of ascent thereby gained carried me too abruptly, without sufficient gradation, into a highly rarefied belt of the air, and the consequence had nearly proved deadly to my adventure and to myself. I was suddenly seized with a convulsion lasting more than five minutes, and even when it subsided in part, I could snatch breath only at long intervals and with gasping efforts—bleeding copiously the whole time from nose and ears, and even slightly from the eyes. The pigeons seemed distressed beyond measure and struggled to get free; while the cat mewed miserably, and, with tongue lolling from her mouth, reeled to and fro in the car as if poisoned. I now too late perceived the extreme recklessness of casting off the ballast, and my agitation was extreme. I expected nothing short of death—and death within a few minutes.”}"}

{"request_id":"54e39072d33175c44b899ba6","rewritten_text":"He was certainly diverting enough, and all that, yet I felt terribly let down; and when I inquired about the coat of mail, he merely chuckled and declared it was far too chilly to wear such things in England. Ah, here comes Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I wish you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, do remove your glove. No, not the left one, the other.”

“Dear Gladys, I truly doubt whether this is altogether proper,” muttered the Duchess, weakly undoing a rather grubby kid glove.

“Nothing that is interesting ever is,” replied Lady Windermere; “on a fait le monde ainsi. However, I must present you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my tame cheiromantist. Mr. Podgers, the Duchess of Paisley; and if you pronounce her mountain of the moon larger than mine, I shall never trust you again.”

“I am convinced, Gladys, nothing of that sort exists in my palm,” the Duchess said, quite solemnly.

“Your Grace is entirely correct,” observed Mr. Podgers, surveying the plump little hand with its short, square fingers. “The mountain of the moon is undeveloped. The life-line, however, is magnificent. Be so good as to bend the wrist. Thank you. Three separate lines on the rascette! You will reach a very advanced age, Duchess, and enjoy remarkable happiness. Ambition—modest enough, the line of intellect not overdrawn, the line of heart—”

“Do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,” Lady Windermere interrupted.

“Nothing would delight me more,” Mr. Podgers said with a bow, “if the Duchess had ever been indiscreet, but I regret I perceive a great stability of affection allied to a powerful sense of duty.”

“Please continue, Mr. Podgers,” said the Duchess, now distinctly gratified.

“Economy ranks high among your Grace’s qualities,” Mr. Podgers went on, while Lady Windermere fell into peals of laughter.

“Economy is an admirable virtue,” the Duchess said serenely; “when I married Paisley he possessed eleven castles and not one habitable house.”

“And at present he owns twelve houses and not one castle,” Lady Windermere cried.

“Well, my dear,” the Duchess began, “I prefer—”

“Comfort,” supplied Mr. Podgers, “and the latest improvements, and hot water laid on in every bedroom. Your Grace is perfectly justified. Comfort is the sole benefit our civilisation provides.”

“You have described the Duchess to perfection, Mr. Podgers, and now you must tell Lady Flora’s,” and, responding to the smiling hostess’s nod, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and prominent shoulder-blades moved awkwardly from behind the sofa, extending a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

“Ah, a pianist, I perceive,” said Mr. Podgers, “a splendid pianist, though perhaps scarcely a musician.”"}

{"request_id":"6dd0f43eb61df90e7ccf01a5","rewritten_text":"At last we arranged to share quarters during my visit in the city; and since my finances were a bit less straitened than his, I was allowed to shoulder the cost of leasing and fitting up—according to the somewhat eccentric gloom of our shared temper—a time-worn, grotesque mansion, long abandoned thanks to superstitions we never examined, and tottering on the verge of ruin in a secluded, desolate nook of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had the public been aware of the routine of our existence there, we would have been deemed lunatics—though, perhaps, lunatics of a harmless strain. Our isolation was absolute. No guests were admitted. Indeed, the location of our retreat was carefully concealed even from my former acquaintances; and Dupin had for years ceased either to know or be known in Paris. We lived entirely within ourselves.

It was one of my friend’s whims (for what else can it be called?) to love the night for her own sake; and into this bizarrerie, as into all his others, I quietly yielded, surrendering myself to his eccentric humors with perfect abandon. The sable goddess would not always remain with us in person; yet we could mimic her presence. At the first breath of dawn we shut up the dusty shutters of our antique pile, lighting a pair of tapers which, strongly scented, cast only the most ghastly, feeble glimmer. By their aid we devoted our spirits to daydreams—reading, writing, or conversing—until the clock gave notice of the coming of real Darkness. Then we would issue into the streets, arm in arm, carrying on the themes of the day, or roaming abroad till late, seeking in the wild lights and shadows of the teeming city that limitless mental excitement which quiet observation can provide.

During these hours I could not help noticing and admiring—though his lavish ideality had prepared me for it—a singular analytic power in Dupin. He appeared, moreover, to take keen delight in exercising it—if not precisely in displaying it—and freely admitted the enjoyment he derived. With a low, chuckling laugh he would boast to me that most men, in relation to himself, wore windows in their chests, and he would be apt to follow such claims with direct, startling demonstrations of his intimate knowledge of my own thoughts. In those instants his demeanor was chill and abstract; his eyes held a vacant look; while his voice, ordinarily a rich tenor, climbed into a treble that might have seemed petulant were it not for the deliberate and perfectly distinct articulation."}

{"request_id":"99037f9b0d4c4f106a700e5d","rewritten_text":"“Stop the starboard! Ting-a-ling-ling! Halt the larboard! Come on with the starboard! Stop her! Let the outside wheel turn slow! Ting-a-ling-ling! Chow-ow-ow! Run out that head-line! lively now! Come—get that spring-line free—what’re you doing there! Take a turn round that stump with the bight! Stand by the stage—let her drop! Engines finished, sir! Ting-a-ling-ling! SH’T! S’H’T! SH’T!” (testing the gauge-cocks).

Tom kept whitewashing—paid the steamboat no heed. Ben stared a second, then called: “Hi-Yi! You’re up a tree, ain’t you!”

No response. Tom admired his latest stroke with an artist’s eye, gave the brush another tender sweep, and inspected the outcome again. Ben sidled up alongside. Tom’s mouth longed for the apple, but he clung to his task. Ben said:

“Hallo, old fellow, you’re made to labor, hey?”

Tom whirled and answered:

“Why, it’s you, Ben! I wasn’t paying attention.”

“Say—I’m off for a swim, I am. Don’t you wish you could? But naturally you’d prefer work—wouldn’t you? Sure you would!”

Tom studied the boy a moment and asked:

“What do you call work?”

“Why, ain’t that work?”

Tom went back to the fence, replying casually:

“Well, maybe it is, maybe it ain’t. All I know is it suits Tom Sawyer.”

“Oh now, you don’t pretend you like it?”

The brush kept gliding.

“Like it? Well, I don’t see why I shouldn’t. Does a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day?”

That shifted the perspective. Ben stopped chewing his apple. Tom swept the brush delicately back and forth—stepped away to note the effect—touched up a spot or two—criticized the effect once more—Ben watching each motion, growing steadily more engrossed, more fascinated. Soon he begged:

“Say, Tom, let me whitewash a bit.”

Tom pondered, almost consented, then changed his mind:

“No—no—I reckon it wouldn’t hardly answer, Ben. You see, Aunt Polly’s dreadful particular about this fence—right here on the street, you know—but if it was the back fence I’d not mind and she wouldn’t either. Yes, she’s mighty particular about this one; it’s got to be finished real careful; I reckon there ain’t one boy in a thousand, maybe two, that can do it the way it has to be done.”

“No—really? Oh come, now—let me try. Just a little—I’d let you, if you were me, Tom.”

“Ben, I’d like to, honest injun; but Aunt Polly—why, Jim wanted the job, and she said no; Sid wanted it, and she turned Sid down.”"}

{"request_id":"8319d567c34078369355a72f","rewritten_text":"I wish to see you permanently well connected, and for that purpose it will be wise to keep as few peculiar acquaintances as possible; therefore, I tell you that if you remain in this country when Mr. Martin marries, I hope you will not be led, through your closeness with the sisters, into knowing the bride, who will likely be some mere farmer’s daughter, untaught.”

“Certainly. Yes. Not that I imagine Mr. Martin would marry anyone who had not received some education—and been properly brought up. Still, I do not intend to set my opinion against yours—and I am sure I shall not desire his wife’s acquaintance. I shall always feel great regard for the Miss Martins, Elizabeth especially, and should be very sorry to give them up, for they are just as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, coarse woman, undoubtedly I had better avoid visiting her, if possible.”

Emma observed her through the variations of this speech, and detected no threatening sign of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted he had no other hold, and that there would be no serious hindrance, on Harriet’s side, to any friendly plan of her own.

They encountered Mr. Martin the following day, while walking along the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after gazing respectfully at Emma, he looked with unmistakable delight at Harriet. Emma did not regret such a chance for inspection; and moving a few steps ahead while they conversed, she soon allowed her sharp eye to grow sufficiently acquainted with Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was extremely neat, and he presented the air of a sensible young man, yet his person offered no further advantages; and when she compared him with gentlemen, she believed he must surrender all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s preference. Harriet was not indifferent to manners; she had voluntarily noticed her father’s civility with admiration mixed with wonder. Mr. Martin looked as though he had no notion of what manners were.

They remained together only a few minutes, as Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting; and Harriet then came running back with a smiling face, full of fluttering excitement, which Miss Woodhouse hoped soon to calm.

“Only think of our happening to meet him!—How extraordinary! It was quite by chance, he said, that he had not gone round by Randalls. He never thought we walked this road. He imagined we took the way towards Randalls most days.”"}

{"request_id":"e511728b24ec2238eddd6da6","rewritten_text":"Suddenly Mr. Podgers let go of Lord Arthur’s right hand and grabbed his left, bending so low to examine it that the gold rims of his spectacles almost touched the palm. For an instant his face became a pale mask of terror, but he quickly regained his composure, and looking up at Lady Windermere with a forced smile, said, ‘It is the hand of a charming young man.’

‘Of course it is!’ replied Lady Windermere. ‘But will he be a charming husband? That is what I want to know.’

‘All charming young men are,’ said Mr. Podgers.

‘I don’t think a husband should be too fascinating,’ murmured Lady Jedburgh thoughtfully. ‘It is so dangerous.’

‘My dear child, they never are too fascinating,’ cried Lady Windermere. ‘But I want details. Details are the only interesting things. What will happen to Lord Arthur?’

‘Well, within the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—’

‘Oh yes, his honeymoon, of course!’

‘And lose a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I hope?’ said Lady Jedburgh in a pleading voice.

‘Certainly not his sister,’ answered Mr. Podgers, waving his hand as if to calm her. ‘Only a distant relative.’

‘I am dreadfully disappointed,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘I have nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one cares about distant relatives now. They went out of fashion years ago. Still, I suppose she should have a black silk dress on hand; it always works for church, you know. And now let us go to supper. They are sure to have eaten everything, but we might find some hot soup. François used to make excellent soup once, but he is so agitated about politics now that I never feel quite sure about him. I wish General Boulanger would be quiet. Duchess, I’m sure you are tired?’

‘Not at all, dear Gladys,’ answered the Duchess, waddling toward the door. ‘I have enjoyed myself immensely, and the chiropodist—I mean the chiromantist—is most interesting. Flora, where is my tortoise-shell fan? Oh, thank you so much, Sir Thomas. And my lace shawl, Flora? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, very kind of you.’ And the good creature finally got downstairs without dropping her scent bottle more than twice.

All this time Lord Arthur Savile had stood by the fireplace, feeling the same dread, the same sickening sense of coming trouble. He gave his sister a sad smile as she swept past on Lord Plymdale’s arm, looking lovely in her pink brocade and pearls, and he barely heard Lady Windermere call him to follow. He thought of Sybil Merton, and the idea that anything might come between them filled his eyes with tears."}

{"request_id":"1f2c22ea864cd4794a0ce7bf","rewritten_text":"Goodness, she could talk. It wouldn’t have been polite to hint that it was very late and I was worn out and ready to drop. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to see it through; there was no other option. So she kept chattering on and on, in the otherwise profound, ghostly silence of the sleeping castle, until eventually there rose, as if from deep beneath us, a distant sound like a muffled scream—with such agony in it that it made my flesh crawl. The queen stopped, her eyes lighting with pleasure; she tilted her graceful head like a bird listening. The sound bored up through the stillness again.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and it endures long. It has been many hours now.”

“Endures what?”

“The rack. Come—you shall see a merry sight. If he still refuses to yield his secret, you shall watch him torn apart.”

What a silky smooth hellion she was, so composed and serene while the muscles all down my legs were aching in sympathy with that man’s suffering. Led by armored guards bearing blazing torches, we marched along echoing corridors and down dank, dripping stone stairs, smelling of mold and centuries of imprisoned night—a chilly, uncanny journey, and a long one, not made shorter or cheerier by the sorceress’s conversation, which centered on this victim and his crime. He had been accused by an anonymous informant of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony isn’t quite right, your Highness. It would be fairer to confront the accused with the accuser.”

“I had not considered that, it being of little consequence. But even if I wished it, I could not, for the accuser came masked at night and told the forester, then immediately left again, so the forester knows him not.”

“Then this Unknown is the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“Indeed, no man saw the killing, but this Unknown saw the daring miscreant near the spot where the stag lay, and came with loyal zeal to betray him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was also near the dead stag? Isn’t it possible he did the killing himself? His loyal zeal—behind a mask—looks a bit suspicious. But why is your Highness racking the prisoner? What’s the gain?”

“He will not confess otherwise; without confession his soul would be lost. His life is forfeit by law for his crime—and I will make sure he pays it—but it would endanger my own soul to let him die without confession and absolution.”"}

{"request_id":"6c639d03fc8bcd8a063fa2ab","rewritten_text":"Their arrival ignited a spark in the heart of Saint Antoine, spreading quickly as they moved along, flaring in the faces at most doors and windows. Yet no one followed them, and not a word was spoken when they entered the wine shop, though every man’s eyes were on them.

“Good day, gentlemen!” said Monsieur Defarge.

It might have been the cue for everyone to speak. A chorus of “Good day!” answered him.

“It’s bad weather, gentlemen,” Defarge said, shaking his head.

At that, every man looked at his neighbor, then they all lowered their eyes and sat in silence. Except for one man, who stood up and walked out.

“My wife,” Defarge said loudly to Madame Defarge, “I have traveled several leagues with this good mender of roads, called Jacques. I met him—by chance—a day and a half outside Paris. He’s a good soul, this mender of roads named Jacques. Give him something to drink, my wife!”

A second man stood up and left. Madame Defarge set wine in front of the mender of roads called Jacques. He removed his blue cap to the company and drank. He carried coarse dark bread in his blouse, eating in between sips, sitting near Madame Defarge’s counter munching and drinking. A third man rose and left.

Defarge refreshed himself with a draft of wine—but took less than the stranger, being a man to whom wine was no rarity—and stood waiting until the countryman finished his breakfast. He looked at no one there, and no one looked at him now; not even Madame Defarge, who had taken up her knitting and was working.

“Are you done with your meal, friend?” he asked at the proper time.

“Yes, thank you.”

“Come, then! You shall see the room I told you you could have. It will suit you perfectly.”

Out of the wine shop into the street, out of the street into a courtyard, out of the courtyard up a steep staircase, out of the staircase into a garret—once the garret where a white-haired man sat on a low bench, bent forward and hard at work making shoes.

No white-haired man was there now; but the three men who had left the wine shop one by one were there. And between them and the distant white-haired man was the single small link: they had once watched him through cracks in the wall.

Defarge shut the door carefully and spoke quietly:

“Jacques One, Jacques Two, Jacques Three! This is the witness encountered by appointment by me, Jacques Four.”"}

{"request_id":"0d28082847f1ffbba2f2e6d1","rewritten_text":"Recent reports from Rotterdam suggest the city is in a frenzy of philosophical excitement. Phenomena there have been so completely unexpected—so entirely new—so utterly at odds with accepted beliefs—that I have no doubt by now all Europe is in an uproar, every branch of physics is in turmoil, and reason and astronomy are at each other’s throats.

It seems that on the—— day of—— (I am uncertain of the date), a vast crowd, gathered for reasons not specified, filled the great square of the Exchange in the well-ordered city of Rotterdam. The day was warm—unusually so for the season—with hardly a breath of air. The crowd did not mind being occasionally sprinkled by brief, friendly showers falling from large white clouds that flickered across the blue sky. Nevertheless, around noon, a slight but remarkable stir began among the assembly: the chatter of ten thousand tongues followed; and a moment later, ten thousand faces turned skyward, ten thousand pipes dropped at once from the corners of ten thousand mouths, and a shout comparable only to the roar of Niagara echoed long, loud, and furious through every quarter of Rotterdam.

The cause of this commotion soon became clear enough. From behind the massive bulk of one of those sharply defined clouds already mentioned, a strange, mismatched, yet apparently solid object slowly emerged into a patch of open blue. It was so oddly shaped, so whimsically assembled, that the crowd of solid townsmen standing open-mouthed below could make nothing of it and never master their amazement. What could it be? For the love of every wife and devil in Rotterdam, what could it mean? No one knew, no one could guess; not even the burgomaster Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk had the slightest clue to unravel the mystery. So, as nothing more sensible could be done, everyone carefully replaced his pipe in the corner of his mouth, cocked his right eye at the phenomenon, puffed, paused, waddled about, and grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally—puffed again.

Meanwhile, the object of all this curiosity—and the cause of so much smoke—was descending lower and lower toward the respectable city. Within a few minutes it came close enough to be clearly seen. It appeared to be—yes! it was without doubt a kind of balloon; yet surely no balloon like this had ever been seen in Rotterdam before."}

{"request_id":"572a10dcd110cff648667921","rewritten_text":"Of course he was very entertaining and all that, but I was terribly disappointed; and when I asked him about the coat of mail, he only laughed and said it was much too cold to wear in England. Ah, here is Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you must take off your glove. No, not the left hand, the other one.’

‘Dear Gladys, I really don’t think it is quite proper,’ said the Duchess, weakly unbuttoning a rather dirty kid glove.

‘Nothing interesting ever is,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘We made the world that way. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favorite palm reader. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley, and if you say she has a higher Mount of the Moon than I have, I will never believe in you again.’

‘I am sure, Gladys, there is nothing like that in my hand,’ said the Duchess seriously.

‘Your Grace is entirely right,’ said Mr. Podgers, glancing at the little plump hand with its short square fingers. ‘The Mount of the Moon is not developed. The life line, however, is excellent. Please bend your wrist. Thank you. Three distinct lines on the bracelet! You will live a very long life, Duchess, and be very happy. Ambition—very moderate; head line not exaggerated; heart line—’

‘Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Nothing would give me greater pleasure,’ said Mr. Podgers with a bow, ‘if the Duchess ever had been, but I am sorry to say I see a great constancy of affection combined with a strong sense of duty.’

‘Please go on, Mr. Podgers,’ said the Duchess, looking quite pleased.

‘Economy is one of your Grace’s chief virtues,’ continued Mr. Podgers, and Lady Windermere burst out laughing.

‘Economy is a very good thing,’ remarked the Duchess comfortably; ‘when I married Paisley he had eleven castles and not a single house fit to live in.’

‘And now he has twelve houses and not a single castle,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Well, my dear,’ said the Duchess, ‘I like—’

‘Comfort,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘and modern improvements, and hot water in every bedroom. Your Grace is quite right. Comfort is the only thing our civilisation provides us.

‘You have described the Duchess perfectly, Mr. Podgers, and now you must read Lady Flora,’ and in answer to a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and high shoulder blades stepped awkwardly from behind the sofa and held out a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

‘Ah, a pianist! I see,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘an excellent pianist, though perhaps not quite a musician.’"}

{"request_id":"2a1f140b60260957250b019d","rewritten_text":"The heft of the insect was astonishing, and, considering everything, I could hardly fault Jupiter for his opinion of it; but I could not fathom why Legrand agreed with him.

“I sent for you,” he said grandly after I finished examining the beetle, “to get your counsel and help in carrying out the plans of Fate and of the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I broke in, “you must be unwell and should take precautions. You shall go to bed, and I will stay with you a few days until you recover. You are feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I felt it and, honestly, found no trace of fever.

“But you can be ill without a fever. Let me prescribe for you just this once. First, go to bed. Next—”

“You are mistaken,” he interrupted. “I am as well as I could expect under the excitement I feel. If you truly wish me well, you will ease this excitement.”

“And how am I to do that?”

“Very easily. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and we need someone we can trust. You are the only one. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me will fade.”

“I want to oblige you in every way,” I replied, “but do you mean to say this cursed beetle is linked to your expedition?”

“It is.”

“Then, Legrand, I cannot join such nonsense.”

“I’m sorry—very sorry—for we’ll have to go alone.”

“Go alone! The man is mad! But wait—how long will you be gone?”

“Probably all night. We leave at once and return by sunrise, no matter what.”

“And will you promise, on your honor, that when this whim of yours is done and the bug business (good heavens!) resolved to your satisfaction, you will come home and follow my advice entirely, as that of your physician?”

“Yes, I promise; now let us go, for we have no time to lose.”

With a heavy heart I went with my friend. We set out around four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and me. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, insisting on bearing everything—more from fear of leaving the tools within reach of his master than from any extra energy or good nature."}

{"request_id":"f2d5c7705e5d18f120584a18","rewritten_text":"These deputies had been sent on ahead to Adrian, who had been chosen arbitrator; they had travelled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and laid waste countryside, nourishing fierce animosity all the way, and now urged their respective claims with unabated factional zeal.

By questioning the envoys separately and after long inquiry, we discovered the actual condition of Paris. Since parliament had appointed him Ryland’s substitute, every surviving English person had yielded obedience to Adrian. He was our commander to lead us from our homeland into unexplored territories, our legislator and guardian. When we first arranged our emigration project, continual division among our members had not been intended, and the chain of authority culminated with the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen events reshaped our plans and caused the majority of our people to be severed for nearly two months from their supreme head. They had crossed in two distinct contingents, and upon meeting at Paris dissension broke out between them.

They discovered Paris abandoned. When the pestilence first arose, returning travellers and merchants, along with letters, had kept us constantly informed of the havoc wrought in Europe. Yet as mortality increased, this contact dwindled and stopped. Even within England communication from one end of the island to the other grew sluggish and scarce. No vessel crossed the channel between Calais and Dover; or if some sad wanderer, anxious to learn the fate of his kin, launched again for our coast, often the ravenous sea engulfed his tiny boat, or after a day or two he caught the contagion and expired before he could recount the ruin of France. Thus we remained in large part ignorant of continental affairs, still cherishing some obscure hope of discovering many fellow-sufferers along its breadth. But the very influences that had so dreadfully thinned England had worked with wider license in the neighboring realm. France was a blank; along the whole road from Calais to Paris no single living soul appeared. In Paris itself perhaps a hundred persons remained, who, resigned to their approaching doom, flitted through the capital’s streets and gathered to talk of former days, showing that vivacity and even cheerfulness that rarely fails the sons and daughters of that nation.

The English took undisputed possession of Paris. Its towering houses and cramped streets were devoid of life. A few wan figures could be discerned at their usual haunt in the Tuileries; they marvelled why islanders should draw near their luckless city—for in extremity of misery, sufferers invariably imagine their share of calamity the sharpest, as, when racked by intolerable agony, we would exchange the very torment we endure for any other that might seize a different part of the frame."}

{"request_id":"8a8f7261a9f976cb7775e728","rewritten_text":"“I hope I’ll soon have the pleasure of introducing my son to you,” Mr. Weston said.

Mrs. Elton, very ready to imagine a special compliment meant for her, smiled graciously.

“You’ve heard of a certain Frank Churchill, I presume,” he went on, “and know that he is my son, though he doesn’t carry my name.”

“Oh yes, and I shall be delighted to meet him. I’m sure Mr. Elton won’t delay in calling on him; we’ll both be very pleased to have him at the Vicarage.”

“You’re very kind. Frank will be thrilled, I’m sure. He’s supposed to be in town next week, if not sooner. We were told so in a letter today. I met the post on my way this morning, and seeing my son’s handwriting, I took the liberty of opening it—even though it wasn’t addressed to me; it was for Mrs. Weston. She’s his main correspondent, I can tell you. I hardly ever get a letter.”

“And you really opened a letter addressed to her! Oh, Mr. Weston—” she laughed affectedly, “I must protest. That sets a terribly dangerous example! I do hope you won’t let the neighbours imitate you. Goodness, if this is what we’re in for, we married women will have to start asserting ourselves. Oh, Mr. Weston, I never would have believed it of you!”

“Well, we men are rascals. You must watch out for yourself, Mrs. Elton. This letter tells us—it’s brief, written in haste just to let us know—that they are all coming to town immediately because of Mrs. Churchill. She hasn’t been well all winter and thinks Enscombe is too cold, so they’re all to head south without delay.”

“Really? From Yorkshire, I think. Enscombe is in Yorkshire?”

“Yes, about a hundred and ninety miles from London—a long trip.”

“Yes indeed, very long. Sixty-five miles farther than from Maple Grove to London. But what is distance, Mr. Weston, to people of great wealth? You would be astonished to hear how my brother, Mr. Suckling, dashes about. You may scarcely believe it, but twice in one week he and Mr. Bragge went to London and back with four horses.”

“The problem with the distance from Enscombe,” Mr. Weston said, “is that Mrs. Churchill, as we hear it, hasn’t been able to get off the sofa for a full week at a time. In Frank’s last letter she complained, he said, that she was too weak to go into her conservatory unless she had both his arm and his uncle’s.”"}

{"request_id":"a783ad6a4fe3b589261e715b","rewritten_text":"“Well, monsieur le mauvais sujet,” the old lady exclaimed as he entered, “why haven’t you come to see me all this time?”

“My dear Lady Clem, I haven’t had a moment to myself,” Lord Arthur replied with a smile.

“I suppose you mean you spend all day with Miss Sybil Merton, buying chiffons and talking nonsense? I can’t understand why people make such a fuss about getting married. In my day we never dreamed of billing and cooing in public, or in private either.”

“I assure you I haven’t seen Sybil for twenty-four hours, Lady Clem. As far as I can tell, she belongs entirely to her milliners.”

“Of course; that’s the only reason you visit an ugly old woman like me. I’m surprised you men don’t take warning. On a fait des folies pour moi, and here I am, a poor rheumatic creature, with a false front and a bad temper. If it weren’t for dear Lady Jansen, who sends me all the worst French novels she can find, I don’t think I could get through the day. Doctors are useless except for taking one’s money. They can’t even cure my heartburn.”

“I’ve brought you a cure for that, Lady Clem,” said Lord Arthur solemnly. “It’s an extraordinary invention by an American.”

“I don’t think I like American inventions, Arthur. I’m quite sure I don’t. I read some American novels lately, and they were utter nonsense.”

“Oh, but there’s nothing nonsensical about this, Lady Clem! I promise you it’s a perfect cure. You must promise to try it.” Lord Arthur pulled a small box from his pocket and handed it to her.

“Well, the box is charming, Arthur. Is it really a present? How kind of you. And is this the marvelous medicine? It looks like a bonbon. I’ll take it right now.”

“Good heavens, Lady Clem,” Lord Arthur cried, grabbing her hand, “you mustn’t do anything of the sort. It’s a homeopathic medicine, and if you take it without having heartburn, it could do you terrible harm. Wait until you have an attack, and take it then. You’ll be amazed by the result.”

“I’d like to take it now,” Lady Clementina said, lifting the little transparent capsule to the light, its bubble of liquid aconitine suspended inside. “I’m sure it’s delightful. The truth is, although I hate doctors, I adore medicines. Still, I’ll save it for my next attack.”

“And when will that be?” Lord Arthur asked eagerly."}

{"request_id":"475d2d637213dca3e3c54a8a","rewritten_text":"Shall I be lifted to the skies, on flowery couches of ease, while others struggle to win the crown and drift through bloody seas?

He had the reputation of being a marvelous reader. At church “sociables” he was invariably asked to recite poetry; and when he finished, the ladies would fling up their hands and let them drop limp into their laps, roll their eyes heavenward, and shake their heads as if to say, “Words fail us; it surpasses all expression, FAR too lovely for this mortal realm.”

When the hymn ended, the Rev. Mr. Sprague transformed himself into a bulletin-board and rattled off “notices” of gatherings and societies and whatnot until it seemed the list would run on to judgment day—a peculiar custom still practiced in America, even in big cities, despite this age of abundant newspapers. Frequently the less reason there is for an inherited custom, the more stubbornly it resists extinction.

Then the minister prayed. It was a generous, sweeping prayer that descended into particulars: it entreated blessings on the church, and the children of the church; on the neighboring churches; on the town; on the county; on the State; on the State’s officials; on the United States; on the churches of the United States; on Congress; on the President; on the government officers; on poor sailors tossed upon stormy waters; on the oppressed millions groaning beneath European monarchs and Eastern tyrannies; on those who have the light and glad tidings yet lack eyes to see or ears to hear; on the heathen scattered through distant islands; and it ended by imploring that the words he was about to utter might win grace and favor, like seed falling into fertile soil and yielding in due season a thankful harvest of good. Amen.

A rustle of skirts followed, and the standing congregation settled into their seats. The boy whose tale this book tells found no delight in the prayer; he merely endured it—if that. He was restless throughout; he mentally kept count of the prayer’s particulars without meaning to—for he was not truly listening, but he knew the familiar ground and the preacher’s well-worn path over it—and whenever a scrap of fresh matter got mixed in, his ear caught it and his whole being objected to it; he deemed additions unfair and knavish. Midway through the prayer a fly alighted on the pew-back before him and tormented his soul by calmly rubbing its forelegs together, folding its arms around its head, and polishing it so zealously it seemed about to detach, exposing the slender thread of a neck; scraping its wings with its hind legs and smoothing them against its body as though they were coat-tails; completing its entire toilet as serenely as if certain it was in no danger at all."}

{"request_id":"a9d718cd3115f46b065a64fd","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Massa Will—indeed I be,” the negro answered at once—“near bout to de very eend now.”

“_Out to the end!_” screamed Legrand, “you mean you’re all the way at the tip of that limb?”

“’Most to de eend, massa—o-o-o-o-oh! Lord-golly-mercy! what dis thing up here in de tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, in high delight, “what do you see?”

“Why, ’tain’t nuthin but a skull—somebody done left his head up in de tree, and de crows eat every scrap o’ meat off it.”

“A skull, you say! Very good—how’s it fixed there? What keeps it fast?”

“Sure ’nough, massa; lemme look. Why dis mighty queer, sure—there’s a big nail through de skull nailing it to de tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly as I direct—do you hear me?”

“Yes, massa.”

“Listen close—find the left eye of the skull.”

“Hum! hoo! dat a funny notion! why ain’t no eye left at all.”

“Confound your dullness! you do know right hand from left?”

“Yas, I knows dat—knows dat fine—’tis wid my lef hand I chops wood.”

“Of course! you’re left-handed; so your left eye’s on the same side as that hand. Now you should manage to find the skull’s left eye, or where it once was. Have you got it?”

A long silence followed. Finally the negro asked,

“Do de skull’s left eye stay on same side as de skull’s left hand, too?—’cause de skull ain’t got nary bit o’ hand—never mind! I got the left eye now—here de left eye! what I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it, as far down the cord will let it go—but mind you don’t lose hold of the string.”

“All done, Massa Will; real easy to send de bug through de hole—watch for him down there!”

Through all this exchange no part of Jupiter’s body was visible; but the beetle he had lowered now shone at the string’s end, glimmering like a polished golden globe in the last glimmers of the setting sun that still faintly lit the hill where we stood. The _scarabæus_ dangled free of every branch and, if released, would have dropped straight to our feet. Legrand at once seized the scythe and swept out a circular patch, three or four yards across, just under the insect; and when he finished, he told Jupiter to release the string and climb down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"fb8013c95839411dcc7534af","rewritten_text":"The nephew cast him a futile look while passing out to the door.

“Good night!” said the uncle. “I anticipate the pleasure of seeing you again in the morning. Rest well! Escort Monsieur my nephew to his chamber there!—And burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you please,” he muttered to himself before he rang his tiny bell once more and called his valet to his own room.

After the valet came and went, Monsieur the Marquis paced back and forth in his loose robe to ready himself gently for sleep on that stifling still night. Rustling about the room with his soft slippers soundless on the floor, he moved like a polished tiger—resembled some bewitched marquis of the incurably wicked stories, whose periodic transformation into a tiger was either fading or beginning.

He strode from one end of his sumptuous chamber to the other, revisiting the fragments of the day’s journey that intruded on his thoughts: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the sinking sun, the descent, the mill, the prison on the crag, the small village nestled below, the peasants at the fountain, and the road-mender in his blue cap pointing at the chain beneath the carriage. That fountain brought to mind the Paris fountain, the small bundle lying on the steps, the women bending over it, and the tall man with upheld arms crying, “Dead!”

“I am calm now,” observed Monsieur the Marquis, “and may retire to bed.”

So, leaving a single light burning on the broad hearth, he let the thin gauze curtains fall around him and heard the night shatter its silence with a long sigh as he settled to sleep.

The stone faces on the outer walls stared blankly at the black night for three weighty hours; for three weighty hours, the horses in the stables clattered at their mangers, the dogs barked, and the owl emitted a sound bearing little resemblance to the note poets traditionally credit it with. Yet such creatures obstinately refrain from uttering what is recorded for them.

For three heavy hours, the chateau’s stone visages, leonine and human, gazed vacantly into the night. Dead darkness shrouded the entire landscape; dead darkness added its own hush to the hushed dust along the roads. The burial-ground reached a state where its small tufts of meager grass were indistinguishable from one another; the figure on the Cross might have stepped down for any trace there was to see. In the village, both taxers and taxed slept deeply. Dreaming perhaps of feasts, as the starved often do, and of ease and rest, as the beaten slave and the yoked ox may, its gaunt inhabitants slumbered soundly and were nourished and unburdened."}

{"request_id":"6d4035ffeb1457a6fbf7aae1","rewritten_text":"“They know how sharp he is; they’ll give Artful nothing less than life,” said the first speaker. “They’ll send the Artful away for good.”

“What do you mean by ‘lagging’ and ‘a lifer’?” demanded Mr. Bolter. “What’s the use of talking that way to me? Why don’t you speak so I can follow you?”

Fagin was about to explain these mysterious terms in plain language, and Mr. Bolter would have learned that they meant “transportation for life,” when the conversation was cut short by the arrival of Master Bates. His hands were shoved in his breeches pockets, and his face twisted into a look of half comic, half miserable distress.

“It’s all over, Fagin,” said Charley once he and his new companion had been introduced.

“What do you mean?”

“They’ve found the gentleman who owns the box; two or three more are coming to identify him; and the Artful’s booked for the voyage,” replied Master Bates. “I’ll need a full suit of mourning, Fagin, and a hatband to visit him in before he sets off. To think of Jack Dawkins—lummy Jack—the Dodger—the Artful Dodger—being sent abroad for a miserable twopenny-halfpenny snuffbox! I never believed he’d do it for less than a gold watch with chain and seals. Oh, why didn’t he rob some rich old gentleman of all his valuables and leave like a gentleman, instead of going like a common prig without any honour or glory!”

With this burst of feeling for his unlucky friend, Master Bates dropped onto the nearest chair, looking sour and hopeless.

“What do you mean by saying he has no honour or glory?” cried Fagin, shooting an angry look at his pupil. “Wasn’t he always the best hand among you all? Was there one of you who could match him on a job? Eh?”

“Not one,” answered Master Bates, his voice rough with grief. “Not one.”

“Then what are you talking about?” demanded Fagin sharply. “What are you bawling for?”

“Because it’s not on the record, is it?” said Charley, stung into open defiance by his sorrow. “Because it won’t show up in the indictment. Because nobody will ever know half of what he was. How will he be listed in the Newgate Calendar? Maybe he won’t be there at all. Oh, my eye, my eye, what a blow it is!”

“Ha! ha!” laughed Fagin, stretching out his right hand and turning to Mr. Bolter, shaking with chuckles as if he had the palsy. “See what pride they take in their trade, my dear.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"c211f745db280d53dfd10394","rewritten_text":"“I know she would!” The Widow Douglas’s lavish hospitality proved a tempting lure. It, joined with Tom’s coaxing, soon won the argument. They resolved to keep the evening’s plans to themselves. Then it struck Tom that Huck might turn up that very night and give the signal. The thought damped much of his excitement, yet he could not surrender the fun awaiting him at the Widow’s. And why should he, he reasoned—the signal had failed to come the night before, so what made tonight any more certain? The guaranteed merriment outweighed the doubtful treasure; in boyish fashion he chose to follow the stronger desire and banish the money box from his thoughts for the rest of the day. Three miles below town the ferry halted at the mouth of a wooded hollow and made fast. The passengers swarmed ashore, and soon the distant glades and craggy ridges were ringing with shouts and laughter. Every conceivable method of getting hot and tired was tried, and eventually the wanderers straggled back to camp, armed with hefty appetites, whereupon the feast fell to. Afterward came a cool spell of lounging and talk beneath the shelter of spreading oaks. Presently someone cried out: “Who’s ready for the cave?” All were. Bundles of candles were fetched, and instantly the crowd was scampering up the hill. The entrance lay on the slope, shaped like a great letter A. Its thick oaken door stood unbarred. Inside was a small chamber, chilly as an icehouse, its limestone walls beaded with a cold sweat. It felt romantic and mysterious to stand in that deep gloom and gaze out upon the sunlit green valley. Yet the solemn mood quickly faded, and the frolicking recommenced. The instant a candle was lit, a general rush descended upon its owner; there followed a tussle and valiant defense, but the candle would soon be dashed down or puffed out, and then came delighted shrieks and another chase. But all things end. In time the party filed down the steep slope of the main avenue, the wavering line of lights barely exposing the towering stone walls nearly to their meeting point sixty feet above. The main passage was scarcely eight or ten feet across. Every few steps other high, narrower fissures branched away to either side—for McDougal’s cave was merely a vast maze of crooked corridors winding into each other and out again and leading nowhere."}

content.text: {"request_id":"3bcefabdb17b203deed47bdf","rewritten_text":"To my mind that quaint fib had been told in the simplest, loveliest way; but I had only heard it once, and that does matter; when everything was new, it must have sounded delightful to the others. Sir Dinadan the Humorist woke first, and roused everyone else with a rather shabby practical joke. He fastened some metal mugs to a dog’s tail and let him loose, and the poor beast tore madly around the place in panic, with the other dogs baying after him, smashing into anything in their path and producing absolute chaos and a perfect storm of racket; the entire crowd laughed till their eyes ran, and a few people toppled from their chairs and rolled on the floor in bliss. They were exactly like a pack of children. Sir Dinadan gloried in his prank so much that he kept repeating, till everyone was tired of it, how this immortal idea occurred to him; and, as with humorists of his sort, he was still laughing after everyone else had stopped. He was so puffed up he had to make a speech—naturally a humorous one. I doubt I ever heard so many stale, worn-out gags strung together. He was worse than the minstrels, worse than any circus clown. It felt oddly mournful to sit here, thirteen centuries before my birth, and listen again to the same poor, moth-eaten jokes that had given me the dry gripes as a boy thirteen hundred years later. It nearly persuaded me no new joke can ever exist. People laughed at those antiquities, of course—they always do; I had noticed that centuries afterwards. But the scoffer, that is, the boy, didn’t laugh. No, he mocked; there was nothing he wouldn’t scoff at. He declared most of Sir Dinadan’s jokes were rotten and the remainder petrified. I said “petrified” was fine; I myself thought the only proper method of classifying some of those jokes’ majestic ages was by geologic periods. Yet that tidy idea went right past the boy, because geology hadn’t been invented yet. I made a note of it, though, planning to educate the realm up to it if I survived. A good notion shouldn’t be discarded merely because the market isn’t ready. Then Sir Kay got up and started cranking his history-mill, with me as the stock for it."}

{"request_id":"2f3d2ef20eab585fdfe098f5","rewritten_text":"Year after year, Dorian Gray remained under the spell of that book, or perhaps it is truer to say he never wished to shake its hold. He obtained no fewer than nine large-paper copies from Paris, each one bound in a different hue to answer the shifting moods and wayward whims of a nature he seemed, at moments, almost to have surrendered. The hero, that marvellous young Parisian whose romantic and scientific temperaments were so curiously interwoven, became for him a prototype of his own being. Indeed, the entire volume appeared to recount the tale of his life, inscribed before he had lived it.

In one respect he stood more fortunate than the novel’s extravagant protagonist. He never experienced—nor had any reason to experience—that grotesque terror of mirrors, shining metal, and still water that overwhelmed the young Parisian so early, prompted by the swift ruin of a beauty once apparently so extraordinary. With something like a cruel delight—and perhaps in almost every delight, as surely in every pleasure, cruelty lies—he would read the final portion, with its truly tragic, albeit somewhat overwrought, chronicle of the grief and anguish of a man who had forfeited what, in others and in the world, he had held most dear.

The exquisite loveliness that had so enthralled Basil Hallward, and so many others beside, seemed never to desert him. Even those who had heard the darkest whispers about him—since odd rumours respecting his way of life from time to time stole through London and became club gossip—could not accept any tale to his discredit when they beheld him. He bore always the aspect of one untainted by the world. Men who spoke coarsely fell silent upon Dorian Gray’s entrance. There was a purity in his face that reproved them; his mere presence seemed to awaken in them recollections of innocence they had marred. They marvelled that one so gracious and winning could have escaped the stains of an age both sordid and sensual.

Often, returning home from those enigmatic and prolonged disappearances that provoked such conjecture among those who deemed themselves his friends, he would steal upstairs to the locked chamber, open the door with the key he now never relinquished, and stand, mirror in hand, before the portrait Basil Hallward had painted, shifting his gaze between the wicked, time-worn visage upon the canvas and the fair, youthful face that laughed back at him from the polished glass."}

{"request_id":"e47e8b8c39b1f366905943e0","rewritten_text":"These envoys had been sent to Adrian, who had been chosen judge; they had traveled from Paris to Calais through empty towns and desolate countryside, seething with hatred for each other, and now they argued their cases with unchecked party spirit.

By questioning the deputies separately and investigating extensively, we discovered the real situation in Paris. Since Parliament had made him Ryland’s deputy, every remaining English person had submitted to Adrian. He was our commander to lead us from our homeland to unknown regions, our lawgiver, and our protector. When the emigration plan was first organized, no one imagined that the group would be separated for long, and the chain of command ended with the Earl of Windsor. But unforeseen events altered our plans and caused most of us to be separated from the supreme leader for nearly two months. The people had crossed over in two distinct groups, and once they reached Paris, conflict broke out between them.

They had discovered Paris deserted. When the plague first appeared, travelers, merchants, and letters regularly told us about the disease’s progress on the continent. But as the death toll rose, those communications dwindled and finally stopped. Even within England, contact from one end of the island to the other became slow and rare. No ship crossed the channel between Calais and Dover; or if some grieving traveler, desperate to confirm the fate of his relatives, left the French shore to return to us, the hungry sea often swallowed his small boat, or after a day or two he caught the infection and died before he could describe France’s ruin. We were therefore largely ignorant of conditions on the continent and clung to a faint hope of finding many companions along that broad route. But the same forces that had devastated England had worked even more violently in that neighboring land. France was empty; along the entire road from Calais to Paris not a single person was seen. In Paris there remained a handful, perhaps a hundred, who, accepting their approaching deaths, drifted through the streets of the capital and gathered to talk about earlier days, with that liveliness and even cheerfulness that hardly ever abandons individuals of that nation.

The English took undisputed possession of Paris. Its tall houses and narrow streets were lifeless. A few pale figures could be seen at their usual meeting place in the Tuileries; they wondered why these islanders would enter their doomed city—for in extreme misery, sufferers always imagine their share of the calamity is the worst, just as, when in intense pain, we would trade the particular agony we endure for any other that might strike another part of the body."}

Then I remembered, with a shudder, that the creature I’d left in my apartment might still be there, alive and roaming about. I flung the door open, as children do when they expect a ghost to be waiting on the other side; but nothing was there. I stepped inside cautiously. The room was empty, and my bedroom was free of its ghastly guest. I could hardly believe I’d been granted such good fortune, but once I was certain my enemy had really fled, I clapped my hands in joy and ran downstairs to Clerval.

We went back up to my room, and the servant soon brought breakfast; but I couldn’t control myself. It wasn’t simply joy that gripped me; my skin tingled with hypersensitivity, and my pulse raced. I couldn’t stay still for even a moment; I leapt over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed out loud. At first Clerval thought my unusual liveliness came from being thrilled to see him, but when he studied me more closely, he noticed a wildness in my eyes he couldn’t explain, and my loud, unrestrained, unnatural laughter frightened and astonished him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “for God’s sake, what’s the matter? Don’t laugh like that. You’re so ill! What’s causing all this?”

“Don’t ask me,” I cried, covering my eyes, because I imagined I saw the dreaded specter slipping into the room; “he can tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I thought the monster seized me; I fought wildly and collapsed in a fit.

Poor Clerval! What must he have felt? A meeting he had looked forward to with such joy turned to misery. But I didn’t witness his sorrow, for I lay unconscious and didn’t regain my senses for a very long time.

That was the start of a nervous fever that kept me bedridden for several months. During all that time, Henry was my only nurse. I later learned that since my father was too old and unfit for such a long trip, and my illness would have crushed Elizabeth, he spared them the grief by hiding how serious my condition was."}

{"request_id":"cb496487d7e4349559bbb94c","rewritten_text":"“But do not think I considered it anything but a misfortune in itself.”

“Depend upon it, they were all quite comfortable.”

“I should not like them any better for that, perhaps. Such a crowd of women and children have no right to be at ease aboard ship.”

“My dear Frederick, you are talking absolute nonsense. What would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who so often wish to be transported from one port to another in pursuit of our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“My feelings, you see, did not stop me from bringing Mrs Harville and her entire family to Plymouth.”

“But I cannot bear to hear you talk like some fine gentleman, as though women were fine ladies instead of rational creatures. None of us expect to sail on smooth seas all our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “once he has a wife, he will sing another song. When he is married, if we are fortunate enough to live through another war, we shall witness him doing as you and I, and many more, have done. He will be grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Ay, indeed we shall.”

“Now I have finished,” cried Captain Wentworth. “As soon as married folks begin attacking me with, ‘Oh! you will think quite differently when you are married,’ I can only answer, ‘No, I shall not;’ and then they retort, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that settles it.”

He rose and walked away.

“What an extensive traveller you must have been, ma’am!” exclaimed Mrs Musgrove to Mrs Croft.

“Pretty well, ma’am, through the fifteen years of my marriage; though many ladies have accomplished more. I have crossed the Atlantic four times, and been once to the East Indies and home again, but just that once; besides visiting various places nearer home: Cork, Lisbon, and Gibraltar. But I never went past the Straits, and never was in the West Indies. We do not count Bermuda or the Bahamas, you know, as the West Indies.”

Mrs Musgrove could not contest it; she could not accuse herself of ever having called them anything at all in her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” continued Mrs Croft, “nothing surpasses the accommodations of a man-of-war; I refer, of course, to the larger classes. When you come to a frigate, naturally you are more cramped; yet any sensible woman may be perfectly content there; and I can truly say the happiest portion of my life has been spent on shipboard. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d9fc837d259b374e6d845e9f","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was too stunned to think clearly. I knew my design differed in its details from this one, even though the general outline was similar. Soon I picked up a candle, sat at the far end of the room, and examined the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I found my own sketch on the back exactly as I had drawn it. My first reaction was simple astonishment at the remarkable similarity of the outlines—at the strange coincidence that, without my knowledge, a skull had been on the other side of the parchment directly beneath my drawing of the scarab, and that this skull matched my drawing so closely in both shape and size. That coincidence truly stunned me for a while. This is how such coincidences usually affect us. The mind tries to establish some link, a causal chain, and when it can’t, it falls into a kind of temporary paralysis. But when I emerged from that stupor, another conviction gradually formed, one that alarmed me even more than the coincidence itself. I began to remember, clearly and without doubt, that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I made my sketch of the scarab. I became absolutely certain, because I recalled flipping first one side and then the other, searching for the cleanest spot. If the skull had been there then, I couldn’t possibly have missed it. This mystery seemed beyond explanation; yet even then, a faint, firefly-like idea flickered in the darkest, most hidden corners of my mind—a hint of the truth that last night’s adventure would prove so magnificently. I stood up at once, put the parchment away safely, and put the matter out of my mind until I could be alone.\n\n“When you had gone and Jupiter had fallen fast asleep, I began a more methodical investigation of the situation. First, I considered how the parchment had come into my possession. The place where we found the scarab was on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and just above the high-water mark. When I first picked it up, it bit me sharply, and I dropped it. Jupiter, ever cautious, refused to grab the insect as it flew toward him until he found a leaf or something similar he could use to handle it."}

{"request_id":"366c8e82fffd6921babde56e","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that always brings misery must have been broken, and the cruel fate that rules it would not allow this break in her eternal laws. But why should I regret that? Misery was my element, and only what was miserable could come near me; if Woodville had been happy I would never have known him. And can I, who for many years was fed by tears and raised under the dew of grief, stop to tell a tale of sorrow and death?

Woodville had to travel into the country and was held there day after day, away from his lovely bride. He received a letter from her saying she was slightly ill, but urging him to hurry to her, that health would return from his eyes and his presence was her surest medicine. He was delayed three more days and then rushed to her. His heart, he knew not why, warned him of misfortune; he had heard nothing more from her; he feared she might be worse, and this fear made him restless to see her again standing before him in health and beauty. A sinister voice seemed always to whisper, “You will never again behold her as she was.”

When he reached her home it was silent. He moved through several rooms; in one he saw a servant weeping bitterly. Weak with fear, he could hardly ask, “Is she dead?” and just heard the dreadful answer, “Not yet.” These shocking words felt less terrifying than those he had expected; learning that she was still alive and that he might still hope brought some relief. He remembered her letter and clung to the wild idea that his kisses, breathing warm love and life, would give her new spirit, and that with him near her she could not die, that his presence was the talisman of her life.

He hurried to her sickroom; she lay with cheeks burning from fever, yet her eyes were closed and she seemed unconscious. He wrapped her in his arms, pressed breathless kisses on her burning lips, and called to her in a voice of subdued anguish by the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am with you; your life, your love. Return, dearest; you promised me this gift, that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die near me. What is death? To see you no more? To part from what is part of myself, without whom I have no memory and no future?”"}
