content.text: {"request_id":"dd134b348c9be40fc351447c","rewritten_text":"I now hurry to the more stirring part of my tale, to events that stirred such feelings in me that they shaped who I have become. Spring moved in quickly; the weather grew mild and the sky clear. It astonished me that what had been barren and gloomy now bloomed with flowers and green plants. My senses rejoiced in countless delightful scents and sights. On one of those days, when the cottagers rested from their work—the old man played his guitar while the children listened—I noticed Felix looked indescribably sad. He sighed often, and once the old man stopped his playing. From his manner, I guessed he asked why his son was upset. Felix answered cheerfully, and the old man was about to resume his music when someone knocked at the door. A lady on horseback stood there, guided by a countryman. She wore a dark outfit and a thick black veil. Agatha asked her something, but the stranger only replied by softly saying Felix’s name. Her voice was musical yet unlike any of my friends’. Hearing it, Felix rushed to her, and she lifted her veil. I saw a face of angelic beauty. Her hair shone raven-black and was carefully braided; her eyes were dark yet gentle and lively; her features were perfectly proportioned, and her complexion was fair with a pink flush on each cheek. Felix was seized with joy at the sight of her, all traces of sorrow disappearing as his face shone with such ecstasy I could hardly believe it. His eyes sparkled and his cheeks reddened with happiness, and just then I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She showed different emotions; wiping away a few tears, she offered her hand, which Felix kissed passionately, calling her, as best I could tell, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him but smiled. He helped her down from her horse, dismissed the guide, and brought her inside the cottage. There he spoke with his father, and the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet, trying to kiss his hand, but he lifted her up and embraced her. I soon realized that though the stranger spoke clearly in her own language, neither the cottagers understood her, nor did she understand them."}

{"request_id":"74b0eb7ed83115d2eb02dc6a","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, one would have thought Nemesis had stolen Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed turned to stone, his face marble with sadness. He had lived the refined and easy life of a young man with wealth and rank, a life free from common worries and full of carefree charm; and now, for the first time, he understood the terrible mystery of Destiny, the dreadful meaning of Doom.

How absurd and monstrous it all seemed! Could it be that on his hand, in letters he could not read but another could, there was some dreadful secret of guilt, some blood-red mark of crime? Was there no escape? Were we only chess pieces moved by an unseen power, vessels shaped by a potter’s whim, set apart for honour or disgrace? His reason rebelled, yet he felt some tragedy hung over him and he had been suddenly forced to carry an unbearable burden. Actors are lucky. They can decide whether to appear in tragedy or in comedy, whether to suffer or to be merry, to laugh or to cry. But in real life it is different. Most men and women must play parts for which they are unsuited. Our Guildensterns play Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets must joke like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the play is poorly cast.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers entered the room. When he saw Lord Arthur he started, and his coarse, fat face turned a greenish yellow. The two men looked at each other, and for a moment there was silence.

“The Duchess has left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and has asked me to bring it to her,” said Mr. Podgers at last. “Ah, I see it on the sofa! Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I insist on a straightforward answer to a question I am going to ask you.”

“Another time, Lord Arthur, but the Duchess is waiting. I’m afraid I must go.”

“You shall not go. The Duchess is in no hurry.”

“Ladies should not be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,” said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. “The fair sex tends to be impatient.”

Lord Arthur’s finely shaped lips curled in irritated scorn. The poor Duchess seemed to him of very little importance at that moment. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and held out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw there,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I must know it. I am not a child.”"}

{"request_id":"9cad8657980ac682d3af1042","rewritten_text":"“Men get married because they’re exhausted; women do it out of curiosity, and both end up disappointed.”

“I don’t think I’m likely to marry, Harry. I’m too much in love. That’s one of your aphorisms. I’m applying it, just as I do everything you tell me.”

“Who are you in love with?” Lord Henry asked after a pause.

“With an actress,” Dorian Gray said, blushing.

Lord Henry lifted his shoulders. “That’s a rather ordinary beginning.”

“You wouldn’t say that if you saw her, Harry.”

“Who is she?”

“Her name is Sibyl Vane.”

“Never heard of her.”

“No one has. People will, though. She’s a genius.”

“My dear boy, no woman is a genius. Women are the decorative sex. They never have anything to say, but they say it beautifully. Women embody the triumph of matter over mind, just as men embody the triumph of mind over morals.”

“Harry, how can you?”

“My dear Dorian, it’s perfectly true. I’m analyzing women right now, so I should know. The subject isn’t as complicated as I expected. I’ve concluded there are only two kinds of women: plain and painted. Plain women are very useful. If you want a reputation for respectability, you only have to take them to supper. The others are very charming, but they make one mistake: they paint to look young. Our grandmothers painted to sound brilliant. Rouge and wit used to go together. That’s finished now. As long as a woman can seem ten years younger than her own daughter, she’s completely content. As for conversation, there are only five women in London worth talking to, and two of them can’t be invited to decent gatherings. Anyway, tell me about your genius. How long have you known her?”

“Ah! Harry, your opinions frighten me.”

“Forget that. How long have you known her?”

“About three weeks.”

“And where did you come across her?”

“I’ll tell you, Harry, but you mustn’t be unsympathetic. After all, it never would have happened if I hadn’t met you. You filled me with a wild desire to know everything about life. For days after meeting you, something seemed to pulse through my veins. When I lounged in the park or strolled down Piccadilly, I looked at everyone who passed and wondered, with a kind of mad curiosity, what lives they led. Some of them fascinated me. Others filled me with dread. There was a delicate poison in the air. I craved sensations...”"}

{"request_id":"314577e3400300898d257177","rewritten_text":"After a while we’d wake up and look around to see what made the noise, and maybe there’d be a steamboat chugging upstream, way over by the far bank, so far away you couldn’t tell anything about it except if it had a stern-wheel or a side-wheel. Then for about an hour there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just thick loneness. Next a raft would slip by in the distance, and maybe some fellow on it would be chopping, because raft men are mostly at it. You’d see the axe flash and swing down—no sound yet; you’d see the axe rise again, and only when it was above his head would the _k’chunk!_ reach you—it took that long to cross the water. That’s how we spent the day, lazing around, listening to the quiet. Once a heavy fog rolled in, and the rafts and such rattled tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run over them. A scow or a raft went by so close we could hear them talking and cussing and laughing—clear as could be—but we couldn’t see a sign of them. It gave you the crawls; sounded like spirits carrying on in the air. Jim said he figured they were spirits; but I says:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Dern the dern fog.’”

As soon as night fell we shoved off; once we got her out near the middle we left her be and let the current take her wherever it pleased. Then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about everything—we stayed naked day and night whenever the mosquitoes would let us. The new clothes Buck’s family made me were too fine to feel easy in, and besides I never cared much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we’d have that whole river to ourselves for ages. Over yonder were the banks and islands across the water, and maybe a spark in the distance—which would be a candle in some cabin window; and sometimes you’d catch a spark or two on the water—on a raft or a scow, you know; and maybe a fiddle tune or a song would drift over from one of those crafts. It’s grand living on a raft. We had the sky above, all dotted with stars, and we’d lie on our backs, staring up, and argue about whether they were made or just happened. Jim said they were made, but I said they just happened; I reckoned it would’ve taken too long to _make_ that many."}

{"request_id":"0da004a24345fe99410e62e1","rewritten_text":"To examine a star in quick glances—to look at it from the side by directing the outer parts of the retina toward it, those parts being more receptive to faint light than the center—is to see the star clearly and truly appreciate its brilliance. That brilliance dims in proportion to how directly we look at it. More rays strike the eye when we stare straight at it, but the sidelong view has the finer capacity to grasp what we see. By being too intense we confuse and weaken our thoughts; we can even make Venus herself disappear from the sky by watching too long and too hard or too directly.

“As for these murders, let’s conduct an investigation ourselves before forming any opinion about them. An inquiry will amuse us”—I found that a strange choice of word but kept quiet—“and besides, Le Bon once did me a favor, and I’m not ungrateful. We’ll go and see the premises with our own eyes. I know G——, the Prefect of Police, and I can easily obtain the necessary permission.”

He did obtain it, and we went straight to the Rue Morgue. It is one of those wretched streets between Rue Richelieu and Rue Saint-Roch. We arrived late in the afternoon, since that part of the city is far from where we lived. The house was easy to find, as many people still stood across the street staring up at the closed shutters with pointless curiosity. It was an ordinary Parisian residence, with a gateway, and on one side a glassed-in watch box with a sliding window panel marking the concierge’s lodge. Before entering we walked up the street, turned down an alley, and, turning again, passed behind the building—Dupin all the while examining the entire neighborhood, as well as the house itself, with such painstaking attention that I couldn’t see any purpose in it.

We retraced our steps to the front door, rang, and, after presenting our credentials, were admitted by the officers in charge. We went upstairs into the room where Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s body had been found, and where both bodies still lay. The disorder of the room had been left as it was. I noticed nothing beyond what had been reported in the Gazette des Tribunaux. Dupin inspected everything, including the bodies of the victims. Then we went through the other rooms and out into the yard, a gendarme accompanying us the entire time."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7d910b3b56de94d2f9804eea","rewritten_text":"Those elderly, frail men were always seen by the public in the act of bowing, and people joked that after bowing a customer out, they kept bowing in the empty office until they bowed another customer in. The barrister was sharp enough to realize that the banker wouldn’t speak so strongly without the kind of confidence that borders on certainty. Unprepared for the huge pill he had to swallow, he managed it. “And now,” Mr. Stryver said, wagging his forensic forefinger at the Temple at large once he had swallowed it, “my escape from this mess is to prove you all wrong.” It was a trick from the repertoire of an Old Bailey tactician, and it always gave him great satisfaction. “You won’t get the chance to make me look wrong, young lady,” Mr. Stryver said; “I’ll take care of that myself.” So when Mr. Lorry arrived that night at as late as ten o’clock, Mr. Stryver, with piles of books and papers strewn about for effect, acted as though nothing weighed on his mind less than the morning’s subject. He even looked surprised to see Mr. Lorry, and appeared entirely distracted and preoccupied. “Well!” said the good-natured messenger after half an hour of fruitless attempts to steer him back to the subject. “I’ve been to Soho.” “To Soho?” Mr. Stryver echoed coolly. “Oh, of course! What am I thinking!” “And I’m confident,” Mr. Lorry said, “that my instincts during our conversation were correct. My view is confirmed, and I stand by my advice.” “Believe me,” Mr. Stryver replied with great friendliness, “I regret it for your sake, and for the poor father’s sake. I know it must be a painful topic for the family; let’s drop it.” “I don’t understand you,” Mr. Lorry said. “I’m sure you don’t,” Stryver said, nodding in a smoothing, concluding way. “Never mind, never mind.” “But it does matter,” Mr. Lorry insisted. “No it doesn’t; I promise you it doesn’t. I believed there was intelligence where there isn’t, and noble ambition where there is none, and now I’m relieved of my mistake, so no harm done. Young women have made such foolish choices many times before, and have regretted them in poverty and obscurity many times before. Unselfishly, I’m sorry things ended, because it would have hurt me from a worldly perspective; selfishly, I’m glad it ended, because it would have hurt me from a worldly perspective—in other words, it’s obvious there was nothing for me to gain.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"253b626d25bfdadc3a91fe03","rewritten_text":"In the acrid tirade against Chantilly that yesterday’s “Musée” carried, the satirist, having made some disgraceful jibes about the cobbler’s adopted stage-name, quoted a Latin line we ourselves have often discussed: “Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.” “I had mentioned to you that it referred to Orion, once written Urion; and, from certain barbed associations tied to that explanation, I knew it was impossible you could have forgotten. It followed that you would connect both notions—Orion and Chantilly. That you did make this connection I saw in the cast of the smile that flitted across your lips. You envisioned the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Up to then you had been leaning in your walk; now I watched you straighten to full height. I knew at once your thoughts had flown to Chantilly’s tiny stature. At that juncture I cut into your reflections to point out that, since he was such a diminutive fellow—that Chantilly—he ought rather to try the Théâtre des Variétés.” Not long after, we were scanning an evening issue of the “Gazette des Tribunaux,” when these paragraphs drew our eyes: “Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, about three o’clock, residents of the Quartier St. Roch were startled from sleep by a series of dreadful screams apparently emanating from the fourth floor of a house on the Rue Morgue, known to be occupied exclusively by Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After some delay, caused by an unsuccessful attempt to gain entrance in the usual way, the gate was forced with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors went in with two gendarmes. By this moment the cries had ended; but as the group took the first stairs, two or more rough voices in angry dispute were heard and seemed to come from the upper stories. On reaching the second landing, these sounds also ceased and everything fell utterly silent. The party divided and rushed through room after room. Arriving at a large back chamber on the fourth story—the door, found locked with the key inside, having been broken open—they were confronted by a sight that filled each witness with awe no less than horror. The room lay in the wildest confusion—furniture shattered and flung about every which way. There was only a single bedstead; its bedding had been stripped off and tossed to the center of the floor. Upon a chair rested a razor, smeared with blood.”}"}

content.text: {"request_id":"0125cf0d5a125755a00df20a","rewritten_text":"Mary never wrote to Bath herself; all the tedious and unsatisfying correspondence with Elizabeth was left to Anne. Breakfast had barely finished when Captain and Mrs. Harville and Captain Benwick joined them for their final walk around Lyme. They were supposed to leave for Uppercross by one o’clock, and until then intended to stay together and outdoors as long as possible. As soon as they reached the street, Anne found Captain Benwick drawing near her. Their conversation the night before had not discouraged him, and they walked side by side for some time, once again discussing Mr. Scott and Lord Byron, still unable—like any other two readers—to agree completely on either’s merits, until something caused a broad shift in the group and she suddenly had Captain Harville beside her instead. “Miss Elliot,” he said quietly, “you’ve done a good deed by making that poor man talk so much. I wish he could have company like yours more often. It’s bad for him, I know, to be shut up the way he is; but what can we do? We can’t separate.” “No,” Anne replied, “I can easily believe that to be impossible; but in time, perhaps—we both know what time can do for every sorrow. Remember, Captain Harville, that your friend is still a young mourner—only last summer, I’ve heard.” “Yes, indeed,” he said with a deep sigh, “only June.” “And he didn’t learn of it right away, perhaps.” “Not until the first week of August, when he came home from the Cape, newly placed on the Grappler. I was at Plymouth, dreading news of him; he sent letters, but the Grappler had orders for Portsmouth. The news had to reach him there, yet who could tell him? Not I. I’d rather have been hauled up to the yardarm. No one could do it except that good man”—he pointed toward Captain Wentworth. “The Laconia had reached Plymouth the week before; there was no danger she’d be sent out again. He accepted the risk of the rest: requested leave, but without waiting for the answer, traveled day and night to Portsmouth, immediately rowed out to the Grappler, and stayed with our poor friend for a week. That’s what he did, and no one else could have saved poor James. You can imagine, Miss Elliot, how dear he is to us!” Anne considered the question with perfect conviction and said as much as her feelings allowed and as much as Captain Harville could bear, for he was too moved to continue and, when he spoke again, the subject was entirely different."}

{"request_id":"db8ac683d25bcc037c91e68e","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced the room in anger. I stood ready to take whatever blame he threw at me. Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is absurd,” he said. “Even schoolboys couldn’t behave more irrationally.”

“You don’t understand,” Raymond answered. “This is part of a whole system—a plan of tyranny I will never accept. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the only slave in the realm? My privacy invaded, my actions judged, my friends insulted? I’ll end it all at once. Bear witness.” He removed the star that marked his office from his chest and tossed it onto the table. “I renounce my office. I give up my power. Let anyone else take it!”

“Let whoever claims it,” cried Adrian, “prove himself your superior, or be judged so by the world. No such man exists in England. Know yourself, Raymond, and the anger will fade and your calm return. Only months ago, whenever we prayed for the prosperity of our country and ourselves, we also prayed for the Protector’s life, so tightly were our fortunes tied to yours. Your time was devoted to our welfare; your ambition was our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, founded institutions, and made the land fertile. The powerful and unjust trembled before your tribunal, and the poor and oppressed rose like dawn-lit flowers under your protection.

“How can you wonder that we are shocked and mourning when all this seems lost? But no, this bitter mood has already passed. Take up your duties again; your supporters will cheer you, your enemies will be quiet, and our love, respect, and loyalty will once more surround you. Control yourself, Raymond, and the world will yield.”

“All this would make sense if you were addressing someone else,” Raymond muttered. “Learn the lesson yourself, and you, the first noble in the land, may become its sovereign. You, the good and wise and just, could rule every heart. But I have learned—too soon for my own peace, too late for England—that I took on a task beyond me. I cannot rule myself. My passions govern me; even my slightest impulse is a tyrant. Do you think I gave up the Protectorate—yes, I have—during a moment of sulkiness? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that trinket again. I will never again load myself with the weight of care and misery signified by that insignia.”"}

{"request_id":"b68e89e136c01735e78911ff","rewritten_text":"Country folk, butchers, drovers, hawkers, boys, thieves, idlers, and vagabonds of every low sort merged into one mass; the whistling drovers, barking dogs, the bellowing and lunging oxen, the bleating sheep, the pigs grunting and squealing, the hawkers’ calls, the shouts, curses, and fights on every side; the bells ringing and voices roaring out of every public house; the jostling, shoving, driving, beating, whooping, and yelling; the hideous, clashing noise echoing from every corner of the market; and the unwashed, unshaven, filthy, ragged figures constantly rushing in and out of the throng made it a deafening, dizzying scene that overwhelmed the senses.

Mr. Sikes, hauling Oliver after him, shouldered his way through the thickest part of the crowd and paid very little attention to the countless sights and sounds that amazed the boy. He nodded a few times to passing friends, and, turning down the invitations to take an early drink, pushed straight ahead until they had left the uproar behind and made their way through Hosier Lane into Holborn.

“Now, youngster!” said Sikes, glancing up at St. Andrew’s Church clock, “just about seven! Step it up. Come on, don’t start lagging already, Lazy-legs!”

Sikes jerked his young companion’s wrist as he spoke. Oliver picked up his pace into a hesitant trot, somewhere between a fast walk and a run, and did his best to match the burglar’s long strides.

They kept up this pace until they passed Hyde Park Corner and were heading for Kensington. Then Sikes eased off until an empty cart some distance behind caught up. Seeing “Hounslow” painted on it, he asked the driver, as politely as he could manage, for a ride as far as Isleworth.

“Hop in,” said the man. “Is that your boy?”

“Yes, he’s mine,” Sikes answered, staring hard at Oliver and slipping his hand into the pocket where the pistol was.

“Your father walks a bit too fast for you, doesn’t he, lad?” the driver asked, noticing Oliver was out of breath.

“Not at all,” Sikes cut in. “He’s used to it. Here, hold my hand, Ned. Up you go!”

With that, he helped Oliver into the cart. The driver pointed to a pile of sacks and told him to lie down there and rest.

As they passed each mile marker, Oliver grew more and more puzzled about where his companion planned to take him. Kensington, Hammersmith, Chiswick, Kew Bridge, Brentford—all slipped by, yet they kept going just as steadily as if the journey had only begun."}

{"request_id":"a9ec9abcd05a5614325f216c","rewritten_text":"Once everything was settled both amicably and to their satisfaction, they ceremoniously sealed the contract with another teacup of peppermint cordial, which was all the more necessary given how fluttery and agitated the lady felt. As she finished the drink, she told Mr. Bumble about the old woman’s death.

“Very good,” said the gentleman, sipping his peppermint. “I’ll stop by Sowerberry’s on my way home and tell him to send over in the morning. Was that what frightened you, my love?”

“It wasn’t anything specific, dear,” the lady answered evasively.

“It must have been something, my love,” Mr. Bumble pressed. “Won’t you tell your own B.?”

“Not now,” she replied. “One of these days. After we’re married, dear.”

“After we’re married!” exclaimed Mr. Bumble. “It wasn’t any impertinence from any of those male paupers that—”

“No, no, love!” the lady interrupted quickly.

“If I thought it was,” Mr. Bumble went on, “if I thought any one of them had dared to lift his vulgar eyes to that lovely face—”

“They wouldn’t have dared, love,” she answered.

“They’d better not!” said Mr. Bumble, clenching his fists. “Let me see any man, parish or extraparish, presume to try it, and I can promise he wouldn’t try it twice!”

Without those colorful gestures, the statement might not have sounded like much of a compliment. But since Mr. Bumble accompanied the warning with several martial flourishes, she was deeply moved by this proof of devotion and declared admiringly that he was a regular dove.

The dove promptly flipped up his coat collar and set his cocked hat on his head, and after exchanging a long, loving embrace with his future bride, he once more faced the cold night wind. He paused for a few minutes in the men’s ward to scold the paupers a bit, just to reassure himself that he possessed the necessary harshness for the workhouse-master’s job. Satisfied with his qualifications, Mr. Bumble left the building in high spirits, buoyed by bright visions of future promotion, which occupied his thoughts until he reached the undertaker’s shop.

Mr. and Mrs. Sowerberry were out for tea and supper, and since Noah Claypole rarely took on more exertion than was required for eating and drinking, the shop remained open though it was past closing time. Mr. Bumble rapped his cane on the counter several times; receiving no response and seeing light shining through the glass window of the little back parlor, he boldly peered in to see what was happening—and when he saw it, he was significantly surprised."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ccc405825c3059cd023fc172","rewritten_text":"Back in my era, in my own land, the revenue was raised through imposts, and the citizen liked to imagine the foreign importer footed the bill, which comforted him; yet the truth was, the American people themselves paid it, shared so evenly that the yearly cost to the hundred-millionaire and to the day laborer’s nursing infant was identical—each shelled out six dollars. Nothing could be more equal than that, I suppose. Now, Scotland and Ireland paid tribute to Arthur, and the combined population of the British Isles totaled just under a million. A mechanic’s daily wage was three cents when he had to meet his own living expenses. By that reckoning, the national government’s budget came to ninety thousand dollars a year, or roughly two hundred and fifty a day. So by replacing gold with nickels during a king’s-evil ceremony, I harmed nobody, displeased nobody, delighted everyone involved, and trimmed four-fifths off that day’s government expenditure—saving as much as eight hundred thousand dollars would have been in my American times. For that substitution I tapped wisdom from a very distant source—the wisdom of my boyhood—for the genuine statesman scorns no wisdom, however humble its origin: as a youngster, I always hoarded my pennies and donated buttons to the foreign missions. The buttons suited the ignorant savage as well as coins did, the coins suited me better than buttons; everybody was pleased, and nobody suffered.\n\nMarinel handled the sufferers one by one. He examined each applicant; if the fellow couldn’t meet the standard he was sent away; if he could, he was passed on to the king. A priest intoned, “They shall lay their hands on the sick, and they shall recover.” Then the king stroked the sores while the reading went on; at last, the patient graduated, received his nickel—with the king slipping it on a cord about his neck—and was dismissed. Would you suppose that would heal? It most certainly did. Any ritual will cure, provided the patient’s faith in it is firm. Near Astolat stood a chapel where the Virgin had once appeared to a girl who pastured geese nearby—the girl swore it herself—and they raised the chapel there and hung a painting depicting the miracle—a picture you’d think dangerous for a sick person to approach; yet, on the contrary, thousands of the lame and the ill came annually, prayed before it, and departed hale and sound; and even the healthy could gaze upon it and live."}

content.text: {"request_id":"33055f131a9cf4fc56348d63","rewritten_text":"The mental traits we describe as analytical are themselves difficult to dissect. We recognize them only through their results. What we do know, among other things, is that for someone who possesses them to excess, they become a source of intense enjoyment. Just as a strong man rejoices in his physical prowess, taking delight in exercises that set his muscles in motion, the analyst glories in the moral activity that untangles. He takes pleasure even in the smallest task that lets him exercise his talent. He loves riddles, puzzles, hieroglyphs, showing in each solution a level of sharpness that seems uncanny to the ordinary mind. His results, born from pure method, seem to be intuition itself.\n\nThe ability to solve things may be greatly strengthened by studying mathematics, especially that highest branch which, unfairly and merely because of its backward workings, has been called analysis, as if it deserves the title above all others. Yet to calculate is not the same as to analyze. A chess player, for example, calculates without needing to analyze. It follows that the influence of chess on mental character is greatly misunderstood. I am not writing a treatise now, but only prefacing a somewhat peculiar story with a few random observations; so I’ll take the opportunity to say that the higher powers of the reflective mind are more thoroughly and more usefully exercised by the modest game of checkers than by all the elaborate fuss of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different, odd ways and have various values, complexity is mistaken (a common error) for depth. Attention is taxed to the utmost. If it lapses for a moment, an oversight occurs that leads to harm or defeat. Since the possible moves are not just numerous but intertwined, the chances of such mistakes multiply; in nine cases out of ten it is the more focused rather than the more perceptive player who wins. In checkers, on the other hand, where the moves are uniform and have little variation, the likelihood of a slip is reduced, and because attention is far less occupied, any advantage gained by either player comes from superior sharpness. To be less abstract, imagine a game of checkers reduced to four kings, where, of course, no blunder is expected. It’s obvious that victory here (assuming both players are equally matched) can be decided only by some exquisite move, the result of a strong exertion of intellect."}

Well-seasoned wood is a costly commodity, sir; and all the iron handles come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” observed Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its inconveniences. A reasonable profit is, naturally, allowable.”

“Exactly so, exactly so,” returned the undertaker; “and if I fail to gain on this or that specific article, I make it up in the long run, you understand—he! he! he!”

“Precisely,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must state,” the undertaker resumed, picking up the thread of comments the beadle had stopped, “though I must state, Mr. Bumble, I labor under one major drawback: namely, that the stout folk are the first to depart. Those who have lived better and paid rates for years are the earliest to sink when they enter the house; and let me assure you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches beyond one’s estimate cuts deeply into one’s profits, particularly when there’s a family to maintain, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry delivered this with the proper indignation of a man mistreated, and as Mr. Bumble sensed it cast something of a slur on the parish’s honor, he decided to shift the topic. Oliver Twist being foremost in his thoughts, he made him the subject.

“By the bye,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t happen to know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A parochial ’prentice who is now a dead weight; a veritable millstone, if I may say, about the parochial throat? Favorable terms, Mr. Sowerberry, favorable terms?” As he spoke, Mr. Bumble lifted his cane to the bill above and tapped three distinct times on the words “five pounds,” printed there in Roman capitals of enormous size.

“Gadso!” exclaimed the undertaker, catching Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That’s precisely what I intended to mention to you. You know—dear me, what a remarkably elegant button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I deem it rather handsome,” replied the beadle, casting a proud glance downward at the large brass buttons adorning his coat. “The die matches the parochial seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and bruised man. The board presented it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I recall putting it on for the first time to attend the inquest on that reduced tradesman who perished in a doorway at midnight.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"711ab0b4eee965b2aae0b073","rewritten_text":"The stupor and shock caused by this sudden change in my situation were, perhaps, the parts of the adventure hardest to explain. The upheaval itself was natural and bound to happen, and I had long expected it once I reached that exact point in my voyage where the planet’s pull would give way to the satellite’s—in other words, where the balloon would feel less gravity from the earth than from the moon. Still, I had been fast asleep and woke with my senses in disorder to face a very startling sight, one I knew would come but not at that precise instant. The shift must have been smooth and gradual, and it is far from certain that, even if I had been awake, I would have felt any sign of upside-down change—no discomfort, no disturbance of my body or equipment.\n\nIt almost goes without saying that once I truly grasped my situation and shook off the terror that had taken hold of my soul, my first thoughts turned entirely to the moon’s general appearance. It stretched beneath me like a map, and though I believed it was still some distance away, the grooves and markings on its surface stood out to me with astonishing and inexplicable clarity. What struck me first was the total absence of ocean, sea, lake, river—any water at all—which seemed the strangest part of its geology. Yet, oddly enough, I saw vast level plains that looked distinctly alluvial, even though most of the visible hemisphere was packed with countless volcanic mountains, cone-shaped and more like artificial bulges than natural ones. The tallest rose no more than three and three-quarter miles straight up, but a map of the Campi Phlegraei volcanic regions would give your Excellencies a better idea of their layout than any weak description I could offer. Most of the mountains were clearly erupting, and they made me acutely aware of their rage and force through the repeated thunder of the so-called meteoric stones that now flew upward past the balloon with increasingly frightening speed."}

{"request_id":"ee972bdfc14e60d41c557872","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was greatly troubled by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the genial peer remained resolute and ultimately persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift bestowed by the ghost. When, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire appeared at the Queen’s first drawing-room following her wedding, her jewels drew universal admiration. For Virginia was given the coronet—the due of all exemplary little American girls—and married her boy-lover as soon as he reached his majority. They were both so attractive and so devoted that everyone rejoiced in the match, save for the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had hoped to secure the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had even held three costly dinner-parties to snare him, and, oddly enough, Mr. Otis himself. Though Mr. Otis was very fond of the young Duke personally, in principle he disapproved of titles, confessing that he feared ‘lest the true principles of republican simplicity might be lost amid the enervating influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy.’ His protests, however, were entirely overborne, and I daresay that, as he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter on his arm, there was not a prouder man anywhere in England.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went down to Canterville Chase, and the next afternoon strolled to the lonely churchyard beside the pine-woods. Much difficulty had arisen at first regarding the inscription on Sir Simon’s tomb, but it was finally settled to mark it simply with the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess had brought some exquisite roses, which she scattered upon the grave, and after they had lingered there awhile they wandered into the crumbling chancel of the ancient abbey. There the Duchess seated herself on a fallen pillar, while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up into her lovely eyes. Suddenly he flung away the cigarette, clasped her hand, and said, ‘Virginia, a wife ought to have no secrets from her husband.’

‘Dear Cecil! I keep nothing back from you.’

‘Yes, you do,’ he replied with a smile. ‘You have never told me what occurred when you were shut in with the ghost.’

‘I have never told anyone, Cecil,’ Virginia answered gravely."}

content.text: {"request_id":"82495d068e78b9bb09469755","rewritten_text":"The next day the ghost felt very weak and tired. The terrible excitement of the last four weeks was finally catching up with him. His nerves were completely shattered, and he jumped at the slightest noise. For five days he stayed in his room and at last decided to give up on the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family didn’t want it, they clearly didn’t deserve it. They were obviously people stuck on a low, material level of existence and unable to appreciate the symbolic value of sensory phenomena. The matter of ghostly apparitions and the growth of astral bodies was, of course, quite different and not really under his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week and to gibber from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesdays of every month, and he did not see how he could honorably escape these obligations. It was true his life had been very wicked, but on the other hand he was extremely conscientious in every matter relating to the supernatural. So for the next three Saturdays he went down the corridor as usual between midnight and three o’clock, taking every possible precaution to avoid being heard or seen. He took off his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old worm-eaten boards, wore a huge black velvet cloak, and carefully used the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit it took a good deal of effort for him to consider this last form of protection. However, one night while the family were at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and carried off the bottle. He felt a little humiliated at first, but then was sensible enough to realize that much could be said in favor of the invention, and to a certain degree it served his purpose. Still, despite all his efforts, he was not left in peace. Strings were constantly stretched across the corridor, and he tripped over them in the dark. Once, while dressed for the role of “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he slipped badly after stepping onto a butter-slide the twins had built from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This last insult enraged him so much that he resolved to make one final attempt to assert his dignity and social standing. He decided to visit the insolent young Etonians the following night in his famous character of “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.”\n\nHe had not appeared in this disguise for more than seventy years, not since he had frightened the charming Lady Barbara Modish so much with it that she immediately broke off her engagement to the current Lord Canterville’s grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with the handsome Jack Castleton, saying nothing on earth would make her marry into a family that allowed such a horrible phantom to pace up and down the terrace at twilight."}

{"request_id":"947c540ccb66857475b0ee4d","rewritten_text":"“But,” said I, handing back the slip, “I am as lost as before. Even if the treasure of Golconda lay waiting upon my solution of this riddle, I am convinced I could never win it.”

“And yet,” Legrand replied, “the answer is far less formidable than one might conclude from a hurried glance at the symbols. These marks, as any person could quickly suspect, compose a cipher—in other words, they contain a meaning. Still, judging from what is known of Kidd, I could not imagine him equal to devising any very intricate cryptograph. I concluded, from the start, that it was of a simple kind—one which, to the rough mind of a mariner, would appear utterly hopeless without a key.”

“And you actually unriddled it?”

“With ease; I have unraveled others ten thousand times more perplexing. Circumstances, along with a certain inclination of mind, have led me to take interest in such puzzles, and it is doubtful that human ingenuity can frame a cipher beyond the reach of human wit, properly applied. Once the characters were connected and legible, I scarcely gave a thought to the difficulty of interpreting them.”

“In this instance—indeed, in all cases of secret writing—the first inquiry concerns the language of the cipher; for the methods of solution, particularly for the simpler kinds, depend upon, and vary with, the nature of the idiom. Generally, nothing remains but trial, guided by probability, of every tongue known to the solver, until the right one is hit upon. Yet, with the cipher before us, every difficulty vanished with the signature. The pun upon the name ‘Kidd’ can be appreciated in no language except English. Without that clue, I should have begun with Spanish and French, being the languages in which a pirate of the Spanish Main would most likely hide such a secret. As it turned out, I deemed the cryptograph English.”

“You notice there are no spaces between words. Had there been, the task would have proved comparatively simple. I would then have started by collating and analyzing the shorter words, and, had a single-letter word appeared—as is very likely—(a or I, for instance,) I should have felt the solution assured. But lacking divisions, my first move was to determine the most common letters, and those least often appearing.”"}

{"request_id":"671603d258373ecadfb5cd79","rewritten_text":"Though his character and disposition differed from hers, they would have satisfied all her hopes. Such a marriage must have proved advantageous to both: her lightness and vivacity might have softened his temper and refined his manners; while his discernment, experience, and worldly knowledge could have bestowed on her a more substantial good.

But the admiring public was not to be instructed by such an example of true marital felicity. Another alliance, incompatible with the former and of a very different nature, was on the point of taking place in their family.

She could not conceive how Wickham and Lydia would ever support themselves with anything like comfort. Yet she could readily predict how little real happiness could fall to a pair united only because desire had overpowered principle.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote again to his brother. To Mr. Bennet’s thanks he replied briefly, assuring him how eager he always felt to promote any member of his family; and he ended with entreating that the topic never be mentioned to him again. The chief aim of his letter was to notify them that Mr. Wickham had resolved to resign his post in the militia.

"It has long been my wish that he should do so," he continued, "as soon as his marriage was determined. I trust you will agree with me that his removal from that corps is highly advisable both for him and my niece. Mr. Wickham intends entering the Regulars, and he still counts among his former companions some who are able and willing to aid his advancement. He has been promised an ensigncy in General ----'s regiment, now stationed in the north. It is advantageous that it should be so distant from this district. He gives reasonable assurances; and I hope that among different associates, where each must maintain a reputation, they will both show greater prudence. I have written to Colonel Forster to acquaint him with our arrangements and to request that he satisfy Mr. Wickham’s various creditors in and around Brighton with promises of prompt payment, for which I have pledged myself. And will you undertake the trouble of giving the same assurances to his creditors in Meryton, whose names I shall attach according to his report? He has set down all his debts; I trust he has not misled us. Haggerston has our orders, and everything will be settled within a week. They will then join his regiment, unless they are first invited to Longbourn; and Mrs. Gardiner tells me my niece is ardently desirous of seeing you all before she leaves the south.""}

{"request_id":"2ff4a0d0a006ac8f14479f27","rewritten_text":"If not for me, he never would have been released. Morgan le Fay hated him with all her heart, and she never would have softened toward him. Still, his offense came from carelessness rather than true wickedness. He had said she had red hair. Well, she did, but that was no way to describe it. When red-haired people belong to a higher social class, their hair is called auburn.

Think about this: among these forty-seven prisoners, there were five whose names, offenses, and imprisonment dates were no longer known. One woman and four men, all bent, wrinkled, and mentally wasted elders. They themselves had forgotten these facts long ago; at best they had vague guesses about them, nothing clear and nothing they would tell the same way twice. The line of priests whose duty it had been to pray daily with the prisoners and remind them that God had placed them there for some wise purpose, and to teach them that patience, humility, and submission to oppression were what He loved to see in people of lower status, had traditions about these poor ruins of humanity, but nothing else. These stories went only so far, describing the length of their imprisonment but not the offenses. Even with tradition, the only thing certain was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years; how much longer they had been kept in darkness could not even be guessed. The king and queen knew nothing about these poor creatures except that they were heirlooms, assets inherited, along with the throne, from the previous rulers. Nothing of their history had been passed along with their bodies, so the inheriting owners considered them worthless and felt no interest in them. I asked the queen:

“Then why in the world didn’t you set them free?”

The question stumped her. She didn’t know why she hadn’t; the idea had never even entered her mind. So there she was, unknowingly predicting the real history of future prisoners of the Castle d’If. It now seemed obvious to me that, with her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were simply property—nothing more, nothing less. When we inherit property, it doesn’t occur to us to throw it away, even when we don’t value it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open world and the glare of the afternoon sun—first blindfolding them, out of kindness to eyes unused to light—they were a striking sight. Skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, pathetic horrors, every one of them; the truest possible children of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"943b0601681a935059aa4acc","rewritten_text":"Biddy was crying; the garden growing darker, the lane, and the stars coming out were all blurred to me as well.

“Nothing was ever found out, Biddy?”

“Nothing.”

“Do you know what’s become of Orlick?”

“Judging by the color of his clothes, I’d say he’s working in the quarries.”

“Then you’ve seen him, of course?—Why are you staring at that dark tree in the lane?”

“I saw him there the night she died.”

“That wasn’t the last time, was it, Biddy?”

“No; I’ve seen him there since we’ve been walking here.—It’s no use,” said Biddy, putting her hand on my arm as I was about to run out, “you know I wouldn’t deceive you; he was there for barely a minute, and now he’s gone.”

My anger flared at learning that she was still being stalked by that man, and I felt relentless toward him. I told her so, and that I would spend whatever money or effort it took to drive him out of the region. Little by little she guided me into calmer conversation, and she told me how Joe loved me and never complained about anything—she didn’t have to say “about me”; I knew what she meant—always doing his duty in his own way, with strong hands, a quiet voice, and a gentle heart.

“Honestly, you could hardly praise him too much,” I said. “And Biddy, we have to talk about these things often, since I’ll be down here a lot now. I’m not leaving poor Joe alone.”

Biddy didn’t say a word.

“Biddy, don’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Besides your calling me Mr. Pip—which seems in poor taste, Biddy—what do you mean?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, with a righteous air, “I insist on knowing what you mean by this.”

“By this?” said Biddy.

“Don’t repeat me,” I snapped. “You didn’t used to do that, Biddy.”

“Didn’t used to!” cried Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! ‘Used to’!”

Well, I thought it best to drop that point too. After another silent turn in the garden, I returned to the main subject.

“Biddy,” I said, “I made a comment about coming down here often to see Joe, and you answered with a very pointed silence. Be so kind, Biddy, as to tell me why.”

“Are you quite sure, then, that you will come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping in the narrow garden path and looking at me beneath the stars with a clear, honest gaze."}

{"request_id":"37e3b39c9ea3c7e1d6e7e3fa","rewritten_text":"“Joseph! Joseph!” He shook his head and tapped his temple, as if lamenting Joseph’s shortcomings.

“But my dear young friend,” said Mr. Pumblechook, “you must be famished, you must be worn out. Sit down. Here’s a chicken brought over from the Boar, here’s a tongue from the same, here are one or two little extras from the Boar, which I trust you won’t disdain. But do I,” said Mr. Pumblechook, popping up the instant he had sat, “behold before me the very one I sported with in his days of cheerful infancy? And may I—may I—?”

The question was whether he might shake hands. I consented, he did so with great zeal, and then re-seated himself.

“Here’s wine,” said Mr. Pumblechook. “Let us drink, Thanks to Fortune, and may she continue to select her darlings with equal wisdom! And yet I cannot,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “look upon One—and likewise drink to One—without once more expressing—May I—may I—?”

I told him he might, and he shook hands again, drained his glass, and inverted it. I followed suit; and if I had upended myself before drinking, the wine could scarcely have rushed to my head faster.

Mr. Pumblechook carved the liver wing for me, and the prime slice of tongue (none of those eccentric No Thoroughfares of Pork now), and scarcely regarded his own plate. “Ah! poultry, poultry! Little you dreamed,” said Mr. Pumblechook, addressing the bird, “when you were a small chick, what awaited you. Little you thought you’d be sustenance in this humble home for one who—Call it a weakness if you choose,” said Mr. Pumblechook, rising again, “but may I? may I—?”

It became needless to repeat that he might, so he simply did it. How he managed it so often without slashing himself with my knife, I cannot tell.

“And your sister,” he went on after a spell of steady eating, “who had the honour of rearing you by hand! It’s a melancholy picture, to think she’s no longer capable of wholly comprehending the honour. May—”

I saw him preparing to make another attempt at me, and I stopped him.

“We’ll drink her health,” I said.

“Ah!” cried Mr. Pumblechook, leaning back in his chair, limp with admiration, “that’s how you know ’em, sir!” (Whoever Sir might be, it certainly wasn’t myself, and nobody else was there.) “That’s how you spot the noble-hearted, sir!”"}

{"request_id":"bde0df7ba5bfe6ea834821cb","rewritten_text":"She would be settled among those who loved her and had more sense than she did; secluded enough to be safe, yet busy enough to stay cheerful. She would never be drawn into temptation or left exposed to it. She would be respectable and content; and Emma admitted she was the luckiest creature alive to have inspired such steady, persistent affection in such a man—or, if not quite the luckiest, then second only to herself.

Harriet, inevitably occupied with the Martins, spent less and less time at Hartfield; which was not to be lamented. The closeness between her and Emma had to fade; their friendship had to change into a calmer goodwill; and luckily, what should happen and must happen seemed already beginning, in the most gradual, natural way.

Before September ended, Emma accompanied Harriet to church and saw her hand placed in Robert Martin’s with such complete satisfaction that no memories, not even of Mr. Elton standing before them, could lessen it. Perhaps, indeed, at that moment she barely saw Mr. Elton except as the clergyman whose blessing at the altar might next fall on herself. Robert Martin and Harriet Smith, the last of the three couples to become engaged, were the first to marry.

Jane Fairfax had already left Highbury and returned to the comforts of her beloved home with the Campbells. The Mr. Churchills were also in town, waiting only for November.

The month between was the one Emma and Mr. Knightley chose, as far as they dared. They had decided their wedding should take place while John and Isabella were still at Hartfield, so they could enjoy a fortnight’s trip to the seaside, which was the plan. John and Isabella, and every other friend, agreed it was wise. But Mr. Woodhouse—how could he be persuaded to consent? He had never mentioned their marriage except as something far off.

When the subject was first raised, he was so miserable that they nearly lost hope. A second mention, though, caused less pain. He began to think it would happen and that he could not stop it—an encouraging step toward acceptance. Still, he was not content. In fact, he seemed so unhappy that his daughter’s courage faltered. She could not bear to see him suffer, to know he imagined himself neglected; and although her reason nearly accepted the assurance from both Mr. Knightleys that once the event was over his distress would soon fade, she hesitated—she could not move forward."}

{"request_id":"46d17a25ae7a43328cb2f47f","rewritten_text":"He made sure she understood that Frank entertained the highest admiration of her—considered her exceedingly lovely and altogether delightful; and with so much speaking in his favour, she felt she ought not to condemn him too severely. As Mrs. Weston remarked, “all young people will have their little fancies.”

Among his new Surry acquaintances, there was one individual who showed far less indulgence. Generally, throughout the parishes of Donwell and Highbury, he was regarded with much fairness; generous allowances were granted for the small irregularities of so handsome a youth—one who smiled so readily and bowed so gracefully. Yet there was one spirit not to be appeased, despite all the smiles and bows—Mr. Knightley. The story was conveyed to him at Hartfield; he made no comment at first; but Emma soon heard him mutter to himself over the newspaper he held, “Hum! precisely the frivolous, foolish fellow I always imagined.” She was nearly affronted; still, a moment’s study convinced her he had spoken merely to ease his own feelings, not to provoke; thus she let it go.

Though Mr. and Mrs. Weston brought unwelcome news in one regard, their visit that morning proved especially well-timed in another. Something occurred while they were at Hartfield that made Emma wish for their counsel; and, fortunately, it was exactly the counsel they offered.

This was the occurrence: the Coles had been settled in Highbury for several years, and were excellent people—amiable, generous, and unassuming; but on the other hand, they were of humble stock, in trade, and only moderately genteel. When they first came into the neighbourhood, they lived within their means, quietly, entertaining little, and that little inexpensively; but within the last year or two, they had gained a substantial increase of fortune—the house in London had yielded greater profits, and luck in general had favoured them. With their growing wealth, their ambitions expanded; they felt the want of a larger house, and a desire for more company. They enlarged their residence, increased their servants, and heightened every expense; by now, in fortune and manner of living, they stood second only to the family at Hartfield. Their delight in society and their new dining-room led everyone to expect they would host dinner parties; and a few gatherings, chiefly of single gentlemen, had already occurred. As for inviting the more established and best families, Emma hardly believed they would dare—neither Donwell, nor Hartfield, nor Randalls. Nothing could induce her to accept, even if they tried; and she lamented that her father’s well-known habits would make her refusal carry less significance than she desired."}

content.text: {"request_id":"ab508893988d033687f831a9","rewritten_text":"Saturday nights in our village had a pleasant sense of tidying up and pausing quietly before starting life anew, and that feeling pushed Joe to stay out half an hour longer than usual. As that extra half hour and his rum and water ran out together, Joe stood up to leave and took my hand. “Hold on a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the strange man. “I think I have a shiny new shilling somewhere, and if I do, the boy shall have it.” He dug through a handful of small coins, wrapped the shilling in crumpled paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Remember, it’s yours.” I thanked him and stared far beyond what was polite, clinging to Joe. He wished Joe good night, he wished Mr. Wopsle good night (who left with us), and he gave me only a glance with his aiming eye—no, not even a glance, because he closed it, yet you can do wonders with an eye by hiding it. On the way home, if I had been in the mood to talk, I would have had to do it all myself. Mr. Wopsle parted from us at the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe kept his mouth wide open all the way home to rinse the rum out with as much air as possible. But I was too stunned by this reminder of my old wrong and my old acquaintance, and I could think of nothing else. My sister was not in a very bad temper when we came into the kitchen, and Joe felt bold enough, that rare mood of hers, to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll be bound,” Mrs. Joe said with triumph. “Otherwise he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.” I took it out of the paper, and it turned out to be good. “But what is this?” Mrs. Joe cried, dropping the shilling and grabbing the paper. “Two one-pound notes?” Nothing less than two thick, sweaty one-pound notes that seemed to have kept close company with every cattle market in the county. Joe snatched up his hat again and ran to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, sure the man would be gone. Soon Joe came back, saying the man had indeed disappeared, but that he had left a message at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

content.text: {"request_id":"8471ebabf9b97c06a9fff36a","rewritten_text":"April 19th. Early this morning, around nine o’clock, when the moon’s surface loomed dangerously near and my anxiety was at its height, the pump of my condenser finally showed unmistakable signs that the atmosphere had changed. By ten I had good grounds to think the air had grown considerably denser. By eleven the apparatus required very little effort; and at noon, after some hesitation, I risked unscrewing the tourniquet. Finding no ill effects, I threw open the gum-elastic chamber and detached it from the car. As was predictable, cramps and a fierce headache immediately followed that rash, perilous experiment. However, since these and other breathing difficulties were not severe enough to endanger my life, I resolved to endure them as best I might, trusting that I was rapidly leaving them behind in my swift approach to the denser layers near the moon. Still, the descent remained violently rapid; and it soon became alarmingly evident that, while I had likely not erred in expecting an atmosphere dense in proportion to the satellite’s mass, I had erred in assuming its density, even at the surface, would suffice to uphold the heavy load in my balloon’s car. It ought to have done so, and to the same degree it does at Earth’s surface, if we suppose true the ratio of gravity to atmospheric condensation on either world. That it failed was demonstrated by my headlong fall; the cause, I can only attribute to those possible geological upheavals previously mentioned. In any case, I was now almost upon the planet, plunging with dreadful speed. Not wasting an instant, I cast overboard first my ballast, then the water-kegs, then the condensing apparatus and gum-elastic chamber, and finally every item inside the car. All in vain. I still plunged with ghastly velocity, now less than half a mile above the surface. As a last resort, after shedding coat, hat, and boots, I severed the car itself—which was quite heavy—from the balloon, and clung with both hands to the net-work. I scarcely had time to note that the entire landscape, as far as I could see, was thickly dotted with tiny dwellings before I pitched headlong into the heart of a bizarre-looking city and into the midst of a vast crowd of ugly little beings. Not one uttered a word or made the slightest move to help me; instead they stood like a troop of idiots, grinning absurdly, arms akimbo, and eyeing me and my balloon with sidelong glances."}

{"request_id":"7a3666d39a77e6ded0ad9b15","rewritten_text":"“You have not been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy the evening parties here.”

“Oh! no. They have nothing for me. I do not play cards.”

“You did not before, I know. You used to dislike cards; but time changes many things.”

“I am not yet so changed,” Anne exclaimed, then stopped, worried about how her words might be taken. After a short pause he said, as if from sudden feeling, “It truly is a long time. Eight years and a half is a long time.”

Whether he meant to say more was left for Anne to imagine later in calmer moments; for while his words still echoed, she was interrupted by Henrietta, eager to use the spare time to go out, urging her companions to hurry before anyone else arrived.

They had to get ready. Anne talked as if she were perfectly willing, and tried to look so; but she felt that if Henrietta had known the regret and reluctance in her heart as she left that chair, as she prepared to leave the room, she would have felt, in all her own certainty about her cousin’s affection, a reason to pity her.

Yet their preparations were suddenly stopped. Alarming sounds were heard; other visitors were arriving, and the door opened for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose presence seemed to chill everyone. Anne felt an immediate heaviness, and wherever she looked she saw the same reaction. The warmth, ease, and cheerfulness of the room were over, replaced by stiff calm, forced silence, or flat conversation, to suit her father and sister’s heartless elegance. How painful to feel it was so!

Her jealous watchfulness was satisfied in one way. Captain Wentworth was acknowledged again by both, Elizabeth even more gracious than before. She spoke to him once, looked at him more than once. Elizabeth was, in fact, planning something important. Soon it became clear. After wasting a few minutes on polite nonsense, she began to give the invitation that was to cover all the remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; nothing formal.” It was all done very elegantly, and the cards she had ready, “Miss Elliot at home,” were laid on the table with a polite, inclusive smile to all, and one card and one smile more directly for Captain Wentworth. The truth was, Elizabeth had been in Bath long enough to understand the value of a man with his manner and appearance."}

{"request_id":"720a296dfe7607a53b14373c","rewritten_text":"She studied me sharply for a moment before asking quietly, “What do you want for them?”

“Only,” I replied, “that you wouldn’t lump them in with the others. They might share the same blood, but believe me, they’re not the same kind.”

Still watching me intently, Miss Havisham repeated, “What do you want for them?”

“I’m not clever enough,” I admitted, feeling myself flush a little, “to hide from you, even if I wished to, that I do want something. Miss Havisham, if you would spare the money to do my friend Herbert a lasting favor, which by its nature must be done without his knowledge, I can show you how.”

“Why must it be done without his knowing?” she asked, settling her hands on her stick so she could study me more closely.

“Because,” I said, “I began helping him over two years ago without his knowing, and I don’t want to be exposed. Why I can’t finish what I started, I can’t explain. It’s part of a secret that belongs to someone else, not me.”

She slowly turned her gaze from me to the fire. After staring at it for what felt like a long time in the stillness and dim candlelight, she was startled by a collapsing heap of red coals and looked back at me—first blankly, then with growing focus. Throughout, Estella kept knitting. When Miss Havisham had fully fixed her attention on me, she spoke as if no time had passed in our conversation: “What else?”

“Estella,” I said, turning to her and trying to steady my shaking voice, “you know I love you. You know I’ve loved you deeply for a long time.”

She raised her eyes to my face, her fingers still moving, her expression unchanged. I saw Miss Havisham glance between us.

“I would have said this sooner, if not for my long-standing misunderstanding. It made me hope Miss Havisham intended us for each other. While I believed you had no choice in it, I held back from speaking. But I must say it now.”

Still expressionless and still working her needles, Estella shook her head.

“I know,” I said in response. “I know. I have no hope of ever calling you mine, Estella.”"}

{"request_id":"53f2a893555e2fd74c1d3bb8","rewritten_text":"PS.—Do let me know about the bows. Jennings swears they are the latest thing.

Lord Arthur’s face grew so grave and woeful as he read the letter that the Duchess burst into fits of laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she exclaimed, “I shall never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what reply am I to make about the clock? I consider it an admirable invention, and I should be delighted to own one myself.”

“I don’t much care for them,” Lord Arthur answered with a melancholy smile, and, after kissing his mother, he quitted the room.

Upon reaching his chambers he threw himself on a sofa, and his eyes brimmed with tears. He had endeavoured with all his strength to commit this murder, yet twice he had failed, and through no fault of his own. He had tried to fulfil his duty, but it seemed Destiny herself had turned renegade. He felt oppressed by the sterility of good intentions, by the uselessness of striving to be noble. Perhaps it might be wisest to break off the marriage altogether. Sybil would suffer, admittedly, yet such suffering could hardly injure a nature so splendid as hers. As for him, what did it signify? There is always some war in which a man may fall, some cause to which he may devote his life, and since life held no delight for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny accomplish his fate; he would not raise a finger to aid her.

At half-past seven he dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he was compelled to dine in their company. Their trifling chatter and empty witticisms left him bored, and once the coffee appeared he excused himself with an invented engagement to escape. As he was leaving the club, the hall-porter handed him a letter. It came from Herr Winckelkopf, requesting him to call next evening to inspect an explosive umbrella that discharged the moment it was opened. It was the newest contrivance, fresh from Geneva. He tore the letter into shreds. He had resolved to attempt no further experiments. Then he strolled down to the Thames Embankment and sat for hours beside the river. The moon looked through a mane of tawny clouds like the eye of a lion, and countless stars bespangled the hollow sky, like gold dust strewn upon a purple dome. Now and again a barge swung out upon the muddy current and drifted with the tide, while the railway signals shifted from green to crimson as the trains shrieked across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"2c0452a0640bef78a699f0c7","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis, at Lady Canterville’s urgent request, had agreed to keep on. She gave them each a low curtsey as they stepped down and said in a quaint, old-fashioned tone, “I bid you welcome to Canterville Chase.” Following her, they walked through the grand Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room paneled in black oak, with a large stained-glass window at one end. Tea was laid out for them there, and after removing their wraps, they sat down and looked around while Mrs. Umney waited on them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor near the fireplace and, not realizing what it meant, said to Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” replied the old housekeeper quietly, “blood has been spilled on that spot.”

“How awful,” said Mrs. Otis. “I do not like bloodstains in a sitting room. It must be removed at once.”

The old woman smiled and, still speaking in that low, mysterious voice, said, “It is the blood of Lady Eleanore de Canterville, who was murdered on that very spot by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon lived nine more years and then vanished in very mysterious circumstances. His body has never been found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The bloodstain has been greatly admired by visitors and cannot be removed.”

“That is nonsense,” cried Washington Otis. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it up right away,” and before the terrified housekeeper could stop him, he knelt down and began scrubbing the floor with a small stick that looked like a black cosmetic. In a few moments no trace of the bloodstain remained.

“I knew Pinkerton would do it,” he said triumphantly, looking around at his admiring family, but as soon as he spoke a terrible flash of lightning lit the gloomy room, a violent peal of thunder made them all jump to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What a monstrous climate!” said the American Minister calmly, lighting a long cheroot. “I suppose the old country is so crowded they don’t have enough decent weather for everyone. I have always thought emigration is the only solution for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” cried Mrs. Otis, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge it to her like breakages,” answered the Minister. “She won’t faint after that,” and in a few moments Mrs. Umney indeed recovered."}

{"request_id":"9932b0c531de374e61c3933c","rewritten_text":"The party was split between two adjoining benches: Anne sat on the front one, and Mr. Elliot had maneuvered, with help from his friend Colonel Wallis, to take the seat beside her. Miss Elliot, surrounded by cousins and the focus of Colonel Wallis’s gallantry, felt perfectly satisfied.

Anne’s mind was in the ideal state for enjoying the evening; it was just the right level of engagement. She felt tender emotions, lively spirits, attentiveness to the scientific, and patience for the dull, and she had never enjoyed a concert more—at least through the first act. Towards its end, during the pause after an Italian song, she explained the lyrics to Mr. Elliot. They held the program between them.

“This,” she said, “is roughly the sense—or rather the meaning—of the words, since one mustn’t talk about the literal sense of an Italian love song; but it is as close to the meaning as I can manage, for I can’t claim to understand the language. I’m a very poor student of Italian.”

“Yes, yes, I see you are. You clearly know nothing at all. You have just enough knowledge of the language to translate on sight these convoluted, inverted Italian lines into clear, elegant English. You needn’t say anything more about being ignorant. Here’s proof enough.”

“I won’t argue against such kind politeness; still, I’d be sorry to be examined by a real expert.”

“I haven’t been visiting Camden Place for so long,” he replied, “without learning something about Miss Anne Elliot; and I consider her someone whose modesty hides half her gifts from the world, and whose accomplishments are so remarkable that her modesty would seem unnatural in any other woman.”

“For shame! For shame! This is too much flattery. I’ve forgotten what’s next,” she said, turning to the program.

“Perhaps,” Mr. Elliot murmured, “I’ve known your character longer than you suspect.”

“Indeed? How so? You could only have known me since I came to Bath, unless my family mentioned me beforehand.”

“I knew of you long before you came to Bath. I heard you described by people who knew you well. I’ve been acquainted with you in reputation for many years. Your appearance, your temperament, your accomplishments, your manner—they were all familiar to me.”

Mr. Elliot was not disappointed in the curiosity he aimed to spark. No one can resist the allure of such a mystery."}

{"request_id":"b9ec7dabbf828a5220abb866","rewritten_text":"Just past noon the boys borrowed a little skiff from a townsman who wasn’t home and set off right away. A few miles below Cave Hollow, Tom said, “Now you see how this bluff looks exactly the same all the way down from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood yards, nothing but identical bushes. But see that white patch up ahead where a landslide happened? That’s one of my markers. We’ll pull in now.”

They beached the skiff.

“Now, Huck, right where we’re standing you could touch the hole I crawled out of with a fishing pole. Try to find it.”

Huck searched all around and came up empty. Tom strutted into a dense clump of sumac and announced, “Here it is! Look at it, Huck; there isn’t a cozier hole in the whole county. You keep quiet about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I had to have a place like this, and figuring out where to find it was the hard part. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret—except we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in. You’ve got to have a gang or else there’s no style to it. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds grand, doesn’t it, Huck?”

“It sure does, Tom. Who do we rob?”

“Oh, pretty much anybody. We ambush folks—that’s the usual way.”

“And kill them?”

“No, not every time. We stash them in the cave till they pay ransom.”

“What’s ransom?”

“Money. You make them raise every bit they can from their friends, and if you’ve kept them a whole year and they still haven’t come up with it, then you kill them. That’s the general method. Only you never kill the women. You lock the women up, but don’t hurt them. They’re always beautiful and rich and scared stiff. You take their watches and jewelry, but you always take off your hat and talk polite. No one is as polite as robbers—you can see that in any book. The women end up falling for you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two they stop crying, and then you couldn’t get them to leave. If you drove them out, they’d spin right around and come back. That’s how it happens in all the stories.”

“It’s really prime, Tom. I think it beats being a pirate.”

“Yeah, it’s better in some ways because it’s close to home and circuses and all that.”

By then they had everything ready, and the boys climbed into the hole, Tom leading the way. They slogged to the far end of the tunnel, tied off their spliced kite strings, and pushed on."}

{"request_id":"c4bc7314fe8e7375ee4de162","rewritten_text":"At the center of this fissure I noticed a pale speck, though at first I could not tell what it might be. After readjusting the telescope’s focus, I looked once more and now discerned it to be a human skull.

“Upon this discovery I grew so confident that I considered the puzzle settled; for the phrase ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could point only to the skull’s location upon the tree, and ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ permitted but a single meaning when it came to seeking buried treasure. I realized the plan was to drop a bullet from the skull’s left eye, then draw a bee-line—meaning a straight line—from the nearest spot of the trunk through ‘the shot’ (the place where the bullet landed), and to extend that line for fifty feet. This would mark a fixed point—and beneath that spot I thought it at least plausible that some valuable deposit might be hidden.”

“All this,” I observed, “is extremely plain, and despite being clever, it remains straightforward and definite. After you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what occurred?”

“Why, having carefully noted the tree’s bearings, I set off for home. The moment I stepped away from ‘the devil’s seat,’ though, the circular opening vanished; no matter how I turned, I never glimpsed it again. What strikes me as the principal ingenuity in the whole affair is the fact—repeated trials assure me it is fact—that the circular gap can be seen from no other accessible viewpoint than the narrow ledge on the rock’s face.

“During this excursion to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel’ I was accompanied by Jupiter, who, I have no doubt, had noticed my absent manner for some weeks past and took special care not to leave me unguarded. But the next morning I rose very early, managed to elude him, and went into the hills to search for the tree. After much labor I located it. When I returned that night my valet threatened to flog me. Of the remainder of the adventure I believe you know as much as I do.”

“I suppose,” said I, “you missed the mark on the first digging attempt because Jupiter stupidly let the bug fall through the right instead of the left eye of the skull.”

“Exactly so. That error caused a difference of about two and a half inches in the ‘shot’—meaning the peg nearest the tree; and had the treasure lain beneath the ‘shot,’ the mistake would have mattered little. But the ‘shot’ and the tree’s nearest point served only to fix a line of direction; naturally, an error however slight at the start grew as we carried the line forward, and by the time we had reached fifty feet it had led us entirely astray.”"}
