content.text: {"request_id":"44c8da1e704f73ba07e3dfad","rewritten_text":"“Next, we built a wire fence.”  “A wire fence?”  “Yes. You hinted at the idea yourself, two or three years ago.”  “Oh, I remember—when the Church first tested its strength against us, then decided to wait for a better season. So, how did you set up the fence?”  “I run twelve extremely strong wires—bare, not insulated—from a large dynamo in the cave, a dynamo with only a positive brush and a negative brush.”  “Yes, that’s correct.”  “The wires leave the cave and enclose a circle of flat ground, a hundred yards across; they form twelve separate fences, ten feet apart—meaning twelve concentric circles—and their ends return to the cave.”  “Right; continue.”  “The fences are attached to heavy oak posts only three feet apart, and those posts are sunk five feet deep.”  “That’s sturdy.”  “Yes. The wires have no ground connection outside the cave. They go out from the dynamo’s positive brush; the negative brush is grounded; the other ends of the wires come back to the cave, and each one is grounded separately.”  “No, no, that won’t work!”  “Why not?”  “Too expensive—it wastes power. You need only one ground connection, through the negative brush. The other end of every wire has to be brought back into the cave and fastened separately, without any ground connection. Now note the efficiency. A cavalry charge storms the fence; you’re using no power and spending no money, because there’s only one ground connection until those horses hit the wire. The instant they touch it, they make contact with the negative brush through the ground and drop dead. Don’t you see? You don’t use energy until it’s needed; your lightning is waiting there like a loaded gun, but it doesn’t cost you a penny until you fire it. Ah yes, the single ground connection—”  “Of course! I can’t imagine how I missed that. It’s cheaper and more effective than the other setup, because if wires snap or tangle, it doesn’t matter.”  “No, especially if we have a sensor in the cave to disconnect the broken wire. All right, proceed. The Gatlings?”  “Yes—that’s taken care of. In the center of the innermost circle, on a broad platform six feet high, I’ve arranged a battery of thirteen Gatling guns and stocked plenty of ammunition.”  “Perfect. They cover every approach, and when the Church’s knights show up, there’ll be music. On the cliff edge above the cave—”  “I’ve put a wire fence there, too, and a Gatling gun.”"}

{"request_id":"c6abf92fe12eef690013e13d","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, will you? Oh, you precious fool!”

“It’s naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll end up strung up, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver answered.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. He grabbed the end of his neckerchief, held it straight up, dropped his head to his shoulder, and pushed a strangled sound through his teeth, giving a lively pantomime that made it plain that “being scragged” meant “being hanged.”

“That’s what it means,” said Charley. “Look at him staring, Jack! I’ve never seen such grand company as that boy; he’ll kill me with laughter, I swear he will.” Master Charley Bates, after another hearty laugh, picked up his pipe again, tears in his eyes.

“You’ve been raised badly,” said the Dodger, admiring his boots with great satisfaction once Oliver had finished polishing them. “Fagin will make something out of you, though, or you’ll be the first one he’s ever had that turned out useless. You’d better start right away, because you’ll take up the trade long before you imagine, and you’re only wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates backed up this advice with various moral sayings of his own; and when those ran out, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into a glowing account of the countless delights of the life they led, spiced with plenty of hints that the smartest thing Oliver could do was to win Fagin’s favor without delay, using the same means they had used themselves.

“And always remember this, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as they heard the Jew unlocking the upstairs door, “if you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the use of saying it like that?” interrupted Master Bates; “he doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take pocket handkerchiefs and watches,” said the Dodger, lowering his speech to Oliver’s level, “some other chap will; so the folks who lose them will be just as bad off, and you’ll be no better, and no one else will be a bit better either, except the fellows who grab them—and you’ve got just as much right to them as they do.”

“Of course, of course!” said the Jew, who had slipped in without Oliver noticing. “It’s all very simple, my dear; take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands with delight as he confirmed the Dodger’s reasoning, and chuckled with pleasure at his pupil’s skill.

The talk went no farther then, because the Jew had returned with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen before, whom the Dodger hailed as Tom Chitling. Tom, having lingered on the stairs to exchange a few gallant remarks with the lady, now stepped into the room."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6300859d1cf00a09c011f2cd","rewritten_text":"Count Rouvaloff stared at him in amazement for some moments and, realizing he was quite serious, wrote an address on a slip of paper, initialed it, and handed it across the table. “Scotland Yard would pay dearly for this address, my dear fellow.” “They won’t get it,” Lord Arthur said with a laugh. After a warm handshake with the young Russian, he ran downstairs, read the paper, and told the coachman to drive to Soho Square. He dismissed the carriage there and walked down Greek Street until he reached Bayle’s Court. Passing under an archway, he entered a curious cul-de-sac apparently dominated by a French laundry, with clotheslines crisscrossing the space and white linen fluttering in the morning air. He went to the far end and knocked on a small green house. After a delay during which every window in the court filled with blurred faces peering out, the door opened to a rough-looking foreigner, who asked in very poor English what he wanted. Lord Arthur gave him the paper from Count Rouvaloff. The man read it, bowed, and led him into a shabby front parlor on the ground floor. A few moments later Herr Winckelkopf, as he was known in England, bustled in wearing a wine-stained napkin around his neck and holding a fork in his left hand. “Count Rouvaloff has introduced me to you,” Lord Arthur said with a bow. “I need a short interview with you on a business matter. My name is Smith, Robert Smith, and I want you to provide me with an explosive clock.” “Delighted to meet you, Lord Arthur,” said the friendly little German, laughing. “Don’t look so startled—it’s my duty to know everyone, and I remember seeing you one evening at Lady Windermere’s. I hope she is quite well. Sit with me while I finish breakfast. There’s an excellent pâté, and my friends insist my Rhine wine beats anything at the German Embassy.” Before Lord Arthur could recover from being recognized, he found himself in the back room, sipping exquisite Marcobrünner from a pale yellow hock glass marked with the Imperial monogram, chatting amiably with the famous conspirator. “Explosive clocks,” Herr Winckelkopf said, “aren’t ideal for shipping abroad because even if they slip past Customs, the trains are so unreliable that they usually go off before reaching their destination.”"}

{"request_id":"c11f78d78ee72d8be9c59fe6","rewritten_text":"Winters on Sullivan’s Island are rarely harsh, and even in autumn it is unusual to need a fire. Yet in mid-October, 18—, one day turned bitterly cold. Just before sunset I pushed through the evergreens to my friend’s hut, where I had not been for several weeks; I was living in Charleston then, nine miles away, and travel between the city and the island was nothing like it is now. I knocked, as usual, but no one answered. Knowing where the spare key was hidden, I found it, unlocked the door, and stepped inside. A bright fire blazed on the hearth—a welcome surprise. I shrugged off my overcoat, settled into an armchair by the crackling logs, and waited for my hosts.

They came soon after dark and greeted me warmly. Jupiter, grinning widely, hurried to prepare marsh hens for supper. Legrand was in one of his spells—what else could I call them?—of excitement. He had discovered a new kind of bivalve, enough to create a new genus, and, more than that, with Jupiter’s help he had tracked down and captured a scarab he believed no one had ever seen before. He wanted my opinion on it the next day.

“And why not tonight?” I asked, rubbing my hands before the fire and cursing all scarabs.

“If only I’d known you were here!” said Legrand. “It’s been so long since I saw you; how could I guess you’d visit me on this very night? As I was coming home I met Lieutenant G—— from the fort, and foolishly I lent him the bug, so you can’t see it until morning. Stay the night, and I’ll send Jup down for it at sunrise. It’s the loveliest creature alive!”

“What?—sunrise?”

“Nonsense! Not sunrise—the bug. It’s a brilliant gold, about the size of a large hickory nut, with two jet-black spots near one end of its back and another longer spot at the other end. The antennae are—”

“Dey ain’t no tin in him, Massa Will, I keeps tellin’ you,” Jupiter broke in. “De bug is a gold bug, solid all through, ’cept his wings—I never felt a bug half so heavy in my life.”"}

{"request_id":"089e281eafb41c9a808aa169","rewritten_text":"Enough of that. I will begin my story: it is my final task, and I hope I still have the strength to complete it. I confess to no crimes; any faults of mine can easily be forgiven, for they arose not from malicious intent but from poor judgment; and I think few would claim that, with different choices and greater wisdom, they could have escaped the misfortunes that have claimed me. My fate has been ruled by necessity, a monstrous necessity. It would have taken hands stronger than mine—stronger than any human power, I believe—to shatter the thick, adamantine chain that bound me: once breathing only joy, filled with warm love and a delight in goodness, only to be consigned to misery that could end only in death, and is now about to end. But I forget myself; my tale remains untold. I will pause for a moment, wipe my dim eyes, and try to lose this vague but heavy sense of present unhappiness in the sharper emotions of the past.

I was born in England. My father was a man of rank: he lost his own father early and was raised by a weak mother who gave him all the indulgence she thought due a wealthy nobleman. He was sent to Eton and later to university, and from childhood he was allowed free access to large sums of money, thus claiming from his earliest youth the independence that a boy with such advantages inevitably secures at a public school.

Under those conditions his passions found rich soil where they could take root and flourish, whether as flowers or as weeds, depending on their nature. Because he was always permitted to act for himself, his character quickly grew strong and distinct, displaying a varied surface on which any sharp-eyed observer might discern the seeds of both virtues and future misfortunes. His careless extravagance, which led him to squander vast sums to gratify fleeting whims—whims he elevated to the status of passions because of their seeming intensity—often manifested as boundless generosity. Yet even as he dedicated himself to meeting others’ needs, his own desires were indulged to the fullest. He gave his money, but none of his own wishes were sacrificed to his gifts; he offered his time, which he did not value, and his affections, which he was glad to have stirred in any way.

I do not claim that, had his desires been set against another’s, he would necessarily have shown undue selfishness; but that test was never applied. He was nurtured in prosperity and surrounded by all its benefits; everyone loved him and sought to please him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"deb688b60b637486c27867c0","rewritten_text":"The chain of necessity that always brings misery must have snapped, and the malignant fate that governs it would never allow such a break in her eternal laws. But why should I complain? Misery was my natural element, and only what was miserable could come near me; if Woodville had been happy, I would never have known him. And I, who for years have been sustained by tears and raised under the dew of grief, can I hesitate to recount a tale of suffering and death? Woodville had to travel into the country and was kept away day after day in weary separation from his beautiful bride. He received a letter from her saying she was slightly ill, begging him to hurry to her, certain that his eyes would grant her health and his company would be her surest medicine. He was delayed three more days, and then he rushed to her. His heart, for reasons he could not name, foretold disaster; he had heard nothing further from her; he feared she might be worse, and this worry made him impatient and restless, desperate for the moment when he would see her again, glowing with health and beauty. A sinister voice seemed to whisper to him, “You will never again see her as she was.” When he reached her home, everything within it was silent. He passed through several rooms; in one, he saw a servant weeping bitterly. He was weak with fear and could barely ask, “Is she dead?” and then he just listened to the dreadful reply, “Not yet.” Those shocking words struck him as less terrifying than what he had expected; to learn she was still alive and that hope remained was a relief. He remembered her letter and indulged the wild thought that his kisses, filled with warm love and life, would revive her, that with him near, she could not die; that his presence was the talisman of her life. He hurried to her sickroom; she lay with fever-flushed cheeks, yet her eyes were closed and she seemed senseless. He wrapped her in his arms; he pressed breathless kisses on her burning lips; in a voice muted by anguish he called her by the tenderest names: “Come back, Elinor; I am here with you, your life, your love. Come back, dearest; you promised me this gift, that I would bring you health. Let your sweet spirit revive; you cannot die near me. What is death? Never to see you again? To lose what is part of myself, without whom I have no past and no future?”"}

{"request_id":"f9604f91a98655a55685ec76","rewritten_text":"They went on past desolate brickfields. The fog thinned a little here, letting him see the odd kilns shaped like bottles, with orange tongues of flame spreading like fans. A dog barked as they passed, and somewhere far off in the murk a stray sea-gull screamed. The horse caught a rut, swerved, and suddenly broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road behind and clattered once more over rough-laid streets. Nearly every window lay in darkness, yet now and again grotesque shadows were cut out against some lamplit blind. He stared at them in fascination. They moved like gigantic puppets, gesturing as if alive. He loathed them. A sullen fury burned in his heart. When they took a corner, a woman shouted something after them from an open doorway, and two men dashed after the hansom for nearly a hundred yards. The cabman lashed at them with his whip.

People say passion makes the mind move in circles. Certainly, with ghastly repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips shaped those subtle phrases that dealt with soul and sense, until he had drawn from them, as it were, the full expression of his mood and, with intellectual sanction, excused passions that would have ruled him even without such excuse. From cell to cell of his brain ran the single thought, and the fierce craving to live, that most dreadful of appetites, nerved every trembling fibre. Ugliness, once hateful to him because it made things real, grew precious for that same reason. Ugliness became reality. The vulgar brawl, the foul den, the raw violence of chaos, the sheer vileness of thief and pariah, struck more vividly, by their intense actuality, than all the gracious forms of art, all the dreamy echoes of song. These were what he needed to forget. In three days he would be free.

All at once the cabman jerked to a halt at the head of a dim lane. Above the low roofs and jagged chimneys rose the black spars of ships. White wreaths of mist clung to the yards like spectral sails.

“Somewhere along here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian started, glanced around. “This will do,” he said, and, springing out, pressed on the extra fare he had promised. He strode swiftly toward the quay. Here and there a lantern glimmered at the stern of some hulking merchantman, its light shaking and shattering in the puddles. A crimson glare poured from an outward-bound steamer taking on coal. The slimy paving looked like drenched rubber."}

{"request_id":"875cef49c27d45955a455d5c","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter had taken an excellent house in Camden Place, lofty and dignified, suited to a man of consequence. He and Elizabeth were settled there, quite satisfied with everything.

Anne entered with a sinking heart, expecting to be imprisoned there for many months, silently wondering, “Oh! when shall I leave you again?” Yet the unexpected warmth of her welcome did her good. Her father and sister were pleased to show her the house and furniture and met her kindly. They even remarked that making a fourth at dinner was an advantage.

Mrs Clay was pleasant and smiling, but her politeness felt routine. Anne had expected her to act properly upon arrival, but the friendliness from the others surprised her. They were clearly in high spirits, and soon she would hear why. They had no interest in listening to her. After waiting for compliments about being missed in their old neighborhood, which Anne could not give, they asked a few shallow questions before taking over the conversation. Uppercross meant nothing to them, Kellynch very little: everything was about Bath.

They delighted in telling her that Bath exceeded their hopes in every way. Their house was unquestionably the best in Camden Place; their drawing rooms had clear advantages over any others they had seen or heard of, and their superiority extended to the style of the decor and the taste of the furnishings. Their acquaintance was highly sought after. Everyone wanted to visit them. They had declined many introductions, yet still had cards left by people they did not know.

There was plenty to enjoy. Could Anne wonder they were happy? Perhaps not, but she had to sigh that her father felt no loss in this change, saw nothing to miss in the duties and dignity of a resident landholder, and found so much to be proud of in the small vanities of town life. She also had to sigh, and smile, and marvel as Elizabeth flung open the folding doors and walked with pride from one drawing room to the other, boasting of their size; at how the woman who had once been mistress of Kellynch Hall could find anything to brag about in space measured by two walls perhaps thirty feet apart.

And there was more to make them happy. They had Mr Elliot as well."}

{"request_id":"0de6eadb341403adc9090720","rewritten_text":"That was all the encouragement she needed.

“Why, my dear, you must know, Mrs. Long says Netherfield has been leased by a young man of great fortune from the north of England. He arrived on Monday in a coach and four to inspect the place, liked it so much that he struck a deal with Mr. Morris on the spot, plans to move in before Michaelmas, and some of his servants are expected to occupy the house by the end of next week.”

“What is his name?”

“Bingley.”

“Is he married or single?”

“Oh, single, my dear, of course! A single man of great fortune—four or five thousand a year. What a splendid opportunity for our girls!”

“How so? How could it matter to them?”

“My dear Mr. Bennet,” his wife answered, “how can you be so provoking? Surely you realize I’m thinking of him marrying one of them.”

“Is that why he’s settling here?”

“Why would you call it a plan? Don’t be ridiculous! But he might easily fall in love with one of them, and therefore you must visit him the moment he arrives.”

“I see no need for that. You and the girls can go—or you could send them alone, which might be even better; since you’re as attractive as any of them, Mr. Bingley might prefer you to the rest.”

“My dear, you flatter me. I’ve had my share of beauty, certainly, but I no longer claim anything extraordinary. Once a woman has five grown daughters, she ought to stop thinking about her own looks.”

“In such situations, a woman usually hasn’t much beauty left to consider.”

“But, my dear, you truly must go and call on Mr. Bingley when he arrives in the neighborhood.”

“I make no promises, I assure you.”

“But think of your daughters. Imagine what an establishment it would mean for one of them. Sir William and Lady Lucas are determined to go for that very reason, for you know they rarely visit newcomers. You absolutely must go, because it will be impossible for us to call on him if you do not.”

“You’re being excessively scrupulous. I’m sure Mr. Bingley will be delighted to see you, and I’ll send a short note with you to give him my full permission to marry whichever of the girls he chooses—though I must recommend my little Lizzy.”

“I insist you do no such thing. Lizzy is not the least bit better than the others, and I’m sure she isn’t half as pretty as Jane or half as good-natured as Lydia.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1d4fbee9a7ddcea2598f50a3","rewritten_text":"At least he believed so. But who could know for sure? No, there had been nothing more. From vanity he had spared her. Out of hypocrisy he had worn the mask of virtue. From curiosity he had tried self-denial. Now he understood that. But this murder—would it haunt him for the rest of his life? Would he always carry his past like a weight? Would he actually confess? Never. There was only one piece of evidence left against him. The picture itself—that was proof. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it so long? Once he had enjoyed watching it change and grow old. Recently there had been no such pleasure. It had kept him awake at night. Whenever he was away, terror gripped him that other eyes might see it. It had spread sadness over his passions. Its mere memory had spoiled many joys. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it. He looked around and saw the knife that had killed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it over and over until no stain remained. It shone, gray and gleaming. As it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work and everything tied to it. It would kill the past, and once that was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous secret life of the soul, and without its ugly warnings he would be at peace. He grabbed the knife and stabbed the picture with it. A cry rang out, followed by a crash. The cry was so full of pain that the startled servants woke and crept from their rooms. Two gentlemen walking past in the square below stopped and looked up at the large house. They walked on until they met a policeman and brought him back. The man rang the bell again and again, but no one answered. Apart from a light in one of the top windows, the house lay in darkness. After a while he stepped away and waited in a neighboring doorway. “Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older gentleman. “Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” said the policeman. The gentlemen looked at each other as they walked off and sneered. One was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle. Inside, in the servants’ wing, the half-dressed staff whispered among themselves. Old Mrs. Leaf wept and twisted her hands. Francis was as pale as death. After about fifteen minutes he gathered the coachman and a footman and slowly climbed the stairs."}

{"request_id":"4e15a55946002a8a589569b8","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I believe, sir,” the spy said in his humblest manner, turning to Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your age and kindness to put it to this other gentleman, so much younger than you, whether he can in any situation justify himself in playing that Ace he mentioned. I admit that I am a spy, and that it is considered a dishonorable occupation—though somebody must do it; but this gentleman is no spy, so why should he degrade himself by becoming one?”

“I’ll play my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking the reply on himself and glancing at his watch, “without any hesitation, in just a few minutes.”

“I would have hoped, gentlemen,” said the spy, always trying to pull Mr. Lorry into the conversation, “that your respect for my sister—”

“I could not better show my respect for your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” said Sydney Carton.

“You don’t think so, sir?”

“My mind is completely made up about it.”

The spy’s smooth manner, oddly out of tune with his deliberately rough clothes and probably with his usual behavior, ran into a wall when faced with the impenetrability of Carton—a man who was a mystery even to wiser and more honest men than he. The spy faltered and lost his footing. While he floundered, Carton said, slipping back into the pose of a man contemplating his cards:

“And actually, now that I think again, I have a strong feeling I possess another good card, not yet mentioned. That friend and fellow-Sheep who said he grazed in the country prisons—who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” the spy answered quickly.

“French, eh?” Carton repeated, reflecting, and seeming not to notice him at all, though he echoed the word. “Well; he might be.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy; “though it’s not important.”

“Though it’s not important,” Carton repeated in the same automatic way—“though it’s not important—No, it’s not important. No. Yet I know the face.”

“I think not. I’m sure not. It can’t be,” said the spy.

“It can’t be,” Sydney Carton muttered, thinking back and absently turning his glass (luckily a small one) again. “Can’t be. Spoke good French. Yet like a foreigner, I thought?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” Carton shouted, slapping his open hand on the table as sudden clarity struck. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had that man before us at the Old Bailey.”

“Now there you’re rash, sir,” said Barsad, smiling in a way that made his aquiline nose tilt further to one side; “there you really hand me the advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"0e105e1fe4dcc70f22eb1751","rewritten_text":"“One more word, Rose. Dearest Rose, just one more!” Harry cried, throwing himself in front of her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as people would say—if my fate had been some quiet, hidden life—if I had been poor, sick, helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or is this hesitation born from my likely rise to wealth and honour?”

“Please don’t force me to answer,” Rose replied. “The question doesn’t exist, and never will. It’s unfair, almost unkind, to push it.”

“If your answer is what I hardly dare to hope,” Harry returned, “it will cast a ray of happiness on my lonely road and light what lies ahead. It isn’t trivial to do so much, with only a few words, for someone who loves you beyond all else. Oh, Rose, in the name of my fervent and lasting devotion, in the name of all I have suffered for you and all you condemn me to endure, answer this one question!”

“Then, if your life had been different,” Rose replied, “if you had been only a little, but not too far, above me—if I could have been a help and comfort to you in any quiet, humble place, instead of a stain and burden in ambitious, distinguished circles—I would have been spared this trial. I have every reason to be happy, very happy, now; but then, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

Old hopes she had cherished as a girl rushed back into Rose’s mind as she confessed this; yet they brought tears with them, as old hopes do when they return withered, and the tears eased her heart.

“I can’t help this weakness, and it only strengthens my resolve,” Rose said, holding out her hand. “I truly must leave you now.”

“I ask for one promise,” said Harry. “Just once more—say within a year, perhaps much sooner—I may speak to you again about this, for the last time.”

“Not to press me to change my rightful decision,” Rose answered with a sad smile. “It will be useless.”

“No,” said Harry. “Just to hear you repeat it, if you will—repeat it for good! I will lay at your feet whatever rank or fortune I possess, and if you still hold to your present resolve, I will never try, by word or deed, to alter it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose replied. “It is only one more pang, and by then I may be better able to bear it.”

She held out her hand again."}

{"request_id":"0bfd3f5281e9b8d3a565a0d7","rewritten_text":"April 12. A remarkable shift occurred in the balloon’s course, and although I had fully expected it, I was unmistakably delighted. After reaching about the twentieth parallel south, it abruptly veered sharply eastward and continued that way all day, remaining almost, if not entirely, in the precise plane of the lunar ellipse. What stood out was a noticeable rocking of the car caused by this change in direction—a rocking that persisted, to varying degrees, for several hours.

April 13. Once again I was badly frightened by the return of the loud, crackling sound that had terrified me on the tenth. I thought about it for a long time but could reach no satisfying conclusion. The earth’s apparent diameter shrank dramatically, now spanning an angle from the balloon of just over twenty-five degrees. The moon was invisible, nearly at my zenith. I remained in the plane of the ellipse but made little headway eastward.

April 14. The earth’s diameter diminished at an extremely rapid rate. Today I became firmly convinced that the balloon was actually racing up the line of apsides to the point of perigee—in other words, following the direct path that would bring it straight to the moon at the part of its orbit closest to Earth. The moon itself was directly overhead and thus out of sight. I had to work long and hard to condense the atmosphere.

April 15. By now even the outlines of the continents and seas on Earth were too blurred to make out. Around noon I noticed, for the third time, that dreadful noise that had so astonished me before. This time it lasted several moments and grew louder as it went on. Finally, while I stood stunned and terrified, expecting some monstrous disaster, the car shook violently, and a colossal, flaming mass of some unknown material streaked past the balloon with the roar of a thousand thunderclaps. When my fear and shock had eased a little, it was easy to assume it was a massive volcanic fragment flung from the world I was approaching—most likely one of that peculiar class of objects occasionally found on Earth and called meteoric stones for lack of a better name.

April 16. Today, straining to look upward through each side window in turn, I was thrilled to see a tiny portion of the moon’s disk jutting, so to speak, beyond the enormous circumference of the balloon."}

{"request_id":"7a64c31f92f851709c4bb234","rewritten_text":"At the center of the gap I noticed a white spot, but at first I could not tell what it was. I adjusted the telescope’s focus, looked again, and realized it was a human skull.

“At that discovery I was so confident I thought the puzzle solved. The words ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only describe the skull’s position on the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ could mean only one thing when searching for buried treasure. I understood that the plan was to drop a bullet through the skull’s left eye. A straight line drawn from the nearest part of the trunk through the ‘shot’ (where the bullet landed) and out fifty feet would mark a specific spot—and I figured something valuable might lie buried beneath it.”

“All that,” I said, “is very clear—clever, but still straightforward. After you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened?”

“Well, after carefully taking the tree’s bearings, I headed home. The moment I left the ‘devil’s seat,’ though, the circular gap disappeared, and no matter how I turned, I could not see it again. The great ingenuity here is that the circular opening (and I am certain it is a fact) can be seen only from that narrow ledge on the rock face.

“Jupiter had accompanied me on my trip to the ‘Bishop’s Hotel.’ He had likely noticed my distracted manner for weeks and made sure I was never alone. But the next morning I got up very early, managed to slip away, and went into the hills to find the tree. After a lot of effort I located it. When I returned that night, my valet threatened to flog me. You know the rest of that episode as well as I do.”

“I imagine,” I said, “that you missed the spot on your first dig because Jupiter let the bug fall through the skull’s right eye instead of the left.”

“Exactly. That mistake changed the ‘shot’—the position of the stake closest to the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been right under the ‘shot,’ the error would have meant little. But the ‘shot’ and the nearest point of the tree were only anchor points to establish a line of direction. Naturally, the small error at the start grew as we extended the line, and by the time we went fifty feet, it had led us completely off course.”"}

{"request_id":"4da3c155639981040d5e1ad8","rewritten_text":"Emma did not regret lowering herself to visit the Coles. The visit supplied her with many pleasant memories the next day, and whatever dignity she might have sacrificed by leaving her seclusion was more than repaid by the glow of popularity. She must have delighted the Coles—good people who deserved happiness—and left a name behind that would not fade quickly.

Perfect happiness, even in memory, is rare, and there were two points that still troubled her. She wondered if she had broken the duty of woman to woman by sharing her suspicions about Jane Fairfax’s feelings with Frank Churchill. It was scarcely right; but the thought had been so strong that it slipped out, and his willingness to believe everything she said was such a compliment to her insight that she could not be sure she ought to have kept quiet.

The other regret also concerned Jane Fairfax, and there she had no doubt. She honestly and clearly regretted that her own playing and singing were inferior. She truly mourned the idleness of her childhood, sat down, and practised hard for an hour and a half.

She was then interrupted by Harriet’s arrival; and if Harriet’s praise could have satisfied her, comfort would have come quickly.

“Oh! if only I could play as well as you and Miss Fairfax!”

“Don’t group us together, Harriet. My playing is no more like hers than a lamp is like sunshine.”

“Oh dear—I think you play best. I think you play just as well as she does. I would much rather listen to you. Everyone said last night how well you played.”

“Anyone who knew anything must have felt the difference. The truth is, Harriet, my playing is only good enough to be praised, but Jane Fairfax’s is far better.”

“Well, I will always think you play just as well as she does, or that if there is any difference nobody would ever notice it. Mr. Cole said you had so much taste; and Mr. Frank Churchill talked a great deal about your taste, and that he valued taste much more than execution.”

“Ah! but Jane Fairfax has both, Harriet.”

“Are you sure? I saw she had execution, but I did not know she had any taste. Nobody mentioned it. And I hate Italian singing—there is no understanding a word of it. Besides, if she plays so very well, you know, it is simply her duty, because she will have to teach.”"}

{"request_id":"49b11616328c3386ef55dcce","rewritten_text":"The weight of the insect was remarkably heavy, and considering everything, I could hardly blame Jupiter for his opinion about it; what baffled me completely was how Legrand could agree with him.

“I sent for you,” he declared in a grand tone once I’d finished examining the beetle, “I sent for you so I might have your counsel and assistance in carrying out the plans of Fate and this bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I broke in, “you’re definitely unwell, and should take some precautions. You’ll go to bed, and I’ll stay with you a few days until you’re better. You’re feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I did, and honestly found not the slightest sign of fever.

“But you can be sick without having a fever. Let me prescribe just this once. First, go to bed. Next—”

“You’re mistaken,” he interrupted. “I’m as well as I can expect to be under the excitement I’m feeling. If you truly wish me well, you’ll help relieve it.”

“And how am I supposed to do that?”

“Very easily. Jupiter and I are going on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and we need help from someone we can trust. You’re the only one. Whether we succeed or fail, this excitement you see in me will be calmed either way.”

“I want to help however I can,” I said, “but do you mean to tell me this damned beetle has anything to do with your trip into the hills?”

“It does.”

“Then, Legrand, I can’t take part in any such ridiculous business.”

“I’m sorry—truly sorry—because we’ll have to attempt it alone.”

“Try it alone! The man has to be mad!—but wait! How long do you plan to be away?”

“Probably all night. We’re leaving immediately and will be back by sunrise at the latest.”

“And will you promise, on your honor, that once this crazy phase is over and this bug business—good God!—is settled to your satisfaction, you’ll come home and follow my advice completely, as your physician?”

“Yes, I promise. Now let’s go; we have no time to waste.”

Heavy-hearted, I went along with my friend. We set out around four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and myself. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades—insisting on bearing the whole lot—more out of fear, it seemed to me, of letting either tool stay within his master’s reach than from any great industry or politeness."}

{"request_id":"53d3604174aa1fee59fbdb32","rewritten_text":"She was right about the rats. Every so often one would poke its nose out of a hole in the corner. She said she needed things close by to throw at them when she was alone or they wouldn’t leave her be. She showed me a bar of lead twisted into a knot and said she was usually a good shot with it, but she had wrenched her arm a day or two ago and wasn’t sure she could throw straight. Still, she waited for a chance and soon hurled it at a rat; she missed by a mile and cried “Ouch!” because it hurt her arm so much. Then she told me to try for the next one. I wanted to get gone before her husband came back, but of course I didn’t let her see that. I took the lead, and when the first rat showed his nose I let fly; if he’d stayed put, he would have been a mighty sick rat. She said that was fine, and she figured I’d get the next one. She fetched the lump of lead again and also brought a hank of yarn she wanted help with. I held up my hands and she laid the hank over them, and she kept talking about her and her husband. Then she stopped to say:

“Keep your eye on the rats. You better keep the lead in your lap, ready.”

She dropped the lump into my lap right then, and I clamped my knees on it while she kept talking. That lasted barely a minute. Then she lifted the yarn off, looked me straight in the face, smiling, and said:

“Come now, what’s your real name?”

“Wh—what, ma’am?”

“What’s your real name? Is it Bill, or Tom, or Bob—what is it?”

I reckon I shook like a leaf and didn’t know what to do. But I said:

“Please don’t make fun of a poor girl like me, ma’am. If I’m in the way, I’ll—”

“No, you won’t. Sit down and stay put. I’m not going to hurt you, and I’m not going to tell on you either. Just tell me your secret and trust me. I’ll keep it, and what’s more, I’ll help you. So will my old man, if you want him to. You’re a runaway apprentice, that’s all. It’s nothing. There’s no harm in it. You’ve been treated bad, so you made up your mind to leave. Bless you, child, I wouldn’t tell on you.”"}

{"request_id":"408b82e1467171a3fa3e76d3","rewritten_text":"“I reckon it among the earliest refinements of well-bred societies.”

“Most assuredly, sir; and it enjoys the additional merit of being fashionable even among the least polished communities; every savage can dance.”

Sir William merely smiled. “Your friend acquits himself charmingly,” he resumed, after a pause as Bingley joined the dancers; “and I dare say, Mr. Darcy, that you are yourself no mean proficient in the art.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, if you remember, sir.”

“Indeed I did, and was by no means ill-pleased with the spectacle. Do you frequently honour St. James’s with your dancing?”

“Never, sir.”

“Do you not consider it a fit compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment which I bestow on no place, whenever it can be avoided.”

“I presume you possess a house in town?”

Mr. Darcy inclined his head.

“I once contemplated settling in town myself, being partial to superior society; but I doubted whether the London air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, expecting a response, but his companion showed no inclination to give one; and at that very moment Elizabeth approaching, he conceived the gallant notion of calling to her,—

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, permit me to recommend this young lady to you as a most desirable partner. Surely you cannot decline when such beauty solicits.” And, seizing her hand, he would have given it to Mr. Darcy, who, though much surprised, was not reluctant to accept it, when she instantly withdrew, and said, with some agitation, to Sir William,—

“Indeed, sir, I have not the slightest intention of dancing. I beg you will not imagine that I came this way to solicit a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with grave propriety, requested the honour of her hand, but to no purpose. Elizabeth remained resolute; nor did Sir William shake that resolution by his renewed entreaties.

“You dance with such excellence, Miss Eliza, that it is unkind to deny me the pleasure of witnessing it; and though this gentleman dislikes the pastime in general, I am sure he cannot object to oblige us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is politeness itself,” Elizabeth replied, smiling.

“So he is: but considering the temptation, my dear Miss Eliza, we need not wonder at his complaisance; for who could reject such a partner?”

Elizabeth cast a playful look and turned away. Her refusal had not lessened her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was regarding her with some complacency when Miss Bingley thus accosted him,—"}

{"request_id":"4070a37702b834a289081637","rewritten_text":"“I swear,” he cried, “by the sun, by the blue sky, and by the fire of love burning in my heart, that if you grant my request, you shall never see me again while they live. Go home and begin your work; I will watch its progress with unbearable anxiety, and when you are ready I will appear.”

With that, he abruptly left me, afraid, perhaps, that my resolve might change. I watched him run down the mountain faster than an eagle’s flight, soon vanishing among the rolling waves of the icy sea.

His story had lasted the entire day, and the sun was sinking when he departed. I knew I should hurry down to the valley before darkness trapped me, yet my heart was heavy and my steps slow. The effort of threading the narrow mountain paths and keeping my footing wearied me, while my mind churned with the day’s events. Night was well advanced when I reached the halfway rest and sat beside the fountain. The stars appeared when the clouds drifted away; dark pines stood before me, and broken trees lay scattered on the ground. The solemn scene stirred strange thoughts. I wept bitterly, and clasping my hands in agony, I cried, “Oh stars and clouds and winds, you are all ready to mock me; if you pity me, crush my feeling and memory—let me become nothing. But if not, leave me—leave me in darkness.”

They were wild, miserable thoughts, yet I cannot explain how the endless sparkle of the stars oppressed me, or how each gust of wind sounded like a dull, hateful sirocco coming to destroy me.

Dawn broke before I reached the village of Chamounix. I rested nowhere but went straight back to Geneva. Even inside my own heart I could not express what I felt—they weighed on me like a mountain, and their very excess dulled my anguish. Thus I returned home, and when I entered the house and stood before my family, my gaunt, frantic look filled them with alarm. I answered no questions, hardly spoke. I felt as if I were under a curse—unworthy of their sympathy—as if I could never again share their companionship."}

{"request_id":"abcff132916a610ea6bcbc78","rewritten_text":"In the middle of this gap I spotted a white speck, though at first I couldn’t tell what it was. I refocused the telescope, looked again, and now realized it was a human skull. 

“After that, I was confident I’d solved the riddle. The phrase ‘main branch, seventh limb, east side’ could only describe where the skull sat in the tree, while ‘shoot from the left eye of the death’s head’ could only mean one thing when hunting for buried treasure. I understood the plan was to drop a bullet from the skull’s left eye, then draw a straight line—what they call a bee-line—from the closest spot on the trunk through the ‘shot,’ meaning where the bullet landed. Extending that line fifty feet would mark a precise point, and beneath that point I thought there might well be something valuable hidden.” 

“All of this,” I said, “is very clear—ingenious, yes, but still straightforward. Once you left the Bishop’s Hotel, what happened?” 

“Well, after carefully taking the tree’s bearings, I headed home. The moment I stepped away from the ‘devil’s seat,’ though, the circular slit vanished; no matter how I turned, I couldn’t see it again. What strikes me as the cleverest part of this whole affair is that the circular opening can’t be seen from any other accessible position than that narrow ledge on the rock face—repeated tests have convinced me of it.” 

“On that trip to the Bishop’s Hotel I was accompanied by Jupiter, who had clearly noticed my distracted mood for weeks and made sure not to leave me alone. But the next morning I got up very early, managed to sneak away from him, and went into the hills to find the tree. After a lot of hard work I found it. When I came home that evening, my valet threatened to give me a whipping. The rest of the adventure you know as well as I do.” 

“I suppose,” I said, “that on your first attempt at digging you missed the spot because Jupiter foolishly let the bug fall through the skull’s right eye instead of the left.” 

“Exactly. That mistake shifted the ‘shot’—meaning the peg closest to the tree—by about two and a half inches. If the treasure had been right under the shot, it wouldn’t have mattered much; but the shot and the nearest point of the trunk were just two points to set a line. So even a small initial error grew worse along the line, and by the time we measured off fifty feet, we were completely off track.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"db2d977ad7f0f22108336ece","rewritten_text":"There was a pleasant feeling of tidying up and taking a quiet breath before starting life anew in our village on Saturday nights, and it encouraged Joe to stay out half an hour later on Saturdays than on other evenings. When that extra half-hour ended and his rum and water was gone, Joe stood up to leave and took my hand. “Wait half a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the stranger. “I believe I have a bright new shilling in my pocket, and if I do, the boy shall have it.” He fished it out of a handful of small coins, wrapped it in a scrunched-up piece of paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he said. “Remember! Your own.” I thanked him, staring at him far beyond what was polite, while clinging to Joe. He wished Joe good night, and he wished Mr. Wopsle good night (who left with us), and he gave me only a look from that aiming eye—no, not even a look, because he shut it, yet astonishing things can be done with an eye by hiding it. On the way home, even if I had been in the mood to talk, any conversation would have had to come from me, because Mr. Wopsle left us at the door of the Jolly Bargemen, and Joe walked all the way home with his mouth wide open to rinse out the rum with as much air as he could. But I was stunned by the reappearance of my old wrongdoing and old acquaintance, and I couldn’t think of anything else. My sister was not in a particularly bad temper when we walked into the kitchen, and Joe took that rare chance to tell her about the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” Mrs. Joe declared triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see it.” I unwrapped the paper, and it turned out to be a good shilling. “But what’s this?” cried Mrs. Joe, tossing down the shilling and snatching up the paper. “Two one-pound notes?” Nothing less than two thick, sweaty one-pound notes that looked as if they’d been on the friendliest terms with every cattle market in the county. Joe grabbed his hat and ran back to the Jolly Bargemen to return them to their owner. While he was gone, I sat on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, fairly certain the man would be gone. Soon Joe returned, saying the man had indeed left, but he, Joe, had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"0f24888b0d4c9216c595189b","rewritten_text":"Great God! Had I for one moment guessed the infernal design of my demonic enemy, I would sooner have exiled myself forever from my homeland and roamed the world a lonely exile than have consented to this wretched marriage. Yet, as though wielding some sorcery, the monster obscured his true purpose; and while I imagined I had secured only my own destruction, I hastened the doom of one infinitely dearer.

As the appointed time for our union approached, whether through cowardice or some prophetic instinct, my heart faltered. Still I hid my agitation beneath a semblance of mirth that drew smiles and delight to my father’s face, though it scarcely escaped the vigilant, discerning eye of Elizabeth. She anticipated our joining with serene contentment, yet not untouched by the slight dread, born of former miseries, that the happiness now appearing so certain and palpable might dissolve into mere vapour, leaving nothing save deep, enduring regret.

Arrangements went forward for the celebration, congratulatory calls were exchanged, and all wore an aspect of cheer. I locked, as best I might, the gnawing anxiety in my heart and engaged with apparent zeal in my father’s schemes, though they might prove but the adornments of my tragedy. Thanks to my father’s efforts, a portion of Elizabeth’s inheritance had been restored by the Austrian government. A small estate on the shores of Como was hers. It was settled that immediately after our wedding we would set out for Villa Lavenza and pass our first days of happiness beside the lovely lake near which it stood.

Meanwhile I took every precaution to safeguard myself should the fiend attack openly. I bore pistols and a dagger at all times and kept ceaseless watch against any stratagem, and by such means won a measure of tranquillity. Indeed, as the day drew near, the menace seemed more an illusion, unworthy to trouble my peace, while the bliss I anticipated in my marriage assumed greater certainty as the date of its solemnization approached and I heard it constantly mentioned as an event chance itself could not prevent.

Elizabeth appeared content; my outward calm helped greatly to soothe her spirits. Yet on the day destined to fulfil both my wishes and my fate, she grew melancholy, oppressed by a presentiment of evil; perhaps, too, she remembered the terrible secret I had pledged to unveil to her on the morrow."}

{"request_id":"ed2229cc8ca1a5960cbfefdb","rewritten_text":"“Now,” said Mr. Lorry, once more resting his hand on the Doctor’s arm after a brief silence, “to what do you attribute this seizure?”

“I believe,” Doctor Manette replied, “that there was a powerful and unusual resurgence of the chain of thoughts and memories that first produced the illness. Certain intense associations of a deeply distressing cast came back to him vividly, I think. It is likely that he had long harboured a fear that such associations would resurface—perhaps under specific conditions—perhaps on a certain occasion. He tried to brace himself in vain; perhaps the effort to steel himself left him less able to endure it.”

“Would he retain any recollection of what happened during the relapse?” Mr. Lorry asked, naturally hesitant.

The Doctor cast a desolate glance around the room, shook his head, and answered softly, “Not in the least.”

“Now, concerning the future,” Mr. Lorry hinted.

“As for the future,” said the Doctor, regaining firmness, “I should feel great hope. Since it pleased Heaven in mercy to restore him so quickly, I should feel great hope. He, succumbing under the weight of some complicated thing—long feared, long dimly foresighted and resisted—and then recovering when the storm had broken and passed, gives me hope that the worst is done.”

“Well, well! That is good comfort. I am grateful!” cried Mr. Lorry.

“I am grateful!” echoed the Doctor, bowing his head reverently.

“There are two further points,” said Mr. Lorry, “on which I wish to be informed. May I proceed?”

“You cannot render your friend a better service.” The Doctor extended his hand.

“To the first, then. He is of studious habits, remarkably energetic; he devotes himself with great ardour to gaining professional knowledge, to conducting experiments, to many undertakings. Does he overdo it?”

“I think not. The nature of his mind may be to crave constant occupation. That might be partly inherent, partly the outcome of suffering. The less it engaged itself with healthy pursuits, the more risk there would be of its turning in an unhealthy direction. He may have watched himself and made that discovery.”

“You are confident he is not under excessive strain?”

“I think I am quite confident.”

“My dear Manette, if he were overworked at present—”

“My dear Lorry, I doubt that could readily occur. There has been a violent tension in one direction, and it requires a counterweight.”

“Pardon me, as a persistent man of business. Suppose for a moment that he _were_ overworked; would it manifest itself in some recurrence of this disorder?”"}

{"request_id":"d4c20c21486db8e264eece5d","rewritten_text":"“But don’t think I didn’t feel it was wrong in itself.”

“Trust me, they were all perfectly comfortable.”

“I might not have liked them any better for that. So many women and children have no right to be comfortable on board.”

“My dear Frederick, you’re talking nonsense. What would become of us poor sailors’ wives, who often need to travel from one port to another after our husbands, if everyone felt as you do?”

“You see, my feelings didn’t stop me from taking Mrs. Harville and her whole family to Plymouth.”

“But I hate to hear you talk like a fashionable gentleman, as if women were delicate ladies instead of sensible creatures. None of us expects smooth water all our lives.”

“Ah, my dear,” said the Admiral, “when he has a wife, he’ll sing a different tune. Once he’s married, if we’re lucky enough to see another war, we’ll watch him do as you and I and many others have done. He’ll be grateful to anyone who brings him his wife.”

“Oh, we certainly will.”

“Now I’m done,” Captain Wentworth declared. “Once married people start in on me with, ‘Oh! you’ll think differently when you’re married,’ I can only say, ‘No, I won’t,’ and then they reply, ‘Yes, you will,’ and that’s the end of it.”

He stood up and walked away.

“What a great traveler you must have been, ma’am!” Mrs. Musgrove said to Mrs. Croft.

“Not bad, ma’am, for the fifteen years of my marriage, though plenty of women have done more. I’ve crossed the Atlantic four times, been to the East Indies and back once, and besides that, been in various places closer to home: Cork, Lisbon, Gibraltar. But I never went beyond the Straits, and never to the West Indies. We don’t call Bermuda or the Bahamas the West Indies, you know.”

Mrs. Musgrove had nothing to argue; she couldn’t remember ever calling them anything in her life.

“And I assure you, ma’am,” continued Mrs. Croft, “nothing beats the accommodations on a man-of-war—speaking of the higher ranks, of course. On a frigate, naturally, you’re more cramped, though any sensible woman can be perfectly content there; and I can say with confidence, the happiest part of my life was spent on board a ship. While we were together, you know, there was nothing to fear.”"}

{"request_id":"82e83234228323225b8bb5a4","rewritten_text":"In fact, he was dressed as “Jonas the Graveless, or the Corpse-Snatcher of Chertsey Barn,” one of his most striking roles, and one the Cantervilles had every reason to remember, since it was the true origin of their quarrel with their neighbor, Lord Rufford. It was about a quarter past two in the morning, and, as far as he could tell, no one was awake. As he wandered toward the library to see if any trace of the bloodstain remained, two figures suddenly sprang out at him from a dark corner, waving their arms wildly over their heads and screaming “BOO!” in his ear.

Seized with a panic that was entirely understandable in the circumstances, he bolted for the staircase, only to find Washington Otis waiting there with the big garden syringe. Hemmed in by his enemies on every side and almost cornered, he vanished into the great iron stove, which was fortunately unlit, and had to make his way home through the flues and chimneys, reaching his room in a dreadful state of dirt, disarray, and despair.

After that, he was never seen again on any nighttime excursion. The twins lay in ambush for him several times and scattered the passages with nutshells every night, to the great annoyance of their parents and the servants, but it did no good. It was obvious his feelings were so injured that he refused to show himself. Mr. Otis therefore returned to his monumental work on the history of the Democratic Party, which he had been pursuing for years; Mrs. Otis organized a spectacular clam bake that astonished the entire county; the boys devoted themselves to lacrosse, euchre, poker, and other American national games; and Virginia rode through the lanes on her pony, accompanied by the young Duke of Cheshire, who had come to spend the last week of his holiday at Canterville Chase. Everyone assumed the ghost had departed, and Mr. Otis even wrote to Lord Canterville to say so; in reply, Lord Canterville expressed great satisfaction at the news and sent his warmest congratulations to the Minister’s admirable wife.

The Otises, however, were mistaken, for the ghost was still in the house, and though nearly an invalid now, he had no intention of letting matters drop, especially when he heard that the guest list included the young Duke of Cheshire, whose grand-uncle, Lord Francis Stilton, had once wagered a hundred guineas with Colonel Carbury that he would play dice with the Canterville ghost. He was found the next morning lying on the card-room floor in such a helpless, paralyzed state that, although he lived to a great age, he was never able to say anything again except “Double Sixes.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"343840b569e328d21c336146","rewritten_text":"He sprang up and gripped her arm hard. “Show him to me. Which man is he? Point him out. I must see him!” he cried; but right then the Duke of Berwick’s four-in-hand drove between them, and once it had passed, the carriage they were seeking had already rolled out of the park. “He has gone,” Sibyl said sadly. “I wish you had seen him.” “I wish I had, for as surely as there is a God in heaven, if he ever does you harm, I shall kill him.” She stared at him in horror. He said it again. The words slashed the air like a knife. People nearby began to gawk. A lady beside her gave a little laugh. “Come away, Jim; come away,” she murmured. He trailed after her stubbornly as she moved through the crowd. What he had declared filled him with grim satisfaction. When they came to the Achilles Statue, she turned back. Pity rested in her eyes, yet her lips broke into laughter. She shook her head at him. “You are foolish, Jim, utterly foolish; nothing but a bad-tempered boy. How can you utter such dreadful things? You have no idea what you’re saying. You’re simply jealous and cruel. Oh! I wish you would fall in love yourself. Love makes people kind, and what you said was wicked.” “I am sixteen,” he retorted, “and I know what I’m doing. Mother is no protection to you. She hasn’t a clue how to take care of you. I almost wish I were not heading to Australia. I feel tempted to throw it all up. I would, if my articles weren’t already signed.” “Oh, don’t look so solemn, Jim. You are like one of those melodrama heroes Mother loved acting in. I won’t quarrel with you. I have seen him, and oh! seeing him is perfect happiness. We won’t quarrel. I know you would never harm anyone I love, would you?” “Not while you love him, I suppose,” he muttered. “I shall love him forever!” she cried. “And he?” “Forever as well!” “He had better.” She recoiled from him, then laughed and laid her hand on his arm. After all, he was only a boy. At the Marble Arch they hailed an omnibus, which carried them close to their shabby place on the Euston Road. It was past five o’clock, and Sibyl needed to lie down a couple of hours before performing. Jim insisted on it. He said he preferred to say goodbye while their mother was absent. She would surely make a scene, and he loathed scenes of every sort."}

{"request_id":"2ec8bb0973973c041b0a4b2f","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were thrilled to see their dear friend again, declared it felt like ages since they had met, and kept asking what she had been doing since they’d parted. They barely acknowledged the rest of the family, avoided Mrs. Bennet whenever possible, spoke little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. They left again soon, springing up with an energy that surprised their brother and hurrying off as if desperate to escape Mrs. Bennet’s polite attentions.

The thought of the Netherfield ball delighted every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to see it as a tribute to her eldest daughter and felt especially flattered that Mr. Bingley delivered the invitation himself rather than sending a formal card. Jane imagined a joyful evening with her two friends and their brother’s attentions, while Elizabeth looked forward to dancing often with Mr. Wickham and watching Mr. Darcy’s expressions and manners confirm everything she believed. Kitty and Lydia’s happiness depended less on any single event or person; though both intended, like Elizabeth, to dance half the night with Mr. Wickham, he was far from the only partner who could please them, and a ball was, after all, a ball. Even Mary assured her family she felt no reluctance about attending.

“As long as my mornings remain my own,” she said, “that’s enough. I don’t think it’s any sacrifice to take part in evening engagements now and then. Society makes claims on all of us, and I count myself among those who believe that periods of recreation and amusement are desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so high that, though she rarely spoke to Mr. Collins without cause, she had to ask whether he meant to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation and, if so, whether he considered it proper to join the evening’s entertainment. She was somewhat surprised to find he had no reservations and did not remotely fear a reprimand, from either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh, for daring to dance.

“I assure you, I am far from thinking that a ball of this sort, hosted by a young man of character for respectable people, could have any harmful influence,” he said, “and I am so little opposed to dancing myself that I hope to be honored with the hands of all my fair cousins over the course of the evening. I will seize this chance to request yours, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances in particular—a preference I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the proper reason and not to any disrespect toward her.”"}

{"request_id":"b44349d1e61fc894fe186e34","rewritten_text":"After a while midnight pealed from the tall Westminster tower, each resonant chime making the night quiver. Then the railway lamps faded, save for a lone lantern glowing like a great ruby atop its mast, and the city’s roar subsided to a distant murmur.

At two o’clock he rose and sauntered towards Blackfriars. How unreal the whole world appeared! How dreamlike! The houses across the river seemed shaped out of darkness itself. One might have sworn that silver and shadow had re-created everything. The massive dome of St. Paul’s swelled like a bubble through the dim air.

As he neared Cleopatra’s Needle he caught sight of a man leaning over the parapet; drawing closer, he saw the fellow glance up, the gaslight flooding his features.

It was Mr. Podgers, the cheiromantist! That pudgy, flaccid face, the gold-rimmed spectacles, the wan and feeble smile, the sensuous mouth—no mistaking them.

Lord Arthur halted. A dazzling inspiration struck him, and he glided quietly forward. In an instant he grasped Mr. Podgers by the legs and hurled him into the Thames. There came a coarse curse, a heavy splash, then silence. Lord Arthur peered anxiously downward but saw only a tall hat, twirling in a pool of moonlit water. Soon that too sank, leaving no sign of the cheiromantist. For a moment he fancied he detected the bulky, twisted figure swimming towards the bridge staircase, and a dreadful sense of failure seized him, but it proved only a reflection, disappearing when the moon emerged from a cloud. At last he felt he had fulfilled destiny’s command. He drew a deep breath of relief, and Sybil’s name rose to his lips.

“Dropped something, sir?” said a sudden voice behind him.

He spun around to face a policeman with a bull’s-eye lantern.

“Nothing worth speaking of, sergeant,” he replied with a smile, and, hailing a passing hansom, he jumped in, directing the driver to Belgrave Square.

For the next few days he swayed between hope and apprehension. At times he half expected Mr. Podgers to step into the room; at others he felt Fate could not treat him so harshly. Twice he walked to the cheiromantist’s lodgings in West Moon Street, yet he could not bring himself to ring. He craved certainty, and dreaded it.

At last it arrived. He was seated in the club smoking-room, sipping tea and listening listlessly to Surbiton’s recounting of the latest comic song at the Gaiety, when the waiter entered with the evening papers."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d4903654dc5c33766a22d07f","rewritten_text":"Colonel Grangerford was a thorough gentleman. He was a gentleman clear through, and every member of his household the same. He came of good stock, as folks say, and that counts in a man just like it does in a horse, so Widow Douglas declared; and nobody ever disputed that she ranked among the very first aristocrats in our town. Pap was forever declaring it, too, though he himself didn’t have any more breeding than a mudcat. Colonel Grangerford stood mighty tall and slender, with a darkish, pale complexion that didn’t show a trace of red anywhere. He shaved clean every morning, all over that lean face; his lips were the thinnest I ever saw, and his nostrils were just as fine, while his nose rose high, topped by heavy brows, and his eyes were the darkest, sunk so far back they looked as if they peered at you out of caves, so to speak. His forehead was lofty, his hair jet black and straight, falling to his shoulders. His hands were long and narrow, and every day he put on a fresh shirt and a complete suit of linen so white it almost dazzled you; on Sundays he added a blue tailcoat with brass buttons. He carried a mahogany cane capped with silver. Not a speck of frivolity about him, not the slightest, and he was never loud. He was as kind as could be—you just sensed it, and that gave you assurance. Once in a while he smiled, and it was pleasant to behold; but when he drew himself up like a liberty pole and the lightning started to dance under his eyebrows, you felt like climbing a tree first and finding out what was wrong afterward. He never needed to tell anyone to behave—everyone was polite whenever he was around. Folks liked his company, too; he was nearly always like sunshine—I mean he made everything feel fine. When he turned into a cloud bank it was terribly dark for half a minute, and that was plenty; nothing would dare go wrong again for a week.\n\nWhen he and the old lady came down in the morning, the whole family rose from their chairs and gave them good-day, and none of them sat again until the colonel and his lady had seated themselves. Then Tom and Bob went to the sideboard where the decanter stood, and mixed a glass of bitters to hand him. He took it and waited till Tom’s and Bob’s drinks were ready too, and then they bowed, saying, “Our duty to you, sir, and madam;” and the colonel and his lady bowed the tiniest bit and said thank you, and all three drank. After that Bob and Tom poured a spoonful of water over the sugar and the little splash of whiskey or apple brandy in the bottoms of their tumblers, and handed them to me and Buck, and we drank to the old folks as well."}

{"request_id":"bb71c96f7a5a3e928d79a31b","rewritten_text":"“I have not the nerves for that sort of thing.”

“But could you feel at ease spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; his papa can, so why should not I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour how he was. I really think Charles might as well have told his father we would all come. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. Yesterday I was terribly frightened, but it is very different today.”

“Well, if you do not think it too late to let them know, suppose you go as well as your husband. Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot think it wrong while I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” cried Mary, her eyes lighting up. “Dear me! that is an excellent idea, very excellent. I may as well go as stay, for I am no use at home—am I?—and it only tires me. You, who do not have a mother’s feelings, are much better suited. You can make little Charles do anything; he always listens to you at once. It will be far better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh! I shall certainly go; I am sure I ought if I can, just as much as Charles, for they are desperate to have me meet Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left alone. An excellent thought of yours, indeed, Anne. I will go tell Charles and get ready at once. You can send for us in a moment if anything is wrong; but I dare say there will be nothing to worry you. I would not go, you may be sure, if I were not perfectly at ease about my dear child.”

She was instantly knocking at her husband’s dressing-room door, and Anne, following her upstairs, arrived in time for the whole conversation, beginning with Mary’s triumphant declaration—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, for I am no more use at home than you are. Even if I shut myself up forever with the child, I could not make him do anything he dislikes. Anne will stay; Anne agrees to stay home and take care of him. It is Anne’s own suggestion, so I shall go with you, which will be much better, for I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I would be very glad to have you go; but it does seem rather hard that she should be left home by herself to nurse our sick child.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"544719fb69affd0bbaf47707","rewritten_text":"So two years went by. Day after day hundreds of dull hours wore on; they brought no visible change, yet slowly altered my mind as I drifted toward death. I began to study more, to feel the thoughts of others through books, to read history, and to lose myself among the multitudes who lived before me. Perhaps as the immediate pain faded, I became more human. Solitude also lost some of its charm: I started to long again for sympathy. I never felt drawn to crowds, but I did wish for one friend who would love me. You might say I was gradually becoming ready to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I wanted had to be so pure, so free from any influence of circumstance, that the world’s coarse alloys—present even in its noblest feelings—could only deceive me. Believe me, I was even less prepared for human company than before. When I left them, they had tormented me like pain and sickness—irritations outside the mind that I could cast off. But now I would have longed for sympathy; I would have wanted to bind my soul to someone else’s and would have only stocked up on disappointment and suffering, for I was as tender as a sensitive plant, all raw nerve. I did not crave sympathy for ambition or wisdom, but for gentle, mutual affection: smiles to cheer me and soft words to comfort me. I wished for one heart where I could pour out my complaints without restraint, so that the heavenly nature of that soil might make blessed fruit spring from bad seed. Yet how could I find it? The love that animates friendship is a delicate spirit rarely found except when two kind souls grow together from youth, or when they are joined by shared suffering and purpose. It comes to some chosen few unbidden; it descends like gentle dew on selected spots which, though barren before, become fertile with sweet flowers under its benign influence. But when it is sought it flees; it mocks the prayers of its devotees; it gives freely, yet cannot be hunted down.\n\nI knew all this and did not go looking for sympathy. But there on my lonely heath, under my humble roof surrounded by wilderness, it came to me like a winter sunbeam that adorns and melts the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone on blighted fruit; I did not revive beneath its light, for I was too utterly undone to feel its kindness."}

content.text: {"request_id":"25dd443f4f45934da1a6275c","rewritten_text":"Dawn had arrived when I set the manuscript aside. The rain had nearly stopped, the world looked gray and mournful, and the worn-out storm was sighing and sobbing itself to sleep. I went to the stranger’s room and listened at his door, which stood slightly open. I heard his voice, so I knocked. There was no reply, though his voice continued. I peeked in. He lay on his back in bed, speaking in fits and starts but with energy, flinging his arms about restlessly like someone fevered and delirious. I slipped in quietly and bent over him. His mutterings and exclamations went on. I spoke—just a word to get his attention. His glassy eyes and ashen face instantly lit up with pleasure, gratitude, joy, welcome.\n\n“Oh, Sandy, you’ve come at last—how I have longed for you! Sit beside me—don’t leave me—never leave me again, Sandy, never again. Where is your hand?—give it to me, dear, let me hold it—there—now everything is well, all is peaceful, and I’m happy again—we are happy again, aren’t we, Sandy? You’re so dim, so vague, you’re only a mist, a cloud, but you are here, and that’s blessing enough; and I have your hand; don’t take it away—it’s only for a little while, I won’t need it long.... Was that the child? ... Hello—Central! ... she doesn’t answer. Asleep, maybe? Bring her when she wakes, and let me touch her hands, her face, her hair, and tell her goodbye.... Sandy! Yes, you’re there. I drifted for a moment and thought you were gone.... Have I been sick long? It must be so; it feels like months to me. And such dreams! such strange and terrible dreams, Sandy! Dreams as real as reality—delirium, of course, but so real! I thought the king was dead, I thought you were in Gaul and couldn’t get home, I thought there was a revolution; in the wild frenzy of these dreams, I imagined that Clarence, my cadets, and I fought and destroyed all of England’s chivalry! But even that wasn’t the strangest. I seemed to be a creature torn from some unborn age far in the future, and even that felt as real as the rest! Yes, I seemed to rush back from that age into our own, then forward again, and was dropped, a stranger, lonely in that unfamiliar England, with a gulf of thirteen centuries yawning between me and you! between me and my home and my friends! between me and all that I hold dear, all that could make life worth living!”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"77e8819577bfa24f5ab6cb4b","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General was obliged to inform the jury that the accused, though youthful in appearance, was seasoned in treasonous dealings demanding his life. This correspondence with the public foe was no matter of today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before, but had gone on much longer. The prisoner, it was certain, had long been passing back and forth between France and England on secret missions for which he could offer no honest explanation. Had treasonous enterprises been of a nature to prosper—which, happily, they never were—the true wickedness and guilt of his work might have remained concealed. Providence, however, had inspired an individual beyond fear or reproach to ferret out the prisoner’s designs and, horrified, reveal them to His Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot, Mr. Attorney-General assured them, would appear before the court. His stance and bearing were, on the whole, sublime. Once the prisoner’s friend, he had, in a moment both auspicious and tragic, uncovered his infamy, and resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer shelter in his bosom upon the sacred altar of his country. Were statues in Britain decreed to benefactors as in ancient Greece and Rome, this illustrious citizen would certainly merit one; as they were not, he likely would go without. Virtue, as the poets—whose verses the jury, of course, knew by heart, though their faces confessed they did not—had observed, was contagious, especially that radiant quality called patriotism or love of country. The lofty example of this immaculate and unimpeachable witness for the Crown, to mention whom at all was an honour, had inspired the prisoner’s servant to a holy resolve to inspect his master’s table-drawers and pockets and to secrete his papers. Mr. Attorney-General anticipated attempts to disparage this admirable servant but, generally speaking, he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters and honoured him above his father and mother. He called upon the jury with confidence to share that sentiment. The testimony of these two witnesses, together with the documents they had discovered and which would be produced, would demonstrate that the prisoner had been supplied with lists of His Majesty’s forces, their arrangement and readiness by sea and land, and would leave no doubt that he habitually transmitted such intelligence to a hostile power."}
