content.text: {"request_id":"98205408536d7f2e15be293e","rewritten_text":"Perdita’s name never arose; still I could not doubt that affection for her caused the wavering of purpose he displayed. And who merited love more than my high-souled sister? Who better deserved the hand of that self-elevated monarch than she, whose very look befitted a queen among nations? She cherished him even as he loved her; though frustration subdued her fervor, and ambition waged fierce war with his. We went together to the House that evening. Raymond, though aware that his projects and prospects must be debated and resolved in the coming discussion, wore an air of gaiety and unconcern. A hum like that of ten thousand swarming beehives deafened us as we entered the coffee-room. Clusters of politicians stood with harried faces and raised or hushed tones. The aristocratic faction—the wealthiest and most influential men in England—seemed less disturbed than the rest, for the issue would be argued without requiring their intervention. By the fire sat Ryland with his adherents. Ryland, of humble birth yet immense fortune, had inherited his riches from his manufacturer father. In youth he had witnessed the king’s abdication and the merging of the two Houses of Lords and Commons; he had approved these popular advances, and his life’s work had been to confirm and expand them. Since then the influence of landowners had grown; at first Ryland had not disapproved of Lord Raymond’s plots, which drew away many supporters from his adversaries. But now matters were going too far. The poorer nobility welcomed the revival of sovereignty as a means to regain the authority and privileges they had forfeited. The half-slumbering spirit of royalty stirred again in men’s minds; they, willing serfs, self-made subjects, stood ready to bow their necks beneath the yoke. A few stalwart spirits endured, pillars of the state; yet the word republic had become trite to the common ear, and many—an event soon to prove whether it was the majority—yearned for the glitter and display of kingship. Ryland was aroused to defiance; he declared that only by his forbearance had this faction been allowed to thrive; the season for leniency had passed, and with a sweep of his arm he would brush away the cobwebs clouding his countrymen. When Raymond stepped into the coffee-room, his arrival drew near-shouts from his allies. They crowded about him, tallied their supporters, and laid out their reasons for expecting new recruits from members who had not yet announced themselves."}

{"request_id":"267d698bbecf657bb7d79b6e","rewritten_text":"“I’m going, Master Will—truly I am,” the Black man replied promptly. “Almost out to the end now.”

“Out to the end?” Legrand practically screamed. “Are you saying you’re all the way out on that limb?”

“Almost to the end, sir—o-o-o-oh! Lord have mercy! what’s this on the tree?”

“Well!” cried Legrand, delighted. “What is it?”

“Why, it’s nothing but a skull—someone left his head up here, and the crows picked every bit of flesh off.”

“A skull, you say! All right—how’s it fastened to the branch? What’s holding it there?”

“Sure enough, sir; let me look. Why, this is mighty curious, I swear—there’s a big nail in the skull fastening it to the tree.”

“Now, Jupiter, do exactly what I tell you—understand?”

“Yes, sir.”

“Pay attention, then—find the skull’s left eye.”

“Huh! That’s good! There isn’t any eye left at all.”

“Curse your stupidity! Do you even know your right hand from your left?”

“Yes, I know that—I know everything about that—it’s my left hand I chop wood with.”

“Of course! You’re left-handed, and your left eye is on the same side as your left hand. Now, I assume you can find the skull’s left eye, or where it used to be. Have you found it?”

There was a long silence. At last the man asked, “Is the skull’s left eye on the same side as its left hand too? Because the skull hasn’t got a bit of a hand—never mind! I’ve got the left eye now—here’s the left eye! What should I do with it?”

“Let the beetle drop through it as far as the string will reach—but be careful not to let go of the string.”

“All done, Master Will; mighty easy thing to put the bug through the hole—watch out down there!”

During this exchange no part of Jupiter’s body could be seen, but the beetle he let down was now visible at the end of the string, glimmering like a polished gold globe in the last rays of the setting sun, some of which still faintly lit the high ground where we stood. The scarab hung clear of any branches and, if released, would have fallen at our feet. Legrand immediately grabbed the scythe and cleared a circular space three or four yards across directly beneath the insect, and, once he finished, he ordered Jupiter to drop the string and come down from the tree."}

{"request_id":"c06e39517506ac2f4e3bd867","rewritten_text":"It was early February, and after a month in Bath, Anne was growing very anxious for news from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted to hear far more than Mary had shared. It had been three weeks since she had heard anything at all. She only knew that Henrietta was back home, and that Louisa, though said to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. She was thinking of all of them very intently one evening when a thicker-than-usual letter from Mary arrived—and, adding to the pleasure and surprise, it came with Admiral and Mrs. Croft’s compliments.

The Crofts must be in Bath! That was something to excite her. They were people her heart naturally turned toward.

“What is this?” exclaimed Sir Walter. “The Crofts have come to Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they brought you?”

“A letter from Uppercross Cottage, sir.”

“Oh! Those letters are convenient passports. They ensure an introduction. Still, I should have called on Admiral Croft in any case. I know what is owed to my tenant.”

Anne could not listen any longer; she could not even have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion fared under her father’s remarks, because her letter absorbed her entirely. It had been started several days earlier.

“February 1st.

“My dear Anne,

“I make no apology for my silence, because I know how little people care about letters in a place like Bath. You must be much too happy to bother with Uppercross, which, as you well know, offers very little to write about. We have had a remarkably dull Christmas; Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove did not host a single dinner party the whole holiday. I do not count the Hayters as anybody. The holidays are over at last, though; I doubt any children ever had such long ones. They certainly were longer than mine. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear they still have not gone home. Mrs. Harville must be an odd mother to be separated from them so long. I do not understand it. They are not at all pleasant children, in my opinion; but Mrs. Musgrove seems to like them every bit as much as, if not more than, her own grandchildren. What dreadful weather we have had! Perhaps it is not felt in Bath with your nice pavements, but in the country it matters. I have not had a soul call on me since the second week of January, except for Charles Hayter, who has been visiting much more often than is welcome. Between ourselves, I think it was a great pity Henrietta did not stay in Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her out of his way a little.”"}

{"request_id":"9e6033e112e40ef0121eab5f","rewritten_text":"They were bringing along a fine-looking elderly gentleman, and a handsome younger fellow with his right arm trussed up in a sling. And land sakes, how the crowd hooted and hollered, and kept it going. But I couldn’t spy any humor in it, and figured it’d take all the duke and king had to spy any, either. I expected they’d go white as sheets. But no, not a bit of color did they lose. The duke never let on he guessed the game, just kept goo-gooing around, cheerful and contented, like a jug gurgling out buttermilk; and the king, he only stared and stared down mournful at them new arrivals like it gave him a stomach cramp in the very heart to think the world held such cheats and scoundrels. Oh, he played it masterly. A heap of the leading folks crowded up around the king, to show they stood by him. That elderly gentleman newly arrived looked plum bewildered. After a minute he began to speak, and I could tell right off he talked _like_ an Englishman—not the king’s fashion, though the king’s was tolerable for a sample. I can’t give the old gent’s exact talk, nor mimic him; but he swung round to the crowd, and said something like this:

“This here is an astonishment to me that I wasn’t expecting; and I confess, free and open, I ain’t in good shape to meet it and answer it; for my brother and me has suffered misfortunes; he’s cracked his arm, and our trunks got put off at a town up the river last night by a mistake. I’m Peter Wilks’ brother Harvey, and this here is his brother William, who can’t hear nor speak—and can scarce make signs fit to count, now he’s only got one hand to do it with. We are who we claim; and in a day or two, when I fetch the baggage, I can prove it. Till then I won’t say any more, but go to the hotel and wait.”

So him and the fresh mute walked off; and the king he chuckles, and blurts out:

“Broken his arm—_very_ likely, _ain’t_ it?—and mighty handy, too, for a cheat that’s got to talk with signs and don’t know how. Lost their baggage! That’s _powerful_ rich!—and mighty clever—considering the _fix!_”

Then he laughed once more; and so did the rest, except maybe three or four, or maybe six. One of those was that doctor; another was a keen-faced gentleman, with an old-style carpet-bag made of carpet-cloth, that had just stepped off the steamboat and was speaking to him in a low tone, darting glances at the king now and again and nodding together—it was Levi Bell, the lawyer that had gone up to Louisville; and another was a big rough husky chap that had come along and listened to every word the old gentleman said, and was listening to the king now."}

content.text: {"request_id":"617adaf861a6c5edba25d0ff","rewritten_text":"Lay down your arms, fellow men, brothers! Forgiveness, help, and brotherly love await your repentance. You are dear to us because you wear the fragile form of humanity; each of you will find a friend and host among these ranks. Shall man remain the enemy of man while the plague, the enemy of all, hovers above us, rejoicing in our slaughter, more cruel even than itself?”  Each army paused. On our side the soldiers gripped their weapons and fixed hard stares on the foe. The others still held their arms, more from fear than defiance; they looked at each other, each waiting for someone to lead, but they had no commander. Adrian leaped from his horse and approached one of the newly slain. “He was a man,” he cried, “and now he is dead. Quickly, bind the wounds of the fallen—let none die; let no more souls escape through your merciless blows to recount before the throne of God the tale of fratricide. Bind their wounds—restore them to their friends. Cast off the tiger hearts burning in your breasts; throw down those tools of cruelty and hate; in this brief pause granted by pitiless destiny, let every man be brother, guardian, and support to the other. Away with those blood-stained weapons, and hurry—some of you—bind up these wounds.”  As he spoke, he knelt and lifted into his arms a man from whose side the warm tide of life poured out. The poor wretch gasped. Both armies were so still that his moans were clearly heard, and every heart, moments ago bent on total slaughter, now beat anxiously with hope and fear for this single man. Adrian tore off his military scarf and bound it around the sufferer. It was too late. The man breathed a deep sigh, his head dropped back, his limbs slackened. “He is dead,” Adrian said, as the body slipped from his arms to the ground, and he bowed his head in grief and awe. The fate of the world seemed tied to the death of this one man. On both sides the forces threw down their arms; even the veterans wept, and our men extended their hands to their foes while a rush of love and deepest friendship filled every heart. The two armies mingled, unarmed and hand in hand, speaking only of how each might help the other. The adversaries joined, each repenting—the one side for their former cruelties, the other for their recent violence—and they obeyed the General’s orders to march toward London."}

{"request_id":"8fd8db7a15820600e9b280ec","rewritten_text":"“I have not nerves for that kind of thing.”

“But could you really feel comfortable spending the entire evening away from the poor boy?”

“Quite. His papa can do it, so why may not I? Jemima is meticulous; she could send word every hour how he fares. In fact, I rather think Charles might have told his father we should all come. I am no more anxious about little Charles now than he is. Yesterday I was terribly frightened, but it is a very different case to-day.”

“Then if you do not consider it too late to give notice for yourself, why should you not go as well as your husband? Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot deem it improper while I remain with him.”

“Are you serious?” cried Mary, her eyes lighting up. “Bless me! that is an excellent idea, really excellent. To be sure, I may just as well go as stay, for I am of no use at home—am I?—and it only worries me. You, who do not have a mother’s feelings, are infinitely the fitter person. You can manage little Charles in anything; he obeys you instantly. It will be far preferable to leaving him solely with Jemima. Oh! I shall certainly go; I am sure I ought, if I have the chance, quite as much as Charles, for they are desperately anxious I should become acquainted with Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not object to being left alone. A capital idea of yours, indeed, Anne. I will go tell Charles and get ready at once. You can have us sent for, you know, at a moment’s warning if anything is amiss; but I dare say nothing will alarm you. I would not go, you may rely on it, if I did not feel entirely at ease about my dear child.”

The next instant she was tapping at her husband’s dressing-room door, and Anne, following her upstairs, arrived in time for the whole discussion, which opened with Mary’s saying, in triumphant tones—

“I mean to go with you, Charles, for I am no more use at home than you. If I were to confine myself forever with the child, I could not induce him to do anything he disliked. Anne will remain; Anne pledges herself to stay at home and care for him. It is Anne’s own scheme, and so I shall accompany you, which will be far better, for I have not dined at their house since Tuesday.”

“This is very considerate of Anne,” her husband replied, “and I should be delighted to have you go; but it seems somewhat unfair that she should be left at home alone to nurse our sick child.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"3309894a9e9f860f17029d75","rewritten_text":"I could still recall how matters stood during our great civil war in the nineteenth century. Up North a carpenter earned three dollars a day in gold value; down South he received fifty—paid in Confederate shinplasters that were worth about a dollar a bushel. Up North a pair of overalls cost three dollars—equal to a day’s wages; in the South they cost seventy-five—which meant two days’ pay. Everything else kept the same ratio. So wages really stood twice as high in the North, because the northern wage bought just twice what the southern one could. \n\nSure enough, I made several acquaintances in the little village, and it pleased me immensely to see our fresh coins moving about—plenty of milrays, plenty of mills, plenty of cents, a fair lot of nickels, and some silver; all in the hands of the artisans and common folk generally; yes, even a trace of gold—but that lay in the bank, meaning the goldsmith’s shop. I stepped in while Marco, son of Marco, was dickering with a shopman over a quarter pound of salt, and I asked for change for a twenty-dollar gold piece. They obliged me—after first gnawing the coin a bit, ringing it on the counter, touching it with acid, and demanding where I had got it, who I was, whence I hailed, whither I was bound, when I expected to arrive, and perhaps a couple hundred more inquiries. And when their questions ran dry, I kept right on and volunteered all sorts of details; told them I owned a dog named Watch, that my first wife was a Free Will Baptist, her grandfather a Prohibitionist, and that I once knew a man with two thumbs on each hand and a wart inside his upper lip who died hopeful of a glorious resurrection, and so forth, and so forth, and so forth, until even that famished village inquisitor began to look content—and a trifle annoyed. Still he had to show due deference to a man of my financial standing, so he offered no impudence, though I noticed he vented it on his assistants, which was perfectly natural. Yes, they broke my twenty, yet I could tell it strained the bank a little; and that was no surprise, for it was like walking into a shabby country store back in the nineteenth century and suddenly asking the proprietor to break a two-thousand-dollar note. He could manage it, perhaps, but he would still marvel how a modest farmer came to be lugging such a sum in his pocket—which was likely what this goldsmith wondered, too; for he followed me to the doorway and stood there staring after me with reverent admiration."}

{"request_id":"cdf6a52c8aae46bb2f86f9a8","rewritten_text":"“In English, the letter that appears most often is e. After that, the order runs this way: a, o, i, d, h, n, r, s, t, u, y, c, f, g, l, m, w, b, k, p, q, x, z. E shows up so much that almost every sentence of any length uses it more than any other letter.

“Right away, this gives us more than a simple guess. The table’s general use is obvious, but for this cipher we’ll only need it a little. Since 8 is the most common symbol here, we’ll start by assuming it stands for e in the regular alphabet. To test that idea, let’s see whether 8 appears in pairs, because e is doubled very often in English—in words like meet, fleet, speed, seen, been, agree, and so on. In this cryptogram, we see it doubled five times, even though the message is short.

“So we take 8 as e. Now, the word ‘the’ is the most common word in the language. Let’s look for any repeated group of three symbols, always in the same order, with 8 as the last character. If we find such repetitions, they will probably stand for ‘the.’ When we look closely, we find seven instances of the sequence ;48. We can then assume ; means t, 4 means h, and 8 means e—the last now firmly confirmed. That is a significant advance.

“Once we have identified one word, we can figure out something else very important: the beginnings and endings of other words. Look at the next-to-last appearance of ;48, close to the end of the cipher. We know the ; that follows immediately after marks the start of a new word, and, among the six symbols after this ‘the,’ we already know five. Let’s write them out with the letters they represent, leaving an empty space for the unknown one—

t eeth.

“Right away, we drop the ‘th’ from the word starting with that first t, because if we test every letter of the alphabet for the blank spot, no word appears that could contain that th there. That narrows it to

t ee,

and when we go through the alphabet again, if needed, we find the only possible word is ‘tree.’”"}

{"request_id":"e66773b6ae0fa676acb477c3","rewritten_text":"Dear me, she could talk endlessly. It wouldn’t do for me to hint that it was getting very late and that I was exhausted and sleepy. I wished I had gone to bed when I had the chance. Now I had to stay; there was no escape. So she kept tinkling along, and the sleeping castle was otherwise silent and ghostly, until at last there rose from somewhere deep below a distant sound, like a muffled shriek with such agony that it made my skin crawl. The queen stopped, her eyes lighting with delight; she tilted her graceful head like a bird listening. The sound forced its way up through the stillness again.

“What is it?” I asked.

“It is truly a stubborn soul, and it endures long. It has been many hours now.”

“Endures what?”

“The rack. Come—you shall see a joyful sight. If he does not yield his secret now, you shall see him torn apart.”

What a silky smooth hellion she was; so calm and composed, while the cords down my legs tightened in sympathy with that man’s pain. Guided by armored guards carrying blazing torches, we tramped through echoing corridors and down stone stairways that were damp and dripping and smelled of mold and ages of shut-up night—a chill, eerie journey and a long one, and not made shorter or cheerier by the sorceress’s talk about the sufferer and his crime. He had been accused by an anonymous informant of killing a stag in the royal preserves. I said:

“Anonymous testimony isn’t quite right, your Highness. It would be fairer to bring the accused face to face with the accuser.”

“I had not thought of that, it being of little importance. But even if I wished to, I could not, for the accuser came masked by night, told the forester, then left at once, so the forester doesn’t know him.”

“Then is this Unknown the only person who saw the stag killed?”

“No man saw the killing, but this Unknown saw this bold wretch near the spot where the stag lay and came with loyal zeal and betrayed him to the forester.”

“So the Unknown was near the dead stag too? Isn’t it possible he did the killing himself? His loyal zeal—in a mask—seems a bit suspicious. But what is your Highness’s reason for racking the prisoner? Where is the gain?”

“He will not confess otherwise; and then his soul would be lost. For his crime his life is forfeit by the law—and surely I will see he pays it!—but it would endanger my own soul to let him die unconfessed and without absolution.”"}

{"request_id":"27785ef5053f0beec69d01a1","rewritten_text":"I want you to stay well connected, and to do that it is best to have as few odd acquaintances as possible. So if you are still here when Mr. Martin marries, I hope you will not let your friendship with his sisters draw you into knowing his wife, who will likely be a farmer’s daughter with no education.”

“Of course. Yes. Not that I think Mr. Martin would ever marry anyone who had not had some schooling and been brought up well. Still, I am not going to argue with you, and I am sure I will not wish for his wife’s acquaintance. I will always think highly of the Miss Martins, especially Elizabeth, and I would be very sorry to give them up, for they are as well educated as I am. But if he marries a very ignorant, coarse woman, of course I had better not visit her, if I can help it.”

Emma watched her through this wavering speech and saw no worrying signs of love. The young man had been her first admirer, but Emma trusted he had no other hold on her and that Harriet would offer no serious resistance to any friendly plans she might make.

They met Mr. Martin the very next day while walking on the Donwell road. He was on foot, and after looking very respectfully at Emma, he gazed with clear pleasure at her companion. Emma was glad to have the chance to inspect him, and by walking a few yards ahead while they talked, soon satisfied her sharp eye about Mr. Robert Martin. His appearance was neat, and he looked like a sensible young man, but there was no other advantage, and she felt sure that when compared with real gentlemen he would lose all the ground he had gained in Harriet’s regard. Harriet was sensitive to manners; she had often admired her father’s gentleness with both admiration and surprise. Mr. Martin looked as though he did not even know what manners were.

They stayed together only a few minutes, since Miss Woodhouse must not be kept waiting, and Harriet came running back with a smiling face and fluttering spirits, which Miss Woodhouse hoped to calm soon.

“Only think of us happening to meet him! How very strange! He said it was pure chance that he had not gone round by Randalls. He did not think we ever walked this road. He thought we usually walked toward Randalls.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"b9c0cec4802c39f8492dc244","rewritten_text":"Once we had seen our friend securely installed in his new post, our thoughts shifted toward Windsor. The place lay so near to London that parting from Raymond and Perdita hardly felt like a true separation. We bade them farewell within the Protectoral Palace. It delighted me to watch my sister seem to enter into the spirit of a performance, striving to sustain her rank with suitable grace. Her innate pride and humility of demeanour clashed now more than ever. Her nervousness was genuine, born from a fear of being undervalued, from that slight regard for the world’s neglect which Raymond also possessed. Yet Perdita thought of others more than he ever did, and some of her shyness stemmed from wanting to ease any sense of inferiority in those around her—an impression that never visited her own mind. Idris, by her birth and education, was better suited to ceremonial routine, although the same ease that made such actions instinctive for her also rendered them dull. Despite every drawback, Perdita plainly relished her role. Brimming with fresh ideas, she scarcely felt sorrow when we left. She embraced us warmly, promised to come soon, and did not lament the circumstances that separated us. Raymond’s spirits were irrepressible; he scarcely knew how to employ his newly acquired power. His mind teemed with schemes, though none were settled, and he vowed that the era of his Protectorship would be marked by some deed of sublime renown. Thus we spoke of them, moralizing as we made our reduced way back to Windsor Castle. We rejoiced at our escape from political tempests and pursued solitude with heightened eagerness. Though our occupations were not lacking, my restless nature now strove only in the realm of intellectual effort; intense study proved a fine remedy to soothe the fever of spirit that idleness would surely have provoked. Perdita allowed Clara to accompany us to Windsor, and she, along with my two beautiful infants, became constant sources of fascination and delight.\n\nOnly Adrian’s health troubled our serenity. It plainly declined without any symptom to suggest the cause, unless his luminous eyes, animated expression, and flushed cheeks made us fear consumption; yet he felt neither pain nor dread. He threw himself ardently into books, finding respite from study in the company he cherished most—his sister and myself."}

{"request_id":"41ea3d0ce48621dc2bcb5803","rewritten_text":"But now she wished it had never happened. She was sure he had been drinking too much of Mr. Weston’s good wine and fully expected he would start talking nonsense.

To keep him in check as much as possible through her own composure, she was getting ready to speak with perfect calmness and gravity about the weather and the night; but she had barely begun, had barely passed the sweep-gate and joined the other carriage, when her subject was snatched away—her hand seized—her attention demanded—and Mr. Elton was actually making forceful love to her: taking advantage of the priceless opportunity, declaring feelings that ought to be well known, hoping and fearing, adoring, ready to die if she refused him; yet flattering himself that his ardent devotion, incomparable attachment, and unmatched passion could not fail to have some effect, and, in short, thoroughly determined to be seriously accepted as soon as possible. It was truly happening. Without hesitation, apology, or much sign of shyness, Mr. Elton, Harriet’s suitor, was declaring himself her suitor. She tried to stop him, but it was useless; he would continue and say everything. Furious as she was, the thought of the moment made her resolve to keep hold of herself when she did speak. She felt that half this foolishness must be drunkenness, and so she hoped it belonged only to the passing hour. Accordingly, with a mix of seriousness and playfulness that she hoped suited his half-and-half condition, she answered,

“I am very surprised, Mr. Elton. This to me! You forget yourself—you mistake me for my friend—any message to Miss Smith I’ll gladly deliver; but no more of this to me, if you please.”

“Miss Smith! A message to Miss Smith! What could she possibly mean?” He repeated her words with such confident emphasis, such swaggering pretense of amazement, that she could not help replying briskly,

“Mr. Elton, this is the most extraordinary behavior! I can explain it only one way: you are not yourself, or you couldn’t speak either to me or of Harriet like this. Get hold of yourself enough to say no more, and I will try to forget it.”

But Mr. Elton had drunk only enough wine to lift his spirits, not enough to muddle his thoughts. He knew exactly what he meant; and after vehemently protesting that her suspicion was most unfair and briefly mentioning his respect for Miss Smith as her friend—though admitting he was astonished she was mentioned at all—he returned to the subject of his own passion and pressed hard for a favorable answer."}

{"request_id":"a6157446fbec168a4ea8571b","rewritten_text":"This was Mrs. Umney, the housekeeper, whom Mrs. Otis had agreed to retain at Lady Canterville’s earnest request. She made them each a deep curtsey as they stepped down and said in a quaint, old-fashioned tone, “I welcome you to Canterville Chase.” Following her lead, they walked through the grand Tudor hall into the library, a long, low room paneled in black oak with a large stained-glass window at the far end. There tea was already laid out for them, and after removing their wraps, they sat down and began to look around while Mrs. Umney served them.

Suddenly Mrs. Otis noticed a dull red stain on the floor beside the fireplace and, unaware of its true meaning, said to Mrs. Umney, “I’m afraid something has been spilled there.”

“Yes, madam,” replied the old housekeeper quietly, “blood was spilled on that spot.”

“How dreadful,” exclaimed Mrs. Otis. “I dislike bloodstains in a sitting room. It must be removed at once.”

The old woman smiled and answered in the same hushed, mysterious tone, “It is the blood of Lady Eleanor de Canterville, who was murdered on that very spot by her husband, Sir Simon de Canterville, in 1575. Sir Simon outlived her by nine years and then vanished under very mysterious circumstances. His body was never found, but his guilty spirit still haunts the Chase. The bloodstain has been greatly admired by tourists and cannot be removed.”

“That’s nonsense,” declared Washington Otis. “Pinkerton’s Champion Stain Remover and Paragon Detergent will clean it up in no time.” Before the frightened housekeeper could stop him, he dropped to his knees and began vigorously scrubbing the floor with a small stick that looked like black cosmetic. In moments the bloodstain had vanished.

“I knew Pinkerton would handle it,” he said triumphantly, glancing around at his admiring family—but no sooner had he spoken than a terrible flash of lightning lit the gloomy room, a thunderclap made them all jump to their feet, and Mrs. Umney fainted.

“What a monstrous climate,” said the American Minister calmly as he lit a long cheroot. “I suppose the old country is so crowded they don’t have enough decent weather for everyone. I have always thought emigration is the only solution for England.”

“My dear Hiram,” cried Mrs. Otis, “what can we do with a woman who faints?”

“Charge it to her like breakages,” answered the Minister. “She won’t faint again after that.” And in a few moments Mrs. Umney indeed revived."}

content.text: {"request_id":"079312abe279ab1a0487f3b1","rewritten_text":"The stupor and astonishment this extraordinary turn of events produced in me was perhaps, when all is said and done, the least explainable part of the adventure. The sudden shift itself was natural and inevitable, and I had long expected it to occur the moment I reached the point in my voyage where the planet’s pull would be replaced by that of the satellite—or, more accurately, when the balloon’s attraction toward Earth became weaker than its attraction toward the moon. Admittedly, I woke from a deep sleep with my senses in disorder to find a startling phenomenon that, although anticipated, caught me off guard at that immediate moment. The reversal must have happened gently and gradually, and it is far from certain that, had I been awake, I would have noticed any internal sign of the inversion—no discomfort, no disruption either to myself or to my equipment. \n\nIt goes almost without saying that, once I fully grasped my situation and emerged from the terror that had gripped every faculty of my soul, my attention was first fixed entirely on the moon’s general physical appearance. It lay beneath me like a map—and although I judged it still to be at a considerable distance, the indentations of its surface appeared to my eyes with a striking and inexplicable clarity. The complete absence of ocean or sea—or even lakes, rivers, or any body of water whatsoever—stood out at first glance as the most extraordinary aspect of its geology. Yet, strangely enough, I saw vast flat regions unmistakably alluvial, although most of the hemisphere visible to me was covered with countless volcanic mountains, conical in shape, and looking more like artificial structures than natural formations. The highest of these rises no more than three and three-quarter miles vertically; but a chart of the volcanic districts of the Campi Phlegraei would give you a better sense of their general surface than any poor description I could attempt. Most of them were clearly erupting, making me dread their fury and power with the repeated thunder of the so-called meteoric stones, which now shot upward past the balloon with increasing, terrifying frequency."}

{"request_id":"fc7437b957c7ca43768f836d","rewritten_text":"But there was no laughter in the little town that same calm Saturday afternoon. The Harpers and Aunt Polly’s household were being dressed in mourning, overwhelmed with grief and tears. A strange quiet settled over the village, though heaven knows it was usually quiet enough. The villagers went about their business with distant looks and spoke little, but sighed often. The Saturday holiday felt like a burden to the children. They had no heart for their games and slowly abandoned them. 

That afternoon Becky Thatcher found herself wandering gloomily around the empty schoolyard, feeling very sad. But nothing there eased her sorrow. She murmured to herself:

“Oh, if only I still had that brass andiron knob! But I don’t have anything left to remember him by.” She swallowed back a small sob. 

Soon she stopped and said quietly:

“It was right here. Oh, if I could do it over, I wouldn’t say that again—not for the whole world. But he’s gone now; I’ll never, never, never see him again.” 

That thought broke her, and she drifted away with tears streaming down her cheeks. Then a band of boys and girls—Tom’s and Joe’s playmates—came by, leaned over the picket fence, and spoke in solemn tones about how Tom did this or that the last time they saw him, and how Joe said this little thing or that (which now, they were sure, held dreadful meaning!)—and each one pointed to the exact spot where the missing boys had stood, then added something like “and I was standing right here—just like this, and if you were him—I was that close—and he smiled, just like this—and then something washed over me, like—terrifying, you know—and I never guessed what it meant, of course, but now I understand!” 

Then they argued about who saw the dead boys last, and many laid claim to that gloomy honor and offered proof, somewhat embellished to favor the storyteller. When it was finally settled who truly had seen the departed last and exchanged their final words, the fortunate winners took on a sort of sacred importance, and the rest stared at them with envy. One poor fellow, having no other glory to brag about, said with very evident pride: 

“Well, Tom Sawyer beat me up once.” 

But that bid for fame was a failure. Most of the boys could say the same, so it cheapened the distinction too much. The group drifted away, still sharing memories of the lost heroes in hushed voices."}

{"request_id":"12931bf6a5ace348f8222f51","rewritten_text":"Right in front of him, in the pale moonlight, stood an old man of terrifying appearance. His eyes glowed like burning coals; long gray hair hung over his shoulders in tangled ropes; his antique-cut clothes were filthy and torn, and heavy manacles and rusty shackles dangled from his wrists and ankles.

“My dear sir,” said Mr. Otis, “I really must insist that you oil those chains, and I have brought you a small bottle of Tammany Rising Sun Lubricator for that purpose. They say one application works completely, and there are several testimonials on the label from our most distinguished homegrown divines. I’ll leave it here by the bedroom candles, and I’ll be happy to provide more if you need it.” With that, the United States Minister set the bottle on a marble table, shut his door, and went to bed.

For a moment the Canterville ghost stood perfectly still in natural outrage; then he smashed the bottle against the polished floor and raced down the corridor, groaning hollowly and radiating a ghastly green glow. But just as he reached the top of the great oak staircase, a door flew open, two little white-robed figures appeared, and a large pillow whizzed past his head! There was clearly no time to waste, so he quickly slipped into the Fourth Dimension of Space as a way of escape, vanished through the wainscoting, and the house fell silent.

When he reached a small hidden chamber in the left wing, he leaned against a moonbeam to catch his breath and tried to absorb what had happened. Never in a brilliant and uninterrupted three-hundred-year career had he been so grossly insulted. He thought of the Dowager Duchess, whom he had scared into a fit as she stood before her mirror in lace and diamonds; of the four housemaids who had fallen into hysterics when he merely grinned at them through the spare bedroom curtains; of the parish rector whose candle he had blown out as the man came late one night from the library, and who had been under Sir William Gull’s care ever since, a complete martyr to nervous disorders; and of old Madame de Tremouillac, who, after waking one early morning and seeing a skeleton in an armchair by the fire reading her diary, had been confined to bed for six weeks with brain fever and, when she recovered, had reconciled with the Church and severed ties with that notorious skeptic Monsieur de Voltaire."}

{"request_id":"c4833b0c38bb9e90b3719805","rewritten_text":"Biddy was in tears; the garden growing dim, the lane, and the stars beginning to show were blurred to me as well.

“Nothing ever came to light, Biddy?”

“Nothing at all.”

“Do you know what has become of Orlick?”

“Judging from the state of his clothes, I should imagine he is labouring at the quarries.”

“Then you have seen him?—Why fix your eyes on that dark tree down the lane?”

“I saw him there, the night she died.”

“That wasn’t the final time, either, Biddy?”

“No; I have noticed him there since we have been walking here.—It is useless,” said Biddy, laying her hand on my arm while I was ready to rush off, “you know I would not mislead you; he was scarcely there a minute, and he has gone.”

The discovery that she was still dogged by this man flamed up my hottest anger, and I felt implacable toward him. I told her so, and said I would spend any money or endure any effort to hound him out of that district. Gradually she led me into calmer speech, and she spoke of Joe’s love for me, and how Joe never murmured at anything,—she didn’t name me; she had no need; I understood her,—but always did his duty in his station, with strong hands, a quiet tongue, and a tender heart.

“Indeed, one could hardly praise him too highly,” said I; “and Biddy, we must often talk of these matters, for of course I shall frequently be down here now. I have no intention of leaving poor Joe lonely.”

Biddy did not utter a word.

“Biddy, can’t you hear me?”

“Yes, Mr. Pip.”

“Besides your addressing me as Mr. Pip—which strikes me as rather poor form, Biddy—what is your meaning?”

“What do I mean?” Biddy asked, timidly.

“Biddy,” I said, with righteous self-assertion, “I must insist on knowing what you mean by this?”

“By this?” repeated Biddy.

“Now, do not repeat,” I snapped. “You used not to repeat, Biddy.”

“Used not!” Biddy exclaimed. “O Mr. Pip! Used!”

Well! I thought it best to drop that matter also. After another silent round through the garden, I returned to the principal point.

“Biddy,” said I, “I made a remark about my coming down here frequently to visit Joe, which you met with marked silence. Be so good as to tell me why.”

“Are you quite certain, then, that you WILL come to see him frequently?” asked Biddy, pausing in the narrow garden path, and gazing at me beneath the stars with a clear and honest eye."}

content.text: {"request_id":"82dd230d9e4a3d71a78d0858","rewritten_text":"“What, then, has ensued? What impression have I made on your imagination?” Dupin asked, and a chill ran through me. “A lunatic,” I replied, “committed this crime—some raving madman escaped from a nearby asylum.” “In certain respects,” he said, “your idea isn’t irrelevant. Yet even the wildest ravings of the insane never match the peculiar voice heard on the stairs. Every madman belongs to some nation, and their language—however incoherent—still keeps the coherence of syllables. Besides, the hair of a madman isn’t like the tuft I’m holding. I disentangled this little tuft from the tightly clenched fingers of Madame L’Espanaye. Tell me what you make of it.” “Dupin!” I cried, thoroughly shaken. “This hair is extremely unusual—it isn’t human.” “I haven’t claimed it is,” he replied. “But before deciding, look at the sketch I’ve drawn on this paper. It’s an exact copy of what one witness described as ‘dark bruises and deep indentations of finger nails’ on Mademoiselle L’Espanaye’s throat, and what Messrs. Dumas and Etienne called ‘a series of livid spots, clearly the impression of fingers.’ “You’ll see,” he continued, spreading the paper on the table, “that the drawing conveys the sense of a firm, locked grip. There’s no sign of slipping. Each finger kept—perhaps until the victim’s death—the terrible hold it first took. Now, try to place all your fingers at once in the impressions as they appear.” I tried, but in vain. “Perhaps we’re not giving this a fair test,” he said. “The paper lies flat, while a human throat is cylindrical. Here’s a billet of wood with about the same circumference. Wrap the drawing around it and try again.” I did so, and the difficulty was even more obvious. “These,” I said, “are not the marks of any human hand.” “Read this,” Dupin answered, handing me a passage from Cuvier. It was a precise anatomical and descriptive account of the large tawny Orangutan of the East Indies. The enormous size, incredible strength and agility, savage ferocity, and imitative tendencies of these animals are known to everyone. I grasped the horror of the murders at once. “The description of the fingers,” I said when I finished reading, “matches this drawing exactly.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"0c456ccb40c0efc47049e737","rewritten_text":"I had tucked my handkerchief and a few other things into my helmet, which turned out to be the kind you can’t take off by yourself. That hadn’t occurred to me when I loaded it up; I didn’t even know it at the time. I thought it would be especially handy there. So now the thought of the handkerchief sitting right there, within reach but impossible to touch, made everything worse and harder to endure. The thing you can’t get is the thing you want most; everyone knows that. My mind locked onto that handkerchief, mile after mile, picturing it and longing for it, while the salty sweat trickled into my eyes and I couldn’t wipe it away. It might sound minor on paper, but it was real misery. I wouldn’t say it if it weren’t so. I decided I’d carry a handbag next time, no matter how it looked or what people said. Those iron-clad Round Table fellows would call it scandalous and raise a fuss, but I say comfort first, style later. We jogged along, and now and then we hit dusty patches that billowed into clouds, stinging my nose and making me sneeze and cry, and yes, I swore when I shouldn’t have. I’m no better than anyone else. We couldn’t seem to meet a soul in this lonely Britain, not even an ogre; and in the mood I was in, that was lucky for any ogre who had a handkerchief. Most knights would go for his armor, but if I could get his bandanna, he could keep his hardware for all I cared. Meanwhile, it kept getting hotter in there. The sun beat down, heating the iron more every minute. When you’re hot like that, every little thing grates on you. When I trotted, I rattled like a crate of dishes, which annoyed me; and I couldn’t bear the shield flapping and banging, first against my chest, then against my back. If I slowed to a walk, my joints squeaked and screeched like a wheelbarrow, and without the breeze from moving faster, I was roasting in that stove. On top of that, the slower I went, the heavier the armor seemed, as if it were piling on more tons every minute."}

{"request_id":"40163624a860aab8a01a4fcc","rewritten_text":"But no, something even more dazzling came to him. He would be a pirate! That was it! Now his future lay open before him, blazing with unimaginable glory. His name would shake the world and make people shudder. He would sweep across the bright, choppy seas in his long, low, black-hulled racer, the Spirit of the Storm, with its grim flag flying at the mast. At the height of his fame he would suddenly appear in the old village and stride into church, sun-darkened and weather-beaten, in his black velvet doublet and trunks, huge jackboots, crimson sash, belt stuffed with pistols, crime-stained cutlass at his side, slouch hat with waving plumes, black flag spread wide with skull and crossbones, and he would listen in swelling delight to the whispers, “It’s Tom Sawyer the Pirate—the Black Avenger of the Spanish Main!”

Yes, it was settled; his path was chosen. He would run away from home and begin at once. He would leave the very next morning. So he had to get ready now. He would gather his supplies. He went to a rotten log nearby and began digging under one end of it with his Barlow knife. Soon he hit wood that sounded hollow. He slipped his hand in and recited in a solemn voice:

“What hasn’t come here, come! What’s here, stay here!”

Then he scraped away the dirt and uncovered a pine shingle. He lifted it and revealed a neat little treasure-box whose bottom and sides were made of shingles. Inside lay a marble. Tom’s astonishment had no bounds. He scratched his head in confusion and said:

“Well, that beats anything!”

Then he flung the marble away in annoyance and stood there thinking. The truth was that one of his superstitions had failed, a superstition he and all his comrades had considered foolproof. If you buried a marble with the required spell, left it alone for two weeks, and then used the incantation he had just spoken to open the spot, you were supposed to find every marble you had ever lost gathered there, no matter where they had been scattered. But now, the charm had plainly failed. Tom’s whole belief system was rocked. He had often heard of the trick succeeding, never of it failing. It never crossed his mind that he himself had tried it several times before and then could not locate the hiding places afterward. He puzzled over it for a while and finally decided some witch had meddled and broken the spell."}

{"request_id":"f95ebcc60a969b12fa577518","rewritten_text":"“I consider it one of the first refinements of civilized societies.”

“Definitely, sir; and it also has the advantage of being fashionable among the less civilized societies of the world: every savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend dances wonderfully,” he went on after a pause, having watched Bingley join the group. “And I don’t doubt that you’re quite skilled yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and took considerable pleasure in the sight. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Don’t you think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”

“It’s not a compliment I pay to any place if I can avoid it.”

“You have a house in town, I suppose?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once considered settling in town myself, for I’m fond of first-rate company; but I wasn’t entirely sure London’s air would suit Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for a response, but his companion clearly wasn’t inclined to give one; and just then Elizabeth moved toward them, which inspired him to attempt a very gallant gesture. He called out to her,

“My dear Miss Eliza, why aren’t you dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must allow me to present this young lady to you as a highly desirable partner. You surely can’t refuse to dance when so much beauty is before you.” And, taking her hand, he would have placed it in Mr. Darcy’s, who, though quite surprised, wasn’t unwilling to accept it, when she immediately pulled back and said, a little flustered, to Sir William,

“Honestly, sir, I have no intention of dancing. Please don’t assume I came this way to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with grave courtesy, asked for the honor of her hand, but it was useless. Elizabeth was resolved; nor did Sir William shake her resolve with his attempt at persuasion.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it’s cruel to deny me the pleasure of watching you; and though this gentleman usually dislikes the amusement, I’m sure he won’t object to indulging us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is the very picture of politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He truly is. But with such enticement, my dear Miss Eliza, who can be surprised at his courtesy? Who would refuse such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave him an impish look and turned away. Her refusal hadn’t hurt her in the gentleman’s estimation, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him in this way,—"}

content.text: {"request_id":"da83665cd387b745dda8d7e1","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so thoroughly content with this conversation that he never again troubled himself, or irked his dear sister Elizabeth, by referring to it; and she was gratified to learn she had said enough to keep him still. The day for his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived, and Mrs. Bennet had to yield to a parting which, as her husband would not hear of their all traveling to Newcastle, promised to last at least a twelvemonth. “Oh, my dear Lydia,” she exclaimed, “when shall we meet once more?” “Oh, Lord! I cannot tell. Not these two or three years, perhaps.” “Write to me often, my dear.” “As often as I am able. But you know married women have little leisure for writing. My sisters may write to me. They will have nothing else to occupy them.” Mr. Wickham’s farewells proved far more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, looked charming, and uttered many graceful phrases. “He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, once they were out of the house, “as ever I beheld. He simpers, he smirks, and he pays court to us all. I am prodigiously proud of him. I defy Sir William Lucas himself to produce a more valuable son-in-law.” The loss of her daughter rendered Mrs. Bennet very dull for several days. “I often think,” said she, “that parting with one’s friends is the worst of all. One feels so forlorn without them.” “This, you see, madam, is the result of marrying a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It should reconcile you to the single condition of your remaining four.” “Nothing of the sort. Lydia is not leaving me because she is married; only because her husband’s regiment lies so far away. Had it been nearer, she would not have gone so soon.” Yet the low spirits into which this affair had cast her were soon relieved, and her mind reopened to the flutter of hope, by a report then beginning to circulate. The housekeeper at Netherfield had received orders to get ready for her master, who was coming down in a day or two, to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet was quite in a fret. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head alternately. “Well, well, and so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for Mrs. Philips first conveyed the tidings). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care in the least. He is nothing to us now, you know, and I am sure I never desire to see him again. Still, he is perfectly welcome to come to Netherfield, if it suits him.”"}

{"request_id":"7a7b55bb22d8af7ef48ba96e","rewritten_text":"“I’m in. It’s the best plan. Should we just hold hands and swear that we—”

“Oh no, that’s no good for this. That kind of thing only works for small, silly stuff—especially with girls, because they’ll turn on you anyway and spill everything if they get mad. But something this big needs writing. And blood.”

Tom’s whole being cheered this idea. It was deep, grim, and frightening; the hour, the situation, the setting all matched it. He picked up a clean pine shingle glinting in the moonlight, took a small piece of red chalk from his pocket, angled it toward the moon, and slowly scratched out these lines, biting his tongue on each downward stroke and easing up on the upward ones.

“Huck Finn and Tom Sawyer swear they will keep quiet about This and they wish they may drop dead on the spot if they ever tell and rot.”

Huckleberry was awed by Tom’s skill with a pencil and the grandeur of his words. He immediately pulled a pin from his lapel to prick himself, but Tom stopped him.

“Wait! Don’t do that. A pin’s brass. It might have verdigris on it.”

“What’s verdigris?”

“It’s poison, that’s what. Just swallow some once—you’ll find out.”

So Tom unwound the thread from one of his needles, and each boy jabbed the pad of his thumb and squeezed out a drop of blood. After many squeezes, Tom finally managed to sign his initials, using the tip of his little finger as a pen. Then he showed Huckleberry how to make an H and an F, and the oath was sealed. They buried the shingle near the wall with some gloomy rites and muttered spells, and the bonds that held their tongues were declared locked with the key thrown away.

A figure crept stealthily through a gap at the far end of the ruined building just then, but they didn’t see it.

“Tom,” Huckleberry whispered, “does this mean we can never tell—ever?”

“Of course it does. No matter what happens, we have to stay quiet. We’d drop dead—don’t you know that?”

“Yeah, I guess that’s true.”

They kept whispering for some time. Suddenly a dog began a long, mournful howl just outside—barely ten feet away. The boys grabbed each other, shaking with terror.

“Which one of us is he warning?” Huckleberry gasped.

“I don’t know—peek through the crack. Hurry!”

“No, you do it, Tom!”

“I can’t—I can’t do it, Huck!”"}

{"request_id":"0c74fbbdadbee494bf1e6efd","rewritten_text":"In my youth, discontent never touched my mind, and if I ever felt ennui, the sight of nature’s beauty or the study of humanity’s finest achievements always stirred my heart and revived my spirits. Now I am like a blasted tree; the bolt has struck my soul, and I felt even then that I would live on only to display what I shall soon stop being—a miserable ruin of a person, pitied by others and unbearable to myself.

We lingered at Oxford for quite a while, wandering through its surroundings and trying to find every place linked to the most inspiring era of English history. Our little voyages of discovery often stretched on because of the many sights that appeared. We visited the tomb of the great Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my spirit rose above its degrading fears to consider the divine ideas of liberty and self-sacrifice these places honored and recalled. For an instant I dared to cast off my chains and look around with a free and noble spirit, but the iron had already eaten into my flesh, and I sank again, trembling and hopeless, into my miserable self.

We left Oxford reluctantly and moved on to Matlock, our next resting place. The countryside near this village resembled the scenery of Switzerland more closely, but everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the distant white Alps that always rise around the pine-covered mountains of my homeland. We visited the miraculous cave and the little natural history cabinets, where the curiosities are arranged just as they are in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. Hearing the latter name spoken by Henry made me shudder, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which was now tied in my mind to that terrible experience.

From Derby, still traveling north, we spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself back among the Swiss mountains. The small patches of snow clinging to the mountains’ northern sides, the lakes, and the crashing rocky streams were all familiar and beloved sights. Here we also met a few acquaintances who nearly managed to trick me into happiness. Clerval’s joy was far greater than mine; his mind grew in the company of talented men, and he discovered within himself far more abilities and resources than he had ever guessed he possessed while he kept company with those beneath him."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6dc4ec2241d1ac057048a7b3","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the luxuries of the dead was astonishing. Then he turned his attention to embroideries and to tapestries that served as frescoes in the chilly rooms of northern Europe. As he delved into the subject—and he had an extraordinary talent for becoming completely absorbed in whatever he took up—he was almost saddened by the thought of the ruin time inflicted on beautiful and marvelous things. He, at least, had escaped that. Summer followed summer, yellow jonquils bloomed and died again and again, nights of horror repeated their tale of shame, yet he remained unchanged. No winter scarred his face or dulled his flower-like complexion. How different it was with material things! Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe on which the gods battled the giants, worked by brown-skinned girls for Athena’s pleasure? Where was the massive velarium that Nero stretched across the Colosseum in Rome, that titanic purple sail representing the starry sky and Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white, gilt-reined horses? He longed to see the curious napkins crafted for the Priest of the Sun, showing every delicacy and dish a feast might require; the burial cloth of King Chilperic, adorned with three hundred golden bees; the fantastic robes that outraged the Bishop of Pontus, covered with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—everything, in fact, that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, with sleeves embroidered with a song that began “Madame, je suis tout joyeux,” the musical accompaniment wrought in gold thread and each square-shaped note formed with four pearls. He read about the room prepared in the palace at Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, made in embroidery and blazoned with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies whose wings were likewise adorned with the queen’s arms, all worked in gold.” Catherine de’ Medici had a mourning bed made of black velvet scattered with crescents and suns. Its curtains were damask, patterned with leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver ground, fringed along the edges with pearl embroidery, and it stood in a room hung with rows of the queen’s emblems in cut black velvet on cloth of silver. Louis XIV had gold-embroidered caryatids fifteen feet high in his apartment."}

{"request_id":"559019709cef518b29534d22","rewritten_text":"After dinner the whole gang went out to hunt turtle eggs on the sandbar. They jabbed sticks into the sand, and when they found a soft spot they dropped to their knees and dug with their hands. Sometimes they pulled fifty or sixty eggs from one hole. The eggs were round, white, and a little smaller than an English walnut. That night they had a famous fried-egg feast, and another on Friday morning.

After breakfast they ran yelling and dancing onto the bar, chasing each other in circles, peeling off their clothes as they went until they were naked. Then they kept up the game far up the shallow water of the bar, fighting the strong current, which kept knocking their legs out from under them and made everything even funnier. Now and then they bent together and splashed water into each other’s faces with their palms, edging closer with their faces turned away so they would not choke on the spray. Finally they grabbed each other and wrestled until the winner dunked his friend, and then they all went under in a knot of pale arms and legs and came up at once, blowing, sputtering, laughing, and gasping for air.

When they were worn out, they ran ashore, sprawled on the dry hot sand, and covered themselves with it, only to bolt for the water again and repeat the whole show. At last it struck them that their bare skin looked like flesh-colored tights; so they traced a ring in the sand and staged a circus—with three clowns, because none of them would surrender that proud role.

Next they fetched their marbles and played knucks and ringtaw and keeps until they got bored. Then Joe and Huck took another swim, but Tom refused because when he had kicked off his trousers he had also kicked off his string of rattlesnake rattles, and he wondered how he had avoided cramps so long without that mysterious charm. He would not go back into the water until he found it, and by then the other boys were tired and ready to rest. They drifted apart, grew listless, and stared across the wide river toward the village dozing in the sun. Tom caught himself writing “BECKY” in the sand with his big toe; he erased it and scolded himself for being weak. But he wrote it again anyway; he could not stop himself. He wiped it out once more and then pulled himself away from temptation by herding the other boys together and joining them."}

{"request_id":"fcea21d87a5fee3184f99e70","rewritten_text":"The doctor was an old man, real pleasant and kind-looking when I roused him. I told him my brother and I had been hunting over on Spanish Island yesterday afternoon, camped on part of a raft we’d found, and around midnight he must have kicked his gun in his sleep, because it went off and shot him in the leg. We wanted the doctor to go over there and patch him up without saying anything to anyone, since we planned to come home this evening and surprise the family.

“Who is your family?” he asks.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. After a moment he asks, “How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I say, “and it shot him.”

“Odd dream,” he says.

Then he lit his lantern, grabbed his saddle-bags, and we headed out. But when he saw the canoe he didn’t like the look of it—said it was big enough for one but didn’t seem safe for two. I say:

“Oh, you don’t need to be scared, sir; it carried all three of us just fine.”

“What three?”

“Well, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

Still, he put his foot on the gunwale and rocked it, shook his head, and said he figured he’d look for a bigger one. But they were all locked and chained, so he took my canoe instead. He told me to wait till he got back, or I could look around more, or maybe I ought to go home and get everyone ready for the surprise if I wanted. But I said I didn’t, so I told him exactly how to find the raft, and then he left.

An idea hit me pretty soon. I says to myself, suppose he can’t fix that leg in a snap like folks say? suppose it takes him three or four days? What would we do—stay there till he lets the secret out? No way; I knew what I’d do. I’d wait, and if he came back saying he had to go again, I’d get down there too, even if I had to swim. We’d tie him up, keep him, shove out down the river, and when Tom was done with him we’d pay him what it was worth, or everything we had, and then let him make it to shore.

So I crawled into a lumber pile to sleep, and the next time I woke the sun was already high overhead. I jumped up and ran to the doctor’s house, but they said he’d gone out sometime in the night and hadn’t come back yet."}

{"request_id":"0f8977f231b325afd161f22c","rewritten_text":"If it hadn’t been for me, he’d never have gotten out. Morgan le Fay hated him with everything in her, and she never would have softened. Yet his offense was more careless than deliberately wicked. He had said she had red hair. Well, she did; but that wasn’t the way to describe it. When red-haired people belong to a certain social level, their hair is called auburn.

Think of it: among these forty-seven captives there were five whose names, crimes, and dates of imprisonment were no longer known. One woman and four men—each stooped, wrinkled, their minds gone, like ancient relics. They themselves had long since forgotten those details; at best they nursed vague guesses about them, never the same twice. The succession of priests whose duty it was to pray daily with the captives and remind them that God had placed them there for some wise reason, teaching them that patience, humility, and submission to oppression were the virtues He prized in people of lower rank, had traditions about these crumbling human ruins, but nothing more. Those traditions went only so far; they dealt with duration of imprisonment, not the nature of the offenses. Even with tradition, the only fact that could be proven was that none of the five had seen daylight for thirty-five years; how much longer the darkness had lasted was beyond conjecture. The king and queen knew nothing about these poor souls except that they were heirlooms, assets inherited along with the throne from the previous regime. Nothing of their history had been handed down with their persons, so the inheriting rulers considered them worthless and felt no interest in them. I asked the queen:

“Then why on earth didn’t you set them free?”

The question stumped her. She didn’t know why she hadn’t; the idea had simply never crossed her mind. So there she was, foreshadowing the true history of future prisoners of the Château d’If without realizing it. It was now clear to me that, with her upbringing, those inherited prisoners were merely property—nothing more, nothing less. And when we inherit property, it doesn’t occur to us to throw it away, even when we don’t value it.

When I led my procession of human bats into the open world and the harsh afternoon sun—after blindfolding them out of pity for eyes so long unused to light—they were a spectacle. Walking skeletons, scarecrows, goblins, sad terrors, every one of them; the truest possible offspring of Monarchy by the Grace of God and the Established Church."}

{"request_id":"4b6d10b4bba10c2a25acb753","rewritten_text":"At these cries, many of the women, whipped into blind frenzy, spun around, striking and clawing their own friends until they collapsed in wild swoons. Only the men who belonged to them kept them from being trampled underfoot.

Still, not a moment was wasted; not one moment! Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville and might be freed. Never, if Saint Antoine remembered his suffering, insults, and wrongs! Armed men and women poured out of the Quarter so quickly, pulling even the last dregs with them as if by suction, that in fifteen minutes only a few old crones and wailing children were left in Saint Antoine’s heart.

No, by that time they were all jammed into the Hall of Examination where the old ugly villain sat, overflowing into the open space and streets. The Defarges, husband and wife, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three pushed in with the first crowd and stood close to him.

“Look!” cried Madame, pointing with her knife. “Look at the old monster bound with ropes. It was well done to tie that bundle of grass on his back. Ha, ha! Well done. Let him eat it now!” She tucked the knife under her arm and clapped like she was watching a play.

People immediately behind Madame Defarge explained what pleased her to those behind them, who passed it farther along, and so on, until the nearby streets echoed with clapping. Likewise, during two or three hours of slow talk and endless words, Madame Defarge’s bursts of impatience were caught and repeated, almost instantly, even far away. Certain men had amazingly climbed the outside of the building to stare through the windows. They knew Madame Defarge well and acted like telegraphs between her and the crowd outside.

At last the sun rose high enough to shine a kind, hopeful beam directly on the old prisoner’s head. The mercy was too much to stand; in a heartbeat the wall of dust and chaff that had held surprisingly long was blown away, and Saint Antoine had him.

The news spread at once, all the way to the edges of the crowd. Defarge had barely leaped over a railing and a table and squeezed the miserable creature in a deadly embrace—Madame Defarge had barely followed and twisted one of the ropes that bound him—The Vengeance and Jacques Three hadn’t yet reached them, and the men at the windows hadn’t yet swooped into the Hall like hawks from their high perches—when the cry seemed to rise across the city: “Bring him out!”"}

{"request_id":"d53bb55b15f446c65aac90f1","rewritten_text":"“I wrapped him in the paper and shoved a piece into his mouth—like I said.”

“And you really think your master was bitten by the beetle, and that the bite made him ill?”

“I ain’t guessing—I know. Why else he dream ’bout the gold so much if it ain’t ’cause the gold-bug bit him? I’ve heard about them gold-bugs before now.”

“But how do you know he dreams about gold?”

“How I know? Because he talks about it in his sleep—that’s how.”

“Well, Jup, maybe you’re right. But what lucky event do I owe the honor of your visit today?”

“What’s wrong, massa?”

“Did you bring a message from Mr. Legrand?”

“No, massa, I brought this here letter.” Jupiter handed me a note that read:

“My dear —— Why have I not seen you for so long? I hope you haven’t been foolish enough to take offense at some little brusqueness of mine; but no, that seems unlikely. Since I saw you I’ve had great cause for worry. I have something to tell you, yet hardly know how to tell it, or whether I should at all.

“I haven’t been well for a few days, and poor old Jup almost drives me mad with his well-meant care. Would you believe it?—he prepared a huge stick the other day to beat me for slipping away and spending the day alone in the hills on the mainland. I truly think my sickly looks saved me from a whipping.

“I’ve made no additions to my cabinet since we met.

“If you can manage it, come over with Jupiter. Do come. I want to see you tonight on business of importance. I assure you it is of the highest importance.

“Ever yours,
“William Legrand.”

The tone of this note filled me with uneasiness. Its whole style was unlike Legrand’s. What could he be thinking? What new whim seized his excitable mind? What “business of the highest importance” could he have? Jupiter’s story did not sound hopeful. I feared that steady misfortune had finally unhinged my friend’s mind. So without hesitation, I got ready to go with the man.

When we reached the wharf, I saw a scythe and three spades, all apparently new, lying in the bottom of the boat we were to take.

“What’s the meaning of this, Jup?”"}

{"request_id":"696690b86da8202a123e8fc3","rewritten_text":"“I do not have the nerves for that sort of thing.”

“But could you really feel comfortable spending the whole evening away from the poor boy?”

“Yes; his father can do it, so why shouldn’t I? Jemima is so careful, and she could send us word every hour how he is. I honestly think Charles could have told his father we would all come. I am no more worried about little Charles now than he is. I was terribly frightened yesterday, but today is very different.”

“Well, if you do not think it too late to let them know for yourself, suppose you go as well as your husband? Leave little Charles to my care. Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove cannot think it wrong while I stay with him.”

“Are you serious?” Mary cried, her eyes lighting up. “Goodness, that is a very good idea, very good indeed. Of course I might as well go as not, because I am no use at home, am I? It only aggravates me. You, who do not have a mother’s instincts, are much the better person. You can get little Charles to do anything; he always obeys you immediately. It will be much better than leaving him only with Jemima. Oh, I will certainly go; I am sure I should, if I can, just as much as Charles, because they are desperate for me to get to know Captain Wentworth, and I know you do not mind being left alone. A wonderful idea of yours, Anne. I will go tell Charles and get ready at once. You can send for us, you know, in a moment if anything is wrong; but I dare say nothing will upset you. I would not go, you may be sure, if I were not completely at ease about my dear child.”

The next moment she was knocking on her husband’s dressing-room door, and as Anne followed her upstairs, she caught the entire conversation, which began with Mary saying, in a triumphant tone—

“I am going with you, Charles, because I am no more useful at home than you are. Even if I shut myself up with the child forever, I could not make him do anything he dislikes. Anne will stay; Anne has offered to stay home and take care of him. It is Anne’s own suggestion, so I will go with you, which is much better, because I have not dined at the other house since Tuesday.”

“This is very kind of Anne,” her husband answered, “and I would be very glad to have you go; but it still feels rather unfair that she should be left at home alone to nurse our sick child.”"}

{"request_id":"52837843cfa50948cd266597","rewritten_text":"And if he asked why I wanted it, or why I thought I had any right to it, I would tell him—though he cared little for such poor dreams—that I had loved Estella dearly and for a long time, and that though I had lost her and must live a bereaved life, anything concerning her was still closer and dearer to me than anything else in the world. Seeing Mr. Jaggers stand silent and apparently unmoved by this plea, I turned to Wemmick and said, “Wemmick, I know you to be a man with a kind heart. I have seen your pleasant home, your old father, and all the innocent, cheerful, playful ways with which you lighten your workday. I beg you to speak for me to Mr. Jaggers and tell him that, considering all the circumstances, he ought to be more open with me.”

I had never seen two men look more strangely at each other than Mr. Jaggers and Wemmick did after this. At first, I feared Wemmick would be dismissed on the spot; but that fear faded as Mr. Jaggers relaxed into something like a smile, and Wemmick grew more confident.

“What’s all this?” asked Mr. Jaggers. “You with an old father, and you with pleasant and playful ways?”

“Well!” answered Wemmick. “If I don’t bring them here, what does it matter?”

“Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, placing his hand on my arm and smiling openly, “this man must be the most cunning impostor in all London.”

“Not at all,” replied Wemmick, growing bolder. “I think you’re the one.”

Again they traded their odd looks, each still suspicious that the other was deceiving him.

“You with a pleasant home?” said Mr. Jaggers.

“If it doesn’t interfere with business,” said Wemmick, “let it be so. Now, looking at you, sir, I wouldn’t be surprised if you were planning to have a pleasant home of your own one day, when you’re tired of all this work.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded thoughtfully two or three times and even sighed. “Pip,” he said, “we won’t talk about ‘poor dreams;’ you know more about such things than I do, being fresher to that kind of experience. But now to this other matter. I’ll put a case to you. Mind! I admit nothing.”

He waited for me to say I understood he was admitting nothing.

“Now, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, “consider this case. Suppose a woman, under the circumstances you mentioned, kept her child hidden and had to tell her lawyer about it when he said he needed to know, to understand how things stood regarding that child.”"}

{"request_id":"e1884652f06f085366ba4f28","rewritten_text":"“So now, let’s hear the whole thing.”

“Well, you see, it was like this. Old missus—that’s Miss Watson—picks on me all the time and treats me pretty rough, but she always said she wouldn’t sell me down to Orleans. But I noticed there was a slave trader hanging around the place a lot lately, and I started getting uneasy. Well, one night I creep to the door pretty late, and it wasn’t quite shut, and I hear old missus tell the widow she’s going to sell me down to Orleans. She didn’t want to, but she could get eight hundred dollars for me, and it was such a big pile of money she couldn’t resist. The widow tried to get her to promise she wouldn’t do it, but I didn’t wait to hear the rest. I lit out mighty quick, I tell you.

“I took off and slid down the hill, planning to steal a skiff along the shore somewhere above the town, but there were still people up, so I hid in the old run-down cooper shop on the bank to wait for everyone to clear out. Well, I stayed there all night. There was somebody around all the time. Around six in the morning skiffs started going by, and by eight or nine every skiff that passed was talking about how your pap came over to town and said you were killed. The last skiffs were full of ladies and gentlemen going over to see the place. Sometimes they’d pull up at the shore and rest before they started across, so from their talk I learned all about the killing. I was real sorry you were killed, Huck, but I sure ain’t now.

“I lay there under the shavings all day. I was hungry, but I wasn’t scared, because I knew old missus and the widow were going to start for the camp meeting right after breakfast and be gone all day, and they know I go off with the cattle about daylight, so they wouldn’t expect to see me around, and wouldn’t miss me until after dark in the evening. The other servants wouldn’t miss me, because they’d take off and have a holiday as soon as the old folks were out of the way.

“Well, when it got dark I headed up the river road and went about two miles or more to where there weren’t any houses. I’d made up my mind what I was going to do. You see, if I kept trying to get away on foot, the dogs would track me; if I stole a skiff to cross over, they’d notice that skiff missing, see, and they’d know about where I’d land on the other side and where to pick up my trail.”"}
