{"request_id":"89955239416180acb9c78f00","rewritten_text":"It is truly curious that she always manages to catch what Jane says better than what I do. Jane’s articulation is so precise! Still, she will find her grandmama no more deaf than she was two years ago; and that is saying much for my mother’s age—and it has really been a full two years, you know, since she was here. We had never gone so long without seeing her before, and as I was just remarking to Mrs. Cole, we shall scarcely know how to lavish sufficient attention on her now.”

“Do you expect Miss Fairfax here soon?”

“Oh yes; next week.”

“Indeed!—that must give you great pleasure.”

“Thank you. How kind you are. Yes, next week. Everyone is astonished, and everyone repeats the same civil expressions. I am sure she will be as delighted to meet her friends at Highbury as they will be to greet her. Yes, Friday or Saturday; she cannot specify which, because Colonel Campbell wants the carriage one of those days. So extremely kind of them to send her all the way! But that is their custom, you know. Oh yes, Friday or Saturday next. That is what she writes about. That is why she has written out of the usual order, as we term it; for ordinarily we should not have expected a letter before next Tuesday or Wednesday.”

“Yes, that was my supposition. I feared there would be little prospect of my hearing anything of Miss Fairfax to-day.”

“So obliging of you to say so! No, we should not have heard, except for this special circumstance of her coming so soon. My mother is in raptures!—for she is to stay with us at least three months. Three months, she says so expressly, as I am about to have the pleasure of reading to you. The situation, you see, is that the Campbells are going to Ireland. Mrs. Dixon has persuaded her parents to cross over and see her immediately. They had not planned to go before the summer, but she is so impatient to have them near her again—for until she married, last October, she had never been away from them for even a week, which must make it feel very odd to be in separate kingdoms, I was going to say, but at any rate in different countries—and so she wrote a pressing letter to her mother—or to her father, I protest I cannot tell which it was, but we shall find out presently in Jane’s letter—she wrote in Mr. Dixon’s name as well as her own, urging them to come straightaway, and they would meet them in Dublin and escort them back to their estate, Bally-craig, a place I hear is exquisitely beautiful.”"}

{"request_id":"d083bc22ced6158742b95ebf","rewritten_text":"In fairness to the young lady, it must be noted that she did not flatly declare she would refuse, but only voiced with great emphasis and earnestness her wish to be “blessed” if she did; a courteous, tactful dodge revealing that innate refinement which cannot endure causing another the sting of an outright denial.

The Jew’s expression sank. He turned from this young lady, who was cheerily—one might even say resplendently—arrayed in a scarlet gown, green boots, and yellow curl-papers, to the other woman.

“Nancy, my dear,” asked the Jew softly, “what is _your_ opinion?”

“That it’s no go; so there’s no use trying it, Fagin,” Nancy answered.

“What’s that supposed to mean?” growled Mr. Sikes, glancing up.

“What I said, Bill,” replied the lady calmly.

“Why, you’re just the very one for it,” argued Mr. Sikes. “No soul around here knows you.”

“And seeing as I prefer they shouldn’t,” Nancy returned in the same steady tone, “I’d say it’s more no than yes with me, Bill.”

“She’ll go, Fagin,” insisted Sikes.

“No, she won’t, Fagin,” retorted Nancy.

“Yes, she will, Fagin,” Sikes repeated.

And Mr. Sikes proved correct. By turns of threats, promises, and bribes, the lady was at last induced to accept the errand. She was not hindered by the concerns that troubled her vibrant companion; having only lately shifted to the Field Lane quarter from the distant yet respectable suburb of Ratcliffe, she felt little fear of being recognised by any of her many acquaintances.

Thus, with a spotless white apron tied over her gown and her curl-papers tucked under a straw bonnet—both items drawn from the Jew’s limitless supplies—Miss Nancy made ready to depart on the mission.

“Hold a moment, my dear,” said the Jew, producing a small lidded basket. “Carry this in one hand. It lends you respectability, my dear.”

“Give her a door-key for the other hand, Fagin,” suggested Sikes. “Makes it look proper and reg’lar.”

“Indeed, you’re right, my dear,” the Jew agreed, suspending a hefty street-door key from the forefinger of the young lady’s right hand. “There; excellent! Excellent, my dear!” he said, rubbing his palms.

“Oh, my brother! My poor, dear, sweet, innocent little brother!” cried Nancy, bursting into sobs and wringing the little basket and the key in anguish. “What’s become of him! Where’ve they taken him! Oh, have mercy, and tell me what’s been done with the dear child, gentlemen; do, gentlemen, if you please, gentlemen!”"}

{"request_id":"2b2a212a7ac8405644a5feff","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind except the memory that those days had existed.

Anne had not set foot in Kellynch since leaving Lady Russell’s house in September. She had no reason to go, and on the few occasions when she might have gone to the Hall, she found ways to dodge and slip away. Her first return was to reclaim her place in the fashionable, elegant rooms of the Lodge and to please its mistress.

Lady Russell’s delight at seeing her again carried a trace of worry. She knew exactly who had been spending time at Uppercross. Fortunately, either Anne truly looked fresher and rounder, or Lady Russell imagined it; and as Anne accepted the compliments, she couldn’t help linking them to her cousin’s quiet admiration and indulging the hope that she might be granted a second blooming in youth and beauty.

Once they began to talk, Anne quickly felt a shift in herself. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, that she had felt slighted and forced to stifle among the Musgroves, now mattered less. Recently she had hardly thought about her father, her sister, or Bath. Their concerns had sunk beneath those of Uppercross; and when Lady Russell brought up their old hopes and fears, expressing pleasure in the Camden Place house they had secured and regret that Mrs. Clay still stayed with them, Anne would have been mortified to reveal how much more her thoughts were occupied with Lyme and Louisa Musgrove, and everyone she knew there; how much more compelling she found the home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick than her father’s residence in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness with Mrs. Clay. She actually had to make an effort to meet Lady Russell with even the appearance of equal concern for matters that naturally should have been foremost.

Another topic brought a touch of awkwardness at first. They had to discuss the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had been in the house less than five minutes the previous day when the full story was poured out to her; but even so, they had to talk it through—she had to ask questions, deplore the rashness, mourn the outcome, and both of them had to say Captain Wentworth’s name. Anne knew she wasn’t handling it as smoothly as Lady Russell. She couldn’t speak his name and meet Lady Russell’s eyes until she resorted to briefly explaining what she believed about the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"6a71ba99b82a0867a45cb238","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, fell into deep thought about whether an honest life wasn’t ultimately the best. Convinced that it was, he turned away from his former life, determined to rebuild it somewhere new. He struggled and suffered for a long time; but with a contented spirit and steadfast purpose, he succeeded at last, and from being a farmer’s drudge and a carrier’s boy, he is now the happiest young grazier in all Northamptonshire.

Now the hand writing these words trembles as it nears the end of its work and would keep weaving the thread of these adventures just a little longer.

I would still like to stay awhile with a few of those whose lives I have shared for so long, and enjoy their happiness by trying to capture it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of early womanhood, casting a soft, gentle light on her quiet path in life, a light that touched everyone who walked it with her, and warmed their hearts. I would depict her as the life and joy of the fireside circle and the lively summer group; I would follow her through the hot fields at noon and listen to the low tones of her sweet voice on moonlit evening walks; I would watch her practicing kindness and charity in the world, and tending to her domestic duties at home with a cheerful, tireless spirit. I would show her and her sister’s orphaned child rejoicing in their love for each other, spending hours describing the friends they lost so tragically. I would summon again the joyful little faces that gathered around her knee and listen to their bright chatter; I would recall the sound of her clear laugh and summon the sympathetic tear that shone in her soft blue eye. These, and a thousand looks and smiles and turns of thought and speech—I would gladly call them all back.

How Mr. Brownlow went on day by day filling his adopted child’s mind with knowledge, growing more attached to him as his character unfolded and revealed the thriving seeds of everything Mr. Brownlow hoped he would become—how he recognized in him new traits of his old friend, awakening in his own heart memories that were melancholy yet sweet and soothing—how the two orphans, forged by hardship, remembered its lessons in mercy toward others, in mutual love, and in heartfelt gratitude to Him who had guarded and preserved them—these things do not need to be told."}

{"request_id":"8bc705e5b452060d6f5d1cb3","rewritten_text":"“You need to learn a bit of my philosophy. Think of the past only when remembering it brings you happiness.”

“I cannot credit you with possessing such philosophy. Your memories must be so entirely free from blame that the peace they give you is ignorance, which is far better than philosophy. With me it is different. Painful memories intrude and cannot, should not, be driven away. I have lived selfishly all my life—my behavior has been selfish even if my principles were not. As a child I was taught what was right, but no one taught me to master my temper. I received good principles, but was allowed to follow them with pride and conceit. I was unfortunately an only son (for many years an only child), spoiled by my parents, who, though good themselves—my father especially, the kindest, most amiable man—still allowed, encouraged, even taught me to be selfish and domineering, to care for no one beyond my own family circle, to look down on everyone else, to want to believe that their sense and worth were inferior to mine. That is who I was from eight to twenty-eight; and that is who I might still be, were it not for you, dearest, loveliest Elizabeth! What do I not owe you! You taught me a lesson—hard at first, but invaluable. Through you I was properly humbled. I came to you with no doubt of my welcome. You showed me how inadequate were all my pretensions to win a woman who deserved to be won.”

“Did you truly believe I would accept you?”

“I did. What must you think of my vanity? I imagined you were wishing for and expecting my proposal.”

“Then my manners must have been at fault, though never intentionally. I never meant to mislead you, but my spirits often led me astray. How you must have despised me after that evening!”

“Despise you? I was angry at first, perhaps, but my anger soon found its proper target.”

“I am almost afraid to ask what you thought of me when we met at Pemberley. Did you blame me for coming?”

“No, not at all. I felt only surprise.”

“Your surprise could not exceed mine at receiving any notice from you. My conscience told me I deserved no special politeness, and I certainly did not expect more than what was due.”

“My aim then,” Darcy replied, “was to show you, with every civility I could offer, that I was not so petty as to hold grudges; and I hoped to gain your forgiveness, to soften your poor opinion of me, by proving I had taken your rebukes to heart.”"}

{"request_id":"d6dcc512fec5108a05ee1f60","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at last, “it can’t be denied that since the new feeding system started, the coffins have grown a bit narrower and shallower than they used to be; but we have to turn some profit, Mr. Bumble. Quality timber costs dearly, sir, and all the iron handles come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its drawbacks. A reasonable profit is, of course, acceptable.”

“Of course, of course,” the undertaker replied. “And if I don’t make money on one item, I make it up over time, you understand—he! he! he!”

“Exactly so,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Yet I must say,” the undertaker went on, picking up the train of thought the beadle had broken, “I must say, Mr. Bumble, I face one big disadvantage: every stout person dies the quickest. The folks who’ve been better off and paying rates for years are the first to sink when they enter the workhouse; and let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, three or four inches beyond the estimate cuts deep into one’s profits—especially with a family to support, sir.”

Mr. Sowerberry delivered this with the righteous annoyance of a man unfairly treated, and Mr. Bumble sensed the hint of a slur on the parish’s honor, so he thought it wise to change the topic. Oliver Twist was foremost in his mind, so he made the boy his subject.

“By the way,” said Mr. Bumble, “do you know anyone who needs a boy? A parish apprentice who’s presently a dead weight, a millstone around the parish’s neck, you might say? Favorable terms, Mr. Sowerberry, favorable terms.” As he spoke, Mr. Bumble lifted his cane toward the bill above him and gave three crisp taps on the words “five pounds,” printed in enormous Roman capitals.

“Gadso!” exclaimed the undertaker, taking hold of the gilt-edged lapel of Mr. Bumble’s official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to talk to you about. You know—dear me, what a remarkably elegant button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it rather handsome,” said the beadle, glancing proudly down at the large brass buttons that adorned his coat. “The die matches the parish seal—the Good Samaritan tending the sick and wounded man. The board presented it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember wearing it for the first time at the inquest on that fallen tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"cc94edd1547db5cda9c9dd4f","rewritten_text":"He stood up and left the room with my nurse, and a moment later my father came in.

Nothing could have pleased me more than his arrival. I reached out my hand and cried, “Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

My father calmed me by assuring me they were well and tried, by speaking about the people I loved, to lift my spirits; but he soon realized that cheerfulness cannot live in a prison. “What a place this is for you, my son!” he said, looking sadly at the barred windows and the wretched room. “You travelled to find happiness, yet misfortune seems to hunt you. And poor Clerval—”

Hearing the name of my murdered friend upset me too much in my frail state, and I wept.

“Alas! Yes, Father,” I replied. “Some horrible fate is fixed on me, and I must live to see it done, or I would have died on Henry’s coffin.”

We were not allowed to talk for long, because my fragile health required every effort to keep me calm. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted I not waste my strength. Yet my father’s presence felt like that of a good angel, and I slowly regained my health.

As the sickness left me, a dark and heavy sadness filled me. The image of Clerval, ghastly and slain, stood constantly before me. More than once the agitation of these thoughts made my friends fear a dangerous relapse. Alas! Why did they keep alive such a miserable, hated life? It must be so I could fulfil my fate, which was nearing its end. Soon, very soon, death would quiet my pounding heart and free me from the crushing weight of grief. In carrying out justice, I would also find rest. Then, though death still seemed far away, I wished for it without cease; I often sat for hours silent and still, longing for some great upheaval that would bury both me and my destroyer in its ruins.

The season of the assizes neared. I had already spent three months in prison, and though I was still weak and in constant danger of relapse, I had to travel nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court met. Mr. Kirwin took on every task of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence."}

{"request_id":"f152ae40aff7b68afd9596bc","rewritten_text":"This brief talk with Mr. Knightley gave Emma great pleasure. It was one of the pleasant memories of the ball that she replayed while walking around the lawn the next morning. She was very glad they now understood each other about the Eltons, and that their opinions of both husband and wife were so similar. His praise of Harriet, his concession in her favour, was especially gratifying. The Eltons’ impertinence, which had threatened for a few minutes to ruin the rest of her evening, ended up producing some of its best moments; and she looked forward to another happy result—the end of Harriet’s infatuation. From Harriet’s way of speaking of the night before they left the ballroom, Emma had strong hopes. It seemed as if Harriet’s eyes had suddenly opened and she now saw that Mr. Elton was not the superior creature she had imagined. The fever had broken, and Emma felt little fear that the pulse would race again from harmful politeness. She counted on the Eltons’ spite to provide all the pointed neglect still needed. Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not too much in love, and Mr. Knightley not wishing to quarrel with her—what a happy summer she must have ahead! 

She was not to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her he could not allow himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, since he had to be home by midday. She did not regret it. 

Having settled all these thoughts, reviewed them, and set them straight, she was turning to the house, spirits braced for the demands of the two little boys and their grandpapa, when the great iron sweep-gate opened and two people entered whom she had never less expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet on his arm—actually Harriet! One moment was enough to show her something extraordinary had happened. Harriet looked pale and frightened, and he was trying to steady her. The iron gates and the front door were not twenty yards apart; the three of them were soon in the hall, and Harriet at once sank into a chair and fainted. 

A young lady who faints must be revived; questions must be answered, and surprises explained. Such events are very interesting, but their suspense cannot last long. In a few minutes Emma knew the whole story. 

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another parlour boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also been at the ball, had walked out together and taken the Richmond road, which, though seemingly public enough for safety, had led them into alarm. About half a mile beyond Highbury, the road made a sudden turn and, shaded on both sides by elms, became for a good stretch very secluded; and when the young ladies had gone some way along it, they suddenly saw, a short distance ahead on a broader patch of greensward by the roadside, a group of gypsies."}

content.text: {"request_id":"588c63c01b19b89f08141388","rewritten_text":"A little after noon the boys borrowed a small skiff from a citizen who was away and pushed off right then. When they were several miles below Cave Hollow, Tom said: “See how this bluff looks the same all the way down from the cave hollow—no houses, no wood-yards, just the same bushes. But do you see that white spot up there where a landslide happened? That’s one of my marks. We’ll go ashore now.” They landed. “Now, Huck, where we’re standing you could touch that hole I came out of with a fishing pole. See if you can find it.” Huck searched all around and found nothing. Tom proudly stepped into a thick bunch of sumach bushes and said: “Here it is! Look at it, Huck; it’s the tightest little hole in this country. Keep quiet about it. I’ve always wanted to be a robber, but I knew I needed a place like this, and finding one was the trouble. Now we’ve got it, and we’ll keep it secret, though we’ll let Joe Harper and Ben Rogers in—because of course there has to be a Gang, or else it wouldn’t have any style. Tom Sawyer’s Gang—it sounds grand, doesn’t it, Huck?” “It sure does, Tom. Who will we rob?” “Oh, almost anyone. We’ll ambush people—that’s mostly how.” “And kill them?” “No, not always. Hide them in the cave until they come up with a ransom.” “What’s a ransom?” “Money. You make them get all they can from their friends; and after you’ve kept them a year, if it isn’t raised, then you kill them. That’s the usual way. Only you don’t kill women. You shut up the women, but you don’t kill them. They’re always beautiful and rich and terribly scared. You take their watches and things, but you always take off your hat and talk polite. Nobody is as polite as robbers—you can see that in any book. Well, the women start loving you, and after they’ve been in the cave a week or two they stop crying, and after that you couldn’t get them to go away. If you drove them out they would turn right around and come back. It’s that way in all the books.” “Why, that’s real bully, Tom. I think it’s better than being a pirate.” “Yes, it’s better in some ways, because it’s close to home and circuses and all that.” By then everything was ready and the boys went into the hole, Tom leading. They worked their way to the far end of the tunnel, fastened their spliced kite strings, and moved on."}

{"request_id":"2863c7853b545791ef15b8e3","rewritten_text":"“But that hardly matters.”

“I might as well ask,” she answered, “why, if you meant to offend and insult me, you chose to confess that you liked me against your will, against your reason, and even against your character. Wasn’t that enough excuse for me to be rude, if I was? But I have other grievances—you know I do. Even if my feelings hadn’t already been against you, even if they were neutral, or even favorable, do you imagine anything would persuade me to accept the man who has probably ruined, perhaps forever, the happiness of a sister I love more than anyone?”

At these words, Mr. Darcy changed color; but the feeling quickly passed, and he listened without interrupting her while she went on—

“I have every reason in the world to think the worst of you. No motive can excuse the unjust and ungenerous part you played there. You wouldn’t dare, you couldn’t deny that you were the main—if not the sole—cause of separating them, leaving one to be judged by the world for caprice and instability, the other to its ridicule for disappointed hopes, and dragging them both into the sharpest misery.”

She stopped and, with growing anger, saw that he listened with an expression that showed he felt no remorse. He even gave her a smile of false disbelief.

“Can you deny you did it?” she repeated.

With forced calm he replied, “I have no desire to deny that I did everything I could to separate my friend from your sister, or that I’m pleased it worked. Toward him I’ve been kinder than toward myself.”

Elizabeth refused to acknowledge this polite remark, though she understood it perfectly, and it certainly did nothing to soften her.

“But my dislike isn’t based solely on that,” she continued. “Long before that happened, my opinion of you was settled. Your character was revealed in the account I heard months ago from Mr. Wickham. What can you possibly say about that? What supposed act of friendship can you claim now? With what distortion can you deceive people here?”

“You seem very interested in that gentleman’s affairs,” Darcy said, less calmly and with a flush of anger.

“Who that knows his misfortunes could fail to care about him?”

“His misfortunes!” Darcy repeated with scorn. “Yes, they’ve certainly been great.”

“And all caused by you,” Elizabeth cried passionately. “You’re the one who has brought him to his current state of poverty—relative poverty.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"a42962f9b92e6139ea0c96e0","rewritten_text":"“You have hardly stayed in Bath long enough,” said he, “to sample the evening parties here.” “Oh! no. Their usual style offers nothing to me. I am no card-player.” “You never were, I know. Cards were not to your taste then; but time alters many things.” “I am not yet so altered,” Anne exclaimed, then faltered, uneasy at she scarcely knew what misconstruction. After a brief silence he spoke again, as if prompted by sudden feeling, “It is a span indeed! Eight years and a half is a span.” Whether he meant to say more was left to Anne’s imagination for a quieter moment; for even as his words still sounded in her ear, Henrietta, eager to seize the present leisure for an outing and urging her companions to make haste lest someone else arrive, startled her attention to other matters. They had to stir. Anne declared herself perfectly ready, and tried to seem so; yet she felt that had Henrietta known the regret and unwillingness in her heart at leaving that chair, at preparing to leave the room, she would have found in her own feelings for her cousin, in the very assurance of his attachment, ample cause to pity her. Their preparations, however, were abruptly checked. Alarming noises were heard; other visitors were approaching, and the door flew open for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose entrance produced a general chill. Anne felt oppression at once, and wherever her eye roved she saw signs of the same. The comfort, freedom, and liveliness of the room vanished, subdued into cold composure, resolved silence, or flat talk, in order to match the heartless elegance of her father and sister. How mortifying to perceive it so! Her watchful eye was satisfied on one point. Captain Wentworth was recognized again by both, Elizabeth even more gracious than before. She spoke to him once, and looked at him more than once. Elizabeth was in truth meditating a great move. The result made it clear. After frittering away a few minutes with the proper nothings, she began to issue the invitation that was to cover all the remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends: no formal party.” It was delivered very gracefully, and the cards she had brought, “Miss Elliot at home,” were placed on the table with a polite, inclusive smile for everyone, and one smile and one card most pointedly for Captain Wentworth. The fact was, Elizabeth had been in Bath quite long enough to appreciate the value of a gentleman whose air and appearance were like his."}

{"request_id":"3a535a019d2466306006a565","rewritten_text":"The two ladies were thrilled to see their dear friend again, said it felt like ages since they last met, and kept asking what she had been up to while they were apart. They paid little attention to the rest of the family; they avoided Mrs. Bennet as much as they could, said little to Elizabeth, and nothing at all to the others. They soon left again, springing from their seats with an energy that surprised their brother, and hurried out as if desperate to escape Mrs. Bennet’s polite attentions.

The upcoming Netherfield ball delighted every woman in the family. Mrs. Bennet chose to see it as a compliment to her eldest daughter and felt especially flattered to receive the invitation directly from Mr. Bingley instead of through a formal card. Jane imagined a happy evening with her two friends and their brother’s attentions; Elizabeth looked forward to dancing much with Mr. Wickham and to confirming everything through Mr. Darcy’s expression and behaviour. Catherine and Lydia’s excitement relied less on any single event or person; though each, like Elizabeth, planned to dance half the evening with Mr. Wickham, he was not the only partner who could satisfy them, and a ball was, after all, a ball. Even Mary assured the family she had no objection to attending.

“As long as I have my mornings to myself,” she said, “that is enough. I do not consider it a sacrifice to take part in evening engagements now and then. Society has claims on us all; and I count myself among those who think breaks for recreation and amusement are desirable for everyone.”

Elizabeth’s spirits were so high that, though she usually avoided speaking to Mr. Collins more than necessary, she could not resist asking if he intended to accept Mr. Bingley’s invitation and whether he would think it proper to join the evening’s entertainment. She was rather surprised to learn he had no doubts at all on that point and did not fear a rebuke from either the Archbishop or Lady Catherine de Bourgh for daring to dance.

“I assure you, I do not believe,” he said, “that a ball of this kind, hosted by a young man of good character for respectable people, can have any harmful effects; and far from objecting to dancing myself, I hope to be honoured with the hands of all my fair cousins over the course of the evening. I also take this opportunity to ask you, Miss Elizabeth, for the first two dances especially; a preference I trust my cousin Jane will attribute to the proper reason, and not to any lack of respect for her.”"}

{"request_id":"62541b6d548577541b890929","rewritten_text":"These thoughts calmed me, and by afternoon I fell into a deep sleep, though the fever in my blood kept peaceful dreams away. The awful scene from the day before played endlessly before my eyes: the women fleeing, Felix dragging me from his father’s feet in fury. I awoke weak, saw it was already night, slipped out of my hiding place, and searched for food.

Once my hunger was satisfied, I followed the familiar path to the cottage. All was quiet there. I crept into my hovel and waited silently for the usual hour when the family would rise. That hour passed, the sun climbed high, yet no one appeared. I shook with fear, imagining some terrible misfortune. The inside of the cottage was dark, and no sound came from within; the agony of waiting is beyond words.

Two countrymen soon walked by, and when they paused near the cottage they began talking with fierce gestures. I could not understand them, for they spoke the local language, not that of my protectors. Soon afterward Felix arrived with another man; I was astonished, for he had not left the cottage that morning, and I listened anxiously to learn the meaning of these strange events.

“Do you realize,” his companion asked, “that you will have to pay three months’ rent and lose the harvest from your garden? I do not want to treat you unfairly, so please take a few days to think about your decision.”

“It is completely useless,” Felix answered. “We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in extreme danger because of the horrible event I told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. Do not try to argue with me any longer. Take back your house and let me escape from this place.”

Felix shook violently as he spoke. He and his companion went into the cottage, stayed only a few minutes, and then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

I remained in my hovel for the rest of the day, sunk in dull despair. My protectors had gone and severed the only bond that tied me to the world. For the first time, feelings of revenge and hatred filled my heart, and I did nothing to resist them. Letting the current carry me, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death."}

{"request_id":"7d9dfdf7f0cf787125fdc4ed","rewritten_text":"That mighty voice—if such a thing could be termed inorganic, since no contrivance of pipe or key could be connected with it—let fall its resonant note, and the girl, turning back to aid her aged companion, finally noticed us.

He was her father; ever since childhood she had guided those obscured steps. Natives of Saxony, they had emigrated here only a few years earlier and woven new bonds with the neighboring villagers. Near the outbreak of the pestilence a young German student had joined them. Their simple tale was easily read: a nobleman loved the fair daughter of the impoverished musician, and followed them when he fled his friends’ persecutions. Yet soon the remorseless leveler came, sweeping down the lofty flowers with the common grass. The youth fell among the earliest victims. She preserved herself for her father’s sake. His blindness enabled her to maintain a deception, accidental at first; now, these solitary beings, sole survivors in the region, left him unaware of the transformation, nor did he know that when he listened to his child’s playing, the mute mountains, unfeeling lake, and unconscious trees, save himself, composed her only audience.

On the very day we arrived, symptomatic illness seized her. She was petrified with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, sightless father solitary upon the void earth; yet she lacked courage to tell him the truth, and sheer desperation drove her to extraordinary efforts. At the usual vesper hour she led him to the chapel; though trembling and drenched in tears for his sake, she played faultlessly, neither missing time nor erring in note, the hymn composed to celebrate the creation of this beauteous globe, now to become her tomb.

We came to her like messengers from heaven; her overwrought courage, her scarcely sustained fortitude, vanished at the sight of rescue. With a cry she rushed towards us, clasped Adrian’s knees, and, uttering only “O save my father!” loosened, with sobs and hysteric screams, the long-barred floodgates of her sorrow.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut that shadows her lover’s grave—she had indicated it to us as she died. Her father, at last aware of his daughter’s peril, unable to behold the alteration of her beloved face, obstinately clasped her hand until it grew chill and rigid in death. Nor then did he stir or speak, until twelve hours afterward compassionate death bore him to unbroken rest. They sleep under the sod, the tree their monument—a sacred spot etched upon my memory, girdled by craggy Jura and the far immeasurable Alps; the church spire they frequented still peers out of the embracing trees; and though her hand is icy, it seems to me that the heavenly music they cherished still wanders there, comforting their gentle spirits."}

{"request_id":"402d09aceb457284abed336c","rewritten_text":"“But I must forewarn you that I shall tell Sybil everything. She is coming to lunch with me to-morrow to discuss bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers you have a foul temper, or a leaning toward gout, or perhaps a wife hidden away in Bayswater, I shall certainly inform her on the spot.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I have no fear,” he replied. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Ah! I am rather sorry to hear you say that. The soundest foundation for matrimony is a mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical; I merely possess experience, which amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is eager to have his palm examined. Do not tell him he is engaged to one of the loveliest girls in London, for that was mentioned in the _Morning Post_ a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” exclaimed the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “please let Mr. Podgers remain here a little longer. He has just informed me I ought to appear on the stage, and I am terribly interested.”

“If he told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I shall certainly remove him. Come over at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, pulling a slight _moue_ as she rose from the sofa, “if I cannot be permitted to go on the stage, I must at least be allowed to be part of the audience.”

“Certainly; we shall all be part of the audience,” said Lady Windermere. “And now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is among my special favourites.”

However, when Mr. Podgers beheld Lord Arthur’s hand he turned strangely pale and kept silent. A shudder seemed to pass through him, and his great shaggy eyebrows twitched convulsively in that odd, vexing fashion they assumed when he was bewildered. Then heavy beads of sweat sprang out across his yellow forehead like some poisonous dew, and his plump fingers grew cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur failed not to remark these singular signs of agitation, and, for the first time in his life, fear touched him. His impulse was to rush from the room, yet he restrained himself. Better to know the worst, whatever it might be, than remain in this ghastly suspense.

“I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We are all waiting,” cried Lady Windermere in her quick, impatient tone, yet the cheiromantist did not reply.

“I believe Arthur is going on the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh, “and that, after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is nervous about telling him so.”"}

{"request_id":"834d75d60c0c764ac7260238","rewritten_text":"He never tried again. The boys lay there counting the dragging moments until it felt like time itself had finished and eternity was turning gray; when they finally noticed the sun beginning to set they felt a rush of gratitude.

Then one of the snores stopped. Injun Joe sat up, looked around, gave his companion—whose head hung toward his knees—a grim smile, nudged him with his foot, and said:

“Hey! You call yourself a lookout, huh? All right, though—nothing happened.”

“Man! Was I asleep?”

“Oh, partly, partly. It’s nearly time to move, pard. What do we do with the little bit of loot we’ve got left?”

“I don’t know—leave it here like always, I guess. No sense carrying it off till we head south. Six hundred and fifty in silver is a load.”

“Well—fine—it won’t hurt to come back here once more.”

“No—but I say we come at night like we used to—it’s better.”

“Yeah; but listen, it might be a good while before I get the right chance at that job; things can happen; it ain’t in such a safe spot; let’s bury it proper—and bury it deep.”

“Good plan,” said the partner, who walked across the room, knelt, lifted one of the rear hearthstones, and pulled out a bag that jingled nicely. He took twenty or thirty dollars for himself and the same for Injun Joe, then handed the bag to him. Joe was on his knees in the corner now, digging with his bowie knife.

In a heartbeat the boys forgot every fear, every misery. With hungry eyes they tracked each movement. Luck!—its glory was beyond imagining! Six hundred dollars could make half a dozen boys rich! This was treasure-hunting under the best conditions—no annoying doubts about where to dig. They nudged each other repeatedly—speaking nudges, and easy to understand; they simply meant, “Oh, aren’t you glad now we’re here!”

Joe’s knife hit something.

“Hey!” he said.

“What is it?” asked his partner.

“Half-rotten plank—no, it’s a box, I think. Here—lend a hand and let’s see what it’s doing here. Never mind, I’ve busted a hole.”

He reached in and pulled something out—

“Man, it’s money!”

The two men examined the handful of coins. They were gold. The boys above were just as excited and just as thrilled.

Joe’s partner said:

“We’ll make short work of this. There’s an old rusty pick over in the weeds on the other side of the fireplace—I spotted it a minute ago.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"10810a5e83ecd13f5333e532","rewritten_text":"In this manner two years slipped away. Day after day hundreds passed, bringing little outward alteration, though a few gradually worked upon my mind as I drifted slowly towards death. I took to study more earnestly, grew more responsive to the thoughts of others as set down in books, read history, and lost my individuality among the throng who had lived before me. Perhaps as the immediate pangs faded, I became more human. Solitude relinquished some of its charms: I again longed for sympathy, not that I ever felt tempted to seek the multitude, but I yearned for a single friend who would love me. You may say I was gradually fitted to return to society. I do not think so. The sympathy I craved had to be so pure, so freed from outward influences, that in the world I must have been thwarted by the coarse materials mingled even with its best emotions. Believe me, at that time I was less suited for fellowship with my kind than ever. When I quitted them they had tormented me, yet it was as pain and sickness torment—something extraneous to the mind that chafed it and that I wished to cast off. Now I should have longed for sympathy; I should have tried to wreathe my soul to another’s, and prepared for myself abundant draughts of disappointment and sorrow; for I was tender as the sensitive plant, all quivering nerves. I desired no sympathy in ambition or wisdom, but in sweet, mutual affection—smiles to gladden me and gentle words to console. I yearned for one heart into which I could pour my complaints unrestrained, that from the heavenly nature of the soil blessed fruit might spring from such poor seed. Yet how could I discover this? The love that forms the soul of friendship is a soft spirit rarely found except when two amiable natures are knit from early youth, or united by common suffering and pursuits; it comes to some of the elect unbidden and unaware, it descends like gentle dew on chosen places which, however barren before, become under its kind influence fertile in all sweet plants; but when sought it flees, it scorns the prayers of its worshipers; it will grant itself, but not be wooed.\n\nI understood all this and went not forth to seek sympathy; yet there on my solitary heath, beneath my lowly roof, while all around lay desert, it came to me like a winter sunbeam lending beauty even as it melts the drifted snow. Alas, the sun shone on blasted fruit; I did not revive beneath its brightness, for I was too utterly ruined to feel its beneficent warmth."}

{"request_id":"2432ecc3934d40e3cd4b970a","rewritten_text":"“I wish we possessed a donkey. Imagine the three of us arriving on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and myself—with my caro sposo walking alongside. I must truly discuss purchasing one with him. In country living, I consider it almost indispensable; for, no matter how many diversions a woman may have, she cannot remain confined at home forever, and long walks, as you know—there is dust in summer, and in winter nothing but mud.”

“You will encounter neither between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and now it is completely dry. Still, come on a donkey if that is your preference. You may borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I would have everything arranged precisely to your liking.”

“That I have no doubt of. I do you complete justice, my dear friend. Beneath that particular dry, blunt exterior, I am aware you possess the warmest of hearts. As I often tell Mr. E., you are a consummate humourist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I thoroughly appreciate your attentiveness to me throughout this plan. You have discovered exactly what delights me.”

Mr. Knightley had another motive for avoiding a shaded table. He wished to persuade Mr. Woodhouse, and Emma as well, to join the outing; and he understood that if any of them were to sit down to eat outdoors, the result would surely be his illness. Mr. Woodhouse must not, under the seductive excuse of a morning drive and an hour or two spent at Donwell, be lured away to suffering.

He had been invited in all sincerity. No hidden terrors were to rebuke him for his trusting acceptance. He did agree. Two years had passed since he last visited Donwell. “Some splendid morning, he, Emma, and Harriet might go perfectly well; he could remain quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls roamed the gardens. He had no reason to suppose they would be damp at midday. He would greatly enjoy seeing the old house again and would be most happy to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton, and any other neighbours. He perceived not the least objection to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there some particularly fine morning. It seemed to him very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—extremely kind and judicious—far superior to dining out. He was not partial to dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was fortunate in everyone’s immediate assent. The invitation met such warm reception everywhere that, much like Mrs. Elton, all seemed to treat the arrangement as though it were a special compliment directed at themselves. Emma and Harriet declared their expectations of enjoyment to be exceedingly high; and Mr. Weston, unsolicited, promised to bring Frank over to join them if it could be arranged—a display of approval and gratitude that they might easily have excused. Mr. Knightley then found himself obligated to state that he would indeed be pleased to see him; whereupon Mr. Weston pledged to write without delay and to spare no persuasive arguments to secure Frank’s attendance."}

{"request_id":"05905f3f01f5b9fffbb37b97","rewritten_text":"“Get up! What are you doing?”

I opened my eyes and tried to figure out where I was. It was after sunrise, and I had been out cold. Pap was standing over me looking sour and sickly. He said, “What are you doing with that gun?”

I guessed he didn’t remember anything about what he’d been up to, so I said, “Somebody tried to get in, so I was waiting for him.”

“Why didn’t you wake me up?”

“Well, I tried, but I couldn’t. I couldn’t budge you.”

“Fine. Don’t stand there yammering all day—get outside and see if there’s a fish on the lines for breakfast. I’ll be along in a minute.”

He unlocked the door, and I headed up the riverbank. I noticed bits of branches and that sort of thing floating past, and pieces of bark sprinkled here and there; that let me know the river was starting to rise. I figured I’d be having a grand time if I were over in town. The June rise always brought me luck, because as soon as the water starts swelling, cordwood floats down, and pieces of log rafts too—maybe a dozen logs together. All you have to do is snag them and sell them to the woodyards and the sawmill.

I walked along the bank with one eye out for Pap and the other for whatever the rising river might bring. Suddenly comes a canoe, a real beauty about thirteen or fourteen feet long, riding high like a duck. I dove headfirst off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and swam for it. I half expected someone to be lying down in it, since people did that to fool passersby, and when some guy pulled his skiff up close they’d pop up and laugh at him. But not this time. It was a real drift canoe. I climbed in and paddled it to shore. I figured the old man would be pleased when he saw it—it was worth ten dollars.

But when I got to land, Pap still hadn’t shown up, and as I was pushing the canoe into a little creek like a gully, all covered over with vines and willows, another idea hit me. I decided I’d hide it well, and then, instead of disappearing into the woods when I ran off, I’d head down the river about fifty miles, make camp in one spot for good, and avoid the rough foot travel.

It was pretty close to the shack, and I kept thinking I heard the old man coming, but I got the canoe hidden. Then I slipped out and looked around a cluster of willows, and there he was, down the path a bit, taking aim at a bird with his gun."}

content.text: {"request_id":"0b538d8d9085e64f34b00254","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was disproportionately wide, lending his whole figure an absurd rotundity. His feet remained invisible, though now and then a horny-looking substance of dubious nature poked through a rip in the bottom of the car—or rather, the top of his hat. His hands were huge, his hair an exceedingly gray queue gathered behind. His nose was monstrously long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes round, gleaming, and sharp; his chin and cheeks, though lined with age, were broad, puffy, and double. Yet no hint of ears could be found anywhere on his head. This curious gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin surtout with snug breeches of the same shade, each knee secured by silver buckles. His waistcoat was fashioned from some vivid yellow cloth; a white taffeta cap perched rakishly to one side; and, to finish his ensemble, a blood-red silk handkerchief swathed his neck and fell lightly on his chest in an elaborate, oversized bow of fantastical design.\n\nAfter descending, as mentioned, to roughly a hundred feet above the ground, the little elder was instantly overtaken by a bout of trepidation and seemed unwilling to come any closer to terra firma. Accordingly, he cast out a measure of sand from a canvas bag he could barely hoist, and in an instant he was motionless. Next, in hurried agitation, he pulled from a side pocket of his surtout a large morocco pocketbook. He balanced it warily in his palm, studied it with pure astonishment, and clearly marveled at its heft. Finally he opened it and produced a huge letter secured with red wax and neatly tied with red tape, which he dropped exactly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to retrieve it. But the air-voyager, still terribly flustered and apparently having no further dealings in Rotterdam, immediately began feverish preparations to depart; and needing to jettison some ballast in order to rise again, he hurled out half a dozen bags, one after another, without bothering to empty them. Each and every one struck the burgomaster squarely in the back and sent him sprawling, somersaulting a full one-and-twenty times before the eyes of the entire city. Needless to say, the mighty Underduk did not allow such insolence from the little old man to go unchecked."}

content.text: {"request_id":"727d3f92be25deb26bde6d36","rewritten_text":"Cut off from usual means, the analyst immerses himself in his adversary’s spirit, identifies with it, and often perceives instantly the single measures (sometimes laughably simple) by which he might lure the other into blunder or hasty miscalculation.\n\nWhist has long been renowned for its effect on what people term the calculating faculty; and thinkers of the highest rank have been known to take a seemingly inexplicable pleasure in it, while dismissing chess as trifling. Beyond question, nothing comparable more severely taxes analytical power. The greatest chess-player in Christendom may remain only the foremost expert at chess; but mastery of whist implies aptitude for triumph in those more vital enterprises where mind contends with mind. By proficiency I mean that faultlessness in the game which embraces a grasp of every source from which legitimate advantage may arise. These are not merely numerous but diverse, and often lie within recesses of thought entirely closed to ordinary intellects. To observe closely is to retain distinctly; and, to that extent, the intensely focused chess-player performs well at whist, while Hoyle’s rules (themselves resting on the bare mechanics of the game) are generally intelligible. Hence to possess a strong memory and to play “by the book” are usually accounted the entirety of sound practice. Yet it is beyond mere rule that the analyst’s art shines forth. He silently amasses a multitude of observations and deductions. So, perhaps, do his associates; but the variance in the volume of information secured depends less on the soundness of the inference than on the quality of the observation. Essential knowledge lies in what to observe. Our player imposes no limits on himself; nor, because the game is central, does he discard inferences drawn from matters outside of it. He scrutinizes his partner’s face, setting it against each opponent’s. He studies how the cards are sorted in every hand; often counting trump after trump, honor after honor, by the glances their holders cast upon each. He registers every change of expression as the play goes on, deriving a rich store of reflection from shifting signs of certainty, surprise, exultation, or vexation. From the way a trick is gathered he judges whether the taker can secure another in that suit. He detects a feint by the manner in which a card is flung upon the table. A stray or unintentional word; the accidental dropping or turning of a card, with the accompanying eagerness or indifference about hiding it; the tallying of tricks, with the order in which they are laid down; awkwardness, wavering, keenness, or agitation—all offer, to his seemingly instinctive insight, clues to the genuine posture of affairs."}

{"request_id":"5b45269ba684b40874592148","rewritten_text":"For years Dorian Gray couldn’t loosen himself from the influence of that book. Or perhaps it’s more accurate to say he never tried to free himself from it. He obtained no fewer than nine large-paper copies of the first edition from Paris and had them bound in different colors so they would suit his varying moods and the shifting whims of a nature he sometimes seemed to have almost entirely lost control over. The hero—the extraordinary young Parisian in whom romantic and scientific temperaments were curiously intertwined—became for him a sort of preview of himself. Indeed, the entire book seemed to him to contain the story of his own life, written before he had lived it.

In one respect he was luckier than the novel’s fantastic hero. He never knew—never had any reason to know—that grotesque fear of mirrors, polished metal surfaces, and still water that struck the young Parisian so early in life, triggered by the sudden decay of a beauty that had once apparently been remarkable. With almost cruel delight—and perhaps in nearly every delight, as surely in every pleasure, cruelty has its place—he would read the latter part of the book, with its genuinely tragic, if somewhat overstated, account of the sorrow and despair of someone who had lost in himself what he prized most in others and in the world.

For the remarkable beauty that had so mesmerized Basil Hallward, and many others besides him, seemed never to abandon him. Even those who had heard the most sinister things about him—and from time to time strange rumors about his lifestyle filtered through London and became club gossip—couldn’t believe anything dishonorable when they saw him. He always looked like someone who had kept himself untainted by the world. Men who talked crudely fell silent when Dorian Gray entered the room. There was something in the innocence of his face that reproached them. His mere presence seemed to revive in them the memory of the purity they had stained. They wondered how someone so charming and graceful could have avoided the corruption of an age that was both sordid and sensual.

Often, returning home from those mysterious and prolonged absences that prompted such odd speculation among the people who were his friends—or thought they were—he himself would creep upstairs to the locked room, open the door with the key he now never parted with, and stand with a mirror in front of the portrait Basil Hallward had painted of him, looking first at the wicked, aging face on the canvas and then at the fair young face that laughed back at him from the polished glass."}

He has four or five thousand a year, and likely more.” Then she turned to her daughter. “Oh, my dear Jane, I am so happy! I am sure I won’t sleep a wink tonight. I knew it would happen. I always said it must, in the end. I was sure you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the moment I first saw him when he came into Hertfordshire last year, I thought how likely it was you would end up together. Oh, he is the handsomest young man ever seen!” Wickham and Lydia were entirely forgotten. Jane was now her unquestioned favorite child; for the moment, she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters quickly tried to secure favors from her future happiness. Mary asked for the use of the Netherfield library, and Kitty begged earnestly for a few dances there every winter. From then on Bingley became a daily visitor at Longbourn, often arriving before breakfast and never leaving until after supper, except when some barbarous neighbor, who could never be detested enough, invited him to dinner and he felt obliged to accept. Elizabeth now had little time to talk with her sister, for while Bingley was there, Jane paid attention to no one else; yet Elizabeth found herself useful to both during the necessary hours of separation. {"request_id":"e73e2919624e4165456cde74","rewritten_text":"From shop to shop I went, purchasing whatever the change in his appearance required. Once that business was settled, I set out for Little Britain on my own account. Mr. Jaggers, though at his desk when I entered, rose at once and planted himself before the fire.

“Now, Pip,” he said, “be cautious.”

“I will, sir,” I replied, for I had arranged in my mind, as I came along, what I meant to say.

“Do not commit yourself,” Mr. Jaggers warned, “and do not commit anyone. You grasp that—anyone. Do not confide in me; I desire no information; curiosity does not trouble me.”

Naturally I perceived he knew the man had arrived.

“I merely desire, Mr. Jaggers,” I said, “to make sure that what I have been told is fact. I cherish no hope of its being otherwise, but at least I may verify it.”

Mr. Jaggers nodded. “But did you say ‘told’ or ‘informed’?” he inquired, with his head inclined and his gaze turned, listeningly, toward the floor. “Told would suggest oral communication. One cannot converse orally with a man in New South Wales, you know.”

“I will say informed, Mr. Jaggers.”

“Good.”

“I have been informed by a person called Abel Magwitch, that he is the benefactor so long concealed from me.”

“That is the man,” said Mr. Jaggers, “in New South Wales.”

“And only he?” I asked.

“And only he,” returned Mr. Jaggers.

“I am not so unreasonable, sir, as to regard you as in any way accountable for my errors and mistaken conclusions; yet I had always supposed it to be Miss Havisham.”

“As you observe, Pip,” replied Mr. Jaggers coolly, taking a bite at his forefinger, “I bear no responsibility for that.”

“Still, it seemed so like her, sir,” I urged, heavy at heart.

“Not a trace of evidence, Pip,” said Mr. Jaggers, shaking his head and drawing up his skirts. “Take nothing on appearances; rest everything on evidence. No better rule exists.”

“I have nothing further,” I sighed, after a brief silence. “I have confirmed my information, and that is the end.”

“And Magwitch—in New South Wales—having now revealed himself,” said Mr. Jaggers, “you will recognize, Pip, how strictly in all my dealings with you I have held to the precise line of fact. There has never been the slightest deviation from the strict line of fact. You are fully aware of that?”

“Entirely, sir.”

“I informed Magwitch—in New South Wales—when he first wrote to me—from New South Wales—that he must not expect me to swerve from the strict line of fact.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"45fa66065756f08e8668e069","rewritten_text":"“You’re not suggesting—” began my sister. “Yes I am, Mum,” said Pumblechook. “But hold on a moment. Go on, Joseph. Good for you! Go on!” “What would everyone here say,” Joe continued, “to twenty pounds?” “Generous would be the word,” my sister replied. “Well, then,” said Joe, “it’s more than twenty pounds.” That wretched hypocrite Pumblechook nodded again and said, with a patronizing laugh, “It’s more than that, Mum. Very good! Keep it going, Joseph!” “Then let’s finish it,” said Joe, happily handing the bag to my sister; “it’s twenty-five pounds.” “It’s twenty-five pounds, Mum,” echoed that lowest of swindlers, Pumblechook, getting up to shake her hand; “and it’s no more than you deserve (as I said when they asked my opinion), and I wish you joy of the money!” If the scoundrel had stopped there, it would have been bad enough, but he made matters worse by proceeding to take me into custody with a show of authority that surpassed all his previous offenses. “Now look here, Joseph and wife,” said Pumblechook, gripping my arm above the elbow, “I’m one of those who always see things through. This boy has to be bound, immediately. That’s my way. Bound without delay.” “Heaven knows, Uncle Pumblechook,” said my sister, clutching the money, “we’re deeply indebted to you.” “Don’t mention it, Mum,” replied that diabolical corn dealer. “A pleasure’s a pleasure, everywhere. But this boy, you understand—we must have him bound. I said I’d take care of it, to tell you the truth.” The Justices were sitting in the Town Hall nearby, and we went straight over to have me bound as Joe’s apprentice in their presence. I say we went, but Pumblechook pushed me over there as if I’d just picked a pocket or set fire to a haystack; in fact, the general impression in court was that I’d been caught in the act. As Pumblechook shoved me through the crowd, I heard some people say, “What’s he done?” and others, “He’s young, too, but doesn’t he look bad?” A kindly-looking man even handed me a tract decorated with a woodcut of a sinister young man loaded with chains like sausages, titled TO BE READ IN MY CELL. The Hall struck me as a strange place, with pews taller than any church’s, people leaning over them to stare, powerful Justices (one with a powdered wig) reclining in chairs, arms folded, or taking snuff, dozing, writing, or reading newspapers, and shiny dark portraits on the walls that my untrained eye thought looked like a mix of hard candy and plaster patches."}

{"request_id":"79f7e1fe00772a77aff9cc9d","rewritten_text":"Watching him in these moods, I often pondered the old idea of the two-part soul and entertained myself by imagining a double Dupin—one creative, one analytical.

Do not think, from what I have just said, that I am describing any mystery or writing a romance. What I have shown in the Frenchman was only the effect of a highly active, perhaps unhealthy mind. But an example of his remarks in these moments will best explain.

One night we were walking down a long, filthy street near the Palais Royal. Both of us seemed deep in thought, and neither had spoken for at least fifteen minutes. Suddenly Dupin burst out with these words:

“He is a very small fellow, that’s true, and would suit the Théâtre des Variétés better.”

“No doubt about that,” I answered without thinking, not immediately noticing (so lost was I in my own thoughts) how perfectly he had matched my reflections. A second later, realization struck me, and my astonishment was immense.

“Dupin,” I said seriously, “this is beyond my understanding. I admit I’m amazed, and hardly trust my senses. How could you know I was thinking of ——?” Here I paused to make sure he really knew the person in my mind.

“—of Chantilly,” he said. “Why stop? You were noting that his tiny figure makes him unfit for tragedy.”

That was exactly what I had been thinking. Chantilly was a former cobbler from the Rue St. Denis who, crazed with the stage, had tried to play Xerxes in Crébillon’s tragedy and had been publicly mocked for it.

“Tell me, for heaven’s sake,” I cried, “the method—if there is one—by which you have managed to read my mind in this matter.” In truth I was more shaken than I cared to admit.

“It was the fruit seller,” my friend replied, “who led you to conclude that the cobbler-turned-actor was too short for Xerxes and the like.”

“The fruit seller! You astonish me—I know no fruit seller.”

“The man who ran into you as we entered the street—perhaps fifteen minutes ago.”

I now remembered that a fruit seller, balancing a large basket of apples on his head, had nearly knocked me down by accident as we left the Rue C—— for the street we were now in; but what that had to do with Chantilly, I could not imagine."}

{"request_id":"df62f495fffe16c111da876d","rewritten_text":"Emma Woodhouse, beautiful, intelligent, and wealthy, blessed with a comfortable home and cheerful disposition, seemed to possess some of life’s greatest advantages, and had spent nearly twenty-one years with hardly anything to trouble or upset her.

She was the younger of two daughters of a deeply loving, indulgent father, and after her sister married, she had been the mistress of his house from an early age. Her mother had died so long ago that Emma could only dimly remember her embrace, and her place had been filled by an excellent governess who came close to being a mother in affection.

Miss Taylor had been in Mr. Woodhouse’s household for sixteen years, serving more as a friend than a governess, very fond of both daughters but especially Emma. Between them it was more like the closeness of sisters. Even before Miss Taylor stopped formally holding the role of governess, her gentle temperament had hardly allowed her to impose any restraint; and since that slight authority had long faded, they had lived together as friends who were mutually devoted, with Emma doing exactly as she pleased, highly valuing Miss Taylor’s judgment but mostly guided by her own.

The real problems in Emma’s situation were that she could too easily have her own way, and she had a tendency to think a little too highly of herself; these were the drawbacks that could tarnish her many pleasures. Yet the danger was so unnoticed at present that she did not consider them misfortunes at all.

Then sorrow came—a gentle sorrow—but not from any unpleasant self-awareness. Miss Taylor married. It was the loss of Miss Taylor that first brought grief. On the wedding day of this beloved friend, Emma first sat in sustained sadness. Once the wedding was over and the bridal party gone, she and her father were left to dine together, with no expectation of a third person to enliven the long evening. After dinner her father, as usual, settled himself to sleep, leaving her only to sit and reflect on what she had lost.

The event offered every promise of happiness for her friend. Mr. Weston was a man of impeccable character, comfortable fortune, suitable age, and agreeable manners; and there was some satisfaction in thinking how selflessly and generously she had desired and encouraged the match. Still, it felt like a bleak day’s work for her. She knew she would feel the absence of Miss Taylor every hour of every day. She thought of the past kindness—the affection of sixteen years—how Miss Taylor had taught and played with her since she was five, how she had dedicated all her efforts to engaging and entertaining her when she was well, and how she had nursed her through every childhood illness."}

{"request_id":"3a338f008671d7c7deb29c4c","rewritten_text":"“Come now, Tom,” says I, “seems like you could tell a body. What’s a bar sinister?”

“Oh, _I_ ain’t certain. But he’s bound to have it. All nobility does.”

That was just his way. If it didn’t hit him to explain something, he wouldn’t, no matter how long you worked at him.

He’d settled all that coat-of-arms notion, so then he set in to finish the rest of that part—which was to lay out a sorrowful inscription—said Jim needed one, same as the lot of them. He cooked up a bunch, wrote them on a sheet, and read them off, this way:

1. _Here a captive heart busted._

2. _Here a poor prisoner, deserted by the world and friends, fretted out his mourning life._

3. _Here a lonely heart broke, and a weary spirit took to its rest, after thirty-seven years of solitary captivity._

4. _Here, homeless and friendless, after thirty-seven years of bitter captivity, died a noble stranger, natural son to Louis XIV._

Tom’s voice shook while he read them, and he nearly went to pieces. After he was done he couldn’t for the world decide which one Jim ought to scratch on the wall, they were all so fine; but in the end he concluded Jim should scratch every one of them. Jim said it would take a whole year to scratch that heap of stuff onto the logs with a nail, and he couldn’t form letters anyway; but Tom promised to mark them out for him, so all Jim had to do was trace the lines. Then pretty soon he says:

“Come to think, the logs won’t answer; they don’t have log walls in a dungeon. We got to dig those words into rock. We’ll fetch a rock.”

Jim claimed a rock was worse than logs; said scraping them into stone would take so cussed long he’d never get loose. But Tom said he’d let me help him. Then he glanced over to see how me and Jim were doing with the pens. It was downright aggravating slow, didn’t give my hands any chance to heal from the sores, and we wasn’t gaining any ground hardly; so Tom says:

“I know the way to manage it. We have to have one rock for the coat of arms and the mourning inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with that very rock.”"}

{"request_id":"6574a1aaa8d2bd794a35108c","rewritten_text":"He rose, left the room with my nurse, and my father entered almost immediately.

Nothing could have delighted me more in that instant than my father’s arrival. I extended my hand to him and exclaimed,

“Are you safe—and Elizabeth—and Ernest?”

He soothed me with assurances about their wellbeing and, lingering on those subjects dearest to me, tried to lift my sinking spirits; yet he soon perceived that cheerfulness cannot dwell in a prison. “What a place for you to inhabit, my son!” he said, casting a sorrowful glance at the barred windows and miserable surroundings. “You set out in search of happiness, yet a cruel fate seems to dog your steps. And poor Clerval—”

The mere mention of my unfortunate, murdered friend was more agitation than my feeble state could bear; tears burst forth.

“Alas, yes, my father,” I answered. “Some most dreadful destiny hangs over me, and I must live to accomplish it, or else I should have died upon Henry’s coffin.”

We were not permitted to talk long, for my fragile health demanded every precaution that might secure calm. Mr. Kirwin entered and insisted my strength not be spent by excessive effort. Yet my father’s presence felt like that of a guardian angel, and little by little my health returned.

As the illness receded, a dark, oppressive melancholy took possession of me, and nothing could dispel it. Clerval’s image appeared incessantly before my eyes, ghastly and slain. More than once the agitation these thoughts provoked made my friends fear a serious relapse. Alas! Why had they preserved so wretched and hateful a life? Surely it was that I might fulfil my fate, which was now nearing its conclusion. Soon—very soon—death would still these pulsings and free me from the crushing weight of anguish that drove me to the dust; and, in satisfying justice, I too would find rest. Then, though death seemed distant, the longing for it never left my mind; for hours I would sit motionless and mute, yearning for some vast upheaval that might entomb both me and my destroyer in its ruin.

The assizes season drew near. I had been three months imprisoned, and though still weak and ever in danger of relapse, I had to journey nearly a hundred miles to the country town where the court convened. Mr. Kirwin himself undertook every duty of gathering witnesses and preparing my defence."}

{"request_id":"a63dd65c9dad621b756a4b11","rewritten_text":"At least he thought so. But who could know? No, there had been nothing else. Out of vanity he had spared her. Out of hypocrisy he had worn a mask of goodness. For curiosity’s sake he had tried to renounce himself. He saw that now.

But this murder—was it going to haunt him forever? Was he always to be weighed down by his past? Was he truly going to confess? Never. Only one piece of evidence remained against him. The portrait itself—that was the evidence. He would destroy it. Why had he kept it so long? Once it had pleased him to watch it change and grow old. Lately, he had felt no such pleasure. It had kept him awake at night. When he was away, he had been terrified that other eyes would look at it. It had thrown gloom over his passions. The mere memory of it had spoiled many moments of joy. It had been like a conscience to him. Yes, it had been his conscience. He would destroy it.

He looked around and saw the knife that had stabbed Basil Hallward. He had cleaned it many times until no stain remained. It was bright and gleaming. Just as it had killed the painter, so it would kill the painter’s work and all it stood for. It would kill the past, and once that was dead, he would be free. It would kill this monstrous soul-life, and without its hideous warnings he would be at peace. He grabbed the blade and plunged it into the portrait.

A scream rang out, followed by a crash. The scream was so full of agony that the startled servants woke and crept out of their rooms. Two gentlemen passing below in the square stopped and looked up at the grand house. They walked on until they met a policeman and brought him back. The man rang the bell several times, but there was no answer. Except for a light in one of the top windows, the house was completely dark. After a while he withdrew to a neighboring portico and kept watch.

“Whose house is that, Constable?” asked the older of the two gentlemen.

“Mr. Dorian Gray’s, sir,” the policeman replied.

They exchanged a look as they walked away and sneered. One of them was Sir Henry Ashton’s uncle.

Inside, in the servants’ quarters, the half-dressed staff were whispering to each other. Old Mrs. Leaf was crying and wringing her hands. Francis was pale as death.

After about fifteen minutes, he gathered the coachman and one of the footmen, and they crept upstairs."}

{"request_id":"051dcb904a50b9e411d9b9b8","rewritten_text":"“It must have been during that very period of Mr. Elliot’s life,” said Anne, “that has always stirred my particular curiosity. It must have been when he first became acquainted with my father and sister. I never met him myself; I only heard about him; but there was something in how he behaved toward my father and sister then, and later in the circumstances of his marriage, that never quite matched what I know of him now. It hinted at a different sort of man.”

“I know everything, I know it all,” cried Mrs. Smith. “He had been introduced to Sir Walter and your sister before I ever met him, but he talked about them constantly. I know he was invited and encouraged, and I know he chose not to go. I can probably satisfy you on points you wouldn’t expect, and as for his marriage, I knew all about it at the time. I was part of every for and against; I was the friend he trusted with his hopes and plans; and though I didn’t know his wife beforehand—her lower social standing made that impossible—I knew her throughout her life afterward, or at least until the last two years, and I can answer any question you might ask.”

“No,” said Anne, “I have no particular question about her. I always understood they weren’t a happy couple. But I would like to know why, at that time in his life, he snubbed my father’s acquaintance the way he did. My father certainly meant to treat him kindly and properly. Why did Mr. Elliot pull away?”

“Mr. Elliot,” replied Mrs. Smith, “at that point in his life had one aim: to make his fortune, and by a faster route than the law. He was determined to make it through marriage. At least he was determined not to ruin it through an imprudent marriage; and I know he believed (whether rightly or not, I cannot say) that your father and sister, with their politeness and invitations, were plotting a match between the heir and the young lady, and such a match could never satisfy his idea of wealth and independence. That was why he withdrew, I assure you. He told me the entire story. He hid nothing from me. It was odd that, after leaving you behind in Bath, my first and closest acquaintance upon marrying should be your cousin, and that through him I should be continually hearing about your father and sister.”"}

{"request_id":"37ab694ac6177c43f9f5a913","rewritten_text":"Other chances for observing them could not but arise. Anne was soon among all four together often enough to form an opinion, though too prudent to confess it at home, where she knew it would please neither husband nor wife; for while she suspected Louisa held the chief place in favour, she could not help thinking, as far as recollection and experience allowed her to judge, that Captain Wentworth was enamoured of neither. They were the more besotted with him; yet even that was hardly love. It was merely a brief fever of admiration; though it might, likely must, ripen into love with some. Charles Hayter seemed conscious of being undervalued, and still Henrietta occasionally looked torn between them. Anne yearned for the ability to show them all what they were doing, to point out the harms they were courting. She never imputed deceit to any. Her greatest comfort was to think Captain Wentworth entirely unaware of the suffering he caused. There was no triumph, no contemptible triumph, in his demeanour. He had likely never heard, and never considered, any claim Charles Hayter might have. His only fault lay in accepting attentions (for accept he must be said to do) from two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw. Three days went by without his appearing once at Uppercross; a very marked alteration. He even declined a standing dinner invitation; and when Mr Musgrove found him then with some large volumes before him, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were certain all was not well, and discussed, with solemn faces, his studying himself into the grave. Mary hoped and believed he had been expressly dismissed by Henrietta, while her husband lived in constant expectation of seeing him the next day. Anne could only regard Charles Hayter as acting sensibly.

One morning, near this time, Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth having gone shooting together, the sisters at the Cottage, seated quietly over their work, received a visit at the window from their counterparts at the Mansion-house.

It was a splendid November day, and the Miss Musgroves crossed the little grounds to stop merely for the purpose of announcing that they meant to take a long walk, and therefore concluded Mary could not wish to accompany them; yet when Mary, feeling some jealousy at not being thought a good walker, instantly answered, “Oh yes, I should like to join you very much, I quite enjoy a long walk,” Anne felt convinced, by the sisters’ looks, that it was exactly what they did not desire, and she once more admired that odd necessity produced by family habits, of everything needing to be told, and everything undertaken together, however unwelcome or inconvenient."}
