{"request_id":"7e658aca159864bcd0f10eae","rewritten_text":"“Allow me to point out, Sir Walter,” Mr Shepherd said one morning at Kellynch Hall as he set down the newspaper, “that the current situation is working in our favour. This peace will send all our wealthy naval officers ashore, and they will all be wanting homes. There could not be a better moment, Sir Walter, to choose among tenants—very responsible tenants. Many a fine fortune has been made during the war. If a rich admiral were to appear in our path, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very fortunate man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter replied. “That is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would be quite a prize for him—perhaps the greatest prize of all, even if he has already claimed any number of others. Wouldn’t you agree, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he must at such wit, and continued, “May I point out, Sir Walter, that when it comes to business, gentlemen of the navy are easy to deal with. I have some experience of their methods, and I freely admit that they think generously and are just as likely to make excellent tenants as any group one might meet. Therefore, Sir Walter, what I would venture to suggest is this: if rumours arise about your intention—which must be expected, because we know how hard it is to keep one part of the world from prying into the actions of another. Consequence has its cost. I, John Shepherd, could hide any family matters I chose, for no one would bother to watch me. But Sir Walter Elliot has many eyes upon him, which may be quite difficult to avoid. Therefore, I take the liberty of saying I would not be greatly surprised if, despite all our caution, some whisper of the truth should leak out. If that happens, and applications inevitably follow, I believe any coming from our wealthy naval officers would be especially worthy of consideration. And let me add that I can be here in two hours at any time to spare you the trouble of replying.”

Sir Walter only nodded. But soon after, as he rose and paced the room, he remarked with sarcasm, “I imagine there are few naval gentlemen who would not be astonished to find themselves in a house like this.”

“They would certainly look around and bless their good fortune,” said Mrs Clay, for she was present; her father had driven her over—nothing was so good for Mrs Clay’s health as a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely agree with my father that a sailor could be a very desirable tenant.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d44eed6ac731dd50b9863612","rewritten_text":"How long I stayed in that stupor I cannot tell. It must have been a fair length of time, for when awareness slowly returned, dawn was breaking, the balloon hung at a tremendous height over a vast wilderness of ocean, and not the faintest strip of land showed anywhere on the wide horizon. Yet my sensations on recovering were not nearly as agonizing as one might expect. In truth, there was an early edge of madness in the calm way I began to examine my situation. I raised each hand to my eyes in turn and wondered what could have caused the swollen veins and the dreadful blackness of my fingernails. Then I carefully felt my head, shaking it again and again and touching it with anxious care, until at last I convinced myself it was not, as I had half suspected, larger than the balloon itself. After that, with a knowing air, I searched both breeches pockets, and, missing a set of tablets and a toothpick case, tried to understand how they could have vanished. Failing to explain it, I felt intensely annoyed. A new sensation of discomfort in the joint of my left ankle occurred to me, and a dim awareness of my situation began to grow. But, strangely, I was neither amazed nor horrified. If I felt anything, it was a kind of smug satisfaction at the cleverness I was about to show in freeing myself from this dilemma; not for a moment did I doubt my final safety. For a few minutes I stayed wrapped in deep thought. I clearly remember pressing my lips together, touching the side of my nose with my forefinger, and making the various gestures and expressions common to men who, settled in their armchairs, ponder complicated or weighty questions. Once I believed I had gathered my thoughts enough, I carefully, step by step, put my hands behind my back and unfastened the large iron buckle on the waistband of my trousers. The buckle had three teeth that, being rusty, turned very hard on their hinges. After some effort I swung them to a right angle with the buckle and was pleased to see they stayed fixed in that spot. Holding this new tool between my teeth, I set about untying the knot of my cravat. I had to pause several times before I managed the trick, but I did manage it at last."}

{"request_id":"91ec32315199e40b2492685d","rewritten_text":"It seemed like a jumble of back lanes, ditches, and tiny gardens, giving off the air of a rather dull retreat. Wemmick’s house was a small wooden cottage surrounded by garden plots, and the rooftop was cut out and painted to resemble a battery with guns.

“My own handiwork,” Wemmick said. “Looks nice, doesn’t it?”

I praised it highly; I think it was the smallest house I’d ever seen, with the oddest Gothic windows (most of them blatantly fake) and a Gothic door barely big enough to squeeze through.

“That’s a real flagpole, you see,” Wemmick continued, “and on Sundays I run up a real flag. Then look here. After I cross this bridge, I haul it up—like so—and cut off the connection.”

The bridge was only a plank spanning a gap about four feet wide and two feet deep. But it was delightful to watch the pride with which he hoisted it and secured it, smiling as he did so, with genuine enjoyment rather than mere routine.

“At nine o’clock every night, Greenwich time,” said Wemmick, “the gun goes off. There he is, you see! And when you hear him fire, I think you’ll agree he’s a Stinger.”

The cannon he mentioned was mounted in a separate little fortress made of latticework. It was shielded from the weather by a clever tarpaulin contraption shaped like an umbrella.

“Then, at the back,” Wemmick said, “out of sight so it doesn’t interfere with the fortification theme—because it’s a principle with me: if you have an idea, carry it through and keep it up—I don’t know whether you agree—”

I answered firmly that I did.

“—At the back there’s a pig, and there are chickens and rabbits; then I knock together my own frames, you see, and grow cucumbers; and you’ll judge at supper what sort of salad I can produce. So, sir,” said Wemmick, smiling again yet with a serious nod, “if you imagine the little place under siege, it would hold out a devilishly long time when it comes to provisions.”

Then he led me to a bower about a dozen yards away, though the path twisted so cleverly that it took a good while to reach; in this hideaway our glasses were already set out. Our punch was chilling in an ornamental lake, on whose edge the bower stood. This pool—circular in shape, with an island in the center that could just as well have supplied the salad for supper—had a fountain he had built. When you set a little wheel going and pulled a cork from a pipe, it sprayed so strongly that it soaked the back of your hand."}

{"request_id":"e4bcaaa51fab67a7e0920802","rewritten_text":"That little conversation with Mr. Knightley gave Emma a great deal of pleasure. As she strolled around the lawn the next morning, it was one of the best memories she savored from the ball. She was delighted they had reached such a good understanding about the Eltons, and that they felt so similarly about both husband and wife; and his praise of Harriet, his admission in her favor, was especially satisfying. The Eltons’ rudeness, which had threatened for a few minutes to ruin the rest of her evening, had actually produced some of its greatest delights; and she anticipated another happy outcome—the end of Harriet’s infatuation. From the way Harriet spoke of the incident before they left the ballroom, Emma felt strong hope. It seemed as if Harriet’s eyes had suddenly been opened and she now saw that Mr. Elton was not the superior man she had believed him to be. The fever had broken, and Emma could scarcely fear that the pulse would quicken again because of dangerous kindness. She was counting on the Eltons’ ill will to provide all the pointed neglect still needed. With Harriet sensible, Frank Churchill not too much in love, and Mr. Knightley not wanting to quarrel with her, how wonderfully happy the summer ahead must be! 

She was not going to see Frank Churchill that morning. He had told her he could not allow himself the pleasure of stopping at Hartfield, as he needed to be home by noon. She felt no regret. 

After sorting through everything and setting it to rights, she was just turning toward the house, spirits refreshed for whatever the two little boys and their grandfather might demand, when the heavy iron gate swung open and two people walked in—people she could scarcely have expected to see together—Frank Churchill, with Harriet leaning on his arm—Harriet herself! One instant was enough to convince her that something remarkable had happened. Harriet was pale and frightened, and he was trying to comfort her. The iron gates and the front door were less than twenty yards apart; in a moment all three were in the hall, and Harriet dropped into a chair and fainted. 

A young lady who faints must be revived; questions must be asked, and surprises explained. Such events are fascinating, but their suspense cannot last long. In a few minutes Emma knew everything. 

Miss Smith and Miss Bickerton, another boarder at Mrs. Goddard’s who had also attended the ball, had gone out for a walk together and taken a route—the Richmond road—which, though apparently public enough to seem safe, led them into danger. About half a mile beyond Highbury, the road took a sudden turn and, shaded by elms on both sides, became quite secluded for some distance; and when the young women had gone some way along it, they suddenly saw, a short distance ahead, on a broader patch of grass to the side, a group of gypsies."}

{"request_id":"b295d75394fe8281368403ff","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted she was somewhat taken aback by the match, yet she spoke more of her heartfelt wish for their happiness than of her surprise, nor could Elizabeth convince her to see it as unlikely. Kitty and Lydia were never tempted to envy Miss Lucas, since Mr. Collins remained merely a clergyman, and the news affected them only as something to circulate about Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant at being able to remind Mrs. Bennet that she now had a daughter advantageously settled, and she visited Longbourn more frequently than usual to proclaim her delight, though Mrs. Bennet’s sour expressions and spiteful comments might have driven delight away.

A constraint between Elizabeth and Charlotte kept both silent on the subject; Elizabeth believed that true confidence could never revive between them. Her disappointment in Charlotte made her cling more tenderly to her sister, whose integrity and sensibility she felt could never be doubted, and whose happiness she watched over with mounting concern, as Bingley had been absent a week and no word of his return had arrived.

Jane had answered Caroline’s letter promptly and now counted the days until she might expect another. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks reached them on Tuesday, directed to their father and written with all the solemn gratitude a year’s residence might have inspired. Having relieved his conscience, he exulted with exuberant phrases over his felicity in winning the affection of their amiable neighbour, Miss Lucas, and declared it was solely to enjoy her company that he so readily accepted their invitation to Longbourn, where he hoped to arrive on Monday fortnight; for Lady Catherine, he added, so warmly endorsed his marriage that she wished it to occur as soon as possible, which he trusted would compel his amiable Charlotte to fix an early day for making him the happiest of men.

Mrs. Bennet could no longer view Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire with pleasure. Rather, she was now as inclined as her husband to complain of it. How odd that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge; it was likewise highly inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She detested having guests in the house when her health was so delicate, and lovers were, of all people, the most irksome."}

{"request_id":"d5f35e34ed0e27746e8facdb","rewritten_text":"“Story!”

He chose to misconstrue the word she had echoed, adding hurriedly, “Yes, customers; in banking we commonly refer to our connection as our customers. He was a French gentleman, a man of science, a person of great accomplishments—a Doctor.”

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Indeed, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman hailed from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was esteemed in Paris. I had the honour of knowing him there. Our dealings were commercial, yet confidential. I was then stationed in our French House, and had been—why, twenty years.”

“At that period—may I ask, in which year, sir?”

“I refer, miss, to twenty years past. He wed—an English lady—and I acted as one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many other French gentlemen and families, were wholly managed by Tellson’s. In a similar fashion, I am, or have been, trustee in some capacity for dozens of our patrons. These are purely business ties, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing resembling sentiment. I have moved from one to another throughout my business life, just as I move from one customer to another in the course of a business day; in short, I possess no feelings; I am simply a machine. To continue—”

“But this concerns my father, sir; and I begin to suspect”—the strangely furrowed forehead bent on him—“that when I was left an orphan because my mother outlived my father by only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost certain it was you.”

Mr. Lorry received the hesitant small hand that trustfully reached for his, raised it with some ceremony to his lips, and then escorted the young lady straight back to her chair; holding the chair-back with his left hand, and using his right alternately to rub his chin, tug his wig at the ears, or emphasize his speech, he stood gazing down into her face while she sat gazing up into his.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how exact my words were just now, when I said I had no feelings, and that all my relations with others are merely business relations, if you consider that I have never seen you since. No; you have been Tellson’s ward ever since, and I have been engaged with the other business of Tellson’s ever since. Feelings! I have neither time nor opportunity for them. I spend my whole existence, miss, in turning a vast pecuniary mangle.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1451be73b5fac1ce673f6ac0","rewritten_text":"The stupefaction and amazement that seized me at this astonishing shift in circumstances were perhaps, in the end, the least explicable portion of the whole adventure. The reversal itself was not merely natural and inevitable, but had long been foreseen as the condition that must ensue when I should reach the distinct point in my journey where the planet’s pull gave way to that of the satellite—or, to be more exact, where the balloon’s gravitation toward the earth was weaker than its attraction toward the moon. Granted, I had awakened from a deep sleep with my senses in disarray, to be confronted by a phenomenon at once startling and, though foreknown, not anticipated at that precise instant. The revolution must, in any case, have transpired smoothly and by degrees, and it is in no sense certain that, even had I been conscious when it happened, I should have detected any inward token of inversion—no discomfort or disorder either in myself or in my rigging.\n\n“It scarcely needs mention that, once I regained proper awareness of my position and shook off the fright that had swallowed every faculty of my spirit, my first concern was entirely fixed upon the general physical spectacle of the moon. It stretched below me like a map—and though I estimated it to be still at a respectable remove, the indentations of its surface stood out to my sight with a startling and wholly inexplicable clarity. The total lack of ocean, sea, lake, river, or any semblance of water struck me, at the first look, as the most astonishing aspect of its geology. Yet, strangely enough, I discerned vast level tracts of decidedly alluvial character, although the larger share of the hemisphere before me was clad in countless volcanic mountains, conical in form, seeming more like artificial heaps than natural projections. The loftiest of these barely rises three and three-quarter miles in height; still, a chart of the volcanic region of the Campi Phlegraei would give your Excellencies a truer notion of their general aspect than any feeble description I might presume to present. Most were plainly in eruption, impressing on me the dread of their ferocity and force through the incessant thunder of the so-called meteoric stones, which now surged upward past the balloon with an ever more terrifying rapidity."}

{"request_id":"f0af7c4ede4215b4ad4bb2e7","rewritten_text":"Great God! Had I for even a moment guessed the hellish intent of my fiendish enemy, I would have exiled myself from my homeland and wandered the world as a friendless outcast rather than agree to this wretched marriage. But as if wielding some spell, the monster kept me blind to his true plan; thinking I had arranged only my own death, I hurried that of someone far more precious.

As our wedding day approached, whether from cowardice or some prophetic dread, my heart sank. I hid my uneasiness behind a show of cheerfulness that lit my father’s face with smiles, though the ever-alert, discerning eyes of Elizabeth were hardly fooled. She looked ahead to our union with calm contentment, tinged with the fear that past misfortunes had left behind—that what now seemed solid happiness might vanish into a dream, leaving only an unending, bitter regret.

Preparations were underway, congratulations arrived, and everything seemed joyful. I locked the anxiety that gnawed at me inside my own heart and, with feigned enthusiasm, joined in my father’s plans, though they might end up serving as the scenery of my tragedy. Through his efforts, part of Elizabeth’s inheritance had been returned by the Austrian government: a small property on the shores of Como. We agreed that immediately after the wedding we would go to Villa Lavenza and spend our first days of happiness beside the beautiful lake it overlooked.

Meanwhile I took every possible precaution in case the fiend attacked me openly. I always carried pistols and a dagger, remained constantly alert to any trick, and gained some measure of calm. As the day drew near, the threat seemed more like a delusion, unworthy of disturbing my peace, while the happiness I anticipated in marriage felt more certain as the date for the ceremony approached and everyone spoke of it as something no accident could stop.

Elizabeth seemed happy; my composed manner helped settle her mind. Yet on the day that was to grant my wishes and seal my fate, she grew sorrowful, sensing impending doom, and perhaps thinking, too, of the terrible secret I had promised to reveal to her the next day."}

content.text: {"request_id":"538b42f3f35ddb01475e7af6","rewritten_text":"Cut off from ordinary resources, the analyst immerses himself in his opponent’s mindset, identifies with it, and often sees in an instant the only tactics—even ridiculously simple ones—by which he can lure that opponent into error or rush him into miscalculation. Whist has long been recognized for its impact on what we call the calculating power, and men of the highest intellect have been known to take an apparently inexplicable pleasure in it while dismissing chess as frivolous. There is unquestionably nothing of a similar kind that tests the faculty of analysis so severely. The best chess player in Christendom may be little more than the best chess player, but mastery of whist implies the ability to succeed in all those more important ventures where mind struggles with mind. By mastery I mean that perfection in the game which includes grasping every source from which legitimate advantage can be drawn. These sources are not only numerous but diverse, often hidden in corners of thought completely inaccessible to the ordinary understanding. To observe closely is to remember clearly, and the chess player with strong concentration will do well enough at whist, while Hoyle’s rules—which rest on the mechanics of the game—are broadly understandable. Thus a good memory and a habit of playing “by the book” are usually seen as the entire secret of good play. But true skill is shown in matters that lie beyond rule. The analyst silently makes a multitude of observations and deductions. His partners may do the same, yet the difference in the scope of information obtained lies not so much in the soundness of the reasoning as in the quality of the observation. The essential knowledge is what to observe. Our player places no limits on himself; nor, simply because the game is everything, does he refuse conclusions drawn from things outside the game. He studies his partner’s face, comparing it carefully with the expression of each opponent. He considers how every player arranges the cards in hand, often counting trump after trump and honor after honor by the glances the holders give them. He notices every change of expression as play advances, gathering insights from the shifts that signal certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way a trick is gathered, he judges whether the taker can secure another in that suit. He recognizes a feint by the way a card is laid on the table. A casual word, the accidental dropping or turning of a card and the anxiety or nonchalance shown in covering it, the counting of tricks and the order in which they are stacked, embarrassment, hesitation, excitement, or agitation—all of these give his seemingly intuitive mind clues to the true state of play."}

{"request_id":"c5ef726f2e7e543b3cc85f7f","rewritten_text":"Yet for all this zeal, the boy grew only gloomier, paler, and more despondent. She added steaming baths, sitz baths, showers, and plunges. Tom stayed as mournful as a hearse. Next she supplemented the water regimen with thin oatmeal gruel and blister plasters. She gauged his capacity like that of a pitcher, stuffing him daily with patent remedies.

By now Tom had ceased to care about being tormented. This new attitude filled the old lady with alarm. The indifference had to be shattered no matter what. Just then she heard of Pain-killer for the first time. She ordered a supply immediately. One taste filled her with gratitude. It was nothing less than fire in liquid shape. She scrapped the water cures and everything else and concentrated her faith on Pain-killer. She delivered Tom a teaspoonful and watched, quivering with anxiety, for the effect. Her distress vanished at once, her soul settling into calm; the “indifference” had been smashed. The boy could not have displayed a livelier or more enthusiastic response if she had kindled a blaze beneath him.

Tom decided it was time to rouse himself; this existence might suit a ruined heart, but it was coming to hold too little romance and too much harrying variety. So he considered different escape plans and finally settled on pretending he fancied Pain-killer. He asked for it so frequently he became unbearable, and his aunt at last told him to serve himself and quit pestering her. Had it been Sid, her delight would have been unmixed; but since it was Tom, she kept a secret watch on the bottle. She noticed the medicine really dwindling, yet never guessed the boy was doctoring a crack in the sitting-room floor with it.

One afternoon Tom was in the act of dosing the crevice when his aunt’s yellow cat strolled by, purring, eyeing the spoon greedily, begging for a sample. Tom said:

“Don’t ask for it unless you want it, Peter.”

But Peter indicated he did.

“You better be sure.”

Peter was certain.

“Now you’ve asked for it, and I’ll hand it over, because there’s nothing mean about me; but if you find it doesn’t suit, you’ve only yourself to blame.”

Peter consented. Tom pried the cat’s jaws apart and poured in the Pain-killer. Peter shot two yards into the air, let out a war-whoop, and tore off around the room, crashing into furniture, knocking over flowerpots, and wreaking general destruction."}

{"request_id":"93cb4e6ec26750d96fc2900d","rewritten_text":"One day, while I was bent over my studies with Mr. Pocket, the post brought me a note whose outer appearance alone sent my heart racing; for although I had never seen the handwriting, I guessed whose it must be. The note had no formal opening—no Dear Mr. Pip, Dear Pip, Dear Sir, nor any such salutation—but ran straight on in these words:—

“I am to be in London the day after to-morrow by the midday coach. I believe it was arranged that you should meet me? At least Miss Havisham thinks so, and I write in compliance with her belief. She sends you her regards.

“Yours, ESTELLA.”

Had there been sufficient time, I would likely have ordered several new suits for the occasion; lacking that, I had to make do with what I already possessed. My appetite vanished on the spot, and I found no peace or rest until the day came. Yet its coming brought no relief; I became more frantic than before and began haunting the coach-office in Wood Street, Cheapside, even before the coach had left the Blue Boar in our town. Though I knew this perfectly well, still I felt it perilous to let the coach-office out of sight for more than five minutes together; and in this unreasonable state I had completed the first half-hour of a four or five hour vigil when Wemmick collided with me.

“Halloa, Mr. Pip,” said he; “how do you do? I should hardly have imagined this was _your_ beat.”

I explained that I was waiting for someone arriving by coach, and asked after the Castle and the Aged.

“Both thriving, thankee,” said Wemmick, “especially the Aged. He’s in rare feather. He’ll be eighty-two next birthday. I have half a mind to fire eighty-two times, if the neighbourhood doesn’t object and that little cannon of mine can stand the strain. However, this isn’t London talk. Where do you suppose I’m bound?”

“To the office?” said I, since he was heading that way.

“Nearest thing to it,” he answered. “I’m going to Newgate. We’re engaged in a banker’s-parcel affair at present, and I’ve been down the road taking a look at the scene, so now I must have a word or two with our client.”

“Did your client commit the robbery?” I inquired.

“Bless your soul and body, no,” replied Wemmick, very dryly. “But he’s charged with it. So might you or I be. Either of us might be accused, you know.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"774bb17d43b071307ee48826","rewritten_text":"He always pretended Peter had written him those letters, but that was a lie; he got every single one out of that young fool we paddled to the steamboat. Mary Jane brought in the letter her father left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. It gave the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls, and it gave the tanyard (which was doing fine business), along with some other houses and land (worth about seven thousand), plus three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and it told exactly where the six thousand in cash was hidden in the cellar. These two crooks said they’d bring it up and keep everything honest and aboveboard, and they told me to come with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag they poured it out on the floor. It was a beautiful sight, all those gold coins. My, how the king’s eyes shone! He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said, “Oh, this is nothing great, oh no, I don’t think so! Why, Bilge, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn’t it?” The duke said it surely did. They pawed at the gold coins, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle on the floor; then the king said, “There’s no use talking; being brothers to a rich dead man and representatives of foreign heirs who got left is the right line for you and me, Bilge. This is what comes from trusting Providence. It’s the best way in the long run. I’ve tried them all, and there ain’t any better way.” Most people would have been satisfied with the pile and taken it on faith, but no, they had to count it. So they counted it, and it came out four hundred fifteen dollars short. The king said, “Damn him, I wonder what he did with that four hundred fifteen?” They worried over it for a while and searched all around. Then the duke said, “Well, he was a pretty sick man, and he probably made a mistake. That must be it. Best to let it go and keep quiet about it. We can spare it.” “Oh, sure, we can spare it. I don’t care about that—it’s the count I’m thinking about. We want to be completely square and open and aboveboard here, you know. We want to haul this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody—so there’s nothing suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

{"request_id":"910885f01ac1f34b967b15b2","rewritten_text":"They passed silent brickfields. The fog thinned a little, and he could see the odd, bottle-shaped kilns with orange tongues of flame fanning out. A dog barked as they went by, and somewhere far off in the dark a stray sea gull screamed. The horse stumbled in a rut, veered aside, and broke into a gallop.

After a while they left the clay road and rattled once more over rough-paved streets. Most windows were dark, but now and then bizarre silhouettes appeared against a lit blind. He watched them with curiosity. They moved like grotesque marionettes and gestured like living things. He loathed them. A dull fury filled his heart. As they turned a corner, a woman shouted something at them from an open door, and two men chased the hansom for about a hundred yards. The driver lashed at them with his whip.

People say passion makes thought run in circles. Certainly, with an awful repetition, Dorian Gray’s bitten lips shaped and reshaped those subtle sentences about soul and sense, until he found in them the complete expression of his mood and, by intellectual approval, justified passions that even without such justification would still have ruled him. From cell to cell of his brain crept the same thought, and the fierce desire to live, the most terrible of all human hungers, sharpened every trembling nerve and fiber. Ugliness, once hateful to him because it made things real, became precious to him now for that very reason. Ugliness was the only reality. The coarse fight, the filth-stained den, the raw violence of chaotic life, the sheer vileness of thief and outcast were more vivid, with their intense immediacy, than all the graceful forms of art, the dreamy shadows of song. They were what he needed for oblivion. In three days he would be free.

Suddenly the driver jerked the carriage to a stop at the top of a dark lane. Over the low roofs and jagged chimney stacks of the houses rose black ship masts. Wreaths of white mist clung to the yards like ghostly sails.

“Somewhere around here, sir, isn’t it?” he asked hoarsely through the trap.

Dorian jolted, looked around, and replied, “This will do.” He jumped out, thrust the driver the extra fare he had promised, and hurried toward the quay. Here and there a lantern glowed at the stern of a huge merchantman. Its light quivered and fractured in the puddles. A red glare spilled from an outbound steamer taking on coal. The slimy pavement gleamed like a soaked raincoat."}

{"request_id":"7a5d2d19cd333023f2af3a50","rewritten_text":"I met the curious stranger I am going to describe while touring Warwick Castle. Three things drew me to him: his open simplicity, his astonishing knowledge of old armor, and the peaceful ease of his company—since he did all the talking. We fell together, as quiet people do, at the back of the guided group, and he immediately began saying things that caught my interest. As he spoke, soft and pleasant and smooth, it was as if he slipped out of this world and into some far-off era, some forgotten country, and he cast such a spell that I seemed to walk among ghosts and shadows and dust and mold of gray antiquity, conversing with a relic of it. He talked of Sir Bedivere, Sir Bors de Ganis, Sir Launcelot of the Lake, Sir Galahad, and the rest of the Round Table exactly as I would talk about my closest friends or enemies or neighbors—and he grew so old, so incredibly old and faded and dry and musty, as he went on. Suddenly he turned to me and said, as calmly as if mentioning the weather or any common topic—

“You know about transmigration of souls; do you know about changing epochs—and bodies?”

I said I had not heard of it. He was so uninterested—like people mentioning the weather—that he did not notice whether I answered or not. There was half a moment of silence, broken by the droning voice of the paid guide:

“Ancient hauberk, sixth century, time of King Arthur and the Round Table; said to have belonged to the knight Sir Sagramor le Desirous; note the round hole through the chain mail in the left breast; can’t explain it; supposed to have been made by a bullet since firearms were invented—perhaps maliciously by Cromwell’s soldiers.”

My acquaintance smiled—not a modern smile, but one that must have vanished from use many centuries ago—and muttered to himself:

“Know you well, I saw it done.” Then, after a pause, added: “I did it myself.”

By the time I recovered from the electric shock of that remark, he had disappeared.

All that evening I sat by my fire at the Warwick Arms, lost in a dream of the old days, while rain beat on the windows and wind roared along the eaves and corners. From time to time I dipped into old Sir Thomas Malory’s enchanting book, fed on its rich feast of wonders and adventures, breathed in the scent of its obsolete names, and dreamed again."}

content.text: {"request_id":"1497a79613e765c9eb9bf00f","rewritten_text":"The ringmaster made a short speech, saying he hoped there wouldn’t be any trouble, and if the man promised to behave he’d let him ride, provided he thought he could stay on the horse. Everyone laughed and agreed, and the man climbed aboard. The instant he was up there, the horse started ripping and tearing, jumping and cavorting while two circus workers clung to its bridle trying to hold it, the drunk man clung to its neck, his heels flying with every leap, and the crowd stood cheering and laughing until the tears ran down their faces. Finally, despite all the circus men’s efforts, the horse broke free and tore around the ring like lightning, that drunk lying flat on him and gripping his neck, first one leg dangling almost to the ground on one side, then the other leg hanging low on the other side, the crowd going absolutely wild. It wasn’t funny to me; I trembled at how close he was to disaster. But soon he managed to sit astride and seize the bridle, lurching this way and that; the next moment he sprang upright, let go of the bridle, and stood there—while the horse ran like a house on fire. He simply stood there, sailing around as easy and steady as if he had never been drunk at all—and then he started peeling off his clothes and flinging them away. He shed them so thick they practically clogged the air, seventeen outfits in all. Then there he was, slim and handsome, dressed in the flashiest, prettiest costume you ever saw, and he laid into that horse with his whip, making it fairly hum—then finally skipped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing room while everyone howled with delight and astonishment.\n\nThen the ringmaster realized how he’d been fooled, and I swear he was the sickest-looking ringmaster you ever saw. Turns out the rider was one of his own men! The fellow had dreamed up the trick all by himself and hadn’t told a soul. I felt foolish enough letting myself get taken in, but I sure wouldn’t have traded places with that ringmaster for a thousand dollars. Maybe there are better circuses than that one, but I haven’t found them yet. Anyway, it was plenty good enough for me, and whenever I run across it, it can have all my business every time."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c3281a6f95233abfd60f4ed9","rewritten_text":"Smallpox! I rushed to the king and whispered in his ear, “Out the door this instant, sire! The woman is dying of the disease that ravaged Camelot two years ago.” He did not move. “Truly I will stay—and lend aid.” I whispered again, “King, you must not. You have to go.” “You mean well, and your words are not unwise. But it would be a disgrace for a king to show fear, and a shame for a knight to hold back his hand when someone needs help. Peace, I will not go. You must go. The Church’s ban spares me but forbids you to be here, and she will deal harshly with you if word reaches her of your trespass.” His position was perilous and might cost him his life, yet arguing was useless. If his knightly honor was engaged, that ended the matter; he would stay no matter what, and I knew it. So I let it go. The woman spoke: “Good sir, in your kindness will you climb the ladder there and tell me what you find? Do not fear to speak plainly, for there are times when even a mother’s heart cannot break any further—having already broken.” “Wait,” said the king, “and give the woman food. I will go.” He set down the knapsack. I turned to head out, but he had already moved. He paused, looking down at a man lying in dim light who had not yet noticed us or spoken. “Is this your husband?” the king asked. “Yes.” “Is he sleeping?” “God be thanked for that mercy, yes—these three hours. Where can I pay the full price of my gratitude, for my heart is overflowing with it for this sleep he sleeps now.” I said, “We will be careful. We will not wake him.” “Ah no, you won’t, for he is dead.” “Dead?” “Yes, and it is a triumph to know it! No one can hurt him or insult him any longer. He is in heaven now and happy—or if not there, then he remains in hell and is content, for there he will find neither abbot nor bishop. We were children together; we have been man and wife these five and twenty years and never apart until today. Think how long that is to love and suffer side by side. This morning he lost his senses, and in his imagining we were boy and girl again wandering through joyful fields; he kept wandering, lightheartedly chatting, and entered those other fields we know nothing of, shut away from mortal sight.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1e68e55c99b501f7975da040","rewritten_text":"Poor Jack was later killed in a duel with Lord Canterville on Wandsworth Common, and Lady Barbara succumbed to a broken heart at Tunbridge Wells before the year ended, so in every respect it had been a tremendous triumph. It was, nonetheless, an exceedingly intricate disguise—if one may use such stage jargon for a mystery among the higher-natural world—and required him a full three hours to ready himself. At last all was in order, and he took great pride in his appearance. The heavy leather riding-boots belonging to the costume were a trifle too big for him, and only one of the pair of horse-pistols could be found, yet overall he was content, and at a quarter past one he slipped out of the wainscot and stole down the corridor. Reaching the chamber occupied by the twins—called the Blue Bed Chamber owing to its blue hangings—he noticed the door slightly open. Desiring a dramatic entrance, he flung it wide, whereupon a hefty jug of water crashed down on him, drenching him through and narrowly missing his left shoulder. At the same instant, he heard muffled peals of laughter coming from the four-poster. The shock to his nerves proved so strong that he bolted back to his own room at top speed, and by the following day he was confined to bed with a violent cold. His sole consolation in the whole misadventure was that he had not taken his head with him, for had he done so the outcome might have been extremely grave.\n\nHe now abandoned the hope of frightening this insolent American clan, and as a rule contented himself with padding through the halls in felt slippers, a thick red muffler round his throat against the draughts, and a small arquebuse in case the twins attacked. The final insult reached him on the nineteenth of September. He had descended to the great entrance hall, convinced he would be safe there, and passed the time by making sardonic comments about the large Saroni photographs of the United States Minister and his wife, which had replaced the Canterville portraits. He wore only a simple long shroud sprinkled with churchyard mould, had bound his jaw with a strip of yellow linen, and carried a small lantern along with a sexton’s spade."}

{"request_id":"d7c0b2a3ba4ddc1e812f73bc","rewritten_text":"These memories weighed on Felix’s heart and made him the most miserable of his family when I first saw him. He could have endured poverty, and as long as it was the price of his virtue he even took pride in it, but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of his beloved Safie were bitter wounds he could not heal. The Arabian’s arrival now brought new life to him.

When word spread in Leghorn that Felix had lost his wealth and status, the merchant ordered his daughter to forget her lover and prepare to return to her homeland. Safie’s generous spirit was angered by this command. She tried to reason with her father, but he stalked away, repeating his harsh order.

A few days later, the Turk hurried into his daughter’s room and told her he had reason to believe his stay in Leghorn had been exposed and that the French government would soon seize him. He had therefore hired a ship to take him to Constantinople and would sail in a few hours. He planned to leave his daughter with a trusted servant, who would follow later with most of his wealth, which had not yet arrived in Leghorn.

Once alone, Safie considered her next steps in this emergency. Living in Turkey repelled her; both her religion and her feelings turned her against it. Some papers of her father’s, which fell into her hands, told her of her lover’s exile and the name of his current refuge. She hesitated for some time, but finally made her decision. Taking a few of her own jewels and some money, she left Italy with an attendant, a native of Leghorn who spoke the common language of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

She reached a town about twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage without trouble, but there her attendant fell gravely ill. Safie nursed her with devoted care, yet the poor woman died, leaving Safie alone, unable to speak the language of the country and completely ignorant of the world’s ways. Even so, she found help. The Italian had given the name of their destination, and after her death the mistress of the house where they had stayed made sure Safie reached her lover’s cottage safely."}

content.text: {"request_id":"8dd7f1d30a651cfa22892baf","rewritten_text":"“Certainly not,” said Duff. “And in order that the ladies may understand the expression yokel, I presume you mean the offender wasn’t a rustic?” Mr. Losberne asked, smiling. “You’ve got it, sir,” answered Blathers. “We’re dealing with the burglary, aren’t we?” “Nothing else,” replied the doctor. “Well then, what’s the story about this boy the servants keep whispering about?” Blathers asked. “It’s nothing,” said the doctor. “One of the scared maids insisted he had a hand in trying to break in; but it’s nonsense—pure absurdity.” “Easily disposed of, if that’s the case,” Duff remarked. “He’s right,” said Blathers, nodding and clicking the handcuffs as though they were castanets. “Who is the boy? What’s his account? Where did he drop in from? He didn’t fall out of the sky, did he, sir?” “of course not,” replied the doctor, sending a nervous look toward the two ladies. “I know his entire story; but we can discuss it later. You’d like to view the spot where the thieves tried to force an entrance first, I suppose?” “Naturally,” replied Mr. Blathers. “Let’s examine the premises before questioning the servants. That’s the proper order of things.” They fetched lights; and Messrs. Blathers and Duff, along with the local constable, Brittles, Giles, and everyone else, went to the little room at the hallway’s end to look out the window; then they went around over the lawn to peer in at the same window; then had a candle passed out to inspect the shutter; then a lantern to trace the footprints; and after that a pitchfork for searching the bushes. This done, amid the absorbed attention of every onlooker, they returned inside, and Mr. Giles and Brittles reenacted their part in the previous night’s drama: repeating it some six times, disagreeing on no more than a single important point at first, and not more than a dozen by the last. Once this climax was reached, Blathers and Duff cleared the room and held so long and solemn a conference that even a consultation of eminent physicians on the most perplexing case imaginable would pale beside it. Meanwhile, the doctor paced the adjoining chamber in great agitation, while Mrs. Maylie and Rose watched with worried faces. “By my word,” he said, pausing after numerous quick strides, “I’m at a complete loss.”"}

{"request_id":"c4ef83ccf938f705c8cfc07e","rewritten_text":"The oaks around us were alive with a tribe of nightingales—there I am now. Idris, glowing with young life, stands at my side—remember, I am only twenty-two, and the beloved of my heart has barely seen seventeen summers. The river, swollen by autumn rains, flooded the low fields, and Adrian in his favorite boat amused himself with the dangerous game of snapping off the topmost branch of a submerged oak. Are you tired of life, Adrian, that you flirt with danger like this?—

He has won his prize, and now he steers his boat through the flood. Our eyes stayed anxiously on him, but the current carried him away from us; he had to land much farther down and make a wide circle before he could return. “He is safe!” said Idris when he sprang ashore and waved the bough over his head in triumph. “We will wait for him here.”

We were alone. The sun had set. The nightingales began their song. The evening star shone sharply in the lingering glow of light in the west. My angel’s blue eyes fixed on that sweet emblem of herself. “How the light pulses,” she said, “that is the star’s life. Its flickering shine seems to tell me its state, like ours on earth, is fragile and restless; it fears, I think, and it loves.”

“Do not gaze on the star, dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Do not read love in its trembling rays. Do not look to distant worlds or speak of the mere idea of a feeling. I have held my peace too long; so long I have been sick with the need to speak to you, to offer you my soul, my life, my whole existence. Do not look on the star, dear love—or do, and let that eternal spark speak for me. Let it be my witness and advocate, silent as it shines. Love is to me as light is to that star; as long as it is not destroyed into darkness, I will love you.”

That moment’s ecstasy must stay veiled forever from the world’s unfeeling gaze. Still I feel her graceful form against my overflowing heart; still my sight, pulse, and breath fail when I recall that first kiss. Slowly and quietly we walked to meet Adrian, whose footsteps we heard approaching.

I begged Adrian to return to me after he brought his sister home. That same evening, strolling along the moonlit forest paths, I poured out to my friend my whole heart—its joy and its hope. For a moment he seemed troubled. “I might have foreseen this,” he said. “What struggle will now arise!”"}

{"request_id":"d3c93c111753624f8e554ead","rewritten_text":"“I must point out, Sir Walter,” Mr Shepherd said one morning at Kellynch Hall as he set down the newspaper, “that the current situation works in our favour. This peace is sending all our wealthy naval officers home. They will all want houses. There could not be a better time, Sir Walter, to have a selection of tenants, very reliable tenants. Many great fortunes have been made during the war. If a rich admiral crossed our path, Sir Walter—”

“He would be a very lucky man, Shepherd,” Sir Walter answered. “That is all I have to say. Kellynch Hall would be a prize for him, the greatest prize of all, no matter how many others he has taken before; wouldn’t it, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd laughed, as he knew he should at such wit, and continued—

“I would note, Sir Walter, that in business, naval gentlemen are easy to deal with. I have some experience with how they conduct business, and I must admit they have generous ideas and are as likely as any group to make good tenants. Therefore, Sir Walter, I suggest that if rumours start spreading about your intention—which we must consider possible, since we all know how hard it is to keep one half of the world from learning what the other half is doing, and fame must pay its price—I, John Shepherd, might hide any family matters I wished, for no one would think it worth watching me; but Sir Walter Elliot has too many eyes upon him to escape notice. So I will say this much: I will not be surprised if, despite our caution, some rumour of the truth leaks out. Assuming it does, as I was about to say, and applications inevitably follow, I think those from our wealthy naval commanders would be especially worth considering. I also beg leave to add that I can be here within two hours at any time, so you need not trouble yourself with replies.”

Sir Walter only nodded. But soon afterward, rising and pacing the room, he said with sarcasm—

“There are few gentlemen of the navy, I imagine, who would not find themselves astonished to be living in such a house.”

“They would look around, certainly, and bless their good luck,” said Mrs Clay, who was present. Her father had brought her over, as a drive to Kellynch was the best thing for her health. “But I entirely agree with my father in thinking a sailor could be a very suitable tenant.”"}

{"request_id":"efb7aa57a0e257277621e5c8","rewritten_text":"I call on you, spirits of the dead, and on you, wandering agents of vengeance, to help and guide me in my work. Let the cursed, hellish monster drink deeply of agony; let him feel the despair that now tortures me.

I began my plea with solemn awe, almost sure the shades of my murdered friends heard and approved my devotion, but fury seized me as I finished, and rage choked my voice.

A loud, fiendish laugh broke through the still night. It rang in my ears, echoed by the mountains, and I felt as if all hell surrounded me with mockery. In that moment I might have gone mad and ended my miserable life, but my vow was heard, and I was kept for vengeance. The laughter faded, and a voice I knew and hated, close to my ear, whispered clearly, “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have chosen to live, and I am satisfied.”

I rushed toward the source of the sound, but the devil slipped from my grasp. Suddenly the broad moon rose and shone on his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with more than human speed.

I chased him, and for months this has been my duty. With only the faintest clues, I followed the twists of the Rhone, but in vain. The blue Mediterranean came into view, and by strange luck I saw the fiend board a ship at night bound for the Black Sea. I took passage on the same vessel, yet he escaped; I know not how.

Through the wilds of Tartary and Russia, though he still evaded me, I kept to his trail. Sometimes the peasants, terrified by his hideous appearance, told me where he had gone; sometimes he himself, afraid I might lose his track, despair, and die, left signs to lead me. Snow fell on my head, and I saw the mark of his huge steps on the white plain. You who are just beginning life, who have yet to know care or agony, how can you grasp what I have felt and still feel? Cold, hunger, and exhaustion were the least of my pains; I was cursed by some devil and carried my eternal hell with me. Yet a spirit of good still followed me, directing my steps and, when I complained most, suddenly freeing me from seemingly impossible dangers. Sometimes, when hunger overcame me and nature gave way, a meal awaited me in the wilderness, restoring my strength and hope."}

{"request_id":"e087da4d92c0eb0863302a17","rewritten_text":"“Good heavens!” the Duchess thought, “he’s some kind of chiropodist after all. How dreadful. I do hope he’s at least foreign—it wouldn’t seem quite so bad then.”

“I absolutely must introduce him to you.”

“Introduce him!” cried the Duchess. “You don’t mean he’s here, do you?” She began searching for a small tortoiseshell fan and a very frayed lace shawl so she could leave at a moment’s notice.

“Of course he’s here; I’d never dream of throwing a party without him. He says I have a perfectly psychic hand, and that if my thumb were the slightest bit shorter I’d be a confirmed pessimist and would have gone into a convent.”

“Oh, I see,” said the Duchess, greatly relieved. “He reads fortunes, I suppose?”

“And misfortunes as well,” replied Lady Windermere. “Plenty of them. Next year I’m apparently in terrible danger on land and sea, so I’m going to live in a balloon and haul up my dinner in a basket every evening. It’s all written on my little finger, or the palm of my hand—I forget which.”

“But surely that’s tempting Providence, Gladys.”

“My dear Duchess, surely Providence can resist temptation by now. I think everyone should have their palms read once a month, just to know what not to do. Of course, you go ahead and do it anyway, but it’s such fun to be warned. If someone doesn’t fetch Mr. Podgers immediately, I shall have to go myself.”

“Allow me, Lady Windermere,” said a tall, handsome young man who had been listening with an amused smile.

“Thank you so much, Lord Arthur, but I’m afraid you wouldn’t recognize him.”

“If he’s as remarkable as you say, I can’t very well miss him. Describe him and I’ll bring him straight back.”

“Well, he’s not the least like a palm reader. I mean he isn’t mysterious or exotic or the least bit romantic-looking. He’s a small, stout man with a funny bald head and big gold-rimmed spectacles—something between a family doctor and a country solicitor. I’m truly sorry, but there’s nothing I can do. People are so exasperating. All my pianists look exactly like poets, and all my poets look exactly like pianists. I remember last season I invited a perfectly dreadful conspirator to dinner—a man who had blown up scores of people, always wore chain mail, and carried a dagger up his sleeve—and when he arrived he looked just like a pleasant old clergyman and spent the evening telling jokes.”"}

{"request_id":"157706416f5fc440782e8a82","rewritten_text":"But in that vicious tirade against Chantilly that ran in yesterday’s Musée, the satirist, tossing out some disgraceful digs about the cobbler changing his name when he took to the stage, quoted a Latin line we’ve often discussed. I mean the line: Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum.

“I told you it referred to Orion, which used to be written Urion, and because that explanation carried certain sharp hints, I knew you couldn’t have forgotten it. So it was obvious you wouldn’t fail to connect the ideas of Orion and Chantilly. I knew you made the connection from the kind of smile that crossed your lips. You thought of the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Up to then, you’d been walking with a stoop, but now I saw you straighten to your full height. Then I knew you were thinking about Chantilly’s small stature. At that point I broke into your thoughts to point out that since he was such a little fellow—that Chantilly—he’d be better suited to the Théâtre des Variétés.”

Not long after that, we were scanning an evening edition of the Gazette des Tribunaux when the following paragraphs caught our eye.

“Extraordinary Murders.—At about three o’clock this morning, the residents of the Quartier St. Roch were jolted from their sleep by a series of terrifying shrieks, apparently coming from the fourth floor of a house on the Rue Morgue, occupied solely by a Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. After a delay caused by failing to gain entry through the usual means, the gateway was smashed with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors entered with two gendarmes. By that time the screams had stopped; but as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, they heard two or more harsh voices arguing angrily, seeming to come from higher up. By the time they reached the second landing, these sounds had also ceased and everything was completely silent. The group spread out and hurried from room to room. When they reached a large back chamber on the fourth floor (the door was found locked with the key inside and had to be forced open), they were confronted with a scene that filled everyone present with horror as much as astonishment.

“The room was in total chaos—the furniture was smashed and scattered in every direction. There was only one bedstead, but the mattress had been removed and dumped in the middle of the floor. On a chair lay a razor, smeared with blood.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"01da9e4a37c4299a81eb52f7","rewritten_text":"He always pretended Peter told him what to write, but that was a lie; he pulled every last bit of it out of that young fool we paddled up to the steamboat. Mary Jane brought the letter her father had left, and the king read it aloud and cried over it. The letter left the house and three thousand dollars in gold to the girls, and it left the tanyard—which was doing good business—plus some other buildings and land worth about seven thousand, and three thousand dollars in gold to Harvey and William, and it told where six thousand in cash was hidden down in the cellar. So those two frauds said they’d go fetch it and make everything honest and aboveboard, and told me to come along with a candle. We shut the cellar door behind us, and when they found the bag they spilled it on the floor. It was a grand sight, all those gold pieces. My, how the king’s eyes shone! He slapped the duke on the shoulder and said: “Oh, this sure isn’t fine, not one bit! No, I reckon not! Why, Bilji, it beats the Nonesuch, doesn’t it?” The duke said it did. They pawed the gold pieces, sifted them through their fingers, and let them jingle down on the floor; and the king said: “No use arguing; being brothers to a rich dead man and speaking for foreign heirs who got left out—that’s the life for you and me, Bilge. This comes of trusting Providence. It’s the best way in the end. I’ve tried them all, and there’s no better way.” Most folks would have been satisfied with the pile and taken it on faith; but no, they had to count it. So they counted, and it came out four hundred and fifteen dollars short. The king said: “Blast him, I wonder what he did with that four hundred and fifteen dollars?” They fretted over it awhile and searched all around. Then the duke said: “Well, he was mighty sick, and likely he made a mistake—I figure that’s it. Best to let it go and keep quiet. We can spare it.” “Oh, sure, we can spare it. I don’t care about that—it’s the count that bothers me. We want to be mighty square and open and aboveboard here, you know. We need to carry this money upstairs and count it in front of everybody—then nothing looks suspicious. But when the dead man says there’s six thousand dollars, you know, we don’t want to—”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"8ef59e1944888aac6262e7f6","rewritten_text":"She left everything behind her, except the memory that it had ever been. Anne had not stepped inside Kellynch since she left Lady Russell’s house in September. There had been no need, and the few chances she had of going to the Hall she managed to avoid. Her first return was to take up her place again in the modern, elegant rooms of the Lodge, and to cheer its mistress. Lady Russell’s happiness at seeing her held a bit of worry. She knew who had been staying at Uppercross. Still, whether Anne truly looked a little fuller and fresher or Lady Russell only imagined it, Anne enjoyed the congratulations. She amused herself by linking them with her cousin’s silent admiration and by hoping she might enjoy a second spring of youth and beauty. Once they began talking, Anne quickly felt a shift in her own mind. The subjects that had filled her heart when she left Kellynch, that she thought dismissed and had had to hide among the Musgroves, now mattered less. Lately she had even lost sight of her father and sister and of Bath itself. Their concerns had been pushed below those of Uppercross. So when Lady Russell returned to their old hopes and fears, praising the house taken in Camden Place and regretting that Mrs. Clay still lived with them, Anne would have been ashamed for anyone to know how much more she was thinking of Lyme and Louisa Musgrove and all the people there. The home and friendship of the Harvilles and Captain Benwick interested her far more than her father’s house in Camden Place or her sister’s closeness with Mrs. Clay. She actually had to work to meet Lady Russell with even the appearance of equal concern for topics that should by nature be her first duty. Their talk on another matter began with a little unease. They had to speak about the accident at Lyme. Lady Russell had heard the whole account within five minutes of arriving the day before, yet there was still more to say: she had to ask, to regret the rashness, to mourn the outcome, and Captain Wentworth’s name had to pass both their lips. Anne felt she did not handle it as well as Lady Russell. She could not speak his name and look straight at Lady Russell until she decided to explain briefly what she believed about the attachment between him and Louisa."}

{"request_id":"c023a89e7ffb153765109966","rewritten_text":"Without warning Mr. Podgers released Lord Arthur’s right hand, caught the left instead, and stooped so close in his scrutiny that the gold rims of his spectacles seemed to graze the palm. For an instant his features froze into a pale mask of terror, but he promptly regained his composure and, glancing up at Lady Windermere with a strained smile, declared, ‘It is the hand of a delightful young gentleman.’

‘Of course it is!’ retorted Lady Windermere. ‘But will he make a delightful husband? That is what interests me.’

‘Every delightful young gentleman does,’ replied Mr. Podgers.

‘I am not sure a husband ought to be too fascinating,’ mused Lady Jedburgh softly; ‘it is frightfully risky.’

‘My dear child, they never are too fascinating,’ cried Lady Windermere. ‘But I require particulars. Particulars are the only things worth hearing. What lies ahead for Lord Arthur?’

‘Within the next few months Lord Arthur will take a voyage—’

‘Oh, certainly, his honeymoon, naturally!’

‘And he will lose a relative.’

‘Not his sister, I trust?’ said Lady Jedburgh anxiously.

‘Most assuredly not his sister,’ answered Mr. Podgers with a soothing gesture, ‘only a distant kinsman.’

‘I am miserably let down,’ exclaimed Lady Windermere. ‘I shall have nothing to tell Sybil tomorrow. No one bothers about distant relatives now. They went out of fashion ages ago. Still, she had better keep a black silk handy; it always suits for church. And now we should get to supper. They will have devoured everything, but we may secure some hot soup. François used to make splendid soup, but politics keep him so excited I never feel secure. I wish General Boulanger would behave himself. Duchess, surely you are worn out?’

‘Not in the least, dear Gladys,’ replied the Duchess, waddling toward the door. ‘I have had an enchanting evening, and the cheiropodist— I mean cheiromantist— is most absorbing. Flora, where is my tortoise-shell fan? Oh, thank you, Sir Thomas, so very much. And my lace shawl, Flora? Thank you again, Sir Thomas, exceedingly kind’; and the good soul contrived to reach the stairs without dropping her scent-bottle more than twice.

Meanwhile Lord Arthur Savile had stayed motionless by the fireplace, oppressed by the same nameless terror, the same nauseating foreboding. He gave his sister a melancholy smile as she swept by on Lord Plymdale’s arm, radiant in pink brocade and pearls, and scarcely registered Lady Windermere’s summons to follow. Sybil Merton filled his thoughts, and the notion that anything might divide them brought tears to his eyes."}

{"request_id":"7d29cc4f017bb7a9dbd86be6","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery horse, the same one that had carried him to victory in Greece. He wore himself out with exhausting exercise, trying to drown the torment of his mind in sheer physical effort.

Slowly he came back to himself. At last, as someone might recover from poison, he raised his head above the feverish haze of passion into the calm air of clear thought. He considered what he ought to do. He was shocked by how much time had passed while madness, not reason, had guided his actions. A month had gone by, and in all that time he had not seen Evadne. Her hold, once bound to the lasting feelings of his heart, had greatly weakened. He was no longer her slave, no longer her lover; he would never see her again, and by this complete return he would earn Perdita’s trust.

Yet when he tried to decide, his imagination summoned the miserable home of the Greek girl— the place she had chosen, from noble and upright motives, instead of a more comfortable one. He thought of her splendour when he first met her, of her life in Constantinople surrounded by every form of eastern luxury; then of her current poverty, her daily labour, her desolate loneliness, her thin face marked by hunger. Compassion rose within him. He would visit her once more; he would find some way to restore her to society and to the privileges of her rank. After that, their parting would come naturally.

Again he remembered how, during this long month, he had avoided Perdita, fleeing her as if she were the rebuke of his own conscience. But he was alert now. All this would be corrected, and future devotion would erase the memory of the single stain on their peaceful life. Thinking of this made him cheerful, and he carefully set out the course he would follow. He recalled promising Perdita that he would attend that very evening—the nineteenth of October, the anniversary of his election as Protector—a festival held in his honour. Let this celebration be a good omen for future happiness. First he would stop by Evadne. He would not stay long, but he owed her some explanation and compensation for his sudden absence. Then he would return to Perdita, to the world he had neglected, to social duties, to the splendour of rank, to the enjoyment of power.

After the events described earlier, Perdita had expected a complete change in Raymond’s behaviour and habits. She looked for open communication and a return to the affectionate companionship that had been the joy of her life."}

{"request_id":"94a552ae380c6add542505e5","rewritten_text":"Mr. Otis was quite upset by Lord Canterville’s refusal and urged him to reconsider, but the good-natured peer stood firm. He eventually persuaded the Minister to let his daughter keep the gift the ghost had given her, and when, in the spring of 1890, the young Duchess of Cheshire appeared at the Queen’s first drawing-room after her marriage, her jewels were the talk of everyone. Virginia received the coronet, which is the reward of all well-behaved little American girls, and married her sweetheart as soon as he came of age. They were both so charming and loved each other so dearly that everyone was delighted with the match, except for the old Marchioness of Dumbleton, who had tried to snare the Duke for one of her seven unmarried daughters and had thrown no fewer than three lavish dinner parties to that end, and, strangely enough, Mr. Otis himself. Mr. Otis liked the young Duke very much personally, but in principle he disapproved of titles and, as he said, “was not without fear that, amid the softening influences of a pleasure-loving aristocracy, the true ideals of republican simplicity might be forgotten.” His objections, however, were completely brushed aside, and I believe that when he walked up the aisle of St. George’s, Hanover Square, with his daughter on his arm, there was not a prouder man in all of England.

After their honeymoon, the Duke and Duchess went down to Canterville Chase, and the day after they arrived they took an afternoon walk to the lonely churchyard near the pine woods. There had been considerable debate at first about the inscription on Sir Simon’s tombstone, but it was finally decided to engrave only the old gentleman’s initials and the verse from the library window. The Duchess brought some lovely roses, which she scattered on the grave, and after they had stood there for a while they wandered into the ruined chancel of the old abbey. The Duchess sat down on a fallen pillar while her husband lay at her feet, smoking a cigarette and gazing up into her beautiful eyes. Suddenly he flicked away the cigarette, took her hand, and said, “Virginia, a wife shouldn’t keep secrets from her husband.”

“Dear Cecil! I have no secrets from you.”

“Yes, you do,” he replied with a smile. “You never told me what happened when you were shut up with the ghost.”

“I have never told anyone, Cecil,” Virginia said gravely."}

{"request_id":"7fdf9635db9eeed219faf4b0","rewritten_text":"This marriage is exactly right. I didn’t think so at first, but I admit it now. The gods made Sibyl Vane for you. Without her you would have been incomplete.”

“Thanks, Basil,” said Dorian Gray, squeezing his hand. “I knew you would understand me. Harry is so cynical that he frightens me. But here comes the orchestra. It’s dreadful, but it only lasts about five minutes. Then the curtain goes up, and you will see the girl to whom I plan to give my entire life, to whom I have already given everything good in me.”

Fifteen minutes later, amid an extraordinary roar of applause, Sibyl Vane stepped onstage. She was indeed lovely—one of the loveliest creatures Lord Henry thought he had ever seen. There was something of a fawn in her shy grace and startled eyes. A faint blush, like the shadow of a rose on silver glass, touched her cheeks as she looked at the packed, excited audience. She stepped back a few paces and her lips seemed to tremble. Basil Hallward jumped to his feet and began applauding. Dorian Gray sat motionless, as if in a dream, staring at her. Lord Henry peered through his glasses, murmuring, “Charming! Charming!”

The scene was the hall of the Capulet house, and Romeo, in his pilgrim’s costume, had entered with Mercutio and his other friends. The band, poor as it was, played a few bars of music, and the dance began. Through the crowd of clumsy, badly dressed actors, Sibyl Vane moved like someone from a finer world. Her body swayed as she danced, like a plant swaying in water. The curve of her throat was like that of a white lily. Her hands seemed carved from cool ivory.

Yet she seemed strangely dull. She showed no joy when her eyes met Romeo’s. The few lines she had to speak—

Good pilgrim, you do wrong your hand too much,
Which mannerly devotion shows in this;
For saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands do touch,
And palm to palm is holy palmers’ kiss—

along with the short dialogue that follows, were spoken in a completely artificial way. Her voice was exquisite, but the tone was entirely wrong. It lacked the right colour. It drained all life from the verse. It made the passion feel unreal.

Dorian Gray grew pale as he watched her, puzzled and worried. Neither of his friends dared say anything to him. To them she seemed utterly incompetent."}

content.text: {"request_id":"cb9ff3541be5411cdaef10e9","rewritten_text":"He did not say a word about it while their guest stayed, but as soon as he had left for the night, he turned to his daughter. “Jane, congratulations. You are going to be a very happy woman.” Jane went straight to him, kissed him, and thanked him for his kindness. “You are a good girl,” he said, “and I am delighted to think you’ll be so well settled. I have no doubt you will suit each other. Your temperaments are so alike that nothing will ever be decided; you are so easygoing that every servant will cheat you; and so generous that you will always spend more than you have.” “I hope not. Carelessness about money would be inexcusable in me.” “Spend more than you have! My dear Mr. Bennet,” exclaimed his wife, “what nonsense are you talking? He has four or five thousand a year, maybe more.” Turning to her daughter, she went on, “Oh, my dear, dear Jane, I am so happy! I’m sure I won’t sleep a wink tonight. I knew it would happen. I always said it would, eventually. I was sure you could not be so beautiful for nothing! I remember, the moment I saw him when he first came to Hertfordshire last year, thinking how likely it was you’d end up together. Oh, he’s the most handsome young man ever seen!” Wickham and Lydia were forgotten. Jane was by far her favorite child; just then she cared for no one else. Her younger sisters soon began currying favor, hoping she might one day grant them whatever pleasures she could share. Mary begged to use the library at Netherfield, and Kitty pleaded for a few dances there every winter. From then on Bingley was naturally at Longbourn every day; he often arrived before breakfast and stayed past supper—unless some barbarous neighbor, who could never be detested enough, had invited him to dinner and he felt obliged to go. Elizabeth now had little chance to talk with her sister, for Jane had no attention to spare while he was around. But she found herself quite useful to both of them in those necessary intervals of separation. When Jane was absent, he always sought out Elizabeth so he could enjoy talking about her; and when Bingley was away, Jane always looked to Elizabeth for the same comfort. “He made me so happy,” she said one evening, “by telling me he had no idea I was in town last spring!”"}

{"request_id":"8b8ace8513c658deebb84ac0","rewritten_text":"Should I ask them? Or Miss Bates? She’s even closer—and I’m not sure she isn’t as likely as anyone to guess what everyone else wants. I think we need a larger council. How about I go invite Miss Bates to join us?”

“Well—if you like,” said Mrs. Weston, a little unsure. “If you think she can help.”

“You’ll get nothing useful from Miss Bates,” said Emma. “She’ll be full of delight and gratitude, but she won’t tell you anything. She won’t even hear your questions. I see no point in consulting Miss Bates.”

“But she’s so amusing, so very amusing! I love listening to Miss Bates talk. And I don’t have to bring the whole family, you know.”

Mr. Weston joined them, and when he heard the plan, he approved immediately.

“Yes, do, Frank—go get Miss Bates, and let’s settle this at once. She’ll enjoy the idea, I’m sure, and I can’t think of anyone better at removing obstacles. Go fetch Miss Bates. We’re getting too particular. She’s a constant lesson in how to be cheerful. But bring both of them. Invite them both.”

“Both, sir! Can the old lady…”

“The old lady! No, the young lady, of course. I’ll think you a fool, Frank, if you bring the aunt without the niece.”

“Oh! I’m sorry, sir. I didn’t immediately remember. Naturally, if you wish it, I’ll try to persuade them both.” And off he ran.

Long before he came back with the short, neat, quick-moving aunt and her graceful niece, Mrs. Weston—being sweet-tempered and a good wife—had already gone over the passage again and found the problems far less serious than she had first thought, really quite minor; and thus the dilemma ended. Everything else, at least in theory, went smoothly. All the small details of tables and chairs, lights and music, tea and supper arranged themselves or were left as trifles for Mrs. Weston and Mrs. Stokes to settle any time. Everyone invited was certainly coming; Frank had already written to Enscombe to request staying a few days past his fortnight, which could not possibly be refused. And it was bound to be a delightful dance.

When Miss Bates arrived, she enthusiastically agreed that it must be. They did not need her as an adviser, but as an enthusiastic supporter (a much safer role) she was truly welcome. Her approval, both broad and detailed, warm and constant, couldn’t fail to please; and for another half hour they walked back and forth through the different rooms, some offering ideas, some following along, all happily enjoying their future plans."}

content.text: {"request_id":"33b8feba3deb6737fea1519f","rewritten_text":"I have no way of knowing how long I remained like that. It must have been quite a while, though, because when I partly regained awareness, dawn was breaking, the balloon was soaring at a tremendous height over a vast emptiness of ocean, and nowhere within the enormous horizon was there even the slightest hint of land. Still, my feelings as consciousness returned were not nearly as full of agony as one might expect. There was, in fact, a touch of budding madness in the calm way I started to survey my situation. I held each of my hands up to my eyes, one after the other, and wondered what could have caused the swollen veins and the dreadful blackness of my fingernails. Then I carefully examined my head, shaking it again and again and feeling it with painstaking attention, until I finally convinced myself it was not, as I had half suspected, actually larger than my balloon. Next, with an air of expertise, I patted both of my breeches pockets, and, finding that a notebook and a toothpick case were missing, tried to figure out what had become of them. Unable to do so, I felt indescribably vexed. It then struck me that the joint of my left ankle was causing considerable discomfort, and a dim awareness of my predicament began to glow in my mind. But, strangely enough, I felt neither shock nor terror. If I felt anything at all, it was a sort of sly delight at the ingenuity I was about to display in getting myself out of this fix; and I never once considered my ultimate survival to be in any real doubt. For several minutes I sat immersed in the deepest thought. I clearly remember repeatedly pressing my lips together, touching my forefinger to the side of my nose, and making all those gestures and grimaces common to men who, comfortably seated in their armchairs, ponder matters of complexity or consequence. Believing I had now gathered my thoughts sufficiently, I carefully and deliberately put my hands behind my back and unhooked the large iron buckle attached to the waistband of my trousers. The buckle had three prongs which, being rather rusty, turned with great difficulty on their pivots. After considerable effort, I managed to bring them to a right angle with the body of the buckle and was pleased to find they stayed firmly in that position. Holding the improvised tool between my teeth, I began to untie the knot of my cravat. I had to pause to rest several times before I could finish this maneuver, but, eventually, it was done."}
