{"request_id":"4b9222f45c2b648adec69699","rewritten_text":"Sydney Carton paused in the street, still uncertain of his direction. “At Tellson’s banking-house at nine,” he murmured, his expression pensive. “Shall I show myself meanwhile? I believe so. These people ought to know that I am here; it’s a sensible precaution, perhaps even an essential preparation. But caution, caution, caution! Let me deliberate!”

Checking the steps that had begun to veer toward a destination, he paced the already dim street once or twice more, tracing the course of his thoughts to their possible outcomes. His first idea stood firm. “It is best,” he said, suddenly determined, “that these people should know there is such a man as I here.” Then he turned his face toward Saint Antoine.

That day Defarge had described himself as the keeper of a wine-shop in the Saint Antoine quarter. For someone well acquainted with the city, locating his house without inquiry was not difficult. After finding the place, Carton emerged from those narrower streets again, dined at a small eating-house, and after dinner fell fast asleep. For the first time in years, he abstained from strong drink. Since the previous night he had taken only a little thin wine; and the night before he had poured the brandy slowly onto Mr. Lorry’s hearth like a man finished with it.

It was as late as seven when he awoke refreshed and ventured into the streets again. On his way to Saint Antoine, he paused before a shop window containing a mirror to slightly tidy the loose knot of his cravat, his coat collar, and his unkempt hair. That done, he headed straight to Defarge’s and went inside.

Only Jacques Three, with his twitching fingers and hoarse voice, stood there as a customer. This man, whom he had seen on the Jury, sipped at the little counter while conversing with Monsieur and Madame Defarge. The Vengeance joined the talk as if she were a regular fixture of the place.

When Carton entered, sat down, and requested (in very indifferent French) a small measure of wine, Madame Defarge gave him a casual look, then a sharper one, sharper again, and finally stepped up to him to ask what he had ordered.

He repeated his request.

“English?” inquired Madame Defarge, inquisitively lifting her dark brows.

After gazing at her, as if even a single French word came slow to him, he responded in the same strong foreign accent."}

{"request_id":"3b0bbd108e414cb88f5241fe","rewritten_text":"His expression was relentlessly determined, and “that cursed bug” were the only words he let slip during the whole trip. I was responsible for a pair of dark lanterns, while Legrand contented himself with the scarab, which he had tied to the tip of a whipcord; he swung it back and forth as he walked, like a magician showing off a trick. When I noticed this latest, obvious sign of my friend’s mental unhinging, I could hardly hold back tears. Still, I decided it was wiser to indulge his obsession, at least for now, until I could try some more forceful tactic with a chance of success. In the meantime I tried, unsuccessfully, to probe him about the purpose of the expedition. Having persuaded me to come with him, he seemed unwilling to discuss any matter of lesser importance, and to all my questions he returned nothing but “we’ll see!”

We crossed the creek at the head of the island in a skiff and, climbing the bluffs on the mainland shore, headed northwest through terrain ferociously wild and barren, where not the slightest sign of a human footprint appeared. Legrand marched in front with firm confidence, pausing only for a moment here and there to note what seemed to be landmarks of his own devising on some earlier visit.

We traveled this way for roughly two hours, and the sun was just setting when we entered a region far more desolate than anything we had yet encountered. It was a kind of plateau near the summit of an almost unscalable hill, thickly forested from the base to the crest, and punctuated by huge boulders that looked as if they were resting loosely on the earth, in many cases prevented from tumbling into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines, branching in every direction, lent the scene an even sterner, more solemn air.

The natural platform we had climbed was choked with brambles, through which we quickly realized we would never have forced a way without a scythe; and Jupiter, at his master’s order, began cutting a path for us to the base of an extraordinarily tall tulip tree. It stood on the level ground with eight or ten oaks, towering over them all—and over every other tree I had ever seen—in the grace of its foliage and shape, the vast spread of its branches, and the general majesty of its bearing."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c8157ef4408685c08bbf7cf3","rewritten_text":"April 7. I rose early and, to my great joy, finally saw what I could only conclude with certainty was the North Pole itself. It was there without question, directly beneath my feet; but sadly I had risen to such an immense height that nothing could be observed with precision. Judging by the sequence of numbers recording my various altitudes at different times between six in the morning on April 2 and twenty minutes before nine on the same day (when the barometer dropped), it could be fairly assumed that by four in the morning on April 7 the balloon had reached an altitude certainly no less than 7,254 miles above sea level. This height may seem enormous, yet the calculation producing it probably fell well short of the truth. In any case, I clearly saw the entire major diameter of the earth; the whole northern hemisphere lay beneath me like an orthographic chart, and the equator itself marked the horizon’s edge. Still, you can easily imagine that the narrow regions of the Arctic circle, though directly below and therefore appearing without foreshortening, were too small and too far from my viewpoint for any very precise examination. Even so, what I could see was strange and exciting. Northward from that massive rim previously described, which with slight qualification may be called the limit of human discovery in these parts, stretched one continuous—or nearly continuous—sheet of ice. In its early degrees its surface visibly flattened, farther on it settled into a plane, and eventually, becoming distinctly concave, it ended at the Pole itself in a sharply defined circular center whose apparent diameter from the balloon formed an angle of about sixty-five seconds. Its dark color, shifting in intensity, was always deeper than any other point on the visible hemisphere and sometimes sank into absolute, impenetrable blackness. Beyond this little could be determined. By noon the circular center had greatly shrunk, and by seven in the evening it disappeared completely; the balloon passed over the western edge of the ice and drifted swiftly toward the equator.\n\nApril 8. I noted a perceptible decrease in the earth’s apparent diameter, along with a significant change in its overall color and appearance."}

content.text: {"request_id":"a22bea607009d547ae9bd1af","rewritten_text":"Lacking his usual tools, the analyst throws himself into his opponent’s mindset, sees through that lens, and often spots at once the only ways—sometimes surprisingly simple—to mislead him into error or rush him into miscalculation. Whist has long been known for sharpening what people call the calculating power, and men of the highest intellect have often found a mysterious pleasure in it while dismissing chess as trivial. Nothing else so similar demands such analysis. The best chess player in Christendom might be little more than that, but real skill in whist shows a mind fit for the more important struggles where minds clash. By proficiency, I mean mastery of the game that understands every source from which legitimate advantage can spring. These sources are many and varied, often hidden in parts of thought that ordinary minds cannot reach. Careful observation leads to precise memory, so a focused chess player will do fairly well at whist, and Hoyle’s rules, based on the mechanics of the game, are clear enough. Having a good memory and playing “by the book” are usually considered the sum of good play. Yet the analyst’s skill shows itself beyond mere rule-following. He silently makes countless observations and deductions. His companions may do so too, but the difference lies less in the logic of their conclusions than in what they observe. The key is knowing what to notice. Our player limits himself in nothing; even though the game is the point, he does not ignore clues from outside the game. He studies his partner’s face, comparing it with each opponent’s. He watches how each hand arranges its cards, often counting trump after trump and honor after honor through the glances of their holders. He tracks every change of expression as the game advances, building a store of insight from looks of certainty, surprise, triumph, or disappointment. From the way someone gathers a trick he judges whether that player can win another in the same suit. He recognizes feints by the way a card is laid down. A careless word, an accidentally dropped or turned card, and the owner’s anxiety or ease about hiding it; the counting of tricks and how they are stacked; every sign of embarrassment, hesitation, eagerness, or nervousness—all feed his seemingly intuitive sense of the real situation."}

content.text: {"request_id":"df41834ef90c082e757eaf7d","rewritten_text":"“Oh, I got you wrong. I thought you said ‘anybody,’ and so I assumed ‘anybody’ included—well, anybody; meaning everybody.” “It does—anybody of high birth; and better still if he’s royal.” “That, it seems to me, might well be,” said the abbot, seizing his chance to smooth things over and head off disaster. “It’s unlikely that so marvelous a gift would be granted for revealing the affairs of lesser folk than those born near the heights of greatness. Our Arthur the king—” “Do you wish to know of him?” the enchanter cut in. “Most gladly, yes, and gratefully.” Instantly everyone was full of awe and interest again, the incorrigible fools. They watched the spells being cast with rapt attention and looked at me with a “There now, what do you say to that?” expression when the announcement came: “The king is weary from the hunt, and has been lying in his palace these two hours, sleeping a dreamless sleep.” “God’s blessing on him!” said the abbot, crossing himself. “May that sleep refresh his body and soul.” “And so it might, if he were sleeping,” I said, “but the king isn’t sleeping; the king is riding.” Trouble again—a clash of authority. No one knew which of us to believe; I still had some reputation. The magician’s scorn was roused, and he said: “I have seen many wonderful soothsayers and prophets and magicians in my day, but never one who could sit idle and perceive the truth of things without so much as an incantation.” “You’ve lived in the woods and missed a lot by it. I use incantations myself, as this good brotherhood knows—but only on important occasions.” When it comes to sarcasm, I can hold my own. That barb made the fellow squirm. The abbot asked after the queen and the court and received this answer: “They’re all asleep, overcome by fatigue, just like the king.” I said, “That’s simply another lie. Half of them are busy with their entertainments; the queen and the other half aren’t sleeping—they’re out riding. Now maybe you can show off a little and tell us where the king and queen, and whoever’s riding with them right now, are heading?” “They sleep now, as I said; but tomorrow they will ride, for they’re going on a journey toward the sea.” “And where will they be the day after tomorrow at vespers?” “Far north of Camelot, with half their journey done.” “That’s another lie—off by a hundred and fifty miles.”"}

{"request_id":"c2e276923220e67f0ec1b5f8","rewritten_text":"The powerful voice—more elemental than mechanical, for we could not imagine pipes or keys producing it—fell silent, and the girl, turning to help her aged companion, finally noticed us.

It was her father, and since childhood she had guided his blinded steps. They were Germans from Saxony who had emigrated here only a few years earlier and forged new bonds with the surrounding villagers. Around the onset of the plague, a young German student had joined them. Their simple story was easy to guess: he, a nobleman, loved the beautiful daughter of the poor musician and followed them when his own friends persecuted him. But soon the great equalizer came with an undulled scythe, mowing down the tall flowers of the field along with the grass. The young man was among the first to fall. She preserved herself for her father’s sake. His blindness allowed her to maintain a deception that had begun by accident, and now, with no one else left alive, he remained unaware of what had happened. When he listened to his daughter’s music, the mute mountains, the senseless lake, and uncomprehending trees were, aside from him, her only audience.

On the very day we arrived she had been stricken with the plague’s symptoms. She was paralyzed with horror at the thought of leaving her aged, sightless father alone on this empty earth, yet she lacked the courage to tell him the truth. The intensity of her desperation drove her to extraordinary effort. At the usual hour of vespers she led him to the chapel, and, though trembling and weeping for his sake, she played—without a misplaced beat or wrong note—the hymn written to celebrate the creation of the adorned world, which was soon to become her tomb.

We appeared to her like messengers from heaven. The courage she had strained to sustain vanished at the sight of help. With a shriek she rushed toward us, threw her arms around Adrian’s knees, and, uttering only “Oh, save my father!” dissolved into sobs and hysterical cries, releasing the sorrow she had suppressed for so long.

Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the great walnut tree that shades her lover’s grave, the spot she indicated to us with her last breath. Her father, at last aware of her peril, could not see the changes in her beloved face, yet he stubbornly held her hand until it grew cold and rigid in death. Even then he neither moved nor spoke, until twelve hours later merciful death granted him endless rest. They sleep beneath the earth, the tree serving as their monument. I still see the sacred spot clearly in my mind, framed by craggy Jura and the far, immeasurable Alps. The spire of the church they once attended still rises from the sheltering trees, and though her hand is cold, I could swear the divine music they cherished still drifts through the air, comforting their tender spirits."}

He deliberately misheard the word she repeated and rushed on, “Yes, customers; in banking we usually call our clients our customers. He was a French gentleman, a scientific gentleman, a man of great accomplishments—a doctor.”

“Not from Beauvais?”

“Why, yes, from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, the gentleman came from Beauvais. Like Monsieur Manette, your father, he was well known in Paris. I had the honor of knowing him there. Our dealings were business, yet confidential. I was then in our French branch, and had been—oh! twenty years.”

“At that time—may I ask, when, sir?”

“I speak, miss, of twenty years ago. He married—an English lady—and I was one of the trustees. His affairs, like those of many French gentlemen and French families, were entirely in Tellson’s hands. In the same way I am, or have been, trustee of one kind or another for scores of our customers. These are purely business relations, miss; there is no friendship in them, no special interest, nothing sentimental. I have moved from one to another in the course of my business life, just as I move from one of our customers to another in the course of my business day; in short, I have no feelings; I am a mere machine. To go on—”

“But this is my father’s story, sir; and I am starting to believe”—the curiously roughened forehead focused on him—“that when I was left an orphan after my mother survived my father only two years, it was you who brought me to England. I am almost sure it was you.”

Mr. Lorry took the hesitant little hand that trustingly reached for his, raised it to his lips with some ceremony, then led the young lady straight back to her chair. Holding the chair-back with his left hand and using his right to rub his chin, tug his wig at the ears, or emphasize his words, he stood looking down into her face while she looked up at his.

“Miss Manette, it was I. And you will see how truthful I was just now, in saying I had no feelings and that all my dealings with others are mere business relations, when you realize that I have never seen you since. No; you have been in Tellson’s care since then, and I have been occupied with the other business of Tellson’s. Feelings! I have no time for them, no opportunity for them. I spend my whole life, miss, turning a vast financial mangle.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"864cdd726e5b05195a06a8cf","rewritten_text":"Master Charles Bates, horrified by Sikes’s crime, began to reflect on whether an honest life was best after all. Convinced that it was, he left his old haunts behind and decided to start fresh in some new kind of work. He struggled hard and suffered for a while, but with his cheerful nature and good intentions he eventually succeeded; from being a farmhand and a carrier’s boy, he has become the happiest young grazier in all Northamptonshire. The hand that writes these lines trembles as it nears the end of its task, wishing to spin out the story a little longer. I long to stay with a few of those with whom I have spent so much time, and share their happiness by trying to describe it. I would show Rose Maylie in all the bloom and grace of young womanhood, casting gentle light on her quiet path in life, which touched everyone who walked it with her and warmed their hearts. I would paint her as the life and joy of the fireside circle and the lively summer group; follow her through the hot fields at noon, and listen to the soft tones of her sweet voice during the moonlit evening walk; watch her kindness and charity abroad, and her calm, tireless care of household duties at home. I would depict her and her dead sister’s child happy in their love for each other, spending long hours together imagining the friends they had so sadly lost. I would call up again the bright little faces that clustered around her knee, and hear their cheerful chatter; I would bring back the sound of that clear laugh, and imagine again the sympathetic tear that shone in her gentle blue eye. These, along with countless looks and smiles, and thoughts and words—I would remember them all if I could. How Mr. Brownlow continued each day to fill his adopted child’s mind with knowledge, growing more attached to him as he saw the seeds of all he had hoped taking root—how he traced in him fresh traits of his old friend, awakening in himself memories that were sad yet sweet and comforting—how the two orphans, tested by hardship, kept its lessons in mercy to others, in mutual love, and in grateful thanks to Him who safeguarded and preserved them—these are things that need not be told."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7d8e7ff42c07b0dbe0340e03","rewritten_text":"The nephew glanced back at him without understanding as he went toward the door. “Good night!” said the uncle. “I look forward to seeing you again in the morning. Sleep well! Light Monsieur my nephew to his room there!—And burn Monsieur my nephew in his bed, if you wish,” he muttered to himself before he rang his small bell again and summoned his valet to his own chamber. When the valet had come and gone, Monsieur the Marquis paced in his loose robe to calm himself for sleep on that hot, still night. Moving around the room, his soft slippers made no sound on the floor; he glided like a refined tiger—like some enchanted marquis of the unrepentant wicked kind in stories, whose regular change into tiger form was either ending or beginning. He crossed his lush bedroom from end to end, thinking again of the scraps of that day’s journey that came uninvited into his mind: the slow climb up the hill at sunset, the setting sun itself, the descent, the mill, the prison perched on the crag, the small village in the hollow, the peasants by the fountain, and the mender of roads with his blue cap pointing out the chain under the carriage. That fountain brought to mind the Paris fountain, the little bundle lying on the step, the women bending over it, and the tall man with his arms raised, crying, “Dead!” “I am calm now,” said Monsieur the Marquis, “and can go to bed.” Leaving only one light burning on the wide hearth, he let his thin gauze curtains drop around him and heard the night break its silence with a long sigh as he settled to sleep. The stone faces on the outer walls stared blankly into the black night for three heavy hours; for three heavy hours the horses in the stable rattled their harness, the dogs barked, and the owl made a sound that little resembled the call that poets assign to owls. Yet such creatures are stubborn in rarely saying what is written for them. For three heavy hours the stone faces of the chateau, lion and human alike, stared blindly at the darkness. Dead blackness lay over the whole landscape, and dead blackness added its hush to the hushed dust on the roads. The burial ground was so far gone that its small heaps of poor grass could not be distinguished from one another; the figure on the Cross might have stepped down for all anyone could see. In the village, tax collectors and the taxed slept soundly. Perhaps they dreamed of feasts, as the starving usually do, and of ease and rest, as the driven slave and the yoked ox may, while its lean inhabitants slept deep, fed and freed in their dreams."}

{"request_id":"cc7aa1554941c50c582126e0","rewritten_text":"“Is that all? That isn’t much! Plenty are out of favor with the Republic and have to stare through the little window. Jarvis Lorry. Banker. English. Which one is he?”

“I’m he. Naturally, since I’m the last.”

It is Jarvis Lorry who has answered every previous question. Jarvis Lorry has climbed down and stands with his hand on the coach door, responding to a group of officials. They stroll around the carriage and slowly climb up to the box to inspect the small pile of luggage on the roof; the country people loitering nearby press closer to the doors and stare greedily inside. A mother holds out her little child’s short arm so it can touch the wife of an aristocrat who has gone to the Guillotine.

“Here are your papers, Jarvis Lorry, countersigned.”

“May we leave, citizen?”

“You may leave. Forward, my postilions! Safe travels!”

“I salute you, citizens.—And the first danger is behind us!”

Again, these words come from Jarvis Lorry, as he clasps his hands and looks up. There is terror in the carriage, there is weeping, there is the heavy breathing of the unconscious traveler.

“Aren’t we going too slowly? Can’t they be urged to go faster?” Lucie asks, clinging to the old man.

“It would look like fleeing, my darling. I mustn’t press them too hard; it would arouse suspicion.”

“Look back, look back, and see if we’re being chased!”

“The road is clear, my dearest. So far, no one is chasing us.”

Houses in pairs and trios pass by, solitary farms, crumbling buildings, dye works, tanneries, and the like, open fields, avenues of leafless trees. Hard, uneven pavement lies beneath us; soft, deep mud borders either side. Sometimes we veer into the bordering mud to avoid the stones that rattle and jolt us; sometimes we are stuck in ruts and bogs there. The pain of our impatience becomes so great that, in our frantic fear, we consider jumping out and running—hiding—doing anything but staying still.

Out of the open country and back again into crumbling buildings, solitary farms, dye works, tanneries, and the like, cottages in pairs and trios, avenues of leafless trees. Have these men tricked us and taken us back by another road? Isn’t this the same place twice over? Thank Heaven, no. A village. Look back, look back, and see if we’re being pursued! Quiet! The posting-house.

Leisurely, our four horses are taken out; leisurely, the coach sits in the small street, without horses and unlikely to move again; leisurely, the new horses appear one by one; leisurely, the new postilions follow, snapping and braiding the lashes of their whips; leisurely, the old postilions count their coins, make wrong totals, and reach unhappy conclusions."}

{"request_id":"376b4d49c4c4f117f8018bb7","rewritten_text":"Jane admitted she was somewhat surprised at the match, yet she spoke more of her genuine wish for their happiness than of her astonishment, and Elizabeth could not make her see it as unlikely. Kitty and Lydia did not envy Miss Lucas at all, since Mr. Collins was only a clergyman, and the matter interested them solely as news to share in Meryton.

Lady Lucas could not help feeling triumphant at having a daughter well married and took every chance to visit Longbourn and declare her happiness, even though Mrs. Bennet’s sour looks and unkind remarks should have chased happiness away.

Between Elizabeth and Charlotte there lay a restraint that kept them silent on the subject, and Elizabeth was convinced they could never again share real trust. Disappointed in Charlotte, she clung more tenderly to her sister, whose sense and sensitivity she believed unshakable, and for whose happiness she worried more each day, since Bingley had been gone a week and there was no word of his return.

Jane had quickly replied to Caroline’s letter and now counted the days until she could reasonably expect an answer. Mr. Collins’s promised letter of thanks arrived on Tuesday, addressed to their father and full of solemn gratitude that might have been expected after living with them for a year. With that duty done, he went on, in many rapturous phrases, about his joy in gaining the affection of their amiable neighbor, Miss Lucas. He then explained that he had so eagerly accepted their kind invitation to Longbourn solely to enjoy her company, and he hoped to return on Monday fortnight; for Lady Catherine, he added, so warmly approved his marriage that she wished it to take place at once, which he hoped would convince his dear Charlotte to set an early date and make him the happiest of men.

Mr. Collins’s return to Hertfordshire was no longer any pleasure to Mrs. Bennet. On the contrary, she was as ready as her husband to complain. It was most odd that he should come to Longbourn instead of Lucas Lodge; it was also highly inconvenient and extremely troublesome. She detested having visitors while her health was so uncertain, and lovers were, of all people, the most disagreeable."}

{"request_id":"99fe9216ddf5760eab126ccd","rewritten_text":"Saturday at noon I went to the well and watched for a bit. Merlin was still burning smoke powders, clawing at the air, and muttering gibberish just as hard as ever, though he looked pretty discouraged, since he hadn’t even managed to bring up a bead of sweat in that well yet. Finally I said, “How are things looking now, partner?”

“Behold, I am right now laboring with the most powerful enchantment known to the princes of the occult arts in the Eastern lands; if it fails me, nothing can help. Silence, until I finish.”

This time he raised a smoke that darkened the whole region and must have made trouble for the hermits, because the wind was blowing their way and it rolled down over their caves in a dense, billowing fog. He poured out torrents of speech to match and twisted his body and slashed the air with his hands in the most extraordinary way. After twenty minutes he dropped down panting, nearly exhausted. Then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, and behind them a crowd of pilgrims and two acres’ worth of foundlings, all drawn by the huge smoke and all in a fever of excitement. The abbot anxiously asked for results. Merlin said:

“If any labor of mortal power could break the spell binding these waters, the one I just tried would have done it. It has failed, which proves what I feared is true. The sign of this failure is that the most potent spirit known to the magicians of the East, whose name no one may utter and live, has set his spell on this well. No mortal breathes now, nor ever will, who can uncover the secret of that spell, and without that secret no one can break it. The water will never flow again, good Father. I have done all a man could. Allow me to go.”

Naturally this threw the abbot into quite a panic. He turned to me, the alarm plain on his face, and said, “You’ve heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all, then, not all! What part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has cast his spell on the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we are ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean, not certainly?”

“That’s it.”

“Therefore, you also mean that when he says none can break the spell—”

“Yes, when he says that, he’s not necessarily telling the truth. There are conditions under which an attempt to break it might have some chance—small, very small, but still a chance—of success.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"e98146eb4c031285c55c77b2","rewritten_text":"So the ring-master got up and made a little speech, saying he hoped there wouldn’t be any disturbance, and if the fellow would swear off causing any more trouble he could ride, provided he figured he could stay on the horse. Everyone laughed and agreed, and up the man climbed. No sooner was he seated than the horse began ripping and tearing and leaping and prancing, while two circus men clung to the bridle trying to keep him in hand, and the drunk clutched his neck, heels shooting sky-high with every bound, while the crowd rose up yelling and laughing till the tears streamed. At last, despite all the circus men’s efforts, the horse busted loose and tore off like all creation around the ring, with that lush lying flat on him and hugging his neck, one leg nearly scraping the ground on one side, then the other leg on the other side, the folks near beside themselves. It wasn’t a bit amusing to me; I shook all over watching his peril. But in a minute he fought his way astride again and caught the bridle, lurching this way and that; the next instant he sprang upright, dropped the bridle, and stood there, with the horse tearing along like a burning house. He simply stood there, floating around as calm and comfortable as if drink had never touched him—and then he commenced peeling off his clothes and flinging them about. He shed them so fast they near clogged the air, and altogether he shed seventeen suits. And there he stood at last, lean and handsome, dressed as gaudy and fine as you ever saw, and he laid into that horse with his whip till the beast fairly buzzed—and finally he hopped off, bowed, and danced away to the dressing-room, the crowd howling with delight and amazement.\n\nThen the ring-master realized how he had been duped, and he was the sickest ring-master you ever set eyes on, I’d bet. Why, the joker was one of his own men! He had dreamed up that whole trick himself and breathed not a word to anyone. I felt plenty foolish being fooled so, but I wouldn’t have stood in the ring-master’s boots for a thousand dollars. Maybe there are bigger circuses than that one, but I haven’t come across them yet. Anyhow, it suited me just fine; whenever I meet up with it again, it can count on getting all my trade every time."}

{"request_id":"9f5610ffd4176e2c5e269ec3","rewritten_text":"“Listen, then! You!” Monks replied. “When his father fell ill in Rome, his wife—my mother—went to join him. They had long been separated, but she left Paris and took me along—maybe to secure his property, for she didn’t care much for him, and he didn’t care for her. He never knew we were there, because his senses had failed. He slept on until the next day and then died. In his desk we found two papers, written the night his illness began, addressed to you”—he turned to Mr. Brownlow—“with a note saying they were not to be sent until after his death. One was a letter to Agnes; the other was a will.”

“What was in the letter?” asked Mr. Brownlow.

“The letter? A sheet covered again and again with lines—a confession full of remorse, begging God for help. He had tricked her with a story about some secret to be revealed one day that kept him from marrying her just then. She trusted him patiently until it was too late and she lost what could never be restored. She was only a few months from giving birth. He explained everything he had planned to do to hide her shame if he lived, and begged her, if he died, not to curse his memory or think the consequences of their sin would fall on her or their child. He said the guilt was all his. He reminded her of the day he gave her the little locket and the ring with her Christian name engraved on it, with a blank for the name he hoped one day to give her. He begged her to keep it and wear it over her heart as before. Then he rambled wildly, repeating the same words over and over, as if he had gone mad. I believe he had.”

“The will,” said Mr. Brownlow, while Oliver’s tears fell fast.

Monks kept silent.

“The will,” Mr. Brownlow continued for him, “was in the same tone as the letter. He wrote of the misery his wife had caused him, of the rebellious nature, vice, malice, and early wicked passions of you, his only son, who had been taught to hate him. He left you and your mother each an annuity of eight hundred pounds. The rest of his property he split into two equal shares—one for Agnes Fleming, and one for their child, if it were born alive and ever reached adulthood.”"}

{"request_id":"64f98984931267948eb176af","rewritten_text":"“But I must warn you in advance that I will tell Sybil everything. She is coming to lunch with me tomorrow to talk about bonnets, and if Mr. Podgers discovers you have a bad temper, or gout, or a wife living in Bayswater, I will certainly tell her all of it.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I am not afraid,” he replied. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Ah! I am a little sorry to hear you say that. The best foundation for marriage is mutual misunderstanding. No, I am not cynical at all; I simply have experience, which amounts to much the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is desperate to have his hand read. Don’t tell him he is engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that was in the Morning Post a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “please let Mr. Podgers stay here a little longer. He just told me I should go on the stage, and I am so interested.”

“If he told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I will certainly take him away. Come over at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, making a little moue as she rose from the sofa, “if I am not allowed to go on the stage, I must at least be in the audience.”

“Of course; we are all going to be in the audience,” said Lady Windermere. “And now, Mr. Podgers, be sure to tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my special favorites.”

But when Mr. Podgers saw Lord Arthur’s hand he turned oddly pale and stayed silent. A shiver seemed to go through him, and his great bushy eyebrows twitched in that irritating way they did when he was confused. Then huge beads of sweat broke out on his yellow forehead like poisonous dew, and his fat fingers grew cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur noticed these strange signs of agitation, and for the first time in his life he felt fear. His impulse was to flee the room, but he held himself back. It was better to know the worst, whatever it might be, than to stay in this horrible uncertainty.

“I am waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We are all waiting,” cried Lady Windermere in her quick, impatient way, but the chiromantist gave no answer.

“I believe Arthur is going on the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh, “and after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to say so.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"d47d62e455fa10f32bd64396","rewritten_text":"The little man’s body was even wider than it should have been, giving his whole figure a laughably round shape. His feet were entirely hidden, though now and then a hard, suspicious-looking object poked through a tear in the floor of the car—or rather, in the top of the hat. His hands were enormous. His hair was very gray and gathered into a queue down his back. His nose was unbelievably long, crooked, and inflamed; his eyes were large, bright, and sharp; his chin and cheeks, though wrinkled with age, were broad, puffy, and doubled; and there wasn’t the slightest sign of ears anywhere on his head. This strange little gentleman wore a loose sky-blue satin overcoat with tight matching breeches fastened at the knees with silver buckles. His waistcoat was made of some vivid yellow fabric; a white taffeta cap was perched jauntily on one side of his head; and to complete his outfit, a blood-red silk handkerchief wrapped his neck and draped stylishly across his chest in an enormous, fanciful bow.\n\nHaving descended, as I mentioned, to about a hundred feet above the ground, the little old gentleman was suddenly seized with a fit of fear and clearly had no desire to get any closer to solid earth. He therefore threw sand from a canvas bag—which he lifted with great effort—and instantly came to a halt. Then, in a rushed and flustered state, he reached into a side pocket of his overcoat and pulled out a large morocco pocketbook. He weighed it suspiciously in his hand, stared at it with astonishment, and seemed surprised by how heavy it was. At last he opened it, took out a massive letter sealed with red wax and carefully tied with red tape, and dropped it directly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to pick it up. But the aeronaut, still greatly disturbed and apparently having no further reason to linger in Rotterdam, began at that moment to make brisk preparations to leave; and since he had to unload some ballast in order to rise again, the half dozen bags he tossed out, one after another, without bothering to empty them, landed, every single one, squarely on the burgomaster’s back and rolled him over and over no fewer than twenty-one times, right in front of everyone in Rotterdam. Nevertheless, one cannot assume that the great Underduk let this impertinence from the little old man go unpunished."}

{"request_id":"165d811b8d0921639a6b44e0","rewritten_text":"These thoughts calmed me, and that afternoon I fell into a deep sleep, but the fever running through my blood kept peaceful dreams away. The horrible scene from the day before replayed endlessly before my eyes: the women fleeing, Felix raging as he tore me from his father’s feet. I woke drained, realized night had already fallen, and crept out of my hiding place in search of food.

Once my hunger was satisfied, I headed along the familiar path that led to the cottage. Everything there was quiet. I slipped back into my hut and waited silently for the time when the family usually rose. That time came and went; the sun climbed high, yet the cottagers never appeared. I shook with dread, afraid some terrible misfortune had occurred. The cottage interior was dark, and I heard no movement; I cannot describe the torture of that suspense.

Soon two countrymen passed by. They stopped near the cottage and began talking in animated gestures, but I could not understand their language, so different from that of my protectors. Shortly after, however, Felix arrived with another man. I was startled, knowing he had not left the cottage that morning, and I watched anxiously for some clue in their conversation to explain these strange events.

“Do you realize,” his companion said, “that you’ll have to pay three months’ rent and lose the harvest from your garden? I don’t want to take unfair advantage, so I beg you to take a few days to think about your decision.”

“It’s completely hopeless,” Felix replied. “We can never live in your cottage again. My father’s life is in grave danger because of the dreadful event I told you about. My wife and sister will never recover from their terror. Please don’t argue with me. Take back your property and let me flee this place.”

Felix shook violently as he spoke. He and the other man went into the cottage, stayed only a few minutes, then left. I never saw any member of the De Lacey family again.

I remained in my hovel the rest of the day, sunk in utter, stupefying despair. My protectors were gone, severing the only tie that bound me to mankind. For the first time, my heart filled with feelings of revenge and hatred, and I made no effort to resist them. Letting myself be carried away by that current, I turned my thoughts toward harm and death."}

{"request_id":"766732f5d485bb3bc3d5f5a5","rewritten_text":"He said that as he left his home and passed through Datchet, he was surprised to see smoke coming from the inn chimney. Thinking travelers might be gathered there, he knocked and was let inside. Only Lucy and her mother were there. Her mother had lost the use of her limbs after a bout of rheumatism, and everyone else in the area had departed in turn, leaving them alone. Lucy begged the man to stay with her; in a week or two her mother would be better, and then they could set out. Without help they would die, left so helpless and abandoned. The man answered that his wife and children were already among the emigrants, so he felt he could not stay. As a last attempt, Lucy gave him a letter addressed to Idris, to be delivered wherever he met us. At least this charge he fulfilled, and Idris read with emotion the letter that followed: 

“HONOURED LADY,

“I know you will remember and pity me, and I dare to hope you will help me; what other hope have I? Forgive the way I write; I am so confused. A month ago my dear mother lost the use of her limbs. She is already better, and in another month I am sure she will be able to travel, as you kindly said you would arrange for us. But now everyone has gone—everyone. As they left, each person said my mother might be better before we were entirely deserted. But three days ago I went to Samuel Woods, who stayed behind because of his newborn child, and as theirs is a large family, I hoped to persuade them to wait a little longer for us; yet I found the house empty. I have seen no one since, until this good man came. What will become of us? My mother does not know our situation; she is so ill that I have hidden it from her.

“Will you not send someone to us? I am sure we will die miserably if nothing changes. If I tried to move my mother now, she would die on the road; and if, when she gets better, I could somehow find the road and travel all those miles to the sea, you would all be in France, and the vast ocean would lie between us, dreadful even to sailors.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"ff5dc25663d1f2e4bac331e4","rewritten_text":"“You ought to be concerned, Dorian. Any gentleman cares for his good reputation. You wouldn’t wish to be spoken of as something foul and debased. Certainly, you possess position and wealth and all that, but rank and riches are not the whole of life. Understand, I do not place any faith in these stories. At least, I cannot accept them when I look at you. Sin stamps itself upon a man’s features; it cannot be hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices, but no such things exist. If a miserable fellow has some vice, it shows in the cut of his mouth, the drop of his eyelids, even in the shaping of his hands. Someone—I won’t give his name, though you know him—approached me last year for a portrait. I had not seen him before and knew nothing of him then, though I have heard plenty since. He offered an extravagant sum. I declined. There was a twist in his fingers that repelled me. Now I know I guessed rightly. His life is appalling. But you, Dorian, with that pure, luminous, innocent face, with your marvellous, untroubled youth—I cannot credit anything evil of you. And yet I rarely see you; you never come down to the studio now, and when I am away from you and hear all these ghastly things whispered in society, I am at a loss. Why is it that the Duke of Berwick rises and quits a club room when you enter? Why is it that so many London gentlemen will neither cross your threshold nor welcome you under theirs? You were once close to Lord Staveley. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up, linked with the miniatures you have lent to the Dudley exhibition. Staveley curled his lip and remarked that you might possess the most artistic tastes, but that you were a man no pure-minded girl should be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should sit with. I reminded him I was your friend and asked his meaning. He told me—plainly, before everyone present. It was dreadful! Why does your friendship prove fatal to young men? There was that unfortunate Guards officer who shot himself—he was your intimate. There was Sir Henry Ashton, forced out of England with a stained name.”"}

{"request_id":"f1bf33c8a64167bdbd031803","rewritten_text":"She suddenly felt a strong urge to go to the front door to see if it was raining. Why should she suspect herself of another motive? Captain Wentworth must be out of sight. She left her seat—she would go. One half of her should not always seem wiser than the other half, nor always suspect the other of worse motives. She would check the weather. But she was stopped at once by Captain Wentworth himself coming in, surrounded by several men and women who were clearly his acquaintances and whom he must have joined just below Milsom Street. He was more visibly startled and flustered on seeing her than she had ever noticed before; he even flushed red. For the first time since they had met again, she felt she showed more feeling than he did. She had the advantage of having had a moment to prepare. The first overpowering shock and confusion were past for her. Still, she had enough to feel—agitation, pain, pleasure—a blend of delight and misery.

He spoke to her and then turned away. His manner showed embarrassment. She could not have called it either cold or friendly, only embarrassed.

After a short pause he came back and spoke again. They exchanged the usual questions about ordinary matters; neither of them seemed much wiser for what they learned, and Anne remained fully aware that he was less at ease than before. By spending so much time together they had managed to speak with an air of indifference and calm, but he could not manage it now. Time had changed him, or Louisa had changed him. There was some kind of self-consciousness. He looked well, not as if he had suffered in health or spirits, and he talked about Uppercross, the Musgroves, even Louisa, with a brief flash of his own mischievous expression when he said her name. Still, it was Captain Wentworth ill at ease, uncomfortable, unable to pretend otherwise.

Anne was not surprised but was saddened to see that Elizabeth refused to acknowledge him. She saw that he saw Elizabeth, that Elizabeth saw him, and that each fully recognized the other. She was convinced he was ready to be greeted, expecting it, and she felt the pain of seeing her sister turn away with unchanging coldness.

Lady Dalrymple’s carriage, for which Miss Elliot had grown very impatient, now pulled up, and the servant entered to announce it."}

{"request_id":"285859b95b480289c5dbb79c","rewritten_text":"“Starve you? Oh, Mr. Ghost—Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my bag. Would you like it?”

“No, thank you. I never eat anything now, but you are very kind, and far nicer than the rest of your nasty, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” Virginia cried, stamping her foot. “You’re the rude, horrid, vulgar one, and talking about dishonesty—how dare you? You stole the paints from my box to try to touch up that absurd bloodstain in the library. You took every shade of red, even the vermilion, and I couldn’t paint another sunset. Then you snatched the emerald green and the chrome yellow, and finally I had only indigo and Chinese white left, so all I could do were moonlit scenes, which are always grim to look at and terribly difficult to paint. I never told on you, though I was furious. The whole thing was ridiculous; who ever heard of emerald-green blood?”

“Well, really,” said the Ghost, rather meekly, “what else could I do? It’s extremely hard to get real blood these days, and since your brother started it with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason I shouldn’t use your paints. As for colour, that is entirely a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, in fact the bluest in England, though I know you Americans don’t care about such things.”

“You know nothing, and the best thing you can do is emigrate and broaden your mind. My father will gladly pay your fare, and although there’s a heavy duty on spirits of any sort, there won’t be any trouble with the Customs because the officers are all Democrats. Once in New York you’ll be an instant success. I know plenty of people there who would pay a hundred thousand dollars for a grandfather, and more than that for a family ghost.”

“I don’t think I should like America.”

“I imagine that’s because we have no ruins or curiosities,” Virginia said tartly.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” the Ghost retorted. “You have your navy and your manners.”

“Good evening. I’ll go ask Papa to get the twins another week’s vacation.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I’m so lonely and unhappy, and I simply don’t know what to do. I want to sleep, and I cannot.”

{"request_id":"8c6d024c0bcad9e950fdb8a9","rewritten_text":"On my return, I found this letter from my father:

“My dear Victor,

“You have probably waited impatiently for a letter setting the date of your return; at first I thought of writing only a brief note telling you when to come. But that would be a cruel kindness, and I dare not do it. How shocked you would be, expecting a joyful welcome, to meet instead with tears and misery. And how, Victor, can I tell you our misfortune? Being away cannot have made you indifferent to our joys and sorrows; still, how can I hurt my long-absent son? I want to prepare you for the dreadful news, yet I know it is impossible; even now your eyes race ahead, looking for the words that carry the terrible message.

“William is dead!—that sweet child whose smile warmed my heart, so gentle yet so merry! Victor, he was murdered!

“I will not try to comfort you; I will simply tell you what happened.

“Last Thursday (May 7th) your two brothers, my niece, and I went for a walk in Plainpalais. The evening was warm and calm, so we stayed out longer than usual. Dusk had fallen before we thought of going home, and then we realized that William and Ernest, who had gone ahead, were nowhere to be seen. We sat on a bench to wait for them. Soon Ernest returned and asked if we had seen his brother. He said they had been playing together; William had run off to hide, and Ernest had looked for him in vain, waited a long time, and still he did not come back.

“This story alarmed us, and we searched for him until night settled in, when Elizabeth guessed he might have gone back to the house. He was not there. We went out again with torches, for I could not rest while I imagined my sweet boy lost and exposed to the damp night air; Elizabeth too was in extreme anguish. Around five in the morning I found my lovely boy, who only the evening before had been blooming with health, lying on the grass, pale and still; the mark of the murderer’s fingers was on his neck.

“We brought him home, and the anguish on my face revealed the truth to Elizabeth. She begged to see the body. At first I tried to stop her, but she insisted, hurried into the room where it lay, examined the victim’s neck, and clasping her hands cried, ‘O God!’”"}

{"request_id":"5db73be757125a3cd7aaa28a","rewritten_text":"Other chances to watch them were bound to come. Anne was soon among all four often enough to form an opinion, though she was too prudent to admit it at home, knowing neither husband nor wife would be satisfied; for while she thought Louisa somewhat preferred, she could not help believing—from memory and experience—that Captain Wentworth was not in love with either. They were more in love with him, though even that was not true love. It was a brief fever of admiration that might, and likely must, become love for some of them. Charles Hayter seemed conscious of being overlooked, yet Henrietta sometimes appeared torn between them. Anne longed to warn them all about what they were doing, and to point out the dangers they were courting. She suspected no deceit. Her greatest relief was believing Captain Wentworth had no idea he was causing pain. There was no triumph, no mean triumph, in his manner. He had probably never heard of, or even considered, Charles Hayter’s claims. His only fault was accepting—accepting was the right word—the attentions of two young women at once.

After a brief struggle, however, Charles Hayter seemed to withdraw. Three days had passed without his visiting Uppercross—a clear change. He even declined a formal dinner invitation; and when Mr Musgrove found him surrounded by large books, Mr and Mrs Musgrove were convinced something was wrong, speaking gravely of his studying himself to death. Mary hoped and believed Henrietta had dismissed him outright, while her husband expected to see him the next day. Anne could only think Charles Hayter showed sense.

One morning around this time, with Charles Musgrove and Captain Wentworth off shooting together, the sisters at the Cottage sat quietly at their work when the sisters from the Mansion-house stopped by the window.

It was a beautiful November day, and the Miss Musgroves crossed the small grounds solely to announce that they were going for a long walk and therefore assumed Mary would not want to join them. When Mary, bristling at the suggestion she was not a good walker, immediately answered, “Oh yes, I should like to join you very much, I am very fond of a long walk,” Anne read in the girls’ expressions that this was exactly what they did not want. She again noted how the family habit seemed to require that everything be announced and everything be done together, no matter how unwelcome or inconvenient."}

{"request_id":"404d626683aae4d57f951b89","rewritten_text":"During dinner Mr. Bennet hardly spoke; but once the servants left, he decided it was time to talk with his guest. He chose a topic that he expected would please him by noting how fortunate he seemed in his patroness. Lady Catherine de Bourgh’s attention to Mr. Collins’s wishes and her concern for his comfort appeared most unusual. Mr. Bennet could not have picked better. Mr. Collins passed at once into eager praise. The subject made him even more solemn than usual, and with an air of great importance he declared he had never seen behavior like hers in a woman of rank—such friendliness and kindness as he had received from Lady Catherine. She had graciously approved both the sermons he had been honored to preach before her. She had also invited him twice to dine at Rosings, and had sent for him only the previous Saturday to complete her evening card game of quadrille. Many people considered Lady Catherine proud, he knew, but he himself had seen only graciousness. She always spoke to him as she would to any other gentleman; she made no objection to his joining the neighborhood society, nor to his leaving his parish now and then for a week or two to visit his relations. She had even condescended to advise him to marry as soon as he could, provided he chose wisely; and she had once paid him a visit in his modest parsonage, where she perfectly approved all the alterations he had made, and even took the trouble to suggest a few herself—some shelves in the upstairs closets.

“That is all very proper and polite, I am sure,” said Mrs. Bennet, “and I dare say she is a very pleasant woman. It is a pity that great ladies in general are not more like her. Does she live near you, sir?”

“The garden in which my humble residence stands is separated from Rosings Park, her Ladyship’s home, only by a lane.”

“I think you said she was a widow, sir? Has she any family?”

“She has only one daughter, the heiress of Rosings and of very great property.”

“Ah,” cried Mrs. Bennet, shaking her head, “then she is better off than many girls. And what sort of young lady is she? Is she handsome?”

“She is a most delightful young lady indeed. Lady Catherine herself says that, in true beauty, Miss de Bourgh far surpasses the most beautiful women; because there is something in her features that marks the young lady of distinguished birth.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"24975ad647b5532a90170cbb","rewritten_text":"The studio swam with the lush perfume of roses, and when the mild summer breeze stirred the garden trees, the heavy fragrance of lilac or the more delicate scent of the pink-blossoming thorn drifted through the open doorway. Reclining on the corner of the divan made from Persian saddle-bags, Lord Henry Wotton lay smoking innumerable cigarettes, as he always did, and from there he could glimpse the honey-sweet, honey-gold sprays of a laburnum, whose quivering branches seemed scarcely capable of supporting such flame-like loveliness. From time to time the fanciful shadows of birds in flight glided across the long curtains of tussore silk that hung before the vast window, creating a fleeting Japanese impression and reminding him of those jade-faced, wan painters of Tokyo who strive, through an art that must remain motionless, to express speed and movement. The sullen drone of bees thrusting their way through the long, uncut grass, or circling with tireless monotony around the dusty gilded horns of the wandering woodbine, only heightened the oppressive stillness. The muffled rumble of London sounded like the bourdon note of a far-off organ. In the middle of the room, fixed to an upright easel, stood the life-size portrait of a young man of exceptional physical beauty, and a short distance before it sat the painter himself, Basil Hallward, whose sudden disappearance several years ago had created such a sensation and sparked countless odd conjectures. As he gazed at the graceful and handsome figure he had captured so deftly in his art, a smile of satisfaction crossed his face and seemed ready to remain. Yet he abruptly sprang up, and shutting his eyes, pressed his fingers against the lids, as if wishing to trap inside his mind some peculiar dream he dreaded might dissolve. “It is your finest work, Basil, the best thing you have ever produced,” Lord Henry remarked languidly. “You ought to send it to the Grosvenor next year. The Academy is much too vast and too common. Every time I have been there, either the crush of people prevented me from seeing the paintings, which was dreadful, or the multitude of paintings kept me from seeing the people, which was worse. The Grosvenor is truly the only suitable place.” “I don’t believe I shall send it anywhere,” he replied, tossing his head back in that queer manner that used to make his friends at Oxford laugh."}

{"request_id":"15b448b12b8e3d89977e4977","rewritten_text":"“You haven’t lived in Bath long enough,” he said, “to get anything out of the evening parties here.”

“Oh, no. Their usual style offers nothing to me. I’m not a card-player.”

“You weren’t before, I know. You never used to like cards; but time changes a lot.”

“I’m not so changed yet,” Anne cried, and then stopped, uncertain what misunderstanding she might cause. After a few moments he added, as if speaking from a sudden feeling, “It’s a long time, indeed. Eight years and a half is a long stretch.”

Whether he meant to go on, Anne had to imagine later; for while his words were still echoing in her ears, Henrietta startled her with other concerns, eager to use the present quiet to get out, urging her companions to hurry before anyone else arrived.

They had to move. Anne said she was perfectly ready and tried to appear so; but she felt that if Henrietta had known how regretful and reluctant she was to leave that chair, to prepare to leave the room, she would have found, in her own secure feelings for her cousin, a reason to pity her.

Their plans, however, were cut short. Disturbing noises sounded; other visitors were arriving, and the door swung open for Sir Walter and Miss Elliot, whose appearance seemed to chill the whole room. Anne felt instantly oppressed, and wherever she looked she saw the same signs. The comfort, ease, and liveliness vanished, replaced by cold composure, forced silence, or dull conversation to match her father and sister’s heartless elegance. How mortifying to realize it!

Her jealous attention was satisfied on one point. Captain Wentworth was again acknowledged by both, and Elizabeth was more gracious than before. She even spoke to him once and looked at him more than once. Elizabeth was actually turning over a grand scheme. The outcome soon showed itself. After wasting a few minutes on the proper niceties, she began issuing the invitation that was meant to cover all remaining obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; no formal party.” She delivered it with perfect grace, laying the “Miss Elliot at home” cards she had brought on the table, smiling warmly at everyone, and adding one extra smile and card directly for Captain Wentworth. The truth was, Elizabeth had spent enough time in Bath to recognize the value of a man with his sort of presence and looks."}

{"request_id":"6d1eb63d15bbf681bb98beff","rewritten_text":"Well, I told him I wanted the watermelon. But he said I didn’t need it for busting out of prison; that’s where the hitch was. He said if I’d wanted it to stash a knife in and slip it to Jim so he could stab the seneschal, that would have been acceptable. So I dropped it, though I couldn’t see what good it did me to stand for a prisoner if I had to sit around and chew over a batch of gilt-edge distinctions like that every time I spotted a chance to swipe a watermelon.

Anyway, like I was saying, we waited that morning till everybody had settled into their work and the yard was empty; then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I hung back a little to keep watch. Soon he came out, and we went and perched on the woodpile to talk. He says:

“Everything’s settled now except tools; and that’s simple enough.”

“Tools?” I says.

“Yep.”

“Tools for what?”

“Why, for digging. We aren’t fixing to gnaw him out, are we?”

“Ain’t those wore-out picks and such in there good enough to dig a nigger out with?” I says.

He wheels around on me, looking mournful enough to make a body cry, and says:

“Huck Finn, did you ever hear of a prisoner keeping picks and shovels and every modern convenience in his closet to dig himself free with? Now I got to ask you—if you’ve got a lick of reason in you—what kind of a chance would that give him to be a hero? They might as well hand him the key and be done. Picks and shovels—why, they wouldn’t even let a king have such things.”

“Well, then,” I says, “if we don’t want the picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of case-knives.”

“To scrape the foundations out from under that cabin with?”

“Yes.”

“Hang it, that’s nonsense, Tom.”

“It don’t matter how silly it seems, it’s the proper way—and the regular way. And there ain’t no other way, that ever I heard of, and I’ve read every book that gives any light on the subject. They always dig out with a case-knife—and not through dirt, mind you; it’s usually solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, and forever besides. Why, think of that prisoner in the lowest cell of the Castle Deef, in the harbor of Marseilles, that carved himself out that way; how long do you calculate he was at it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, make a guess.”

“I don’t know. Six weeks.”"}

{"request_id":"865f9ef08748942fced3f2ab","rewritten_text":"Ten minutes later, his face bleached with terror and his eyes wild with grief, Lord Arthur Savile burst out of Bentinck House, pushing through the crowd of fur-clad footmen surrounding the big striped awning, as if he neither saw nor heard anything. The night was bitter cold, the gas lamps around the square flaring and wavering in the sharp wind; yet his hands burned with fever, and his forehead felt like fire. He kept going, almost staggering like a drunk. A policeman gave him a curious look as he passed, and a beggar who slunk from an archway to ask for alms recoiled, scared by suffering worse than his own. At one point he halted beneath a lamp and stared at his hands, convinced he could already see blood staining them, and a faint cry escaped his trembling lips.

Murder—that was what the chiromantist had read there. Murder! The night itself seemed to recognize it, the lonely wind howling it in his ear. Every dark corner of the streets was filled with the word. It leered at him from the rooftops.

He reached the Park first, drawn to its somber trees. Wearily he leaned against the railings, cooling his brow against the wet iron while he listened to the trembling hush among the branches. “Murder! Murder!” he kept repeating, as though the repetition could dull the terror of the word. The sound of his own voice made him shudder, yet he half hoped some echo would catch it and rouse the sleeping city from its dreams. He fought a wild urge to halt some passerby and confess everything.

After that he drifted across Oxford Street into cramped, disreputable alleys. Two women with painted faces mocked him as he went by. From a dark courtyard came curses, blows, then shrill screams, and on a damp doorstep he saw the bent figures of poverty and old age huddled together. A strange pity surged up in him. Were these children of sin and misery condemned to their fate just as he was to his? Were they, like him, simply puppets in a monstrous spectacle?

Still, it wasn’t the mystery but the absurdity of suffering that struck him—the sheer uselessness of it, the grotesque lack of meaning. Everything felt jumbled, stripped of harmony. He marveled at the clash between the era’s shallow optimism and the harsh truths of life. He was still very young.

Eventually he found himself standing before Marylebone Church. The silent roadway stretched out like a long ribbon of polished silver, dotted here and there with dark arabesques of shifting shadows."}

Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, gave her a look full of wonder. Elizabeth said nothing, yet she was deeply gratified; the compliment must be for her sake. {"request_id":"096875967bdfee1dcd142d20","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologized. He answered, “Not at all,” and went on.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you can imagine she was pursued as a great prize. Her half brother had regained plenty of money, but through debts and new foolishness squandered it again in the worst way. The rift between him and her was even deeper than the one he had had with their father, and it’s suspected he nursed a bitter, deadly grudge against her for stirring up their father’s anger. Now, I reach the cruel part of the story—only pausing, my dear Handel, to point out that a dinner napkin will not fit into a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to stuff mine into my glass, I have no idea. I only know that with determination worthy of a better cause, I exerted myself to force it in. Again I thanked him and apologized, and again he said in the brightest tone, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“There appeared on the scene—whether at the races, the public balls, or anywhere else you like—a certain man who courted Miss Havisham. I never saw him (this was twenty-five years ago, before you and I, Handel), but my father used to say he was flashy, just the type for the role. Yet he could not, without ignorance or prejudice, be mistaken for a gentleman, my father emphatically insists, because he holds that no man who isn’t a gentleman at heart has ever been, since the world began, a gentleman in manner. He says no polish can hide the grain of the wood, and the more polish you apply, the more the grain shows. Well! This man pursued Miss Havisham relentlessly and claimed to be devoted to her. I believe she hadn’t shown much susceptibility before, but every bit she had came out then, and she loved him passionately. She clearly idolized him. He exploited her affection so methodically that he extracted large sums of money from her, and he persuaded her to buy her brother out of his share in the brewery (which their father had weakly left to him) at a huge price, arguing that once he married her he must own and run it entirely. Your guardian wasn’t part of Miss Havisham’s inner circle at that time, and she was too proud and too deeply in love to take anyone’s advice.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9f600706f6dbc5ff026a6d2e","rewritten_text":"He chose Friday, August 17th for his appearance and spent most of the day examining his wardrobe, ultimately settling on a large slouch hat with a red feather, a burial shroud frilled at the wrists and neck, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening a violent storm broke out, and the wind blew so hard that every window and door in the old house shook and rattled. It was exactly the kind of weather he loved. His plan was simple. He would quietly make his way to Washington Otis’s room, gibber from the foot of the bed, and stab himself three times in the throat to the sound of slow music. He held a special grudge against Washington, fully aware that he used Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent to scrub out the famous Canterville bloodstain. After reducing the reckless, foolhardy boy to utter terror, he would go to the room of the United States Minister and his wife, press a clammy hand to Mrs. Otis’s forehead, and hiss into her shaking husband’s ear the awful secrets of the charnel house. As for little Virginia, he was undecided. She had never insulted him and was pretty and gentle. He felt a few hollow groans from the wardrobe would be more than enough, and if that failed to wake her, he might claw at the bedspread with trembling, palsied fingers. He was determined to teach the twins a lesson. First, he would sit on their chests, to give them the suffocating sensation of a nightmare. Then, since their beds were close together, he would stand between them as a green, icy corpse until they were paralyzed with fear, and finally he would throw off the shroud and crawl around the room with bleached bones and one rolling eyeball as “Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton,” a role in which he had repeatedly made a tremendous impression, and which he thought as good as his celebrated part, “Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.”\n\nAt half-past ten he heard the family going to bed. For a while wild bursts of laughter from the twins disturbed him, as they were clearly amusing themselves with schoolboy cheerfulness before turning in, but by a quarter past eleven everything was quiet, and when midnight struck, he set out. An owl beat against the window panes, a raven croaked from the old yew tree, and the wind moaned around the house like a lost soul, but the Otis family slept unaware of their fate, and above the rain and storm he could clearly hear the steady snoring of the United States Minister."}

{"request_id":"cf5e12f64083cd463af765d2","rewritten_text":"“I have two questions to ask you—is that allowed?”

“You can ask,” Monks replied, with a hint of surprise. “Whether I answer is another matter.”

“That makes three,” Mr. Bumble said in a weak attempt at wit.

“Is this what you expected from me?” the matron demanded.

“It is,” said Monks. “And the other question?”

“What are you going to do with it? Could it be used against me?”

“Never,” said Monks. “Not against me either. Look! But don’t take a single step forward, or your life isn’t worth a reed.”

With that, he suddenly dragged the table aside. Grabbing an iron ring set into the floorboards, he yanked open a large trapdoor right at Mr. Bumble’s feet, forcing the man to retreat several paces in a rush.

“Look down,” Monks said as he lowered the lantern into the chasm. “Don’t be afraid of me. I could have dropped you without effort while you sat over it, if that had been my plan.”

Reassured, the matron edged toward the rim, and even Mr. Bumble, driven by curiosity, inched forward. The murky water, swollen by heavy rain, roared below; all other sounds vanished in the rush and swirl against the green, slimy pilings. There had once been a mill there; the tide, foaming and raging around the remaining rotten stakes and scraps of machinery, seemed to race forward with fresh fury once free of the useless barriers that had tried to slow it.

“If you threw a man’s body down there, where would it be by morning?” Monks asked, swinging the lantern over the dark shaft.

“Twelve miles downriver, hacked to pieces,” Bumble answered, shrinking from the idea.

Monks pulled the small packet from inside his coat, where he had stuffed it in haste, tied it to a lead weight from an old pulley lying on the floor, and dropped it into the torrent. It plunged straight down, sliced through the water with barely a sound, and vanished.

The three of them looked at one another and seemed to breathe easier.

“There!” said Monks, letting the trapdoor slam back into place. “If the sea ever gives up its dead like the books claim, it will keep its gold and silver, and that junk with it. We’re finished here; time to dissolve our pleasant gathering.”

“Without question,” Mr. Bumble said quickly.

“You’ll keep your tongue still, won’t you?” Monks asked, throwing him a threatening look."}

{"request_id":"6b0bfcad1be581e3acb2338f","rewritten_text":"If you won’t, and are counting on my patience and the mercy of those you’ve wronged, sit in that chair without a word. It has been waiting for you for two whole days.”

Monks mumbled something indistinct, but still wavered.

“Move quickly,” said Mr. Brownlow. “One word from me, and your other option is gone forever.”

Still the man hesitated.

“I’m not inclined to bargain,” said Mr. Brownlow, “and since I am defending the dearest interests of others, I have no right to.”

“Is there—” asked Monks, his tongue faltering, “is there—no middle ground?”

“None.”

Monks looked anxiously at the old gentleman, but seeing only severity and resolve on his face, walked into the room and, with a shrug, sat down.

“Lock the door from the outside,” Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, “and come when I ring.”

The men obeyed, leaving the two alone.

“This is fine treatment,” said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak, “from my father’s oldest friend.”

“It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,” replied Mr. Brownlow. “Because the hopes and wishes of bright young years were tied to him, and to that beautiful creature of his blood and kin who rejoined her God in youth and left me here, solitary and alone. Because he knelt with me at his only sister’s deathbed when he was still a boy, on the morning that — had Heaven chosen otherwise — would have made her my young wife. Because from that moment my scarred heart clung to him through all his trials and failings until he died. Because old memories filled my heart, and even seeing you brings back thoughts of him. It’s for all these reasons that I’m moved to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to blush for your unworthiness in bearing his name.”

“What does the name have to do with anything?” the other asked, half silently and half in stubborn amazement at the other’s emotion. “What is that name to me?”

“Nothing,” said Mr. Brownlow, “nothing to you. But it was hers, and even after all this time it brings back to me, an old man, the warmth and thrill I once felt just hearing a stranger repeat it. I’m very glad you changed it—very, very glad.”

“This is all very impressive,” said Monks (still holding to his assumed name) after a long silence, during which he had twisted himself in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his face shaded by his hand."}

{"request_id":"62d6b078fb207676db7c7679","rewritten_text":"At the sight, the orangutan immediately sprang through the chamber door, down the stairs, and, through a window that unfortunately stood open, out into the street.

The Frenchman followed in despair; the ape, still clutching the razor, would now and then stop, look back, and gesture at its pursuer until he nearly caught up, then dart away again. The chase went on like this for a long time. The streets were utterly silent, since it was nearly three in the morning. While racing down an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the fugitive spotted a light shining from Madame L’Espanaye’s open window on the fourth floor of her house. Rushing to the building, it noticed the lightning rod, climbed it with unbelievable speed, grabbed the shutter flung back against the wall, and used it to swing straight onto the bed’s headboard. The entire feat took less than a minute. As it entered the room, the orangutan kicked the shutter open again.

Meanwhile, the sailor was both relieved and alarmed. He felt he had a real chance to recapture the creature now, since it could barely escape the trap it had entered except by the rod, where he might catch it on the way down. Yet he also worried intensely about what it might do inside the house. That thought drove him to keep following the runaway. A lightning rod is easy enough to climb, especially for a sailor; but when he reached the height of the window, which lay far to his left, he could go no farther. All he could do was lean over to get a glimpse inside. That glimpse nearly made him lose his grip from sheer horror. At that very moment came the awful screams that had roused everyone on the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, appeared to have been arranging papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been wheeled to the center of the room. It was open, and its contents were scattered on the floor. The victims must have been sitting with their backs to the window; and, judging by the time between the creature’s entry and their screams, it seems likely they didn’t notice it right away. The shutter banging shut would naturally have been blamed on the wind.

As the sailor looked in, the gigantic animal had grabbed Madame L’Espanaye by the hair—left loose because she had been combing it—and was brandishing the razor around her face, mimicking a barber’s motions."}
