{"request_id":"fee64b4df13ba46a81315dc4","rewritten_text":"“I’m not eating at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man replied, leaving the room.

“Now, Alan, we can’t waste a minute. This chest is heavy—I’ll take it for you. You bring the rest.” His words came fast, commanding. Campbell felt overpowered by him. They left together.

At the top landing, Dorian took out the key and turned it in the lock. Then he stopped, a troubled look in his eyes. He shivered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he murmured.

“That’s nothing to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell said coldly.

Dorian pushed the door halfway open. As he did, the face in his portrait leered at him in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that last night, for the first time in his life, he had forgotten to hide the cursed canvas and was about to rush forward when he drew back with a shudder.

What was that disgusting red moisture shining wet and slick on one of the hands, as if the canvas had sweated blood? How terrible it looked!—for a moment worse, he thought, than the silent thing lying stretched out on the table, the thing whose grotesque warped shadow on the stained carpet showed it hadn’t moved, but was still there just as he had left it.

He took a deep breath, opened the door wider, and with half-closed eyes and his head turned away, walked quickly in, determined not to look even once at the dead man. Then he bent down, snatched up the gold-and-purple hanging, and threw it over the picture.

He stopped there, too afraid to turn around, his eyes fixed on the complex patterns before him. He heard Campbell carrying in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other items needed for his gruesome task. He began to wonder if he and Basil Hallward had ever met and, if they had, what they would have thought of each other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, only aware that the dead man had been shoved back into the chair and that Campbell was staring into a gleaming yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was long past seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale but icy calm. “I did what you asked,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"2b4e4c0639664e8a1e5759ab","rewritten_text":"WHEN Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, purchased Canterville Chase, everyone declared he was acting very foolishly, for there was no question that the place was haunted. In fact, Lord Canterville himself, a man of precise honour, considered it his obligation to point this out to Mr. Otis when they began negotiating. 

“We have not wished to occupy the place ourselves,” said Lord Canterville, “ever since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a seizure, from which she never truly recovered, by two skeleton hands laid upon her shoulders as she dressed for dinner. I feel compelled to inform you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family, as well as the parish rector, the Rev. Augustus Dampier, a Fellow of King’s College, Cambridge, have also seen the ghost. After the Duchess’s unhappy mishap, none of our younger servants would stay on, and Lady Canterville often had very little sleep at night because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My Lord,” replied the Minister, “I’ll take the furniture and the ghost at the price. I hail from a modern nation where we can buy anything money will procure; with our lively young men painting the Old World red and carting off your best actresses and prima donnas, I suppose if there were a ghost anywhere in Europe, we’d have it back home soon enough in a public museum or touring as an attraction.”

“I am afraid the ghost is real,” said Lord Canterville with a smile, “even if it has ignored the proposals of your eager impresarios. It has been known for three hundred years, since 1584, in fact, and invariably appears before the death of any family member.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, for that matter, Lord Canterville. But there is nothing like a ghost, sir, and I suspect the laws of Nature will not be suspended for the British nobility.”

“You Americans are certainly very natural,” answered Lord Canterville, who did not quite grasp Mr. Otis’s final remark, “and if you do not mind sharing the house with a ghost, that is fine. Only remember I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was finalized, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family went down to Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis—once Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, a famed belle of New York—was now a striking, middle-aged woman with fine eyes and an excellent profile."}

{"request_id":"aba5e9e5bfcc4dc86af7f5b7","rewritten_text":"“I’m very ignorant, and it troubles me—just a little.”

“Tell me what it is.”

“I have a cousin, my only relative and an orphan like me, whom I love dearly. She’s five years younger than I am and lives on a farm in the south. Poverty separated us, and she knows nothing of what has become of me—for I cannot write, and even if I could, how could I explain everything? It’s better as it is.”

“Yes, yes: better as it is.”

“What I have been thinking as we walked here, and what I still think now as I look into your kind, strong face that gives me so much support, is this: If the Republic truly helps the poor, if they become less hungry and suffer less in every way, she might live a long time. She might even grow old.”

“What then, my gentle sister?”

“Do you think”—the patient eyes, so full of endurance, fill with tears, and her lips part a little more and tremble—“that it will feel long to me while I wait for her in the better world where I trust both you and I will be mercifully sheltered?”

“It cannot be, my child; there is no Time there, and no trouble there.”

“You comfort me so much! I’m so ignorant. Should I kiss you now? Is it time?”

“Yes.”

She kisses his lips; he kisses hers; they bless each other solemnly. His free hand doesn’t shake as he lets go; nothing worse than a sweet, bright steadfastness shows in her patient face. She steps forward before him—she is gone; the knitting women count Twenty-Two.

“I am the Resurrection and the Life, saith the Lord: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.”

The murmur of many voices, faces lifted upward, the push of countless footsteps at the edge of the crowd, swelling forward like one great heave of water, all vanish. Twenty-Three.

*****

They said of him, throughout the city that night, that his was the most peaceful face ever seen there. Many added that he looked sublime and prophetic.

{"request_id":"fb134036b615e4421098ad0b","rewritten_text":"Just then his eyes, and mine as well, fell on the scrap of parchment, which I first thought was plain paper. It lay half buried in the sand, with one corner sticking out. Nearby I noticed the remains of what looked like the hull of a ship’s longboat. The wreck must have been there a very long time, because it was barely recognizable as boat timbers.

“Anyway, Jupiter picked up the parchment, wrapped the beetle in it, and handed it to me. Soon after, we started for home and ran into Lieutenant G——. I showed him the insect, and he begged to take it to the fort. When I agreed, he immediately slipped it into his waistcoat pocket, without the parchment it had been wrapped in, which I still held while he inspected the beetle. Maybe he was afraid I might change my mind and wanted to secure his prize right away—you know how passionate he is about anything related to natural history. At the same time, without realizing it, I must have put the parchment in my own pocket.

“You remember I went to the table to sketch the beetle and found no paper where it was usually kept. I checked the drawer and nothing was there. I searched my pockets, hoping for an old letter, when my hand touched the parchment. I’m giving you the exact details because the whole incident struck me strongly.

“Surely you’ll think I’m fanciful, but I already felt a sort of connection. I had two links in a longer chain: a boat on a shoreline, and near the boat a parchment—not paper—with a skull drawn on it. Naturally you ask, ‘What is the connection?’ I answer that the skull, or death’s-head, is the well-known symbol of pirates. The death’s-head flag is raised in every battle.

“I said the scrap was parchment, not paper. Parchment lasts a long time—almost forever. People rarely use it for trivial matters, since it is not as convenient as paper for everyday writing or drawing. That made me suspect there was some meaning—some purpose—to the death’s-head. I also noticed the shape of the parchment. Even though one corner had been damaged somehow, it was still clear that the original shape was oblong.”}"}

{"request_id":"c6a9464e80eec5509f294f42","rewritten_text":"Her complexion shifted, and she fell silent.

Mrs. Gardiner was standing slightly behind, and when Elizabeth paused, he asked her if she would introduce him to her friends. This was a courtesy she had never expected from him, and she could barely hide a smile at the thought of his now chasing acquaintance with the very people he had looked down on while proposing to her. “What a shock he’ll have,” she thought, “when he learns who they are. He thinks they’re fashionable society.”

The introductions were made immediately, and as she explained their family connection, she glanced at him to see how he took it. She almost expected him to flee from such humiliating relations. He was clearly surprised, yet he bore it well; instead of leaving, he turned back with them and started talking with Mr. Gardiner. Elizabeth couldn’t help being pleased, couldn’t help feeling triumphant. It comforted her that he should know she had relatives no one needed to be ashamed of. She listened closely to every exchange, proud of each word from her uncle that revealed his intelligence, taste, or good manners.

The conversation soon shifted to fishing, and she heard Mr. Darcy, with utmost politeness, invite him to fish there whenever he liked while he remained nearby, offering to lend him tackle and pointing out the stretches of the river where the fish were most plentiful. Mrs. Gardiner, walking arm in arm with Elizabeth, shot her a look full of astonishment. Elizabeth said nothing, but she was deeply gratified; the compliment had to be meant for her. Still, her amazement was intense, and she kept repeating to herself, “Why has he changed so much? What could it come from? It cannot be because of me; it cannot be for my sake that his manners have softened like this. My reproaches at Hunsford could not have produced such a change. It’s impossible he could still love me.”

After walking this way for some time—two ladies in front, two gentlemen behind—they rearranged themselves when they climbed back from the riverbank, where they had gone to examine an unusual water plant. The change came from Mrs. Gardiner, who, tired from the morning’s exertion, found Elizabeth’s arm insufficient and therefore took her husband’s instead."}

{"request_id":"06823ad9dbcc8d361d07c0ca","rewritten_text":"Raymond paced the room in anger. I waited, prepared for his reproaches, while Adrian leaned against the wall. “This is utterly absurd,” he exclaimed. “If you were schoolboys, you could not behave more unreasonably.”

“You do not understand,” Raymond answered. “This is merely part of a system—a scheme of tyranny to which I will never submit. Because I am Protector of England, must I be the sole slave in the nation? My privacy invaded, my actions judged, my friends insulted? I will rid myself of it all. Be witnesses,” he said, removing the star, badge of office, from his breast and flinging it on the table. “I renounce my post; I abdicate my power—let anyone else take it!”

“Let it be taken,” cried Adrian, “by one who can declare himself, or whom the nation will call, your superior. There is no man in England presumptuous enough. Know yourself, Raymond, and your anger will subside; your satisfaction return. Only a few months ago, whenever we prayed for our country or ourselves, we also prayed for the Protector’s life and welfare, so closely were they linked. Your hours were devoted to our good, your ambition to earn our praise. You adorned our towns with buildings, established useful institutions, made the soil abundantly fertile. The powerful and unjust shrank from your tribunal, and the poor and oppressed lifted their heads like flowers awakened at dawn by your protection.

“Can you marvel that we are in shock and lament when all seems altered? Yet this splenetic mood is already ending; resume your duties. Your supporters will greet you, your enemies fall silent, our love, honour, and duty will again surround you. Command yourself, Raymond, and the world lies under your sway.”

“All this might be good advice for someone else,” Raymond answered gloomily. “Learn your own lesson, and you, the first peer of the realm, might become its sovereign. You, the good, the wise, the just, might command every heart. But I see now—too soon for my own peace, too late for England’s benefit—that I took on a task beyond me. I cannot command myself. My passions rule me; my slightest impulse tyrannizes me. Do you believe I abandoned the Protectorate, as I have done, in a fit of spleen? By the living God, I swear I will never take up that bauble again, never again burden myself with the weight of care and misery it represents."}

{"request_id":"481a938ea13e7a18a1091f69","rewritten_text":"With these shrieks, many of the women, whipped into sightless fury, spun around, striking and clawing at their own companions until they collapsed in a passionate faint, saved only by their men from being crushed beneath the feet around them.

Even so, not an instant was squandered; not a single heartbeat! That Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville and might be freed. Never, if Saint Antoine remembered his own torments, insults, and grievances! Men and women under arms poured out of the Quarter with such speed, dragging even these last dregs behind them with a suction so strong, that in fifteen minutes there remained in Saint Antoine’s bosom only a few ancient crones and the crying little ones.

No, by then they packed the Hall of Examination where this old, ugly, wicked man stood, overflowing into the nearby open space and streets. The Defarges, husband and wife, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three pressed forward in the front ranks, not far from him in the Hall.

“Look!” cried madame, pointing with her knife. “Look at the old villain bound with ropes. Well done to tie a bunch of grass on his back. Ha, ha! Well done indeed. Let him feast on it now!” Madame tucked her knife beneath her arm and applauded as though at a spectacle.

The people directly behind Madame Defarge explained the reason for her delight to those behind them, and these to others, and they to more, until the neighbouring streets echoed with the clatter of clapping hands. Likewise, during the two or three hours of tedious drawl, and the winnowing of many bushels of words, Madame Defarge’s frequent bursts of impatience were caught up, with astonishing rapidity, at a distance: all the more because certain men who by some remarkable agility had climbed the exterior of the building to look in through the windows, knew Madame Defarge well and served as a telegraph between her and the throng outside.

At last the sun climbed so high it cast a gentle beam, like hope or protection, straight down upon the old prisoner’s head. That favour was too great to endure; in a heartbeat the barrier of dust and chaff that had lasted so improbably long shattered, and Saint Antoine possessed him!

The news flashed at once to the farthest edges of the multitude. Defarge had merely leapt over a railing and a table, enclosing the wretched creature in a lethal embrace—Madame Defarge had just followed, twining her hand into one of the ropes binding him—The Vengeance and Jacques Three had not yet arrived, and the men at the windows had not yet swooped into the Hall like birds of prey from their lofty roosts—when the shout seemed to rise across the whole city, “Bring him out!”"}

{"request_id":"ffbb680c1ab79e9c07ec15e3","rewritten_text":"I now hurry to the more moving part of my story. I will describe the events that impressed me with feelings that have transformed me from what I once was into what I am now.

Spring advanced quickly; the weather turned fair and the sky remained clear. I was startled that what had seemed barren and gloomy now blossomed with the most beautiful flowers and greenery. My senses were delighted and refreshed by countless scents and countless sights of beauty.

One of those days, when my cottagers took their regular rest from labor—the old man played his guitar while the children listened—I noticed that Felix’s face was indescribably melancholy. He sighed often, and when his father paused in his playing, I guessed from his manner that he was asking the reason for his son’s sadness. Felix answered in a cheerful tone, and the old man was about to resume his music when someone knocked at the door.

It was a lady on horseback, accompanied by a countryman serving as a guide. She wore a dark outfit and was covered with a thick black veil. Agatha asked a question, to which the stranger only replied by speaking Felix’s name in a sweet voice. Her voice was musical but unlike any of my friends’. Hearing this name, Felix hurried to the lady, who, once she saw him, lifted her veil. I saw a face of angelic beauty and expression. Her hair was glossy raven black, intricately braided; her eyes were dark but gentle and lively; her features were perfectly proportioned; her complexion was wondrously fair, each cheek tinted with a lovely pink.

Felix seemed overwhelmed with delight at her sight. Every trace of sorrow vanished from his face, replaced instantly by such ecstatic joy I could hardly believe it possible. His eyes sparkled and his cheeks flushed with pleasure, and in that moment I thought him as beautiful as the stranger. She was moved by different feelings; wiping a few tears from her lovely eyes, she held out her hand to Felix, who kissed it rapturously and called her, as best I could make out, his sweet Arabian. She did not seem to understand him but smiled. He helped her dismount, dismissed her guide, and led her into the cottage. A conversation followed between him and his father, and the young stranger knelt at the old man’s feet, ready to kiss his hand, but he lifted her and embraced her warmly.

I soon realized that although the stranger spoke clearly and had a language of her own, neither she understood the cottagers nor did they understand her."}

{"request_id":"14a281900374e468e7384442","rewritten_text":"Naturally he was very entertaining and all that, but I was terribly disappointed; and when I asked him about the coat of mail, he only laughed and said it was far too cold to wear in England. Ah, here comes Mr. Podgers! Now, Mr. Podgers, I want you to read the Duchess of Paisley’s hand. Duchess, you’ll have to take off your glove. No, not the left hand, the other one.’

‘Dear Gladys, I honestly don’t think it’s quite proper,’ said the Duchess, weakly unfastening a rather grimy kid glove.

‘Nothing interesting ever is,’ said Lady Windermere. ‘_On a fait le monde ainsi_. But I must introduce you. Duchess, this is Mr. Podgers, my favored palmist. Mr. Podgers, this is the Duchess of Paisley, and if you dare say she has a higher Mount of the Moon than I do, I’ll never trust you again.’

‘I’m sure, Gladys, there’s nothing of the sort in my hand,’ said the Duchess seriously.

‘Your Grace is quite right,’ said Mr. Podgers, glancing at the plump little hand with its short square fingers. ‘The Mount of the Moon is not pronounced. The life line, however, is excellent. Please bend the wrist. Thank you. Three clear lines on the rascette! You will live to a great age, Duchess, and be extremely happy. Ambition—very moderate, line of intellect not exaggerated, line of heart—’

‘Now, do be indiscreet, Mr. Podgers,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Nothing would please me more,’ said Mr. Podgers, bowing, ‘if the Duchess had ever been indiscreet, but I regret to say that I see great steadfastness of affection combined with a strong sense of duty.’

‘Please go on, Mr. Podgers,’ said the Duchess, looking delighted.

‘Economy is far from the least of your Grace’s virtues,’ continued Mr. Podgers, and Lady Windermere burst into fits of laughter.

‘Economy is an excellent thing,’ remarked the Duchess complacently. ‘When I married Paisley he had eleven castles and not a single place fit to live in.’

‘And now he has twelve houses and not a single castle,’ cried Lady Windermere.

‘Well, my dear,’ said the Duchess, ‘I like—’

‘Comfort,’ said Mr. Podgers, ‘and modern conveniences, and hot water laid on in every bedroom. Your Grace is absolutely right. Comfort is the only thing our civilization truly gives us.’

‘You’ve described the Duchess’s character perfectly, Mr. Podgers, and now you must tell Lady Flora’s.’ At a nod from the smiling hostess, a tall girl with sandy Scottish hair and high shoulder blades stepped awkwardly out from behind the sofa and held out a long, bony hand with spatulate fingers.

‘Ah, a pianist! I can see it,’ said Mr. Podgers. ‘An excellent pianist, though perhaps not quite a musician.’"}

content.text: {"request_id":"2f2fddb4a2ce33e0ad632988","rewritten_text":"He shivered, then returned and closed the window behind him. Once at the door, he turned the key, opened it, and did not even glance toward the murdered man. He maintained that the secret was to refuse to acknowledge the reality. The friend whose fatal portrait had caused all his misery had vanished from his life. That sufficed. Suddenly he remembered the lamp—a curious Moorish piece of dull silver worked with arabesques of burnished steel and dotted with rough turquoises. Perhaps his servant might notice its absence and start asking questions. He hesitated briefly, then went back to take it from the table. He could not avoid seeing the lifeless figure. How motionless it lay! How ghastly white the long hands appeared! It resembled some hideous wax effigy. After locking the door again, he crept quietly down the stairs. The woodwork creaked, complaining as though in torment. He paused repeatedly to listen. No, all was still. It was nothing but the echo of his own steps. Reaching the library, he spotted the bag and coat in the corner. They had to be hidden. He opened a secret press built into the wainscoting, the same place where he kept his odd disguises, and placed them inside. They could easily be burned later. He took out his watch: twenty minutes to two. He sat and began to think. Year after year—almost month by month—men in England were hanged for what he had just done. Murder seemed within the air, as though some red star had drawn too near the earth.... Yet what proof existed against him? Basil Hallward had left at eleven; no one had witnessed his return. Most of the servants were away at Selby Royal. His valet was asleep.... Paris! Of course. That was where Basil had gone—by the midnight train, just as he had planned. With his strange reserve, suspicions would not rise for months. Months! Everything could be destroyed well before that. A sudden idea jolted him. He put on his fur coat and hat and stepped into the hall. There he halted, hearing the slow, heavy tread of a policeman passing outside and watching the bull’s-eye flash on the window. He waited, holding his breath. After a few minutes he lifted the latch, slipped out, and closed the door softly behind him. Then he began to ring the bell."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b84c3ac3f0396fec96aa484c","rewritten_text":"Saturday nights brought our village a delightful feeling of tidying up and pausing quietly before beginning life anew, and that feeling emboldened Joe to linger half an hour later than usual. When the extra half-hour and the rum-and-water ran dry together, Joe rose to leave and took my hand. “Hold a moment, Mr. Gargery,” said the odd man. “I’m sure there’s a bright new shilling somewhere in my pocket, and if there is, the lad shall have it.” He fished it out from a fistful of small change, wrapped it in wrinkled paper, and handed it to me. “Yours!” he declared. “Remember! All your own.” I thanked him, staring so long that good manners were forgotten, and clung tight to Joe. He bade Joe good-night, wished Mr. Wopsle the same (for he went out with us), and bestowed on me nothing but the intention of his aiming eye—not even that, for he shut it; yet wonders can be worked with an eye by hiding it. Walking home, had I been inclined to chatter, the conversation would have been entirely mine, as Mr. Wopsle left us at the Jolly Bargemen’s door, and Joe trudged home with his mouth gaping, to let as much air as possible wash the rum away. But I was heavy-headed, overwhelmed by the resurfacing of my old misdeed and old acquaintance, and could think of nothing else. My sister was not particularly cross when we appeared in the kitchen, and Joe took that rare mood as license to report the bright shilling. “A bad one, I’ll wager,” cried Mrs. Joe triumphantly, “or he wouldn’t have given it to the boy! Let’s see.” I unfolded the paper, and the coin was sound. “But what’s this?” exclaimed Mrs. Joe, tossing the shilling aside and snatching up the paper. “Two One-Pound notes?” Nothing less than two plump, sweating pound notes, as though they had long fraternized with every cattle market in the county. Joe snatched his hat and ran to the Jolly Bargemen to return them. While he was away, I settled on my usual stool and stared blankly at my sister, fairly certain we would not find the man there. Soon Joe came back to say the man had gone, but he had left word at the Three Jolly Bargemen about the notes."}

{"request_id":"ee012da4c83fdd4b328cb520","rewritten_text":"“I should warn you that I’m going to tell Sybil everything. She’s coming to lunch with me tomorrow to talk about hats, and if Mr. Podgers discovers that you have a bad temper, or a tendency toward gout, or a wife stashed away in Bayswater, I will certainly pass all of it on to her.”

Lord Arthur smiled and shook his head. “I’m not worried,” he said. “Sybil knows me as well as I know her.”

“Oh, I’m a bit sorry you said that. The best foundation for marriage is mutual misunderstanding. No, I’m not being cynical, I’ve simply lived a little, which amounts to the same thing. Mr. Podgers, Lord Arthur Savile is dying to have his palm read. Don’t bother telling him he’s engaged to one of the most beautiful girls in London, because that was in the Morning Post a month ago.”

“Dear Lady Windermere,” cried the Marchioness of Jedburgh, “please let Mr. Podgers stay with me a little longer. He’s just told me I ought to go on the stage, and I’m fascinated.”

“If he’s told you that, Lady Jedburgh, I’ll certainly take him away. Come here at once, Mr. Podgers, and read Lord Arthur’s hand.”

“Well,” said Lady Jedburgh, making a small pout as she rose from the sofa, “if I’m not allowed to go on the stage, I should at least be allowed to watch.”

“Of course; we’re all going to watch,” said Lady Windermere. “And now, Mr. Podgers, do tell us something pleasant. Lord Arthur is one of my special favorites.”

But when Mr. Podgers saw Lord Arthur’s palm he turned strangely pale and kept silent. A shudder ran through him, and his thick eyebrows twitched convulsively, in that odd, irritating way they did when he was confused. Huge beads of sweat broke out on his sallow forehead like some poisonous dew, and his plump fingers turned cold and clammy.

Lord Arthur noticed these unsettling signs, and for the first time in his life, he felt afraid. He wanted to bolt from the room, but he held himself back. Better to know the worst, whatever it might be, than endure this horrible uncertainty.

“I’m waiting, Mr. Podgers,” he said.

“We’re all waiting,” snapped Lady Windermere, but the palm reader still said nothing.

“I’m convinced Arthur is destined for the stage,” said Lady Jedburgh, “and after your scolding, Mr. Podgers is afraid to tell him.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"9522d6c3e0359f3e742e1f68","rewritten_text":"Raymond was energized by the intense sensation of regained health; he felt that serving as general of the Athenians gave him a role worthy of his ambition, and in his hope of conquering Constantinople he counted on creating an event that would stand as a landmark in the ages, an exploit unmatched in human history. A city rich with historic association, its beautiful location celebrated throughout the world, had been the stronghold of the Moslems for centuries; he believed it would soon be rescued from slavery and barbarism and returned to a people distinguished for genius, civilization, and the spirit of liberty. Perdita rested on his restored companionship, on his love, his hopes, and his fame, as comfortably as a Sybarite on a luxurious couch; every thought brought delight, each emotion seemed bathed in a congenial and soft element.\n\nWe arrived at Kishan on the seventh of July. The weather during our journey had been clear. Each day, before dawn, we left our night camp and watched the shadows retreat from hill and valley while the sun’s golden approach spread. The soldiers with us, full of national vivacity, took enthusiastic pleasure in the beauty of nature. The rising of the sun was greeted with triumphant music, while birds, heard in brief intervals, filled the spaces between the tunes. At noon we pitched our tents in some shady valley or wooded hollow among the mountains, while a stream babbling over pebbles lulled us into grateful sleep. Our evening march, calmer, was even more delightful than the restless energy of the morning. When the band played, they instinctively chose melodies of moderated passion; the farewell of love or the lament for absence would be followed and ended by a solemn hymn that suited the gentle loveliness of evening and raised our minds to grand, religious thoughts. Often all sounds ceased so we could listen to the nightingale, while fireflies danced in bright patterns and the soft cooing of the aziolo promised fair weather to the travelers. If we passed a valley, gentle shadows surrounded us, and rocks were tinted with beautiful colors. If we crossed a mountain, Greece lay below like a living map, its famous peaks cutting the sky, its rivers threading silver lines through fertile land. Almost afraid to breathe, we English travelers gazed in ecstasy at this splendid landscape, so different from the muted tones and melancholy graces of our homeland. When we left Macedonia, the fertile yet low plains of Thrace offered fewer beauties, yet the journey stayed interesting. An advanced guard announced our approach, and the country people quickly moved to honor Lord Raymond."}

content.text: {"request_id":"c3f85a0fb3d16a0192ac8702","rewritten_text":"Without pausing to consider, and hardly aware of her own feelings, Elizabeth, upon finishing this letter, immediately snatched up the other and, opening it with extreme impatience, read the following: it was dated a day later than the end of the first. \n\n“By now, my dearest sister, you will have received the hurried note I sent before. I hope this one is clearer, yet though I am not pressed for time, my head is so confused that I cannot promise coherence. Dearest Lizzy, I hardly know what to say, but I have unpleasant news and cannot delay it. Foolish as a marriage between Mr. Wickham and our poor Lydia would be, we are now eager to know it has actually happened, for there is too much reason to fear they never went to Scotland. Colonel Forster arrived yesterday, having left Brighton the day prior, only a few hours after the express. Although Lydia’s brief note to Mrs. F. led them to believe they were headed to Gretna Green, Denny let slip that he believed W. never meant to go there or to marry Lydia at all, and this was repeated to Colonel F., who, instantly alarmed, set out from B., intending to follow their trail. He easily traced them to Clapham, but no farther, for upon entering that town they transferred to a hackney-coach and dismissed the chaise that had brought them from Epsom. All that is known after that is that they were seen continuing on the London road. I am at a loss what to believe. After making every possible inquiry on that side of London, Colonel F. came through into Hertfordshire, diligently repeating his questions at every turnpike, and at the inns at Barnet and Hatfield, yet to no avail—no such persons had passed. With the warmest concern he proceeded to Longbourn and shared his fears with us in a way that does him great credit. I truly pity him and Mrs. F., though no blame can be laid on them. Our distress, dear Lizzy, is extreme. My father and mother imagine the worst, but I cannot think so badly of him. Many circumstances might make a private wedding in town more suitable than continuing with their first plan; and even if he could conceive such a scheme against a girl of Lydia’s connections, which seems unlikely, could she be so lost to all propriety? Impossible! I am pained, however, to find that Colonel F. is not inclined to trust in their marriage: he shook his head when I voiced my hopes and said he feared W. was not a man to be depended on.”"}

{"request_id":"46caa002e0bfdcd465ff068d","rewritten_text":"Looking at him, you would have said Nemesis had snatched Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed turned to stone, his face marble in its sorrow. He had lived the delicate, luxurious life of a young man with rank and money, a life exquisite in its freedom from sordid worry, its beautiful boyish carelessness; and now, for the first time, he became aware of Destiny’s terrible mystery, of Doom’s awful meaning.

How insane and monstrous it all seemed! Could it be that written on his hand, in characters he himself could not read but another could decipher, was some terrible secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime? Was there truly no escape? Were we nothing more than chess pieces moved by an unseen power, vessels the potter shapes at his whim, for honor or for shame? His reason rebelled against it, yet he felt some tragedy hanging over him, that he had been suddenly summoned to bear an unbearable burden. Actors are so fortunate. They can choose whether to appear in tragedy or in comedy, whether to suffer or to revel, to laugh or to weep. But real life is different. Most men and women are forced to play parts for which they have no talent. Our Guildensterns play Hamlet for us, and our Hamlets have to jest like Prince Hal. The world is a stage, but the play is badly cast.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers entered the room. When he saw Lord Arthur he started, and his coarse, fleshy face turned a sort of greenish yellow. The two men locked eyes, and for a moment there was silence.

“The Duchess left one of her gloves here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to bring it to her,” said Mr. Podgers at last. “Ah, I see it on the sofa! Good evening.”

“Mr. Podgers, I insist on your giving me a direct answer to a question I’m about to ask.”

“Another time, Lord Arthur. The Duchess is anxious. I’m afraid I must go.”

“You’re not leaving. The Duchess isn’t in any hurry.”

“Ladies should not be kept waiting, Lord Arthur,” said Mr. Podgers with his sickly smile. “The fair sex tends to lose patience.”

Lord Arthur’s finely cut lips curled in irritated scorn. Just then, the poor Duchess seemed to him of no importance at all. He crossed the room to where Mr. Podgers stood and held out his hand.

“Tell me what you saw there,” he said. “Tell me the truth. I must know. I’m not a child.”"}

{"request_id":"3d60fb291b954106e9e14db0","rewritten_text":"Because of this, I decided to get out as soon as we reached the town and remove myself from his hearing. I carried out this plan without trouble. My small portmanteau was in the boot under my feet; I only had to turn a hinge to pull it out. I dropped it in front of me, followed it down, and found myself standing under the first lamp on the first stones of the town pavement. The convicts stayed with the coach, and I knew where they would be taken to the river. In my mind, I saw the boat with its convict crew waiting at the slime-covered steps, heard again the rough “Give way, you!” like an order to dogs, and saw once more the evil-looking Noah’s Ark resting on the black water.

I could not have said what I feared, because my fear was undefined and vague, but it held me strongly. As I walked toward the hotel, I felt a dread far beyond simply meeting someone unpleasant that made me shake. I am sure it never took a clear shape and that it revived for a few minutes the terror of my childhood.

The coffee-room at the Blue Boar was empty, and I not only ordered dinner there but had started eating before the waiter recognized me. Once he apologized for forgetting me, he asked if he should send Boots for Mr. Pumblechook.

“No,” I said, “certainly not.”

The waiter—the same one who had delivered the Great Remonstrance from the Commercials on the day I was apprenticed—looked surprised and soon slid a dirty old copy of the local paper directly in front of me. I picked it up and read this paragraph:

“Our readers will hear with some interest, concerning the recent romantic rise in fortune of a young ironworker from this area (what a subject, by the way, for the magical pen of our not yet fully appreciated townsman TOOBY, the poet of our columns!), that the youth’s earliest patron, companion, and friend was a highly respected person not entirely disconnected from the corn and seed trade, and whose very convenient and spacious business premises lie within one hundred miles of the High Street. It is not without personal pride that we record HIM as the Mentor of our young Telemachus, for it is good to know that our town produced the founder of the latter’s fortunes.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"6420b95c69dd734039c63957","rewritten_text":"For a moment I was too amazed to think clearly. I knew my planned design differed in detail from this one, even though the general shapes were somewhat alike. Soon I took a candle, sat at the other end of the room, and examined the parchment more closely. When I turned it over, I saw my own sketch on the back, exactly as I had drawn it. At first I was only astonished by the striking similarity in outline—the odd coincidence that, without my knowledge, a skull would be on the other side of the parchment, right beneath my picture of the scarab, and that this skull, in both outline and size, would match my drawing so closely. The strangeness of the coincidence entirely stunned me for a time. Coincidences often act this way. The mind tries to find a connection, a cause and effect, and, unable to do so, falls into a kind of temporary paralysis. Yet when I recovered from this stupor, a new conviction slowly emerged, one that startled me even more than the coincidence itself. I began to remember clearly—positively—that there had been no drawing on the parchment when I sketched the scarab. I was absolutely sure of it; I recalled turning first one side and then the other, hunting for the cleanest spot. Had the skull been there, I certainly would have noticed it. Here was a mystery I could not explain; but even then, there was a faint glow—like a glow-worm—in the deepest corners of my mind, an early hint of the truth that last night’s adventure displayed so brilliantly. I stood up at once, put the parchment away safely, and put off further thought until I could be alone.\n\n“When you had gone, and Jupiter was fast asleep, I began a more methodical study of the matter. First I considered how the parchment came into my hands. The spot where we found the scarab was on the mainland shore, about a mile east of the island, and only a short distance above the high tide line. When I picked it up, it bit me sharply, making me drop it. Jupiter, being his cautious self, before seizing the insect—which had flown toward him—looked around for a leaf or something similar to use to handle it."}

In that pointless unease and anguish of spirit, I would wander the streets at dusk, passing those offices and houses where I’d left the appeals. To this day, the tired western streets of London on a cold, dusty spring night, with their lines of severe, shuttered mansions and their endless ranks of lamps, remain sorrowful to me from that association.

My daily visits to him were curtailed now, and he was kept under stricter watch. Seeing, or imagining, that I was suspected of intending to carry him poison, I asked to be searched before sitting by his bedside, and told the officer always present that I was ready to do anything to convince him of the purity of my purpose. No one was severe with him or with me. There was duty to be done, and it was done, though not harshly. The officer constantly assured me he was worse, and the other sick prisoners in the room, along with the prisoners attending them as nurses—criminals, yet not without kindness, thank God!—always echoed the same news.

As the days passed, I observed ever more that he would lie calmly, gazing at the white ceiling, with no light in his face until some word of mine lit it for a moment, only to fade again. At times he could barely speak, or not at all, and would respond with faint pressures of my hand, which I soon learned well enough to interpret.

The count of days had reached ten when I saw a greater change in him than ever before. His eyes turned toward the door and brightened as I entered.

“Dear boy,” he said when I sat by his bed. “I thought you’d come late. But I knowed you couldn’t be that.”

“It is just the time,” I replied. “I waited for it at the gate.”

“You always waits at the gate; don’t you, dear boy?”

“Yes. So as not to lose a minute.”

“Thank’ee, dear boy, thank’ee. God bless you! You’ve never forsaken me, dear boy.”

I squeezed his hand silently, unable to forget that I had once meant to forsake him.

“And what’s best of all,” he said, “you’ve been more at ease with me when I lay under a dark cloud than when the sun was bright.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"cbc361fd4bf6554f7e4bf8bd","rewritten_text":"He slipped furtively out of the wainscoting, a wicked smile twisting his cruel, lined mouth, and the moon veiled herself in a cloud as he crept past the great oriel window where his own arms and those of his murdered wife shone in azure and gold. Still he glided onward, like some baleful shadow, the very darkness seeming to recoil from him as he went. Once he fancied he heard a cry and halted, but it proved only the hound from the Red Farm baying, so he continued, muttering queer sixteenth-century imprecations and now and then flourishing the rusty dagger through the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the passage leading to unlucky Washington’s room. He paused there for an instant, the wind tossing his long grey locks about his head and twisting into grotesque folds the indescribable horror of the dead man’s shroud. Then the clock struck the quarter, and he knew the hour had come. He chuckled softly and turned the corner; yet scarcely had he done so when, with a piteous cry of dread, he recoiled and hid his blanched face in his lean, bony hands. Directly before him stood a ghastly apparition, motionless as carved stone, monstrous as some lunatic’s dream. Its head was bald and burnished; its face round, bloated, and white; hideous laughter seemed to have contorted its features into an everlasting grin. From its eyes poured rays of crimson light, its mouth gaped like a fiery well, and a dreadful garment, akin to his own, wrapped its Titan frame in voiceless snows. Across its breast hung a placard inscribed with strange letters of antique fashion—a scroll of disgrace, a record of wild transgressions, some awful register of crime—and in its right hand it upheld a falchion of gleaming steel.\n\nHaving never beheld a ghost before, he was naturally seized with profound terror, and after a second hurried glance at the dreadful apparition, he bolted back to his room, tangling himself in his long winding-sheet as he raced down the corridor, and finally dropping the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jack-boots, where the butler discovered it next morning. Once within his own chamber, he flung himself onto a narrow pallet-bed and buried his face beneath the coverings. After a time, however, the stout old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to speak with the other ghost as soon as daylight came. Thus, just as dawn was silvering the hills, he made his way once more to the spot where he had first seen the grisly phantom, convinced that, after all, two ghosts were better than one, and that with his newfound ally he might safely tackle the twins."}

{"request_id":"404dcbcaa281281caf4cb020","rewritten_text":"When Mr. Hiram B. Otis, the American Minister, bought Canterville Chase, everyone said he was making a foolish choice because the place was definitely haunted. Lord Canterville himself, a man of strict honour, felt obliged to mention this to Mr. Otis when they discussed the purchase.

“We have not cared to live there,” said Lord Canterville, “since my grandaunt, the Dowager Duchess of Bolton, was frightened into a seizure—one from which she never truly recovered—when two skeletal hands were laid on her shoulders as she dressed for dinner. I must tell you, Mr. Otis, that several living members of my family have seen the ghost, as has the rector of the parish, the Reverend Augustus Dampier, a fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. After the poor Duchess’s accident, none of our younger servants would stay, and Lady Canterville lost much sleep because of the strange noises coming from the corridor and the library.”

“My lord,” answered the Minister, “I will take the furniture and the ghost at their price. I come from a modern country where we have everything money can buy, and with our lively young men painting the Old World red and running away with your best actresses and prima donnas, I’m sure that if there were a ghost in Europe, we would have it at home very soon, either in one of our public museums or travelling as a show.”

“I am afraid the ghost is real,” said Lord Canterville, smiling, “even if it has ignored the offers of your daring impresarios. It has been known for three centuries—since 1584, in fact—and it always appears before a member of our family dies.”

“Well, so does the family doctor, Lord Canterville. But there is no such thing as a ghost, and I don’t believe the laws of nature will be suspended for the British aristocracy.”

“You are certainly very matter-of-fact in America,” replied Lord Canterville, who did not quite understand Mr. Otis’s last remark. “If you do not mind a ghost in the house, that is fine. Just remember I warned you.”

A few weeks later, the purchase was completed, and at the end of the season the Minister and his family moved into Canterville Chase. Mrs. Otis—formerly Miss Lucretia R. Tappan of West 53rd Street, a celebrated New York beauty—was now a very handsome middle-aged woman with fine eyes and a striking profile."}

{"request_id":"9eacd2f939f7443a1c19b592","rewritten_text":"In the morning they found her lifeless in bed, having apparently slipped away without suffering. Sir Mathew Reid had been summoned at once, yet naturally nothing could be done, and her burial was arranged for the twenty-second at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death she had drawn up her will, leaving Lord Arthur her little house in Curzon Street along with all her furniture, personal possessions, and paintings, except for her miniature collection, which was destined for her sister, Lady Margaret Rufford, and her amethyst necklace, which she bequeathed to Sybil Merton. The estate was not worth much, but Mr. Mansfield, the lawyer, was particularly anxious that Lord Arthur return immediately, if possible, since a great number of bills awaited settlement, and Lady Clementina had never kept proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s thoughtful remembrance, and felt Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Nevertheless his devotion to Sybil eclipsed every other feeling, and the awareness that he had fulfilled his duty filled him with serenity and solace. Reaching Charing Cross, he felt entirely content.

The Mertons welcomed him with genuine warmth. Sybil exacted a promise that nothing should ever again come between them, and their wedding was fixed for the seventh of June. Life once more appeared bright and splendid to him, and all his former happiness returned.

Yet one afternoon, while he was inspecting the Curzon Street house with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of faded letters and emptying drawers of miscellaneous trifles, the young woman suddenly gave a little cry of pleasure.

“What have you discovered, Sybil?” asked Lord Arthur, glancing up from his task and smiling.

“This charming little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it quaint and Dutch? Do let me keep it! I’m sure amethysts won’t suit me until I’m well past eighty.”

It was the box that had once contained the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, a faint flush rising to his face. He had almost forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as oddly fitting that Sybil, for whom he had endured such dreadful tension, should be the one to remind him of it first.

“Of course you may have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur; and might I have the bonbon as well? I never dreamed Lady Clementina cared for sweets. I imagined she was far too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a ghastly thought flashed through his mind."}

{"request_id":"a3b18df41b9e79fe6ea00628","rewritten_text":"After sharing in the general lament over the dreadful result Elizabeth now regarded as nearly inevitable, and which Miss Bennet could not declare entirely impossible, the former resumed the topic: “But tell me every detail I have not yet heard. I want more particulars. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they no suspicion before the flight occurred? They must have been constantly together.”

“Colonel Forster admitted he had often suspected some preference, particularly on Lydia’s part, yet nothing alarming. I am truly sorry for him. He behaved with the utmost attention and kindness. He _was_ coming to us to express his concern before he had the least notion they had not gone to Scotland; once that fear spread, it sped his journey.”

“And did Denny remain convinced Wickham would not marry? Did he know they meant to run off? Had Colonel Forster seen Denny himself?”

“Yes; yet when questioned by _him_, Denny denied any knowledge of their scheme and refused his true opinion. He did not repeat his assurance they would never wed, and from _that_ I am inclined to hope he might have been misunderstood earlier.”

“And until Colonel Forster arrived, none of you suspected they were not truly married?”

“How could such an idea occur to us? I was a little uneasy—slightly fearful for my sister’s happiness with him in wedlock, because I knew his behaviour had not always been entirely correct. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they only perceived the imprudence of the match. Kitty then confessed, with very natural triumph at knowing more than we did, that in Lydia’s last letter she had been prepared for such a measure. She had known, it seems, of their being enamoured for many weeks.”

“But not before going to Brighton?”

“No, I think not.”

“And did Colonel Forster seem to think ill of Wickham himself? Is he aware of Wickham’s true character?”

“I must admit he did not speak as favourably of Wickham as formerly. He considered him imprudent and extravagant; and since this wretched business occurred, it is reported he quitted Meryton heavily in debt—but I hope that is untrue.”

“Oh, Jane, had we been less silent—had we told what we knew of him—this would never have happened!”

“Perhaps it might have been better,” her sister replied.

“But to expose any person’s past faults without knowing their current sentiments appeared unjustifiable.”"}

{"request_id":"ef58b442699868d19115c58a","rewritten_text":"It was well past midday before he awoke. His valet had glided in several times on tiptoe to see if he stirred, puzzled at what kept his young master abed so late. At last the bell sounded, and Victor entered quietly with a cup of tea and a stack of letters, all arranged on a small tray of old Sèvres porcelain, and drew back the olive satin curtains with their shimmering blue lining before the three tall windows.

“Monsieur has slept admirably this morning,” he remarked with a smile.

“What is the time, Victor?” Dorian Gray asked, still heavy with sleep.

“One hour and a quarter after noon, Monsieur.”

How late indeed! He sat upright, took a sip of tea, and began sorting through his correspondence. One note, delivered by hand that morning, was from Lord Henry. He hesitated briefly, then set it aside. The remaining letters he opened without interest. They contained the usual mix of visiting cards, dinner invitations, tickets to private viewings, programmes for charity concerts, and other such things showered upon young men of fashion every season morning. There was a rather hefty bill for a chased silver Louis Quinze dressing set he had yet to pluck up courage to forward to his guardians, who were so staunchly old-fashioned they did not understand that we live in an era when unnecessary objects are our sole necessities; and there were several very politely phrased notes from Jermyn Street money-lenders, offering instant advances of any amount at the most moderate interest.

After some ten minutes he rose, wrapped himself in an elaborate dressing gown of silk-embroidered cashmere, and moved into the onyx-floored bathroom. The cool water revived him after his prolonged sleep. He seemed to have forgotten all he had endured. Once or twice a faint sense of having been involved in some strange tragedy crossed his mind, yet it all possessed the unreality of a dream.

Fully dressed, he went into the library and sat down to a light French breakfast set for him on a small round table near the open window. The day was exquisite. The warm air seemed saturated with spices. A bee flew in and circled the blue-dragon bowl filled with sulphur-yellow roses before him. He felt entirely content.

Suddenly his gaze fell on the screen he had positioned in front of the portrait, and he gave a start.

“Too cold for Monsieur?” the valet asked, placing an omelette on the table. “Shall I close the window?”

Dorian shook his head. “I am not cold,” he murmured."}

content.text:
{"request_id":"9e3368261c22abbd86afecc7","rewritten_text":"During my younger years discontent never crossed my mind, and whenever boredom threatened, the beauty of nature or the study of humanity’s finest and most sublime works always stirred my heart and lifted my spirits. Now I’m a blasted tree; the lightning has struck my soul, and I felt then that I would live on only to display what I would soon stop being—a miserable example of ruined humanity, pitied by others and unbearable to myself.

We spent quite some time at Oxford, wandering its surroundings and trying to identify every place connected to the most inspiring period of English history. Our little expeditions often stretched on as new sights appeared. We visited the tomb of the illustrious Hampden and the field where that patriot fell. For a moment my soul rose above its degrading, miserable fears to consider the sacred ideals of liberty and self-sacrifice these monuments commemorated. For an instant I dared to shake off my chains and look around with a free, noble spirit, but the iron had bitten deep, and I sank back, trembling and hopeless, into my wretched self.

We left Oxford reluctantly and headed to Matlock, our next stop. The countryside around the village resembled Swiss scenery more than anything else, though everything was on a smaller scale, and the green hills lacked the distant white Alpine crowns that always accompany the pine-clad mountains of my homeland. We toured the astonishing cave and the little natural history cabinets, where the curiosities were arranged just as they are in the collections at Servox and Chamounix. Hearing that last name spoken by Henry made me shudder, and I hurried to leave Matlock, which now seemed tied to that terrible memory.

From Derby we continued north and spent two months in Cumberland and Westmorland. I could almost imagine myself among the Swiss mountains again. The small patches of snow that still clung to the northern slopes, the lakes, and the crashing rocky streams were all familiar and beloved sights. We made acquaintances there who nearly persuaded me I was happy. Clerval’s joy was even greater than mine; his mind opened up in the company of men of talent, and he discovered in himself more abilities and resources than he’d ever suspected while keeping to his inferiors."}

{"request_id":"9c948e95ae75eaf22a006a1b","rewritten_text":"Such were the happenings that gnawed at Felix’s heart and made him, when I first met him, the most desolate member of his family. Poverty alone he could have borne—indeed, while want had been the reward of his virtue, he took pride in it—but the Turk’s ingratitude and the loss of beloved Safie were afflictions sharper and beyond remedy. Now, however, the Arabian’s arrival breathed new vigor into his spirit.

Once the tidings reached Leghorn that Felix had been stripped of fortune and rank, the merchant ordered his daughter to dismiss every thought of her lover and get ready to return to her native land. Safie’s generous soul rebelled against such commands; she tried to reason with her father, but he angrily departed, repeating his despotic decree.

A few days later the Turk entered his daughter’s rooms and abruptly informed her that he had grounds to think his presence in Leghorn had been exposed and that he would soon be seized by the French authorities; therefore he had secured a vessel bound for Constantinople, on which he intended to sail within hours. He planned to leave his daughter with a trusted servant, who was to follow when she pleased, bringing most of his property, which had not yet been transported to Leghorn.

Left alone, Safie pondered what course of action would best suit this crisis. The idea of living in Turkey repelled her; both her faith and her feelings were opposed to it. Among some papers of her father’s that fell into her possession she learned of her lover’s banishment and discovered the name of the place where he now lived. She wavered for a time, but in the end fixed her resolve. Taking certain jewels that were hers and a sum of money, she left Italy accompanied by an attendant native to Leghorn, who spoke the common tongue of Turkey, and set out for Germany.

She arrived safely at a town some twenty leagues from De Lacey’s cottage, when her companion was seized with a dangerous illness. Safie tended her with devoted care, yet the unfortunate girl died, leaving the Arabian alone, unable to speak the country’s language and wholly unversed in the customs of the world. She nevertheless found herself among kind people. The Italian had revealed the name of their destination, and after her death the mistress of the house where they had boarded ensured that Safie reached her lover’s cottage unharmed."}

{"request_id":"a21d74176a2f0e4b7e09a728","rewritten_text":"Three or four months went by, and winter had set in for real. I’d been going to school almost every day and could spell, read, and write a little. I could recite the multiplication table up to six times seven is thirty-five, and I doubt I’d ever get any farther even if I lived forever. I don’t care much for math anyway.

At first I hated school, but after a while I learned to put up with it. Whenever I got too bored I’d skip, and the beating I got the next day actually did me good and perked me up. The longer I went to school, the easier it got. I was getting used to the widow’s ways, too, and they didn’t chafe me so much anymore. Living in a house and sleeping in a bed still pulled on me pretty hard, but before the cold weather hit I used to sneak out to sleep in the woods sometimes, which felt like a relief. I liked the old ways best, but I was starting to like the new ones a bit too. The widow said I was coming along slow but steady, and doing very well. She said she wasn’t ashamed of me.

One morning at breakfast I accidentally knocked over the salt cellar. I grabbed for the salt as fast as I could to toss some over my left shoulder and ward off bad luck, but Miss Watson beat me to it and slapped my hand away. She said, “Take your hands off that, Huckleberry; what a mess you’re always making!” The widow spoke up for me, but I knew that wouldn’t keep the bad luck away. After breakfast I went out feeling nervous and shaky, wondering when it was going to hit me and what it would be. There are ways to fend off some kinds of bad luck, but not this kind, so I didn’t do anything except shuffle along gloomy and watchful.

I went down to the front garden and climbed over the stile where you pass through the tall board fence. There was about an inch of fresh snow, and I saw some tracks. They had come up from the quarry, lingered around the stile for a while, and then moved on around the garden fence. It was strange that whoever it was hadn’t come in after hanging around like that. I couldn’t make sense of it. It was really curious somehow. I was about to follow the tracks around, but I bent down to take a closer look at them first."}

{"request_id":"a2fb3dd74e9eeee476f8097c","rewritten_text":"“Well, well, Mr. Bumble,” he said at last, “since the new feeding system began, the coffins are indeed narrower and shallower than before; but we must make some profit, Mr. Bumble. Well-seasoned timber is costly, sir, and all the iron handles come by canal from Birmingham.”

“Well, well,” said Mr. Bumble, “every trade has its drawbacks. A fair profit is certainly allowed.”

“Of course, of course,” the undertaker replied. “And if I don’t make money on one item, I make it up later, you see—he! he! he!”

“Exactly so,” said Mr. Bumble.

“Though I must say,” continued the undertaker, picking up the thread Mr. Bumble had broken, “I must say, Mr. Bumble, I face one great disadvantage: all the stout people die the fastest. Those who have been better off and paid rates for years are the first to sink when they come into the house. And let me tell you, Mr. Bumble, that three or four inches over one’s estimate cuts deeply into one’s profits, especially when one has a family to support, sir.”

As Mr. Sowerberry spoke with the rightful anger of a man ill-used, and as Mr. Bumble felt it hinted at the parish’s honor, the latter thought it wise to change the subject. With Oliver Twist on his mind, he turned to him.

“By the bye,” said Mr. Bumble, “you don’t know anyone who wants a boy, do you? A parish apprentice who’s currently a dead weight, a millstone, so to speak, around the parish’s neck? Liberal terms, Mr. Sowerberry, liberal terms?” As he spoke, Mr. Bumble lifted his cane and tapped three times on the words “five pounds,” printed above him in huge Roman letters.

“Gadso!” exclaimed the undertaker, taking Mr. Bumble by the gilt-edged lapel of his official coat. “That’s exactly what I wanted to discuss with you. You know—dear me, what an extremely fine button this is, Mr. Bumble! I never noticed it before.”

“Yes, I think it rather attractive,” said the beadle, looking proudly at the large brass buttons on his coat. “The design is the same as the parish seal—the Good Samaritan healing the injured man. The board gave it to me on New Year’s morning, Mr. Sowerberry. I remember wearing it for the first time when I attended the inquest on that ruined tradesman who died in a doorway at midnight.”"}

{"request_id":"34be6060f67164d00b3b4cd1","rewritten_text":"I command you, spirits of the departed, and you, wandering agents of vengeance, to strengthen and guide me in my task. Let the accursed, infernal creature quaff the bitterness of agony; let him endure the despair that now preys on me.”

I began this curse with such solemn reverence that it seemed my slain companions heard and approved my dedication, yet by the end the furies mastered me, and rage strangled my speech.

Out of the night’s stillness came an answering peal—a loud, demonic laugh. It lingered upon my ears, the mountains gave it back, and I felt as if all hell enclosed me with scorn and mirth. In that instant I should have yielded to madness and ended my wretched life, had not my vow been acknowledged and my fate preserved for revenge. The laughter faded, and then a voice I knew and loathed, seeming close beside me, murmured distinctly, “I am satisfied, miserable wretch! You have resolved to live, and I am content.”

I sprang toward the spot from which the sound issued, but the fiend slipped from my grasp. Suddenly the full orb of the moon rose and revealed his ghastly, twisted form as he fled with more than human speed.

I pursued him, and for many months this has consumed me. With the faintest clue, I traced the windings of the Rhone in vain. The blue Mediterranean spread before me, and by a strange turn I saw the demon board by night and conceal himself in a vessel bound for the Black Sea. I secured passage on the same ship, yet he escaped me—I know not how.

Through the wilderness of Tartary and Russia, though he eluded capture, I followed his trail. Sometimes peasants, terrified by his abhorrent presence, indicated his route; sometimes he himself, fearing that I might lose him, despair, and die, left markers for my pursuit. Snow settled upon my head, and I saw the impression of his enormous stride across the white expanse. You who are just entering life, unfamiliar with care and untouched by anguish, how can you imagine what I have endured and still endure? Cold, hunger, and weariness were the lightest of my torments; a demon’s curse clung to me, and I bore my private inferno wherever I wandered; yet some benevolent spirit also accompanied and steered my course, and when I complained most bitterly, it would suddenly free me from seemingly insuperable perils. At times, when the body, overcome by starvation, faltered from exhaustion, a meal awaited me in the desolation that revived and emboldened me."}

{"request_id":"6eeeb0c82d3a743fabbaf56f","rewritten_text":"“Charles Evrémonde, known as Darnay,” was finally brought to trial.

His judges sat on the Bench wearing feathered hats; but everywhere else the rough red cap with its tricolor cockade dominated. Looking at the jury and the rowdy crowd, he might have thought the usual order of things was reversed—that criminals were judging honest men. The lowest, cruelest rabble of the city—any city’s supply of such people—controlled the room: chatter, cheers, jeers, predictions, and demands ran unchecked. Most of the men were armed with something; among the women, some carried knives or daggers, some ate and drank as they watched, many knitted. One of the knitters kept an extra piece of work tucked under her arm. She sat in the front row beside a man Darnay hadn’t seen since arriving at the Barrier, yet instantly recognized as Defarge. He noticed that she whispered to him once or twice and that she seemed to be his wife; but what struck him most about them was that though they sat as close to him as they could, they never looked at him. They waited for something with stubborn resolve, fixing their eyes on the jury and nowhere else. Below the President sat Doctor Manette, dressed as usual. As far as Darnay could tell, he and Mr. Lorry were the only people present unconnected to the Tribunal who wore their everyday clothes instead of the coarse Carmagnole outfit.

Charles Evrémonde, called Darnay, was charged by the public prosecutor as an emigrant, whose life was forfeit to the Republic under the decree that banished all emigrants on pain of Death. It didn’t matter that the decree was dated after his return to France. He was here, and the decree was here; he had been captured in France, and they demanded his head.

“Off with his head!” shouted the crowd. “An enemy of the Republic!”

The President rang his bell to quiet them and asked the prisoner if it was true he had lived many years in England.

Undeniably, it was.

Was he not then an emigrant? What did he call himself?

He hoped he was not, according to the meaning and intent of the law.

Why not, demanded the President.

Because he had willingly given up a title and position that repelled him and had left his country—he argued that this happened before the word emigrant was used with the Tribunal’s current meaning—to support himself in England by his own labor rather than live on the labor of France’s already overburdened people."}

{"request_id":"baa118783689a67fb431caaa","rewritten_text":"While these events unfolded in the country workhouse, Mr. Fagin sat in the old lair—the very one from which the girl had whisked Oliver away—musing over a dim, smoky fire. He balanced a pair of bellows on his knee, with which he had apparently tried to coax the coals into livelier blaze; yet he had sunk into profound thought, and, folding his arms atop it with his chin resting on his thumbs, stared absently at the corroded bars.

Behind him, the Artful Dodger, Master Charles Bates, and Mr. Chitling sat at a table, wholly absorbed in a whist match; the Dodger taking dummy against Master Bates and Mr. Chitling. The face of the first-named gentleman, always keen, assumed fresh interest through his close watch of the cards and his careful reading of Mr. Chitling’s hand; upon which, whenever opportunity arose, he cast a succession of intent glances, prudently directing his own play by what he perceived in his neighbor’s cards. As the night was cold, the Dodger kept his hat on, as he often did indoors. He also gripped a clay pipe between his teeth, removing it only briefly when he felt compelled to reach for the quart pot on the table, standing ready with gin-and-water for the party’s refreshment.

Master Bates likewise paid heed to the game; yet, being more high-strung than his accomplished associate, he resorted more often to the gin-and-water, and additionally indulged in numerous jokes and off-hand remarks, all sorely unfit for a serious rubber. Indeed, the Artful, relying on their close friendship, more than once seized the chance to lecture his companion soberly on such improprieties; every admonition Master Bates accepted with excellent temper, merely begging his friend to be “blowed,” or to thrust his head in a sack, or replying with some other neatly crafted quip of the same order, whose apt delivery stirred great admiration in Mr. Chitling. It was noteworthy that the latter gentleman and his partner unfailingly lost; and that this fact, far from irritating Master Bates, seemed to give him the highest delight, for he roared with laughter at the end of each hand and declared he had never witnessed so merry a game in all his born days.

“That makes two doubles and the rubber,” said Mr. Chitling, with a face miles long, as he pulled half-a-crown from his waistcoat pocket. “I never met such a chap as you, Jack; you scoop it all.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"aabf7fc4c78af05dbdeedbc9","rewritten_text":"It was early February, and after a month in Bath, Anne grew very eager for word from Uppercross and Lyme. She wanted much more than Mary had told her. Three weeks had passed since any news had come. All she knew was that Henrietta was back home, and that Louisa, though said to be recovering quickly, was still in Lyme. She was thinking of them all one evening when a thicker-than-usual letter from Mary arrived, delivered with Admiral and Mrs. Croft’s compliments, making the surprise and pleasure even greater. The Crofts must be in Bath! That interested her; her heart naturally turned toward them. “What is this?” cried Sir Walter. “The Crofts have arrived in Bath? The Crofts who rent Kellynch? What have they sent you?” “A letter from Uppercross Cottage, Sir.” “Oh! Those letters serve nicely as passports. They guarantee an introduction. I would have called on Admiral Croft anyway. I know what is due to my tenant.” Anne could listen no longer; she could not have said how the poor Admiral’s complexion survived. The letter absorbed her, and she saw it had been started several days earlier. “February 1st. “MY DEAR ANNE, I make no apology for being silent, because I know how little people care about letters in a place like Bath. You must be far too happy to mind Uppercross, which, as you know, offers little to write about. We had a very dull Christmas; Mr. and Mrs. Musgrove did not give a single dinner party during the holidays. I do not count the Hayters as anyone. The holidays are over at last: I believe no children ever had such long ones. I certainly did not. The house was cleared yesterday, except for the little Harvilles; but you will be surprised to hear they have never gone home. Mrs. Harville must be an odd mother to part with them for so long. I do not understand it. They are not pleasant children, in my opinion; but Mrs. Musgrove seems to like them as much as, if not more than, her own grandchildren. What dreadful weather we have had! Perhaps it is not noticed in Bath, with your neat pavements, but in the country it matters. No one has called on me since the second week of January, except Charles Hayter, and he has been calling far more often than welcome. Between ourselves, I think it is a great pity Henrietta did not stay in Lyme as long as Louisa; it would have kept her a little out of his way.”"}

{"request_id":"d4dd7f2b607993f0c8b8ac26","rewritten_text":"The doctor proved to be an elderly fellow; a very pleasant, gentle-looking old gentleman when I roused him. I told him me and my brother had been over on Spanish Island hunting yesterday afternoon, and we’d camped on a bit of raft we’d found, and around midnight he must have kicked his gun while dreaming, because it went off and hit him in the leg, and we wanted the doctor to go over there and patch him up and not breathe a word about it or let anyone find out, since we planned to come home this evening and surprise the folks.

“Who are your folks?” he asks.

“The Phelpses, down yonder.”

“Oh,” he says. After a pause he asks:

“How’d you say he got shot?”

“He had a dream,” I says, “and it shot him.”

“Queer sort of dream,” he says.

So he lit his lantern, grabbed his saddle-bags, and we set out. But when he spotted the canoe he didn’t like her looks—said she’d do for one person, but she didn’t seem safe for two. I says:

“Oh, don’t be uneasy, sir, she carried the three of us easy enough.”

“What three?”

“Why, me and Sid, and—and—and the guns; that’s what I mean.”

“Oh,” he says.

Still, he put his foot on the gunwale and rocked her, shook his head, and said he guessed he’d look for a bigger one. But they were all locked and chained up; so he took my canoe, told me to wait till he came back, or I could keep searching, or maybe I’d better head home and get them ready for the surprise if I fancied. But I said I wouldn’t; so I gave him exact directions how to find the raft, and off he went.

I struck on an idea soon after. I says to myself, suppose he can’t patch that leg in three shakes of a sheep’s tail, like the saying goes? Suppose it takes three or four days? What then? Do we sit there till he spills the secret? No, sir; I know what I’ll do. I’ll wait, and when he comes back, if he says he has to go again, I’ll get down there too, even if I’ve got to swim; and we’ll tie him up and hold him, and push off down the river; and once Tom’s through with him we’ll pay him what it’s worth, or everything we’ve got, and then let him reach shore.

After that I crawled into a lumber-pile to grab some sleep; and the next time I woke the sun was high overhead! I rushed out and headed for the doctor’s house, but they said he’d gone out sometime during the night and hadn’t come back yet."}

{"request_id":"dfe0974d58b2a88c05e575cd","rewritten_text":"“Starve me to death? Oh, Mr. Ghost—I mean Sir Simon—are you hungry? I have a sandwich in my bag. Do you want it?”

“No, thank you. I never eat anything now. But it’s very kind of you, all the same, and you’re much nicer than the rest of your dreadful, rude, vulgar, dishonest family.”

“Stop!” Virginia cried, stamping her foot. “You’re the one who’s rude and dreadful and vulgar, and as for dishonesty, you know perfectly well you stole the paints from my box to touch up that ridiculous bloodstain in the library. First you took all my reds, even the vermilion, so I couldn’t paint any more sunsets. Then you took the emerald green and the chrome yellow, and finally I had nothing left but indigo and Chinese white, so I could only paint moonlit scenes, which are always depressing to look at and not at all easy to paint. I never told on you, though I was very angry, and the whole thing was absurd—who ever heard of emerald-green blood?”

“Well, really,” said the Ghost, rather meekly, “what else could I do? It’s very hard to get real blood these days, and since your brother started it with his Paragon Detergent, I saw no reason why I shouldn’t use your paints. As for color, that’s a matter of taste. The Cantervilles have blue blood, the very bluest in England, but I know you Americans don’t care about such things.”

“You don’t know anything about it, and the best thing you can do is emigrate and broaden your mind. My father would be delighted to give you a free passage, and though there’s a high duty on spirits of every kind, there won’t be any trouble at Customs, because the officers are all Democrats. Once you’re in New York, you’ll be enormously popular. I know plenty of people who would pay a hundred thousand dollars to have a grandfather and much more than that to have a family ghost.”

“I don’t think I’d like America.”

“I suppose that’s because we have no ruins and no curiosities,” Virginia said sarcastically.

“No ruins! No curiosities!” the Ghost replied. “You have your navy—and your manners.”

“Good evening. I’ll go ask Papa to give the twins an extra week off school.”

“Please don’t go, Miss Virginia,” he cried. “I’m so lonely and so unhappy, and I really don’t know what to do. I want to go to sleep, and I can’t.”

“That’s ridiculous. You just go to bed and blow out the candle.”"}
