content.text: {"request_id":"72489608ecb2a3490e5f3ebf","rewritten_text":"He slipped silently out of the wainscoting, an evil smile twisting his cruel, wrinkled mouth, and the moon hid behind a cloud as he crept past the great oriel window where his own arms and those of his murdered wife were blazoned in azure and gold. On and on he glided like a malevolent shadow, even the darkness seeming to recoil as he went. Once he thought he heard someone call and stopped, but it was only the baying of a dog from the Red Farm, so he moved on, muttering strange sixteenth-century curses and now and then brandishing the rusty dagger in the midnight air. At last he reached the corner of the passage leading to unlucky Washington’s room. For a moment he paused there, the wind whipping his long gray locks around his head and twisting into grotesque folds the nameless horror of the dead man’s shroud. Then the clock struck the quarter hour, and he knew the moment had come. He chuckled to himself and rounded the corner—but no sooner had he turned than, with a pitiful wail of terror, he stumbled back and buried his blanched face in his long, bony hands. Right in front of him stood a ghastly apparition, motionless as a carved statue and monstrous as a madman’s dream. Its head was bald and gleaming, its face round and fat and white, and hideous laughter seemed to have twisted its features into an eternal grin. From its eyes streamed rays of scarlet light, its mouth was a wide pit of fire, and a ghastly robe, like his own, sheathed in silent whiteness that titanic form. On its chest hung a placard with strange writing in ancient characters—some scroll of disgrace, it seemed, some record of wild sins, some dreadful ledger of crime—and in its right hand it held aloft a falchion of gleaming steel.\n\nNever having seen another ghost before, he was naturally terrified, and after one more quick glance at the fearful phantom he fled back to his room, tripping over his long winding-sheet as he rushed down the corridor and finally dropping the rusty dagger into the Minister’s jackboots, where the butler found it in the morning. Once in the privacy of his chamber, he flung himself onto a narrow pallet bed and hid his face under the covers. After a while, however, the brave old Canterville spirit reasserted itself, and he resolved to go speak to the other ghost as soon as daylight came. So, just as dawn was silvering the hills, he returned to the spot where he had first seen the grisly phantom, feeling that, after all, two ghosts were better than one and that, with the help of his new ally, he might finally deal with the twins."}

{"request_id":"c8de1f99fc9ad38f1987d718","rewritten_text":"Yet my father remained beside me, consoling and chasing away the bitter recollections with radiant hopes: it seemed a tender pleasure to weep merely that he might brush away my tears.

Again he diverted my mourning by setting it beside the despair he had felt when my mother died. Even then I quailed at the portrait he sketched of his own passions: endowed with a poet’s fancy, he so animated his description of the tempest that had rent his feelings that his speech became living truth, and I believed while I shivered. I wondered how he could ever have resumed the ordinary duties of existence after thoughts so wild had allied him with something unearthly; while he spoke, the conceptions he communicated were so tremendous that the human heart seemed too narrow to contain them. His emotions appeared more fitting for a spirit whose dwelling is the earthquake and the volcano than for one bound to a mortal frame and human features. Yet these belonged to the past; he was altered now. He had become all affection and gentleness; and when I lifted my eyes in astonishment as he spoke, the smile on his lips showed me his heart was filled with the mildest feelings.

Two months after my aunt’s death we moved to London, where my father led me to engage in deeper studies than I had ever pursued. My progress was his joy; he remained with me through every lesson, assisting or sharing in each. We mingled much with society, and there was no day that he did not try to adorn with some fresh enjoyment. The tender devotion he bore me, together with the love and reverence I returned, cast an enchantment over every instant. The hours seemed slow because each minute was occupied; we lived more in a single week than many do in several months, and the variety and novelty of our pleasures added flavour to each.

We were forever taking excursions together. Whether it was to behold lovely landscapes, to view fine paintings, or simply to wander without plan in search of whatever diversion might arise, I was always content near my father. It grieved me whenever a third person joined us; yet if I turned toward him with a troubled expression, his gaze, fixed on me and shining with tenderness, instantly restored joy to my heart. O hours of fervent delight! Brief as ye were, ye stretch to the length of an entire life when I look back through the mist of sorrow that rose immediately afterward as though to veil you from my sight."}

{"request_id":"c9e75a889a91750f15f3f7cc","rewritten_text":"Mr. Merton was greatly troubled by the marriage being delayed a second time, and Lady Julia, having already ordered what she meant to wear, used every means to persuade Sybil to abandon the engagement. Yet Sybil, devoted as she was to her mother, had committed her whole life to Lord Arthur, and nothing Lady Julia urged could shake her trust. As for Lord Arthur, it was several days before he recovered from the crushing setback, and his nerves went quite to pieces for a while. His excellent common sense, however, soon reasserted itself, and his sound, practical mind left him in no doubt as to his next step. Poison having proved a thorough failure, dynamite or some other explosive was clearly the proper course.

He therefore ran through the list of his acquaintances again, and, after careful deliberation, resolved to blow up his uncle, the Dean of Chichester. The Dean, a man of wide culture and erudition, was particularly fond of clocks and had amassed an extraordinary collection of timepieces, from the fifteenth century down to the modern day, and Lord Arthur felt this passion of the worthy Dean’s provided an ideal opening for his plan. Where to obtain an explosive device was, of course, another matter entirely. The London Directory afforded him no guidance, and he considered it of little use to appeal to Scotland Yard, as they never appeared to know anything about the activities of the dynamitards until after a blast had occurred, and not much even then.

All at once he remembered his friend Rouvaloff, a young Russian with very revolutionary leanings, whom he had encountered at Lady Windermere’s during the winter. Count Rouvaloff was reputed to be writing a biography of Peter the Great, and to have come to England to examine the papers concerning the Tsar’s stay in this country as a shipwright; but it was widely believed he was actually a Nihilist agent, and the Russian Embassy certainly did not regard his presence in London with favour. Lord Arthur felt he was precisely the person he needed, and one morning drove down to his Bloomsbury lodgings to ask for counsel and aid.

‘So you have gone in for politics in earnest?’ said Count Rouvaloff, when Lord Arthur had explained why he had come; but Lord Arthur, who loathed any sort of swagger, was bound to confess that he took no interest in social problems, and wanted an explosive machine solely for a strictly family affair in which no one but himself was involved."}

{"request_id":"a0ef26e428b01e51e22904a0","rewritten_text":"Yesterday’s “Musée” carried that bitter tirade against Chantilly, where the satirist, making a few disgraceful remarks about the cobbler changing his name when he took to the stage, quoted a Latin line we have often discussed: Perdidit antiquum litera prima sonum. I had told you it referred to Orion, once written Urion; and because there is a sharp joke tied to that explanation, I knew it was impossible for you to have forgotten it. It was obvious you would connect Orion with Chantilly. I knew you had done so from the smile that crossed your face. You were picturing the poor cobbler’s sacrifice. Until then you had been bent over in your walk, but I saw you straighten to your full height. At that moment I was sure you were thinking about Chantilly’s tiny stature. I broke into your thoughts to remark that, since he truly was a very small fellow, he would fit better at the Théâtre des Variétés.

Soon after, we were reviewing an evening issue of the “Gazette des Tribunaux” when the following notice caught our eyes.

“Extraordinary Murders.—This morning, around three o’clock, the residents of Quartier St. Roch were jolted from sleep by a stream of terrible screams apparently coming from the fourth story of a house on Rue Morgue. The building was known to belong solely to Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, Mademoiselle Camille L’Espanaye. There was a delay when the initial attempts to gain entry in the usual way failed, but at last the gateway was broken with a crowbar, and eight or ten neighbors entered, joined by two gendarmes. By then the cries had stopped; yet as the group rushed up the first flight of stairs, they heard two or more rough voices in angry dispute, seeming to come from the upper part of the house. On reaching the second landing, those sounds also ceased, and everything fell perfectly still. The group spread out, hurrying from one room to another. When they reached a large back chamber on the fourth floor, they found the door locked with the key on the inside, so they forced it open. A sight awaited them that shocked everyone with both horror and astonishment.

“The room was in complete chaos. Furniture had been smashed and tossed everywhere. There was only one bedstead, and the mattress had been stripped from it and flung into the middle of the floor. A razor lay on a chair, its blade coated with blood.”"}

{"request_id":"b90be8ed621f6840276b9b8f","rewritten_text":"The heft of the insect was genuinely astonishing, and, all things considered, I could scarcely condemn Jupiter for his notion of it; yet how Legrand could be in accord with that notion baffled me entirely.

“I sent for you,” he began, with a lofty air, once I had finished examining the beetle, “I sent for you to gain your counsel and help in promoting the plans of Fate and of the bug—”

“My dear Legrand,” I broke in, “you are truly unwell and would do well to take precautions. You shall go to bed, and I will stay with you for a few days until you recover. You are feverish and—”

“Feel my pulse,” he said.

I felt it and, to be honest, found not the faintest hint of fever.

“But someone may be ill without fever. Let me prescribe just this once. First, go to bed. Next—”

“You are mistaken,” he cut in. “I am as well as one might expect, given the excitement I endure. If you truly wish me well, you must ease this agitation.”

“And how is that to be managed?”

“Quite simply. Jupiter and I are setting out on an expedition into the hills on the mainland, and for this expedition we need someone we can trust. You are the only person suitable. Whether we succeed or fail, the excitement you see in me will be calmed either way.”

“I’m eager to oblige you in any fashion,” I answered. “But do you mean this cursed beetle is tied to your trip into the hills?”

“It is.”

“Then, Legrand, I cannot lend myself to such an absurd enterprise.”

“I regret it—deeply—for we shall have to undertake it alone.”

“Do it alone! The man must be insane!—but wait!—how long do you expect to be away?”

“Most likely all night. We are leaving at once and shall return, in any event, by sunrise.”

“And will you pledge me, on your honor, that once this whim of yours is concluded and the bug affair (good heavens!) resolved to your liking, you will go home and follow my advice implicitly, as though it came from your physician?”

“Yes, I promise. Now let us go, for we have no time to waste.”

With a heavy heart I went along with my friend. We set out around four o’clock—Legrand, Jupiter, the dog, and myself. Jupiter carried the scythe and spades, insisting on bearing the whole set—more, it seemed to me, from fear of leaving any implement within his master’s reach than from any particular zeal or docility."}

{"request_id":"9ed54c2d4b648b977ed6e727","rewritten_text":"He was of low stature yet strikingly upright, and his voice was the most melodious I had ever heard. He opened his discourse with a review of the history of chemistry and the advancements brought about by various learned men, uttering with fervent emphasis the names of the foremost discoverers. He next gave a brief survey of the science in its present condition and clarified many of its fundamental terms. After conducting a few introductory experiments, he closed by delivering a eulogy on modern chemistry, the expressions of which are unforgettable to me:

“The old instructors of this discipline,” he declared, “vowed impossibilities and achieved nothing. The modern adepts promise scarcely anything; they are aware that metals cannot be changed into other metals and that the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands appear created only to plunge into dirt and whose eyes seem destined to peer through microscopes or into crucibles, have in truth wrought wonders. They pierce the hidden retreats of nature and reveal her operations in their secret haunts. They climb into the skies; they have worked out the circulation of the blood and the constitution of the air we inhale. They have gained fresh and nearly boundless powers; they can summon the thunderbolts of heaven, counterfeit the earthquake, and confront the unseen world with its own phantoms.”

Such were the professor’s utterances—rather, such were the words of fate, spoken for my ruin. While he continued, I felt as though my soul contended with a tangible foe; each key that composed the mechanism of my being was pressed in turn; note after note resounded, and swiftly my mind filled with a single idea, a single notion, a single aim. So much has already been accomplished, cried the spirit of Frankenstein—still more, immeasurably more, shall I accomplish; keeping to the footsteps that have been traced, I will blaze a new trail, probe uncharted forces, and unveil for mankind the most profound secrets of creation.

No sleep visited me that night. My inner self was in revolt and agitation; I sensed that order must spring from it, yet I lacked the strength to effect it. Gradually, after daybreak, slumber came. When I awoke, my thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. Only a determination remained—to return to my former studies and to consecrate myself to a science for which I believed I had an innate aptitude. That same day I called upon M. Waldman. In private his demeanour was even gentler and more engaging than before the public, for the dignity that marked him during his lectures was in his own home replaced by the utmost friendliness and warmth."}

{"request_id":"8794f9b4788410d034312907","rewritten_text":"Yet he kept one secret from his dear friends, a secret he had guarded since childhood. Although he loved his fellow collegians, he would not trust their delicate judgment or sympathy. He was in love. He feared they would mock the intensity of his passion, and he could not bear to have them profane it by calling it a brief or trivial fancy when to him it was the very core of his life.

A gentleman of modest means lived near his family estate and had three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the most beautiful, yet her beauty only enhanced her other qualities: her mind was clear and strong, and her disposition angelically gentle. She and my father had been playmates since infancy. Diana had been a favorite of his mother even as a child; this partiality grew with the years of the lively and lovely girl, and thus my father spent every school and college vacation constantly in her company. Novels and other means by which young people in civilized society learn about passions before they truly feel them had a powerful effect on him, as he was unusually receptive to every impression. At eleven Diana was his favorite playmate, yet he already spoke the language of love. Although she was nearly two years older, her education made her more childish, at least in knowledge and expression of feeling. She met his fervent declarations with innocence and returned them without understanding their meaning. She had read no novels and kept company only with her younger sisters. What chance had she to know the difference between love and friendship? When her maturing mind finally revealed the true nature of their relationship, her affection was already given to her friend, and her only fear was that other charms or his own fickleness might make him break his childish vows.

But each day their attachment grew more ardent and tender. It was a passion that had grown with his growth, entwined with every faculty and feeling, and could only end with his life. No one knew of their love except themselves. Yet although he dreaded the disapproval of his companions, who might scorn him for loving someone beneath him in fortune, nothing ever shook his resolve to marry her as soon as he could find the courage to face the obstacles he was determined to conquer.

Diana was fully worthy of his deepest affection."}

{"request_id":"02ce60e1379c8628b0f520cb","rewritten_text":"“What’s wrong?”

I said,

“Pap, and Mom, and Sis, and—”

Then I choked up. He said,

“Oh, darn it now, don’t take it so hard; we all have to face trouble, and this one’ll turn out fine. What’s happened to them?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the watchman on this boat?”

“Yeah,” he said, sounding downright pleased. “I’m the captain and the owner and the mate and the pilot and the watchman and the head deckhand; and sometimes I’m the freight and the passengers too. I’m not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be as blasted generous and nice to Tom, Dick, and Harry as he is, throwing money around like it’s nothing; but I’ve told him plenty of times I wouldn’t swap places with him, because, says I, a sailor’s life is the life for me, and I’ll be darned if I’d live two miles out of town where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and twice that besides. Says I—”

I cut in and said,

“They’re in a terrible lot of trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, Pap and Mom and Sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferry boat and head up there—”

“Head up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there’s only one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good heavens! What on earth are they doing there, for goodness’ sake?”

“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”

“I’ll bet they didn’t! Why, my Lord, they don’t stand a chance if they don’t get off real quick! How in the world did they ever get into a mess like that?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting up there in town—”

“Yeah, Booth’s Landing—keep going.”

“She was visiting at Booth’s Landing, and right toward evening she started across with her enslaved woman on the horse ferry to stay the night at her friend’s place, Miss What’s-her-name—I can’t remember—and they lost their steering oar, and swung around and drifted down, stern first, about two miles, and ran aground on the wreck, and the ferryman and the enslaved woman and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker grabbed hold and got onto the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we came drifting down in our trading scow, and it was so dark we didn’t see the wreck until we were right on top of it; so we ran aground too; but all of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best soul!—I almost wish it had been me instead, I do.”

“My word! That’s the most unbelievable thing I ever heard.”"}

{"request_id":"f83bc2d3db62a227747840a3","rewritten_text":"“Do you come back often?”

“I have never been here since.”

“Nor I.”

The moon began to rise, and I thought of that calm face turned to the white ceiling, now gone. The moon rose higher, and I thought of the pressure of his hand when I spoke the last words he ever heard.

Estella broke the silence between us.

“I have often wanted and planned to return, but many things stopped me. Poor, poor old place!”

The silver mist caught the first moonlight, and the same light shone on the tears that fell from her eyes. Not knowing I saw them, and trying to master them, she said quietly,

“Were you wondering, as you walked, how it came to be left like this?”

“Yes, Estella.”

“The ground belongs to me. It is the only thing I have kept. Everything else has slipped away bit by bit, but I held on to this. It was the only thing I fought for in all those miserable years.”

“Will they build on it?”

“At last, they will. I came to say goodbye before it changes. And you,” she added, her voice tender to a wanderer, “do you still live abroad?”

“Still.”

“And are doing well, I am sure?”

“I work hard enough for a decent living, and so—yes, I do well.”

“I have often thought of you,” Estella said.

“Have you?”

“Lately, very often. For a long hard time I kept away any memory of what I had thrown away when I didn’t know its value. But since duty no longer forbids that memory, I have given it a place in my heart.”

“You have always had your place in my heart,” I replied.

We were silent again until she spoke.

“I never thought,” Estella said, “that I would say goodbye to you while saying goodbye to this place. I am very glad to do so.”

“Glad to part again, Estella? Parting is painful to me. The memory of our last parting has always been sad and painful.”

“But you said to me,” Estella answered earnestly, “‘God bless you, God forgive you!’ If you could say that then, you won’t hesitate to say it now—now, when suffering has taught me more than anything else, and taught me what your heart once was. I have been bent and broken, but—I hope—into a better shape.”"}

{"request_id":"1baa460774d38e4fe3de15de","rewritten_text":"“Jupiter,” he said when we reached the tree’s base, “come here! Was the skull nailed to the branch facing outward, or turned toward the limb?”

“The face was out, massa, so the crows could reach the eyes easy, without trouble.”

“Then was it this eye or that eye where you dropped the beetle?” Legrand touched each of Jupiter’s eyes.

“It was this eye, massa—the left eye—just like you told me.” Yet he pointed to his right eye.

“That settles it—we must try again.”

My friend, whose madness now seemed to show a method, moved the peg marking where the beetle fell about three inches west of its previous spot. He measured from the trunk to the peg as before, then continued the straight line for fifty feet, marking a point several yards from where we had been digging.

Around this new spot he traced a circle, larger than the first, and we resumed work with the spades. I was exhausted, but somehow the change in my thoughts had removed much of my dislike for the task. I was strangely drawn in—even excited. Maybe something about Legrand’s wild behavior carried a hint of planning or calm that impressed me. I dug with enthusiasm, and now and then caught myself truly expecting the treasure that had obsessed my poor companion. While these odd thoughts held me fully, and after we had worked for perhaps an hour and a half, the dog’s fierce howling interrupted us again. At first, his restlessness had seemed playful or willful, but now it turned grim. When Jupiter tried to muzzle him again, the dog fought back, leaped into the hole, and tore at the soil furiously with his claws. In moments he revealed a pile of human bones, two full skeletons tangled together with several metal buttons and what looked like the dust of rotted wool. A few strokes of a spade unearthed the blade of a large Spanish knife, and as we dug deeper, three or four loose pieces of gold and silver coin appeared."}

{"request_id":"984d484e4f746f2936a22c76","rewritten_text":"“Unless you’re calling Miss Havisham a man. And I doubt even you would go that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up in town?” Joe said.

“Is there a Miss Havisham down in town?” my sister replied.

“She wants this boy to go play there. And of course he is going. And he had better go play there,” my sister said, shaking her head at me as if urging me to be very light and playful, “or I’ll deal with him.”

I had heard of Miss Havisham in town—everyone for miles around had heard of her—as an immensely rich, severe woman who lived in a large, gloomy house locked up against thieves and who lived in seclusion.

“Well, imagine that!” Joe said, astonished. “I wonder how she came to know Pip!”

“Idiot!” my sister cried. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Because some person,” Joe politely suggested again, “mentioned she wanted him to go there to play.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go there and play? Isn’t it just barely possible that Uncle Pumblechook is one of her tenants, and that he sometimes—we won’t say every quarter or half-year, because that would be asking too much of you—but sometimes—goes there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then ask Uncle Pumblechook if he knew of a boy to go play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, being always considerate and thoughtful for us—though you may not think so, Joseph,” she added in the most reproachful tone, as if he were the most heartless of nephews, “then recommend this boy, standing prancing here”—which I solemnly swear I was not doing—“to whom I’ve always been a willing slave?”

“Good again!” Uncle Pumblechook cried. “Well said! Nicely put! Excellent! Now Joseph, you know the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister continued reproachfully, while Joe apologized by rubbing the back of his hand across his nose over and over, “you do not yet—though you may not realize it—know the situation. You might think you do, but you do not, Joseph. Because you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, sensible that for all we know this boy’s fortune might be made by going to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him into town tonight in his own chaise-cart, keep him overnight, and take him with his own hands to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lord have mercy on me!” my sister cried, flinging off her bonnet in sudden despair, “here I am talking to a pair of Mooncalves, with Uncle Pumblechook waiting, the mare catching cold at the door, and the boy filthy with soot and dirt from the hair on his head to the soles of his feet!”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"fcd7976aafca93c39172b2b5","rewritten_text":"Mr. Attorney-General had to tell the jury that the prisoner before them, though young, had long been involved in treason, which now put his life at risk. This correspondence with the public enemy was not a matter of today, yesterday, last year, or even the year before. It was certain that for longer than that, the prisoner had been traveling back and forth between France and England on secret business he could not honestly explain. If treason ever prospered—which fortunately it never did—the true wickedness of his work might have stayed hidden. But Providence had moved a person beyond fear or reproach to discover the prisoner’s schemes and, horrified, report them to his Majesty’s Chief Secretary of State and most honourable Privy Council. This patriot would be presented to them. His position and bearing were, overall, sublime. He had once been the prisoner’s friend, but when he discovered his infamy in a moment both fortunate and terrible, he resolved to sacrifice the traitor he could no longer hold close on the sacred altar of his country. If statues were awarded in Britain as in ancient Greece and Rome to public benefactors, this shining citizen would surely have one. Since they were not, he probably would not. Virtue—so the poets had observed in many passages the jury surely had at their fingertips (though their guilty expressions revealed they knew nothing of them)—was in some way contagious, especially the bright virtue called patriotism, or love of country. The noble example of this flawless and unassailable witness for the Crown, whom it was an honour even to mention, inspired the prisoner’s servant. That example planted in him a holy resolve to search his master’s desk drawers and pockets and hide his papers. Mr. Attorney-General expected to hear attempts to discredit this admirable servant, but as a rule he preferred him to his own brothers and sisters and honoured him more than his own father and mother. He confidently urged the jury to follow suit. The evidence of these two witnesses, along with the documents they would produce, would show that the prisoner had been supplied with lists of his Majesty’s forces and their locations and readiness by sea and land, leaving no doubt that he had routinely passed such information to an enemy power."}

{"request_id":"ac9762f5261dc1370eeaa362","rewritten_text":"“I won’t be dining at home tonight, so I shall have no need of you.”

“Very good, sir,” replied the servant, withdrawing.

“Now, Alan, we can’t waste a second. This chest weighs a ton! Let me carry it. You gather the rest.” His orders came fast, sharp; Campbell felt mastered by him. Together they left the room.

Upon reaching the upper landing, Dorian drew out the key, turned it in the lock, then paused, a cloud of distress crossing his expression. A tremor ran through him. “I don’t know that I can go in, Alan,” he whispered.

“That is of no consequence to me. I have no need of you,” Campbell answered icily.

Dorian pushed the door half open. Instantly he caught sight of his portrait’s face grinning in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay across the floor before it. He suddenly remembered that, for the first time in his life, he had neglected the previous night to conceal the cursed canvas and was about to dash forward when a shiver drove him back.

What was that disgusting crimson moisture beading, slick and gleaming, upon one of the painted hands, as though the canvas itself sweated blood? How awful it looked—more awful, it struck him for the instant, than the mute object he knew lay stretched upon the table, the object whose grotesquely distorted shadow on the mottled carpet told him it had not shifted, but remained precisely where he had left it.

Drawing a long breath, he forced the door wider and, eyes narrowed and head turned aside, stepped in swiftly, determined not to send even a single glance toward the corpse. Bending to snatch up the gold-and-purple drapery, he flung it completely over the picture.

He halted there, dreading to turn, his gaze fastening on the complex pattern before him. He heard Campbell hauling in the weighty chest, the irons, and the other apparatus demanded for his terrible task. A strange curiosity took him—had he and Basil Hallward ever encountered each other, and if they had, what impressions had passed between them?

“Leave me,” came the harsh voice behind him.

He wheeled and rushed out, just aware that the dead body had been shoved back into the chair and that Campbell stared into a slick yellow face. Descending the stairs, he caught the sound of the key turning again in the lock.

It was well after seven when Campbell returned to the library. His complexion was ashen, yet his composure perfect. “I have done what you asked,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"a66ddcf585daadd6eaf2bb9c","rewritten_text":"“She would make such a charming companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse concurred in everything, but added, “Our little friend Harriet Smith, for that matter, is another equally lovely young creature. You will like Harriet. Emma could not wish for a better companion than Harriet.”

“I am delighted to hear it—but only Jane Fairfax is known to be so accomplished and superior!—and precisely Emma’s age.”

This subject was talked over very cheerfully, and others of equal weight followed and faded away with the same concord; yet the evening did not end without a slight recurrence of agitation. The gruel arrived and offered abundant material for conversation—copious commendations and observations—decided assurances of its suitableness for every constitution, and some rather sharp invectives against the many households where it was rarely produced tolerably;—but, unfortunately, among the failures the daughter had to cite, the latest, and therefore the most vivid, was her own cook at South End, a young woman temporarily engaged, who never could apprehend what she meant by a basin of fine smooth gruel, thin, but not excessively so. However often she had wished for it and sent orders, nothing decent had ever been achieved. It was a perilous entry.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and fixing his eyes on her with tender concern.—The exclamation in Emma’s ear conveyed, “Ah! there is no end to the melancholy consequences of your going to South End. It is quite unfit to dwell upon.” And for a little time she hoped he would avoid speaking of it, that a silent pondering might restore his enjoyment of his own smooth gruel. After a pause of several minutes, though, he began:

“I shall always regret that you chose the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why must you regret it, sir?—I assure you, it benefited the children greatly.”

“And besides, if the sea was necessary, it ought not to have been South End. South End is unhealthy. Perry was astonished you had selected South End.”

“I know many people entertain that notion, but truly it is entirely a mistake, sir.—We were all perfectly healthy there, never experienced the slightest inconvenience from the mud; and Mr. Wingfield insists it is quite wrong to suppose the place unhealthy; and I am sure he is reliable, for he thoroughly understands the nature of the air, and his own brother and family have been there repeatedly.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if anywhere.—Perry spent a week at Cromer once, and he considers it the finest of all the sea-bathing places.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"1c23d1c672a29402f88aacc1","rewritten_text":"For an instant I was too astonished to reason clearly. I knew my design differed in its particulars from this one—though its general form bore a certain likeness. Soon I took up a candle, and seating myself at the opposite end of the room, examined the parchment more intently. On flipping it over, I saw my own sketch on the reverse, precisely as I had drawn it. My first reaction was simple amazement at the truly striking similarity of outline—at the curious accident that, unbeknown to me, there lay a skull on the other side of the parchment directly beneath my figure of the scarabæus, and that this skull matched my drawing not only in shape but in dimensions. I declare, the oddity of this coincidence completely stunned me for a while. This is a common effect of such coincidences. The mind strives to forge a link—to find a chain of cause and effect—and, failing, lapses into a kind of momentary numbness. Yet, once I emerged from the stupor, another conviction dawned on me gradually, startling me even more than the coincidence. I began distinctly, unequivocally, to recall that no drawing had appeared on the parchment when I made my sketch of the scarabæus. I grew utterly certain; I remembered turning up first one side, then the other, searching for the cleanest portion. Had the skull been there then, I must have observed it. Here, indeed, was a mystery I felt incapable of explaining; but even at that early stage, there seemed to flicker, deep in the most hidden recesses of my mind, a glow-worm spark of the truth which last night’s adventure later proved so splendidly. I rose at once, secured the parchment, and set aside all further speculation until I could be alone.\n\n“When you had left, and Jupiter was sound asleep, I undertook a more systematic inquiry into the matter. First of all, I reviewed the way the parchment had come into my hands. The spot where we found the scarabæus lay on the mainland coast, about a mile east of the island and only a short distance above the high-water line. When I grasped it, it nipped me smartly, causing me to drop it. Jupiter, with characteristic caution, before seizing the insect, which had flown towards him, looked around for a leaf—or something of the sort—with which to take hold of it.”"}

I long to return to my family and my home; and in exchange for any further information from me—considering the insight I can offer into many significant branches of physical and metaphysical science—I must request, through the influence of your honorable body, a pardon for the crime I committed in causing the death of the creditors when I left Rotterdam. This is the purpose of the present paper. Its bearer, a resident of the moon whom I persuaded and properly instructed to serve as my messenger to Earth, will await Your Excellencies’ decision and bring back the requested pardon, if it can be obtained in any fashion.

“I have the honor to be, etc., Your Excellencies’ very humble servant,

“HANS PFAALL.”

After finishing this extraordinary document, Professor Rub-a-dub dropped his pipe in pure shock, and Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, having removed his spectacles, wiped them, and placed them in his pocket, forgot both himself and his dignity so completely that he spun around three times on his heel in the purest astonishment and admiration. There was no doubt—the pardon must be secured. So swore Professor Rub-a-dub in a hearty oath, and so decided the illustrious Von Underduk, as he took the arm of his fellow scholar and, without a word, headed straight home to consider what steps to take. However, when they reached the burgomaster’s door, the professor dared to suggest that since the messenger had chosen to disappear—no doubt terrified by the fierce appearance of the burghers of Rotterdam—the pardon would be useless, as no one but a man from the moon would undertake a journey of such distance. The burgomaster agreed, and so the matter was finished. Rumors and theories, however, were far from over. The letter, once published, sparked endless chatter and speculation. Some of the self-important even made fools of themselves by declaring the whole affair nothing but a joke. But “hoax” seems to be a catchall term for these people, used for anything beyond their understanding. For my part, I do not see what evidence they rely on for such a claim. content.text: {"request_id":"fa8363d3ef4eecf2939ef0b1","rewritten_text":"They must matter to you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You don’t want people speaking of you as something vile and corrupt. Of course, you have your position, your wealth, and all that. But position and wealth aren’t everything. Understand, I don’t believe these rumors at all. At least, I can’t believe them when I look at you. Sin writes itself across a man’s face. It can’t be hidden. People talk about secret vices, but there’s no such thing. If a miserable man has a vice, it shows in the lines of his mouth, the droop of his eyelids, even the shape of his hands. Someone—I won’t mention his name, but you know him—came to me last year to sit for a portrait. I had never seen him before and hadn’t heard anything about him then, though I’ve heard plenty since. He offered an absurdly high price. I refused. There was something about the shape of his fingers that repelled me. Now I know I was right about him. His life is awful. But you, Dorian, with your pure, radiant, innocent face, and your astonishingly untroubled youth—I cannot believe anything against you. And yet I see you so rarely, and you never come to the studio now, and when I’m away from you, hearing all these hideous things people whisper about you, I don’t know what to think. Why is it, Dorian, that a man like the Duke of Berwick leaves a club room when you enter? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse either to visit you or to invite you into their homes? You used to be Lord Staveley’s friend. I met him at dinner last week. Your name came up in conversation, connected with the miniatures you’ve lent to the Dudley exhibition. Staveley curled his lip and said you might have the most refined artistic tastes, but that you were the sort of man no pure-hearted girl should be allowed to know, and no chaste woman should share a room with. I reminded him I was your friend and asked what he meant. He told me. He said it right there in front of everyone. It was dreadful! Why is your friendship so disastrous for young men? There was that poor boy in the Guards who killed himself. You were his close friend. Then there was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with a ruined name."}

content.text: {"request_id":"57bfb30b1823ac1b190f050d","rewritten_text":"Soon his voice rang out in something like a halloo. “How much fudder I got for go?” “How high up are you?” asked Legrand. “Ebber so fur,” the negro answered; “kin see de sky fru de tip ob de tree.” “Never mind the sky—pay attention to me. Look back along the trunk and count the limbs on this side beneath you. How many have you gone by?” “One, two, tree, four, fibe—I done pass fibe big limb on dis side, massa.” “Then climb one branch higher.” Within a few minutes the voice called again, declaring he had reached the seventh limb. “Now, Jup,” cried Legrand, plainly much agitated, “work your way out along that branch as far as you can; if anything odd catches your eye, let me know.” Whatever slight doubts I still harbored about my unfortunate friend’s sanity were finally dispelled; I could only conclude he was quite deranged, and began to worry in earnest about getting him home. While I was debating the best course, Jupiter’s voice came once more. “Mos’ afeard to go fur on dis limb—him dead limb pritty much all de way.” “You said the limb is dead, Jupiter?” Legrand cried, his voice shaky. “Yes, massa, dead as any door-nail—done for sartin—done depart dis life.” “In the name of heaven, what am I to do?” Legrand exclaimed in deep distress. “Do?” said I, glad for a chance to intervene. “Why, come home and go to bed. Come along!—be sensible. It’s late, and you remember your promise.” “Jupiter,” he shouted, ignoring me entirely, “do you hear?” “Yes, Massa Will, hear you plain enough.” “Then test the wood with your knife and tell me if it seems very rotten.” “Him rotten, massa, sure nuff,” the negro replied shortly, “but not so berry rotten as he might be. Could venture little ways on de limb by myself, dat’s true.” “By yourself?—what are you talking about?” “Mean de bug, sir. ’Tis _berry_ heavy bug. Spose I drop him down fus, den de limb won’t crack wid only one nigger.” “You infernal rascal!” Legrand cried, evidently relieved, “what nonsense is that? If you let that beetle fall I’ll wring your neck. Look here, Jupiter, do you hear me?” “Yes, massa; no need for hollerin’ so at poor nigger.” “Very well, then pay attention! If you will hazard the limb only as far as you judge safe, keeping the beetle secure, I’ll give you a silver dollar the instant you come down.”"}

{"request_id":"8c2c8ddc7cbac77aea1e7468","rewritten_text":"“What’s the trouble?”

I said, “Pap, and Mam, and Sis, and—” Then I broke down. He said, “Oh, dang it, don’t get so upset; we all have our troubles, and this one will come out all right. What’s wrong with them?”

“They’re—they’re—are you the boat’s watchman?”

“Yes,” he said, sounding pretty pleased. “I’m the captain, owner, mate, pilot, watchman, and head deckhand; and sometimes I’m the freight and the passengers, too. I’m not as rich as old Jim Hornback, and I can’t be as generous to Tom, Dick, and Harry as he is, throwing money around the way he does; but I’ve told him plenty of times I wouldn’t trade places. I said, a sailor’s life is the life for me, and I’m darned if I’d live two miles out of town where nothing ever happens, not for all his money and twice more on top. I said—”

I cut in and said, “They’re in terrible trouble, and—”

“Who is?”

“Why, Pap and Mam and Sis and Miss Hooker; and if you’d take your ferryboat and go up there—”

“Up where? Where are they?”

“On the wreck.”

“What wreck?”

“Why, there’s only one.”

“What, you don’t mean the Walter Scott?”

“Yes.”

“Good heavens! What are they doing there, for goodness’ sake?”

“Well, they didn’t go there on purpose.”

“I’ll bet they didn’t! Why, great goodness, they won’t stand a chance if they don’t get off quick! How in the world did they get into such a mess?”

“Easy enough. Miss Hooker was visiting up in the town—”

“Yes, Booth’s Landing—go on.”

“She was visiting there at Booth’s Landing, and near evening she set out with her Black woman in the horse ferry to stay overnight at her friend’s house, Miss What’s-her-name—I forget her name—and they lost their steering oar, swung around, and floated down stern first about two miles, and slammed into the wreck. The ferryman, the Black woman, and the horses were all lost, but Miss Hooker grabbed hold and got on the wreck. Well, about an hour after dark we came down in our trading scow, and it was so dark we didn’t notice the wreck till we were right on it; so we hit it too. All of us were saved except Bill Whipple—and oh, he was the best creature! I almost wish it had been me instead.”

“My George! It’s the strangest thing I ever ran into.”"}

{"request_id":"3637d0ac1f3ebfcb17605d36","rewritten_text":"When the wedding took place about three weeks later, St. Peter’s was packed with a crowd of fashionable people. The Dean of Chichester read the service with great solemnity, and everyone agreed they had never seen a more striking couple than the bride and groom. They were more than attractive—they were happy. Lord Arthur never once regretted what he had endured for Sybil, and she gave him the best gifts a woman can give a man—devotion, tenderness, and love. Their romance stayed alive despite daily life. They always felt young.

Some years later, after they had two beautiful children, Lady Windermere visited Alton Priory, a lovely old place that had been the Duke’s wedding gift to his son. One afternoon, she sat with Lady Arthur beneath a lime tree in the garden, watching the little boy and girl running up and down the rose walk like flickering sunbeams. Suddenly she took her hostess’s hand and asked, “Are you happy, Sybil?”

“Dear Lady Windermere, of course I’m happy. Aren’t you?”

“I have no time to be happy, Sybil. I always like the last person introduced to me, but once I really know them I usually grow bored.”

“Don’t your lions satisfy you, Lady Windermere?”

“Heavens, no! Lions are only amusing for one season. Once their manes are trimmed, they become the dullest creatures imaginable. Besides, they behave terribly if you’re truly kind to them. Do you remember that awful Mr. Podgers? He was a complete fraud. I didn’t mind that, and I even forgave him when he tried to borrow money, but I couldn’t tolerate his flirting with me. He made me detest palmistry. I’ve taken up telepathy now. It’s much more entertaining.”

“You mustn’t speak poorly of palmistry here, Lady Windermere; it’s the one topic Arthur doesn’t like people to joke about. I assure you he takes it very seriously.”

“You don’t mean he actually believes in it, Sybil?”

“Ask him, Lady Windermere—here he is.” Lord Arthur came up the garden path carrying a large bunch of yellow roses, his two children dancing around him.

“Lord Arthur?”

“Yes, Lady Windermere?”

“You can’t mean you believe in palmistry?”

“Of course I do,” the young man replied with a smile.

“But why?”

“Because I owe all the happiness of my life to it,” he said quietly, as he sank into a wicker chair."}

{"request_id":"209440b93e16765ce541db94","rewritten_text":"I thanked him and apologized. He replied, “Not at all,” and went on.

“Miss Havisham was now an heiress, and you may guess she was watched as a great prize. Her half-brother had plenty of money again, but between debts and renewed wildness he squandered it terribly once more. He and she clashed even more fiercely than he had with their father, and it is suspected he nursed a deep grudge against her for provoking their father’s anger. Now comes the cruel part of the story—only stopping, my dear Handel, to point out that a dinner napkin does not fit in a tumbler.”

Why I was trying to cram mine into my tumbler, I cannot explain. I only know I was, with a determination worthy of a better cause, working hard to squeeze it in. Again I thanked him and apologized, and again he cheerfully replied, “Not at all, I’m sure!” and continued.

“There appeared on the scene—say at the races, or the public balls, or wherever you please—a certain man who courted Miss Havisham. I never saw him (for this was five-and-twenty years ago, before you and I were, Handel), but my father often mentioned that he was a flashy man, suited to his purpose. Yet my father insists he could never be mistaken for a gentleman, except by ignorance or prejudice, because he holds that no man lacking a true gentleman’s heart was ever, since the world began, a true gentleman in manner. He says no varnish can hide the grain of the wood, and the more varnish you apply, the more the grain shows. Well! This man chased Miss Havisham closely and claimed to adore her. I believe she had not shown much tenderness before then; but whatever capacity she had broke out, and she loved him passionately. There is no doubt she worshiped him. He played upon her affection so methodically that he drew large sums of money from her, and persuaded her to buy her brother’s share in the brewery (weakly left to him by their father) at a huge price, arguing that when he became her husband he had to hold and run the whole concern. Your guardian was not in Miss Havisham’s confidence then, and she was too proud and too infatuated to take advice from anyone.”"}

{"request_id":"8690d07d304df90e0a5a3628","rewritten_text":"After a while we’d wake up and figure out what roused us, maybe spotting a steamboat chugging upstream so far away on the other side we couldn’t tell much about her except whether she was a stern-wheeler or a side-wheeler. Then for about an hour there’d be nothing to hear and nothing to see—just steady loneliness. Next you’d notice a raft slipping by way off yonder, maybe with some fellow chopping, because they’re almost always chopping on a raft; you’d see the axe flash and swing down—you don’t hear a thing; you see that axe rise again, and by the time it’s over the man’s head you finally hear the k’chunk—it took all that time to travel over the water. So we spent the day lazing around, listening to the silence. Once the fog got so thick the rafts and other craft going past were banging tin pans so the steamboats wouldn’t run them down. A scow or a raft came so close we could hear the men talking and cussing and laughing—clear as anything—but we couldn’t see a sign of them; it gave you the creeps; it was like spirits carrying on in midair. Jim said he figured it was spirits, but I said:

“No; spirits wouldn’t say, ‘Darn the darn fog.’”

As soon as it got dark we shoved off; when we reached the middle we left the raft alone and let the current take her wherever it pleased; then we lit our pipes, dangled our legs in the water, and talked about all sorts of things—we were always naked, day and night, whenever the mosquitoes allowed it—the new clothes Buck’s folks made for me were too fine to feel comfortable, and besides I never cared much for clothes anyway.

Sometimes we had that whole river to ourselves for the longest stretch. Over yonder were the banks and islands across the water, and maybe a spark or two—which meant a candle in a cabin window; and sometimes you’d see a spark or two on the water—on a raft or a scow, you know; and maybe you’d catch a fiddle tune or a song drifting over from one of those craft. Living on a raft is wonderful. We had the sky above us, sprinkled with stars, and we’d lie on our backs and stare up at them and argue whether they were made or just happened. Jim said they were made, but I said they simply happened; I figured it would take too long to make that many."}

{"request_id":"2bc89fb7e7260cf687ecd66e","rewritten_text":"“Good-bye, Uncle George. I’ll be late for lunch if I stay any longer. Thanks for the information. I like to know everything about new friends, and nothing about the old ones.”

“Where are you having lunch, Harry?”

“At Aunt Agatha’s. I invited myself and Mr. Gray. He’s her newest protégé.”

“Humph! Tell your Aunt Agatha to stop pestering me with charity requests. I’m fed up. The good woman thinks I have nothing better to do than write cheques for her silly whims.”

“Fine, Uncle George, I’ll tell her, but it will do no good. Philanthropic people lose all sense of real kindness. That’s how you spot them.”

The old gentleman growled in approval and rang for his servant. Lord Henry walked through the low arcade onto Burlington Street and headed toward Berkeley Square.

So that was the story of Dorian Gray’s family. Even told clumsily, it had stirred him with its hint of a strange, almost modern romance. A beautiful woman risking everything for a mad passion. A few wild weeks of happiness cut off by a hideous, treacherous crime. Months of silent agony, and then a child born in suffering. The mother taken by death, the boy left alone under the rule of an old, loveless man. Yes, it made an interesting background. It framed the lad, made him seem more perfect. Behind every exquisite thing lurked tragedy. Worlds had to labor so that even the humblest flower could bloom....

And how charming he had been at dinner the night before, with wide, startled eyes and lips parted in frightened pleasure as he sat across from him at the club, the red candle shades tinting the awakening wonder of his face a deeper rose. Talking to him was like playing a fine violin. He reacted to every touch of the bow.... There was something dangerously absorbing in wielding influence. Nothing else was like it. To project one’s soul into some graceful form and let it linger there for a moment; to hear one’s own ideas echoed back with the added music of passion and youth; to pour one’s temperament into another as if it were a subtle liquid or strange perfume—there was real joy in that, perhaps the most satisfying joy left in an age as narrow and vulgar as theirs, gross in its pleasures and common in its goals....

He was a marvellous type, this lad whom he had met by chance in Basil’s studio, or could be shaped into one, at least."}

I started talking slow and easy, as if I were just passing time; the oldest man alive couldn’t have figured out where I was starting from and guessed where I’d end up. “Boys, there are a lot of curious things about law, and custom, and usage, and all that, if you take a close look, and about the drift and progress of human opinion and movement, too. There are written laws—they die; but there are unwritten laws—those are eternal. Take the unwritten law of wages: it says they have to rise, little by little, straight through the centuries. And look how it works. We know what wages are now, here and there and all around; we take an average and call that today’s wage. We know what wages were a hundred years ago, and two hundred; that’s as far back as we can reach, but it’s enough to tell us the law of progress, the measure and rate of periodic increases. So without any documents to help us, we can come very close to figuring out what wages were three, four, and five hundred years ago. Good so far. Do we stop there? No. We stop looking back; we turn around and apply the law to the future. My friends, I can tell you what people’s wages will be at any future date you want to name, for hundreds of years.” “What, goodman, what!” “Yes. {"request_id":"3f9aaed5d5bc475228ad33b5","rewritten_text":"He was short but impressively upright, and his voice was the sweetest I had ever heard. He opened his lecture with a recap of chemistry’s history and the many improvements made by different learned men, passionately sounding the names of its most distinguished discoverers. He then gave a brief overview of the current state of the science and clarified several of its basic terms. After performing a few introductory experiments, he finished with praise for modern chemistry, in words I will never forget:

“The old teachers of this science,” he said, “promised the impossible and achieved nothing. The scientists of today promise very little; they know metals cannot be transmuted and the elixir of life is a fantasy. Yet these philosophers, whose hands seem destined only to dabble in dirt and whose eyes pore over microscopes or crucibles, have truly performed miracles. They penetrate nature’s recesses and show how she works in her hidden places. They rise into the heavens; they have discovered how blood circulates and the nature of the air we breathe. They have gained new and almost limitless powers; they can command heaven’s thunder, imitate the earthquake, and even tease the invisible world with its own shadows.”

Such were the professor’s words—or rather, let me say, the words of fate—pronounced to destroy me. As he spoke I felt as if my soul was struggling with a tangible enemy; one by one the different keys of my being were struck, chord after chord resonated, and soon my mind held only one thought, one idea, one goal. So much has been done, cried the soul of Frankenstein—more, far more, will I accomplish; following the paths already laid down, I will break new ground, discover unknown forces, and reveal to the world the deepest secrets of creation.

I did not close my eyes that night. My inner self was in rebellion and turmoil; I sensed order would arise from it, yet I could not bring it about. Little by little, after dawn, sleep came. When I awoke, my thoughts of the previous night seemed like a dream. All that remained was a resolve to return to my former studies and devote myself to a science for which I believed I had a natural gift. That same day I visited M. Waldman. In private his manners were even more gentle and appealing than in public, for the certain dignity he showed during his lecture was replaced in his own home by the greatest friendliness and kindness."}

{"request_id":"595904e5aa61efbb05926aa4","rewritten_text":"“I wish we had a donkey. The perfect scene would be all of us arriving on donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and me—with my dear husband walking beside us. I really must talk to him about buying one. In country life a donkey seems almost essential; no matter how many diversions a woman has, she cannot stay shut up indoors forever, and long walks are impractical—dust in summer, mud in winter.”

“You will not meet either between Donwell and Highbury. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and right now it is perfectly dry. Still, come on a donkey if you like. You can borrow Mrs. Cole’s. I want everything arranged exactly to your taste.”

“That I am sure you do. Indeed, I give you full credit, my good friend. Beneath that dry, blunt manner, I know you have the warmest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are a real humorist. Yes, believe me, Knightley, I am very aware of your attentiveness to me in this whole plan. You have found exactly what will please me.”

Mr. Knightley had another reason for avoiding a table in the shade. He wanted to convince Mr. Woodhouse, as well as Emma, to join the outing, and he knew that any of them sitting outside to eat would certainly make Mr. Woodhouse ill. Mr. Woodhouse must not be lured under the harmless excuse of a morning drive and a few hours at Donwell only to suffer for it afterward.

He was invited in good faith. No hidden dangers would reproach him for his easy trust. He agreed to go. He had not visited Donwell for two years. “Some fine morning he, Emma, and Harriet could go quite well; he could sit quietly with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls walked through the gardens. He did not think they could be damp at midday. He would greatly enjoy seeing the old house again and would be very glad to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any other neighbors. He saw no objection at all to his, Emma’s, and Harriet’s going there on some fine morning. He thought it very well done of Mr. Knightley to invite them—very kind and sensible—far better than dining out. He did not care for dining out.”

Mr. Knightley was lucky that everyone accepted at once. The invitation was so well received that it seemed, like Mrs. Elton, they each took the plan as a personal compliment. Emma and Harriet declared they expected great pleasure from it, and Mr. Weston, without being asked, promised to bring Frank over if possible—proof of appreciation and gratitude that could have been spared. Mr. Knightley then had to say he would be glad to see him, and Mr. Weston promised to write immediately and urge Frank to come with every argument he could muster."}

His nerves were completely shot, and he jumped at the slightest sound. For five days he stayed in his room, and eventually decided to give up on the bloodstain on the library floor. If the Otis family didn’t want it, they clearly didn’t deserve it. They obviously lived on a dull, material level of existence and were incapable of appreciating the symbolic value of sensuous phenomena. The issue of ghostly apparitions and the growth of astral bodies, however, was quite different and really outside his control. It was his solemn duty to appear in the corridor once a week, and to gibber from the large oriel window on the first and third Wednesday of each month, and he didn’t see how he could honorably get out of those duties. It was quite true that he had lived a wicked life, but on the other hand he was very conscientious in everything connected to the supernatural. For the next three Saturdays, therefore, he walked the corridor as usual between midnight and three in the morning, taking every possible precaution not to be heard or seen. He removed his boots, stepped as lightly as he could on the old worm-eaten boards, wore a large black velvet cloak, and made sure to use the Rising Sun Lubricator to oil his chains. I must admit it took him considerable effort to bring himself to adopt this last protective measure. Still, one night while the family was at dinner, he slipped into Mr. Otis’s bedroom and took the bottle. At first he felt a bit humiliated, but afterward he was sensible enough to realize that the invention had a lot to recommend it, and to some extent it served his purpose. Even so, he was not left in peace. Wires were constantly being stretched across the corridor, tripping him in the dark, and on one occasion, while dressed as “Black Isaac, or the Huntsman of Hogley Woods,” he suffered a serious fall after stepping on a butter-slide the twins had built from the entrance of the Tapestry Chamber to the top of the oak staircase. This final insult infuriated him so much that he resolved to make one last attempt to assert his dignity and social standing, and decided to visit the insolent young Etonians the next night in his famous role of “Reckless Rupert, or the Headless Earl.” He had not appeared in that disguise for more than seventy years, in fact not since he had so terrified pretty Lady Barbara Modish with it that she abruptly broke off her engagement to the present Lord Canterville’s grandfather and ran away to Gretna Green with handsome Jack Castleton, insisting that nothing on earth would make her marry into a family that allowed such a ghastly ghost to parade up and down the terrace at dusk."}

{"request_id":"a7784d4a8328371995635366","rewritten_text":"“Why, that’s how everybody does, Huck.”

“Tom, it don’t make any odds. I ain’t everybody, and I can’t abide it. It’s dreadful being so tied down. And vittles come so easy I don’t care for ’em that way. I’ve got to ask to go fishing; got to ask to go swimming—derned if I don’t have to beg leave for every last thing. Then I’ve got to talk so proper there ain’t no comfort in it—I have to sneak up in the attic and let loose awhile every day, just to get some savor, or I’d ’a’ died, Tom. The widder wouldn’t let me smoke; she wouldn’t let me holler, or gape, or stretch, or scratch before folks—” [Here a spasm of special vexation and grievance seized him]—“And dad fetch it, she prayed constant! Never saw such a woman! I _had_ to pull out, Tom—I just had to. Besides, that school’s fixing to open, and I’d ’a’ had to attend—well, I wouldn’t stand _that_, Tom. Looky here, Tom, being rich ain’t what it’s claimed to be. It’s nothing but fretting and fretting, sweating and sweating, and wishing you was dead all the while. These clothes suit me, this bar’l suits me, and I’m done shedding ’em. Tom, I wouldn’t have fallen into all this misery if it hadn’t been for that cash; now you take my share along with your own, and slip me a ten-center now and then—not too often, because I don’t set any store by a thing unless it’s tolerable hard to come by—and you go and plead me off with the widder.”

“Oh, Huck, you know I can’t. It wouldn’t be square; and besides, if you’ll just give this way a bit more of a try you’ll learn to like it.”

“Like it! Yes—like I’d enjoy a hot stove if I sat on it long enough. No, Tom, I won’t be rich, and I won’t live in those cussed smothery houses. I favor the woods, and the river, and hogsheads, and I’ll stick by ’em. Blame it! just as we’d got guns, and a cave, and everything fixed to rob, this dern foolishness had to rise up and spoil the whole layout!”

Tom caught his chance—

“See here, Huck, being rich sha’n’t keep me from turning robber.”

“No! Oh, good-licks; are you in real dead-wood earnest, Tom?”

“As dead earnest as I’m sitting here. But Huck, we can’t let you into the gang unless you’re respectable, you know.”

Huck’s gladness sank.

“Can’t let me in, Tom?”"}

{"request_id":"c4f5e3234e9fb142f50794fb","rewritten_text":"“You won’t, won’t you? Oh, you precious fool!”

“It’s being naughty, isn’t it, Oliver?” asked Charley Bates. “He’ll end up scragged, won’t he?”

“I don’t know what that means,” Oliver replied.

“Something like this, old fellow,” said Charley. He grabbed the end of his neckerchief, held it up, dropped his head to his shoulder, and made a strange noise through his teeth to show that scragging and hanging were the same thing.

“That’s what it means,” Charley said. “Look how he stares, Jack! I never saw such fun as this boy; he’ll be the death of me, I swear.” Master Charley Bates laughed hard again and returned to his pipe with tears in his eyes.

“You’ve been brought up badly,” said the Dodger, admiring his boots after Oliver polished them. “Fagin will make something of you, though, or you’ll be the first he ever had who turned out useless. You’d better start right away; you’ll take to the trade before you expect it, and you’re just wasting time, Oliver.”

Master Bates backed this up with various moral lectures of his own; and when those ran out, he and his friend Mr. Dawkins launched into a glowing description of all the pleasures in their line of work, adding plenty of hints that Oliver’s best move was to secure Fagin’s favor quickly by doing what they themselves had done.

“And always keep this in mind, Nolly,” said the Dodger, as the Jew’s key turned in the door above, “if you don’t take fogels and tickers—”

“What’s the use of talking like that?” Master Bates cut in. “He doesn’t know what you mean.”

“If you don’t take handkerchiefs and watches,” the Dodger explained in simpler terms, “some other guy will; so the people who lose them will still be worse off, and you’ll be worse off, too, and nobody will be a bit better except the chaps who grab them—and you’ve got just as much right to them as they do.”

“Of course, of course!” said the Jew, who had come in without Oliver noticing. “It’s all in a nutshell, my dear; a nutshell—take the Dodger’s word for it. Ha! ha! ha! He knows the catechism of his trade.”

The old man rubbed his hands with pleasure as he confirmed the Dodger’s logic, and chuckled with delight at his student’s skill.

The conversation went no further then, because the Jew had returned home with Miss Betsy and a gentleman Oliver had never seen, whom the Dodger greeted as Tom Chitling. After Tom lingered on the stairs to exchange a few flirtatious words with the lady, he came in at last."}

{"request_id":"3b872f80533f5b25a2a83f68","rewritten_text":"Why, we could probably spin a very dramatic superstition from this idea. I assume you’ll call the bug scarabaeus caput hominis, or something along that line—Natural History books are full of such names. But where are the antennae you mentioned?”

“The antennae!” said Legrand, who seemed to be getting inexplicably heated about the matter. “I’m sure you must see the antennae. I made them as clear as they are on the actual insect, and I think that should be enough.”

“All right, all right,” I said. “Maybe you did—still, I don’t see them.” I handed him the paper without further comment, not wanting to ruffle his temper, though I was amazed at how the situation had shifted. His bad mood confused me, and the drawing itself showed absolutely no antennae; in fact, the whole thing really did look a lot like the standard illustrations of a death’s-head.

He took the paper with clear irritation and was about to crumple it up, apparently to toss it in the fire, when a casual glance at the design seemed to seize his attention. In an instant his face flushed a deep red, and in another it went ghostly pale. For a few minutes he stayed where he was, studying the drawing closely. Finally he got up, took a candle from the table, and sat on a sea chest in the far corner of the room. There he examined the paper again, anxiously, turning it this way and that. He said nothing, and his behavior astonished me; but I thought it wiser not to aggravate his growing moodiness with any remarks. Soon he took a wallet from his coat pocket, placed the paper carefully inside, and put both into a desk, which he locked. He seemed calmer now, but his earlier excitement had vanished. He didn’t seem sulky so much as preoccupied. As the evening wore on he sank deeper into his reverie, and none of my attempts at conversation could break it. I had planned to spend the night in the hut, as I often did, but seeing my host in this state, I decided I ought to leave. He didn’t urge me to stay, yet when I left he shook my hand with even more warmth than usual.

About a month later (and during that time I hadn’t seen Legrand once), I was visited in Charleston by his man, Jupiter. I’d never seen the good old man look so downhearted, and I feared some serious misfortune had struck my friend."}

content.text: {"request_id":"82796fb4b1c8677c435e7bc3","rewritten_text":"No letter of consolation had ever been dispatched to Ireland. The omission had recoiled upon the head of the offender; when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no note of condolence arrived at Kellynch, thus giving full cause to believe the Dalrymples deemed the kinship at an end. How to mend this uneasy affair and be received once more as cousins was the problem, and it was not one which, in a judicious sense, either Lady Russell or Mr Elliot considered insignificant. “Family ties were always worth preserving; good society always worth courting; Lady Dalrymple had taken a house for three months in Laura Place, and would be living in proper style. She had been in Bath the preceding year, and Lady Russell had heard her praised as a delightful woman. It was highly desirable that the connection be renewed, if it might be achieved without any sacrifice of propriety on the Elliot side.” Sir Walter, nevertheless, must choose his own method, and ultimately penned a most polished letter of ample explanation, regret, and appeal to his right honourable cousin. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot could admire this letter, but it secured everything necessary by drawing three scribbled lines from the Dowager Viscountess: “She felt greatly honoured, and should be happy in their acquaintance.” The labour of the affair was ended; the pleasures began. They called in Laura Place, they displayed the cards of Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret wherever they would be most conspicuous; and “Our cousins in Laura Place,”—“Our cousin, Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret,” were topics for everyone. Anne was mortified. Even had Lady Dalrymple and her daughter been exceedingly agreeable, she would have been mortified by the commotion they raised; but they were nothing. There was no distinction of manners, accomplishments, or intellect. Lady Dalrymple bore the title of “a charming woman” simply because she had a smile and civil reply for each person. Miss Carteret, with even less to contribute, was so plain and so ungainly that only her birth gained her admittance at Camden Place. Lady Russell admitted she had anticipated something better; yet “the acquaintance was worth maintaining,” and when Anne dared voice her opinion of them to Mr Elliot, he agreed they amounted to nothing individually, but still insisted that, as relatives, as reputable society, as people who would draw other reputable society about them, they had their usefulness. Anne smiled and replied, “My notion of good company, Mr Elliot, is the company of intelligent, well-informed people, who have plenty to talk about; that is what I call good company.”"}

Why are you looking at that dark tree in the lane?” “I saw him there, the night she died.” “That wasn’t the last time either, Biddy?” “No; I have seen him there while we have been walking. It’s no use,” Biddy said, laying her hand on my arm as I was about to run out. “You know I wouldn’t deceive you. He wasn’t there a minute, and now he’s gone.” My anger flared at the thought that he still followed her, and I felt a deep hatred for him. I told her so, and that I would spend whatever it took to drive him from the area. She gradually calmed me, and told me how Joe loved me, how he never complained—she didn’t have to mention of whom, I knew—and always did his duty in his life, with a strong hand, quiet tongue, and gentle heart. “Indeed, it would be hard to praise him too much,” I said. “And Biddy, we must speak of these things often, because I shall be down here often now. I won’t leave poor Joe alone.” Biddy said not a word. “Biddy, don’t you hear me?” “Yes, Mr. Pip.” “Besides your calling me Mr. Pip, which I find poor manners, Biddy, what do you mean?” “What do I mean?” Biddy asked timidly. “Biddy,” I said, putting on a virtuous tone, “I must insist on knowing what you mean by this.” “By this?” said Biddy. “Don’t echo,” I retorted. “You didn’t use to echo, Biddy.” “Didn’t use to!” cried Biddy. “Oh, Mr. Pip! Didn’t!” Well! I thought I might give up that point as well. After another silent turn in the garden, I returned to the main subject. “Biddy,” I said, “I mentioned coming down here often to see Joe, and you answered with a very pointed silence. Please, Biddy, tell me why.” “Are you quite sure that you will come to see him often?” Biddy asked, stopping in the narrow garden path and looking at me with clear, honest eyes under the stars."}

{"request_id":"6bfabdd249f1ae07fcd93bf2","rewritten_text":"Tom managed to scrape the cupboard with it and was about to commence on the bureau when a summons came for him to dress for Sunday-school.

Mary handed him a tin basin of water and a cake of soap, and he stepped outside to the little bench by the door, set the basin down, dipped the soap once, and laid it aside. He rolled up his sleeves, poured the water gently onto the ground, then slipped back into the kitchen to rub his face industriously on the towel behind the door. But Mary snatched the towel away, saying:

“Now aren’t you ashamed, Tom. You mustn’t act that way. Water won’t harm you.”

Tom felt slightly taken aback. The basin was filled anew, and this time he lingered over it, collecting courage; he drew in a great breath and set to work. When he shuffled into the kitchen again with both eyes shut, feeling about for the towel, suds and water provided credible evidence on his face. Yet when he emerged from the towel he still failed inspection: the clean portion halted at his chin and jaw like a mask, while below stretched a gloomy sweep of untouched earth that ran down his front and around his neck. Mary seized control, and when she finished he was a man and a brother, color distinctions swept away; his soaked hair was neatly brushed, its short curls coaxed into a dainty, even arrangement. [He secretly worked the curls out with hard effort and plastered his hair flat to his head, for he thought curls effeminate and his own tormented him endlessly.] Mary fetched a suit that had been worn only on Sundays for two years—simply called his “other clothes”—which tells us all we need about his wardrobe. After he dressed, the girl put him in order: she buttoned his trim roundabout up to his chin, pulled his broad collar down over his shoulders, brushed him off, and set his speckled straw hat atop him. He looked greatly improved and extremely uncomfortable. He felt exactly as ill at ease as he appeared; whole garments and cleanliness pinched him. He hoped Mary would overlook his shoes, but that wish perished; she smeared them well with tallow, as was customary, and brought them forth. He lost his temper and complained that he was forever being driven to do what he least desired."}

{"request_id":"4a4ba7df0123f22e4532c430","rewritten_text":"At one point, though, the lieutenant asked why he had come so far over the ice in such an unusual vehicle.

His face immediately fell into profound darkness, and he answered, “To find someone who ran away from me.”

“And did the man you were chasing travel the same way?”

“Yes.”

“Then I think we saw him, because the day before we picked you up we spotted some dogs pulling a sledge with a man in it across the ice.”

This caught the stranger’s attention, and he asked countless questions about the route the demon, as he called him, had taken. Soon after, when he was alone with me, he said, “I’ve undoubtedly stirred up your curiosity, as well as that of these good people; but you’re too considerate to pry.”

“Certainly; it would be very rude and inhumane of me to trouble you with my questions.”

“And yet you rescued me from a strange and deadly situation; you kindly brought me back to life.”

Soon after this he asked whether I thought the breakup of the ice had destroyed the other sledge. I answered that I couldn’t say for sure, because the ice didn’t break until nearly midnight, and the traveler might have reached safety before then; but I couldn’t judge.

From then on a new vigor seemed to animate the stranger’s failing body. He showed the greatest urgency to be on deck to watch for the sledge that had appeared before; but I’ve convinced him to stay in the cabin, since he’s far too weak to endure the harsh air. I’ve promised that someone will keep watch for him and alert him immediately if anything new comes into view.

Such is my journal of this strange episode up to today. The stranger’s health has slowly improved, but he is very quiet and seems uneasy when anyone but me enters his cabin. Yet his manners are so gracious and gentle that the sailors are all interested in him, even though they’ve had little conversation with him. As for myself, I’m beginning to love him like a brother, and his constant deep sorrow fills me with sympathy and compassion. He must have been a noble soul in his better days, being so attractive and kind even now in ruin.

I told you in one of my letters, dear Margaret, that I expected to find no friend on the vast ocean; yet I have found a man who, before suffering crushed his spirit, I would have been delighted to call the brother of my heart."}
