“William Bird, tailor, testifies that he was one of the group who entered the house. He is English. Has lived in Paris two years. Was among the first to go up the stairs. Heard the argument. The gruff voice belonged to a Frenchman. Managed to catch several words but cannot recall them all now. Clearly heard ‘sacré’ and ‘mon Dieu.’ At that moment there was a noise like several people struggling—a scraping and scuffling. The shrill voice was very loud—louder than the gruff one. He is sure it was not an Englishman’s voice. It seemed to be German. Might have been a woman’s voice. Does not understand German.

“Four of the previously named witnesses, when recalled, testified that the door of the room where Mademoiselle L.’s body was found was locked from inside when they reached it. Everything was completely silent—no groans or any other sounds. When they forced the door, no one was inside. The windows, in both the front and back rooms, were shut and firmly fastened from within. A door between the two rooms was closed but not locked. The door leading from the front room into the hallway was locked, with the key inside. A small front room on the fourth floor at the head of the hallway was open, the door ajar. This room was packed with old beds, boxes, and similar items. These were carefully moved and searched. Not an inch of the house was left unchecked. Chimney sweeps were sent up and down the chimneys. The house had four stories with garrets (mansardes). A trapdoor on the roof was nailed down tightly—seemed not to have been opened in years. The witnesses gave varying estimates of the time between hearing the argument and breaking open the door—some as short as three minutes, some as long as five. The door was difficult to open.

“Alfonzo Garcio, undertaker, testifies that he lives on the Rue Morgue. He is Spanish. Was one of the party who entered the house. Did not go upstairs. Is nervous and feared the effects of agitation. Heard the argument. The gruff voice was that of a Frenchman. Could not make out the words. The shrill voice was that of an Englishman—he is certain of it.”"}

{"request_id":"3cac0e531e181ede8d4e398d","rewritten_text":"Were our lofty visions destined to vanish thus? Our title had proclaimed us “a little lower than the angels,” and lo, we proved no more enduring than ephemeral beings. We had styled ourselves “the paragon of animals,” yet behold—only a “quintessence of dust.” We lamented that the pyramids survived the embalmed forms of their ancient builders. Alas! even the humble shepherd’s straw hut we met along the road held within its frail frame a stronger promise of longevity than the entire human race. How could we square this melancholy transformation with our former aspirations and imagined powers?

Suddenly an inward voice, distinct and even, seemed to speak:—Thus was it decreed from eternity: the steeds that race with Time bore this hour and this fulfilment linked to them, ever since the void first yielded its burthen. Would you attempt to reverse the immutable ordinances of Necessity?

Mother of the world! Handmaid of the Almighty! eternal and unchanging Necessity! thou who with tireless fingers art forever weaving the inextricable chain of events!—I will not complain of thy workings. If my mortal mind cannot confess that all that exists is perfect; yet since whatever exists must be, I will sit amid the wreckage and smile. Verily we were born not for delight, but for submission and for hope.

Would the reader grow weary if I minutely chronicled our tedious pilgrimage from Paris to Geneva? Were I, day by day, to register in journal form the pressing miseries of our condition, could my hand achieve, or could language supply phrases sufficient, to declare the variety of our unhappiness—the jostling and piling of one woeful event upon another? Patience, oh reader! whoever thou art, wherever thou abidest—whether of spiritual lineage, or descended from some surviving pair—thy nature shall still be human, thy dwelling-place the earth; thou shalt peruse here the deeds of the extinct race, and shalt demand in astonishment whether they who endured what is set down before thee were beings of fragile flesh and tender organization like thyself. Most true, they were— therefore weep; for surely, solitary one, thou wilt be of kindly disposition; shed pitying tears; yet meanwhile lend thine ear to the narrative, and learn the actions and sufferings of those that came before thee.

Nevertheless the final occurrences that attended our passage through France were so crowded with uncanny horrors and dismal griefs that I dare not dwell upon them long. Were I to analyze every incident, each fleeting breath of a second would comprise a heart-rending history, whose slightest syllable would freeze the blood in thy young veins. It is fitting that I raise for thy instruction this memorial of the vanished race; but it is not meet that I drag thee through hospital wards or the hidden chambers of the charnel-house."}

{"request_id":"b9621fa28612766e3549007b","rewritten_text":"Mr. Wickham was so entirely satisfied with that conversation that he never again troubled himself, or annoyed his dear sister Elizabeth, by bringing it up, and she was pleased to see she had said enough to keep him quiet.

The day for his and Lydia’s departure soon arrived, and Mrs. Bennet had no choice but to accept the separation. Since her husband had no intention of following her scheme of the whole family going to Newcastle, the separation was likely to last at least a year.

“Oh, my dear Lydia,” she cried, “when will we meet again?”

“Oh, Lord! I have no idea. Not for two or three years, perhaps.”

“Write to me very often, my dear.”

“As often as I can. But you know married women never have much time for writing. My sisters can write to me. They’ll have nothing else to do.”

Mr. Wickham’s farewells were far more affectionate than his wife’s. He smiled, looked handsome, and said a great many pretty things.

“He is as fine a fellow,” said Mr. Bennet, as soon as they left the house, “as ever I saw. He simpers and smirks and charms us all. I am exceedingly proud of him. I challenge even Sir William Lucas to produce a more valuable son-in-law.”

Losing her daughter made Mrs. Bennet very low for several days.

“I often think,” she said, “that there is nothing so dreadful as parting from one’s friends. One feels so abandoned without them.”

“This is the result, you see, madam, of marrying off a daughter,” said Elizabeth. “It should make you more content that your other four remain single.”

“That’s not the case at all. Lydia isn’t leaving me because she is married; it is only because her husband’s regiment is so far away. If it had been closer, she wouldn’t have gone so soon.”

But the listless state this event had thrown her into was soon eased, and her mind revived with new hope, by a piece of news then beginning to spread. The housekeeper at Netherfield had been ordered to prepare for her master, who was arriving in a day or two to shoot there for several weeks. Mrs. Bennet became wholly agitated. She looked at Jane, smiled, and shook her head by turns.

“Well, well, so Mr. Bingley is coming down, sister,” (for it was Mrs. Philips who brought her the news). “Well, so much the better. Not that I care about it, of course. He is nothing to us, you know, and I am sure I never wish to see him again. However, he is very welcome to come to Netherfield if he likes.”"}

{"request_id":"d7289305cad4017e0b4b0758","rewritten_text":"At the sight of him, the Ourang-Outang instantly bounded through the chamber door, darted down the staircase, and then, through an unfortunately open window, leaped into the street.

The Frenchman chased it in desperation; the ape, still clutching the razor, paused now and again to look back and make grim gestures at its pursuer, until the man nearly overtook it, when it darted off once more. Thus the pursuit lasted for a considerable time. The streets lay utterly silent, for it was near three in the morning. While slipping into an alley behind the Rue Morgue, the runaway’s attention was caught by a light shining from the open window of Madame L’Espanaye’s room on the fourth floor. Dashing to the house, it spotted a lightning rod, scaled it with astounding speed, gripped the window shutter, which was flung wide against the wall, and used it to swing itself straight onto the bed’s headboard. The entire maneuver took less than a minute. As it entered, the Ourang-Outang kicked the shutter open once more.

Meanwhile, the sailor felt both relief and dread. He hoped to recapture the creature now, for it could scarcely escape the trap it had entered except by the rod, where he might intercept it on the descent. Yet he was deeply uneasy about what havoc it might wreak inside. This anxiety drove him to keep up the chase. A lightning rod is not difficult to climb, especially for a seaman; but once he reached the height of the window, which was far to his left, he could go no further, managing only to lean over enough to gain a glimpse into the room. At that sight he almost lost his grip from sheer horror. Now burst forth those dreadful shrieks in the night that had roused the sleepers of the Rue Morgue. Madame L’Espanaye and her daughter, dressed in their nightclothes, seemed to have been arranging some papers in the iron chest already mentioned, which had been rolled to the center of the chamber. It stood open, with its contents strewn on the floor beside it. The victims must have sat with their backs to the window, and from the interval between the creature’s entrance and the screams, it appears they did not notice it at once. The clapping of the shutter would naturally have been taken for the wind.

As the sailor peered in, the massive brute had gripped Madame L’Espanaye by the hair (which hung loose from recent combing) and was brandishing the razor about her face, mimicking a barber’s motions."}

content.text: {"request_id":"6aeff31f7c8821cfe9b1ca23","rewritten_text":"No imagination could capture how sublime this spectacle would have been if it had occurred in the darkness of night. Hell itself might have served as an apt comparison. Even as it was, my hair stood on end while I stared into the gaping depths, letting my mind descend, as if wandering through those strange vaulted halls, fiery gulfs, and red, gruesome chasms of hideous, unfathomable flame. I had truly escaped by a hair’s breadth. If the balloon had stayed in the cloud just a little longer—if I had not decided to dump ballast simply to avoid getting wet—I would have been ruined. Such dangers, though rarely considered, may be the greatest faced in ballooning. By this point, however, I was too high to worry about that anymore.\n\nI was rising fast, and by seven o’clock the barometer showed an altitude of nine and a half miles. Breathing became extremely difficult. My head throbbed, and after feeling dampness on my cheeks for some time, I realized it was blood pouring from my eardrums. My eyes troubled me as well; when I ran my hands over them, they felt distinctly swollen and pushed out of their sockets, and everything in the car—and even the balloon itself—looked warped. These symptoms were worse than I expected and frightened me. At that moment, rashly and without thinking, I tossed three five-pound bags of ballast out of the car. The sudden surge upward carried me too quickly, without gradual adjustment, into a highly rarefied layer of the atmosphere, and it nearly cost me my expedition and my life. A violent spasm seized me for more than five minutes, and even after it eased somewhat, I could draw breath only in short, gasping intervals, while blood streamed from my nose and ears and even trickled slightly from my eyes. The pigeons were in visible distress and fought to break free, while the cat cried miserably and staggered across the car with her tongue hanging out, as though poisoned. I realized too late how reckless I had been in dumping the ballast, and my panic was overwhelming. I expected nothing less than death—and death within minutes."}

content.text: {"request_id":"1cd0f2a89992a96ed969be27","rewritten_text":"Even reading about the luxury of the dead seemed amazing. He turned his attention to embroideries and to tapestries that served as frescoes in the cold rooms of the northern nations of Europe. As he studied the subject—he always had a remarkable ability to become completely absorbed in whatever he took up—he felt almost saddened by how time ruined beautiful, extraordinary things. He, at least, had escaped that. Summer followed summer, yellow jonquils bloomed and died again and again, nights of horror repeated their shame, yet he remained unchanged. No winter marked his face or stained his flowerlike bloom. How different it was with objects! Where had they gone? Where was the great crocus-colored robe, showing gods fighting giants, worked by brown-skinned girls for Athena’s pleasure? Where was the huge velarium Nero stretched across the Colosseum, that massive purple sail showing the starry sky and Apollo driving a chariot drawn by white, gold-reined steeds? He longed to see the curious table-napkins made for the Priest of the Sun, which displayed every dish needed for a feast; the mortuary cloth of King Chilperic, with its three hundred golden bees; the fantastical robes that angered the Bishop of Pontus and were decorated with “lions, panthers, bears, dogs, forests, rocks, hunters—all that a painter can copy from nature”; and the coat Charles of Orleans once wore, whose sleeves bore the verses of a song beginning “Madame, je suis tout joyeux,” with a musical accompaniment wrought in gold thread and each square note formed with four pearls. He read of the room prepared at the palace at Rheims for Queen Joan of Burgundy, decorated with “thirteen hundred and twenty-one parrots, embroidered with the king’s arms, and five hundred and sixty-one butterflies, whose wings carried the queen’s arms, all worked in gold.” Catherine de’ Medici had a mourning bed made of black velvet sprinkled with crescents and suns. Its curtains, of damask with leafy wreaths and garlands on a gold and silver ground, were edged with pearl embroidery, and the room was hung with rows of the queen’s emblems in cut black velvet on cloth of silver. Louis XIV had gold-embroidered caryatids fifteen feet high in his apartment."}

content.text: {"request_id":"b3e862244f503a3eaf0adadb","rewritten_text":"The mighty voice—if we can call it that, for we could not connect it with any organ or keyboard—fell silent, and the girl, turning to help her elderly companion, at last saw us. It was her father; ever since childhood she had guided his blind steps. They were Germans from Saxony who had emigrated a few years earlier and formed new ties with the surrounding villagers. Around the time the plague began, a young German student had joined them. Their simple story was easy to guess. He, a nobleman, loved the fair daughter of the poor musician and followed them into exile from his family’s disapproval. Soon the great leveller came, its scythe cutting both the grass and the tall flowers. The youth died early. She kept herself alive for her father’s sake. His blindness let her preserve a fiction born by accident, and now these solitary survivors in the land let him remain unaware of the change; he did not know that when he listened to his child’s music, the mute mountains, senseless lake, and unfeeling trees were, besides himself, her only audience. The very day we arrived she had been struck by the first symptoms of illness. She was frozen with dread at the thought of leaving her old, sightless father alone on the empty earth; yet she had not the courage to tell him, and the very height of her desperation drove her to extraordinary effort. At the usual evening hour she guided him to the chapel, and though she trembled and wept for his sake, she played without missing a beat or note the hymn celebrating the creation of the adorned earth, soon to be her tomb. We seemed to her like visitors from heaven. Her strained courage and barely sustained strength vanished at the sight of help. With a shriek she rushed toward us, embraced Adrian’s knees, and with the single cry, “O save my father!” she broke down in sobs and hysterical cries, opening the long-sealed floodgates of her grief. Poor girl! She and her father now lie side by side beneath the tall walnut tree where her lover rests, the place she pointed out to us moments before her death. Her father, finally aware of his daughter’s danger yet unable to see the changes in her dear face, clung stubbornly to her hand until it grew cold and stiff in death. Even then he did not move or speak, until twelve hours later when merciful death took him to unbroken rest. They sleep beneath that sod, the tree their monument. The blessed spot is clear in my memory, ringed by craggy Jura and the far immeasurable Alps. The spire of the church they once frequented still rises from the sheltering trees; and though her hand is cold, I still imagine the holy music they loved drifting through the air, soothing their gentle spirits."}

{"request_id":"aa0752e47a441f502c2a90e6","rewritten_text":"Soul and body, body and soul—how unfathomable they remained! The soul harbored animal impulses, and the body, in turn, experienced spells of spirituality. The senses could become refined, while the intellect might descend. Who could identify where the bodily urge ended or the psychic impulse began? How superficial were the rigid definitions of typical psychologists! Yet how hard it was to adjudicate the claims of each competing school! Was the soul merely a shade dwelling within the house of sin? Or did the body actually reside within the soul, as Giordano Bruno believed? The divorce of spirit from matter was mysterious, and their union proved equally mysterious.

He began to muse whether psychology could ever become such an exact science that each tiny spring of existence would be laid bare. As things stood, we endlessly misread ourselves and seldom grasped others. Experience held no ethical worth. It was simply the label men affixed to their errors. Moralists generally treated it as a warning mechanism, endowed it with a certain moral efficacy in shaping character, extolled it as something that instructed us what to pursue and what to shun. But experience provided no driving force. It was no more an active cause than conscience itself. All it truly showed was that our future would mimic our past, and that the wrongdoing we once committed reluctantly we would commit repeatedly, even joyfully.

It was evident to him that only the experimental method could yield any scientific dissection of the passions; and Dorian Gray was certainly a subject ready to hand, offering promise of abundant and rewarding results. His sudden, frenzied love for Sibyl Vane was a psychological curiosity of considerable import. There could be no question that curiosity played a large part in it, curiosity paired with the thirst for novel experiences, yet it was not a straightforward, but a highly intricate passion. Whatever portion of it sprang from the purely sensuous instinct of youth had been reshaped by imagination, altered into something that seemed to the boy himself removed from sense, and for that very reason all the more perilous. It was those passions about whose origins we misled ourselves that most tyrannized over us. Our weakest motives were the ones whose nature we recognized. Frequently, while we imagined we were experimenting on others, we were in fact experimenting on ourselves.

As Lord Henry sat brooding over these reflections, a knock sounded at the door, and his valet entered to inform him that it was time to dress for dinner."}

{"request_id":"ba751b0679802ff322a8755d","rewritten_text":"“I consider it one of the first refinements of polite society.”

“Certainly, sir; and it also has the advantage of being popular among the less refined societies of the world—every savage can dance.”

Sir William only smiled. “Your friend dances wonderfully,” he continued after a pause, watching Bingley join the dancers. “And I have no doubt you are an expert yourself, Mr. Darcy.”

“You saw me dance at Meryton, I believe, sir.”

“Yes, indeed, and I took considerable pleasure in watching. Do you often dance at St. James’s?”

“Never, sir.”

“Do you not think it would be a proper compliment to the place?”

“It is a compliment I never pay to any place if I can avoid it.”

“You have a house in town, I assume?”

Mr. Darcy bowed.

“I once thought of settling in town myself, for I enjoy superior society; but I was not quite sure the air of London would agree with Lady Lucas.”

He paused, hoping for an answer, but his companion seemed unwilling to give one. Just then Elizabeth moved toward them, and Sir William, thinking it would be very gallant, called out to her:

“My dear Miss Eliza, why are you not dancing? Mr. Darcy, you must let me present this young lady to you as a most desirable partner. You cannot refuse to dance when so much beauty stands before you.” And taking her hand, he would have given it to Mr. Darcy, who, though very surprised, did not refuse, when she immediately drew back and said with some agitation to Sir William,

“Indeed, sir, I have no intention of dancing. I beg you not to imagine that I came this way to ask for a partner.”

Mr. Darcy, with solemn propriety, requested the honor of her hand, but it was useless. Elizabeth was resolute; nor did Sir William’s attempt at persuasion weaken her resolve.

“You dance so well, Miss Eliza, that it is cruel to deny me the pleasure of seeing you; and though this gentleman dislikes the amusement in general, I am sure he cannot object to oblige us for half an hour.”

“Mr. Darcy is all politeness,” said Elizabeth, smiling.

“He is, indeed; but considering the incentive, my dear Miss Eliza, we cannot be surprised at his politeness, for who would object to such a partner?”

Elizabeth gave him an arch look and turned away. Her refusal had not hurt her in Mr. Darcy’s opinion, and he was thinking of her with some satisfaction when Miss Bingley addressed him."}

{"request_id":"f2906f29e89eb1a8d329d921","rewritten_text":"Not every one would have so kindly persisted as she did, refusing to take Jane’s answer; she flatly insisted she would not write such a refusal yesterday, as Jane wanted; she meant to wait—and sure enough, by yesterday evening everything was arranged for Jane to go. Quite a surprise to me! I had not the faintest suspicion!—Jane drew Mrs. Elton aside and told her at once that, on reconsidering the benefits of Mrs. Smallridge’s position, she had resolved to accept it.—I never heard a syllable until all was concluded.”

“You spent the evening at Mrs. Elton’s?”

“Yes, every one of us; Mrs. Elton insisted on our coming. It was decided on the hill, while we were strolling with Mr. Knightley. ‘You must all spend your evening with us,’ she said—‘I positively must have every one of you come.’”

“Mr. Knightley was present too, was he?”

“No, Mr. Knightley was not; he excused himself at once; and though I imagined he would appear, because Mrs. Elton vowed she would not let him escape, he never did;—but my mother, Jane, and I were there, and we passed a very agreeable evening. Such considerate friends, you know, Miss Woodhouse, must always be pleasant company, though everyone looked rather worn after the morning’s party. Even enjoyment, as you know, is exhausting—and I cannot say that any of them seemed to have derived much delight from it. Still, I shall always remember it as a charming party, and feel deeply grateful to the considerate friends who included me.”

“Miss Fairfax, I assume, though you did not perceive it, had spent the whole day deciding?”

“I dare say she had.”

“Whenever the time arrives, it must be unwelcome to her and to all her friends—but I trust her appointment will have every relief possible—I mean with regard to the family’s character and manners.”

“Thank you, dear Miss Woodhouse. Indeed, there is everything imaginable to make her content. Besides the Sucklings and Bragges, there is not another nursery establishment so generous and refined within Mrs. Elton’s acquaintance. Mrs. Smallridge is the most delightful woman!—Her style of living is nearly on par with Maple Grove—and regarding the children, excepting the little Sucklings and little Bragges, there are no other youngsters so elegant and sweet. Jane will meet such respect and kindness!—It will be nothing but delight, a life of delight.—And her salary!—I truly dare not mention her salary to you, Miss Woodhouse."}

{"request_id":"b495e7d87909222dc4f0da5c","rewritten_text":"I have already remarked that he was a poet: at three-and-twenty he put forth his first poem, and the whole nation greeted it with fervour and delight. Fortune attended him without fail; never had a reputation risen so swiftly, nor spread so completely. The crowd praised the very verses that amazed the scholar secluded in his study: not a single voice dissented.

It was at this zenith of his fame that he met Elinor. She was a youthful heiress of rare loveliness, living under her guardian’s charge: from the first sight of them together it was plain they were created for one another. Elinor lacked Woodville’s genius, yet she was generous and noble, exalted by her youth and the admiration she everywhere inspired above knowledge of anything except virtue and goodness. She was fair; her manners candid and unaffected; her dark-blue eyes shone with a radiance bestowed only by sensibility wedded to wisdom.

Destined for each other, they soon loved. Woodville tasted love’s happiness for the first time; Elinor was transported by winning the heart of one so splendid and honoured among men. Could aught but pure joy spring from such a union?

Woodville, the Poet, was sought by every circle, all eyes fixed upon him when he entered; yet he was merely the son of a poor clergyman, while Elinor possessed wealth. Her guardian did not oppose their attachment: Woodville’s merit was too great for anyone to cavil at his lack of fortune; but her father’s dying injunction forbade her to wed before reaching her majority, and her inheritance depended on strict obedience. She had just completed her twentieth year, and both lovers were compelled to endure the delay. Nevertheless they were always together, their bliss like that of Eden: they studied side by side, contrived plans for future pursuits, and, drinking love and joy from each other’s eyes and lips, they scarcely lamented the pause before full union. Woodville’s glory ever increased, while under his accomplished guidance Elinor grew yet more lovely and wise.

In two months Elinor would reach one-and-twenty; every preparation for their wedding was complete. How can I tell the catastrophe that befell such joy? Yet this earth, shrouded in blight and sorrow, would cease to be itself if two such angelic beings had been permitted to exist solely for one another. Search the world over and you will not find the faultless felicity their marriage promised; only a revolution in the order appointed for us wretched earth-dwellers could have allowed such perfect happiness to endure."}

{"request_id":"9d8bb9afe072bdc411f2afed","rewritten_text":"“One more word, Rose. Dearest Rose, just one more!” Harry pleaded, stepping in front of her. “If I had been less—less fortunate, as people say—if I’d been meant for some quiet, hidden life—if I’d been poor, sick, helpless—would you have turned away from me then? Or did this doubt come only because of my likely rise to wealth and honor?”

“Please don’t push me to answer,” Rose replied. “That situation hasn’t come up and never will. It’s unfair, almost unkind, to insist.”

“If your answer is what I hardly dare hope it is,” Harry said, “it will cast a ray of happiness on my lonely road and light what lies ahead. It isn’t trivial to do so much, with just a few short words, for someone who loves you above everything. Oh, Rose, in the name of my passionate and steady devotion; in the name of all I’ve suffered because of you, and all you consign me to endure; answer me this one question!”

“Then if your fate had been different,” Rose answered, “if you’d been only a little, but not so far, above me; if I could have helped and comforted you in any modest life of peace and seclusion, and not been a stain and hindrance among ambitious, distinguished crowds, I would have been spared this ordeal. I have every reason to be happy—very happy—now; but then, Harry, I admit I would have been happier.”

Memories of her girlhood hopes rushed back to Rose as she said this, but they brought tears with them, as old hopes do when they return dead and gone; and they eased her heart.

“I can’t help this weakness, and it only makes my resolve stronger,” Rose said, holding out her hand. “I have to leave you now, truly.”

“I ask one promise,” Harry said. “Once, and only once more—within a year, though it might be sooner—I may speak to you again about this, for the last time.”

“Not to push me to give up a right decision,” Rose answered with a sorrowful smile; “it would be pointless.”

“No,” Harry said. “Just to hear you repeat it, if you will—repeat it for good. I’ll lay whatever position or fortune I have at your feet; and if you still hold to your decision, I won’t try, by word or deed, to change it.”

“Then let it be so,” Rose said. “It’s just one more pain, and by then I may be able to bear it better.”

She held out her hand again."}

{"request_id":"4b5028760402fc8a4ad1d9a9","rewritten_text":"But I question how long you would have persisted without interference. When would you have spoken if I had not forced the moment? My resolve to thank you for your kindness to Lydia certainly had tremendous effect. Too much, perhaps, for what becomes of morality if our comfort arises from a broken promise, since I should not have touched on the topic? This cannot stand.”

“There is no need for you to be troubled. The moral remains quite intact. Lady Catherine’s unwarrantable attempts to divide us swept away all my uncertainties. I do not owe my current happiness to your impatient wish to show gratitude. I was in no temper to wait for the opening you might offer. My aunt’s report gave me hope, and I resolved to learn everything immediately.”

“Lady Catherine has been infinitely beneficial, which should delight her, given she adores being useful. But tell me, why did you come down to Netherfield? Simply to ride to Longbourn and feel awkward? or did you plan something more decisive?”

“My true intention was to see you, and to judge, if possible, whether I might ever hope to inspire your affection. My announced motive, or what I told myself it was, involved discovering if your sister still cared for Bingley, and, if she did, making to him the admission I have since made.”

“Do you ever expect to muster the courage to inform Lady Catherine of what awaits her?”

“I am more apt to lack time than courage, Elizabeth. Yet it must be done; give me a sheet of paper, and it shall be done at once.”

“And were I not obliged to write a letter myself, I might sit beside you and admire the steadiness of your hand, as another young lady once did. But I too have an aunt who must no longer be neglected.”

From a reluctance to confess how much she had overrated her intimacy with Mr. Darcy, Elizabeth had still not replied to Mrs. Gardiner’s lengthy letter; yet now, possessing news she knew would please most, she felt almost ashamed to realize her uncle and aunt had already been deprived of three days of joy, and she immediately penned the following:--

“I would have thanked you earlier, my dear aunt, as duty required, for your long, kind, and satisfying collection of particulars; but, truthfully, I was too vexed to write. You imagined more than truly existed. Yet now imagine whatever you please; give your fancy free rein, let your imagination soar along every possible path the subject permits, and unless you deem me already married, you cannot be much mistaken.”"}

{"request_id":"4561cd97f4a8f538a383f699","rewritten_text":"“She and the children might very well stay.”

“Ah, papa—you have never been able to make that happen, and I do not think you ever will. Isabella cannot stand being away from her husband.”

That was too true to argue. Though the idea displeased him, Mr. Woodhouse only gave a resigned sigh, and as Emma saw how the thought of his daughter’s devotion to her husband weighed on him, she quickly turned the talk to a part of the subject that would cheer him.

“Harriet must give us as much of her company as she can while my brother and sister are here. I know she will be delighted with the children. We are very proud of the children, are we not, papa? I wonder which one she will find the handsomest, Henry or John?”

“Yes, I wonder which she will. Poor little things, how happy they will be to come. They are very fond of being at Hartfield, Harriet.”

“I dare say they are, sir. I do not know who is not.”

“Henry is a fine boy, but John looks very much like his mother. Henry is the eldest; he was named after me, not after his father. John, the second, was named after his father. Some people think it odd that the eldest was not named for his father, but Isabella insisted on Henry, which I thought very sweet of her. And he is a very smart boy indeed. They are all remarkably clever, and they have so many charming ways. They will come and stand by my chair and say, ‘Grandpapa, can you give me a bit of string?’ and once Henry asked me for a knife, but I told him knives were meant only for grandpapas. I think their father is too rough with them quite often.”

“He seems rough to you,” said Emma, “because you are so gentle yourself; but if you could compare him with other fathers, you would not think him rough. He wants his boys to be active and strong; and if they misbehave, he gives them a sharp word now and then, but he is a loving father—certainly Mr. John Knightley is a loving father. The children are all fond of him.”

“And then their uncle comes in and throws them up to the ceiling in a very frightening way!”

“But they enjoy it, papa; there is nothing they like more. It is such a delight for them that if their uncle did not insist on taking turns, whoever started would never let the other have a turn.”

“Well, I cannot understand it.”

“That is how it is with all of us, papa. Half the world cannot understand the pleasures of the other half.”"}

{"request_id":"0226ac5b3432829a8c0f893d","rewritten_text":"“Unless you’re about to call Miss Havisham a he. And I doubt even you would stretch it that far.”

“Miss Havisham, up town?” Joe repeated.

“Is there a Miss Havisham down town?” snapped my sister.

“She wants this boy to go there and play. Naturally he’s going. And he’d better play there,” my sister declared, wagging her head at me as a cue to be airy and lively, “or I’ll put him to work.”

I already knew of Miss Havisham in town—every soul for miles knew of Miss Havisham in town—as a monstrously wealthy, forbidding lady living in a vast, cheerless house fortified against thieves, leading a reclusive existence.

“Well, to be sure!” cried Joe, amazed. “How ever did she come to know Pip?”

“Noodle!” my sister shrilled. “Who said she knew him?”

“—Which a certain person,” Joe ventured again with courtesy, “remarked that she desired him to go and play there.”

“And couldn’t she ask Uncle Pumblechook whether he knew of a boy to go and play there? Isn’t it remotely possible that Uncle Pumblechook is one of her tenants, and that sometimes—we won’t impose quarterly or even half-yearly, that would overtax you—but sometimes goes there to pay his rent? And couldn’t she then inquire of Uncle Pumblechook if he knew a boy to go and play there? And couldn’t Uncle Pumblechook, ever mindful and considerate toward us—though you may fail to recognize it, Joseph,” she added in her deepest tone of reproach, as though he were the most unfeeling nephew alive, “then suggest this boy, standing here Prancing”—which I do solemnly affirm I was not—“for whom I have eternally been an obedient drudge?”

“Good again!” exclaimed Uncle Pumblechook. “Nicely stated! Sweetly put! Very good! Now, Joseph, you’re aware of the situation.”

“No, Joseph,” my sister insisted, still reproachful, while Joe sheepishly passed the back of his hand back and forth across his nose, “you do not yet—despite what you may suppose—understand the situation. You may think you do, but you do _not_, Joseph. Because you don’t know that Uncle Pumblechook, perceiving that for aught we can say this boy’s fortune could be sealed by his visit to Miss Havisham’s, has offered to take him to town this very night in his own chaise-cart, to lodge him tonight, and to deliver him with his own hands to Miss Havisham’s tomorrow morning. And Lor-a-mussy me!” cried my sister, flinging off her bonnet in a flash of despair, “here I am chattering to a pair of Mooncalfs, while Uncle Pumblechook waits, the mare catches her death at the door, and the boy stands smeared with soot and grime from the crown of his head to the sole of his foot!”"}

{"request_id":"bb151c55f216ce8b0cae67eb","rewritten_text":"“After that, we put up a wire barrier.”

“Wire barrier?”

“Yes. You suggested it yourself two or three years back.”

“Oh, I recall—the first time the Church tested its power against us and soon judged it wiser to wait for a more promising season. Well, how have you set up the barrier?”

“I run twelve very sturdy wires—bare, not insulated—out of a large dynamo in the cave—a dynamo with nothing but a positive and a negative brush.”

“Yes, correct.”

“The wires leave the cave and enclose a level circle of ground a hundred yards across; they form twelve separate barriers, each ten feet apart—meaning twelve concentric circles—and their ends reenter the cave.”

“Right; proceed.”

“The barriers are lashed to massive oaken posts only three feet apart, and the posts are sunk five feet deep.”

“Excellent strength.”

“Yes. The wires have no ground-contact outside the cave. They leave the positive brush of the dynamo; the negative brush provides the ground-connection; the other ends come back to the cave, and each one is grounded independently.”

“No, no, that will never do!”

“Why not?”

“It’s too costly—wastes power for nothing. You need only one ground-connection, through the negative brush. Each opposite end must return into the cave and be fastened separately, without any ground-contact. Now see the thrift of it. Suppose a cavalry charge flings itself against the barrier; you are consuming no power, spending no coin, because there’s just one ground-connection until those horses strike the wire; the instant they touch it they complete a circuit to the negative brush through the earth, and fall dead. Don’t you see? You don’t expend energy till it is required; your lightning waits like a loaded gun, but it costs you nothing until you fire it. Oh yes, the single ground-connection—”

“Certainly! I can’t imagine how I missed it. It’s not only cheaper, but more effective than the other plan, since if wires snap or tangle, no damage follows.”

“None, particularly if we have a telltale in the cave and cut off the broken wire. Now, proceed. What about the gatlings?”

“Yes—set up. In the middle of the innermost circle, on a wide platform six feet high, I’ve assembled a battery of thirteen gatling guns with ample ammunition.”

“Perfect. They command every path, and when the Church’s knights show up, there’ll be lively music. The brow of the cliff above the cave—”

“I’ve mounted a wire barrier there too, and a gatling gun.”"}

{"request_id":"392e61461ebd1bb6f6125d51","rewritten_text":"April 12th. A remarkable change occurred in the balloon’s direction which, though fully expected, filled me with unalloyed delight. After following its previous path as far as roughly the twentieth parallel south, it suddenly veered sharply eastward and spent the entire day moving in that course, maintaining nearly, if not precisely, the plane of the lunar ellipse. Noteworthy, this shift produced a distinct rocking of the car, a swaying that endured for many hours in varying strength.

April 13th. Was again greatly disturbed by a renewal of the loud, crackling sound that frightened me on the tenth. I meditated long on it without reaching any satisfactory interpretation. The apparent diameter of the earth diminished greatly, now spanning scarcely more than twenty-five degrees beneath the balloon. The moon remained invisible, almost directly over my zenith. I still kept to the plane of the ellipse, though with little advancement eastward.

April 14th. The earth’s diameter shrank with extreme rapidity. Today I felt strongly persuaded that the balloon was ascending along the line of apsides toward perigee—in plain terms, taking the exact route that would bring it straight to the moon at the nearest point of its orbit to the earth. The moon itself was vertically above me and therefore out of sight. Condensing the air required prolonged and arduous labor.

April 15th. No outlines of continents or oceans could now be distinguished on the earth with any clarity. Around noon I detected, for the third time, that horrifying noise which had so completely alarmed me earlier. This time it persisted, intensifying as it went on. Finally, while I stood numb with terror, expecting some unimaginable catastrophe, the car shook with tremendous force, and an enormous blazing mass of unknown material swept past the balloon with the clamorous bellowing of a thousand thunders. Once my fear and astonishment had somewhat abated, I readily concluded it must be a colossal volcanic fragment hurled from the very world I was approaching, likely one of those peculiar substances occasionally discovered on earth and labeled meteoric stones for want of a better term.

April 16th. Today, straining to look upward through the side windows in turn, I saw, to my great joy, a tiny portion of the moon’s disk projecting, as if encircling, beyond the vast circumference of the balloon."}

{"request_id":"ac092fe42562b27aefc603b7","rewritten_text":"“If I cannot exist on that, I will not ask aid from any man. Is it content?”

A tremendous roar of acclamation burst forth, and above it the king cried:

“Loose his bonds, give him liberty! Pay him homage, high and low, rich and poor alike, for he has become the king’s right arm, vested with might and authority, and his seat is upon the highest step of the throne! Now chase away this crawling night, bring back the light and gladness, that all the world may bless thee.”

But I answered:

“That a common fellow be humbled before the world is nothing; yet it were dishonor to the king if any who saw his minister unclad did not also see him freed from his disgrace. Might I request that my garments be returned?”

“They are unfitting,” the king interposed. “Bring raiment of a nobler sort; apparel him as a prince!”

My scheme prospered. I needed things to remain just so until the eclipse reached its height; otherwise they would pester me again to shoo away the darkness, which I plainly could not do. Calling for clothing bought me a bit of delay, though not sufficient. So I devised a fresh excuse: I declared it reasonable to suppose the king might reconsider, might somewhat repent of what frenzy had made him do; therefore I would let the gloom deepen, and if after a proper interval he still held his purpose, the night should be banished. The king disliked it, and so did the rest, but I held fast.

It became ever darker, blacker, while I fought with those clumsy sixth-century clothes. At last the place was in utter blackness, and the crowd groaned with horror as chill uncanny winds stole through and the stars pricked out above. When the eclipse reached its utter fullness I was thankful, though all others suffered, as was only natural. I proclaimed:

“The king, by his silence, yet abides by the compact.” I raised my hands, held them aloft a moment, then intoned with dreadful solemnity: “Let the enchantment melt away and pass without harm!”

There came no immediate answer in that profound gloom, that graveyard stillness. But when the bright rim of the sun thrust forward a breath later, the whole assembly erupted with a colossal cheer and swept toward me like a flood to bury me under blessings and thanks—and Clarence, rest assured, was not the last of the tide."}

{"request_id":"8d7a12ca2c0ec860afe1d41a","rewritten_text":"“Git up! What you doin’ there?”

I blinked awake and peered around, trying to figure out my whereabouts. Sun was well up, and I’d been dead asleep. Pap loomed over me looking sour and sickly, too. He says:

“What you meddlin’ with this gun for?”

I reckoned he didn’t remember a lick of what he’d been up to, so I says:

“Somebody aimed to break in, so I was laying for him.”

“Why didn’t you fetch me?”

“Well, I tried; but I couldn’t stir you—couldn’t move you a hair.”

“Well, fine. Quit standing there palaverin’ all day; hustle out and see if there’s a fish on them lines for breakfast. I’ll be along directly.”

He slipped the bolt, and I scooted off up the river-bank. I noticed bits of limbs and such drifting down, with specks of bark, so I knowed the river was starting to swell. I allowed I’d be having big times now if I was over at the town. The June rise always used to bring me luck; soon as it commenced here’d come cordwood floating along, and hunks off log rafts—sometimes a dozen logs bunched up; all you had to do was snag them and sell to the woodyards and the sawmill.

I kept on up the bank with one eye peeled for pap and the other watching what the rise might fetch. All at once here come a canoe; a real dandy, too, thirteen or fourteen foot, sitting high like a duck. I dove head-first off the bank like a frog, clothes and all, and struck out for the canoe. I half expected somebody was stretched out in it, because folks often played that trick, and when a chap had dragged a skiff pretty near they’d pop up and laugh at him. But it warn’t that way now. It was a drift-canoe sure enough, and I clambered in and paddled her to shore. I thought, the old man’ll be tickled when he spies this—she’s worth ten dollars. But when I made land pap wasn’t in sight yet, and as I was running her into a little creek like a gully, all wrapped in vines and willows, another notion struck me: I figured I’d stash her fine, and then, instead of lighting out for the woods when I made my break, I’d head down the river about fifty miles and fix a camp in one place for good, and not have so rough a time hoofing it.

It was nigh the shanty, and I fancied I heard the old man coming every minute; but I got her stowed, and then I stepped out and peeked around a clump of willows, and there was the old man down the trail a spell, already drawing a bead on a bird with his gun."}

{"request_id":"117f9933561312f739c825a6","rewritten_text":"A few days later, Virginia and her curly-headed cavalier went riding over Brockley meadows, where she tore her riding habit so badly squeezing through a hedge that, upon returning home, she resolved to slip up the back staircase to avoid notice. As she hurried past the Tapestry Chamber, its door chanced to stand open, and she imagined she saw someone inside. Assuming it was her mother’s maid, who occasionally came there with her work, she stepped in to ask for help mending the damage. To her utter astonishment, it was the Canterville Ghost himself! He sat by the window, watching the ruined gold of the yellowing trees whirl through the air and the red leaves caper wildly down the long avenue. His head rested on his hand, his entire posture one of deep dejection. Indeed, he looked so forlorn and so worn-out that little Virginia, whose initial impulse had been to flee and fasten herself in her room, felt a sudden compassion and resolved to console him. Her tread was so light, and his melancholy so absorbing, that he did not realize she was there until she spoke.

“I am very sorry for you,” she said, “but my brothers return to Eton to-morrow, and then, if you behave properly, no one will bother you.”

“It is ridiculous to ask me to behave,” he replied, turning in amazement toward the pretty child who had dared address him, “quite ridiculous. I must clank my chains, groan through keyholes, and pace about by night, if that is what you mean. It is my sole justification for existing.”

“It is no justification for existing at all, and you know you have been dreadfully wicked. Mrs. Umney told us the day we arrived that you had murdered your wife.”

“Well, I fully admit it,” said the Ghost peevishly, “but it was entirely a domestic affair and concerned no one else.”

“It is very wrong to kill anybody,” said Virginia, who sometimes had a sweet Puritan gravity inherited from some old New England forebear.

“Oh, I detest the cheap severity of abstract morals! My wife was exceedingly plain, never starched my ruffs properly, and understood nothing of cookery. Why, there was a buck I shot in Hogley Woods, a magnificent pricket, and do you know the way she had it served? However, it is of no consequence now—it is all past—and I must say it was hardly considerate of her brothers to starve me to death, even though I did kill her.”"}

{"request_id":"6b910acc2e999bf8b015c422","rewritten_text":"Saturday at noon I went to the well and watched for a while. Merlin was still burning smoke powders, flailing at the air, and muttering nonsense as hard as ever, but he looked discouraged, for he still hadn’t raised even a sweat out of that well. Finally I said:

“How does it look now, partner?”

“Behold, I am now trying the strongest spell known to the princes of the Eastern occult arts; if this fails, nothing will work. Be quiet until I finish.”

This time he raised a smoke that blackened the whole region and must have made things miserable for the hermits, because the wind was blowing toward them and the fog rolled over their dens in thick waves. He poured out torrents of words to match, twisting his body and chopping the air with his hands in the strangest way. After twenty minutes he dropped, panting and nearly spent. Then the abbot arrived with several hundred monks and nuns, and behind them a crowd of pilgrims and acres of foundlings, all drawn by the monstrous smoke and in a great state of excitement. The abbot anxiously asked about the results. Merlin said:

“If any human effort could break the spell on these waters, what I have just tried would have done it. It has failed, which proves what I feared—this failure shows that the strongest spirit known to Eastern magicians, whose name none may speak and live, has laid his spell on this well. No mortal breathes, or ever will, who can uncover the secret of that spell, and without it nothing can break it. The water will never flow again, good Father. I have done all that man can do. Let me go.”

Naturally this threw the abbot into a panic. He turned to me, showing it plainly, and said:

“You heard him. Is it true?”

“Part of it is.”

“Not all, then? What part is true?”

“That the spirit with the Russian name has put a spell on the well.”

“God’s wounds, then we are ruined!”

“Possibly.”

“But not certainly? You mean, not certainly?”

“That’s right.”

“Wherefore, you also mean that when he says no one can break the spell—”

“Yes, when he says that, he isn’t necessarily right. There are conditions under which trying to break it might have a chance—a small, tiny chance—of success.”"}

{"request_id":"f60b8567fbbfa8d5c9c2f454","rewritten_text":"Nothing Emma learned later made her take back her bad opinion of Mrs. Elton. Her first impression had been right. However often they met, Mrs. Elton always appeared the same—full of herself, presumptuous, overly familiar, ignorant, and ill-bred. She had a little beauty and some skill, yet so little good sense that she believed she came armed with superior worldly knowledge to brighten and improve a country neighbourhood, and she imagined Miss Hawkins had held a social standing that only Mrs. Elton’s own importance could surpass.

There was no reason to think Mr. Elton saw her differently. He seemed not only happy but proud, as if congratulating himself on bringing to Highbury a woman even Miss Woodhouse could not match. Most of her new acquaintances, either inclined to approve or unused to judging for themselves, followed Miss Bates’s goodwill or assumed the bride must be as clever and charming as she claimed, and were easily satisfied. Mrs. Elton’s praise thus spread from mouth to mouth as it should, unhindered by Miss Woodhouse, who continued her initial polite contribution and spoke graciously of Mrs. Elton as “very pleasant and very elegantly dressed.”

In one respect, Mrs. Elton grew even worse. Her feelings toward Emma cooled. Likely offended by Emma’s lukewarm response to her offers of friendship, she pulled back and became noticeably colder and more distant. The change suited Emma, but the malice behind it only deepened her dislike. Both Mrs. Elton’s and Mr. Elton’s manners toward Harriet were also unpleasant—sneering and careless. Emma hoped this would quickly cure Harriet, yet the mentality that caused such conduct lowered both Eltons in her eyes. It was clear poor Harriet’s feelings had been offered up to marital confidence, and Emma’s part in the story had probably been coloured to make Harriet look worst and Mr. Elton feel best. Harriet had become the focus of their shared dislike. Whenever they ran out of conversation, it was easy for them to start criticizing Miss Woodhouse; any hostility they dared not show Emma directly spilled out in their contemptuous treatment of Harriet.

From the very start, Mrs. Elton took a strong liking to Jane Fairfax—not just when conflict with one young lady might make the other more appealing, but immediately. Mere natural admiration did not satisfy her. Unasked, without any right or invitation, she insisted on helping and befriending Jane. Before Emma lost Mrs. Elton’s confidence, and by about their third meeting, she heard all about Mrs. Elton’s knight-errantry on the subject."}

{"request_id":"928f06bcb7980193e5761c21","rewritten_text":"There comes a point in every well-made boy’s life when he suddenly burns to go dig for hidden treasure. That urge came over Tom one day. He marched out to find Joe Harper, but couldn’t. Then he tried Ben Rogers; Ben had gone fishing. Soon Tom ran into Huck Finn the Red-Handed. Huck would do. Tom led him to a private spot and quietly explained the plan. Huck was willing. Huck was always willing to join any scheme that promised fun and didn’t need money, because he had too much of the kind of time that isn’t money. “Where’ll we dig?” Huck asked.

“Oh, almost anywhere.”

“Why, is treasure buried everywhere?”

“No, not a bit. It’s hidden in very particular spots, Huck—sometimes on islands, sometimes in rotten chests under the tip of a branch on an old dead tree right where the shadow falls at midnight; but mostly under the floor of haunted houses.”

“Who hides it?”

“Why, robbers, of course—who else? Sunday-school superintendents?”

“I don’t know. If it was mine I wouldn’t hide it; I’d spend it and have a good time.”

“So would I. But robbers don’t. They always hide it and leave it.”

“Don’t they come back for it?”

“No. They mean to, but they usually forget the signs, or they die. Anyway, it sits there a long time and gets rusty. After a while somebody finds an old yellow paper that tells how to find the signs—a paper that takes about a week to work out because it’s mostly symbols and hieroglyphics.”

“Hyro-what?”

“Hieroglyphics—pictures and such that don’t seem to mean anything.”

“Have you got one of those papers, Tom?”

“No.”

“Well then, how are you going to find the signs?”

“I don’t need signs. They always bury treasure under a haunted house or on an island or under a dead tree with one limb sticking out. We’ve tried Jackson’s Island some already, and we can try it again later. There’s that old haunted house up the Still-House branch, and there are plenty of dead-limb trees—loads of them.”

“Is it under all of them?”

“What a question! No!”

“Then how do you know which one to dig at?”

“Dig at them all!”

“Why, Tom, that’ll take all summer.”

“Well, so what? Suppose you find a brass pot with a hundred dollars in it, all rusty and dull, or a rotten chest full of diamonds. How about that?”

Huck’s eyes lit up.

“That’s great. Plenty great for me. Just give me the hundred dollars and I won’t need any diamonds.”"}

{"request_id":"2ae2b556e376c5676eed2e47","rewritten_text":"Ever since the night we took him to the stairs and sent him abroad, I had watched carefully for any sign that we were suspected. I saw none. We certainly had not been, and were not then, followed or watched by any boat. If a boat had trailed us, I would have rowed to shore and forced her either to pass on or to show her purpose. But we kept on without any sign of interference.

He wore his boat-cloak and, as I have said, looked like a natural part of the scene. It was notable—though perhaps the miserable life he had led explained it—that he worried least of all of us. He was not careless, for he told me he hoped to live to see his gentleman become one of the best gentlemen in a foreign country. He was not passive or resigned, as I understood it, but he refused to go out of his way to meet danger. When danger came, he faced it, yet he would not bother about it until it arrived.

“If you knew, dear boy,” he said to me, “what it is to sit here next to my dear boy and have my smoke, after being shut up day after day between four walls, you’d envy me. But you don’t know what it is.”

“I think I know the pleasures of freedom,” I answered.

“Ah,” he said, shaking his head gravely. “But you don’t know it like me. You’d have to be locked up, dear boy, to know it like me—but I ain’t going to be low.”

It seemed inconsistent to me that he would risk his freedom and even his life for any pressing idea. Yet I thought that perhaps freedom without danger was too far from the life he had always known to be to him what it would be to another man. I was not far off, since he said after smoking a little:

“You see, dear boy, when I was over yonder, on the other side of the world, I was always looking this way; and it grew dull to stay there, even though I was getting rich. Everyone knew Magwitch, and Magwitch could come and go, and nobody would be troubled about him. They ain’t so easy about me here, dear boy—wouldn’t be, at least, if they knew where I was.”

“If all goes well,” said I, “you will be completely free and safe again in a few hours.”

“Well,” he said, drawing a long breath, “I hope so.”

“And you believe so?”"}

{"request_id":"1cd67545de6e102b669718fa","rewritten_text":"Meanwhile, gravity would keep weakening in proportion to the square of the distance, and with a wildly increasing speed I would eventually reach those distant regions where the earth’s pull gives way to the moon’s. With this in mind, I decided it was pointless to burden myself with more provisions than would last forty days.

“Another difficulty still troubled me. It has been noted that during balloon ascents to great altitudes, besides the pain involved in breathing, people suffer intense discomfort in the head and body, often with nosebleeds and other alarming symptoms, which grow worse the higher one goes. This was a disturbing thought. Was it not likely these symptoms would continue to intensify indefinitely, or at least until death ended them? I eventually concluded otherwise. Their origin lay in the gradual removal of normal atmospheric pressure on the body’s surface and the resulting swelling of the superficial blood vessels—not in any actual breakdown of the organism, as happens with respiratory distress when the air is too thin to renew the blood in a heart’s ventricle. Unless that renewal failed, I saw no reason life could not continue even in a vacuum; the expansion and contraction of the chest—what we call breathing—is purely muscular action, the cause rather than the result of respiration. In short, I believed that as the body adapted to the lack of atmospheric pressure, the pain would gradually lessen, and while it lasted I trusted my iron constitution to bear it.

“Thus, honorable sirs, I have described some, though not all, of the considerations that led me to plan a journey to the moon. I will now present the outcome of an attempt so apparently bold in theory and, in any case, so completely without precedent in human history.

“After reaching the height previously mentioned—three and three-quarter miles—I tossed a quantity of feathers from the gondola and saw that I was still rising quickly enough. There was therefore no need to throw out ballast. I was pleased, for I wanted to keep as much weight aboard as possible, for reasons that will become clear later.”"}

{"request_id":"33a9f6052b201b22ecb658b8","rewritten_text":"“I’m not dining at home, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man said as he left the room.

“Now, Alan, we can’t waste a moment. This chest is heavy—I’ll carry it. You take the other things.” His words came fast and commanding. Campbell felt overpowered by him. They left the room together.

At the top landing, Dorian took out the key, turned it in the lock, and then stopped. A worried look crossed his face, and he shuddered. “I don’t think I can go in, Alan,” he murmured.

“That’s your concern. I don’t need you,” Campbell replied coldly.

Dorian pushed the door half open. His portrait’s face sneered in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor in front of it. He remembered that last night, for the first time ever, he had forgotten to cover the cursed canvas, and he started to rush forward, then recoiled with another shudder.

What was that vile red dew gleaming wet on one of the painted hands, as if the canvas had sweated blood? How dreadful it looked—more dreadful, he felt for a moment, than the silent thing stretched across the table, the thing whose twisted shadow on the stained carpet told him it hadn’t moved and still lay as he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, opened the door wider, and with half-closed eyes and his head turned away, walked quickly inside, determined not to look even once at the dead man. Stooping, he lifted the gold and purple drape and flung it over the picture.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around, staring at the tangle of patterns before him. Behind him he heard Campbell bringing in the heavy chest, the irons, and the other tools he had demanded for the grim task. He wondered if Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever met, and what they had thought of each other if they had.

“Leave me now,” said a harsh voice behind him.

He turned and hurried out, barely aware that the corpse had been pushed back into the chair and that Campbell was studying a gleaming yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was well after seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale but completely composed. “I’ve done what you asked,” he muttered."}

{"request_id":"1a69396b62219d378c1deb0b","rewritten_text":"I hastened along and soon reached my college. Then the recollection came over me, with a chill, that the creature I had abandoned in my chamber might still be roaming there. I trembled at the idea of confronting the monster, yet dreaded even more that Henry might encounter him. So I begged him to stay a few minutes at the foot of the stairs, and I flew up to my own quarters. My hand was already on the latch before I regained my senses; then I halted, seized with a cold shudder. I flung the door wide open, as children do when they fancy a spectre waits behind it; yet nothing met my sight. I entered on tiptoe: the room was empty, and my bedroom likewise cleared of its odious inmate. I could scarcely credit so extraordinary a piece of good fortune; but once convinced my adversary had escaped, I clapped my hands with delight and ran back to Clerval.

We mounted to my chamber, and the servant soon served breakfast; yet I could not master myself. It was not mere happiness that seized me; my skin prickled with overpowering nerves, and my pulse raced. I could not stay still for a moment; I leaped over chairs, clapped my hands, and laughed unstoppably. At first Clerval attributed my unwonted gaiety to the joy of seeing him again, but as he watched me more carefully, he detected a frenzy in my eyes he could not explain, and my loud, uninhibited, unfeeling laughter both startled and alarmed him.

“My dear Victor,” he cried, “what on earth is the matter? Do not laugh so. How wretched you look! What has caused this?”

“Ask me nothing,” I exclaimed, covering my eyes, for I imagined the dreaded spectre gliding into the room; “_he_ could tell. Oh, save me! Save me!” I thought the monster clutched me; I struggled madly and dropped down in a convulsion.

Poor Clerval! What must his emotions have been? A reunion he had expected with such happiness so horribly changed into sorrow. Yet I did not witness his anguish, for I was insensible and remained without consciousness for a very long time.

Thus began the nervous fever that held me prisoner for many months. Throughout that period Henry was my only caretaker. I later learned that, aware of my father’s advanced years and unfitness for so lengthy a journey, and how my illness would torment Elizabeth, he spared them distress by concealing the true severity of my malady."}

{"request_id":"e53b20a98a35d8ca2e1168e8","rewritten_text":"“Please think about it, ma’am,” Oliver pleaded, tears forcing their way out despite his efforts to hold them back. “Please think how young and good she is, and how much happiness and comfort she brings to everyone around her. I am sure—completely certain—that for your sake, because you are so kind; for her sake; and for everyone she fills with joy; she will not die. Heaven cannot let her die so young.”

“Hush,” Mrs. Maylie said, laying her hand on Oliver’s head. “You think like a child, poor boy. Yet, even so, you remind me of my duty. I forgot it for a moment, Oliver, and I hope I may be forgiven, for I am old and have seen enough illness and death to know the agony of being parted from those we love. I have also seen enough to know that it is not always the youngest and best who are spared to those who love them; but that knowledge should comfort us in our grief. Heaven is just, and such things teach us powerfully that there is a brighter world than this, and that the passage to it can be swift. God’s will be done! I love her, and He knows how dearly!”

Oliver was surprised to see that, as Mrs. Maylie spoke, she silenced her sobs at once, straightened herself, and became composed and resolute. He was even more astonished that this steadiness endured, and that throughout the care and constant watching that followed, Mrs. Maylie remained calm and prepared: carrying out all her new duties steadily and, outwardly at least, even cheerfully. But he was young and did not yet understand what strong minds can endure under trial. How could he, when even such minds rarely know their own strength?

A tense night followed. By morning, Mrs. Maylie’s fears proved sadly accurate. Rose was entering the first stage of a severe, dangerous fever.

“We must act, Oliver, and not sink into useless grief,” said Mrs. Maylie, pressing a finger to her lips while fixing her eyes on him. “This letter must reach Mr. Losberne as quickly as possible. It has to be taken to the market town, only four miles away by the footpath across the fields, and from there sent by express rider straight to Chertsey. The people at the inn will send it, and I know I can rely on you to see it done.”

Oliver could not answer, but his face showed how eager he was to set out immediately."}

{"request_id":"a265733a6c5a41562a55d905","rewritten_text":"So I said I needed the watermelon. But he answered that I didn’t need it to bust out of prison with; that was the difference. He said if I’d wanted it to hide a knife in and smuggle it to Jim so he could kill the seneschal, then it would’ve been fine. I let it drop after that, though I couldn’t see the point of representing a prisoner if I had to sit there chewing over a bunch of gold-leaf distinctions every time I saw a chance to swipe a watermelon.

Anyway, like I was saying, we waited that morning until everyone was settled down to their tasks and nobody was in sight around the yard; then Tom carried the sack into the lean-to while I stood back a bit to keep watch. Soon he came out, and we went over and sat on the woodpile to talk. He said:

“Everything’s set now except for tools, and that’s easy to fix.”

“Tools?” I said.

“Yeah.”

“Tools for what?”

“To dig with. We’re not going to gnaw him out, are we?”

“Aren’t those old busted picks and things in there good enough to dig a slave out with?” I said.

He spun on me, looking so pitying it would make you want to cry, and said:

“Huck Finn, did you ever hear of a prisoner having picks and shovels and all the modern conveniences in his wardrobe to dig himself out with? Now I want to ask you—if you’ve got any reason in you at all—what kind of chance would that give him to be a hero? They might as well lend him the key and be done with it. Picks and shovels—why, they wouldn’t hand them to a king.”

“Well then,” I said, “if we don’t want the picks and shovels, what do we want?”

“A couple of table knives.”

“To dig the foundations out from under that cabin with?”

“Yeah.”

“Dang it, that’s ridiculous, Tom.”

“It doesn’t matter how ridiculous it is, it’s the right way—and the proper way. And there isn’t any other way I ever heard of, and I’ve read every book that gives information about these things. They always dig out with a table knife—and not through dirt, either; usually it’s through solid rock. And it takes them weeks and weeks and weeks, forever and ever. Why, think about that prisoner in the bottom dungeon of the Château d’If, in the harbor of Marseilles, who dug himself out that way; how long do you figure he worked at it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Well, guess.”

“I don’t know—maybe a month and a half.”"}

{"request_id":"89d3a3b3d1518c75d981818e","rewritten_text":"He mounted a fiery steed—the same one that had carried him to triumph in Greece; he wore himself out with mind-numbing exertion, drowning the torment of a restless spirit in sheer physical sensation.

By degrees he rallied; at length, as if recovering from poison, he raised his head above the mists of fever and passion into the tranquil air of calm deliberation. He pondered what course to pursue. First the lapse of time struck him, the interval in which frenzy rather than reason had directed every act. A month had passed, and throughout it he had not seen Evadne. Her sway, tied to few of the lasting affections of his heart, had immensely diminished. He was her captive no longer—nor her lover: he would never behold her again, and through this complete return deserve Perdita’s trust.

Yet as he resolved thus, his imagination painted the wretched dwelling of the Greek maiden—one she had clung to from lofty and generous motives, refusing an abode of greater comfort. He recalled her splendour when he first encountered her; he remembered her existence at Constantinople, surrounded by every token of eastern luxury; then her current destitution, her daily toil, her loneliness, her wan, famine-pinched face. Pity surged within him; he would see her once more; he would contrive some scheme to restore her to society and the privileges of her station; their parting would then naturally ensue.

Again he reflected how through this long month he had shunned Perdita, fleeing her as he would the stings of his own conscience. But he was roused now; all should be set right; future devotion would efface the single stain on the peace of their union. He grew almost light-hearted at the thought, and with sober resolve traced the path he meant to follow. He recalled that he had promised Perdita to be present that very evening—the nineteenth of October, anniversary of his elevation to Protector—at a festival held in his honour. Let this festivity presage the felicity of coming years. First, he would visit Evadne; he would not linger; yet he owed her some explanation, some amends for his silent, prolonged absence; then onward to Perdita, to the ignored world, to the duties of his station, the brilliance of rank, the savour of power.

After the scene portrayed in the preceding pages, Perdita had anticipated an entire alteration in Raymond’s manners and conduct. She looked for unrestrained conversation, and the renewal of those affectionate habits of intimacy that had been the joy of her life."}

{"request_id":"29e672229bab3160473e7f7e","rewritten_text":"Recent reports from Rotterdam say the city is in a frenzy of philosophical excitement. Events there were so unexpected—so new, so completely against accepted beliefs—that I am sure all Europe is now in uproar, physics in turmoil, and reason and astronomy at each other’s throats.

On the —— day of —— (I am not sure of the date), a great crowd gathered for unspecified reasons in the large square before the Exchange in tidy Rotterdam. The weather was warm—unusually so for that time of year—with barely a breath of wind. The crowd did not mind being occasionally sprinkled by brief friendly showers that fell from large white clouds, which mottled the blue sky in a restless pattern. Still, around noon, a slight but notable agitation ran through the gathering. Ten thousand tongues began clattering, and a moment later ten thousand faces turned upward, ten thousand pipes dropped from ten thousand mouths, and a shout, compared only to Niagara’s roar, rang long and loud through the outskirts of Rotterdam.

The cause of this uproar soon became clear. From behind the massive bulk of one of those sharply defined clouds emerged, very slowly into a patch of blue sky, a strange, mixed, yet apparently solid object. It was so oddly shaped, so whimsy in construction, that the crowd of strong burghers could neither grasp it nor admire it enough. What could it be? In the name of all the housewives and devils in Rotterdam, what sign could it hold? No one knew, no one could guess; not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, had the slightest clue to solve the mystery. So, as nothing else could be done, everyone carefully replaced his pipe in the corner of his mouth, cocked his right eye at the phenomenon, puffed, paused, waddled about, grunted meaningfully—then waddled back, grunted, paused, and finally puffed again.

Meanwhile the object of so much curiosity—and so much smoke—descended lower and lower toward the admirable city. Within a few minutes it was close enough to see clearly. It seemed to be—yes! it was definitely a kind of balloon; but surely no balloon like this had ever floated over Rotterdam before."}

content.text: {"request_id":"7ac4f6e69670243a09b41a05","rewritten_text":"We were united in our affection for Adrian, though she, still scarcely past childhood, lacked my capacity to gauge the width of his virtues or to echo his pursuits and judgments as I could. I was ever in his company. His nature held a tenderness and ethereal sweetness that lent our conversations a gentle, almost otherworldly tone. Yet he could also be as mirthful as a skylark singing aloft, his thoughts soaring like an eagle’s, pure as the gentle dove. He could lighten Perdita’s gravity and blunt the sharp spur of my own restless activity. I looked back on my impatient desires and vexed struggles with others as on a stormy dream, feeling as altered as if I had migrated into a new form whose fresh senses and nerve-work changed how the seeming universe was mirrored in my mind. Yet in truth I remained the same in strength, in that deep hunger for sympathy, and in my longing for vigorous action. My manly virtues did not abandon me, for the enchantress Urania spared Samson’s locks even as he rested at her feet; but everything grew softened and humanized. Nor was Adrian limited to instructing me in the chilly certainties of history and philosophy. As he used these to teach me to curb my wild and unrefined spirit, he also revealed the living manuscript of his own heart, granting me insight into its marvelous nature.\n\nEven in his earliest years, the former queen of England had tried to plant bold and ambitious schemes in her son’s mind. She discerned that he possessed genius and extraordinary gifts; she nurtured these with the aim of later turning them to the advantage of her own designs. She fostered his thirst for knowledge and his impetuous courage; she even tolerated his untamed devotion to liberty, trusting that such a passion would, as so often happens, ripen into a craving for dominion. She sought to raise him to harbor resentment against those who had forced his father to abdicate, urging him to seek retribution. In this she failed. Reports—however warped—of a great and wise people asserting its right to self-rule stirred his admiration; from early youth he became a republican by conviction. Yet his mother did not relinquish hope. To her love of authority and proud birth she added determined ambition, patience, and restraint. She dedicated herself to studying her son’s character. Through praise, rebuke, and exhortation she endeavored to discover and strike the responsive chords; and though the music that flowed at her touch sounded discordant to her ear, she grounded her expectations in his talents and felt assured that eventually she would prevail over him."}
