{"request_id":"2e949022ead1caa6237dc0e3","rewritten_text":"“Do you play?”

“I think, sir,” replied the spy, in his humblest tone as he turned toward Mr. Lorry, “I may appeal to a gentleman of your years and kindness to persuade this other gentleman, so much your junior, that he cannot possibly reconcile it with his rank to use the Ace he speaks of. I grant that I am a spy, and that it is counted a discreditable role—though someone must perform it; but this gentleman is not a spy, and why should he descend to make himself one?”

“I lay down my Ace, Mr. Barsad,” said Carton, taking up the reply himself and glancing at his watch, “without a qualm, in just a few minutes.”

“I should have hoped, gentlemen,” said the spy, always trying to draw Mr. Lorry into the exchange, “that your regard for my sister—”

“I could pay no better homage to your sister than by finally freeing her from her brother,” Sydney Carton interposed.

“You do not think so, sir?”

“I am completely resolved.”

The spy’s smooth manner, oddly at odds with his ostentatiously coarse attire and likely with his usual behavior, met such resistance from Carton’s impenetrability—Carton who baffled wiser and more honest men—that it faltered and failed him. While he hesitated, Carton resumed his former pose of studying the cards:

“And indeed, now that I reconsider, I have a distinct impression I hold another strong card uncounted. That friend and fellow-Sheep who mentioned pasturing in the rural prisons; who was he?”

“French. You don’t know him,” the spy answered quickly.

“French, eh?” Carton echoed, musing, seeming not to notice, though he repeated the word. “Well; perhaps.”

“He is, I assure you,” said the spy; “though it doesn’t matter.”

“Though it doesn’t matter,” Carton repeated in the same mechanical tone—“though it doesn’t matter—No, it doesn’t matter. No. Yet I recognize the face.”

“I think not. I’m certain not. It’s impossible,” said the spy.

“It’s-impossible,” Sydney Carton muttered, thinking back, toying again with his glass (luckily a small one). “Impossible. Spoke excellent French. Yet I thought like a foreigner?”

“Provincial,” said the spy.

“No. Foreign!” Carton cried, striking his open palm on the table as a flash of understanding lit his mind. “Cly! Disguised, but the same man. We had him before us at the Old Bailey.”

“There, you are rash, sir,” Barsad replied, with a smile that gave his aquiline nose even more of a tilt; “there you actually put me at an advantage over you.”"}

{"request_id":"3cd4215d1f309cc5688eb32a","rewritten_text":"His stubbornness was extreme, and “dat deuced bug” were the only words he let fall the whole way. I myself was entrusted with two dark lanterns, while Legrand contented himself with the scarabæus, dangling it from the end of a whip-cord; he swung it back and forth like some prestidigitator as he walked. Seeing this latest, undeniable sign of my friend’s disturbed mind, I could hardly keep from weeping. Yet I judged it prudent to indulge his whim for the time being, or at least until some more forceful remedy might promise success. Meanwhile I tried, though fruitlessly, to draw him out concerning the object of the excursion. After securing my company, he showed no inclination to discuss any matter of lesser moment, and to all my inquiries he answered only, “we shall see!”

We crossed the creek at the island’s head in a skiff, then climbed the high ground on the mainland shore and moved northwestward through a tract desolately wild, where not the faintest trace of human passage appeared. Legrand marched ahead resolutely, stopping only for a moment now and again to consult certain landmarks, apparently of his own devising on some former visit.

Thus we went for nearly two hours, and the sun was just setting when we entered a region even more cheerless than any before. It was a kind of table-land near the crest of an almost inaccessible hill, thickly forested from base to summit, broken by huge crags that seemed to rest loosely on the earth and were, in many instances, kept from plunging into the valleys below only by the trees against which they leaned. Deep ravines running in various directions lent the scene a still more solemn austerity.

The natural platform we had climbed was choked with brambles, through which we soon found passage would have been impossible without a scythe; and Jupiter, acting under his master’s orders, set about cutting a path for us to the foot of an extraordinarily tall tulip-tree. This tree stood with eight or ten oaks on the level and towered above them all—and above every other tree I had ever seen—in the elegance of its leaves and shape, the spread of its branches, and its overall majestic presence."}

content.text: {"request_id":"d0044591bffc09c7b5536752","rewritten_text":"The mental qualities we call analytical are themselves hard to analyze. We recognize them only through their effects. We do know that when someone possesses them in excess, they become a source of deep enjoyment. Just as a strong man delights in exercises that test his muscles, so the analyst rejoices in the moral effort of untangling. He takes pleasure even in small tasks that let him use his gift. He loves riddles, conundrums, and hieroglyphics, and his solutions show a sharpness that to ordinary minds seems almost supernatural. His results, driven by pure method, seem intuitive.\n\nStudying mathematics, especially its highest branch that ironically bears the name analysis because of its reverse steps, may greatly strengthen the faculty of resolving. Yet calculating is not the same as analyzing. For instance, a chess-player may calculate without truly analyzing. This means people misjudge the game’s effect on the mind. I am not writing a treatise but merely introducing an unusual tale with random observations; I will therefore claim that the higher powers of reflection are more fully and usefully engaged by the modest game of checkers than by all the elaborate fuss of chess. In chess, where the pieces move in different and odd ways and have different values, people often mistake mere complexity for depth. Here the attention is the quality most demanded. If it lapses for even a moment, a mistake happens that brings harm or defeat. Because the possible moves are numerous and tangled, the chances of such mistakes multiply, and nine times out of ten the more concentrated, rather than the more acute, player wins. In checkers, however, where moves are uniform and have little variation, the chance of errors drops, and since mere attention is barely employed, whatever advantage a player gains comes from superior sharpness. To make this less abstract, imagine a checkers match reduced to four kings, with no errors expected. There, if both players are equal, victory can come only from some refined move born of a powerful intellectual effort."}

{"request_id":"0b72fda5a349e1a92549ac35","rewritten_text":"Sir Walter Elliot of Kellynch Hall, Somersetshire, amused himself with no other book than the Baronetage; it filled any idle interval and comforted him in moments of anxiety. While he pored over the scant surviving earliest patents his thoughts were lifted to admiration and respect; whenever domestic vexations intruded they melted into disdain or pity as he perused the near endless creations of the last century; and when nothing else on the page served, he could always turn to his own history with unfailing interest. The favourite volume regularly opened to this entry:

“ELLIOT OF KELLYNCH HALL.

“Walter Elliot, born March 1, 1760, married, July 15, 1784, Elizabeth, daughter of James Stevenson, Esq., of South Park, Gloucester, by which lady (who died 1800) he has issue Elizabeth, born June 1, 1785; Anne, born August 9, 1787; a still-born son, November 5, 1789; Mary, born November 20, 1791.”

Exactly thus had the paragraph issued from the press; but Sir Walter had embellished it for the benefit of himself and his household by adding after Mary’s birth: “Married, December 16, 1810, Charles, son and heir of Charles Musgrove, Esq., of Uppercross, Somerset,” and by noting with precision the day of his wife’s death.

Next came the chronicle and advancement of the ancient and reputable line, in customary language: its original settlement in Cheshire; its mention in Dugdale; the service as high sheriff; representation of a borough in three successive parliaments; displays of loyalty; and the creation of the baronetcy in the first year of Charles II, together with all the Marys and Elizabeths they wed; altogether composing two neat duodecimo pages, closing with the arms and motto: “Principal seat, Kellynch Hall, in the county of Somerset,” followed again by Sir Walter’s script—

“Heir presumptive, William Walter Elliot, Esq., great grandson of the second Sir Walter.”

Vanity encompassed every facet of Sir Walter Elliot’s nature—vanity of appearance and of station. He had been singularly handsome in early life, and at fifty-four retained the traits of a very fine man. Scarcely any woman could be more devoted to her looks; nor could the valet of a newly ennobled peer cherish more satisfaction in his master’s rank than Sir Walter did in his own. He regarded beauty as second only to the privilege of a baronetcy, and the Sir Walter Elliot who combined these blessings commanded the deepest homage of his heart.

His good looks and title had at least this fair justification for his affection: through them he had secured a wife far superior in character to what he could ever have merited on his own account."}

{"request_id":"b652c15ef5cc74fbb77a5781","rewritten_text":"But when I saw you become the object of another’s love—when I pictured someone cherishing you not just as a sacred symbol of beauty and virtue, or you loving someone else with a fiercer passion than you felt for me—the fiend inside me awoke. I sent your lover away, and from that instant I have known no peace. I have begged for sleep and rest in vain; my eyes would not close, and my blood never settled. I woke to a new existence like one who dies in hope and finds himself in hell. I will not stain your thoughts by revealing my inner battles, my fury at myself, or my despair. Let a veil cover the unimaginable feelings of a guilty father; the secrets of such a tortured heart cannot be laid bare. Everything became noise, crime, remorse, and hatred, yet also the tenderest love; and what first drove me to vow that I would conquer my passion and restore a father to my child was seeing your bitter, compassionate grief. That is what brought me here: I believed that if I could awaken again the grief I felt at your mother’s death, and revive the many memories of her that had lain dormant for seventeen years, any love for her child would fade. In a burst of heroism I resolved to come alone, to leave you—the very life of my life—and not see you again until I could do so without guilt. But it failed: I overvalued my strength or undervalued my love. I would surely have died if you had not hurried to my side. I almost wish I had been extinguished.

And now, Mathilda, I must make my final confession. I was wretchedly wrong to think I could overcome my love for you; I never can. The sight of this house, these fields and woods where my first love once lived has only deepened it. In my madness I dared to tell myself—Diana died to bring her child into the world; her spirit passed into her daughter, and you should be Diana to me. The harder I try to cast off this love, the tighter it clings—this guilty passion, more unnatural than hatred, that withers your hopes and destroys me forever.

Better to have fallen in love with despair, and safer to have kissed her.

No stretch of time or distance can tear from my soul what has become part of it. Since I arrived here, not even for a moment has the hell of passion left me, implanted to burn until all is cold, rigid, and dead."}

{"request_id":"b0d54a36efa68ec76fa2f02a","rewritten_text":"Recent intelligence from Rotterdam indicates that the city is in a state of unusual philosophical agitation. Events have taken place there so wholly unlooked for, so strikingly new, so absolutely opposed to every former conception, that I have no hesitation in believing that by this time all Europe is in commotion, physics is boiling over, and reason and astronomy are locked in noisy debate.

It seems that upon the —— day of —— (the exact date escapes me), a vast concourse of people, for purposes not particularly specified, had gathered in the great square of the Exchange of that well-ordered city. The weather was hot—exceptionally so for the season—scarcely a stirring of wind; and the multitude felt no annoyance at being now and then gently refreshed by brief sprinklings which descended from large white cloud-masses that fitfully checkered the blue dome overhead. Yet, about midday, a slight yet singular movement ran through the assembly: after that came the clatter of ten thousand tongues, and instantly ten thousand faces turned skyward, ten thousand pipes simultaneously dropped from ten thousand mouths, and a shout, comparable only to Niagara’s thunder, rang long and loud, raging through all the quarters of Rotterdam.

The cause of this commotion soon became plain enough. From beyond the huge bulk of one of those sharply defined cloud-masses already mentioned, there slowly slid into an open tract of blue a curious, jumbled, but seemingly solid object, so strangely formed, so fantastically assembled, that no amount of staring would suffice for the hardy burghers standing open-mouthed below. What might it be? In the name of all the vrouws and devils of Rotterdam, what omen was this? No one knew, no one could conjecture; not even the burgomaster, Mynheer Superbus Von Underduk, possessed the slightest clew to the enigma. Consequently—as nothing more sensible suggested itself—each man replaced his pipe with care in the accustomed corner of his mouth, and, cocking his right eye toward the prodigy, puffed, waited, waddled, and grunted meaningly—then waddled away, grunted, paused, and once more—puffed.

Meanwhile the object of such wonder, and occasion of so much smoke, sank lower and lower toward the worthy city. Within a very few minutes it came near enough for precise observation. It seemed—indeed, it undeniably was—a kind of balloon; yet surely no balloon of that description had ever before been witnessed in Rotterdam."}

{"request_id":"7e85d1040a0c3e86a8862c11","rewritten_text":"“Well, Jup,” said I, “what's wrong now?—how is your master getting on?”

“Why, to tell de truth, massa, him ain’t so monstrous well as he might be.”

“Not well! I’m very sorry to hear that. What does he complain of?”

“Dat’s jes it!—him neber grumble ’bout anyt’ing—yet him mighty sick all de same.”

“Very ill, Jupiter!—why not say so at once? Is he laid up in bed?”

“No, not a bit!—he ain’t tied down nowhere—that’s the very rub—my mind is getting mighty heavy ’bout poor Massa Will.”

“Jupiter, I’d like to be clear what you’re telling me. You insist your master is ill. Hasn’t he told you what troubles him?”

“Why, massa, ’taint worth while to take offense ’bout it—Massa Will says nothing at all’s wrong wid him—but den why he go round looking like dis, wid his head drooped and his shoulders humped, and as pale as a goose? And den he keeps a siphon de whole time—”

“Keeps a what, Jupiter?”

“Keeps a siphon wid figures on the slate—the oddest figures I ever did see. I’m starting to feel scared, I tell ye. Hab to keep a mighty sharp eye on his moves. T’other day he slipped me ’fore sunrise and stayed gone all de blessed day. I had a big switch cut ready to give him a smart thrashing when he showed up—but I’m such a fool I couldn’t do it after all—he looked so terribly poorly.”

“Eh?—what?—oh yes!—all things considered, I think you’d better not be too harsh with the poor fellow—don’t whip him, Jupiter—he’s hardly fit for that—but can’t you guess what’s brought on this illness, or rather this change in behavior? Has anything disagreeable happened since I last saw you?”

“No, massa, nothing bad’s happened since den—it was before den, I fear—it was the very day you was dere.”

“How? what are you implying?”

“Why, massa, I mean the bug—there now.”

“The what?”

“The bug,—I’m mighty certain Massa Will got bit somewhere about the head by dat goold-bug.”

“And on what grounds, Jupiter, do you rest that notion?”

“Plenty o’ grounds, massa, and mouth besides. I never seen such a cursed bug—he kicks and bites everything he comes near. Massa Will caught him first, but had to let him go again right quick, I tell ye—then must ha’ been the moment he got bit. I didn’t like the looks of the bug’s mouth myself, nohow, so I wouldn’t touch him wid my finger, but I nabbed him with a scrap of paper I picked up.”"}

content.text: {"request_id":"115c3d5e63282178cf4e1f70","rewritten_text":"All the young people were quite set on seeing Lyme. Captain Wentworth spoke of going again himself, for it was merely seventeen miles from Uppercross. Though it was November, the weather was far from unpleasant; and, in short, Louisa, being the keenest of them all and having decided on it, now fortified by the notion that insisting on her will showed commendable firmness, overruled her parents’ wish to defer the trip until summer. So to Lyme they would go—Charles, Mary, Anne, Henrietta, Louisa, and Captain Wentworth. The first heedless plan had been to depart in the morning and return at night; but Mr. Musgrove, for his horses’ sake, objected. Once considered sensibly, a November day would hardly allow much time for exploring a new place, after taking away the necessary seven hours for travel. They were therefore to stay overnight and not be looked for until dinner the following day. This was deemed a considerable improvement; and though they all gathered at the Great House to breakfast rather early and started very punctually, it was well past noon before the two carriages—Mr. Musgrove’s coach with the four ladies, and Charles’s curricle driven by him with Captain Wentworth—were descending the long hill into Lyme, entering its even steeper main street, and making it quite certain that they would barely have time to look around before the light and warmth disappeared. After securing rooms and ordering a meal at an inn, their next obvious step was to walk straight down to the shore. They had arrived too late in the year for any diversion or variety Lyme might offer as a resort. The public rooms were closed, nearly all lodgers gone, scarcely any families but the residents remaining; and as the buildings themselves hold little to admire, it is the town’s striking situation—the main street seeming to rush into the sea, the walk to the Cobb tracing the cheerful little bay, busy in season with bathing machines and visitors—the Cobb itself, with its ancient curiosities and recent improvements, and the beautiful ridge of cliffs extending eastward—that attracts a stranger’s eye. A person would have to be very singular indeed not to find charms in Lyme’s immediate surroundings that make him wish to know the place better."}

{"request_id":"5dbd0aefac9d62257a07368a","rewritten_text":"“She would make such a wonderful companion for Emma.”

Mr. Woodhouse agreed wholeheartedly, but added, “Our dear little friend Harriet Smith is another lovely young woman. You’ll like Harriet. Emma couldn’t have a better companion than Harriet.”

“I’m delighted to hear it—but Jane Fairfax, everyone knows, is utterly accomplished and exceptional! And she’s exactly Emma’s age.”

They continued happily on that topic, then moved on to others of similar importance, all discussed in the same harmony. But the evening did not end without a slight return of agitation. The gruel arrived and gave them plenty to say—lavish praise, numerous comments, unquestioned declarations of its healthfulness for every constitution, and rather sharp criticism of all the households where it was never prepared properly. Unfortunately, among the failures the daughter mentioned, the most recent and therefore the most vivid was with her own cook at South End, a temporary hire who never could grasp what she meant by a properly smooth bowl of gruel, thin but not too thin. No matter how often she requested and ordered it, she never got anything acceptable. This was a dangerous topic.

“Ah!” said Mr. Woodhouse, shaking his head and looking at her with tender concern. The exclamation in Emma’s ear meant, “Ah! there’s no end to the sad consequences of your going to South End. It ought not to be spoken of.” For a short time she hoped he would hold his tongue, that silent reflection would be enough to restore his appreciation of his own smooth gruel. After a few minutes, however, he began, “I’ll always regret that you went to the sea this autumn instead of coming here.”

“But why should you regret it, sir? I assure you, it did the children a world of good.”

“And besides, if you had to go to the sea, it shouldn’t have been South End. South End is unhealthy. Perry was surprised you chose South End.”

“I know many people think that, but it’s quite a mistake, sir. We were all perfectly well there, never had the least discomfort from the mud, and Mr. Wingfield says it’s entirely wrong to believe the place unhealthy. I’m sure he can be trusted; he understands the air and his own brother’s family has gone there several times.”

“You should have gone to Cromer, my dear, if you went anywhere. Perry spent a week at Cromer once and says it’s the best of all the seaside bathing places.”"}

{"request_id":"d26b590a17b6aa7f359faeb1","rewritten_text":"In the morning she was found dead in her bed, apparently without pain. Sir Mathew Reid had been called at once, but there was nothing he could do, and she was to be buried on the 22nd at Beauchamp Chalcote. A few days before her death she made her will, leaving Lord Arthur her little house in Curzon Street and all her furniture, personal effects, and pictures, except for her miniature collection, which went to her sister Lady Margaret Rufford, and the amethyst necklace, which Sybil Merton was to have. The estate was not worth much, but Mr. Mansfield, the solicitor, was very eager for Lord Arthur to return immediately, if possible, because there were many bills to settle and Lady Clementina had never kept proper accounts.

Lord Arthur was deeply moved by Lady Clementina’s thoughtful remembrance of him and felt that Mr. Podgers had much to answer for. Still, his love for Sybil outweighed every other feeling, and knowing he had done his duty gave him peace and comfort. When he arrived at Charing Cross, he felt completely happy.

The Mertons greeted him warmly. Sybil made him promise never again to let anything come between them, and the wedding was set for the 7th of June. Life seemed bright and beautiful once more, and his old joy returned.

One day, however, while he was going through the house in Curzon Street with Lady Clementina’s solicitor and Sybil, burning bundles of faded letters and emptying drawers full of odds and ends, the young woman suddenly gave a little cry of delight.

“What have you found, Sybil?” said Lord Arthur, looking up from his work with a smile.

“This lovely little silver bonbonnière, Arthur. Isn’t it charming and Dutch? Do give it to me! I know amethysts won’t suit me until I’m over eighty.”

It was the box that had held the aconitine.

Lord Arthur started, and a faint blush touched his cheek. He had almost forgotten what he had done, and it struck him as a strange coincidence that Sybil, for whom he had endured all that terrible tension, should be the first to remind him of it.

“Of course you can have it, Sybil. I gave it to poor Lady Clem myself.”

“Oh, thank you, Arthur; and may I have the bonbon too? I never guessed Lady Clementina liked sweets. I thought she was far too intellectual.”

Lord Arthur turned deathly pale, and a horrible idea crossed his mind."}

content.text: {"request_id":"758342e0fbb5ddb74191cbff","rewritten_text":"He fixed upon Friday, the 17th of August, for his reappearance, and devoted most of the day to inspecting his wardrobe, ultimately favouring a broad slouch hat with a crimson plume, a winding-sheet trimmed at the neck and cuffs, and a rusty dagger. Toward evening a fierce rainstorm burst, the wind blowing so fiercely that every window and door in the old house rattled and shook, precisely the weather that pleased him most. His course of action was arranged thus: he would slip quietly into Washington Otis’s chamber, gibber at him from the foot of the bed, and plunge the dagger into his own throat three times to the accompaniment of slow music. He cherished a particular rancour against Washington, fully aware that he was the one accustomed to erase the celebrated Canterville bloodstain with Pinkerton’s Paragon Detergent. Once the bold, heedless lad had been reduced to utter terror, he would move on to the room of the United States Minister and his wife, lay a clammy palm upon Mrs. Otis’s brow, and whisper into her trembling husband’s ear the dreadful secrets of the charnel-house. Regarding little Virginia, he remained undecided. She had never offended him, and was both lovely and sweet. A few hollow groans from the wardrobe ought, he thought, to suffice, or, should that fail to rouse her, he might claw at the bedspread with palsied twitching fingers. As for the twins, he meant to give them a thorough lesson. First, he must of course sit upon their chests to induce the suffocating sensation of nightmare. Then, as their beds stood close together, he would position himself between them in the guise of a green, icy-cold corpse until they were paralysed with fright, and finally tear away the winding-sheet and creep round the chamber with bleach-white bones and one rolling eyeball as ‘Dumb Daniel, or the Suicide’s Skeleton,’ a rôle in which he had on more than one night produced a stunning impression, and which he deemed fully equal to his famed portrayal of ‘Martin the Maniac, or the Masked Mystery.’\n\nAt half-past ten he heard the household retire. For a while the twins’ shrill peals of laughter, the merry mirth of schoolboys amusing themselves before sleep, disturbed him, but by a quarter past eleven all was quiet, and as the clock struck midnight he set out. The owl battered the windowpanes, the raven croaked from the ancient yew-tree, and the wind wandered round the house, moaning like a lost soul; yet the Otis family slumbered unaware of their fate, and above the rain and gale he could plainly catch the steady snore of the Minister of the United States."}

{"request_id":"ddf55c41daef2e0dbf1354da","rewritten_text":"P.S.—Please tell me about the bows. Jennings swears they’re the latest style.

Lord Arthur looked so grave and miserable over the letter that the Duchess burst into fits of laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she exclaimed, “I’ll never show you a young lady’s letter again! But what shall I say about the clock? I think it’s a brilliant invention, and I should like one myself.”

“I don’t think much of them,” Lord Arthur replied with a wistful smile, and after kissing his mother he left the room.

Once upstairs, he threw himself on a sofa, eyes brimming with tears. He had done everything possible to commit this murder, yet both attempts had failed through no fault of his own. He had tried to do his duty, but Destiny herself seemed to have betrayed him. He was weighed down by the emptiness of good intentions, the futility of trying to be noble. Perhaps it would be better to break off the engagement altogether. Sybil would suffer, of course, but suffering could never truly damage such a noble nature. As for himself, what did it matter? There is always some war in which a man can die, some cause to which he can give his life, and since life held no pleasure for him, death held no fear. Let Destiny carry out her sentence. He would not lift a finger to help her.

At seven-thirty he got dressed and went down to the club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he was obliged to dine with them. Their shallow talk and mindless jokes left him cold, and as soon as coffee arrived he made up an excuse and left. As he was walking out, the hall porter handed him a letter. It was from Herr Winckelkopf, inviting him to come by the next evening to look at an explosive umbrella that detonated the moment it was opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. Arthur tore the letter to pieces. He had resolved to attempt no more experiments. Then he wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat for hours by the river. The moon glared through a mane of tawny clouds, like a lion’s eye, and countless stars studded the hollow vault of sky, like gold dust scattered on a purple dome. Every so often a barge swung out into the muddy current and drifted away on the tide, while the railway signals flicked from green to red as trains screamed across the bridge."}

{"request_id":"019b508e5e49627b31ec7920","rewritten_text":"The chain of doom that forever drags misery must have snapped, and the malignant destiny that rules it would never suffer such a rupture of her eternal decrees. Yet why should I grieve at this? Misery was my native air, and only what was wretched could draw near me; had Woodville been content, I never would have met him. And can I, who for years lived on tears and was reared beneath the showers of grief, hesitate to recount a story steeped in woe and death?

Woodville was compelled to travel into the country and lingered there day after day in intolerable separation from his lovely bride. A letter reached him from her, saying she was somewhat ailing, yet urging him to hasten to her, declaring that health would flow from his eyes and that his presence would prove her surest medicine. Three more days held him away, and then he hurried toward her. His heart, he knew not why, foreshadowed disaster; no further letters had come; he dreaded that her illness had worsened, and this fear made him feverish and impatient for the instant when she would again stand before him, clothed in bloom and grace; for a sinister voice kept whispering, “You shall never behold her as she was again.”

When he reached her dwelling, it lay silent: he passed through several rooms; in one a servant sobbed violently. He grew faint with terror and could hardly ask, “Is she dead?” barely hearing the dreadful answer, “Not yet.” Those astounding words fell on him with less horror than what he had dreaded; to find she still lived, that hope remained, was a bittersweet relief. He recalled her letter, and indulged the wild belief that his kisses, warm with love and life, would breathe new energy into her, that she could not perish while he was near; that his presence was the talisman sustaining her existence.

He sped to her sick chamber; she lay with flaming cheeks and closed eyes, apparently insensible. He enfolded her in his arms; he pressed breathless kisses upon her burning lips; in a voice of hushed anguish he summoned her by the tenderest names: “Return, Elinor; I am here—your life, your love. Return; dearest, you granted me this boon, that I should restore you. Let your gentle spirit rekindle; you cannot die beside me. What is death? To see you no more? To be sundered from what is part of myself; without whom I possess neither recollection nor future?”"}

{"request_id":"f4564886c4a95b1580cbdee2","rewritten_text":"The day went by much like the one before. Mrs. Hurst and Miss Bingley spent several hours of the morning with the patient, who kept getting better, though slowly, and in the evening Elizabeth joined everyone in the drawing-room. The loo table, however, was missing. Mr. Darcy was writing, and Miss Bingley sat nearby, watching his letter take shape and repeatedly distracting him with messages for his sister. Mr. Hurst and Mr. Bingley were playing piquet, while Mrs. Hurst observed their game.

Elizabeth picked up some needlework and was well entertained by the exchange between Darcy and his companion. The lady’s constant praise—of his handwriting, the straightness of his lines, or the length of his letter—and his complete indifference to it all made a curious conversation that matched Elizabeth’s opinion of both of them.

“How delighted Miss Darcy will be to get such a letter!”

He gave no reply.

“You write unusually fast.”

“You are mistaken. I write rather slowly.”

“How many letters you must have to write in a year! Business letters, too! How dreadful I would find them!”

“It is lucky, then, that they fall to me and not to you.”

“Please tell your sister that I long to see her.”

“I have already told her so once, at your request.”

“I am afraid you do not like your pen. Let me mend it for you. I mend pens remarkably well.”

“Thank you—but I always mend my own.”

“How can you manage to write so evenly?”

He said nothing.

“Tell your sister I am delighted to hear of her progress on the harp, and do let her know I am thrilled with her beautiful little design for a table, and I think it far better than Miss Grantley’s.”

“Will you allow me to save your thrills for when I write again? At the moment I have no space to do them justice.”

“Oh, it does not matter. I will see her in January. But do you always write such lovely long letters to her, Mr. Darcy?”

“They are usually long; but whether always lovely is not for me to decide.”

“I have a rule: anyone who can write a long letter with ease cannot write badly.”

“That will not work as a compliment to Darcy, Caroline,” her brother cried, “because he does not write with ease. He thinks too hard about words with four syllables. Don’t you, Darcy?”

“My style of writing is very different from yours.”

“Oh,” cried Miss Bingley, “Charles writes in the most careless way imaginable.”"}
